title: Emergency call centers utilizing Convey911 for translation services
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Emergency call centers utilizing Convey911 for translation services

 September 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Public safety agencies up and down the Shore are reaping the benefits of a new translation service called Convey911.The service has been added to the arsenal of many emergency call centers, including in Talbot and Dorchester counties. With a network of around 10,000 on-demand human interpreters, the service runs 24/7 and can connect callers in just seconds.
Convey911 CEO Jeff Bruns said the service allows emergency call specialists to quickly bring an interpreter after detecting the language of the caller.
"The technology is listening to that person's voice, is making a determination around what language they speak, and is transcribing and translating their voice in real time, and putting it on the screen so the 911 call taker is able to read and understand what you're saying," Bruns said.
Over 180 languages are supported by Convey911's text translation services, Bruns said.
The service has around 110 languages on demand for human interpreters and around 120 using artificial intelligence.
Artificial intelligence helps at the beginning of a call, Bruns said, detecting the language spoken by the caller. But the service doesn't rely on AI.
"The call taker always has control," Bruns said. "They have the ability to hit a button and pull in a real, live human. But what we're doing in the background is understanding how accurately, or lack thereof, we're transcribing. And if we find that the accuracy is not within a certain level of expectation, for example 80% accuracy, then we're going to prompt the call taker on the screen (to bring in an interpreter)."
Holley Guschke, the chief of Talbot County's 911 communications division, said the department is fully trained on Convey911's services. It is the department's hope that the service will assist residents in Talbot and surrounding counties.
"When you do need to translate, it is important to be able to do that as quickly as possible in order to send police, fire or medical personnel," Guschke said.
"Working with Convey911 translation services will be invaluable to 911 operations by enabling clear and immediate communication with non-English speakers, reducing response times, and ensuring that all individuals receive the critical help they need during emergencies," said Brian LeCates, Talbot County's emergency services director, in an emailed statement.
In Dorchester County, Emergency Communications Chief Robbie Larimer says the county's call center receives one to two calls per day from non-English speakers. Partnering with Convey911 has helped the department quicken its translation times since June, he said.
"They've been very willing to work with us," Larimer said. He added that the company "embraces the understanding" of the need for public safety.
Larimer said Eastern Shore agencies embraced the service at the Maryland Association of Counties' conference last year. Convey911 was at the conference, and representatives from different counties took notice.
"We saw what they had to offer," Larimer said.
Bruns emphasized the service helps not just public safety agencies, but other departments as well. The Caroline County Health Department has been using the service since June.
Holly Trice, the health department's director of nursing, lauded the Convey911 service as an "everyday" tool to communicate with residents.
"Our previous platform did not have an interpreter immediately available, so there were times we would sit on the phone for 15 minutes or so trying to find an appropriate interpreter," Trice said. "We don't have that with Convey911. As soon as we initiate the call, we immediately assign an interpreter, and everyone has been extremely professional."
Bruns said feedback has been "exceptional" so far. He noted two "pain points" that the service addresses: quality of interpretation and the time it takes to get an interpreter on the line.
While Convey911 serves around 50 departments in around 14 states, its Maryland roots as a Baltimore-based company are important to Bruns.
"It's very important for us to ensure that we're doing everything we can to canvass Maryland, and really support Gov. (Wes) Moore's platform of leave no one behind," Bruns said. "We had a huge advocate in (Larimer) … in bringing all of the counties together so that we could do this as a group."

title: Political signs vandalized
author: Staff Writer
content:
Political signs vandalized

 September 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 330
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot Republican Central Committee (TCRCC) has worked hard to promote our candidates, including the erection of a couple dozen large Trump, Andy Harris and Hogan signs around the county. In just a week we have had one large sign near Trappe stolen, replaced and stolen again, and last night (Saturday, Aug. 31) had two signs spray-painted on St Michaels Road just outside of St Michaels. These signs cost an average of $100 each plus $15 for lumber and sweat equity to dig post holes and erect the signs.Vandalism of political signs is against the law and is punishable by jail time and hefty fines. Complaints have been filed with the Sheriff's Office. Many signs are now monitored by trail cameras. If we catch the responsible parties, we will prosecute vigorously. TCRCC will pay a $500 reward to anyone whose testimony leads to conviction.
While spending two hours cleaning the paint off of the signs, I was cursed at twice … "F--k You" and "F--k Trump" by people driving by. (It was offset by some dozen or more friendly honks and thumbs-up, and two people who stopped to ask if they could help.)
This behavior is typical of people who have no respect for the Constitution, and specifically the First Amendment or of the election process in which we all express our opinions by peaceful, respectful means.
Sadly, the Democratic Party has encouraged behavior that stifles freedom of expression for several years (witness Obama's "get in their face" remarks), and seems to have little regard for the First Amendment (as shown by the pressuring of Facebook and Twitter by the Biden/Harris Administration to censor conservative thought).
If we are to have a democracy of, by and for the people, we must respect each other's right to think and say what we will. I hope that Democrats who are put off by this behavior will chastise their brethren for acting this way. It isn't pretty.
To be silent is to condone this behavior.
KENT ROBERTSON
Royal Oak

Assault at Easton High School sends student to hospital

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 EASTON — The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is investigating the circumstances surrounding an assault that took place at Easton High School, located on the 700 block of Mecklenburg Avenue, on Sep. 10.At approximately 12:06 p.m., the deputy assigned as the school resource officer at Easton High School was alerted to an assault occurring inside of the school.
Deputies initiated an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the assault, in conjunction with the Easton High School administrative staff and the Talbot County State's Attorney's Office.
Pursuant to the investigation, two juveniles, who are students at the school, were identified and arrested in relation to the assault. Deputies were also able to identify two victims of the assault. One of the victims is an Easton High School staff member and the second victim is a juvenile student at the school.
The juvenile victim was transported to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton via the Talbot County Department of Emergency Services for treatment of non-life-threatening injuries.
The juvenile suspects were transported to the Talbot County Sheriff's Office for booking and processing. They were charged with first- and second-degree assault, reckless endangerment and several other charges relating to the incident.
The Talbot County Sheriff's Office will be contacting the Department of Juvenile Services to obtain a release disposition for both suspects.
Easton High School was placed on a brief lockdown during this event.
If anyone has information they are requested to contact the Talbot County Sheriff's Office at 410-822-1020, by email at sheriff@talbotcountymd.gov, on Facebook at Talbot County Sheriff or on our website at talbotsheriff.org.

title: Bradford House residents share concerns with community, management
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Bradford House residents share concerns with community, management

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 656
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Bradford House Apartments residents, community members, and service providers gathered at Anchor Point on Monday afternoon to talk about unsafe conditions at the apartment complex on Race Street and what is needed to remedy the situation.The community conversation, which was facilitated by Mid Shore Mediation, was born out of a concern from Dorchester County District Court Judge Melvin Jews. Jews is presiding over multiple rent escrow cases filed against Bradford House residents by Millennia Housing Management, the Cleveland-based company that manages Bradford House.
Residents have expressed concerns about safety in the building.
In September 2023, the property — which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs — received a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development inspection score of 30c*. The score indicated health and safety deficiencies and other problems identified with building systems, the building's exterior and individual apartments.
Wendy Schneider, alternative dispute resolution programs manager for Eastern Shore district courts, said Jews was concerned residents who don't have a case in court or who are not comfortable appearing in court weren't getting heard.
"And there also might have been people outside of those that were actually in the courtroom that might need to hear what's going on," Schneider said. "So that's why we came up with the idea of hosting this meeting. Just to give everyone an open and safe space to have conversation and just say whatever they feel comfortable saying without that pressure of court."
Representatives from Millennia, including the chief operating officer, regional manager and Bradford House property manager, listened in on the meeting virtually. At the end of the meeting, one representative said they appreciated the residents taking the time to voice their concerns.
During the conversation, residents talked about a variety of concerns from bed bug infestations, to frequent changes in management, to elevators not working, to a lack of security.
Residents Anna Walker and Stephanie Robinson talked about the in-unit call-for-aid systems, many of which were found inoperable during the September 2023 HUD inspection.
Walker said that she learned her call-for-aid chord didn't work in December when no one came to help her on the floor of her bathroom. Walker said she had to crawl down the hallway of the building to get a neighbor to call 911.
Robinson, who has epilepsy, recalled falling in the bathtub and having to yell for help "for the longest time." She said more than two pull chords are needed in each apartment.
Walker said her grandchildren can't visit her because of safety and security concerns, and she hasn't been able to get a home health care provider because no one wants to come to the Bradford House.
"The worst part is the isolation," she said.
Resident Jerome Jones, who is on dialysis, said he has also had a difficult time getting services because people don't want to come to the apartment complex.
Jones talked about being scared to bring furniture into his home because he doesn't want to draw bed bugs, which multiple residents at the meeting talked about experiencing.
La-Shon Foster, who is running for mayor of Cambridge, said during the conversation that these problems have existed for more than four years and residents aren't getting the help they need.
"The mediation is good," she said. "But if nothing is done to follow it in six months from now, we're right back at this table (and) it does no good."
Local psychiatrist Gene Bautista, who serves Bradford House residents, suggested that the Health Department open a station in the Bradford House and that everyone who serves the apartment receive sensitivity training.
"Just a little bit more sensitivity would go a long, long way," he said.
Resident Linda Johnson, who is a member of the apartment's tenant association, said she just wants management to respect residents, talk with residents and know what's happening on the property.
"At the end of the day, I'm just glad that we had this mediation, and I'm glad that Millennia finally heard us," she said.

title: Cambridge man gets 25 years after taking plea deal in murder trial
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Cambridge man gets 25 years after taking plea deal in murder trial

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Crime 
 
 289
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge teen was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Sept. 6 in connection to the 2021 fatal shooting of Ja'Len Woolford.Daeveon Johnson, 19, faced a first-degree murder charge in the shooting that occurred on Nov. 18, 2021. Johnson entered an Alford plea for the charge in November 2022.
As part of the plea deal, Johnson will serve 25 years at the Patuxent Youthful Offenders Program. Once 50% of the sentence is served, Johnson will be eligible for parole.
Johnson's sentence will begin dating back to Jan. 4, 2022, the day he was arrested by Cambridge police. He will also serve five years probation.
The sentence orders Johnson to have no contact with Key'Marion Ennals. Ennals, 19, was found not guilty on 12 charges relation to the fatal shooting, including first-degree murder, at a trial this August.
Johnson's sentencing was delayed as part of his plea agreement, which included Johnson testifying during Ennals' trial last month.
In his initial interview with police, Johnson admitted to carrying a .40 caliber firearm. An autopsy revealed that Woolford died from a single gunshot wound from a .40 caliber firearm.
Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard provided a statement following the sentencing of Johnson.
"The State recommended a sentence of life imprisonment, suspending all but forty years of active incarceration," the statement read. "The Court heard heartfelt victim impact statements from three members of the victim's family, each expressing their choice to forgive Mr. Johnson, and each requesting the Court consider a lesser period of active incarceration for Mr. Johnson given his cooperation and remorse.
"The State continues to offer condolences to all family and loved ones impacted by the loss of Ja'Len Woolford, and thanks the Court for its mindful consideration of all circumstances at sentencing."

title: Everbridge becomes Kent's new emergency alert system
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Everbridge becomes Kent's new emergency alert system

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Even at 3 a.m. from his home, with a tap of a button Emergency Preparedness Planner Brian Pearsall can send out an alert to a majority of Kent County residents.He hopes he never has to do that, but it's beneficial the option's there.
In the basement of the Kent County Sheriff's Office, where the Office of Emergency Services is housed, he demonstrates how efficient he can be in sending notifications with the department's new software, Everbridge.
On July 1, they made the switch from their old system Code Red, a commendable program in its own right.
Why the switch?
"It allows us to be more effective to the community with updated information regarding weather forecasts and gives us a larger environment to do that with their technology," Pearsall said.
Pearsall explained there are three levels of communication.
Everbridge is a TSP level 3 certification, designated Public Health, and receives restoration priority just under Federal government certifications. It is required to be backed up and restored in order to provide for public health.
He pointed out, Everbridge is used widely throughout the state right now making communicating between counties convenient.
"We can coordinate better as far as resource needs," Pearsall said.
Everbridge can target specific areas within the county as well.
In a simulation, a test, on his cell phone, Pearsall uses the map on the Everbridge application to send out a storm warning to just Kennedyville residents.
Narrowing it down even further, if needed, he could send notifications to just a specific housing community within Kennedyville.
These alerts are available to residents who have phones in a contract with Everbridge. But also residents can receive specific notifications by signing up to receive alerts at https://www.kentcounty.com/oes.
Those who sign up get alerts for weather conditions, tornados, flash floods, and even water line repairs and other infrastructure information.
So far, the new software has gone off without a hitch as they've sent out 10 alerts since the time of the interview in late August.
Along with other administrators, Director Pete Landon and Chief of Communications Brad Russum, Pearsall meets regularly over Zoom with the Everbridge team to increase their knowledge of technology which always seems to be adapting.
The emergency team is always looking to learn as much as they can to increase the public's awareness and safety.
Like for example, in a few months time they will be able to provide IPAUS, Integrated Public Alert and Warning System.
"When you receive an amber alert on your phone, you can't stop that from coming through. So soon I'll be able to provide this to our residents and visitors," Pearsall remarked.
In the case of an impending tornado for example, he can interrupt every phone in Kent County warning residents.
He's been taking FEMA courses online, and when the time comes, will take an exam for certification along with quarterly tests.
The team's also looking to expand public's awareness like the recent Maryland Mesonet Weather Station, set up at the back of the A.F. Whitsitt Center. It's one of 70 weather stations in the state in partnership with the University of Maryland, Maryland Department of Emergency Management, Maryland Environmental Service and Maryland Department of Health.
These stations are spaced about 10 miles apart and solar powered, measuring rainfall, snow, even the temperature of the top soil.
"It has all manner of capabilities and allows us to be more effective in predicting and forecasting weather events," Pearsall added.
Like the Everbridge program, the station provides opportunities to cooperate with various local, state and federal entities.
All these expansions are part of an effort, "To create a safer Kent County by getting the resources to the community, residents and visitors."
Pearsall noted, "We're doing everything we can to ensure the public is safe as possible."

title: Talbot community remembers victims of 9/11
author: Tom McCall
content:
Talbot community remembers victims of 9/11

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 401
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Around 100 people gathered at the corner of Dover and West streets Wednesday morning in a solemn and patriotic remembrance of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. A fire engine ladder with a giant American flag waved above the gathering.There was prayer and the laying of a wreath as the prelude.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Talbot County Council Member Keasha Haythe and Council Vice President Pete Lesher all came to the podium. Council President Chuck Callahan gave the greeting.
"We are here today for a day to remember 9/11, The National Day of Service and Remembering," Haythe said.
"On this day of remembrance, on this day of service, our focus is on what we have in common, what we value together as a community and as a nation," Lesher said.
The ceremony featured musical tributes, including performances by the Easton Middle School band and a spirited group of singers, including Thalia Turner, who sang the "Star Spangled Banner " Deputy John Coleman, who sang "God Bless America " and Ta'Vea Roberts, who sang "America The Beautiful."
The crowd was solemn as the silver bell was tolled by firefighter Rich Williamson. He rang out three sets of five, symbolizing the code for loss of life of a firefighter. It is an honorific signal for the ultimate sacrifice.
2,977 people died on 9/11, Callahan said. On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners, crashing the first two planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and one into the Pentagon in Arlington County, Virginia. The fourth plane crashed in rural Pennsylvania during a passenger revolt.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said, "We are here today to ensure its lessons of courage, of loss and of unity are never forgotten. Let us forever honor the bravery of first responders, who without hesitation ran towards danger."
Dressed in formal wear, Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Easton Chief of Police Alan Lowery placed a wreath in the memorial space across from the library. The stone bench behind them was carved with "You Are Not Forgotten."
Pastor Reginald Pinkett of Asbury United Methodist Church invoked the holy presence. And Pastor Dave Griffin of Grace Fellowship gave a short sermon.
Pinkett said, "We comfort the firefighters, the paramedics, the police officers, all the ones who gave lives trying to help and protect on that crucial day."
Many heads were bowed. Many hands were crossed as the victims of 9/11 were brought to mind.

title: Easton police officer found guilty of misconduct
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton police officer found guilty of misconduct

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 662
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An Easton police officer was found guilty on Tuesday of misconduct in office. Sgt. Jason Dyott, 38, was convicted of two separate instances of engaging in physical sexual conduct with two different teenage girls while on duty.Judge C. Carey Deeley Jr. found Easton Police Department Dyott guilty on two counts of misconduct in office. Dyott — who had served as an Easton police officer since approximately June 2008 — was found guilty under three theories of misconduct: malfeasance, misfeasance and nonfeasance.
The charges stem from allegations that Dyott used his departmental cell phone to communicate in a sexual manner with several teenagers and students at local high schools and met up with them while on duty. Two teenage girls are mentioned in a charging document from the Office of the State Prosecutor.
During opening statements of the trial, Senior Assistant State Prosecutor Mary Setzer said that in the fall of 2022, Dyott engaged in physical acts with two teenage girls in separate instances. She said that on Nov. 11, Dyott picked up an 18-year-old from her friend's house in his police vehicle and had sex with her in the vehicle while on duty.
Setzer said that two days later, Dyott met with a 17-year-old in the Target parking lot while he was on duty and made out with her. According to the charging document, Dyott leveraged his position as a police officer to engage in this sexual relationship and sent her multiple photographs of him in his police uniform with sexually provocative language attached.
Dyott's defense attorney Shaun Owens said during opening statements that Dyott is not denying the relationships with the teenagers. Owens said the conduct was not criminal, however, and that he does not believe there is evidence to support that Dyott's actions constituted misconduct.
Owens said the state would need to prove that Dyott engaged in the acts because he was a police officer or because he had been afforded that privilege as a police officer. Owens said that in any profession, Dyott could have engaged in the exact same behavior.
During the trial, both of the then-teenagers mentioned in the charging document testified. The then-17-year-old said that when the investigation into Dyott began, Dyott told her to deny what happened, and he said they didn't do anything wrong because she was old enough to consent.
The then-18-year-old recounted the night she met up with Dyott. She said that while in the police vehicle, the police radio was on, and after she heard a badge number spoken over the radio, Dyott turned the radio down. She said that she and Dyott didn't have any conversations about Dyott's job during their interaction, and Dyott didn't respond to work during that time.
During closing arguments, Owens brought up that the radio call, which the then-18-year-old talked about during testimony. He said that it was not clear what the call was about, if it was for Dyott specifically or if it required Dyott's response.
Deputy State Prosecutor Sarah David said that in the two incidents, Dyott acted in his official capacity. Not only was he on duty, she said, but he was presenting himself to the public and to the teenage girls as an officer.
A sentencing hearing is set for Nov. 1.
According to a news release from the Office of the State Prosecutor, State Prosecutor Charlton T. Howard III said, "Law enforcement officers who abuse the power of their position, and betray the trust of the community, must be held accountable."
In an interview with the Star Democrat Wednesday, Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey said Dyott is suspended with pay. He has been suspended with pay since the beginning stages of the investigation in 2023.
In 2014, Dyott was named the Easton's department's officer of the year.
According to a Wednesday press release, "upon this conviction, the Easton Police Department will now seek to impose the appropriate administrative penalties upon Mr. Dyott."
Lowery said he could not say at this time when those administrative penalties will be imposed.

title: Family seeks answers to St. Mary's man's death while in custody in Calvert jail
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Family seeks answers to St. Mary's man's death while in custody in Calvert jail

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 According to descriptions provided by his family, Angel Manuel Jimenez was always the life of the party. They described him as "a flirt, a charmer, always cracking jokes and tearing up the dance floor."Jimenez, a native of the Bronx, a resident of Great Mills and an electrician by trade, was 50 years old when he died on Dec. 4, 2023, while in custody at the Calvert County Detention Center in Barstow.
"What led him there is not important," Elena Jimenez, one of Angel's sisters, said of the fact her brother was in jail, adding the real question is, "What led up to his death?"
A certificate issued by the state department of health's division of vital records lists Jimenez's cause of death as "restraint complicated by hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease." The document cites his manner of death as "homicide."
"He was just detained at the time," Elena Jimenez told Southern Maryland News. "No medical attention was given to him. He died at the detention center. What occurred during the last hours? We don't have anything. It's already been nine months and we don't have any answers."
According to documents on file in the Maryland Judiciary system, Jimenez was the defendant in an ongoing paternity case, which dated back to December 2008. He was served a warrant last Dec. 1, just days before his death.
On Aug. 16, after other local media outlets reported on the family's call for answers from authorities, the Calvert County Sheriff's Office, which oversees the detention center, issued a statement about the Jimenez case.
"As soon as we became aware of the incident, we immediately contacted the independent investigations division of the [state] attorney general's office," the sheriff's office statement reads. "However, they determined this case would not fall under their purview and declined to investigate it. Determined to ensure an impartial investigation, we reached out to the Maryland State Police, who agreed to handle the case from start to finish."
Southern Maryland News contacted the state police's Pikesville office headquarters, which advised to "contact the Calvert County State's Attorney's Office as they are handling all media inquiries for the Jimenez case."
"Our office is reviewing the entire case," Calvert County State's Attorney Robert H. Harvey Jr. (R) told Southern Maryland News. "We are going to be following up with the state medical examiner's office. We will then prepare a written report."
Harvey said he was hopeful the report would be completed by the end of September. He added that the case may or may not be reviewed by a grand jury.
The Jimenez family and members of the Calvert community received some surprising news during the Aug. 28 meeting of the county's police accountability board.
While reviewing the year-to-date complaints the panel has received, chairman Wilson H. Parran said the detention center and the correctional deputies are "not an area of responsibility" for the accountability board, adding that those officers "have their own bill of rights."
John Norris, county attorney who provided council to the board at the August meeting, explained that correctional deputies are "disciplined through their internal structure."

title: Cambridge City Council extends juvenile curfew another year
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council extends juvenile curfew another year

 September 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a four-to-one vote on Sept. 9, the Cambridge City Council extended its temporary juvenile curfew for another 12 months.The curfew — which was originally passed in September 2023 — makes it so that juveniles under 16 cannot be in a public place within the city between the hours of 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. on Sundays through Thursdays and 11 p.m. through 5 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.
There are exceptions to this, including when the juvenile is with a parent or when the juvenile is on the way home from work or a school activity.
The extension will keep the curfew in place through Sept. 30, 2025.
At the City Council meeting on Sept. 9, a public hearing was held before the commissioners took a vote. Resident Shay Lewis-Sisco, who is running for Cambridge's Ward 2 commissioner seat, said that during a community visioning session at Mace's Lane Middle School, most of the students involved said they were in favor of the curfew.
Commissioner Sputty Cephas brought up a conversation he had with one young person. He said the curfew made the child think twice about going out at night.
Cephas, who voted to extend the curfew, asked the other commissioners whether they thought the curfew should be reviewed annually or on a longer-term basis.
Commissioners Jameson Harrington, Brian Roche and Laurel Atkiss all said they think the curfew should be reviewed on an annual basis.
Harrington, who voted against the extension, said an annual review allows the council to more easily end the curfew if it isn't working.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Harrington said he voted against the curfew as a principle. He said he has been against it from the start and data shows it is not effective, but he said he is proud of how it is working in Cambridge.
Roche and Atkiss both spoke about the curfew's effectiveness in allowing Cambridge Police to have conversations with children and employ community policing.
"But definitely an annual reevaluation is great because we hope to make progress and maybe not need such structures at some point in the future," Atkiss said.
Before the vote, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said he thinks the curfew is a good tool. He said there has been less juvenile crime during the hours of the curfew compared to 2023 "when it was a real crisis." He said the curfew has made children think twice about going out at night and has allowed the department to reach more children.
At the end of the meeting, Todd thanked the council.
"I just want to thank everyone for the support of the curfew and the continuation of it for another year," he said. "It's much appreciated."

title: Man handed life sentence for Federalsburg murder
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Man handed life sentence for Federalsburg murder

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Quandre Winder, 27, was handed a life sentence on Wednesday for the September 2023 murder of 27-year-old Caryn Faye Brown in Federalsburg.Judge Brett Wilson handed Winder a life sentence with all but 50 years suspended for first-degree murder and a consecutive 20-year sentence for firearm use in a violent crime with eligibility for parole after five years.
Winder's incarceration will be followed by five years of supervised probation.
In July, Winder pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and using a firearm in a violent crime. Although Winder received 10 charges relating to Brown's death, the remaining eight charges — including manslaughter, assault and additional firearm charges — were abandoned by the state.
Shortly after midnight on Sept. 4, 2023, Brown was found dead in front of an apartment complex in the 700 block of Gardens Court in Federalsburg. Officers from the Federalsburg Police Department were called to the scene and found her lying in the grass with apparent gunshot wounds to the head and chest.
At a plea hearing on July 8, Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin said Winder, who had a handgun on him and had been arguing with Brown before she was killed, was seen shooting Brown multiple times. Franklin said the two were in a "volatile relationship," which Brown had ended due to domestic violence.
During the sentencing hearing on Wednesday, Franklin said the system had failed Brown, who had cases against Winder for domestic violence.
Brown's siblings, mother and eight-year-old son all provided statements at the sentencing hearing. Brown's son Dominic's statement read, "My mommy was a beautiful person, and you took her away from me."
Brown's mother, Nancy Geeslin, recounted the night she got the call that her daughter had been killed. She spoke about how Brown's death has affected each of Brown's children.
Brown's younger sister, Tyrah Banks, said she didn't know if Winder would every fully grasp what he did to their families.
"This will never not hurt," she said.
Banks said she has found peace in the fact that her sister can't be hurt again and peace in the fact that Brown lives on through her children.
Winder's attorney Dana Boston, who is with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender, said Winder committed a terrible act that shouldn't have happened. Boston said Winder had a rough upbringing and developed a drug addiction. He said Winder was on Percocet and Xanax the night of Brown's death.
Boston said Winder expressed "heartfelt remorse" for his actions and is dealing with the psychological repercussions of those actions.
Before handing down Winder's sentence, Wilson said it wasn't the system, but the nature of law that failed Brown. He said when it comes to domestic violence, peace orders are just pieces of paper.
"They're not bullet-proof vests," he said.
Wilson said Winder's criminal history, including firearm and assault charges, show a pattern of disregard for law, authority and others.
Wilson said he is sorry anybody has to grow up in imperfect conditions. But he said this "senseless" act should not have happened.
After the hearing, Jennifer Roberts, Brown's aunt, said in an interview with the Star Democrat that their family is happy to have closure after this has hung over their heads for a year. She said they have no choice but to be satisfied with the outcome, and they have to put their faith in the court system.

On Friday, TCPS students were put in a modified lockdown following a threatening social media post made that morning. According to the Sheriff's Office, the threat originated outside of the United States and similar threats were made to schools in Easton, Pennsylvania.
Gamble said the Sheriff's officer is aware of jurisdictions in other states that "have had 40 or 50 of these types of threats."
"It's happening all over our country where, for whatever reason, somebody is trying to disrupt school operations and put our kids in fear," he said.
Gamble said that a few years back, the district experienced something similar where about half a dozen non-specific threats were made during the course of the school year. He said he would expect to see more of these threats this year.
"This just seems like the thing to do these days for some reason," he said.

title: Child dies after Dundalk house fire
author: JOEL LEV-TOV jlev-tov@chespub.com
content:
Child dies after Dundalk house fire

 September 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOEL LEV-TOV jlev-tov@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 353
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As neighbor Zack Richardson tells it, it was eerily quiet for such a dramatic night. Fire trucks lined Dunleer Road in the early hours of Wednesday, Sept. 4, but didn't turn on their sirens.Had he not gotten up to feed his newborn, he said, he would have missed the house fire across the street from him at 3220 Dunleer Road. The Baltimore County Fire Department ruled that an electrical malfunction caused the fire.
According to a fire department press release, fire engines arrived at the house at 3:44 a.m.
Owner Kevin Mars' 8-year-old son Nolan was hiding on the second floor of the house. Firefighters found and rescued him by 4 a.m., radio traffic indicates. Richardson said Nolan's body was "limp" as he was carried out of the burning house.
Nolan was taken to a local hospital. He died Sept. 9, according to a fire department press release. Only one pet survived, owner Kevin Mars said. Nine cats died in the blaze, according to the fire department.
Mars and four other children in the house escaped with minor injuries, the fire department said.
Despite the dramatic scene, few signs of tragedy remained just a few hours later. The only hints were charred grass, boarded up windows, small pieces of glass strewn around the outside of the house and the back of packaging for an oxygen mask. A faint smell of burning lingered if you got close enough. Even closer, burned wood was visible.
The birds in the tree next to the house kept chirping.
By Sept. 10, the oxygen mask packaging had been removed. In addition to a sign directing people to drop off packages at Richardson's house, a sign warning people that "any alteration or removal of items in this area" would be punished because an ongoing fire investigation was taking place.
Richardson, the neighbor, started a GoFundMe campaign to help the family. As of Tuesday, it had already raised over $23,000 out of the $30,000 goal. His wife set up a clothing drive for the family.
"The support has been amazing and unexpected but sometimes uncomfortable," Mars wrote in a text to the Eagle, "being we're usually quiet people."

title: Justice Department sues companies for bridge collapse
author: CAIT KELLEY and CALEY FOX SHANNON Capital News Service
content:
Justice Department sues companies for bridge collapse

 September 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CAIT KELLEY and CALEY FOX SHANNON Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 416
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit Wednesday against the owner and the operator of the ship that collided with the Francis Scott Key Bridge in March, asking for more than $100 million to recoup the cost of extensive cleanup efforts to reopen the Fort McHenry Channel.The Justice Department asserted that the companies' conduct in sending the container ship Dali down the Patapsco River was "outrageous, grossly negligent, willful, wanton, and reckless."
The suit claimed that "the Dali got underway with known unseaworthy conditions in confined waters where a ship of its magnitude had every opportunity to cause catastrophic damage and loss of life, which in fact happened."
The defendants in the civil suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, are the Singapore-based corporations Grace Ocean Private Limited, which owned the Dali, and Synergy Marine Private Limited, the Dali's operator.
Representatives for the companies did not respond to requests for comment.
The bridge collapse resulted in the death of six road workers and impeded operations in the Port of Baltimore until the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and U.S. Navy Supervisor of Salvage and Diving completed the cleanup in June.
"The Justice Department is committed to ensuring accountability for those responsible for the destruction of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, which resulted in the tragic deaths of six people and disrupted our country's transportation and defense infrastructure," Attorney General Merrick Garland said in a statement.
This suit from the DOJ is a response to Grace Ocean and Synergy's petition to the court in April "for exoneration from or limitation of liability" for damages resulting from the collision. In that claim, the companies asked that their liability be limited to $43.67 million for the damage to the ship and its cargo.
In the 53-page filing Wednesday, the Justice Department detailed a litany of mechanical and electrical flaws in the Dali that led to collision with the bridge. The suit alleges that Grace Ocean and Synergy were aware of these issues and that Dali's crew mishandled the ship's approach to the bridge after two power outages occurred in the early hours of March 26.
"This was an entirely avoidable catastrophe, resulting from a series of eminently foreseeable errors made by the owner and operator of the Dali," Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Brian Boynton said in a statement.
On Tuesday, families of the victims of the bridge collapse announced at a press conference they will be filing their own legal claim to hold the owner of the Dali liable.

title: Scammers look to lure voters to get information
author: MORGAN LEASON Capital News Service
content:
Scammers look to lure voters to get information

 September 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MORGAN LEASON Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Scammers posing as election workers are trying to mislead Maryland voters with fraudulent text messages, prompting concerns at the State Board of Elections.The scammers are telling voters they're not registered to vote in November and then urging them to click a false link to remedy that, according to Jared DeMarinis, the board's state administrator of elections.
"They're capitalizing on the hypertension involving this election," DeMarinis said in an interview with Capital News Service. "The text message is urgent, and they're playing on a fear that an individual is not registered to vote when they really are."
He said he worries that texting scams of this nature could have a sweeping impact on the election, especially if they mislead voters about whether they're registered and eligible to vote.
"The impact of this is to create a new narrative and foster disinformation about voter roles," DeMarinis said.
Similar incidents of text scams have been reported in Illinois, Georgia and Pennsylvania already this year. In Peoria County, for example, text scammers also meant to deceive voters into registering to vote by mail through a false link.
Ensuring the integrity of elections and maintaining public trust are critical issues for Maryland election officials and the nation, especially as the 2024 election nears and texting scams become more prevalent.
As the state elections administrator, DeMarinis is tasked with administering and conducting elections and creating consistent policy and application of the laws in Maryland.
The Maryland board was already working to recruit election judges, track mail-in ballots and secure the local elections. Now, they must also battle continuous threats to undermine public trust in elections.
According to the board, the text scam informs recipients that public records show they are not registered at their address. The matter is "URGENT," the text says. The text then invites the recipient to click a fake link to register before the deadline.
The board's website lists the valid sources for voter registration, polling locations, mail-in ballot status and ways to vote. The board is also reminding voters that trusted information will come from a .gov web address.
DeMarinis told CNS he is determined to combat the spread of disinformation by being proactive on social media. He also encouraged people to contact him or the state board to verify information.
"You don't wait until things hit critical mass," he said, "you combat this information and correct the record immediately."
The board created a portal on its website where people can report instances of scamming and disinformation. DeMarinis said he plans to work with social media platforms to help correct false information.
He said that if scam efforts rise to the level of voter disenfranchisement or suppression, the board will work with law enforcement to ensure that Marylanders are "free to vote, without any sort of undue influence."
As the general election approaches with only 48 days left and early voting starting on Sept. 23, the threat of these scammers remains high. The public must remain vigilant and in the meantime, the board will continue its efforts to combat scams and safeguard the integrity of the election, he said.
"These scams are a direct threat to the legitimacy of the electoral process, because, at best, they're just trying to steal identities," DeMarinis said. "But at worst, they're there to kind of sow distrust in an election administration and undermine confidence in the system."

title: Motorists encouraged to watch for deer as breeding season approaches
author: Tom McCall
content:
Motorists encouraged to watch for deer as breeding season approaches

 September 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As deer breeding season nears, motorists are encouraged to keep their eyes peeled for white tails on the road.Local auto repair businesses say they are busier fixing collisions this time of year. Hitting a deer can cause thousands of dollars worth of damage, bending front fenders, crumpling hoods and cracking front windshields.
"It is about 20% to 30% more this time of year," said TJ Jefferson of Grants Automotive in Easton. "I get more calls early in the morning, 'Can you come get my car? I just struck a deer or a deer just struck me.'"
With increased volume during deer season, he says they just get it done with the available manpower that they have.
According to data from State Farm, "U.S. drivers had an estimated 1.8 million animal collision insurance claims in the U.S. between July 2022 and June 2023."
About 1.5 million deer-car accidents happen every year. More than $1 billion in annual insured losses are due to damages caused by deer-car accidents. According to State Farm, Maryland drivers have a one-in-116-vehicle likelihood risk for animal collisions. The highest risk state for deer-car collisions is West Virginia at one in 37 vehicles.
Deer breeding season begins in October and runs through mid-December. During these months, bucks become more active, seeking out female deer. The females move around more to avoid the bucks. All this motion means more deer are on the roads.
Deer are most active between the hours of 5 and 8 a.m. and again from 5 to 8 p.m., which are also hours that many drivers are on the road commuting to or from work.
Trooper Ian Rola of the Easton Barracks of the Maryland State Police said, "The incidents that rise this time of year are car accidents. (Deer) are in rut and are running all over and crossing the roadway. It is usually up this time of year — in the November time frame."
Rola and fellow law enforcement officers work to help keep roadways clear of hazards during these peak months.
"It is between law enforcement and SHA. We try to keep the roads clear. We rely on the public. If you see a carcass, give us a call, and we will come out. If it is a mess, we call SHA (State Highway Administration) to help," Rola said.
Rola emphasized the importance of drivers slowing down and wearing seat belts, especially as deer breeding season approaches.
"You have got to imagine, you hit a dear, you slam on the brakes and you are going forward at the same time. The seat belt will stop that forward momentum. This saves a lot of injuries from deer accidents," he said.
Representatives from the State Highway Administration encouraged drivers to avoid making sudden turns or movements to avoid hitting deer.
"Making sudden, sharp turns is dangerous as it could place the driver in the path of oncoming traffic or cause your vehicle to strike a fixed object such as a tree or utility pole," wrote Charlie Gischlar of the Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration in an email.

 U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers at the Port of Wilmington seized a shipment of counterfeit designer handbags bound for Newark, authorities said.CPB officers initially inspected the shipment on Sept. 4 after it arrived via express air cargo from China. The shipment, which was heading to an address in Newark, consisted of 26 handbags bearing luxury brand names, such as Chanel, Goyard, Gucci, Hermes, Loewe and Louis Vuitton.
Officers suspected that the handbags may be counterfeit and detained the shipment to verify the authenticity of the handbags' trademarks. CBP's trade experts verified that the handbags were counterfeit and subject to seizure pursuant to the agency's statutory and regulatory authorities.
Had the handbags been genuine, they would have been worth more than $150,000.
The international trade in counterfeit consumer goods is illegal, CBP spokesman Steve Sapp said.
"It steals revenues from trademark holders, steals tax revenues from the government, funds transnational criminal organizations, and the unregulated products potentially threaten the health and safety of American consumers," Sapp added.
Counterfeiters often manufacture consumer goods using substandard materials and parts that either break prematurely or that could hurt consumers. Counterfeit consumer goods may also be sourced or manufactured in facilities that employ forced labor.
"Unscrupulous vendors that peddle counterfeit consumer goods continue to place their profits over your health and safety. Customs and Border Protection urges you to protect your families by purchasing authentic consumer products from reputable retailers," said Erik Kelling, CBP's port director for the Port of Wilmington.
The most recent incidents came two weeks after CBP officers in Wilmington seized 277 counterfeit Lululemon Everywhere Belt Bags, valued at nearly $13,000 had they been authentic.

 CHESTERTOWN — Every first and third Wednesday, the Kent County Sheriff's Office K-9 unit, cooperating with law enforcement in Talbot, Dorchester and Caroline counties, train their dogs.On Wednesday, Sept. 18, they trained at Geno's Automotive in Kent County. After that, the K-9 units were invited to the Kent County Middle School to receive something special.
In a gesture of police support, the Kent Puppy Pals 4-H Dog Club donated a Line of fire Defense Street Fighter vest to Addy, a German Shepherd, handled by Dfc. Craig Lewis of the Dorchester County Sheriff's Office.
Going through Kent County Sheriff's Office Sgt. Scott Lockerman's organization, the Maryland Police K9 Foundation, the Puppy Pals donated a check for $300 in June.
Club Leader of Puppy Pals Kim Montooth explained each year they do a service project. Last year, for instance, they raised money for the Humane Society. This year was exciting for the kids and something different, Montooth said.
Molly's Place also donated $1,000 in a vest for Waylon, a K-9 black lab handled by Pfc. Nick Lang of the Easton Police Department.
In front of about 20 people, the dogs modeled the vests, which are lightweight enough yet specially designed to protect their vital organs.
Then the Puppy Pals kids and their families gathered around to pet the dogs.
After the children met with the dogs and 4-H mom Karri Bryant had a playful tug of war with Addy, they were invited into the school where they witnessed a live demonstration of how Addy sniffs out controlled substances.
Controlled substances were stashed in two classrooms. Led by Lewis, sniffing desks and drawers, Addy alerted to the controlled substance in both rooms in about 30 seconds.
Trainer Mark Carr of Tidewater Strategic Services said the dog doesn't go right to the spot because of the nature of scent itself. The K-9 moves around the perimeter of the room, getting the entire scent. Once she gets a complete picture, she can hone in.
President of the club Trenton Montooth was impressed. At 14 years of age, he has decided he wants to be a K-9 officer.
Lockerman thanked the Puppy Pals and Molly's Place, expressing the importance of their giving by showing the positive impact K-9 dogs make.
"K-9's make the community safer with their presence. Crime rates go down. Schools are much safer. Even the town's property values go up," he said.

 An 80-year-old man retrieved a gun when his adult son attempted to break into his Conowingo residence on Tuesday, Sept. 24 and then fatally shot him, according to Maryland State Police.As of Thursday, criminal charges had not been filed against the alleged shooter.
Investigators identified Joe Berry Jr., 53, of Conowingo, as the victim. Police said the father is cooperating with investigators.
Cecil County Department of Emergency Services paramedics pronounced Berry dead at the scene of the incident, which occurred at approximately 2 p.m. Tuesday on a residential property in the 200 block of Mt. Zoar Road — where a fire damaged an adjacent home at about the same time, police reported.
A 78-year-old woman, whom investigators believe to be Berry's mother, suffered injuries during the incident and an ambulance crew transported her to Upper Chesapeake Medical Center in Bel Air for treatment, according to police. Although they did not specify the woman's injuries, MSP officials qualified that her injuries "were not from gunfire."
MSP troopers assigned to the agency's North East Barrack rushed to scene shortly before 2 p.m. Tuesday in response to a reported shooting, police reported.
Troopers found Berry outside the residence and noticed that he had "apparent gunshot wounds," police said. They also located Berry's father at the scene, police added. Berry's father declined medical treatment, according to MSP officials, who did not specify if the 80-year-old man had been injured during the incident or if he had experienced a medical episode.
"Investigators believe an argument between Berry and his father led to the shooting. The preliminary investigation indicates that Berry attempted to break into the residence before his father retrieved a firearm and shot Berry," an MSP spokesperson outlined, noting that the father is "currently cooperating with investigators."
Firefighters responded to that Mt. Zoar Road property, too, and extinguished a blaze at an adjacent home, police said. As of Wednesday night, detectives with the Maryland Office of the State Fire Marshal continued their investigation to determine the cause of that fire, police added. Although it appears to be so, MSP and MOSFM officials have not indicated if that house fire is related to the fatal shooting.
Detectives with MSP's Homicide Unit are leading the fatal shooting investigation, according to the spokesperson.
"Investigators are working to determine a motive," the spokesperson reported, noting, "No charges have been filed at this time. The investigation remains active."

 CAMBRIDGE — Following an incident at Génesis Food Market on Washington Street, the establishment's owner has been arrested for assault.Alex Perez, 38, of St. Michaels, was arrested for first- and second-degree assault and reckless endangerment.
According to a news release from the Cambridge Police Department, officers received a report that someone was shoplifting at the store Perez owns. When the officers arrived, they found one man sitting down and two men standing next to him. Police said one of the men standing was holding a hammer and the man sitting was bleeding from his hand.
The man with the bleeding hand was taken to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Cambridge, police said. According to the news release, while he was at the hospital, the man told officers he had been stopped from leaving Génesis Food Market and was told to sit down. Police said the man reported that Perez had a hammer in his hand and told an employee to grab a machete.
According to the news release, the man told police that Perez put the machete up to his neck and made statements about wanting him to die before swinging the machete and striking his hand.
A petition created on change.org on Sept. 27 is calling for justice for Perez. According to the petition — which had 356 signatures as of Monday afternoon — Perez was arrested for defending his business. It calls on law enforcement and courts to review Perez's case, drop the charges and re-examine the law when it comes to small businesses defending themselves.
Perez's niece Cindy Chun said in an interview with the Star Democrat that the charges should be dropped because there were no cameras, so it is one person's word against another, and the news release doesn't share Perez's side.
Chun said Perez — who also owns three businesses in Easton and one in St. Michaels — is a loving father and husband and a great boss.
"He is the most caring and loving person you'll ever meet," she said.
Chun said the Wednesday incident was the third time in a week that someone had come in to rob the market. She said that after Perez was arrested, a family member of the person Perez is charged with assaulting came into the store and threatened Perez, his business and his family.
"That's why we want justice for this case because trust me, so far no one is listening to us," Chun said. "The whole police department, they are not listening to us.  EASTON — The Talbot County Department of Social Services hosted a child safety presentation Monday evening at the Talbot County Free Library to educate adults and children ages 3 to 12 on best practices to avoid child abuse.Paris Quillet, special projects coordinator for the department, presented the "Empower Me!" presentation, based on resources from the Jacob Wetterling Resource Center, a program that works to prevent child sexual abuse.
The county receives around 400 reports of child sexual abuse, physical abuse or neglect each year, she said.
"We want to talk about safety for our bodies the same way that we talk about fire drills and active shooter safety and bike safety," Quillet said.
Quillet emphasized to parents that the program avoids "stranger danger" terminology since over 90% of child sexual abuse nationwide is perpetrated by someone who the child knows. Instead, the program keys on the behavior aspect.
"We really want to make sure that we're giving these clear (messages) to children to focus on the behavior and how somebody makes us feel or what they're asking us to do, as opposed to the relationship," Quillet said.
In the children's portion of the program, children were encouraged to identify five trusted adults. Quillet encouraged parents and guardians to "be comfortable that (they) might not be the person that (children) come to for everything."
Having trusted adults in different spaces is important not just for young children but also teenagers, Quillet noted. With the dangers of technology and the internet, she said the 12- to 17-year-old age range is "more vulnerable than ever."
"We see a lot of things locally that revolve around technology and often used as a grooming practice," she said.
At the end of the hourlong presentation, Quillet said parents should stay involved in their children's activities and choose caregivers carefully.
"There should never be a time where I'm not allowed to have access to my children or I'm not allowed to watch them," she said. "… Screen all your caregivers carefully. Ask for references, definitely do unannounced visits."

title: Eastern Shore residents assist survivors of Hurricane Helene
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Eastern Shore residents assist survivors of Hurricane Helene

 October 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 394
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to do their part, a group of Eastern Shore residents have come together to send a truck of donated urgent relief supplies for areas affected by Hurricane Helene.Members of the Eastern Shore Hurricane Relief Committee have been in the works with Hurricane Helene Airlift Relief, an organization based at the Statesville Regional Airport in North Carolina using private small planes and helicopters to land donations past multiple bridge and road collapses.
Helene, a monstrous category 4 hurricane, has devastated communities across six states, including North Carolina, where over 56 deaths have been reported thus far.
Mike Detmer, an organizer for the donation drive, said supplies have been donated by Eastern Shore locals through drop off stations they established in Hurlock and Cambridge.
Detmer said they encouraged people to donate only items listed by the Hurricane Helene Airlift Relief. Those items include, but are not limited to, diapers, baby formula, non-perishable food, feminine care products, hand sanitizer, and toothbrushes and toothpaste.
Detmer said he is surprised by the vast amount of support the initiative has received from the Eastern Shore.
"In the face of such a terrible disaster, it's been really encouraging to see the volume of response, and I'm thankful for it, and I hope to be able to work with all of our neighbors here to send it to people who need help," Detmer said.
Lindsay Wheatley, an organizer for the donation drive, said on Monday she and Detmer were casually talking about the devastation in North Carolina and felt the urge to find ways they could help.
Wheatley said they contacted Eddie James, an owner of Koski Trucking in Dorchester County, and the company generously donated a truck and driver to take desperately needed items to the Statesville staging area. According to Wheatley, James, who previously has worked in disaster relief, was eager to do his part.
Wheatley said through social media they were able to quickly gather community resources together.
Additionally, Wheatley said her husband and one of the owners of Koski Trucking will be heading down to North Carolina in their private vehicles with chainsaws, materials and tools to try to help out in anyway they can.
"At the end of the day, community, family, that's really all that you have," Wheatley said. "And in times of need, you just hope that others show up and help, and that's what we're trying to do."

title: Nonprofit hosts meeting to discuss concerns at apartment complex outside Ridgely
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Nonprofit hosts meeting to discuss concerns at apartment complex outside Ridgely

 October 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 548

 HILLSBORO — Residents and community members gathered at Allen AME Church on Saturday to speak about safety concerns at an apartment complex just outside of Ridgely.Residents of the Dayspring Apartments, located off of School Street close to the Ridgely town line, have voiced worries from since early this year. Those worries intensified after a non-fatal shooting outside of the apartment complex in August.
Bridge Maryland Inc., a nonprofit organization based in Baltimore County, organized a public meeting Saturday to facilitate discussion of housing justice, water equity and safety in the area of the complex. More than 50 people were in attendance.
Trina Ewell, a resident of the Dayspring Apartments for five years, outlined her concerns, ranging from safety, to management, to mold found in bedrooms and bathrooms.
"I feel outraged that nothing has been done," Ewell said, "that all families that live back here in the neighborhood are ignored, and we have been ignored for long."
Ewell said property management has been largely unresponsive to tenants. Attempts by The Star Democrat to reach the property manager or the management company, East Coast Property Management, were unsuccessful.
Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker attended the meeting, emphasizing his commitment to work with property management and the local neighborhood association that Bridge Maryland is assisting.
"I met with the management group about a year ago and was promised that a lot of these things would be fixed," Baker said on Saturday. "And we're still waiting on it now. But to my knowledge, the county commissioners have been working, and they have gotten the cameras up and running. They are working on the lighting. They are working on the shrubbery and the other things that affect our job in law enforcement."
As Baker described efforts to improve safety in the area, he was met with applause from the crowd.
"It has to be a working relationship," Baker said. "It has to be law enforcement and the management group to make sure that citizens are safe in that community. And I am absolutely, 100% behind helping and making that community a much better and safer place."
County police responded to a shooting on Aug. 10 outside of the complex in which one man was injured. Residents such as Ewell have expressed lasting effects from the shooting.
"My son's bedroom faces the street," Ewell said. "He could feel the vibration of the gunshots in which brought on (a) panic attack for my son that night. … It has brought ongoing panic attacks for him."
Sandra Pitts lives on School Street, near the apartment complex. She has worked with Bridge Maryland in recent months and spoke at Saturday's meeting, noting flooding concerns on School Street.
Pitts says those who live in Dayspring are often afraid to speak up, a role she doesn't mind taking. She said the work of Bridge Maryland has been critical in advancing efforts of the local residents.
"I think they're doing a good job and I think things have really grown," Pitts said in an interview.
As president of Bridge Maryland and pastor of Allen AME Church, the Rev. Angelique Mason spoke during Saturday's meeting. She thanked attendees and explained that Bridge Maryland's water equity team assembled environmental leaders to focus "on the failing waste system that sits on Daysprings."
"This is what community looks like," Mason said. "This is what real power looks like."

title: Maryland spends millions to settle lawsuits every year, officials don't like it
author: SOFIA APPOLONIO Capital News Service
content:
Maryland spends millions to settle lawsuits every year, officials don't like it

 October 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SOFIA APPOLONIO Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 322
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The state of Maryland is spending millions of dollars to settle lawsuits every year, and top elected officials aren't happy about it.At a meeting of the Board of Public Works on Wednesday, two officials questioned why the state was being asked to approve yet another payout – this one having to do with strip searches by public safety employees.
Although the board approved the $50,000 settlement request, Comptroller Brooke Lierman and Treasurer Dereck E. Davis questioned the prison agency's decision to settle instead of heading to trial.
"If somebody has been wronged, we should be paying that person and the employees should be retrained or released, but we can't have strip searches that were done properly cost the state $50,000 each," Lierman said.
The request stems from a lawsuit alleging misconduct by employees during a strip search, but the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services did not detail the case at the public meeting.
Joseph Sedtal, the agency's deputy secretary of administration, told the board that the employees involved in the suit followed proper procedures regarding strip searches.
But, Sedtal said, it's difficult to go to trial and prove this because, due to privacy concerns, there are no cameras allowed in the strip search room.
Often, he said a case is the defendant's word against that of the facility.
Even though the board voted to approve the settlement, Lierman asked that the agency come back with more information.
She asked for follow-up on how many such cases are filed, how often the state fully litigates them and how many result in complete dismissals.
State Treasurer Dereck E. Davis questioned the logic, asking whether juries would be more inclined to believe the defendants over the correctional officers if the officers proceeded with proper protocol.
"I would like to think settlements are more of a rarity as opposed to a regularity," Davis said. "It bothers me because this is money, public dollars that I know could be put to good use."

title: Trey Rider sentenced to 15 months at detention center for house fire
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Trey Rider sentenced to 15 months at detention center for house fire

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Fred "Trey" Rider III has been ordered to turn himself into the Talbot County Detention Center on Monday morning to serve 15 months for reckless endangerment. His charges stem from a fire he started at his home in November 2022.At a sentencing hearing Friday, Judge Thomas G. Ross also handed Rider a 20-year sentence for first-degree arson with all but the time he's already served suspended. Rider was given five years of probation with conditions that include attending Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous meetings and completing an abuser intervention program.
In August, Rider pleaded guilty to first-degree arson and five counts of reckless endangerment for a fire started at his home in Easton on Nov. 24, 2022. He faced up to 30 years in prison and $50,000 in fines for first-degree arson and up to 25 years in prison and $25,000 in fines for the five counts of reckless endangerment.
Rider had also been charged with second-degree arson, first-degree malicious burning, two counts of arson threat, two counts of malicious destruction of property, obstruction of emergency assistance and two additional counts of reckless endangerment. As part of a plea deal, the state did not prosecute Rider for those nine additional charges.
Forty-five firefighters responded to the fire in Rider's two-story, single-family home at 27930 Peach Orchard Road in Easton. Through investigation, officials classified the fire as incendiary.
According to court documents, Rider's reckless conduct in igniting the house on fire "clearly" put the firefighters who responded in danger.
At Rider's plea hearing, Talbot County Deputy State's Attorney Joyce Jones said Rider blocked his two driveways with vehicles before setting fire to the house.
That night, Rider was located a short distance from his home and transported to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton for emergency care. Rider's attorney Christine DuFour said at the plea hearing that Rider was under the influence of alcohol during the incident and had slit his wrists.
At the sentencing hearing Friday, Jones asked that Rider's sentencing include incarceration. She said the fire was a planned event, citing threatening texts he sent his wife, Kari Rider, who is currently in the midst of a divorce from Trey Rider.
At the sentencing, Kari Rider said the night of the fire has caused her and their two sons lasting emotional and psychological effects. She said she and Trey Rider had been in a "horribly abusive relationship" and he had been destroying her things for years.
A restitution hearing, which Kari Rider asked for Friday, is set to be scheduled after the divorce proceedings.
DuFour, Trey Rider's attorney, said that over the past seven months, Trey Rider has put in hard work at a recovery center and a sober living home. She said that while he has a ways to go, Rider's goal is to become a sponsor for others struggling with addiction. DuFour said Rider also hopes to participate in reunification therapy with his sons.
A variety of people gave statements on Rider's character during the sentencing, including friends, family and counselors.
Rider said he was ashamed of his conduct, which has "caused immense harm and pain" in the lives of his wife and children. Before apologizing to his family, he said he has "fallen very far" and has reached out to get as much support as possible so he can continue down a road of recovery.
Before handing down the sentence, Ross called Rider's actions the night of the fire "calculated," "planned" and "self-serving." He said Rider has been given opportunities that most people don't get, including getting to begin rehab before being sentenced.

title: Ridgely police vehicles, equipment were sold, transferred this summer
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely police vehicles, equipment were sold, transferred this summer

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 671
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The town of Ridgely has sold seven vehicles and three firearms once belonging to the Ridgely Police Department since the police department was disbanded, according to records obtained by the Star Democrat.The vehicles and firearms were sold to the the Caroline County sheriff and other Eastern Shore municipalities.
Residents in Ridgely have been without the service of the Ridgely Police Department since a state investigation into the town's police chief was opened in March. Ridgely's commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department on March 12.
The town entered into a short-term agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide police coverage in place of the suspended officers. When the Ridgely officers were officially laid off at the start of the fiscal year on July 1, the town entered into a new memorandum of understanding with the county sheriff's office for fiscal year 2025.
Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker says he is committed to ensuring his office provides Ridgely residents with adequate police coverage.
"We have had positive feedback from a large number of residents who are happy with the service," Baker said. "I am absolutely here for the citizens of the Town of Ridgely and the citizens of Caroline County."
A July report said state investigators found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity" looking into "suspected" perjury and misconduct by Ridgely Police Chief Jeff Eckrich.
Transaction records from Ridgely show the town began to sell and transfer vehicles and equipment in the weeks before the release of the investigation's report and before officers were officially laid off.
In June, the town transferred three pistols and three radios to the Caroline County Sheriff's Office with no charge associated.
Three police vehicles — two 2022 Ford Interceptors and one 2020 Ford Interceptor — were sold to the Sheriff's Office for $1 apiece on June 18, transaction records show.
On July 12, the town sold a 2023 Chevy Tahoe to the Town of Denton for just over $44,000. On July 27, Ridgely sold three vehicles to the City of Salisbury — a 2014 stripped K-9 Ford Interceptor for $1,000, a 2015 Ford Interceptor for $4,000 and a 2017 Ford Interceptor for $8,000.
Ridgely Town Commissioners did not respond to questions from the Star Democrat regarding the vehicle and equipment sales. Commissioners have maintained that a statement provided at a Sept. 9 town meeting, which did not address the vehicles and equipment, will be the town's final statement regarding the police department.
COUNTY COVERAGEBaker said the vehicles and equipment acquired by the county are being used by the deputies providing coverage to the town. The vehicles and equipment those deputies previously had will go back to the Sheriff's Office inventory to be used by county officers.
The current memorandum of understanding between the town and county outlines that the Sheriff's Office provides 480 hours of coverage per month.
Baker said the end goal is to have three full-time deputies providing coverage in Ridgely. At this time, there are only two full-time deputies, with a third in the police academy.
Sgt. Keith Collison, a former Ridgely officer, is overseeing daily operations in the town. The second full-time deputy is Cpl. Tracy Ferguson, who has more than seven years of law enforcement experience.
When the deputies stationed in Ridgely are not working, the Sheriff's Office and Maryland State Police are supplementing that temporary gap with patrol checks, Baker said.
Baker added that at one point during the current agreement, there were two officers training in the academy that were planned to be stationed in Ridgely. During that time, the county brought an "experienced" officer to serve as the second full-time deputy and assumed the cost of one of those officers in training at the academy.
By February or early March, Baker says he plans to transfer a third full-time deputy to Ridgely, which he says will "more than fulfill the agreement set out in the MOU."
The Ridgely Police Department office within the town hall building is serving as a substation for the Sheriff's Office deputies, Baker said. It is "up and functional" with fiber optics, computer systems and phone lines.

title: Dorchester County unveils restructuring plan for emergency services, corrections
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County unveils restructuring plan for emergency services, corrections

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words
