title: Attorney general releases immigration guidances; local officials react
author: Konner Metz
content:
Attorney general releases immigration guidances; local officials react

 February 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the days since President Donald Trump signed executive orders bringing sweeping changes to immigration policy, Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown has released immigration enforcement guidance for local law enforcement agencies and healthcare providers.Last week, Brown joined 10 other attorney generals across the United States in addressing the president's federal immigration directives.
In a joint statement, they wrote that state and local law enforcement agencies "cannot be commandeered" to assist federal immigration agents.
"As state attorneys general, we have a responsibility to enforce state laws — and we will continue to investigate and prosecute crimes, regardless of immigration status," the statement read. "We will not be distracted by the President's mass deportation agenda."
LAW ENFORCEMENT
In Brown's guidance toward law enforcement, the attorney general stated, "the federal government cannot compel state and local law enforcement to enforce immigration laws."
"This guidance ensures that law enforcement agencies understand the scope and limitations of their authority and makes clear that the rule of law does not change depending on the federal government's priorities," Brown wrote.
The guidance outlines that police officers cannot do the following: extend detentions to investigate immigration status, give names and addresses to federal authorities without a warrant, or ask about immigration status if it's not relevant to an investigation.
Dorchester County Sheriff James Phillips said his department won't overstep boundaries, but they will assist federal authorities if requested.
"If they ask for police assistance, we're going to help them," Phillips said.
"It's his opinion, it's how he's interpreting the law, and I understand that," said Phillips of Brown's guidance, later adding that "I'm not going to turn my back on another police officer doing his job."
Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker said as he's aware, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, is "going after hardened criminals that are in Caroline County."
Baker said the sheriff's office will assist federal immigration agents in ways that federal and Maryland laws permit. He said that U.S. Homeland Security Investigations has had a presence in recent weeks.
"I think that HSI has peaked as far as going after people who are here illegally and are committing crimes," Baker said of what he's heard from his deputies.
HEALTHCARE FACILITIESIn his guidance to healthcare providers, Brown wrote that "no Marylander, regardless of immigration status, should have to choose between their health and safety."
If an immigration agent enters a healthcare facility, Brown's guidance instructs staff to request the agent's credentials and contact legal counsel.
The attorney general said healthcare staff shouldn't give out patient information unless shown a warrant, subpoena or summons. Brown added that staff shouldn't "attempt to bar the officer from public spaces" or "take other action to thwart the investigation."
Trena Williamson, regional director of communications and marketing for the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health, said the medical system "has a consistent approach" for interactions with all law enforcement officers.
"We remain committed to complying with federal and state laws while ensuring all Marylanders have access to essential health care services," Williamson wrote. "Recent executive orders from the president have not resulted in any changes to our approach."

title: QA, Kent approve regional jail agreement, Caroline not yet on board
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QA, Kent approve regional jail agreement, Caroline not yet on board

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A proposed new regional detention center to be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill would house detainees from Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties. But all counties have yet to reach an agreement. The Queen Anne's commissioners gave their approval to the Mid-Shore Regional Detention Center Cooperative Service Agreement final draft Jan. 28, as did Kent. Caroline remains uncommitted.The new jail facility aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
The corrections facility is proposed to be owned by Queen Anne's County with employment also falling under Queen Anne's County; the goal being to assimilate the current Kent and Caroline correctional officers.
The agreement has been a collaboration between the three counties for several months, Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn said.
With Kent County also approving the final draft, the agreement is still waiting on a public hearing from Caroline County. If Caroline doesn't sign, Kent Commissioners said they would renegotiate with Queen Anne's alone.
Kent Commissioner John Price made the motion to a unanimous vote. The facility will be built regardless, he said, noting the number of beds would be the primary change if Caroline dropped out.
In a recent meeting of the Caroline County commissioners, they said they still have not received exact numbers for how much everything will cost and how much the county will save by joining the agreement with the other counties.
Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested that the county should do an independent evaluation of the operating cost.
"This decision is going to depend on the operational cost and I'm talking long range operational cost," Porter said. "Would it make sense for us to engage someone to do an independent evaluation of these operating cost?"
Each county is currently operating their own jails and have either exceeded inmate capacity or need extensive renovation.
With the State of Maryland willing to fund up to 50% of the costs of the design and construction, a regional detention center is anticipated to be of less cost to the citizens.
Queen Anne's County Commissioner Phil Dumenil noted the regional and state effort, "is a savings for all three counties."
At about 100 years old, Caroline's facility in particularly is in need of improvement, according to Queen Anne's commissioners.

title: Maryland man gets 8 years in crossbow killing of girlfriend
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Maryland man gets 8 years in crossbow killing of girlfriend

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A man who fatally shot his live-in girlfriend with a crossbow arrow inside their Conowingo residence — maintaining that it was an accident — received an eight-year sentence on Tuesday, after a jury had convicted him of involuntary manslaughter but acquitted him of murder and assault two months earlier.Cecil County Circuit Court Administrative Judge Brenda A. Sexton imposed the eight-year sentence on 41-year-old Jeffrey Allen Lander, who also had been found guilty of reckless endangerment. At sentencing, however, that lesser charge merged into Lander's conviction for involuntary manslaughter, which carries a maximum 10-year penalty.
The victim — Judy Elizabeth Gee, 45 — was shot through the back inside the couple's residence in the 700 block of Bell Manor Road at approximately 4:40 p.m. on Jan. 14, 2024, causing heavy internal bleeding. An ambulance crew transported Gee to Lancaster General Hospital in Lancaster, Pa., where she died on an operating table at 7:13 p.m., about two and half hours later.
Sexton remarked from the bench Tuesday that Lander's "conduct was heinous," and she agreed with Assistant State's Attorney Robert Sentman's assessment that Lander exhibited a "lack of remorse or acceptance of responsibility for Gee's death," prosecutors summarized.
Sentman, who prosecuted Lander at trial, recommended a maximum 10-year sentence — exceeding state sentencing guidelines that set a penalty range of three to eight years of active incarceration for Lander. Those guidelines are based on a defendant's criminal record, the seriousness of the offense and other factors.
Lander's lawyer, Assistant Public Defender Jason Ricke, requested a sentence at the lower end of state sentencing guidelines.
Landers will serve his eight-year term in a Maryland Department of Corrections prison, and he received credit for approximately seven months that he spent in jail after his June arrest.
In November, at the conclusion of a three-day-long trial, jurors deliberated for approximately four hours before finding Lander guilty of involuntary manslaughter and reckless endangerment.
Involuntary manslaughter applies when the defendant unintentionally kills someone while acting with gross negligence, meaning the defendant should have known the risk of his or her actions. Other elements also can apply under the statute.
The jury, however, acquitted Lander of second-degree murder, first-degree assault and second-degree assault — criminal offenses that involve an intentional act, to varied degrees. Second-degree murder is punishable by up to 40 years in prison. First-degree assault and second-degree assault carry maximum sentences of 25 years and 10 years respectively.
At trial, Sentman maintained that Lander intentionally shot Gee because, during an argument moments earlier, Gee had informed Lander that she was ending their two-year relationship and that she was leaving him.
Aside from Gee, Lander was the only person present when the fatal shooting occurred — and he provided the narrative of the incident to investigators.
While police and paramedics were at the shooting scene, Gee was seated on a couch, with the arrow protruding out the entrance and exit wounds on her upper torso. She was barely conscious and was not alert. Gee wasn't capable of giving investigators her account of the incident.
The day of the fatal shooting started for Lander at about 4 p.m., with Gee jolting him awake and starting an argument with him. "She was kicking me in the knee. It was a rude awakening. I woke up angry," Lander told investigators.
Lander volunteered all of that information to investigators at the outset, after he had called 911. But in a police interview about two months later, Lander denied that he and Gee had been arguing directly before the fatal shooting.
The defense contended that Lander accidentally shot Gee with the arrow when he tripped over a cat seconds after removing his loaded crossbow from a wall rack in the living room while she was seated on a nearby couch, possibly leaning toward an end table to retrieve something.
Lander, who elected not to testify on his own behalf, told investigators that he thought the crossbow's safety was engaged and that he always stored his crossbow locked and loaded during hunting season.
In addition, Lander told investigators that he was preparing to go deer hunting that late afternoon, noting that there was about one hour of daylight left. Lander also told investigators that he liked going into the woods to decompress after confrontations with Gee.
Cecil County Sheriff's Office detectives testified that they believe Lander shot Gee in the "heat of the moment" amid the argument and that he immediately experienced regret and emotional aguish, prompting him to call 911.
Ricke, however, categorized the deadly shooting this way when addressing the jury in his opening statement: "It was a tragic accident — nothing more. It is not a murder. It is not a crime."
Police arrested and charged Lander on June 28, six months after the incident, at the conclusion of an investigation that included consulting with a crossbow expert.

title: Cleanup launched at former homeless camp in Maryland woods near I-95
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Cleanup launched at former homeless camp in Maryland woods near I-95

 February 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 594
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Nearly 30 contracted workers wearing hazmat suits and protective masks and gloves spent about 30 hours collecting garbage left at a former homeless encampment in the woods adjacent to the North East Station Shopping Center, marking the latest step in restricting the property.The cleanup started on Monday morning (Feb. 3) and continued through Thursday, with contractors filling scores of industrial-sized garbage bags by the end of each 7-hour workday. In addition to bottles, cans and other trash, workers gathered the remnants of campsites, including worn blankets, pillows and so forth. Numerous syringes reportedly were found while clearing the area.
Baltimore-based real estate developer Klein Enterprises, which acquired the 87,006-square-foot North East Station Shopping Center for $11.6 million in 2017, also owns approximately 40 acres of adjacent woods, and that company is paying for the cleanup of the homeless encampment that once occupied that area.
Problems associated with the homeless people living in those woods grew over time as the number of campers increased, according to North East Police Chief Stephen Yates, who noted that an NEPD patrol officer checked the area at the start of the cleanup project Monday morning to make sure that no homeless people were on the property.
"Drug overdoses were occurring more and more in those woods and so were medical emergencies in general. And it is not an easy area for paramedics and police officers to access," Yates said, before remarking, "The concern was for everyone's safety."
The police chief also reported that trash created by the homeless people started accumulating in the woods and that the number of complaints regarding malicious destruction of property and vandalism also increased, as the number of campsites grew.
In addition, according to Yates, his agency frequently received complaints about homeless people panhandling outside stores in the North East Station Shopping Center and disturbing patrons in other ways.
The situation reached its boiling point about a year ago, when garbage, rocks and other debris that the homeless people had dropped into an opening after removing a manhole cover clogged a sewer pipe — causing backed-up sewage to spill into the creek.
It reportedly cost Klein Enterprises thousands of dollars to repair the damaged pipe.
But much worse, the seeped sewage triggered a Maryland Department of Environment investigation. Because the environmental incident occurred on property owned by Klein Enterprises, the MDE levied an "astronomical fine" on the company, according to Yates.
And that was the catalyst for Klein Enterprises taking proper measures to get rid of the homeless people in the woods, Yates said.
Following eviction procedures, the company first posted "no trespassing" signs in and around the woods and then gave people in that makeshift homeless community notice that they must vacate the property within at least two months, Yates added, noting that circumstances later pushed that deadline back.
After the homeless people were gone, Klein Enterprises was free to embark on the next phase — cleanup of the former campground. Contractors started removing the garbage left behind by the banished homeless people on Monday morning and, as of late Thursday afternoon, it wasn't clear when the cleanup project will end.
Once the cleanup is completed, Klein Enterprises will erect a high fence around that entire wooded area, in an effort to keep people from entering the property, Yates said. It also will install security cameras in and around that wooded area, he added.
The Cecil Whig reached Klein Enterprises representatives Thursday and asked for more specific information for this story, including the sum of the MDE fine and the cost of the cleanup. As of deadline, however, the Whig had not received that information.

title: "These allegations are despicable': In wake of crematorium scandal, morticians resign, board being reviewed
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
"These allegations are despicable': In wake of crematorium scandal, morticians resign, board being reviewed

 February 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 676
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After a scathing report about a White Plains crematorium began circulating in late January, the Maryland State Board of Morticians had several key figures resign after complaints arose of their inaction over the last several years.Brandon Wylie, Michele Kutta and Patrick Thompson, executive members and officers of the board, all resigned under pressure from Gov. Wes Moore (D).
Soon after their resignation, they were promptly removed from the Maryland Department of Health's website.
Heaven Bound Cremation Services LLC — located in a White Plains building with beauty salons, a pharmacy and a restaurant — had its license suspended last month after it was determined that "the public health, safety or welfare imperatively requires emergency action," the Maryland State Board of Morticians' report said.
Rosa and Brandon Williams, the two operators of the crematorium, were already on probation by the board for prior disciplinary action before the most recent report due to improper storage of human remains.
An August 2019 final order said that Rosa Williams had violated several statutory and regulatory provisions by "commingling cremains, disposing of cremated remains in a receptacle with bio-hazard waste, otherwise improperly storing cremated remains, and failing to send cremated remains to the agent of the decedent."
In January 2021, it was determined that Williams had failed to comply with the order, which set another two-year probationary term on her.
Then, in March last year, the Maryland State Board of Morticians' investigator conducted an inspection that revealed "human bodies in cardboard boxes stacked on top of each other with no support between the boxes, human bodies in ripped body bags with arms and legs hanging out of the body bags, human remains that were not being stored at temperatures below 40 degrees Fahrenheit and blood on the refrigeration unit and bodily fluids on the floor."
By January this year, not much had changed, according to the report.
It was determined that the cremation chamber was not operational and human bodies were "accumulating rather than being cremated in a timely manner."
Also found last month, the door to a refrigeration unit was blocked by an accumulation of boxes with bodies, dried blood and fluids were on the floors, bodies were stored in damaged bags, 18 bodies were stored in temperatures not below 40 degrees, "three visibly decomposing bodies," and one decomposing body that had been in the facility since the March 2024 inspection.
Moore commented on the report, saying, "Firstly, these allegations are despicable, and those responsible need to be held accountable. I know the board is independent, but they have failed these families and I share in their outrage, and I stand with them in demanding justice. There is an active investigation into this matter, and these families deserve better."
Soon after, he announced a review of the board.
Moore asked attorney Charles P. Scheeler to lead the review, which will involve a thorough assessment of the board's structure and operations and whether changes to law or regulations are warranted. Scheeler previously served as a federal prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland.
"The operational review of Maryland's health professional licensing boards is an important step in ensuring these entities are effectively fulfilling their responsibilities," said Del. Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Anne Arundel, Prince George's), who is the chair of the Health Government and Operations Committee. "Given their critical role in safeguarding public health and maintaining professional standards, it is essential that we fully understand any challenges they may be facing. I appreciate the administration's efforts in undertaking this review."
Southern Maryland News visited various businesses in the building, with multiple employees having no idea what was occurring right behind them. Most businesses within the building are front-facing, toward Crain Highway; the crematorium is in the back of the facility.
The Charles County Department of Health issued an abatement order to the crematorium, while the Maryland Department of Health condemned "in the strongest terms" the mistreatment of human remains.
Anyone who may have questions or need guidance regarding concerns for the remains of a loved one can contact the Maryland Department of Health Board of Morticians and Funeral Directors. Visit health.maryland.gov/bom/Pages/home.aspx for contact information.

title: Lawmakers debate the sentencing of youth as adults
author: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service
content:
Lawmakers debate the sentencing of youth as adults

 February 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 1116
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland lawmakers are once again debating whether to scale back the state's practice of automatically placing teenage defendants in adult court if they are accused of serious crimes.After more than a decade of deadlock on the subject, advocates for the reforms had begun to worry that the moment for rethinking automatic sentencing had passed, while Maryland's state's attorneys remained steadfastly opposed. However, a key Senate Democrat kept the debate alive this session by introducing a pared-down version of the proposal that maintains automatic charging as an adult for the most serious crimes.
"We're paying more money, getting worse outcomes, and taking a longer time to get there," said Sen. William Smith, a Democrat representing Montgomery County and the chair of the Senate's Judicial Proceedings Committee.
Smith argues that even his pared-down version of the bill would spare some juvenile defendants from spending weeks or months in the adult system before their charges are dismissed or dropped. Reform advocates say that exposure increases their risk of committing a new, more serious crime in the future.
Maryland prosecutors, however, contend that lawmakers should be more skeptical of the state's Department of Juvenile Services, which is responsible for housing and providing services to those in the juvenile justice system.
"It's unwise to send more juveniles with more complex problems and challenges to a system that has been shrinking for the past three years," said Wicomico County State's Attorney Jamie Dykes, alluding to real and planned closures of juvenile detention and treatment facilities.
Now, Senate lawmakers are once again weighing whether the costs of treating some teenage defendants as adults pencil out for the public's safety.
Smith's bill would give Maryland's juvenile courts default jurisdiction over teenage defendants charged with some violent crimes, allowing prosecutors to request that a case be moved to circuit court to reflect the severity of a crime. That would effectively flip the current system, wherein circuit court automatically has jurisdiction over juvenile defendants charged with certain violent crimes, and defense attorneys can request to transfer cases to juvenile court.
But the bill would leave the most serious violent crimes, including first-degree murder, in the circuit court's jurisdiction by default. That exception is adjustment from past reform bills intended to assuage critics.
"This issue has been studied and debated throughout three governors, multiple committee chairs," said Alice Wilkerson, executive director of Advance Maryland and a part of the coalition of advocacy groups backing the bill.
Ending automatic sentencing of juveniles as adults was that coalition's first policy goal, she added, and years later, it remains "unfinished business."
That coalition has seen victories on other fronts. In 2022, for instance, Maryland lawmakers voted to generally bar police from interrogating children until they have consulted an attorney.
Dayvon Love, director of public policy for the Baltimore-based think tank Leaders of a Beautiful Struggle and a vocal supporter of automatic sentencing reform, says pushback from law enforcement and prosecutors on recent criminal justice reforms, as well as critical media coverage, seemed to doom automatic sentencing reform.
"We are dealing with what I describe as a backlash," he told the Capital News Service.
Smith's emergence as the latest voice of automatic sentencing reform in the Senate, however, may change the reform movement's outlook. As chair of the Judicial Proceedings Committee, Smith is well-positioned to negotiate a path forward for a pared-down bill.
But the policy disagreements surrounding automatic sentencing have largely not budged.
Smith underscores that most teenagers charged as adults in the state eventually see their cases transferred down to juvenile court — 79% in 2023 alone, he told his committee on Tuesday.
Awaiting that transfer, he added, "when someone's languishing in the adult system, they get none of the services and attention that they would get in the juvenile system." Exposing teenagers to the adult court and prison system, he added, increases their chances of committing more serious crimes in the future.
"Based on my 24 years in both juvenile and adult criminal courts, there is a drastic difference in outcomes [between adult and juvenile court] that should be the elephant in the room," said retired Anne Arundel County Circuit Court Judge Philip Caroom, who testified in support of the bill on Tuesday.
The additional hearings and administrative costs involved in transferring hundreds of young defendants between the adult and juvenile systems, Smith added, cost the Department of Juvenile Services roughly $12.3 million a year. "What if you have $12.3 million to reinvest into services, into oversight?" he asked.
But Sen. William Folden, a Republican representing Frederick County and a frequent critic of criminal justice reform bills on the committee, was critical of the Department of Juvenile Services' ability to properly rehabilitate young people placed in its custody by the court system.
"DJS is a mess. DJS is a wreck. DJS has a secretary that spends money on all these shiny new ideas and documented zero of the outcomes," he said. "I don't know if that's someone that can be entrusted with such an important role in molding youth."
Catharine Rosenblatt, chief of the Baltimore City State's Attorney's Office juvenile division, echoed those concerns. She told lawmakers that her office regularly sees cases transferred from adult to juvenile court on the pretense that the Department of Juvenile Services will provide secure housing or behavioral therapy, only for those services never to materialize.
"Unfortunately, what we've found time and time again is that the services available — they're in name only," she said.
But neither Rosenblatt nor any other prosecutor who spoke in opposition to the bill on Tuesday expressed enthusiasm for the services available to teenages in the adult system. Charles County Deputy State's Attorney Karen Piper Mitchell, for instance, questioned why therapeutic services aren't available to teenage defendants tried in adult court, even while arguing against the proposed reforms.
The Department of Juvenile Services is supportive of the proposed reforms, and its legislative director testified in support of Smith's bill, arguing that their agency already serves the substantial share of Maryland's teenage defendants charged as adults who eventually transfer to juvenile court.
If lawmakers do finally implement the reforms, Baltimore County State's Attorney Scott Shellenberger asserted that the forecasted savings on court hearings might not materialize if prosecutors opted to request transfers to adult court in most cases, as public defenders do for transfers to juvenile court in most cases.
"I understand that 80% are being transferred down [to juvenile court]," he told CNS. "If they all started in juvenile, a vast majority of the State's Attorneys would try to waive many of them up, and I don't believe it would approach anything near 80% that would be granted." Nevertheless, he said, lawmakers should not assume that the costs of hearing cases in both adult and juvenile jurisdictions would disappear.
The Judicial Proceedings Committee has yet to vote on the bill.

title: Bill could improve police awareness of unseen disabilities
author: SOfIA APPOLONIO Capital News Service
content:
Bill could improve police awareness of unseen disabilities

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SOfIA APPOLONIO Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 466
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Lawmakers are considering a bill that would make it easier for first responders in Maryland to know when they're dealing with a person who has invisible disabilities.The measure would allow Maryland residents to request a notation on their driver's license or state ID card that identifies their unseen disability, such as autism or hearing impairment.
If adopted, the bill would mandate training for law enforcement on how to improve interactions with people who have hidden disabilities. It would also require the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration to work on awareness programs.
The changes are meant to help protect people with invisible disabilities during encounters with first responders — a special concern for parents of Black children who may be at higher risk during conflict with police.
"The reality of these encounters presents differently when your Black son transitions to adulthood and becomes a legally independent Black man," said bill co-sponsor Del. Kym Taylor, a Democrat representing Prince George's County, who said her son has a hidden disability. "There are no visible signs nor immediate indicators to help first responders understand potential reactions."
The bill, known as Eric's ID Law, is named for Maryland native Eric Blessed Carpenter Grantham, 20, a Black man who lives with autism.
Following the 2020 death of George Floyd — a Black man who died at the hands of Minneapolis police officers — Grantham and his mother Linda worried about Grantham potentially encountering police and failing to respond as expected because of his disability. The two met with Sen. William Smith Jr., a Democrat representing Montgomery County, Senate sponsor of the bill.
Grantham says that he designed special logos that easily identify hidden disabilities to law enforcement.
"Eric's ID Law was created to help save lives for people who cannot use their own voice," he said.
Prince George's County Sheriff John Carr said he supports the proposal, adding that increased resources to aid people with invisible disabilities during encounters with law enforcement are a "must."
"From a law enforcement perspective, we want you to know that we are here to serve you and we want this bill to pass," Carr said. "Any time that we're able to put a citizen at ease during a traffic stop, that is something that helps us interact and keep our community safe."
Similar initiatives exist in Maryland already, such as the MVA "blue card" that people can present to identify their disability. Additionally, the Ethan Saylor Alliance was established in 2015 to "provide increased training for law enforcement and other public service entities" to address situations with people with invisible disabilities.
Its formation follows the death of Saylor, a 26-year-old man with Down syndrome, following a police altercation at a Frederick movie theatre.
The passage of this law would mean Maryland joins 11 other states allowing people with disabilities to identify themselves on their identification cards.

title: Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Police Chief Alan Lowrey raised concerns over a proposed bill in the state legislature that would limit police officers' abilities to make traffic stops for certain violations.Senate Bill 292, cross-filed in the House of Delegates, would shift many primary offenses to secondary offenses, including improper use of headlights and taillights, failing to use turn signals, missing or improper license plates, and excessive noise.
That change would mean police officers can only cite a driver for those offenses if they pull over the driver for a different, primary offense.
During an Easton Town Council meeting Monday, Lowrey, also serving as the interim town manager, said the bill's proposed changes would be "drastic" and negatively impact police in detecting crime.
"There's a number of concerns on my part as the chief of police, and I've spoken with my staff about this," Lowrey said.
Lowrey said offenses such as driving without headlights are common signs indicating potential impaired driving. He said all of the offenses that would be reclassified are safety issues.
"I personally have arrested a number of people, based upon traffic stops, for serious crimes," Lowrey said.
As written, the bill seeks to make evidence gathered during traffic stops inadmissible if an officer fails to state their name, identification number, agency and reason for the stop. Lowrey called that measure "drastic" as well.
Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) is the bill's sponsor. At a Jan. 28 Senate Judicial Proceedings hearing, Sydnor noted Baltimore County statistics that indicated Black and Hispanic drivers face inequities in the rate of citations issued.
"It is these disparities that spurred me to seek and introduce a legislative remedy," Sydnor said.
Sydnor said he worked with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender on the drafted bill. Moving primary violations to fall under secondary violations make way for technologies such as cameras to detect traffic violations, the senator said.
"Technology that can be modified to do what people do today," Sydnor said. "So really, this bill kicks off a conversation about, I would say, a reimagining of how we deal with traffic offenses on the highways."
At the hearing, though, some legislators and law enforcement officials from around the state spoke unfavorably of the legislation.
Those conversations around Maryland have continued in the weeks since. Last month, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed the bill at a meeting and expressed intent to write a letter in opposition.
Monday in Easton, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said the job of being a police officer is "tough enough as it is."
"We don't need to make it any tougher," Abbatiello said. "So I would support anything that the town would like to do in order to try to prevent this from passing."
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Lowrey how the town could express its concerns regarding the bill. Lowrey suggested drafting a letter.
Following discussion, Easton councilmembers voted unanimously to send correspondence to committees in Annapolis opposing the bill.

title: Sometimes red, sometimes blue, sometimes neither: State and local police and Trump's ICE raids
author: MIKE SUNNUCKS APG Media
content:
Sometimes red, sometimes blue, sometimes neither: State and local police and Trump's ICE raids

 February 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MIKE SUNNUCKS APG Media | Section: National 
 
 1547
 Words 

 Read News Document

 President Donald Trump's increased immigration raids and promised mass deportations of undocumented migrants are spotlighting the roles local police are — or are not — playing with the crackdowns.Some conservative states and sheriffs are touting new and existing agreements with the U.S. Immigration & Customs Enforcement (ICE) to hold undocumented immigrants accused of other crimes and promised more cooperation with Trump to deal with international gangs, trafficking rings and drug cartels.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Feb. 19 that state police agencies were entering into agreements with ICE "to execute functions of immigration enforcement within the state."
"Florida is setting the example for states in combating illegal immigration and working with the Trump Administration to restore the rule of law," DeSantis said. "By allowing our state agents and law enforcement officers to be trained and approved by ICE, Florida will now have more enforcement personnel deputized to assist federal partners. That means deportations can be carried out more efficiently, making our communities safer as illegal aliens are removed."
The Florida Highway Patrol, Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE), Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), and the Florida State Guard have entered into 287(g) agreements with ICE.
Those deals allow state and local police to administer federal immigration laws.
GANG INFLUXAs of December 2024, ICE had 287(g) agreements with approximately 135 state and local law enforcement agencies nationally, according to the American Immigration Council.
Some of those agreements have been in place for years.
"Nothing has changed in our approach. If someone is being held on local charges and ICE wants to place a 'hold' on them they do. We do participate in the 287(g) program and this has been active for years," said Dan Springer, sheriff in Gallatin County, Montana (which includes Bozeman and Belgrade).
"We have one person designated as a warrant service officer. This allows that detention Officer to serve warrants generated by ICE."
Springer said his deputies will notify ICE of arrestees potentially being in the country illegally if those persons don't have a U.S. Social Security number or valid immigration visa when they are booked for an alleged crime.
"During the booking process, we also ask everyone their place of birth and if it is a foreign country, that also alerts us to notify ICE," Springer said. "ICE is contacted, they review fingerprints, demographics, etc. and they determine citizenship. If determined to be illegal by the ICE agent and they meet certain criteria set forth by ICE, they place an immigration detainer."
Those holds can also apply to immigrants who overstay their visa or have been convicted of serious crimes and face deportation orders.
ICE also has 48 hours to show up at local jails to pick up those with holds after charges are adjudicated or the defendants are bonded out, Springer said.
Trump has designated Mexican cartels and Latin American gangs as terrorist organizations allowing for more U.S. law enforcement, intelligence and military assets to be deployed against those syndicates with a focus on curtailing fentanyl (a potent and dangerous synthetic opioid) and other smuggling in the U.S.
He's also promised to crack down human trafficking rings and has criticized the prior administration for allowing post-pandemic migration waves into the U.S.
Springer said he's seen an influx of gang members in Montana.
"We have been able to classify some as being illegal aliens and some are not," the sheriff said.
Earlier this month, ICE and U.S. Homeland Security agents arrests six alleged members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua.
'SANCTUARY PROMISE'Immigration advocates and Democrats worry about Trump's raids sweeping up undocumented migrant workers who are in the U.S. to work and have not committed crimes.
Those migrants often take jobs native-born Americans eschew and are key to sectors such as construction, agriculture and restaurants.
Critics of Trump's promised mass deportations also worry about ICE agents going into churches or schools to make arrests.
Thirteen states — including Oregon, California, Illinois, New York and Colorado as well Utah — have sanctuary laws restricting state and local police from cooperating with ICE.
Another 220 cities and counties also have sanctuary laws protecting undocumented migrants and forbidding local police from cooperating with federal immigration agencies, according for the Center for Immigration Studies.
Those include big cities such as Atlanta, Baltimore, Philadelphia and New Orleans as well as college areas such as Dane County, Wisconsin (Madison); Las Cruces, New Mexico; Athens-Clarke County, Georgia; and Franklin County, Ohio (Columbus).
Illegal immigration was center stage in Athens, Georgia after a Venezuelan man, who had been arrested but not detained in New York and Georgia on other charges, killed nursing student Laken Riley in 2022.
The man, José Antonio Ibarra, was convicted of murder and Congress passed and Trump signed a new law last month requiring federal detention of undocumented immigrants accused of burglary and theft.
Trump has spotlighted other high-profile violent crimes committed by migrants illegally in the U.S. That includes the 2024 killing and sexual assault of 12-year-old Jocelyn Nungaray in Houston; two Venezuelan men illegally in the U.S. were charged with the crime.
Public opinion polls show U.S. voters supporting Trump's deportation push with 59% backing the effort in a CBS News/YouGov poll and 63% in a Napolitan News Service survey this month.
Democrats in sanctuary cities and states have promised to stick by their policies of not working with ICE.
"Our immigrant communities are Oregon communities," said Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, in a video statement last month. "I will uphold Oregon's sanctuary promise laws."
Portland (Oregon) Police Chief Bob Day said in a statement that a department directive also eschews immigration enforcements.
"I want everyone to feel safe and protected, which is why it is important to understand that the Portland Police Bureau does not engage in immigration enforcement as outlined … Simply put, we have no legal authority to do so," Day said.
U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Trump's immigration czar Tom Homan have promised to go after states and local jurisdictions who push back or refuse to help enforce immigration laws. New York City Mayor Eric Adams has promised NYPD cooperation with ICE's removal efforts. That move coincided with the Trump administration dropping corruption charges against the mayor brought by the Biden administration.
'OUR MISSION'Some municipal police departments say immigration enforcements are not within their operations especially with county sheriffs frequently handling jails.
In Omaha, Nebraska, Mayor Jean Stothert, a Republican, and Police Chief Todd Schmaderer, posted a social media video last month saying local police will not inquire about immigration status.
"We don't want anyone to be afraid. If you are the victim of a crime or a witness of crime... the Omaha police will not check your legal status," Stothert said.
Dustin Lensing, police chief in Belgrade, Montana, said his small town department does not have a 287(g) agreement but will provide logistical support to ICE and other federal agencies when requested.
"From a local law enforcement perspective, not a lot has changed in our mission. Our mission at the municipal level is to maintain and ensure the safety of all of our residents and visitors, regardless of immigration status. When a crime or incident occurs, we respond and mitigate the situation," Lensing said.
"At this time, we are not directly contacting ICE whenever we have contact with a potential migrant, as a lot of times, we do not truly know their immigration status (resident, non-resident, visa, green card holder) and we have to be careful to follow laws and restrictions as they apply to profiling persons due to their ethnicity," he continued.
The Belgrade chief has also seen "some increase in gang, drug and labor trafficking issues" and an uptick in federal immigration holds.
"What we are seeing is that some of our arrestees are being held on ICE detainers after we book them into jail on local charges. We do not have involvement in the process since this occurs after our officers have left the facility, but this is not something we have seen much of from ICE in several years," Lensing said.
'WE DON'T ASK FOR IMMIGRATION STATUS'On Maryland's Eastern Shore, Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said a unique setup limits his deputies' involvement with immigration cases.
Gamble said in a number of Maryland counties jails are not administered by local sheriffs. They are run by a separate local corrections department. He said his deputies don't delve into legal status.
"We don't ask for immigration status," Gamble said.
He said when defendants are booked into jail, their fingerprints and information get shared with the FBI and in turn other agencies, including ICE.
"They will see that," Gamble said of whether ICE can tell criminal defendants are potentially undocumented or illegally in the U.S.
While Maryland is one of the most Democratic and progressive states in the union, it does not have sanctuary laws.
Maryland Attorney Anthony Brown, a Democrat, issued fresh immigration guidance in January telling state and local police they "are prohibited from asking about a person's immigration status during regular police functions unless it is relevant to a crime being investigated by that officer." He said "state and local law enforcement officers cannot be prohibited from sharing information about a detainee's citizenship or immigration status with federal immigration officials, but they are not required to do so either."
Brown said more detailed information about a defendant requires a warrant.
Gamble said his agency is often at arms length from those interactions because he doesn't operate the jail.
"We don't know about any of this stuff," Gamble said. 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Greensboro Police Department adds Stg. Jeff Adams to staff

content:
Greensboro Police Department adds Stg. Jeff Adams to staff

 GREENSBORO — The Town of Greensboro announced on Feb. 12 that its police department hired Sgt. Jeff Adams as its newest member, ending a long stretch during which Police Chief Lenox Trams was the town's sole officer."Sgt. Adams brings 18 years of law enforcement experience and officially started on February 11," The Town of Greensboro said in a Facebook post. "He's currently completing his 80-hour FTO training, and we can't wait for you to meet him."
Trams has been the lone officer at Greensboro Police Department since September of 2024, and he is pleased to bring Adams on board.
"I've been there since March of 2023, and I've been trying to recruit only the highest best qualified officers, and it's been a struggle," Trams said. "So when I was down to myself I didn't give up, I kept recruiting and I actually had the applicant who kind of met our standards, so he applied, and then he went through the hiring process and a very extensive background investigation, and I just hired him."
Adams' 18 years of law enforcement experience was one of these reasons Trams hired him, the police chief said, but also Adams' 18 years of loyalty.
"Sergeant Adams has been at one agency for 18 years and that track record to me says a lot," Trams said. "He's very loyal to the agency, and he just doesn't bounce around. We also look at like other factors of his application, but I think off the face, just having him be loyal to his one agency for 18 years says a lot."
In September 2024, the town of Greensboro considered closing the police department because the public safety demands were too much for one officer to handle. The Caroline County Sheriff's Office would have taken over the policing duties for the town.
Trams believes with this hire the conversations of dissolving the police department have been "tabled." He hopes to continue to grow the staff at the Greensboro Police Department.
When Trams was by himself, Greensboro moved its offices into the police department's building, with the town's town hall experiencing maintenance concerns. But now there will be talks of moving the police department to another office since the plan will be to continue to grow the department, Trams said.
"I was by myself, so that was the best move at the time," Trams said. "But now that I'm going to build up the agency and hire quality officers, we all can't be in the same building, so there is some talking about putting the police department in another building."

title: Multiple crashes at Easton intersection lead to resident concerns
author: Konner Metz
content:
Multiple crashes at Easton intersection lead to resident concerns

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 630
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A recent string of crashes at the intersection of Brookletts Avenue and South Aurora Street have ignited resident calls for traffic and safety improvements.Monday morning, residents Lydia Pinkney and Tony Ruffini stood on the sidewalk of Aurora Street, discussing their safety concerns for the residential area that is home to many families and children.
"You stand out here for about five, ten minutes, you'll see how fast people go," Ruffini said. "It's insane. They don't care, and they're always in a hurry."
According to the Easton Police Department, the intersection has seen three crashes this month, all due to driver error. There were only 13 in the last 11 years, police said.
Town engineers reviewed the traffic light, which was confirmed as operational. In a Facebook post, the police department encouraged drivers to be cautious and stated the intersection will be monitored.
"While this location is being monitored, officers have begun targeted traffic enforcement and will continue to do so at different hours of the day," the department wrote.
Pinkney said she's worried for the safety of her 9-year-old daughter and her dog when walking up and down Aurora Street near the intersection. She says a car has careened into her yard before, and many neighbors have had their parked cars damaged.
Pinkney believes part of the issue is drivers may be unaware it is a residential area.
"The speed limit's 25, and I know people are going more than 25," she said. "Our kids play out here. And what worries me about everything is if … someone's not paying attention or whatnot, them running the red light or just going way too fast and clipping me and my daughter."
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said the town is looking at what it can do with the intersection's traffic light in terms of safety and timing.
Easton's engineers recently adjusted the timing of the intersection's traffic light, hoping to lower the "chances of a collision if a driver attempts to beat a red light," the Easton Police Department announced Tuesday.
Discussion around safety on Brookletts Avenue has been recurring. This month, the town installed four-way stop signs at two other Brookletts intersections, South Harrison Street and Hanson Street. The intersections previously had two stop signs each.
Van Emburgh said thus far, feedback on the four-way stop signs has been positive. Resident Lisa Stone lives next to the intersections and said she's happy with the change.
"I have seen so many near accidents at the intersections, particularly Hanson and Brookletts," Stone said. " … I think that's a good improvement."
The town also added on-street parking lines to Brookletts Avenue, a measure that Van Emburgh said will improve safety on the wide, two-way street.
"The white lines give the drivers cues as to where they're supposed to be in the travel lanes," Van Emburgh said. "Because one of the things that we struggle with is when you have a road that can accommodate on-street parking, but no one's actually parking on it, it looks like a wide-open raceway."
For many neighbors, traffic and safety concerns only grow as developers revamp a nearby property formerly owned by Perdue AgriBusiness. Last week, Easton's Planning Commission approved the majority of a 123-unit proposal for the site along Brookletts Avenue.
Developers had Lenhart Traffic Consulting prepare a traffic impact study, which recommended project approval. Per Planning Commission documents, the study found redevelopment will have "minimal impact on the surrounding road network."
Ruffini said with the new development and an eventual increase in traffic, South Aurora Street "will be a main road before you know it."
Stone, meanwhile, is excited to see the redevelopment, given it includes commercial space and affordable housing. But she's keeping an eye on its impacts to driver and pedestrian safety.
"Hopefully it will just be an increase in traffic and not a decrease in safety," Stone said.

title: Leaving a timeless mark: Remembering lives lost with roadside memorials
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Leaving a timeless mark: Remembering lives lost with roadside memorials

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 1814
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As one drives along Route 210 through Bryans Road in the area of Livingston Road a metal cross can be seen by anyone with an observant eye. It helps to know it's there if you are looking for it, but if you approach it on foot via sidewalk you can better observe its simplicity.The name "Tiffani" in big capital letters using a decorative font is in the middle of the cross, at the top is a red flower and at the bottom is the insignia for the Bryans Road Volunteer Fire Department and Rescue Squad.
According to Deborah Carrington-Smith, the cross commemorates the life of her daughter, Tiffani Carrington, who was killed near the Indian Head Highway intersection on Dec. 21, 1996.
"She was 19 years old," Carrington-Smith told Southern Maryland News. "Her car, a 1987 Nissan 300ZX, was broadsided by a Charles County sheriff's officer."
The deputy driving the sheriff's office patrol car was responding to a call. Tiffani Carrington, according to information posted by the U.S. National Emergency Medical Service Memorial Service, had logged a lot of volunteer hours with the Bryans Road company.
At the time she was killed, Tiffani Carrington was pursuing a career as a Maryland State Police trooper paramedic.
"This is who Tiffani was to our family," her mother said. "She was a child full of spunk, a teenager wise beyond her years and an EMT with aspirations of becoming a flight paramedic. She was a cheerleader, a softball player, a coach and a mentor to other youth. She was the apple of her father's eye and a bit bossy with her younger brothers. She had so much love to give and was never stingy with her affection."
In 1998, the national EMS memorial service honored Tiffani Carrington, declaring her death was in the line of duty.
Carrington-Smith is quoted in the organization's citation saying that her daughter took the career path toward becoming a paramedic "after she saw a lady collapse from a seizure."
Tiffani Carrington, her mother said, was frustrated that she didn't have the expertise to aid the stricken woman. That led to her career path decision.
Carrington-Smith said that over six months after the tragic death, her daughter posthumously earned her flight paramedic wings.
"She spoke her mind unabashedly, valuing authenticity, honesty and courage," Carrington-Smith said of Tiffani. "Material things were not important to her and she judged people by how they treated others."
Marking the spot of a memorialFor those wishing to have a marking to remember a loved one lost in a road tragedy, the rules in Maryland can be ambiguous.
"State Highway Administration does not track memorials that are placed along state highways in memory of crash victims," SHA spokesman Daniel Allman told Southern Maryland News. "However, state law prohibits the unauthorized placement of anything along state highways that are not approved, highway safety-related signs or devices. The placement of roadside memorials could pose safety and maintenance concerns for motorists, pedestrians and highway workers."
A website called "Roadside Tribute" notes in Maryland, the state highway administration "must comply with the law and has an obligation to motorists to keep roads safe, which includes removing distractions and illegal items from state right-of-way. When doing so, crews keep any intact roadside memorials at the nearest shop to be reclaimed within two weeks. If the owners of the memorials are known, SHA tries to contact them."
Those rules don't stop people from placing memorials, though, as evidenced by the many memorials large and small along the region's roadways.
The state website further noted that there are other options in Maryland that can be used to pay tribute to a loved one lost in a road tragedy. Those options include the Adopt-a-Highway program and Partnership Plantings. In some cases, plantings along the highway are done in honor of someone and can be noted with a sign.
Remembered with flowersNearly 18 years after Tiffani Carrington's death, Charles County lost another volunteer responder in a road crash. Autumn Jenkins was 20 years old when her life was claimed in a collision that occurred April 28, 2015, on Route 424 in the area of Tim's Place in Nanjemoy.
Katelyn Shannon remembered her cousin Autumn Jenkins as a consummate volunteer, someone whose passion was to help people and animals. She had worked at the Charles County Humane Society as a technician and was also a manager at a Waldorf swimming pool.
According to a July 2016 Maryland Independent article on the sentencing of the other driver, an Indian Head man in his early 20s, police investigating the crash said the Chevrolet Silverado the at-fault driver was operating crossed the center line and crashed into the Kia Soul that Jenkins was driving.
Crews desperately worked to free her from the wreckage, but Jenkins was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver of the truck, court testimony stated, registered a 0.14 blood alcohol level. He was sentenced to 10 years with all but three years suspended.
Shannon said the memorial to her cousin "sits in front of a telephone pole. We have a stone that was engraved with a drawing of a dog and the fire shield. We also have her helmet shield up and we actively put flowers and solar lights. We actively attend DUI checkpoints conducted by the La Plata Police Department in memory of her."
The Maryland Independent story on the sentencing mentioned that when the defendant's mother made her plea for clemency to the judge, she mentioned that her son went back to the crash site on the anniversary of Jenkins' death and left flowers.
Memories of a 'bright and positive person'Jonna Jones of Lusby remembers her friend, Lauren Pitt, as someone who loved people and life.
"Her enthusiasm for people made me feel like I could do anything," Jones said. "Such a bright, positive person. We lost a bright light when she passed."
Pitt, who lived in St. Mary's County's Hollywood, was 27 when she was killed Sept. 3, 2015, while riding as a passenger on a motorcycle. The operator of the Harley Davidson, Conrado "Chico" Fabricante Jr., 55, of Broomes Island, also died in the crash at the Route 2/4 and Rousby Hall Road intersection in Lusby.
"This year it will be 10 years, that's hard to believe," Jones said.
Fabricante, the father of three, had worked at Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant for over 30 years. His obituary posted by Rausch Funeral Home said he was an avid motorcyclist and a member of Hells Angels, "who were his second family."
At the time of her death, Pitt was employed at Calvert Orthopedic of Southern Maryland as a radiology technician and part-time by MedStar St. Mary's Hospital.
According to her obituary, Pitt was a 2006 graduate of Leonardtown High, where she played clarinet in the school jazz band. Jones recalled Pitt was in the process of learning to play the mandolin in 2015.
The markers memorializing Pitt and Fabricante — two wooden crosses with their first names — are placed in front of the guardrail on southbound Route 2/4 near the Rousby Hall Road intersection.
Several months after the collision occurred, the Calvert County Sheriff's Office announced that the incident was nobody's fault and no blame would be placed nor charges filed.
Jones said she has never stopped to visit the roadside memorial but has visited Pitt's gravesite in Leonardtown.
"I have done things in her honor," Jones said.
One of the events Jones dedicated to her friend's memory was a half-marathon she trained for and ran in 2016.
"It helped me keep going," Jones said of the 13-mile dash and the inspiration of her late friend. "I finished it with a smile on my face."
'Unknown reasons'It was on a Monday morning, the first day of October 2018, that 24-year-old David Joseph Johnson of Ridge lost his life when his small sedan traveling south of Lexington Park went off Route 235, up a steep embankment, struck a tree and flipped over on its roof.
The Leonardtown High grad was employed as a welder at the time of his passing.
A release from the St. Mary's County Sheriff's Office stated that Johnson's vehicle went out of control "for unknown reasons," before it went off the road and subsequently crashed.
"There's only one person that knows, and that person can't tell us," then-Captain Steve Hall, the county's current sheriff, told The Enterprise the day after the fatality. "There's never any logical explanation."
An array of flowers surrounding a cross with the name "Joseph" in capital letters marks the location of the fatality on Three Notch Road just north of a local bus and car repair shop.
'A gifted swimmer'He was born in a Siberian city in July 1998 and eight months later was adopted by David and Kandia Spain, who brought him to their home in Huntingtown. Zachary David Igor "Zack" Spain attended Plum Point Elementary, Plum Point Middle and Huntingtown High, graduating in 2016.
While he played soccer during his elementary and middle school years, Zack Spain's true passion was swimming, which he did competitively starting at age 5.
"He was a gifted swimmer and swam club team, summer league and for his high school," Kandia Spain told Southern Maryland News. "He was a kind and caring brother, son and friend."
His plan was to study political science with the goal of working for an environmental protection group.
On Thanksgiving Day 2020 — Nov. 26 — Zack Spain was operating a vehicle on Wilson Road in Prince Frederick. He was the lone occupant of the car. According to the Calvert sheriff's office, the vehicle left the road and crashed into two utility poles. Zack Spain was declared dead at the scene. He was 22.
"I keep flowers all year round attached to the utility pole," Kandia Spain told Southern Maryland News.
Remembering 'Lil Bro'It's hard to spot, but somewhere in a sparsely wooded area near the Route 5 and Chingville Road intersection of St. Mary's County a small white cross that had been staked into the earth lays on the ground. Almost one year ago, a horrific, single-vehicle crash occurred there, injuring three — the adult female driver and two small children — and killing a male juvenile who had recently celebrated his 8th birthday.
Brysen McKinley Carter had been a football player for the Pax River Raiders team.
According to the St. Mary's sheriff's office, the three juvenile occupants, including Brysen, "were found to not be correctly restrained."
Brysen was taken to MedStar St. Mary's Hospital and was later pronounced dead.
The crash occurred on March 16, 2024, and more than seven months later the driver, Ashley Nicole Nolan, now 28, of Lexington Park, was served an 18-count indictment, which includes four felony charges for negligent manslaughter and homicide with a motor vehicle while impaired, according to court records. A circuit court jury trial is currently scheduled for early April.
A GoFundMe page in Brysen Carter's honor raised over $19,000 before organizers stopped accepting donations. The Pax River Raiders contributed $500 to the fund.
On a tribute page posted by Briscoe-Tonic Funeral Home, one of Brysen's friends wrote, "I miss you every day, Lil Bro." 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Former councilmember Engle leads way in creating Easton's new highway safety plan
author: Konner Metz
content:
Former councilmember Engle leads way in creating Easton's new highway safety plan

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 611
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Ron Engle has a robust resume of public service.The former National Highway Traffic Safety Administration senior manager and Virginia police officer developed an extensive portfolio in traffic policy and management over more than three decades.
Following retirement, Engle remained busy, serving on many local boards in Talbot County and winning a seat on the Easton Town Council in 2015.
So when Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey asked Engle in 2023 if he would give the town a hand in creating a Strategic Highway Safety Plan, it was a no-brainer.
"The chief grabbed me and said, 'I need help getting grants,'" Engle recalled. "And he said, 'And I know you know how to do it.'"
Though he lost his council seat two years ago, Engle has spearheaded the creation of a traffic safety plan for Easton during the last year.
Approved by the Town Council earlier this month, Easton's new Strategic Highway Safety Plan is expected to bring significant funding opportunities to the town for its transportation and safety efforts, town officials say.
It is 72 pages in length, detailing strategies and action plans for Easton to address vehicular, bicycle and pedestrian safety issues as the town grows. Not every city or town in the state has adopted a strategic plan aligning with the state's vision, Engle noted.
"My gut feeling is that with so few of these programs, we can do pretty well," he said.
The plan goes hand-in-hand with Maryland's Vision Zero law that was established in 2019, which aims to eliminate all vehicle-related deaths by 2030. Traditional approaches to highway safety assume crashes and injuries are inevitable, but Vision Zero lays out that traffic systems can accommodate for human error.
"What I mainly focused on was speeding, distracted driving, impaired driving, bicycling and pedestrians," Engle said, as well as sections dedicated to Route 50 safety and mature drivers, given Talbot County's older population.
In order to lay the groundwork, town leaders worked with Washington College's Geographic Information Systems Program to compile accident data dating back to 2018, culminating in the release of an interactive traffic dashboard.
While Easton doesn't have traffic fatalities often, the numbers depict problem areas in town where the most crashes occurred from 2018-2023, such as Dover Road and Aurora Street.
Engle said the data, combined with sleek and easy-to-read graphic designs and charts made by the town's communications specialist, Greg Mueller, helped the strategic plan come to life.
"It wasn't until I got the data," Engle said. "I would have never thought Dover Street had the most crashes. It just wouldn't occur to me."
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh, one of the plan's main contributors, said it all boils down to making Easton safer. Clear deadlines for goals and improvements will keep the town's progress timely, he said.
"It will hold us accountable," Van Emburgh said.
Lowrey says the Strategic Highway Safety Plan is just one step in Easton's efforts to better safety for residents using all modes of transportation.
"It's an important first step, but it's part of a bigger process that the mayor's undertaking to help us address Easton as it is right now and how it will be in the future," Lowrey said.
Engle, who says he's "fascinated" by public service, has been inspired not just by his traffic safety background, but by local organizations and residents, too.
It's part of the reason he's continued to dedicate hours upon hours of his time to creating a better and safer Easton.
"It's a big bite for the town, because there's a lot of things in here they need to (do that) they may not have the money or may not have the resources (for)," Engle said of the highway safety plan. "But everything in here is something we should do."

 CAMBRIDGE — A Cambridge man has been sentenced to incarceration after being found guilty of charges that stem from an incident with his infant in April 2023.On Feb. 21, Marcus Peak, 28, was sentenced to 28 years of incarceration, with all but 15 of those years suspended, in the Dorchester County Circuit Court. Peak was also sentenced to serve five years of probation with the condition that he not have any unsupervised contact with minors.
In December, Dorchester County Circuit Court Judge William Jones found Peak guilty of of first- and second-degree assault, first- and second-degree child abuse, neglect of a minor and reckless endangerment.
The charges against Peak stem from an incident on April 21, 2023, when Cambridge Police officers responded to assist Dorchester County Emergency Medical Services with an infant who was unconscious and not breathing. EMS treated the infant and transported her to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Cambridge. The baby was then transported to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore.
According to police, Peak told detectives he had just fed his daughter a bottle and placed her in a bassinet for a nap. He said the baby was asleep.
Peak said that when he returned to check on her later, he noticed the baby's head was tilted to the side with fluid coming from her nose and mouth. He said the baby's eyes were partially opened.
At that time, Peak denied any traumatic event that could have caused injury to his daughter.
Detectives were told Peak had lied and did not inform them the baby had fallen to the floor, striking her head. Peak allegedly then picked the baby up and shook her to wake her up, according to a report from the Cambridge Police Department.
During the trial in December, Dr. Eric Klotz, an emergency medicine physician who treated the child that day, said the child's injuries were consistent with a high mechanism of injury. He said it was one of the more severe head injuries he's seen in his career.
Dr. Joseph Scheller, a pediatric neurologist who was asked by Peak's defense to testify, said it is possible the child's injuries were caused by an accidental fall. He said short falls can sometimes cause serious injury.
According to Maryland court documents, Dorchester County Assistant Public Defender Michelle Moodispaw filed a notice to appeal the case on Tuesday.

title: Common sense degrees needed
author: Staff Writer
content:
Common sense degrees needed

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 391
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This past weekend, I was enjoying my morning tea when I got a curious phone call. The gentleman knew me by my nickname, and I quickly became a good listener. Trying to place the voice it took me a few minutes to realize who it was a long-time multigenerational family friend. Let's call him Mike. I would later reflect on what an honor it was for me.For the better part of an hour, he regaled me with stories of yesteryear (none, surprisingly, set in the famed bygone watering hole of that name), featuring my father, grandfather and great-grandfather. My eyes swelled as he began to bring the good old days back to life, first in black and white, then in color. Some stories I had had a taste of, but most were new to me. What gentlemen they were.
I share that story to preface this one. While enjoying the company of "The Thursday Brotherhood" the topic of today's social climate came up. All of our comments were true and valid in their own way; I can only imagine that each generation feels the same, that in any moment in history, there are good times and not-so-good times.
The conversation brought back memories of my great-grandfather Walter Wood; he was the chief of police for then little old Easton. He called it "my town," and used his platform to serve with understanding as only he could. One quality of old Walter I heard about more than a few times was his sensible approach to life. My dad called it his C.S. (common sense) degree.
As it goes, he would leave home after supper, head to the firehouse, and open the door to the locals who needed shelter for the night. Today, we call them homeless. He would lock the door and call it a night. In the morning, the routine played out in reverse. What a novel solution.
Today, we share the same challenges as our predecessors, updated for the 21st century. How we approach them and resolve them is up to us, let's call it perspective. Sometimes what is old is what's new again. Having a bit more compassion and understanding for our neighbors can't be all wrong. Just maybe if we all use our C.S. degrees a bit more, we can all wake up and go to sleep with a smile.
ROO WOOD
Wittman

 Delaware court documents released Tuesday shed new light on how a Kirk Middle School teacher allegedly spent months grooming one of his students by sending her sexual messages and fantasies through an online chat application.Ultimately, the inappropriate behavior expanded to school grounds, where David DiFilippo would spend time alone with the 13-year-old girl in his classroom, making sexual comments to her and, on one occasion, touching her legs, court records allege.
DiFilippo's actions "are clearly and reasonably indicative of an adult grooming and enticing a minor for the purpose of sexual contact and/or a sexual experience," Detective Marc Conway, of the Delaware State Police, wrote in court documents, adding that DiFilippo was trying to build up trust with the girl to "ultimately entice and arouse her sexually."
DiFilippo's alleged behavior took place between September 2023 and February 2024, when DiFilippo was 43 and 44 years old.
During that six-month period, DiFilippo and the girl chatted nearly every day over Discord, a messaging app. The messages were "flirtatious and sexual in nature," and DiFilippo suggested sexual acts with the girl, made comments about her body and clothing and referred to her as "babe" and "baby," court records show.
He sent her several stories detailing explicit sexual fantasies involving her engaging in sexual intercourse, masturbation and oral sex. He would then ask the girl "if the writings were good enough that she could picture them in her mind and if reading them made her feel a certain way," court documents allege.
One story involved a teacher and a student having sexual relations on a school bus during a field trip, and DiFilippo then told the girl he was planing a field trip and asked if she would like to sit with him on the bus, court records indicate.
DiFilippo would delete the messages after the girl read them, but she kept screenshots of the messages on her phone.
DiFilippo's behavior eventually extended into in-person encounters, and he would allow the girl to skip class to hang out with him alone in his classroom during his planning period when he did not have a class to teach. Other times, she would stay in his classroom after class ended and the other students left.
On one occasion, DiFilippo told the girl he liked her "milky white thighs" and said seeing them made him feel "like an animal ready to attack his prey," court documents allege. Another time, he suggested they go into a closet to kiss, but the girl refused. On a different day, the girl brought DiFilippo an assortment of snack food and asked him which he liked best, to which he replied he liked "the snack in the dress," presumably referring to her.
Court records describe one incident in which DiFilippo's behavior turned physical. The girl was sitting on a counter near his desk, and DiFilippo allegedly knelt down and rubbed her legs. The girl told him to stop, which he did.
It's not clear why DiFilippo's behavior ended in February 2024. Court records indicate that the girl told her therapist about it in August 2024, sparking a police investigation.
The girl provided police with screenshots of DiFilippo's Discord messages, and detectives later subpoenaed Discord for a transcript of the messages sent from his account. Investigators interviewed the girl with help from the Child Advocacy Center in Wilmington.
DiFilippo turned himself in to police in February after the months-long investigation.
He was charged with sexual solicitation of a child, enticement for purposes of sexual conduct, dangerous crime against a minor, promoting sexual solicitation of a child, providing obscenity material to a child, sexual abuse of a child by a person of trust and offensive touching. He was released after posting $65,500 secured bond.
Police asked anyone with information or who may be a victim to contact Conway at 302-365-8411.
According to a brief biography posted on Kirk's website, DiFilippo taught in the gifted and talented program and has been a teacher for approximately 15 years. He wrote that his favorite part of the job is "forming strong bonds and relationships with my students."
A spokesperson for the Christina School District did not respond to a request for comment.
