title: Picnic honors treatment center's past, looks to future
content:
Picnic honors treatment center's past, looks to future

 September 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 1157
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Earlier this month, after the 2023 5K Color Fun Run/WalK for Kent Goes Purple, The A.F. Whitsitt Center celebrated its 40th year with an alumni picnic.Hosted at the center, honored guests, professionals in the community and residents showed up, ate a meal together and shared memories.Also in attendance was Maryland Delegate Jay Jacobs, R-36, and a resident of Kent County. He presented a Maryland General Assembly official citation to the Whitsitt Center for their 40 years service.The Kent County House Delegation recognized the establishment, for providing in-patient residential substance treatment services for the Eastern Shore and the State of Maryland.Jacobs reminisced, saying back in 2009, when the state was thinking about closing the center, and he was mayor of Rock Hall, they held a 24 hour vigil to prevent its closing.Fortunately, the center did not shut down, he added, and since then, many people have been positively impacted.Jacobs expressed hope, looking toward the future. "I think we'll see some things take place soon as far as infrastructure goes. The building's going to be restored to its real glory and be a real piece of a thread of the fabric of this county."As folks finished their meals, Director of the Kent County Health Department's A.F. Whitsitt Center, Carla Thorpe, talked about the rich history of the center, handing out awards.She produced a plaque dedicated to the staff who used to work there and had now moved on.Thorpe then recognized the first patient at the Whitsitt Center, the late Bill Walls, bringing his family up to applause.Thorpe pointed out, Walls was one of the first to do harm reduction, keeping sufferers of alcohol addiction from seizures or tremors before they got to treatment.In honor of him, they established the Whitsitt Wonder Impact award."It's for somebody who has been through the program and has given back to those who have been in recovery," Thorpe said.To her left, stood a painting of the founder, the late, A.F. Whitsitt When individuals come through the doors, they will see his picture on the wall, she announced. Thorpe asked his grandchildren, Clay Mitchell and Chris Mitchell, to say some words remembering their grandfather and present an award in his honor."Your grandfather was an advocate. His big thing was to work with those suffering from alcoholism," Thorpe said.His grandchildren had memories to share, speaking of his dedication."This thing wasn't popular when he was the health officer in the 40's, 50's or 60's, but he did it anyway because it was the right thing to do," Chris Mitchell said about his grandfather.Clayton Anderson Mitchell added, "I feel like my grandfather never really died because the mission of this organization lives on through the great staff who work here."Thorpe moved on to recognize a friend of recovery in the founder's honor; someone who represented A.F. Whitsitt's values, presenting Executive Director of Mid Shore Behavioral Health, Katie Dilley, the A.F. Whitsitt award.Thorpe said, "She's working with us to see what other supports she can bring to the region. For me, she's been a mentor, and when it comes down to it, it's about the people we serve, and keeping the services we need here on the shore."Mid Shore Behavioral Health covers five counties, Kent, Queen Anne's, Talbot, Caroline and Dorchester.Dilley said, "It's a gift to be in this job and work hard for you. The hope and drive of everybody in this room is what it's all about. We're here to make sure we're on the right path, and we do not lose the resources that bring life, and strength back into our community."To cap the picnic off, there was a rousing testimony by Shiloh Blackburn, accompanied by his wife, Marian.Blackburn's one of the 25,000 the center's helped over the years, since 1983.Blackburn described his life in great detail, from addiction to recovery, and the men who helped him make that change.He told the audience he came to the center with a trash bag of his belongings. He said he was a manipulator, a chameleon, justifying his addictions, blaming his childhood.But at the center, he was confronted with people serious about beating addictions.In Church Hill, he said he got his first 24-hour chip, noting the late Bill Walls was there.But it was not a full recovery. He said that from 12-years-old onward there was a romance to using drugs and alcohol. It was that romance that he was addicted to.After he had been clean for a while, and things were going right again, he took back his will.He found himself back at the Whitsitt Center, where lead counsellor, the late Katrina Tolliver, spoke "some great sense" into him. Her advice to him was to keep his mouth shut."I was a guy who knew a lot," he said, indicating he was not yielding enough to learn.But something resounded within him this time. He began to listen and learn.Then another life changing event with his sponsor.He was sandpaper, Blackburn noted, and did not just simply say, call me everyday. The sponsor challenged him. First of his advice was to pray every night, a simple prayer, to stay sober one day at a time."For the first day in my life it was man in the mirror time," he said.One day, after months and months of praying, he said, that prayer was answered. It was immediate, not desiring."As I was walking to this job, a calmness that I never felt before, and the compulsion to want to drink and get high was totally gone. At that moment I knew it was God who took that from me because that's the only person I was asking every day."He tried to tell his roofer coworkers about it, but they didn't listen.It didn't matter however.He started becoming "childlike," meaning willing to learn.He described working on himself like a "surgery of the spirit."His sponsor told him it's time to forgive his mother. Not by his words, but with his actions. So he started doing chores for her, asking her what he could do, being a continual presence in her life.One day, he said, she asked him if she could attend a meeting. His mother, since last March, is now 15 years sober, he said.Blackburn now has a life he could have never dreamed. He's married his best friend, and he wanted to thank the men in his life who made him.Health Officer Bill Webb, who sees miracles like Blackburn's at the meetings, said the Whitsitt Center is available for anybody who needs the help. They have 44 beds, 12 beds of which are crisis beds, for opioids and stimulants. They also accept health insurance and offer adult care.

 Maryland SNAP-Ed, a program of University of Maryland Extension in partnership with Maryland Department of Human Services, has written a new original storybook promoting family physical activity.More than 125,000 free copies of the book will be distributed to low-income sites across the state throughout the summer."The Secret to an Extraordinary Day" follows the story of an ordinary family that takes an unexpected adventure, prompted by a series of mysterious notes. "Among the many lasting effects of the pandemic, sedentary behaviors increased due to increased reliance on technology for school and education. While SNAP-Ed's interest in physical activity is as a tool for obesity and chronic disease prevention, our partners also recognize the power of movement to address critical concerns around social-emotional health." Physical activity is a current focus area for SNAP-Ed, due to well-documented impacts on chronic disease prevention. Supporting youth in developing a lifelong relationship with physical activity also benefits overall well-being.Books are being distributed to partnering schools, early childhood sites, out of school programs, Maryland WIC offices, SNAP Outreach community partners, low-income 4-H youth programs, and summer meals sites, allowing SNAP-Ed to deliver health promotion messages while supporting family literacy and summer learning.For more information or to read the book, go to https://extension.umd.edu/active-fun.

title: New cardiac monitors improve emergency aid
author: Will Bontrager
content:
New cardiac monitors improve emergency aid

 October 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 987
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WORTON - In an emergency sit uation, there's no time for equipment to go down. The efficiency of equipment is often the difference between life and death. Even two-seconds difference, Logan Quinn, chief of Emergency Medical Services for Kent County said, are precious to a patient' survivability.Quinn's been researching trends in the medical field, and pre-charging heart monitor machines before administering a rhythm check on a patient for example, is just one of the ways he found is more effective.The new cardiac monitor and defibrillators his staff now possess wil help with that, he added.Seven of them, were delivered this August, from Zoll, replacing the outdated models from their old company, Physio-Control.His crew of 14 paramedics and 12 EMT's, are now better equipped with these Zoll monitors. Each substation in Rock Hall and Galena, the county ambulance vehicle, the primary paramedic unit, and his own vehicle, now have them, he pointed out.Quinn's impressed by these machines, stating that they are top-of-the-line, which will lead to better training practices.Features, exclusive to the Zoll monitors, lend what Quinn calls, "see-through CPR" capabilities. He explained, when a person's in cardiac arrest, they place a CPR feedback puck on the center of the chest, then another on the side. When connected, and compressions are being given, that patient's vital information appears on the monitor's screen.The machine also informs the person administering the compressions. "The monitor shows how deep you compress, how quickly, and really coaches the clinicians," he said.On the monitor's screen, Quinn noted, appears the rhythm of the CPR, the ups and downs, and even reports any changes during defibrillation.Quinn remarked there is also this kind of feedback provided via the bag valve mask sensor, which is connected to the monitor's computer. When they put an airway in a patient, Quinn said, there's a sensor attached to the airway that feeds information back to the monitor. Because of the high cost, they don't carry automatic ventilators, Quinn noted, but the monitor gives them closer control over ventilation required, allowing emerstion required, allowing emergency personnel to set the volume of air they need to administer.From there, the machine tells how many breaths-per-minute, how much volume is being given, and amazingly coaches when to squeeze the bag, with a flashing countdown sequence in the lower left-hand corner.Although they're still using the bags manually to ventilate patients, Quinn said, this helps tremendously, especially because each person's lung capacity's different.The monitors also assist providers treating traumatic brain injuries, provid-ing a trend of the patient's immediate vital signs. Quinn, said it reads how much oxygen is in the patient's blood, how much CO2 they're putting out, reports the blood pressure every five minutes, and takes little readings placing them on the graph, where they can confirm the patient's blood pressure is at a safe level.Quinn received these new monitors after going to the Kent County Commissioners with his request to change the previous contract with Physio-Control to Zoll.During the meeting in July, Quinn provided them a less than stellar review of the previous monitors. Side-by-side with Pete Landon, director of Emergency Services, Quinn gave the commissioners a glimpse of his frustrations with the older machines and his plan to replace them.Quinn said, since he took over as Chief in February, he had ordered two monitors, quickly realizing the shortage was a problem. He then used grant money provided by Maryland Emergency Services, and ordered another one, budgeted for FY24, but lamented that the company he had a contract with was inconsistent with their deliveries.Additionally, Physio-Control had other problems, Quinn added. They didn't upgrade their equipment for some time. He said if something broke inside of the machines, internally, like a chip or a motherboard issue, it didn't get repaired.He said they would be provided loaners, but the problem with those were they were different models - often not compatible with the ones they had.So Quinn, wanting to fix his budget, tired of the inconsistency, sought information from the competitors of these monitors, talking to the Zoll sales representative.He told the commissioners he definitely found something better.All new equipment.A package deal."They'll give us six new monitors up front then put us in a five-year payment plan, replacing all the monitors in our fleet," Quinn said.And, he added, no indeterminate date of delivery either.The contract with Zoll is an annual payment of $59,453 that runs from 2024 through 2028. And it's money well spent.Landon lauded Quinn's efforts, "What he's come up with is a plan that not only will save money for the county in the long run, but also brings together the training and maintenance of the equipment while also being able to replace it in an accelerated fashion."Commissioner John Price saw it was imperative to move with speed in order to get the new contract signed and made a motion to approve. It was an unanimous decision in the yes column.From the commissioner's approval, to signing the contract, and getting the monitors was less than a month.Quinn, who has been with the Kent County Emergency services for nine years, starting out as a dispatcher, sees big possibilities ahead for the department he's now in charge of, at only 30 years of age."I'm very passionate about this system. It has a lot of potential. We're one of the smallest agencies on the Eastern Shore. That can be good or bad, but it gives us the opportunity to work together."He acknowledged the new machines, especially intricate ones, like Zoll, are an adjustment, but commended his crew dealing with the transition training."I'm proud of my staff. Change is hard, but they've been showing they're really committed to not only me, but supporting us as an agency to get better. This was just the first step."

title: Bleach has uses beyond laundry
content:
Bleach has uses beyond laundry

 October 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 281
 Words 

 Read News Document

 That bottle of liquid chlorine bleach sitting in your laundry room has all sorts of uses that have nothing to do with laundry. It can help keep your flowers looking fresh, purify water in emergencies and even lend a hand when you're cleaning up after a disaster.DETER MOSQUITOESWhile bleach may not be the first thing that comes to mind when dealing with mosquitoes, it can effectively deter them from reproducing in stagnant water. Add a small amount of bleach to a birdbath to eliminate mosquito larvae and safe-guard the water's quality. Just 1 tablespoon of bleach can protect up to 50 gallons of water, so use it sparingly. Avoid introducing bleach into natural water bodies and ponds to protect their delicate ecosystems.CUTTING BOARDMaintain a germ-free cut-ting board by rinsing it with a bleach-water mixture (1 teaspoon per gallon) and let-ting it air dry.DEODORIZERTo banish odors and germs from your trash bin, give it a rinse with a bleach-water combination.TOY SANITATION Children's toys can harbor germs. Combat this by soaking toys in a solution of 1 tablespoon of liquid bleach per gallon of water, followed by thorough rinsing.SNEAKER REVIVALBring the whiteness back to your white sneakers with a gentle scrub using a light bleach-water solution.PATIO FURNITURE Revitalize outdoor furniture by scrubbing it with a bleach-water mix (1/3 cup of bleach to 1 gallon of water). Ensure you do this away from plants you wish to protect.Chlorine bleach is an affordable and versatile cleaning agent. Use it wisely and safely to enjoy its bene-fits without any drawbacks. Your home and wallet will thank you.Mary Hunt is the founder of EverydayCheapskate.com, a frugal living blog, and the author of the book "Debt-Proof Living."

title: State sees surge in COVID-19 cases
author: Shifra Dayak; Capital News Service
content:
State sees surge in COVID-19 cases

 October 5, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Shifra Dayak; Capital News Service | Page: 14 | Section: News 
 
 840
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON - Maryland is seeing a surge in COVID cases that mirrors national trends - and experts say it might continue as the state heads into respiratory disease season and as some residents take lax approaches to preventive measures.The rate of reported COVID-19 cases in the state saw an uptick during September. Sept. 11 saw the highest recorded case rate in Maryland, with 6.64 cases per 100,000 people. Case rates have seen a gradual decline since then, but are still sitting above rates during the summer months.Before last month, the last time that case rates in the state were above five cases per 100,000 residents was in March.Data from the Maryland Department of Health shows that in September 2022, reported COVID-19 infection rates ranged from 12.08 to 17.06 cases per 100,000 residents. Case rates last month ranged from 4.54 to 6.64 cases per 100,000 people, meaning this year's numbers look better than last year's.But Kate McPhaul, an associate research professor in the University of Maryland's School of Public Health, said the prevalence of testing is lower now than earlier in the pandemic.Amid the September surge, President Joe Biden's administration announced last week that it is appropriating $600 million to companies that produce COVID-19 testing kits to boost the number of tests manufactured in the nation.The same day, the administration announced that all households in the country can request four free rapid-testing kits through covid. gov/tests. Free COVID-19 tests previously were available via mail from January 2022 until June of this year.McPhaul warned that despite a resurgence in testing options, current case numbers may not be entirely accurate because fewer people overall are testing and milder cases have likely not all been reported to the state.However, there's a general indication that there has been a surge in recent weeks, including through anecdotal evidence, she said.This fall surge indicates that COVID-19 could be showing signs of spiking seasonally, McPhaul said, but since it is still a relatively new virus, predicting its behavior is difficult.In line with the surge in cases, hospitalizations and deaths in Maryland have also increased between the start of summer and now, state health department data shows.These upticks will likely continue in the coming months, according to Kristen Coleman, an assistant professor in the University of Maryland's public health school.Coleman said that reinstating preventive measures like masking and air filtration in public spaces, classrooms and more could help keep the surge at bay."I expect that (cases) will continue to climb," Coleman said. "This fall, because of the uptick, I do see more people masking, but certainly not as many as in the beginning of the pandemic." A poll by the business intelligence company Morning Consult in May showed that only 24% of all United States adults were "very" concerned about COVID-19. It's a number that's steadily declined since the start of the pandemic. In April 2020, comparatively, 65% of adults told Morning Consult they were "very concerned." For McPhaul, this decline in concern is evident through a drop in people masking and seeking out the most recent booster dose of the COVID-19 vaccine."People want the pandemic to be over with and to me right now, it seems like there's a bit of a disconnect with the COVID rate going up. A lot of the behaviors that mitigate getting sick kind of don't seem to be happening," McPhaul said.The U.S. Food and Drug Administration in mid-September approved an updated COVID-19 booster vaccine that targets newer variants that have been fueling a rise in cases. But this booster has not been widely administered, McPhaul said.Only 24% of Maryland's population has received an updated bivalent booster vaccine at all, according to the Centers for Disease Control. Additional tracking shows that few residents in the region and nationally have received the most recent booster dose.In addition to the case surge in Maryland, Virginia and the District of Columbia also are seeing similar trends and similar attitudes when it comes to masking and vaccines.Between the beginning of August and mid-September, Virginia's Department of Health recorded an uptick in reported COVID-19 cases and hospitalizations for COVID-19. In all except four of Virginia's 139 counties and independent cities, fewer than 25% of residents have received all the CDC-recommended doses of the COVID-19 vaccine, according to data from the department.Numbers across the past month in Washington, D.C., align with national trends.The rate of weekly reported cases per 100,000 city residents saw a steady uptick from 11.7 cases on Aug. 19 to 33.6 cases on Sept. 9, according to DC Health.As cases may continue rising in the region, McPhaul encouraged area residents to think about preventive measures in their communities, including masking around high-risk individuals and getting vaccinated against respiratory diseases like COVID-19, RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) and the flu."I think people just need to get that person in their head that they're protecting," she said. "All of that stuff that we were promoting during the pandemic can continue to be utilized in the prevention of all of the airborne infections."

title: Students learn to save a life - St. Michaels Y training session prepares students for emergencies
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Students learn to save a life - St. Michaels Y training session prepares students for emergencies

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News

 ST. MICHAELS-Nine middle school students gained lifesaving skills Wednesday afternoon, thanks to a partnership between the St. Michaels Community Center, St. Michaels Youth & Law Enforcement (SMYLE), Talbot County Emergency Services and the Perkins Family YMCA.Talbot County paramedic Rachael Cox led the afterschool CPR and AED training class at the Y, guiding the young students through the steps to take in an emergency.The class was free for all who participated, thanks to a $200 donation from SMYLE, the St. Michaels Police Department's youth program, that covered certification costs for the students. The St. Michaels Community Center assisted in facilitating the program.Cox began her class by showing how to check if a person is responsive, then asked the students what they thought the next step was.The answer? Calling 911 and staying on the line with the dispatcher.The next step, as Cox demonstrated, is checking if the person is breathing. If not, it's time to start chest compressions, she said.Each student practiced chest compressions on practice manikins and learned how to use an AED before moving on to learning how to do CPR on infants.As a community risk reduction paramedic and CPR and AED coordinator for Talbot County, Cox loves teaching. She likes being able to introduce preteens and teenagers to CPR, first aid and AED skills to prepare them for any emergency situation, even if they're alone without adults present."I feel like we call EMS, police, fire and dispatch first responders, but I really don't believe we're first responders because we're not there when the emergency happens-the community is," she said. "And that's why I feel these types of classes are so important."Amethyst Monroe, a Perkins Family YMCA staffer who supervised Wednesday's class, is continuing to coordinate other developing middle school programs. She's planning another CPR and AED session soon.Monroe's aim is to make sure future programs are lowcost and provide the area's youth with more life skills.Anyone who wishes to support future after-school programming at the Perkins Family YMCA can donate to the center's annual campaign or reach out to Tracy Eutsler, the Y's executive director, at teutsler@ymcachesapeake.org.Those who are interested in scheduling CPR and AED classes can contact Rachael Cox at rcox@talbotdes.org.

title: Unwelcome lecture from a neighbor
content:
Unwelcome lecture from a neighbor

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 22 | Section: News 
 
 272
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DEAR HARRIETTE: I'm 28, and I live in a small apartment complex where everyone knows each other. My neighbor, a gentleman in his 50s, saw me smoking a cigarette the other day and decided to take it upon himself to lecture me on the dangers of smoking.Although I appreciated his concern, his lecture was unwelcome. I intend to quit smoking at some point, but I don't need my neighbor to intervene. I fear that the next time I bump into him, he will give me another lecture. What can I do to make him understand that his unsolicited advice is not helping? I'm a grown adult, and I don't need lectures. - Good IntentionsDEAR GOOD INTENTIONS: As you know, your neighbor expressed his concerns out of genuine care for you. Remember that when you speak to him. It is your right to do whatever you want with your life and your body. Provided that the cigarette smoke is not contaminating your neighbors' air, you should be able to smoke in peace.That said, it is likely that this man will either say something or scowl at you the next time he sees a cigarette in your hand. Can you say something?Yes, but be careful. You can thank him for his concern, but put up a guardrail. Tell him you know what you are doing. When you decide to quit, you will. Politely ask him to refrain from giving you advice on this topic in the future.Harriette Cole is a lifestylist andfounder of Dream Leapers, an initiative to help people access and activate their dreams. title: Critical Condition? - Nursing home industry, group of senators push against Biden's bid to require more nursing staff at facilities
author: Mike Sunnucks; Apg Newspapers
content:
Critical Condition? - Nursing home industry, group of senators push against Biden's bid to require more nursing staff at facilities

 October 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks; Apg Newspapers | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1488
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The nursing home and assisted living industries - along with a number of federal lawmakers - are pushing against a Biden administration plan to require more staffing at facilities including having registered nurses be on-site 24/7.Last month, the White House unveiled details of new rules and regulations on nursing homes - which receive $100 billion annually in Medicare, Medicaid and other U.S. government payments.A centerpiece of the push (and industry opposition to it) centers on federally mandated staffing of registered nurses and nursing aides."If finalized, the proposal would require every facility to have a registered nurse on site 24/7, to have a certain minimum number of registered nurses and nurse aides to help provide routine care, and to staff according to resident needs based on a robust assessment of the facility's residents," the Biden administration said in its September proposal.The rule would apply to approximately 15,000 nursing homes with 1.2 million patients/residents nationwide.The Democratic administration is also promising increased oversight of long-term care facilities spending of Medicare and Medicaid as well as "inappropriate prescribing of antipsychotic medications." The White House is also concerned about private equity firms buying up nursing homes and assisted living centers and subsequent impacts on care.The push would also have facilities provide at least 33 minutes of care to patients from a registered nurse and just under 2.5 hours of care from nursing aides each day."This means a nursing home would need roughly ten nurse aides per each 8-hour shift in a facility with 100 residents," according to the White House briefing report.The rules would not usurp states with even higher personnel requirements.According to an analysis by the Kaiser Family Foundation, more than 80% of facilities would have hire additional nursing staff if the rules go in place - including 90% of for-profit nursing homes and 60% of nonprofit and government-run centers.The Biden administration said understaffed facilities increase the likelihoods of patient injuries and deaths as well as substandard care. "When nursing homes stretch workers too thin, residents may be forced to go without basic necessities like hot meals and regular baths, or even forced to lie in wet and soiled diapers for hours," the White House said in a Sept. 1 briefing paper on the new regulations.To help address the staffing needs, CMS says it is launching a $75 million effort to help train and recruit new nurses including with scholarships and tuition reimbursements.Industry opposition Long-term and congregate care industry groups contend the staffing rules are burdensome and will put facilities out of business - especially in rural and already underserved areas - as their sector faces continued and post-pandemic labor shortages.The American Health Care Association and National Center for Assisted Living say the Biden personnel rules will require nursing homes to hire more than 102,100 new full-time workers (including more than 22,000 registered nurses and more than 80,000 nurses aides).The groups say it will cost the nursing home industry $6.8 billion annually - challenging a $4 billion per year estimate from the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.If nursing homes are required to reduce their numbers of beds available because of staffing rules and shortages that could impact more than 280,000 congregate care residents, many of them on Medicaid, the industry associations argue."If this rule is finalized without the financial support that nursing homes will need to hire these additional workers, hundreds of thousands of seniors will be at risk of losing the care they need," said Cory Rutledge, chief assurance officer at Clifton Larson Allen LLP (CLA), a Minneapolis-based professional service and accounting firm that analyzed the federal proposals for the two industry groups.Political pushback The industry - and its push against the Biden efforts - has some influential friends in Washington.Twenty-eight U.S. senators wrote U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service Administrator Chiquita Brooks-La-Sure Sept. 29 voicing concerns about President Joe Biden's push for new staffing requirements on nursing homes and assisted living centers.The 23 Republican, 3 Democratic and 2 independent senators worried about the "staffing mandates" include Montana Sens. Jon Tester, a Democrat, and Steve Daines, a Republican, as well as U.S. Sens.Marco Rubio, R-Florida, James Lankford, R-Oklahoma.Kyrsten Sinema, I-Arizona, Jean Shaheen, D-New Hampshire, Marsha Blackburn, R-Tennessee, Jim Risch R-Idaho, Thom Tillis, R-NC, and Joe Manchin, D-West Virginia."In many parts of the country, America's longterm care facilities are facing severe workforce shortage issues that are harming access to critical care for our nation's seniors. With this in mind, we are deeply concerned that now is the worst possible time for the United States to establish the nation's first federal staffing mandate for long term care facilities," the senators said in their correspondence."We believe the rule as proposed is overly burdensome and will result in additional closures and decreased access to care." The senators want President Joe Biden to rescind the rule and find "alternative approaches" to labor challenges.Tester previously voiced opposition to the Biden nursing home efforts in September and earlier this year and wants different staffing rules for rural areas."I fear a one-size-fitsall staffing mandate would undermine access to care for patients, particularly in rural communities.Instead, I urge you to work with Congress and rural stakeholders on tailored solutions that address the severe workforce challenges in underserved areas," Tester said in a June letter to the Biden administration. "A blanket staffing mandate would not account for individual facilities' operational capabilities and staffing circumstances." His office cites Montana Health Care Association numbers showing 11 nursing homes have closed statewide since 2021 (including the loss of 850 long-term care bids last year.)Since 2021, Montana has seen the closure of 11 nursing homes, and in 2022 alone, the state lost more than 850 nursing home beds, according to the Montana Health Care Association.U.S. Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers, a Washington state Republican who chairs the House Energy and Commerce Committee, also worries the new mandate will put rural nursing homes in a bind."The rule will put nursing homes - particularly in rural areas - in an impossible dilemma as they grapple with how to manage current occupancy levels with the insufficient workforce available to meet the requirements. This rule fails to adequately balance the needs of seniors and nursing home staff in the face of the current staffing shortage gripping our nation."Nursing homes would have three years in rural areas to abide by the 24/7 RN mandate and five years to get in line with all the new rules. Urban and suburban facilities would have two years to have RN's on staff around-theclock and three years for all the other mandates, according to CMS.Labor unions support There are some hardship provisions for facilities with chronic staffing shortages in underserved areas. Comments on the new rules are being accepted until Nov. 6.In many states, a distinct minority nursing homes are currently in compliance with the proposed staffing levels.Those lower percentages include California (21%), Florida (20%), Texas (4%), New York (14%), Idaho (31%), Maryland (17%), Delaware (16%), Wyoming (38%), Montana (38%), Wisconsin (37%), Georgia (6%) and Louisiana (1%), according to KFF.States with higher current compliance levels based on the proposed nursing staff regulations include Oregon (63%), Washington (49%), North Dakota (76%), Maine (75%), Vermont (75%) and Alaska (100%). Those states have staffing rules above and beyond the current federal benchmarks.Part of Biden's push stems from the coronavirus pandemic which saw more than 200,000 nursing home residents and staff deaths attributed to the virus - approximately one-fifth of all deaths attributed to the pandemic nationally.Nursing homes already report labor struggles with 86% reporting staffing shortages and 96% struggling to hire staff, according to AHCA. That includes nursing aides who sometimes make at or barely above state minimum wage levels with pay at times a kin to service and retail workers.While some patient advocates wanted Biden to go even farther with new requirements, labor unions representing nursing home workers support the new federal push."Our country's long term care system is in the midst of a catastrophic crisis, and nursing home workers and residents have suffered unspeakable consequences. In the absence of a federal staffing standard, nursing home workers have endured complete physical, mental and emotional exhaustion due to understaffed shifts and unsafe working conditions, and nursing home residents have been robbed of the quality care and quality of life they deserve,' said SEIU International President Mary Kay Henry after the rule's release last month.AFLCIO President Liz Shuler also backs Biden's push to require more transparency related to nursing home ownership, finances and use of Medicare and Medicaid funds."Workers and the families of residents have been sounding the alarm for decades about the need for a minimum national staffing standard in nursing homes, and we commend the Biden-Harris administration for answering the call."

title: It's about community - Chesapeake Bay Walk to Defeat ALS set for Oct. 22 in Centreville
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
It's about community - Chesapeake Bay Walk to Defeat ALS set for Oct. 22 in Centreville

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 892
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE - The Chesapeake Bay Walk to Defeat ALS is on track to reach its $35,000 goal on Sunday, Oct. 22, and organizers are hoping last minute walkers and supporters will join the fight.Walkers will sign in at 9 a.m. at Route 18 Park in Centreville. Even those who wake up and decide to participate that day can get in on the action and register at the walk.When Pam Clark Edwards of Centreville, was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), in February 2021, her family and friends not only rallied around her, they lost no time launching the effort to raise funds for the ALS Association.Edwards' daughters, Meredith Kulbacki of Centreville and Morgan Edwards of Winter Garden, Florida, spearheaded the Oct. 2022 Walk that rallied some 140 people who walked, ran and wheeled to raise over $30,000.Their team, Pam's Praying Pineapples, will be joined by 10 additional teams this year.As of the beginning of October, the local walk had raised over 80% of its goal."That's pretty amazing," Kulbacki said. "I think we can definitely get close to that, if not reach it by the walk." The community has reached out to help. Other fundraising in the form of raffles and a 50/50 drawing will be held, and about 40 items were donated by local businesses.For example, "we have a foursome golf outing at Queenstown Harbor, an official NFLfootball signed by Justin Tucker of the Baltimore Ravens, a gift basket from Draper Brothers liquor store, cosmetic gift bags, jewelry and various services," Meredith said.Fun activities include pumpkin decorating for kids.The ALS chapter from D.C., Maryland and Virginia will be sending helpers to be stationed at tables, so people can find out more information about ALS itself, and maybe about how they can help, Kulbacki said."If they have become a caretaker to someone with ALS," she said. "There will be workers there to help them through that." Information will be available for people who have been diagnosed with ALS.In fact, some members of Edwards' care team at Johns Hopkins will be attending the walk Ebb Tide Tent & Party Rentals in Queenstown donated a large tent, while Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation donated the use of the park.Community support has been "just amazing," Edwards said."Having the support of the community helps us as a family deal with all of this," she said.The Clark family has deep roots in the county. Pam and her husband, Fred, and Kulbacki and her family live on the family farm just down the road from the park where the walk will be held.Pam is a retired teacher in Queen Anne's County Public Schools.Pam's mother, June, and her brother Jeff have canvassed local business owners, who are supporting their longtime neighbors.Edwards' longtime friends and colleagues are part of the small committee helping her daughters. Connie Dean, Barb Thompson and Bobbie King have rallied around the Edwards family to help out where they can to help organize the walk.Kulbacki, who was raised in Centreville, spent eight years in York, Pennsylvania, and recently moved back. "It means everything to me. It means family," she said.During the COVID pandemic, she and her family, which includes her husband and two children, decided to move back home "on a whim." "We felt so alone with just no family and (few) friends there," she said. "We had no idea that this would happen.We say it was almost like God told us. He helped us through this, and it was almost a blessing in disguise that we moved home, so that we could help my mom and my dad and my family through this." "So not only to be here with them, and then also to have so much support from everybody in the community and all of our friends and family - it's just amazing and we're so thankful for that," Mer said.Kulbacki knew about the ALS Association's Walk to Defeat ALS through a sad coincidence. The mother of a close friend in Pennsylvania died from ALS about a year before the Kulbackis moved to Maryland, and Kulbacki had participated in a Pennsylvania Walk in memory of Becky Miller's mom."I didn't know that it would affect me so deeply a year later, so it's been amazing to still be friends with her and have support from her because she knows what I'm going through," Mer said."You never know when ALS may affect a friend or family member," Edwards said. "It is becoming, I think, more prevalent. I know five people who have passed away from it, not because I have been in this situation - these are people who have been in my life." "It's a disease that they really do not have a treatment or cure for yet, and we just need to put money into the resources for help for these families, as well as to provide money for research," she said.To register online for the Oct. 22 Walk, visit Walkto-DefeatALS.org.For more information about the ALS Association, donating your time or resources and supporting the Walk to Defeat ALS Chesapeake Bay, visit als.org or contact coordinator Tara Huang at tara.huang@als.org.

title: Husband lacking concern on health
author: Harriette Cole
content:
Husband lacking concern on health

 October 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Harriette Cole | Page: 22 | Section: Advice 
 
 320
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DEAR HARRIETTE: I recently had a physical that included a range of blood work. Some of the tests came back abnormal, and now I have to go back for more blood work.This is so scary to me. I want to talk to someone about it, but whenever I tell my husband about my health concerns, he doesn't listen. Instead, he immediately starts lecturing me about what I should do to improve my health. That is not what I need right now.I need support, someone to hold my hand and help me have the courage and strength to go through this process. - Need Support DEAR NEED SUPPORT: Now is not the time for you to be worrying about hurting your husband's feelings. This is your life and your health. Whatever you need to do to walk through this moment and get the most out of it is what you should be concentrating on. It is perfectly fine for you to ask a friend or your sister to go with you to your doctor's appointments or to talk through the results and recommendations after your visits.It can be helpful to have an advocate to stay apprised of what you discover. That person may also think of questions that you may have missed. It's one thing to get a diagnosis and another to figure out a plan of action for improving your health.Invite the person you think will be most helpful to you.Be sure to get their full agreement.When the time is right, you can inform your husband of what is going on and how you are tackling your health issues - if you so choose.What's most important is that you address your problems and do your part to get healthy.Harriette Cole is a lifestylist and founder of Dreamleapers, an initiative to help people access and activate their dreams. title: UM Shore Regional Health celebrates 'health care heroes' - Luncheons, unveiled murals recognize health care workers' efforts during CO VID-19 pandemic
author: Contributed
content:
UM Shore Regional Health celebrates 'health care heroes' - Luncheons, unveiled murals recognize health care workers' efforts during CO VID-19 pandemic

 October 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 628
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - UM Shore Regional Health's Senior Leadership team recently hosted post-COVID luncheons for team members in each of the five counties UM SRH serves - Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Talbot and Queen Anne's - to celebrate the World Health Organization declaring an end to the COVID-19 public health emergency earlier this year and to honor all team members who served during the pandemic as "caregivers." The luncheons also served as a remembrance for those team members who gave the ultimate sacrifice during the pandemic and lost their lives, Calvin Molock, Jr. and Bronte Johnson.Family members of both Molock and Johnson attended the luncheon in Easton. Plaques honoring Molock and Johnson will be placed at UM Shore Medical Centers at Cambridge, Chestertown and Easton, as well as UM Shore Medical Pavilions at Denton and Queenstown."COVID made us here at Shore, and health care teams and community members everywhere, realize very quickly how nimble and course-corrective we had to be as new information on COVID came to light," said William Huffner, MD, Chief Medical Officer and Senior Vice President, Medical Affairs, UM SRH."There were a lot of unsung heroes during COVID, but especially infection prevention teams everywhere, who helped us address the changes as they came.We all are just so appreciative of everyone who stepped up to help our caregivers and communities during this challenging time and these luncheons are just a small token of our appreciation for our team's dedication." Artwork honoring health care heroes was unveiled during the post-COVID luncheons in Cambridge, Chestertown, Easton and Queenstown.During fall 2022, Kelly Strannahan, Patient Experience Manager at UM SRH, reached out to the Kent Cultural Alliance with an idea of how to honor the commitment of UM SRH team members and health care workers to the communities UM SRH serves in a meaningful and permanent way.The Kent Cultural Alliance proposed having a competition to create mural-size artwork for each UM SRH facility in each county and collaborated with arts councils in Dorchester, Talbot and Queen Anne's counties, working with each to select an artist from their county to complete the commission.Each artist was provided with canvases, made possible with the support of The Finishing Touch in Chestertown.In Dorchester County, the artist is Miriam Moran, for Talbot County, the artist is Kevin Garber, and in Queen Anne's County, then-high school senior Claire Parker was selected.In Kent County, the honor was given to Paul Santori, who early on in the pandemic had a severe case of COVID and was hospitalized at UM Shore Medical Center at Chestertown. Santori succumbed to a non-COVID related health issue in winter 2023.His wife, Inez Santori, made the decision in conversation with Kent Cultural Alliance Director John Schratwieser to transfer the commission to Paul's dear friend, Ron Akins. Paul had sketched his ideas while lying in the hospital for several weeks before his death. With Inez's support, Ron was able to realize Paul's vision for the mural.Each of the county arts councils provided a stipend of $1,250 for their respective artist, and this stipend was supported in part by Kent County's Hedgelawn Foundation.The five arts councils receive funding from the Community Arts Development program of the Maryland State Arts Council, which receives financial support from the National Endowment for the Arts.

title: 'We know stigma is killing people' - Childhood traumas often drive addictions, Societal judgments often hinder recovery
author: Laura Tayman
content:
'We know stigma is killing people' - Childhood traumas often drive addictions, Societal judgments often hinder recovery

 October 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 669
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE - Emily Keller, the Special Secretary of Opioid Response for Maryland's Governor Wes Moore, shared her experience with the opioid epidemic right at the beginning of the Queen Anne's County Community Overdose Action Town Hall."I lost my best friend Ashley to an overdose in 2016. She should have had more treatment options. Unfortunately, my story isn't unique." The town hall held Sept. 21 at Kent Island High School, was the ninth out of 24 counties that the State of Maryland's "Before It's Too Late" team is holding across the state, sponsored by state representatives who are continue to tackle the opioid epidemic. A panel of staff from county offices were on hand to share their efforts and listen to testimony from the community.Major Christopher Amoia, Operations Commander of the Queen Anne's County Sheriff's Office, gave data he believes indicates the collaboration among county agencies is working. "Since 2018 to the present, we had a reduction of overdoses by 380%, and deaths were lowered 267%," he said. Amoia credited expanding programs like DARE and promoting community awareness. Still, as of the day of the meeting, the number of overdoses to date this year is even with all of 2022.Deputy State's Attorney Christine Rickard shared how her team partnered with law enforcement. "We are going after the drug dealers who are dealing this poison to our residents," she said. She is also working with the county's Drug Court. "We know why people are committing crimes-to support their habits. We are working to get them the help they need." There are positive things happening with the county's drug court program, shared the Honorable Judge Lynn Knight, "We used to just lock addicts away," she said. "Now we are getting very involved with the option of plea deals that allow the offender to enter a treatment program, complete 12-18 months, keep checking in with the court, and submit to regular drug tests." County Commissioner Jim Moran said county efforts have also focused on youth, saying, "We tell them we don't want them to be a statistic." Community member Paula Dickerson of Grasonville addressed the panel, "We feel unseen. We have a community center that sits empty despite our area that has crime and an obvious drug problem." Dickerson, who is now 27 years sober, accepted the challenge from Moran to gather community members and arrange for a similar presentation at the Grasonville Community Center.Linda Kohler, Executive Director of Chesapeake Charities, encouraged the panel to consider creating more sober living homes for adults. "Currently, there is one in Talbot County, ready to assist with services like providing drives to rehab and finding jobs." Kohler said they have a grant now to train more peer support specialists.Tom McKnight, (a county resident who says he is 32 years sober) suggested adults who are now sober might be a better way to reach students."We've lived it," said McKnight."We have stories to tell." Madeline Eskew, a student at Kent Island High School, had an uncle die from substance abuse in 2010 and a close cousin had to move out of state to find an acceptable treatment facility. "I just encourage officials to focus more on the mental health side of the problem." Keller told Eskew, "More often than not, addicts are masking an adverse childhood experience and try to suppress their pain." Kent Island High School student Avery Mortimore voiced concern about students who take the big step to access treatment but face hostile peers when they return to school. "They don't want to be judged or shamed. They can't fully re-acclimate and don't fit in." "We know stigma is killing people," said Keller. "It's the reason people aren't getting help. We see it in adults as well." When asked what she would do in that situation, Mortimore said, "I would focus not just on stopping addiction before it starts but on what you do during and after treatment."

She does amazing work on my hair, and I have no interest in finding a new stylist anytime soon.However, every time I am around her, I cannot help but notice her bad body odor. It has become so bad that I find myself holding my breath at certain points during the session. She had to be on set with me for a photoshoot recently, and I know the other people in the room could smell her.I don't want to hurt her feelings or embarrass her, but at the same time, I cannot ignore this any longer.What should I do? - Sensitive to Smells DEAR SENSITIVE TO SMELLS: While it will feel awkward in the moment, telling your friend about her body odor is actually a gift to her.There's no way that you are the first person who has noticed her odor. If she is unable to check it, she may at best lose clients and at worst lose her job.When you do hair, you stand in close proximity to others all day long. Personal hygiene is paramount, especially in roles that bring people into each other's intimate space.Speak to your stylist privately.Tell her what you have noticed and why it is important.Suggest that she figure out what her issue is - it could be medical or basic hygiene. Admit that as much as you like working with her, the odor may require you to find a new stylist.Harriette Cole is a lifestylist and founder of Dreamleapers, an initiative to help people access and activate their dreams.  Earlier this month, the 42nd annual Thomas J. Ewing Dinner Auction was held to benefit Chester-wye, the longtime center to provide care for adults with developmental disabilities. The event was again hosted at the Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department.Event Co-Chair Wheeler Baker welcomed those who attended the Oct. 14 event, thanking the many dedicated attendees and sponsors of the event. Auction donations will go to support critically needed renovation of two of the Chester-wye houses, the Ewing and Nash Houses, noted Baker, "The project will include wheelchair accessible living spaces, new kitchens, wheelchair friendly baths, all customized for individuals with developmental disabilities."Baker also thanked the KIVFD for graciously hosting the event for so many years. Music for the event was provided by the Guthrie Matthews Method Band.The printed program provided a brief history of Chesterwye - originated through the efforts of Bobby Ann and Stuart Nash, who had a little boy, "Chip", with Down syndrome. With laser focus, Bobby Ann pushed the county to provide a place where young and older adults with disabilities could be cared for and learn to live life as fully as possible. Chesterwye was the result.Following the meal of steak and crab cakes, catered by Chesapeake Celebrations, county commissioner Jim Moran spoke briefly. "For over 57 years the Chesterwye has provided homes and support for individuals with developmental disabilities," he said, noting, "Chesterwye was the first organizations in Maryland to provide personalized housing, 'forever homes', as alternative to institutions of the day." Moran also recognized the late Thomas J. Ewing as one of the founders, donating land where the Ewing house now stands.Kay Ewing Maloney, owner of the former famed "Holly's Restaurant" in Grasonville, was the guest speaker. Her late father, Thomas J. Ewing, for whom the dinner-auction is named, founded the restaurant in the early 1950s. It became a landmark for both locals and travelers to the Eastern Shore until is was eventually sold a few years ago.Recounting some of Chesterwye's history, Maloney emphasized, "Remember, we're here to raise money for Chester-wye, which is a great organization! title: Maryland joins DC, 40 other states suing Meta
author: Bridget Byrne; Capital News Service
content:
Maryland joins DC, 40 other states suing Meta

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bridget Byrne; Capital News Service | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 787
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON - Maryland, the District of Columbia and 40 other states are suing Meta alleging that its platforms cause harm to children by building addictive features, Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown announced Tuesday."Our country is facing a youth mental health crisis fueled by young people's extensive and compulsive use of, and reliance on, social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram," Brown said at a press conference outside Hampstead Hill Academy, a Baltimore public school. "This has placed an entire generation of young people in jeopardy."Maryland and 32 other states are filing a joint lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, and the District of Columbia and eight other states are filing separate complaints in federal, state or local courts.The scope of the legal claims may vary, but all are expected to assert that Meta used harmful and manipulative tactics purposefully to keep children on its platforms.In 2021, a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general announced an investigation into Meta, focusing on whether the parent company of Instagram and Facebook violated consumer protection laws by promoting the sites' apps to children and teens."Based on the information obtained during that investigation, we allege that Meta's actions have violated the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act," Brown said.Nationwide, states have seen a surging youth mental health crisis: the number of children ages 3 to 17 who experienced anxiety or depression from 9.4% in 2016 to 11.8% in 2020 - a 25% increase, according to the National Institute of Health. Maryland ranked 19th in the nation for overall child well-being."Just like Big Tobacco did a generation ago, Meta has chosen to maximize its profits at the expense of public health, specifically the health of our children," Brown charged.In the suit Maryland joined, the attorneys general allege that "Meta has harnessed powerful and unprecedented technologies to entice, engage, and ultimately ensnare youth and teens.""Its motive is profit, and in seeking to maximize its financial gains, Meta has repeatedly misled the public about the substantial dangers of its Social Media Platforms. It has concealed the ways in which these Platforms exploit and manipulate its most vulnerable consumers: teenagers and children. And it has ignored the sweeping damage these Platforms have caused to the mental and physical health of our nation's youth," the filing states.Meta said in a statement that it agreed with "the attorneys general's commitment to providing teens with safe, positive experiences online, and have already introduced over 30 tools to support teens and their families."But Meta added: "We're disappointed that instead of working productively with companies across the industry to create clear, age-appropriate standards for the many apps teens use, the attorneys general have chosen this path."Brown was joined by Hampstead Hill Academy Principal Matthew Hornbeck, who said that over the 20 years he has been at the school he has seen the impact the rise in social media use has had on his students. Hornbeck described measures to curb phone use at Hampstead Hill, but stressed they were "merely a workaround.""(Social media) hijacks normal, healthy thinking," Hornbeck said. "It sucks up so much time and keeps the user wanting more and more. It's not an overstatement to say it can steal big chunks of a childhood.""The urge to check your phone is stronger than any consequence we have at school," he said.Treeme Cannizzaro, an 8th grade student at Hampstead Hill, said at the press conference that limiting phone use in schools does not address the impact social media has on mental health when students are not at school."My friends and I can't help but get on our phones to see what we've missed," Cannizzaro said. "Limiting access to social media has had a positive impact on my mental health during the school day, and I hope that social media companies can find more ways to decrease the anxiety and depression my friends and I feel from social interactions online."In May, the Federal Trade Commission proposed barring Meta from monetizing the data it collects for underage users.Also in May, U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy issued an advisory stating that, although there are some benefits, social media use presents a "profound risk of harm" for children and called for further research into social media's impact on youth mental health."Children are exposed to harmful content on social media, ranging from violent and sexual content, to bullying and harassment," Murthy said in a statement. "And for too many children, social media use is compromising their sleep and valuable in-person time with family and friends."Efforts to regulate social media's impact on social media have gained traction this year, but also have faced challenges in court. Federal judges blocked newly-passed children's safety laws in California and Arkansas.

Planning commission OKs new UM Shore facility plan

 EASTON - The Easton Planning Commission on Thursday, Oct. 19 unanimously approved a sketch site plan for the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health's new regional medical center with several conditions.The project, which first received planning commission approval of a sketch site plan over a decade ago, resurfaced so hospital officials could discuss an updated sketch plan for the medical center.The proposed six-story, 340,000-square-foot medical center and roughly 55,000-square-foot medical office building are slated to occupy just over 235 acres off of Longwoods Road near U.S. Route 50 in Easton.The largest part of the complex will include a 147-bed hospital, including 122 acute inpatient beds across several units and 25 observation beds, along with labs and imaging rooms and a helipad. The complex will have 18 more beds than the hospital's existing facility.The other main portion of the complex will be utilized for medical offices.Over 1,100 parking spaces, a 36-acre open space area, stormwater management facilities and landscaping are also included in the plan.The new regional medical center will replace the town's existing hospital, which is 3.5 miles away and tucked into downtown Easton.In addition to the large-scale medical center, the hospital system is proposing removal and relocation of a section of Maryland Route 662C and modifying entrances into the Talbot County Community Center, which is adjacent to the property.At the Oct. 19 meeting, the hospital system also sought a waiver of parking lot landscape hedge and vegetative buffer requirements, or approval to plant native grasses and plants instead of hedges to enable proper drainage flow towards proposed stormwater management facilities and to allow for better visibility at parking lot exits.Questions raised by planning commission members during the meeting centered on parking, accessibility, emergency access, landscaping and traffic.After additional discussion, the planning commission voted to approve the sketch site plan with several conditions for the applicant to meet, including addressing remaining comments from the Easton Staff Development Review, meeting with the commission again to review if additional landscape screening is appropriate and working with the town engineer to explore alternatives for emergency access.Though the town's planning commission approved the sketch plan, the start of construction is dependent on receiving a Certificate ofNeed from the Maryland Health Care Commission. UM Shore Regional Health filed the CON application in early January.The hospital anticipates a response from the state by the end of this year or by January 2024, according to Ken Kozel, president and CEO of UM Shore Regional Health. Hospital officials hope to begin construction in late spring 2024.

title: College junior feels jealous of friend
author: Harriette Cole
content:
College junior feels jealous of friend

 October 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Harriette Cole | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 319
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I am a junior in college, and I'm struggling with feelings of jealousy toward my friend. It seems like everything comes so easily to her, and it's hard for me not to compare our paths.Recently, my friend received a $10,000 scholarship for a study abroad program in Japan and landed an internship at one of the top investment banking firms in the United States. She applied to only one internship and only one scholarship, and things fell into place effortlessly. It's as if a fairy comes in every night while she's sleeping and throws magic pixie dust at her to make everything work out. Meanwhile, I feel like I have to fight tooth and nail just to make half as much progress. Every day is a continuous struggle to accomplish the goals that I have. I try hard to be positive, but obstacles pop up constantly. How can I deal with these feelings of envy and move forward with a more upbeat outlook on life? - Jealous DEAR JEALOUS: It is understandable that you would be envious of your friend for what appears to be an easy life. As you also know, it is toxic to dwell on what other people have. No good will come out of that longing. Instead, you must focus on yourself. Do your best to view your life as your perfect challenge. You are gaining resilience as you live through each experience.Claim your small victories.To keep on track, create a vision board. Look through magazines and newspapers for images that reflect the things you want for your life. Cut them out. Brainstorm words and ideas that represent your dreams.Write them down. Next, on a large piece of cardboard or paper, place the images and words together. Make a simple art piece out of this collection of ideas to create your vision board. When thoughts creep in about your friend's success - or anyone else's - wish them well and pivot back to planning your own life.

The UWCC chose to focus this year's awards on programs and services that address mental health, food insecurity and programs and services for seniors and the elderly."There are so many needs in our community but we felt these three were the most pressing," past President Samantha Parker said."The pandemic and inflation have created special challenges for our must vulnerable residents, especially children, the elderly and those struggling with a mental health condition." The following organizations received awards from UWCC: Mid-Shore Council on Family Violence: MSCFV's Chesapeake Crisis to Self-Sufficiency Model provides domestic violence victims with a pathway to empowerment that includes hotline services, emergency shelter, on-going case management, counseling and mental health services, economic empowerment, basic living needs, transportation, interpretation/translation, pet safety, support groups, abuser intervention programming, community outreach and awareness.Court-Appointed Special Advocates of Caroline: CASA recruits and trains volunteers who advocate for children in the Caroline County foster care system. CASA volunteers are the eyes and ears of the courts and the voices for the children, monitoring each child's well-being and making recommendations to the court that are in the child's best interest.Critical Repairs Caroline County (formerly Rebuilding Together): The mission of this organization is to enable low-income residents in Caroline County to remain safely in their homes by providing necessary repairs and accessibility improvements they cannot afford. These repairs are intended to improve the residents' quality of life, their overall safety and enable them to access life-supporting activities.Martin's House & Barn (formerly St. Martin's Ministries): The organization assists vulnerable families in Caroline County through a wide variety of programs, including its food pantry, thrift shop, family homeless shelter and homelessness prevention program.His Hope Ministries: Its mission is to offer resources to help vulnerable families, individuals, youth, and elderly citizens experiencing homelessness or living in unstable housing. It operates the largest homeless shelter on the Eastern Shore and provides residents with a wide variety of programs to help achieve their housing goals.Aaron's Place: A community resource center aiding Caroline residents with food insecurity, housing, health and wellness and addressing social determinants of health and health disparities.Caroline Medical Adult Daycare: MADC is a program of services designed to allow health-impaired adults of Caroline County to remain in their homes and community. They live as independently as possible, with dignity and a renewed sense of quality of life, through care in the least restrictive setting, while preventing inappropriate or premature institutionalization.The United Way of Caroline County's mission is to support non-profits meeting the human services needs of our community.For more than 40 years, it has taken care of Caroline County and helped families get back on their feet and thrive. title: All hands on deck - How local hospitals handle mass casualty incidents
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
All hands on deck - How local hospitals handle mass casualty incidents

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 757
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - It was all hands on deck Monday morning at two University of Maryland Shore Regional Health facilities as emergency department staff treated patients from a school bus crash in Easton.Ten of the 11 patients involved in the crash between a Caroline County school bus and a SUV were taken to Shore Regional Health facilities - three patients to the hospital in Easton and seven to the freestanding emergency department in Queenstown.The number of patients in need of evaluation and treatment triggered first responders to categorize the crash as a mass casualty incident, or a situation that overwhelms local healthcare systems' resources and capabilities."When (first responders) say, 'we got something bad,' we listen," said Dr.Walter Atha, the regional director of emergency medicine for the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health."They (called) ahead, and that's exactly what happened yesterday: they gave us a heads up and said 'Look, we're going to have numerous (patients), many more' - in fact even (taxing) their own capacity to bring them in," he added.From there, back and forth discussions ensued on which patients could be brought to the hospital in Easton versus the Queenstown facility, though all four of Shore Regional Health's facilities can perform initial resuscitation efforts.An incident command system, or structure that's put in place if there's a large-scale ongoing emergency situation, was also implemented to manage plans to move forward.While emergency medical services personnel triaged patients at the scene Monday morning, a yellow alert, which signifies an internal or external disaster, went out to hospital staff. That partnership between first responders and physicians is crucial in managing an emergent situation.The alert notifies everyone from leadership positions to those on the frontlines to prepare - "just brace yourself" for however the situation may go, Atha said.Sending the systemwide alert lets units far removed from the emergency department prepare to decompress the emergency department's other needs so staff can perform resuscitation if needed.Situational awareness is key when preparing for an influx of patients, Atha said. It's particularly important to evaluate the resources on hand, including personnel needs and the location of certain equipment. The hospital in Easton also can contact an on-call physician in anticipation of increased critical volume.But in preparation for a rush of patients from Monday's crash, an on-call physician wasn't needed - a doctor with expertise in resuscitation concerned about patients needing high level care "came in on his own goodwill" to help, Atha said."So many people in the community say, 'I will come help,'" he said.Treating young patients like those involved in the bus crash can be a challenge though.Atha said physical shock from injuries in children doesn't manifest the same way it does in adults. The resilience of children makes them "notoriously difficult" for first responders to triage because some kids who look well could be seriously injured.Difficulties can also arise with ensuring there is enough staff on hand to answer questions from families and to keep everyone calm.And with any mass casualty incident that occurs in a rural area, distance makes a difference, both positive and negative."Frankly, there's a little advantage in that maybe we have a little extra time if it's far removed in terms of knowing what's coming in, rather than it happening a block away," he said. "On the other hand, you want to get to trauma victims as soon as you can, so that's the challenge: the distance." But still, mass casualty incidents in the Mid-Shore region are "not that frequent," Atha said."This is the largest-scale that I've seen in a while," he said, struggling to remember other serious incidents during his 10-year tenure at the hospital.Even with the low frequency of such incidents in the area, Atha felt the emergency department staff had the resources they needed to respond to it adequately."The feedback I got from the folks on the frontlines who were actually taking care of the patients (said) things went as smoothly as they could," he said.To keep improving emergency department responses to various incidents, hospital staff set up review meetings to debrief on what went well and what didn't. A meeting on the response to the bus crash was held Tuesday morning.Atha commended all who were involved with the Monday's response."It's not just the people who put hands and gloves on those patients; it was everybody at every level stepped up and was ready, I think that's really important," he said.

An emergency department staff member at the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton works at the nurses' station.
