title: County health report shows progress
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
County health report shows progress

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 2B | Section: News 
 
 1004
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - During her biannual report to the Caroline County Commission at its Oct. 24 meeting, Health Officer Robin Cahall touted successes, including significant state grant funding, increased behavioral health services with better outcomes and progress in achieving 2023 initiatives.However, communicable diseases like tuberculosis are present in the county, and the department, along with its partners, is reaching out to vulnerable populations with services.Cahall presented a slide show with Behavioral Health Director Jessica Tuel that provided information on funding, staffing and numbers related to services delivered to county residents.For fiscal year 2023, the health department received about $6.9 million in grant funding. Along with state and local funding, the total is $8.5 million.The approved county match was $409,054 - less than 5% of the total budget for the health department.The department continues to apply for additional grant funding.The fiscal year 2024 budget, however, will increase with a county match of just over $589,000, or about 7% of the department's total budget.Because the state contribution is based on a wealth index, the approximate ratio of state to local percentages of the department's baseline funding is nearly 80% state and just over 20% county.The wealth index hasn't been updated since 1996, Cahall said, but the Maryland Association of County Health Officers has created an ad hoc committee to review the process for determining the formula.Core funding must be used for specific purposes according to the state, and most of that "goes towards our environmental health services," Cahall said.Those local health services include communicable disease control, family planning, maternal and child health, wellness promotion, data management and protective equipment, among others.Among this year's initiatives, the Behavioral Health Program has moved to Denton Plaza, and a second Mobile Treatment Unit is up and running. The department is making progress towards National Public Health Accreditation and expanding chronic disease prevention.The health department's newest partnerships include the ongoing Caroline County Collective Impact."We have several different members of our leadership team that participate in different action teams for collective impact," Cahall said."That's been very successful for us in the sense of collaborating with our community partners and leaders to get some things done." For example, Mobile Integrated Health is a partnership among the Department of Emergency Services, the Basic Life Support Committee and Shore Health, and the Resource Directory Project partners with the Caroline Human Services Council and the Caroline County Public Library.The Communicable Disease, Family Planning and Women and Child Health Division is "definitely one of our priorities," Cahall said.The department performed 180 teburculosis tests and identified 38 latent tuberculosis infections. The department treated 28 of those individuals; primary care providers could treat the others.So far in 2023, the department performed 531 pregnancy tests and a registered nurse handled 1,249 unduplicated office visits. A lot of prenatal care and referrals went to Choptank Community Health providers.commission President Travis Breeding asked about the health department's response to "a really large influx of new English language learners" at the northern end of the county."Are you seeing additional requests for assistance and support among the new American population, the immigrant population?" he asked.Cahall said they were seeing a slight influx in terms of immunization requests, but the department referred people to Choptank Community Health or other providers."We don't want the health department to be primary care for anyone," she said."We have a great immunization team," Cahall said. "We actually have two new nurses and our director of nursing. We can definitely use one more on our communicable disease side.We're trying to work that in, but it's definitely manageable." Cahall said behavioral health is one of the biggest programs within the health department.Cahall said there has been a 37% decrease in visits to receive buprenorphine (the medication used for the management of opioid use disorder), care coordination has increased 84% and maintenance has increased 12%."That data indicates that our clients are shifting from active treatment to maintenance and they're also shifting to discharge," Cahall said. "This is definitely showing improvement in our treatment." She pointed to a 60% decrease in use of the mobile treatment unit (MTU) "because we've worked really hard on discharging and putting our clients into maintenance when it's needed or when they're ready." Cahall reported percentages instead of numbers for drug intoxication deaths because "we're dealing with small numbers" and they may not all be Caroline County citizens.Cahall's last slide listed four top 2024 initiatives. She said the Coordinated Community Supports Project is "going to be huge for us." The department has nearly $400,000 to expand current school-based mental health services; the current capacity is an average of 260 students in five schools.Other initiatives include Mobile Integrated Health, expanding sexually transmitted infections (STI) testing capabilities and establishing organizational performance measures based on the State Health Improvement Plan (SHIP).commissioner Frank Bartz asked how the department is helping those with mental health concerns and if more people were receptive to seeking help."I have seen a huge difference, especially in the last three years," Tuel said. "People are really worried about their mental health and are caring for themselves, which I'm really happy about." Tuel said that most people with "substance use disorder often have mental health concerns, as well. They are treated just like any other patients." "Coordinated community support not only supports children and adolescents' mental health, but the family as a whole," Cahall said. "The other thing we've worked on is an anti-stigma campaign we've seen a shift in the stigma situation." Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who participated in the meeting remotely because of illness, weighed in at the end of the report and thanked Cahall and Tuel for the information."We've come a long way from our health report card that we used to have where we were last in everything you didn't want to be last in, and first in everything we didn't want to be first in," he said.

title: 'Know that you can make a difference' - Nonprofit for children affected by conflict in Ukraine hosts fundraiser at Avalon
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'Know that you can make a difference' - Nonprofit for children affected by conflict in Ukraine hosts fundraiser at Avalon

 November 3, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Short videos and still photos were projected across the screen of the Avalon Theater Wednesday night, including one image of a young girl, maybe 10 years-old.Susan Mathison asked those gathered to consider just this one person and her needs for food during the war in Ukraine."Because of our ability to distribute food, that kid and her family ate that week and they will as well next week," she told dozens of locals who had gathered at the theater to learn about Mathison and her partners' work.On Feb. 24, 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine in an escalation of the Russo-Ukrainian War, which started in 2014. It is estimated that tens of thousands of Ukrainian civilians have died and hundreds of thousands of military members.The Common Man for Ukraine, a non-profit aligned with rotary clubs around the world, feeds, clothes and provides sleeping bags for children affected by the war.Along with feeding those in need, The Common Man for Ukraine brings in mental health workers to help young people cope with losing their homes, and in many cases, their families.Mathison is one of the founders of the group. She and three friends - Alex Reyes, Steve Rand and Lisa Murray, all based in New Hampshire - decided they needed to do something about the suffering they had seen from the conflict.None of them were foreign aid workers or diplomats, she said, but they were determined to figure out how to help."The world has a lot of catastrophes right now. And the media and our hearts can be distracted from one to the other, to the other," Mathison said. "Our challenge as humans is to find a cause that matters to you and makes a difference. Find something and know that you can make a difference in the lives of someone, somewhere." "We are just four people.Alex owns a couple dozen restaurants in New Hampshire.Steve is a hardware store owner, I am a retired forester and Lisa is a public health specialist. We had no humanitarian aid experience.Steve and Alex were rotarians.This was a total start from zero." Their approach was to fly to Ukraine, talk to people and find out what they needed."Steve contacted the district governor of all the rotarians in Poland and Ukraine. Alex put up the first million dollars. We are going to raise a match of a million dollars. So we want to help, what can we do?" Mathison said.The Ukrainian Rotarians recommended some projects, which The Common Man for Ukraine was eager to see put on the ground."What is the one thing we can do really well? We decided to work on kids.They seem the most vulnerable, most innocent victims.We wanted to stay out of the fray of politics. 2.5 million kids are in hiding from Russian bombing and kidnapping.They are internally displaced," she said."They are looking for a place to sleep. They are hid in safe houses and secret locations all over Ukraine." The Rotarian connection helped this nonprofit find safe houses and deliver food on a 40-day rotation. Mathison said they have delivered 800 tons of food, 10,000 sleeping bags and 500 generators to date. They keep two warehouses on the Polish border with Ukraine."The Russians have a history of winning wars by starving people out," Rand said. "They are trying to interrupt every line of resupply.If we had a warehouse in Ukraine, it would be a target to be blown up." The organization brings 30 children a month to a safe place in Poland, where they get art therapy, play therapy, talk therapy and perhaps most importantly, they network with others who have lost a parent, said Mathison."Our three legged stool is food, warmth and love.That last leg is mental health counseling," she said.She said her hope is that these kids will be the ones to rebuild Ukraine when the war is over.To learn more about the nonprofit, visit commonmanforukraine.org.

Steve Rand, in blue vest, hands out cards and receives donations after Susan Mathison is done speaking at the Common Man for Ukraine fundraiser at the Avalon Theater.

title: How to clean a kitchen sponge
author: Mary Hunt
content:
How to clean a kitchen sponge

 November 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Hunt | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When asked, "What is the dirtiest spot in the typical household?" most people say the toilet seat.For sure, that would have been my response, until I discovered studies on bacteria and household diseases by Dr. Chuck Gerba, professor of microbiology at the University ofArizona.Gerbas studies have found that on the average toilet seat, there are 50 bacteria per square inch. But the typical kitchen sponge has around 10 million bacteria per square inch. That's no typo! And it gets worse, so brace for what I am about to tell you.Gerba has discovered that usually there are about 200 times more fecal bacteria on the average kitchen cutting board than on a toilet seat. It doesn't necessarily get there through actual contact with feces, but arrives via raw meat products or the organs from inside of the animal, where a lot ofthe fecal bacteria originate.With all those gazillions of bacteria on kitchen sponges, you may assume the best way to clean our kitchen sponges is by a minute or two in a microwave oven set on High. Seems reasonable, right? Well, it's not!Putting that kitchen sponge through a complete cycle with detergent daily, or as often as you run a load of dishes, is a much better solution. The heat plus detergent are sufficient to kill bacteria and mildew.Another option, especially ifyou don't have a dishwasher, is to soak that daily sponge in a good antibacterial sanitizer for at least 10 minutes up to overnight. But don't spend $8 for a 16-ounce bottle from the store. Make it yourselffor pennies!According to the Food and Drug Administrationl, 1 teaspoon ofliquid chlorine bleach per 1 quart ofclean water can be used to sanitize all kitchen surfaces such as cutting boards, countertops, refrigerator shelves - and sponges!CQPYRIGHT 2023 CREATQRS.COM

author: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com
content:
'We made it' - YMCA opens new facility in Centreville

 CENTERVILLE - "We made it!" shouted YMCA of the Chesapeake Executive Director Robbie Gill, Wednesday afternoon, Oct. 18, to begin the grand opening ceremony at the new Queen Anne's County Family YMCA & Active Aging Center in Centreville.This YMCA is the 11th location in the Chesapeake region, which includes all of the Eastern Shore of Maryland and Virginia, and the largest of them all. The QA YMCA is 70,000 square feet indoors (providing a workout just walking around inside the building?)The project to date cost $22.6 million. Of that, $15,235,000 came from private donations (248 donors thus far). QAC government provided $3.5 million, State Capital Grant provided $3,065,000, and the Maryland Department of Aging another $800,000.The goal of the YMCA is for families to live their healthiest lives and reach their full potential in mind, body and spirit. It offers a stay-and-play space for parents to bring their young children to be cared for by trained members of the Y staffwhile the parents workout. This service is provided free within the cost of the family's membership fee.The Active Aging Center is only the second one located in the Chesapeake region to offer congregate meals for seniors at discounted prices, chronic disease prevention programs, Enhance Fitness, swimming classes, social groups and benefits counseling tailored for ages 55-plus.The QAC Active Aging Center is open to all members of the community age 55 and over, and a YMCA membership is not required to enter. Check with the QA Department of Aging or Active Aging Center for more details about this offer.The pool at the Y has six 25-yard length swimming lanes, one ofwhich will always be open for lap swimming. Children ages 16 and under are required to take a simple swim test administered by the lifeguard to be able to swim in the pool.Gill shared an experience he had during the early years of planning of this Y."A father came to our meeting saying, 'My son drowned in the Corsica River in 1974. Ifwe had a YMCA back then, my son would have received swim lessons there, and would be alive today,'" he said. "That father's comments stuck with me as we have gone forward to where we are today." Among those who spoke at the grand opening ceremony, was Patricia Saelens, QACPS Superintendent of Schools. She said, "We have have already begun partnering with the Y to provide water safety training to our school children starting with our elementary school children. We're very excited about doing this."As a not-for-profit organization, the YMCA provides financial assistance to ensure no one is turned away from membership, programs and services due to the inability to pay. The upkeep of the YMCA facility is at no cost to the county. Every Y is self-supporting, funded by private dollars. The new facility in Centreville will employ over 100 staff members.PHOTO BY DOUG BISHOP Area elected officials are pictured at the ribbon cutting ceremony for the grand opening of the new Queen Anne's County YMCA as Maryland Department of Aging Secretary Carmel Roques, Wednesday afternoon, Oct. 18, in Centreville. To her right, Eastern Shore Excutive Director Robbie Gill is pictured. Gill has overseen this project since it was first conceived 17-years ago. Approximately 200 people attended the event.The completed "Phase 1" facility now exists. Phase 2 will include the addition of an outdoor pool, six outdoor pickleball courts and space for family gatherings and activities, again, at no cost to the county. Phase two is planned to be completed by summer 2024.There are rules at the YMCA that may appear to be "a throw back" to a bygone era. "No profanity. Shoes and shirts must be worn at all times. Fighting will result in suspension of YMCA membership."The heritage of the YMCA is to promote Christian values and an environment of caring for everyone. It is to be a happy place to come and be with others.Centreville Town Councilman Eric Johnson Jr. was present at the grand opening. He said, "The YMCA is a focal point for community health, active aging, fitness, family, community, and so much more. I couldn't be more excited about this perfect addition to our town."County Commissioner Jim Moran added, "What have our active adults using the YMCA, We have our families using the YMCA, and we have our students using the YMCA. This facility checks off so many boxes when it comes to our community and quality of life."To make an appointment to tour the new QA YMCA, or have questions answered, call 443-262-9994. Brian Byrnes is the QA YMCA executive director.

title: Crisis Within A Crisis - The distressing, problematic intersections of homelessness and mental health
author: Mike Sunnucks; APG National Enterprise Editor
content:
Crisis Within A Crisis - The distressing, problematic intersections of homelessness and mental health

 November 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks; APG National Enterprise Editor | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1894
 Words 

 Read News Document

 America's mental and behavioral health crises are no more pronounced than with homeless/unsheltered people.Homeless individuals have higher rates of severe mental illnesses and behavioral health problems - and are far less likely to have received help - than the general U.S. population, according to various studies and analyses.A June study released by North Carolina-based RTI International found approximately 3.7 million American adults, or 1.8%, ofthe general population suffer from schizophrenia spectrum disorders. That number is higher than previous estimates.Among homeless populations in the U.S, individuals suffering schizophrenia, one ofthe most challenging and erratic mental health disorders, total as much as 33%, according to various studies.Nationally, 4.4% of the population suffers from bipolar disorders, according to the National Institute ofHealth. That number is as high as 42% among the homeless.Another 45% ofhomeless people deal with mental health challenges, including anxiety and depression, versus 21% ofthe general population, according to reports from the Brain & Behavior Research Association and Mental Health America.Homeless people also have more than double the rates ofsubstance abuse as the general population, according to numbers from the American Addiction Centers.NO EASY SOLUTIONThe situation also exposes plenty ofwarts in broader systems ranging from health care and mental health to criminal justice and past and contemporary mistreatment of society's poorest and most vulnerable.Women make up 38% of the U.S. homeless population while Indigenous, Hispanic and Black persons make up disproportionate shares of the homeless population - 5%, 24% and 37%, respectively - as compared to their shares of the general population.Chris Bouneff, executive director the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) Oregon, said homelessness is frequently the unfortunate outcome ofuntreated behavioral health situations or the result of mental health systems that have not helped individuals address traumas and other root causes.Bouneff said the approach to helping unsheltered individuals is too often reactionary and pigeonholed into different silos, such as housing, jobs and health services (including behavioral and mental health).Trying to address serious and chronic mental and behavioral health problems once people hit the street with a health care system not aligned to help poor people is an uphill battle, he contends."You will never be able to build out ofthe problem," Bouneff said.The Oregon mental health advocate said there needs to be better coordination between groups helping the unsheltered.That means better linking housing agencies, shelters and mental and behavioral health providers whose operations and funding streams tend to be siloed to those areas."We have a funding dynamic where you do one thing - housing or health care - and never the two shall meet," Bouneff said.It also means offering an "array" of services and options for homeless persons facing struggles, rather than searching for one magic solution."The challenge is we are always looking for one thing to solve the problem," Bouneffsaid. "In behavioral health, it doesn't work that way. You have to have an array ofthings available. You can't just have a housing first solution, for example."The reality across the country is that many homeless shelters are just that - shelters.Many shelters, especially smaller ones in smaller communities, are focused on providing beds, showers and food to homeless neighbors. They offer limited to no mental and behavioral health services to their clients."Our services offer drug-free shelter, hot showers and hot meals. We are not trained on mental health," said Candy Sanders, executive secretary and volunteer coordinator for the Klamath Falls Gospel Mission in southern Oregon.The shelter-which offers 92 beds, including a dozen for homeless women with kids - does partner with local medical and behavioral health providers.Bouneffsaid having a more cohesive approach can also help overcome hesitancies that homeless persons might have toward mental and behavioral systems, including bureaucracies and past bad experiences.Fifty-eight percent ofAmericans who report struggling with mental health (28 million people) receive no treatment, with many citing costs. That challenge is magnified for homeless persons.On top ofthat, there are also segments ofunsheltered homeless populations who resistantly avoid accessing services-including housing and shelters as well as mental and behavioral health assistance. That's a very tough nut to crack for service providers as well as law enforcement."There are certain components ofthis chronic homeless population that like their lifestyle. They want to live on the street," said Pinellas County SheriffBob Gualtieri in the Tampa area, discussing issues with crime and services for unsheltered residents."This isn't a services issue. This isn't an availability of services issue," said Gualtieri, noting the complexity ofthe issue. The Florida sheriff said one shelter in the county (which includes St. Petersburg and Clearwater) is only at about halfofits 425-person capacity.POLICE ON THE FRONT LINESThere are also new approaches being tried across the country aimed at front line interactions with homeless persons, including those experiencing mental and behavioral health crises.Many times that job falls to police officers -who traditionally have not been trained or equipped to address severe and chronic mental illness.Mental health advocates, as well as some law enforcement officials, are trying to change that.A number ofpolice departments have increased mental and behavioral health training for officers, making it a mandatory requirement for new recruits.Other agencies have launched co-responder efforts that pair social workers, as well as mental health crisis professionals, with officers on certain police calls.InWyoming, Cheyenne Regional Medical Center started a co-responder program earlier this year with the Cheyenne Police Department, with plans to expand to the Laramie County Sheriff's Off.ce. The program received money to get going via a state grant totaling just under $345,000.Natalie Villalobos, director ofsocial work at CRMC Behavioral Health Services, said co-responders accompany local police on certain calls related to mental health, as well as domestic incidents. The goal is to assist police, offer help and services to those in need, and build relationships with community members who might gain from mental health or homeless services."You have people in crisis. You have domestic violence situations," Villalobos said.She said in a smaller city such as Cheyenne -with a population ofaround 67,000-police and social service providers often deal with the same individuals on the behavioral and mental health fronts."We are interconnected," Villalobos said.There are currently five social workers and other mental health workers from the hospital -including Villalobos - who ride along with police on calls related to the program.Right now, the effort is based on staffing and certain times of days, and the hospital workers keep their distance during certain police calls.But during other calls, the CRMC co-responders can offer services and counsel family members and victims, and build rapport with residents dealing with homelessness and mental illness.EFFORTS IN FLORIDA, WISCONSINThe St. Petersburg Police Department in Florida launched its own co-responder program in2021 aimed at improving community relations after the 2020 death ofGeorge Floyd in Minnesota sparked civil strife, nationwide protests, and calls for cutting or defunding police budgets.The effort is contracted out to GulfCoast JFCS, a Clearwater, Florida-based behavioral health firm with a staffof20, including 14 "navigators" who accompany patrol officers on calls and a youth engagement specialist that is funded through a grant from the National Football League.Community Assistance and Life Liaison (CALL) navigators respond to homeless-related calls, suicide threats, juvenile truancies, neighborhood disputes, substance abuse situations and responses related to Florida's 72-hour commitment law (the Baker Act).There are 577 officers on the St. Petersburg police force, which received more than 372,600 emergency and other calls for service last year."CALL has made over 10,000 contacts in the community since inception (in) February 2021 and served nearly5,000 unique clients," according to Megan McGee, assistant director ofthe administrative services bureau ofSt. Petersburg Police."Ninety to 95% ofthose calls that are diverted to the CALL team are handled without police. Officers have also sent over2,000 referrals to the team. For the month ofAugust, (the team) received 48 referrals from officers," McGee said.After an $850,000 pilot effort, the CALL program now has a $1.67 million budget and is expanding its hours ofoperation to 8 a.m. to 2 a.m.In Wisconsin, the Madison Police Department has had a mental health unit since 2015. The squad includes six full-time mental health officers and three embedded crisis workers. They assist patrol officers as needed, including those related to homelessness.The Eau Claire Police Department has had a similar effort in place since 2022 aimed at helping unsheltered people access services including for mental and behavioral health.Police departments' mental health outreach also comes as law enforcement agencies face their own rise in suicides and look to overcome historical and stigmas to asking for help. There were also a record number ofsuicides among the U.S. population last year (49,449)."There are certain components of this chronic homeless population that like their lifestyle. They want to live on the street."Bob GualtieriSheriff, Pinellas County, Florida"The suicide rate for police officers is alarming. More police officers die by suicide than they do in the line ofduty," said Jennifer Hannah, a lieutenant with the Madison Police Department in Wisconsin. "MPD has not been immune. Repeated exposure to trauma, ifnot addressed, processed and treated, grows throughout an officer's career and can affect all areas ofan officer's personal and professional life. But oftentimes, the stigma associated with seeking help prevents officers from reaching out for support."Hannah said officers still worry if"they will be perceived as being weak" or face adverse career ramifications ifthey are public about their challenges. Like other agencies, Madison police have launched peer support efforts to help officers talk to their cohorts.Those peer efforts, greater awareness of challenges and overcoming stigmas within their own department can help foster more understanding and empathy on calls dealing with behavioral health crises and incidents, law enforcement officials said.OREGON'S APPROACHBack in Oregon, Bouneffsaid the state is embarking on an effort to send mental and behavioral health specialists - and not police - on some calls.The initiative is part ofa $39 million effort and 40-cents-per-month charge on phone lines to build out 988 call centers to field mental health crisis calls, and $118 million in state spending to bolster mental health services and crisis responses-including for burgeoning homeless populations."Law enforcement is not in the business of responding to mental health calls. They are not trained for it. They are not good at it," Bouneff said.He said Oregon and its localities are still figuring out how to structure those responses and when police will need to be involved or take the lead because ofthreats or incidents involving violence and self-harm.He did note the bipartisan support for dealing with mental health and responding to intersections with homelessness."Some ofthe strongest supporters are rural Republicans," Bouneffsaid. "You can't hide this in a rural community." 
 
 Caption: Homeless persons in the U.S. suffer from higher percentages of mental and behavioral health challenges than the general population. That comes as unsheltered populations have increased in California (pictured), Washington, Oregon, Delaware, Wisconsin and other states.
 
JOEY ZANOTTI/WIKIMEDIA COMMONS
 
SOURCES: HHS, National Coalition to End Homelessness, Security.org
 
ADJOAJO/WIKIMEDIA COMMONS
 
Homelessness is a major challenge in New York City, Los Angeles, Seattle, San Francisco and other big cities. But it is also confronting smaller towns and communities across the country.
 
FRANCO FOLINI/WIKIMEDIA COMMONS There are plenty of hesitations among some homeless persons to access mental and behavioral services. Past and contemporary mistreatment, previous individual traumas, concerns about being committed or put on medications along with siloed service providers are among the challenges for a challenged population.

title: Volunteers 'make a difference'
author: Tamara Forte; Special To The Bay Times Record Observer
content:
Volunteers 'make a difference'

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Forte; Special To The Bay Times Record Observer | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE - Kindness, enthusiasm and a passion for helping exuded from the front doors at Sudlersville Middle School as 75 households and 130 people were served on Saturday, Nov. 4, at the 10th annual "Make a Difference Day." Tables, chairs and volunteers lined the halls, gymnasium and areas outside of the school.This non-profit and free community event began in 2014 as a way to provide county resources and services for families in need.Housing Program Administrator Kelly Huber said "not only do we rely on the committee, (but) it takes a village of volunteers to assist on the day of the event. We had over 70 volunteers from the community to help - including student volunteers from the Boys Scouts, the sea cadets, adult volunteers, and local school volunteers." Volunteers - of all ages - wore "Make a Difference Day" shirts that said: "Ask me a?" on the back. Volunteers spent the day providing information and services throughout the event.While the Division of Housing and Community Services oversees the event, a large committee plans and executes it. Composed of people from local businesses, agencies, and individuals from the community, many of the original Make A Difference Day board members remain on the committee and are active members in both the planning and in volunteering during the day.Sea cadets volunteered their time and politely welcomed each person in attendance by opening the doors and formally greeting them.Sea cadets are 10 to 17 yearolds who participate in the United States Naval Sea Cadet Corps (USNSCC), a youth leadership development program sponsored by the U.S. Navy.Once through the doors, attendees were given a navigator (who spoke their language) to guide and help them through over 50 tables, services and resources, all conveniently in one location.Each person and family could select the services they needed. Services included: legal aid, social services, meals and food access, education, transportation, housing, personal hygiene, and much more. Eddie the Barber, stylist Ashley Calderone and many Queen Anne's County cosmetology students completed 30 to 40 free haircuts on Saturday.The dental van completed over 30 free dental screenings and provided goodie bags to all.Other services included free flu shots and medical testing (blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose testing).The Lions Club helped more than 10 people with vision needs. Additional services were also offered throughout the day.Giveaways were offered to everyone and were crowd pleasers - toiletries, hats, mittens, blankets, slippers, socks, diapers and wipes, and food from the Maryland Food Bank. Many of those were made possible by donations.The entire event is funded through grants, sponsors and monetary donations from the community. And all donated items found homes that day.

title: Perfectionist gets stressed at work
author: Harriette Cole
content:
Perfectionist gets stressed at work

 November 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Harriette Cole | Page: 21 | Section: News 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DEAR HARRIETTE:I'm a perfectionist, and it's causing me a lot of stress. I recently accepted a job that proved to be overwhelming to me.I thought I would be good at it, but I had to stretch a lot, and it just seemed like I was not doing anything right. I ended up quitting after one week. I felt like such a failure.My boss didn't say that I was doing a bad job, but she kept pointing out things that I needed to work on. I just couldn't take it. Now I am unemployed and feel like even more of a loser. How can I regain my confidence when my perfectionism is probably what landed me here in the first place?-Crippling PerfectionismDEAR CRIPPLING PERFECTIONISM:Give yourself credit for recognizing that you may be too much of a perfectionist. In our culture, being a high achiever - being the best■is lauded.Know that you are not alone in your desire to do everything right and likely better than others. Know, too, that this is unhealthy and can lead to situations like you described where you feel compelled to walk away rather than face whatever situation is before you.According to VeryWell-Mind.com, signs of perfectionism include: all-or-nothing thinking, being highly critical, having unrealistic standards, focusing only on unmet goals, fear of failure, procrastination, defensiveness and low self-esteem.You can work to combat those feelings by establishing daily affirmations that speak to your talents and goodness. Give yourself a break. Showing up and doing your best are good. And good is just fine.You may want to see a therapist to help you navigate the current crisis and help you develop strategies for managing your expectations and outcomes.Harriette Cole is a lifestylist andfounder ofDREAM-LEAPERS, an initiative to help people access and activate their dreams. You can send questions toaskharri-ette@harriettecole.com.

title: Patricia 'Pat' Harris remembered at 10th Crabs for a Cure
author: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com
content:
Patricia 'Pat' Harris remembered at 10th Crabs for a Cure

 KENT NARROWS - The 10th annual Crabs for a Cure hosted at Harris Crab House, and sponsored by Bosom Buddies Charities took place with a record turnout of 180 people attending, during the month of October, national Breast Cancer Awareness Month.The event, which originally began 10 years ago with about 40 people, said Harris Crab House President Bill Oertel, has grown every year. The restaurant was at its limit for capacity that weeknight evening.Bosom Buddies Charities, Inc., Chair Claudia Boldyga welcomed all who attended saying, "There's just nothing quite like cracking crabs and enjoying the company of family and friends. BBC's mission is to raise awareness, encourage early detection, support treatment, and celebrate healing. In our 17 years, BBC has raised almost $3 million enabling our organization to purchase state-ofthe-art equipment, including the first digital and later 3D mammography for Anne Arundel Medical Center on Kent Island, and provide invaluable nurse navigator and genetic counseling support for health care facilities on the Eastern Shore and Annapolis." She added, "We're a 100% volunteer organization and the proceeds of our fundraising stays in our local communities.The important work we do to fulfill our mission would not be possible without the support from local businesses like Harris Crab House. We want to thank the entire Harris and Oertel families for this beautiful waterfront venue and delicious food, and we're grateful to Harris Crab House throughout the past 10 years. All the food and drink you are enjoying this evening has been completely donated by Harris Crab House!" She continued, "Ten years ago, a group of ladies came up with the idea to have this crab feast to raise money for breast cancer awareness.One of those ladies was Pat Harris. In her historic battle with this disease, Pat showed courage and tenacity.Tonight, we celebrate Pat - an amazing woman and her unsung contributions to our cause." Harris passed away earlier in 2023 from a 20 year on again, off again battle with breast cancer.Married to Jerry Harris, he and Pat went on the build the restaurant, and have a large family that today includes grandchildren and great grandchildren.The evening's food not only included steamed hard shell crabs, but a wonderful seafood buffet of fried soft shell crab almandine, large steamed shrimp, fried oysters, roast beef, chicken alfredo, and sides of roasted red potato slices, Brussel sprouts, pasta salad and vegetable crab soup.It was announced that the upcoming Bosom Buddies Ball will be held Saturday evening, March 23, 2024, at the Westin Hotel, Annapolis.This event always sells out. This year's theme is "Setting Sail for New Horizons".

title: Grace Street, Sheriff Launch Holiday Program For Children Affected By Addiction
author: Contributed
content:
Grace Street, Sheriff Launch Holiday Program For Children Affected By Addiction

 November 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Grace Street and the Talbot County Sheriff 's Office this week announced a Christmas shopping program for children and teens affected by substance use in Talbot County.Nicole's Promise directly supports young people who have lost a parent to addiction with a special shopping trip hosted by Talbot County Sheriff 's deputies.The program also includes a Christmas gift drive for children and teens with a parent struggling with, or in early recovery from, substance use disorder.The program is in honor of Nicole, a good friend of Bri S., a peer support specialist at Grace Street."Nicole was a vibrant soul, full of life and possibility," Bri said."Addiction took her from us too soon, leaving six children behind without a mother. I cannot take away the pain of those children, who are left motherless, but I can do something meaningful in Nicole's honor."Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble, who says he has long supported recovery and has spearheaded prevention efforts in the region with Talbot Goes Purple and other programs, quickly agreed to partner on Nicole's Promise.In December, deputies will take the children and teens on a holiday shopping trip, before returning to the sheriff 's office for cookies and activities with an elf."I have seen too many families get torn apart by this disease of addiction, and the hardest hit are the children that get left behind when a parent overdoses," Gamble said. "We're glad that we can help bring some holiday cheer to those kids as we continue our fight against the opioid epidemic."Grace Street is accepting donations for Nicole's Promise. To sponsor the program, or to purchase gifts off the wishlist, visit gracestreetrecovery.org.The gift list program also is available in Caroline County.Audra Williamson with Mid-Shore Restoring Hope heard about the program through her volunteer work with Grace Street and partnered to bring the toy drive to Caroline County.Donations are accepted at Aaron's Place at 401 Aldersgate Drive in Denton. title: Seminar Focuses On Trends In Pancreatic Cancer Care
author: Contributed
content:
Seminar Focuses On Trends In Pancreatic Cancer Care

 November 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 698
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NEAVITT - Pancreatic cancer is a relatively rare cancer, representing only 3% of estimated new cancer diagnoses each year.However, it is especially lethal. Presently the third leading cause of cancer death, pancreatic cancer kills more than 50,000 Americans every year.For the Mid-Shore Pancreatic Cancer Foundation Inc., supporting efforts to advance the diagnosis and treatment of pancreatic cancer and educating the public about risk factors and symptoms of the disease are key strategies for saving lives.On this year's World Pancreatic Cancer Awareness Day Nov. 16, the Foundation sponsored a seminar, "New Trends in Pancreatic Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment," in the Cadby Theatre at Chesapeake College in Wye Mills.Designed for clinicians involved in patient care, the evening program featured presentations by three leading University of Maryland Medical System oncology specialists: Nader Hanna, a professor of surgery at UM School of Medicine and director of clinical operations for the Division of General and Oncologic Surgery at the University of Maryland Medical Center (UMMC); Yixing Jiang, a professor of medicine at UM SOM and director of GI medical oncology at the Marlene and Stewart Greenebaum Cancer Center at UMMC; and Jason K. Molitoris, an associate professor of radiation oncology at UM SOM, associate medical director at the Department of Radiation Oncology at UMMC, and director of Clinical Hyperthermia Program.Hanna provided an overview of various risk factors for pancreatic cancer, including heredity (indicating a family history of certain genetic mutations) and smoking, and noted that symptoms of the disease, such as weight loss, back pain, jaundice and adult-onset (over age 65) diabetes, most often don't present until the disease is relatively advanced.He also reviewed various diagnostic strategies and surgical approaches, stressing the importance of surgical resection as the most significant factor for survival.Jiang discussed the genetic aspects of pancreatic cancer and how chemotherapy drugs are tailored to address the specific mutations identified in individual patients.She noted that systemic chemotherapy provides curative results for less than 30 percent of patients and that side effects can be very severe. However, in many cases it does improve survival time and also palliates cancer-related symptoms.Molitoris described the role of radiation in treating pancreatic cancer, including challenges caused by the location of the pancreas near other tissues that can be damaged by radiation.He described the criteria for cases in which radiation is employed prior to surgery to shrink tumor size, or after surgery to palliate complications from the disease and improve quality of life."We were really pleased to have a good turnout for this event, and the presenters provided very clear and detailed updates from the standpoint of their practice," said Bill Shrieves, president of the Mid-Shore Pancreatic Foundation Inc."The Foundation does a lot to support pancreatic cancer patients and to raise funds for research on the disease, but as one of our volunteers commented, this event might be the most important thing we've done as an organization.If just one of the clinicians who attended does something different based on the information that was shared and it improves the outcome for a pancreatic cancer patient, that is the best kind of success," he said.Shrieves also credited support from Tidewater Rotary in making the event possible."A generous grant of $5,000 from Rotary's Flags for Cancer Program made it possible for us to offer this event free of charge, and we are very grateful for that support," he said.Established in 2013, The Mid-Shore Pancreatic Cancer Foundation Inc. sponsors and participates in events that raise awareness about pancreatic cancer in the community, and also helps patients and their families in the Mid-Shore region find assistance, financial support and transportation to and from treatments.The group funds research through direct grants or support for other organizations, such as the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network.For more information about The Mid-Shore Pancreatic Cancer Foundation, Inc., visit midshorepancan.org/or call 410-745-9243.

title: November is national Family Caregivers Month
author: Mary Land Department Of Aging

November is national Family Caregivers Month

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Land Department Of Aging | Page: 12 | Section: News 
 
 757

 Enrollment is now open for Medicare.The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released 2024 premium, deductible, and coinsurance amounts for Medicare Parts A and B, and the 2024 Medicare Part D income-related monthly adjustment amounts.Medicare Part A covers inpatient hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, hospice, inpatient rehabilitation, and some home health care services. However, about 99 percent of Medicare beneficiaries do not have a Part A premium since they have at least 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment, as determined by the Social Security Administration.Medicare Part B covers physicians' services, outpatient hospital services, certain home health services, durable medical equipment, and other medical and health services not covered by Medicare Part A. The standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B enrollees will be $174.70 for 2024, an increase of $9.80 from $164.90 in 2023. The annual deductible for all Medicare Part B beneficiaries will be $240 in 2024, an increase of $14 from the annual deductible of $226 in 2023.A beneficiary's Part D monthly premium adjustment is based on his or her income and affects roughly 8 percent of people with Medicare Part D. These individuals will pay the income-related monthly adjustment amount in addition to their Part D premium.NATIONAL FAMILY CAREGIVERS MONTHCelebrated every November, National Family Caregivers Month is a time to recognize and honor family caregivers, including spouses, adult children, relatives, and friends, who provide invaluable support to older adults and people with disabilities.More than 53 million family caregivers provide unpaid care across the country.AARP estimates that in 2021, family caregivers provided 36 billion hours of care valued at $600 billion, up from 34 billion hours of care valued at $470 billion just two years before. At the same time, at least 2.7 million grandparents-and an unknown number of other relative caregivers-carry the primary responsibility for caring for grandchildren whose parents are unable to do so."We recognize the need for a robust, coordinated approach to supporting family and kinship caregivers," said Maryland Department of Aging Secretary Carmel Roques. "As the youngest Baby Boomers turn 65 in 2029 and lifespans continue to climb into the 80s and beyond, the demand for at-home care is going to soar."MARYLAND FAMILY CAREGIVER SUPPORT PROGRAMIn an effort to help family and informal caregivers care for loved ones at home for as long as possible, the Maryland Department of Aging administers the Family Caregiver Support Program (FCSP) through the Area Agency on Aging (AAA) network. AAAs provide FCSP services including counseling, case management, training, support group resources, information and referral, and respite care. To learn more about the program, funded by the Administration for Community Living, or find events taking place in your county celebrating family caregivers, go to aging.maryland.gov. To find out what local resources are available in your area, contact Maryland Access Point at 1-844-627-5465 or go to www.marylandaccesspoint.info.VA CAREGIVER SUPPORT PROGRAMThe Veterans Administration Caregiver Support Program (CSP) has launched new legal and financial planning support services, as well as a new web-based educational tool, to provide comprehensive support to veterans and promote the health and well-being of veteran caregivers Eligible participants, including primary family caregivers who support veterans, can access licensed attorneys and certified financial counselors who can provide expert-led consultative financial planning and legal services relating to the needs of injured veterans and their caregivers.In addition, these primary caregivers can access essential financial and legal resources at the VA Caregiver Support: Providing Legal and Financial Services to Veteran Caregiver website."Being a primary family caregiver is a noble and challenging role requiring immense dedication and sacrifice," said Dr. Colleen Richardson, CSP Executive Director. "At CSP, we are dedicated to providing caregivers with the resources they need to navigate the encounters of caregiving and achieve their caregiving goals."SUPPORTIVE COMMUNITIES AND VILLAGESThe Maryland Department of Aging (MDOA) was pleased to take part in the National Village Gathering held last month in Silver Spring, MD to increase collaboration with the Village network as part of the MDOA's Supportive Communities Initiative.Villages are community-based, nonprofit organizations formed through a cadre of caring neighbors who connect members to an array of practical support and social services that enable older adults to enjoy an independent quality of life in their homes and communities.Through the Supportive Communities Initiative, MDOA will continue to engage with the Village network, as well as other neighbor-to-neighbor initiatives, faith-based groups, and nonprofit organizations in an effort to improve opportunities for Marylanders to age in place.Learn more about Villages at vtvnetwork.org or find a Village near you at www.wavevillages.org.The above information is courtesy of the Maryland Department of Aging

UM Shore cuts ribbon for renovated interventional radiology suite

 December 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 EASTON - The Interventional Radiology suite at UM Shore Medical Center at Easton recently underwent major renovations to accommodate new X-ray equipment.Due to the size of the new equipment, the room has been completely revamped, including new cabinetry and flooring, an updated control room and a new area for team members to scrub-in. The cost of the project was $2.3 million."Our prior equipment was more than 20 years old," said Penny Olivi, director of Radiology Services at UM Shore Regional Health. "With this completely upgraded room and the state-of-the-art digital X-ray equipment, we are now able to offer new, more complex procedures that will help patients with minimally invasive interventions." The Interventional Radiology suite typically sees about 100 patients each month, and the IR team provides clinical support for all areas within UM SRH; however, the key areas where the team provides the most support are cancer care and dialysis access.The new suite was designed so that it could be completely disassembled, down to the cabinetry, and then reassembled and integrated into UM Shore Regional Health's new regional hospital, set to open in 2028."This is groundbreaking technology and a huge advantage for our Shore communities," said Ken Kozel, president and CEO of UM Shore Regional Health. "Knowing we could safely transfer the equipment to the new regional medical center, we wanted to offer this state-of-the-art advanced care to our patients now."And now patients don't have to travel across the Bay Bridge for this type of expert care and minimally invasive procedures.They're available right here, close to home." Interventional radiologists diagnose and treat disease and a wide range of conditions in the body by utilizing various small tools, such as catheters or wires.X-ray and imaging techniques, such as CT and ultrasound help guide the radiologist.Interventional radiology can be used instead of surgery for many conditions, and in some cases, it can eliminate the need for hospitalization. Interventional radiologists work closely with a patient's care team and play an important role in a patient's treatment plan.UM SRH Radiology Services also partners with the Radiologic Sciences Degree Program at Chesapeake College. The partnership allows X-ray students to attend clinical rotations in all UM Shore Regional Health facilities.Many current members of the Shore Radiology team attended Chesapeake College's program, and this ongoing partnership enables UM SRH staff to share their knowledge and expertise with the next generation of radiologic technologist graduates.Interventional Radiology training is also provided onsite by UM SRH Radiology Services. General X-ray technologists with an interest in this intense, minimally invasive surgical approach to diagnosis and treatment are trained by experienced and skilled techs and the IR Radiologist team, Dale Johnson, MD, and Brian Callahan, MD.There is also an advanced certification in IR available to UM SRH team members.

title: Lead Persists As Problem In Holiday Gifts
author: Cecelia Shilling; Capital News Service
content:
Lead Persists As Problem In Holiday Gifts

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Cecelia Shilling; Capital News Service | Page: B9 | Section: News 
 
 798
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - Lead poisoning has hit the news recently with pollution from leaded aviation gasoline, poisoning from applesauce pouches and federal lead pipe replacement projects.But some lead poisoning threats come during the holiday gift-giving season from jewelry, toys, makeup and other gifts.
In October, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency highlighted the dangers of lead exposure from leaded gasoline still used by some small planes.Communities near general aviation airports experience disproportionate exposure from emissions, the release said.
The Food and Drug Administration is investigating lead found in cinnamon applesauce pouches sold under WanaBana, Weis and Schnucks brands.
As of Nov. 22, there have been 52 cases of elevated blood lead levels in young children potentially linked to these pouches.
On Nov. 30, the EPA announced a proposal to require replacement of lead service lines nationwide within 10 years, according to a press release. The administration is investing $15 billion in replacing lead service lines, providing technical assistance to communities and developing a national inventory of lead pipes.
"The lead dust equivalent of only three granules of sugar is all it takes to poison a child," said a University of Maryland Medical Center release.
Added to all those threats during the holiday season is the lead sometimes hidden in common gifts like jewelry, makeup or toys, said Jay Apperson, a spokesperson for the Maryland Department of the Environment.
Vintage items or things manufactured in other countries are more likely to be contaminated.
"No child should be left behind because of lead poisoning," said Apperson.
"Public education about the importance of getting tested, along with strong enforcement, will all go a long way towards eradicating lead poisoning."
Children are the most vulnerable to lead poisoning and experience symptoms like irritability, issues with attention and learning, delayed growth and hearing issues. Severe cases can cause brain damage and neurological dysfunction, even death.
And lead poisoning can impact cardiac health, pregnancy and hypertension.
In Maryland, children must be tested for blood lead at 12 months and 24 months according to the Maryland Department of Health. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention uses a reference value of 3.5 micrograms per deciliter to identify children with blood lead levels higher than average.
Lead paint found in older homes is a leading cause of lead poisoning, with most childhood exposure coming from hand-to-mouth contact with lead dust.
"If a child has a very elevated blood lead level, that's almost surely the root cause of lead-based paint. If you get down to these relatively lower levels, say in the 3.5 (micrograms per deciliter) range, then you might need to look at other potential sources that might not be so obvious," Apperson said.
Inexpensive jewelry has often been found to contain lead. Lead allows metals to be shaped easily and is cheaper than alternatives like zinc, said the California Department of Toxic Substance Control.
"Lead is also sometimes used as a stabilizer in some plastics, such as polyvinyl chloride (PVC), which is often incorporated into children's jewelry items," said the department.
Another common gift item, makeup, can also be a problem. Kohl eyeliners, used in Asian and African cultures for example, may contain large amounts of lead and other metals, according to the FDA.
One 2013 case from the New Mexico Department of Health began when an Afghan refugee family brought eyeliner to the U.S. An Albuquerque clinic reported that a toddler had a blood lead level of 27 micrograms per deciliter linked to the use of kajal eyeliner, the report said. Lab testing later identified the eyeliner's lead content as 54%.
Inexpensive toys can also have lead in paint, metal or plastic. Vintage toys made before 1978, when lead paint was banned for residential use, or imported toys are more likely to contain the substance.
In 2007, for example, about 253,000 "Sarge" toys, a character from the Cars movie, were recalled by Mattel for containing lead paint, according to the Consumer Product Safety Commission.
About 675,000 Mattel Barbie accessory toys were also recalled that same year due to lead paint. Both toys were manufactured in China.
The non-profit organization Kids in Danger said recalls of children's products due to excessive lead content increased to 19 instances in 2022, the highest rate of lead-related recalls in the last 10 years, according to a 2023 document called "Hidden Hazards: 2022 Children's Product Recalls." Nine lead-related recalls were announced in 2020.
"We really have to focus in on what will be permanent eradication of exposure and poisoning and that job needs to be finished," said Ruth Ann Norton, president and CEO of the Green and Healthy Homes Initiative.
"And that takes both funding and diligence."

title: Complicated Crossroads
author: Mike Sunnucks
content:
Complicated Crossroads

 December 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1754
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After high-profile mass shootings, calls to focus on mental health - including passing more red flag gun confiscation laws and expanding involuntary commitment statutes - have become as frequent as pushes for increased gun control."It's about mental health." has become a common refrain after shootings.
The mental health component of America's longstanding debate over guns and its crossroads with high-profile mass and school shootings is dotted with misperceptions and misunderstandings of the issue, what's already on the books and how red flag and commitment laws are and are not being used to help those in crisis from hurting themselves and others.
There are also civil liberties and constitutional questions regarding allowing the government and/or police to put someone in a mental hospital or take away their guns.
POLICE, 911 CALLS
One of the biggest challenges is that mental health action and interventions often start after an emergency 911 call to police when a crisis situation is already happening.
It's often a police officer rushing to a scene who is the first to deal with someone threatening or already harming themselves or others.
"The de facto response is still law enforcement," said Lisa Dailey, executive director of the Treatment Advocacy Center, a Virginia-based group focused on civil commitment laws and other mental health issues.
She said the mental health system and approaches have to change that dynamic.
"They are not being implemented to get people the care that they need in the right time frame," Dailey said.
Despite the talk of increasing mental health resources and putting a dent in long-held societal and family stigmas, Jack McDevitt, a professor of practice emeritus in criminology and criminal justice at Northeastern University in Boston, said a 911 call is still frequently the entry point to law enforcement and other agencies response to a person going through a mental health crisis and potentially harming themselves or others.
Sometimes those police officers have no background information on a person's mental state or history of mental illness.
McDevitt, who has helped Massachusetts lawmakers with gun policy proposals, said it is important for 911 operators to be able to get information and mental health histories from callers. But that is not always easy in stressful and sometimes violent situations when emergency calls occur.
He sees merits in having counselors and social workers respond to some mental health calls and wellness checks that do not involve violence - with police sometimes in a support role.
That may help diffuse situations.
"They aren't the ones knocking on the door," said McDevitt, referring to programs in Florida, Wisconsin, Wyoming and other states.
'PATCHWORK SYSTEM'
All U.S. states have some form of involuntary or civil commitment laws that allow for temporary or short-term placements in inpatient mental health settings, including hospitals, when a person shows serious signs of committing suicide or harming or killing others.
The landscape for those state laws is mixed with some states allowing for court-order holds and commitments related to substance abuse, according to a report by the Treatment Advocacy Center. five states - including Florida, California, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming - allow for 72-hour holds.
Another seven states (such as Georgia and Texas) and the District of Columbia have 48-hour limits on the time someone can be involuntarily committed.
Eight states - including Maryland (30 hours), Delaware (24 hours) and Montana (the next business day) - have shorter time limits, according to TAC.
Some state laws allow for family members to petition for commitments and there are situations where judges can impose holds related to substance abuse and self-harm.
For example, judges in Colorado can impose 180-days holds for substance abuse treatment.
"Our system is very patchwork," Dailey said.
Dailey said states need to look at how to better match mental health policies, including commitment laws, to the needs of patients. She said proper mental health treatment programs can take six months - not the 72-hour holds on the books in most states.
DISINCENTIVES AND DIFFICULTIES
That varied and piecemeal approach isn't just related to varying state laws related to commitments and gun confiscation.
Mental health systems across the country are challenged by lack of inpatient facility capacity and a system where treatment, housing, employment and substance abuse services can be siloed.
"It's still really difficult to navigate the system," said Dailey, pointing to the lack of a central agency, information or support source for patients and their families.
That can leave individuals dealing with severe mental illness such as schizophrenia, bipolar and borderline personality disorders to navigate various bureaucracies while trying to overcome stigmas and fears of past and contemporary mistreatment of the "mentally ill." "Individuals have often had very bad experiences at inpatient or law enforcement settings," Dailey said.
Stigmas toward mental health continue including hospitalizations for patients worried about reactions from their families, friends and employers.
There are pushes in New York and some other states to allow for longer mandated hospitalizations and to make it easier for police and courts to involuntarily commit seriously mentally ill persons, including homeless people, after a series of high-profile assaults.
Some bioethicists and mental health professionals argue that inpatient hospitalizations are not always the best treatment path for some patients.
Civil libertarians worry expanding forced hospitalizations can lead to discriminatory treatment by courts and police of some classes of patients. There is plenty of history in the U.S. and other countries of political, religious and ethnic minorities as well as women being disproportionately "put away" by government authorities and mental health practitioners.
"Involuntary hospitalization is a serious deprivation of liberty that can be justified only in the narrow circumstance where there is mental illness and an imminent physical danger to the person to be committed or to others, evidenced by observed behavior, and where there is no less restrictive alternative. In such cases, strong procedural safeguards must be in place throughout to ensure that the due process rights of the individual are protected," said the New York Civil Liberties Union in response to state and local efforts to expand civil commitments.
But even if police and courts are more aggressive in pursuing forced hospitalizations, many states and regions lack the number of mental inpatient beds needed to accommodate such a push.
Police officers have to go through a number of legal and bureaucratic hoops to gain temporary and short-term holds.
"It'a big challenge," said Dailey, noting that officers can spend several hours going through the inpatient mental health process.
Some states require specific staffing to transport an individual to a mental health hospital or another inpatient facility. And even then, police will find facilities completely full.
"It's much easier to bring them in and book them," she said.
BY THE NUMBERS
The U.S. has seen a contemporary decline in the number of mental hospitals and institutionalized patients.
In 1955, when state mental asylums and short and long-term commitments were more common there were more than 500,000 beds nationally, according to the American Psychiatric Association.
In 1963, there were 800,000 mentally ill developmentally disabled persons kept in institutional settings - often at overcrowded and toxic mental hospitals, according to the Kennedy administration which pushed for systematic changes away from asylums.
As many as 1.5 million people were treated annually at those sanatoriums in the early 1960s.
A study last year by the National Association of State Mental Health Program Directors Research Institute Inc. showed there were still close to 471,500 patients at government-run, private and other mental hospitals in 1970.
That number stands at just 121,300 in 2020, the most recent data available.
Moves toward de-institutionalization and U.S. health care business models focused away from inpatient settings have driven that trend.
RED FLAG LAWS
Shootings in Maine in October that killed 18 people and injured 13 and at the University of Nevada Las Vegas Dec. 6 that killed three persons have sparked new looks at mental health approaches and red flag gun laws - especially after details of the New England killings by U.S. Army firearms instructor Robert Card emerged.
Twenty-one states have so-called red flag laws on the books allowing for court and law enforcement to temporarily seize guns from individuals deemed likely to harm others or themselves.
Those states include Nevada, Washington, Oregon, California, Florida, Maryland, Delaware, Illinois and New York, according to Everytown for Gun Safety, which supports increased gun control laws.
"Red flag laws are a tool law enforcement and others can use when somebody is clearly at high risk of doing something with a firearm, but they can't be arrested because no crime has been committed and they don't appear to need a mental health hold or qualify for one," said Amy Barnhorst, a psychiatrist at University of California, Davis, Health and a violence prevention expert in an analysis of the issue earlier this year.
Maine's gun confiscation law requires an extra step of those states of having the individual question go through a mental health evaluation.
McDevitt said most of the time gun confiscations are done in response to concerns about potential suicide attempts and firearms are usually returned to their owners.
It can save some people from hurting themselves," said McDevitt, citing research showing for the laws can help reduce suicides.
There were 26,933 suicides committed with firearms in 2022 compared to with 19,592 homicides, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control.
Suicides by firearms made up 56.9% of all gun deaths and 54.4% of all suicides last year, according to CDC figures. McDevitt said owners often get guns back after anywhere between 30 days and six months depending on the state statute.
Pushes for additional red flags in other states face resistance from gun rights advocates. The National Rifle Association's Institute for Legislative Action worries red flag gun laws could be used by the government to take guns from critics and political opponents.
'RARELY USED'
Despite their increased advocacy, McDevitt said gun confiscation proceedings are rare.
"There aren't thousands and thousands of these things. They are pretty rarely used," he said.
A 2022 analysis by the Associated Press said red flag laws have been little used due to lack of awareness and resistance from some sheriff 's offices and police departments to such policies on Second Amendment grounds.
Part of that also stems from families being reluctant to broach the issue, McDevitt said.
"That's a very difficult conversation to have.
Most people don't want to do that," he said.

Firearms account for the majority of suicides in the U.S. and more people take their own lives with guns than commit homicides with firearms.

title: Rabid cat reported in Legion Road, Denton area
author: CAROLINE COUNTY HEALTH DEPARTMENT
content:
Rabid cat reported in Legion Road, Denton area

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CAROLINE COUNTY HEALTH DEPARTMENT | Page: A2 | Section: News 
 
 362
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Maryland Department of Health laboratory has confirmed a positive rabid cat in the Legion Road area of Denton. The cat was turned into the Humane Society, which then contacted the Caroline County Health Department's Environmental Health Division to facilitate rabies testing.Any person in the vicinity of Legion Road should avoid contact with wildlife, feral cats, unknown animals and any animal (including cats or dogs) that appears sick or to exhibit signs of rabies. Additionally, all residents in the area are urged to make sure their pets and mammal livestock are up to date on rabies vaccinations.
To report a potentially rabid animal, contact Animal Control at (410) 820-1600 or the non-emergency line of the 911 Center at (410) 479-2222.
Please contact the Caroline County Health Department immediately if you have had, or may know of anyone who might have had, any possible human or animal exposure to a rabid animal at (410) 479-8045.
If you have an emergency regarding a potential rabid animal or exposure and are calling after normal business hours or on the weekend, call (410) 829-5910.
An exposure can mean contamination of open wounds, abrasions, mucous membranes or scratches by potentially contaminated with infectious material from a rabid animal.
Additionally, any penetration of the skin by teeth constitutes a bite exposure. All bites, regardless of body site, represent a potential risk of rabies transmission, but that risk varies with the species of biting animal, the site of the bite and the severity of the wound.
Rabies is a serious, but preventable viral disease that attacks the nervous system. It is predominantly seen in raccoons, bats and skunks, as well as dogs and cats.
All wild or unknown animals must be avoided whenever possible since the possibility of exposure to rabies can occur anywhere and anytime.
Pet owners should remember that the best way to protect themselves, their families and their pets is to keep their animals up to date on rabies vaccination.
The Health Department regularly offers low-cost rabies clinics to help residents protect their pets. The next clinic will be held in the spring. Please monitor the Health Department's Events Calendar for more information.
For more information about rabies, visit CDC's Rabies Prevention webpage at cdc.gov/rabies/prevention/index.html.

author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Festival of Trees raises $50K for Compass Hospice

 December 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News

 DENTON - Dozens of donated, decorated evergreen trees at the Towers Family Historical Museum in Hobbs were not just a beautiful display of Christmas cheer. They prompted $50,000 in donations for Compass Hospice's work in Caroline County.Despite the rainy weather, the annual Festival of Trees the first weekend of December attracted almost two dozen corporate sponsors who raised over $25,000 of the total proceeds. Sponsorship levels ranged from $5,000 or more to $250.
About 130 people attended the preview party Friday, Dec. 1, to put in their bids for tiny, tabletop trees to elaborately decorated trees with extras, and everything in between.
I think it's the best year yet," said Compass Hospice CEO Heather Guerieri Sunday afternoon.
"A lot of the same people do trees and sponsor over and over, and they just get more talented and more creative every year." Co-chairs of this year's festival were Melanie McMahan and Dave Whaley.
When all the receipts were counted, the result was "the most successful Festival of Trees to date," Baird wrote in a Dec. 15 email.
"It's been great," said Compass Hospice Development Director Shelly Baird Sunday afternoon.
"We have 76 trees, which is the most we've ever had." This is the sixth year the event has been held at the Towers Family Historical Museum on Sennett Road.
Owners Bill and Gail Towers "are so generous," Baird said. "They host this and they donate and they're amazing." "We just want the bids to go up," Gail Towers said, laughing as she imitated the chiming sound of new bids on the Trice Auctions website.
"I just can't wait till it starts bing, bing, bing, bing, bing." The preview party's "Pick of the Tree Lot" raffle raised $3,000. The winner, who could choose any tree in the display, chose "Chestnuts Roasting on an Open Fire," a snowy, woodland-themed tree and extras donated by the Strzempka family. It was won by Jill Pugh of Shore Industries of Denton, one of the festival's sponsors.
The Strzempka family's 2022 tree won the raffle as well. Along with this year's tree, they donated a fire pit and supplies, as well as decorations created by family members from across the country.
Created in memory of the family patriarch who had been cared for by Compass Hospice at the end of his life, "the whole family came three different days to get it perfect," Baird said.
"One of the granddaughters, I believe in Seattle, donated these hand blown icicles. Another grandchild made the skirts. These are handmade mittens by another family member," she said.
"I don't know all the stories, but I'm sure many of these other trees have a story," Baird said.
About four trees sported a Grinch theme. Some trees were rustic, other elegant.
Several tabletop trees were made of seashells. North Caroline High School's Spanish IV class created a "We are Bulldogs!" tree while Choptank Electric Cooperative honored 100 years of Disney.
Some creators donated several trees; florist Sherry Councell created a dozen.
Festival attendees picked up information for online bidding hosted by Trice Auctions of Denton. Bidding ended at 4 p.m. Sunday, and winners picked up their trees the following Monday and Tuesday.
The festival "proceeds stay in Caroline County for hospice services and grief services," Guerieri said. "We don't turn people away based on ability to pay if they don't have insurance for hospice." Baird said fundraisers like the Festival of Trees provides for Compass Hospices services in Caroline, Kent and Queen Anne's counties.
"We have to raise about $500,000 to $700,000 a year through donations" because insurance doesn't cover every hospice service," Baird said.
"Our entire grief services support department is not covered by insurance, so all of about $400,000 of that goes to that department. We provide counseling to close to 800 people a year, and a lot of them were not even involved with hospice." Among them are children in each of the three counties' schools.
Compass Hospice, based in Centreville, provides hospice and supportive care in-home and at the Barnette Center in Centreville and Arcadia Assisted Living in Denton; community grief support; and veterans services.
"This is just such a heartwarming experience to be able to volunteer and be among such a special group of people that do care, and their heart is in it," volunteer Connie Calloway Hutson said. "That's the reason I do it. I'm just so proud that I can do it." Bill Towers said they sponsor fundraisers for hospice "because it's an organization that needs some support." "And he has a heart of gold," Gail Towers said.
"They do a great job.
We've never had to use hospice," Bill Towers said, as his wife added, "It's one of those things that you're glad that they have it." "But you hope you never have to use it," he said.
