 EASTON - The Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday found an amended version of a resolution, which would ensure some county oversight in future expansion of the Lakeside at Trappe wastewater treatment plant, to be consistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.The unanimous finding of consistency comes after several months of discussion on the legislation.If passed by the Talbot County Council, Resolution 338 would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for a wastewater treatment plant serving the Lakeside at Trappe development.The discharge permit at the center of the legislation was issued in October 2022. It's limited to the first phase of the project and allows for an initial annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or 250 gallons perday per equivalent dwelling unit.A major permit modification approved by MDE is required for future expansion of the wastewater treatment plant.The resolution, which was introduced by County Council member Lynn Mielke in February, would also mandate future expansion of the new plant to require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.In October, the resolution was found inconsistent with the comprehensive plan due to a map needing to be reviewed, though planning commission members endorsed the legislation's basic principles.That endorsement led to a chance for reconsideration of the finding in November and into December.The amendment to the resolution considered Tuesday by the planning commission was introduced by Mielke and Council Vice President Pete Lesher on Nov. 28. It adds language requiring a certification from the Talbot County Planning Commission of an expansion amendment's consistency with the comprehensive plan.To Chip Councell, chairman of the planning commission, the amended resolution would be the county's only chance for a review of potential expansion.Councell said it would be "irresponsible" of the county to not look at social factors, including hospitals and schools, when reviewing future expansion, especially considering changes from just the last three years."The world is different, and we don't know what it's going to look like in eight to 10 years, and I just don't see how we can write a blank check," he said. "I trust the Town of Trappe when it comes to their development and what it does. I don't think it's reasonable to put that burden of these other services on all the citizens of Talbot County." The planning commission was also set to consider Resolution 347 and its amendment, along with Resolution 348 - legislation related to Lakeside - on Tuesday, but the five-member board unanimously voted to postpone discussion until they receive a recommendation from the county's Public Works Advisory Board.The two resolutions, introduced in September, address updated information on equivalent dwelling units for all phases of the Lakeside development, along with clarifying Trappe's water and sewer service maps.The Public Works Advisory Board's next meeting is set for Thursday, Dec. 21.No agenda has been made available yet.

title: Highway Administration hears from public on Route 404
author: Maggie Trovato; trovato@chespub.com
content:
Highway Administration hears from public on Route 404

 DENTON - The Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration gave Caroline County residents the opportunity to share their thoughts on state Route 404 between Harmony Road and Greenwood Road at a public open house held at Denton Elementary School on Wednesday.SHA Project Manager Carmeletta Harris said the purpose of the open house is to get feedback from the public on what they would like to see regarding Route 404."We are not presenting any concepts tonight," Harris said. "We want them to tell us what else is out here that we haven't seen yet." At the open house, poster boards lined the school cafeteria to show SHA's findings from its Planning and Environmental Linkages Study.The purpose of the study is to assess transportation needs.Information was broken down into seven sections: Study overview, PEL process, environmental overview, transportation needs, mapping, Title VI and safety.At the mapping station, residents could place post-it notes with their concerns on a map of Route 404.According to the information displayed at the event, the top five dislikes, gathered from stakeholder interviews so far, are congestion, uncontrolled intersections, danger from high speeds and trucks, accidents and that there is not a dual lane all the way through.Harris said SHA wants to listen to residents before presenting any concepts. Currently, SHA plans to develop preliminary improvement concepts this winter and present those concepts for feedback in the spring. It also plans to finalize its study recommendations and identify any potential stand-alone projects in the spring.Harris said the project is not funded for anything outside of the study."Not construction and things of that nature," she said. "That could come down the line But right now, we're tasked to do this study and develop some concepts." Bruce Pepper, who lives on Mitchell Road, said he's most interested in seeing the concepts that the SHA comes up with.One of Pepper's main concerns is traffic. He said that he has noticed Legion Road getting beach traffic."They run 60 miles an hour down that road," he said. "It's hilly, winding.And they think they're getting ahead, but they're not. But the GPS tells them it's a shortcut." Pepper's neighbors, Alyssa and Jamie Taylor, said they have concerns with safety and the accidents."We have only been here for about two and a half years," Alyssa Taylor said. "And we have walked up to, I would say, at least three - I can think of four or five accidents that we hear happen." The Taylors are especially interested to find out if Route 404 will be expanding."I would love to know if 404 is going to be in my front yard," Alyssa Taylor said.If that does happen, the Taylors would consider moving. They said it would affect property values and be a safety concern."Even though my front door right now is probably 160 feet from the centerline - If they do dual-lane, I don't want tractor trailers, cars, motorcycles, whatever, going 80 miles an hour now 60 feet from my door, 80 feet from my door," Jamie Taylor said.Alyssa Taylor said she was happy that SHA wanted to hear from residents and said that they had written down "everything that we're saying." John Booze said everyone from SHA was receptive and willing to listen."Tough forum too because everybody has their own issue," he said."I don't envy them. But they gave everybody a good listen and I think it'll be positive going forward." Booze said traffic volume and getting across Route 404 are some of his major concerns."Getting across the road," he said. "Whether it's somebody coming from a home. Whether it's somebody coming from business The folks that have frontage right on 404 I really am concerned about." Like Pepper, Booze has noticed more drivers taking roads that connect to MD 404."Because of Waze and GPS and Google Maps, people are starting to go farther out on the back roads to get where they want to go," he said.Booze said those drivers are driving fast and its causing the traffic problems to spread outside of Route 404."So you need to take that into consideration as well," he said. "That was one of the things that I wanted to make sure I shared with them when I came."

Residents weigh in on potential improvements to Matthewstown Road

 EASTON - Easton residents voiced desires to see improved pedestrian and bicycle access, left turn lanes and traffic volume mitigation on Matthewstown Road during a transportation open house Tuesday evening.Facilitated by the Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration, the open house served as an opportunity for residents to ask questions about the agency's working study of a 1.6-mile stretch of the busy two-lane road.A SHA team first began considering environmental, community and economic goals in terms of improvements along Matthewstown Road this past spring as part of a Planning and Environmental Linkages Study.According to survey data collected by SHA, residents primarily like the road's traffic lights and convenience.However, concerns were raised about extensive traffic congestion, timing issues with the traffic light at Elliot Road, speeding, excess development and a lack of sidewalks.Those concerns were echoed at Tuesday's open house, where residents were able to view an aerial map of the portion of the road being studied and place sticky notes on areas of concern.Notes included adding left turn lanes at the intersection of Matthewstown Road and Black Dog Alley and the road's intersection with Dyott Court, changing speed limits and coordination of signals to lessen traffic.Residents also highlighted the number of dense housing developments along the road, some of which have yet to be built, like Gannon Range.To Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey, who lives near Matthewstown Road, the lack of pedestrian and bicycle access along the road could stand to be improved.Efforts have been made to improve pedestrian access on the west side of Easton, particularly west of Route 50, but dense development on both sides of the highway necessitate taking steps to handle the additional volume.Adding sidewalks - and dedicated center turn lanes to avoid cars traveling around others on the shoulders - would be great, he said.But above all, Lowrey hopes the community will be engaged with the process of improving the busy road.Hunters Mill resident John Franczak raised concerns about the significant traffic on Matthewstown Road, noting long wait times for lights to change.Franczak said he would be willing to look at the possibility of a traffic circle somewhere along the road stretch in question to slow speeding traffic down, though he also voiced a request to lower the speed limit from 50 mph to 35 mph between the Hunters Mill neighborhood and Route 50.The SHA study is set to finish by spring 2024. title: Strand Beach Project To Be Completed By Summer
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com
content:
Strand Beach Project To Be Completed By Summer

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 839
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - With the first phase of construction complete, Oxford's Shoreline Improvement project along the Strand is expected to be complete by summer.Oxford Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said the first part of the project, to build the shoreline infrastructure, "touched on nearly all parts of the project."
This part, which was completed before Thanksgiving, included building a berm between the road and the water, placing hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to help bring sand in and creating small islands in the water to reduce the waves that come onto the beach.
Lewis said these island structures were built using a combination of rock, wood chips and other components.
"(The structures) will sit over the winter months, which allows them to stabilize," Lewis said. "It allows them to go through weather, high tides, we just had a fairly substantial storm, that sort of stuff."
Oxford Police Chief Eric Kellner said the construction brought in extra traffic, particularly with all of the materials that were brought in using larger vehicles like dump trucks.
In order to allow space for workers to do their job and to prevent damage to civilian vehicles, Kellner said that the police department, with the help of Public Works, closed the beach parking lot.
There were some concerns from residents about the large construction vehicles speeding in the area, Kellner said.
"In response to that, we did a few things," he said.
"One was, obviously, we ran radar to enforce the speed limits. And we also deployed our speed sign to remind the vehicles of their speed in hopes of calming any potential speed issues."
Kellner said that in running radar and collecting data from the speed sign, the police department really sees an issue with speeding.
He said that large and loud vehicles driving down a small, narrow street can sometimes give off the perception that the driver is speeding.
"Our findings were that most of those larger vehicles were following the rules of the road," he said.
In the spring, the second part of the project is set to begin.
"We're estimating April," Lewis said. "I mean a lot of this is dependent on weather temperatures, asphalt, plants, a lot of factors."
Lewis said the second part will include adding plants to the new structures, adding signage, elevating land on the far east end and making improvements to the parking lot.
"The whole concept is to build a higher area all along the Strand to protect it from the stormwaters off the river," Lewis said.
The parking lot will be built with storm management areas underneath it so that storm water can enter it and be filtered before going back out. The parking lot will be paved with asphalt, with a cobble layer underneath it.
"There's a lot of - not just tidal water coming from the river - but also stormwater settling along that road in the parking lot," Lewis said.
"So bringing all of that elevation up to prevent that and allowing the water to go under the road and then back out into the creek will basically build resilience for that whole area."
Lewis said that as the sea level rises and the intensity of storms increase, infrastructure along the Strand becomes more vulnerable.
"Keep in mind, this is the only road we really have that runs along the water," she said. "This area here, it's worthy of this type of resilience protection because a breach in any place, especially up near the parking lot, would be so difficult to repair."
Lewis called it a project for the future.
"With the impacts of sea level rise and stormwater and tidal water management that we're seeing currently," she said, "it's necessary to look at how to build in these areas with natural infrastructure that will help to protect it in the future."
David Ghysels, who walks along the Strand every day, said he thinks the project will be nice when it is complete, particularly if it helps with flooding.
Lewis said she has received positive and negative comments from residents on the project.
"I think the closer you are to the project physically, the more involved you may have been over the last five years," she said. "So I think that one of the impacts will be people who don't go there regularly or aren't involved in the government regularly all of a sudden want to know what happened. So it's really just a continued educational process."
Mac Sommerlatte, who lives next to the beach, said he thinks the project should, when finished, positively impact the town by minimizing shoreline erosion and mitigating the impact of sea level rise. He said the project is a complicated one.
"I think one of the problems is that there are several projects here," he said.
"It's not just one. And people don't seem to have the complete information on all of them. And they may disagree with parts of it."

title: Commissioners Mull Moratorium On Poultry Byproduct Storage
author: Connie Connolly; Cconnolly@Chespub.Com
content:
Commissioners Mull Moratorium On Poultry Byproduct Storage

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; Cconnolly@Chespub.Com | Page: 13 | Section: News 
 
 914
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Following a sometimes spirited discussion of a controversial poultry byproduct treatment system, the three Caroline County Commissioners went into closed session Tuesday, Dec. 12, with the county's attorney to refine language for a temporary moratorium.Crystal Dadds, director of the Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes opened the discussion that focused on a "possible moratorium on the onsite storage of dissolved air flotation, otherwise known as DAF."
Dadds said the department and the commissioners had heard concerns from citizens about the recent construction of a concrete storage pit used to store DAF, or raw food waste.
"And there's some concern that the county does not have any specific regulations to address agricultural storage tanks," she said. At issue is the waste products being trucked into the county from poultry processing plants located elsewhere.
Concerned citizens, an agricultural expert and a trade association spokesman weighed in during the nearly hourlong discussion.
Grayson Middleton, government affairs manager with the Delmarva Chicken Association, argued that DAF is "an agricultural product because it's coming from a product that's being manufactured agriculturally on the Shore, and it's being applied to the Shore in an agricultural manner."
"If there's no place to store this, it makes it extremely hard for application," Middleton said.
However, Commissioner Frank Bartz claimed there was a distinction between a farmer being paid to store a product or being the end user of it.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter was more blunt. "We're not going to become a storage ground in this county for things brought in here from somewhere else and then everybody else is going to have to sit around and deal with it," he said.
The DAF pit is located on River Road outside Ridgely.
Neighbors reported the stench and flies emanating from the open-pit DAF were unlike manure since the DAF contains poultry processing byproducts.
"The smell smacks you in the face," said John Hammer, a farmer and poultry producer who lives about a quarter-mile from the DAF facility.
Sue Ellen and Mike Woodward live on Marblehead Road, and their property borders the land on which the facility sits.
Mike Woodward said the smell is so sickening, he can't work at his sawmill outside, and the flies are "just outrageous. I mean, they just cling right to our house."
Commission President Travis Breeding cited another concern. Hauling the materials in 18-wheelers and tanker trucks "is increasing the weight in traffic and potential damage to roads that, frankly, we struggle to keep up with now," he said.
Bartz placed the responsibility for storing byproducts on the poultry plants.
"It's up to them to expand their holding facilities and processing facilities where they are, instead of sending it to wherever they can just find a room and just to stick it temporarily," he said.
Caroline County Extension agent Jim Lewis said DAF is part of the nutrient management program and regulated by the Maryland Department of Agriculture, but "they very rarely issue fines" for violations.
The Maryland Department of the Environment deals with biosolids and can "pull their permits, they can fine them, shut them down," Lewis said.
However, at this point DAF is not considered a biosolid, but rather a "soil amendment" which should be worked into the soil within a day, Lewis said.
"If you do incorporation, then you're exposing soil to the surface rather than leaving a cover crop with no till," he said. DAF is untreated, Lewis said. "It's a decomposing meat, fat, blood product that potentially, I would think, would carry foodborne diseases.
The residents who commented said the DAF pit in their vicinity is not the only one in the county. The commissioners and planning department have heard of other storage facilities.
Porter asked Middleton if Caroline County had any poultry processing plants.
Middleton said no and added that the county has chicken houses.
"I'm fully aware that we have chicken houses," Porter said. "Are the chicken houses bringing material to these pits directly?" "This is the kind of thing that irritates me to no end," Porter said. "We're not going to subject our citizens to this."
County Attorney Stewart Barroll told the citizens who complained about the DAF pit, "What you've described to us is clearly a nuisance and not protected by the Right to Farm law." He asked if they had sought legal counsel. They answered that they couldn't afford an attorney and were afraid of retaliation.
"I don't know if I can handle that fight, let alone the expense of going through a long, drawn-out process of me trying to prove what the stink is like in the air, or how many flies are around my window or what's in my ditch," Sue Ellen Woodward said. "I don't have the resources or the emotional part to fight that. That's why I come to you."
"I think we're going to attempt to address the issue for you and try to come up with reasonable expectations and guidelines for the storage and application of this product," Breeding said.
The commissioners went into closed session with Barroll to determine the language to place in a resolution to declare a temporary moratorium.
They plan to introduce a resolution at their Dec. 20 meeting.

 Crystal Dadds, director of the Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes, foreground, and Caroline County Extension agent Jim Lewis share their views Dec. 12 about a possible moratorium on the onsite storage of dissolved air flotation, otherwise known as DA F.

title: Bayvanguard Bank Leases Oxford Branch For Another Seven Years
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com
content:
Bayvanguard Bank Leases Oxford Branch For Another Seven Years

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com | Page: B2 | Section: News 
 
 488
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - The Commissioners of Oxford voted unanimously to enter into a lease agreement with BayVanguard Bank at a meeting on Tuesday.With this vote, the bank will keep its branch in the town-owned property at 104 Factory St for another seven years. The current bank lease expires Dec. 31.
At the meeting Tuesday, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said Bay-Vanguard Bank has already reviewed the lease and its board has approved it.
Before the commissioners voted on the draft lease, Ryan brought up the concerns regarding in-branch banking services offered by the bank, which were discussed at an Oct. 23 commissioners meeting.
"I went back to Bay Vanguard and we were able to negotiate some terms of a new draft lease," she said.
For the first six years of the lease, BayVanguard Bank will pay the town $8,568 annually in rent. In year seven, annual rent will increase to $9,684.
The most significant changes, Ryan said, were made under the section about the use of the property.
She said that under the new lease, the bank will have the right to use the property for banking-related services as long as it provides "traditional branch bank services with face-to-face interaction during the entire term."
The bank must be open for a minimum of 15 hours per week Monday through Friday "with the ability to set the hours as the bank deems desirable and necessary."
The bank can reduce its hours from the minimum 15 hours per week if it determines it is no longer feasible to be open for that time as long as it puts "a full-service remote ATM machine, capable of replacing branch bank transaction services, on the premises," Ryan said.
The bank will have the ability to terminate the lease within the first five years by giving the town 120 days prior written notice. The town will only be able to terminate the lease in the last two years of the term as long as it provides 180 days notice.
"And the reason for the town's inability to terminate within the first five years is, obviously, if the bank determines it's no longer feasible to provide the minimum 15 hours of service and they have to provide the expense of the full service ATM, they want to have a long enough term to recognize the cost of making that investment," Ryan said.
The town must provide 180 days notice, rather than 120, due to legal requirements the bank must follow when it comes to provide public notice of a branch closure.
After the vote, Commission President Tom Costigan thanked Ryan for her work on negotiating the lease.
"I know that a lot of work went into this and I think this is a good thing for our town," he said.

title: County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com
content:
County Council Approves Vehicle Weight Limit On Black Dog Alley

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub.Com | Page: B3 | Section: News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday approved legislation establishing a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reduce heavy truck through traffic.Resolution 351, which received unanimous support from council members, will prohibit vehicles over 17,000 pounds from traveling on Black Dog Alley, which runs between Cordova Road and Dover Road.
Some vehicles are exempt from the restrictions, including vehicles owned or operated by government entities and their employees, vehicles involved with agricultural production or operations, emergency vehicles, vehicles belonging to those whose land is located on or is only accessible via Black Dog Alley and vehicles providing services like heating oil delivery, trash pickup or property improvement.
Vehicles over the weight limit can use U.S.
Route 50 as an alternate route, which is better equipped to handle oversized vehicles and higher traffic volume.
The need for the legislation stems from maintenance and safety issues along the narrow roadway.
The concept of a weight limit on the road has previously been considered by the county.
The council introduced similar legislation in late 2019, but the resolution did not progress.
During the legislation's public hearing Tuesday, Talbot County farmer Keith Shortall, who lives off of Black Dog Alley, said while he does utilize the road for agricultural purposes during harvest season, he's noticed many trucks hauling grain from the Port of Baltimore down into Hurlock in Dorchester County year-round.
Shortall emphasized the need for advance signage for the change in vehicle allowance.
He also stressed the need for other improvements on the narrow parts of the road that don't have shoulder lanes.
" Regardless of what you do with this, the work that needs to be done on Black Dog Alley still needs to happen," he said.
Design for improvements to parts of Black Dog Alley is in progress, said Ray Clarke, the county engineer.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble echoed safety concerns, noting that Black Dog Alley is the most accident-prone road in the county.
Gamble also raised a flag to future traffic problems once the new regional medical center is constructed, saying Black Dog Alley will likely see more emergency vehicles coming from southern Caroline County utilizing the road.
Gamble said the sheriff 's office would start enforcement of the new restriction on Black Dog Alley in an educational way at first.
Citations are more likely to be handed out after an adjustment period.
John Trax, a Talbot County farmer and the "self-proclaimed mayor of Black Dog Alley," expressed full support for the resolution. He adding that he wished more could be added to it, namely ways to further address traffic and speeding.
The resolution took effect upon adoption.

title: Oxford To Create Investment Opportunity Task Force
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com
content:
Oxford To Create Investment Opportunity Task Force

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub.Com | Page: B3 | Section: News 
 
 582
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - After months of discussion, the Commissioners of Oxford passed a resolution to create an Investment Opportunity Task Force at a meeting on Tuesday.Both Commission President Tom Costigan and Commissioner Katrina Greer voted in favor of the resolution.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin voted against it.
The resolution for the task force, previously named the Investment Advisory Committee, was introduced by Costigan at a commissioners meeting on Oct. 24.
The task force, made up of three members, will be charged with reviewing the town's investments quarterly, providing recommendations to the commissioners on investment opportunities, responding to other commissioner requests, and annually reviewing and providing recommendations on the town's investment policy.
The task force will receive a packet of documents, which are listed in the proposed resolution, by the town manager.
Members of the task force must be registered to vote in the Town of Oxford and have "experience and training in municipal investment policies and implementation."
Members cannot hold a paid, appointed or elected position in Oxford's government.
At the October meeting, Costigan's resolution was introduced alongside a competing proposed resolution to create a Financial Advisory Committee by Greer.
In Greer's proposal, the committee would be tasked with providing recommendations to commissioners "in matters and issues related to town finances and financial topics" and responding to recommendation requests from commissioners regarding issues related to town finances and financial topics.
The committee would not exercise financial powers of the town. It would have the authority to access any financial information available to the public via the Maryland Public Information Act.
Members would need to be a registered voter, renter, resident or property owner in the town and have "demonstrable, professional experience in finance." Members would not be able to hold a paid, appointed or elected position in Oxford's government.
The commissioners waited to vote on whether to enact one of the two resolutions, or neither of them, until the meeting Tuesday, in order to give residents time to look at both resolutions and share their thoughts and feedback.
Greer's resolution was voted on before Costigan's. Greer voted in favor of it. Costigan and Delean-Botkin voted against it. Greer then voted in favor of Costigan's resolution.
"I want to take the time to thank everyone who took the time to write in and express your opinions on this matter," Costigan said at the meeting.
"Your thoughts have certainly helped me and, I'm sure, the other commissioners, come to a conclusion."
At October and November meetings, some residents shared their support for Greer's proposal, some shared support for Costigan's proposal and others questioned why the town needed a committee or task force in the first place.
Delean-Botkin spoke before both votes to say that, having read letters from residents as well as heard many opinions and comments from residents, she had concerns about both proposals. She said that for this reason, she would be voting against the resolutions.
"My guiding principal is what is the best for the town of Oxford now and in the future," Delean-Botkin said. "On that basis, I don't believe an independent citizen advisory committee is in the best interest of the town."
After the vote, Greer said she was pleased with the result.
"I'm glad that we have come to the legislative process and produced something," she said.
"I think it will be a great benefit."

 Oxford Commission President Tom Costigan (left) and Commissioner Katrina Greer discuss their respective committee proposals at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Oct. 24. At a meeting Dec. 12, the commissioners passed a resolution to create Costigan's proposed Investment Opportunity Task Force.

title: St. Michaels Mulls Proposed Flood Mitigation Improvements - Coastal Engineer Presents Findings Of Study Investigating Town'S Current, Future Flooding
author: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub. Com
content:
St. Michaels Mulls Proposed Flood Mitigation Improvements - Coastal Engineer Presents Findings Of Study Investigating Town'S Current, Future Flooding

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; Njones@Chespub. Com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 672
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - To mitigate increased flooding from sea level rise and stormwater runoff, the Commissioners of St. Michaels are considering investing in improvements to vulnerable shorelines and infrastructure.At the commissioners' Wednesday meeting, BayLand project manager and coastal engineer Anna Johnson presented the San Domingo Creek and West Side stormwater and harbor infrastructure assessment and flood mitigation study.
The study, performed by BayLand, an environmental engineering firm, focused on San Domingo Creek, which hugs the west side of town and opens into Broad Creek. It aimed to examine the town's current flooding sources and investigate what flooding will look like in the future.
The study came as another effort by the town government to address stormwater and coastal flooding. In 2021, the town created the Climate Change/Sea Level Rise Commission, which then worked with the Maryland Department of Natural Resources to obtain a grant for a study.
Much of Maryland, including St. Michaels, is experiencing both global and relative, or local, sea level rise, Johnson said. And according to historic water level measurements taken from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration tide station in Cambridge, sea levels in the lower Chesapeake Bay have risen just over a foot in 80 years.
After the BayLand team assessed existing conditions, current stormwater infrastructure and sea level rise data, further modeling was performed to identify the six most vulnerable areas along San Domingo Creek.
Grace Street was determined to be the highest priority area, Johnson said. The culvert bridging over the creek is undersized, she said, and its low elevation means that by 2050, standing water could occur daily on the road.
A county pump station is also in close proximity to the Grace Street culvert, and that area is also likely to experience daily flooding.
Back Creek Park was ranked as the second highest priority, primarily due to the condition of the bulkhead on its southern shoreline.
West Chestnut Street at Tilden Street, Canton Street at Glory Avenue, the St.
Michaels Nature Trail and Thompson Street were also identified as priority areas.
As for risk mitigation strategies, nature-based, passive solutions are preferred, Johnson said.
"Marshes rebound. A marsh may flood, but then six months later, it's back to being a marsh, whereas if a house floods, it all has to be replaced, or major construction has to be done to fix it," she said.
Nature-based solutions are also grant-friendly, Johnson said.
According to Roy Myers, chair of the town's Climate Change/Sea Level Rise Commission, grant requests are underway for expansion of the living shoreline at Back Creek Park and completion of an assessment and preliminary design for a tide gate under the nature trail bridge.
Once the BayLand team compiled a list of projects based on the needs for mitigation, an implementation plan was developed to determine a timeframe for addressing the needs.
Because of the failing bulkhead, the Back Creek Park living shoreline improvement project was designated as an immediate implementation project.
The project is estimated to cost $204,000.
Installing a tide gate where the St. Michaels Nature Trail bridge crosses San Domingo Creek is another project proposed for immediate implementation.
If installed, the tide gate could prevent coastal flooding in the surrounding area.
However, assessment, preliminary design and implementation for a tide gate come with a hefty price tag - just over $2.4 million.
Johnson recommended the town look into applying for a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant to offset the cost.
Johnson warned of the risk of waiting to implement improvements, pointing out that prices will increase over the next few years.
Improvements to the Grace Street culvert, pipe outfall improvements at the West Chestnut and Tilden Street retention area, stormwater infrastructure replacement along the St. Michaels Nature Trail and raising boating infrastructure at Back Creek Park were listed as shortterm implementation projects.
The total cost for those four projects is estimated at $1.07 million.
Long-term implementation projects, like monitoring flood risk for assessed areas and nourishing living shorelines along Back Creek Park, are designated as such to see if a stronger need develops over time.

title: Land Use Regulations And The Housing Crisis
author: Mid-Shore Board Of Realtors
content:
Land Use Regulations And The Housing Crisis

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mid-Shore Board Of Realtors | Page: 13 | Section: News 
 
 649
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - America has an affordable housing crisis, and for over two decades, supply has not kept up with demand.The result is housing, in both rentals and homeownership, is out of reach for an increasing number of Eastern Shore residents, said MSBR President Shelby Roney.
This is not something impacting only lower income households. It is crushing the workforce's pocketbook. Even if you consider yourself well off, if you buy a house that costs double what it did a few years ago, this has a negative impact on your way of life.
We have seen area businesses close or hold back on expanding because they cannot recruit and retain workers. Many of those who grew up in this area are unable to stay local unless they continue living with relatives or stretch their incomes too thin.
Much of this is because of the housing affordability gap.
When we look at state and local zoning and land regulations, we can see how zoning helped create the nationwide crisis by restricting distinct types of development. Many cities and states are looking to help solve this crisis, and they are adopting new planning and zoning regulations to help increase the housing supply.
This year, Denton amended zoning regulations to allow more multifamily housing areas and streamlined the zoning approval process.
The National Association of Realtors has found that some states that have in the past shunned subsidies and workforce housing programs are now voting for land-use reform.
And other states that may have been viewed as protectionist are now removing restrictions and bringing housing to market faster by reducing the upfront infrastructure costs to encourage development.
It is time for our Eastern Shore counties to consider ways to help create affordable workforce housing and remove the "not in my backyard" mentality.
Many local land use regulations across the country make it nearly impossible to build affordable and what is considered missing middle housing. The missing middle housing refers to the range of housing that fits between single-family detached homes and mid-to-high-rise apartment buildings.
Many people grew up in such housing, but current zoning restrictions tended to eliminate townhouses, fourplexes and segregated housing into only larger-lot, single-family zones, or denser, taller apartment districts.
Some states are beginning to recognize the urgent need for this type of housing and have passed laws that preempt local control over some land-use decisions.
There are jurisdictions that have done away with single-family-only zoning, which makes up most of the zoning in the United States. More local regulations are allowing accessory dwelling units, or even duplexes or triplexes, by right, in single family districts. The Town of Easton allows accessory dwelling units in some areas to help with this housing issue, and they are considering other measures as well.
ADUs, also known as granny flats, are ancillary buildings on a single-family lot.
They could be over a carriage house, in a converted garage or in a stand-alone building, and they are usually about 500 to 750 square feet.
They add gentle density to a neighborhood while creating affordable housing options, a place for relatives, and an income stream for the lot owner to help keep up with those rising costs.
As realtors, we work with families daily who want to live near their employer and who want the American Dream of home ownership. Homeownership does not always start out as a single-family home.
Sometimes it starts out in a duplex, a townhome or a condo unit, said Roney.
As the counties consider zoning reform, let us look to pro-affordable housing regulations that will support our workforce and start individuals and families on the path to the attainable American Dream of homeownership.
The Mid-Shore Board of Realtors' mission is to advocate for its members and the public to preserve the right to own, transfer and utilize real property.
For more information, visit midshoreboardofrealtors.com.

title: St. Michaels Issues Update On Marengo Street Pump Station Fire
author: Town Of St. Michaels
content:
St. Michaels Issues Update On Marengo Street Pump Station Fire

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Town Of St. Michaels | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 420
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Dec. 3, one of two of the Town of St. Michaels' water treatment plants experienced a major fire, making the facility inoperable. The cause of the fire is still being investigated by the State Fire Marshal but does not appear to be arson-related.Fortunately, the Town has plenty of water capacity to serve the community in the coming months when demand is low during winter and early spring.
Nonetheless, with only a single, operable water treatment plant online, there is some potential of temporary domestic water service interruptions.
Please be assured that Town staff has quickly implemented precautionary and proactive measures to minimize any interruptions in water service to our community. To this end, we have implemented the following measures over the past several days: ¡ Hosted a meeting with Talbot County Emergency Services and other agencies to alert them of the issue.
¡ Coordinated with Town engineers and water treatment equipment suppliers to review all treatment processes in the current operable water plant along with securing back-up equipment if a mechanical failure were to occur.
¡ Worked with St. Michaels Fire Department to establish protocols for the use of alternative water sources if a major fire were to occur.
¡ As lead time for replacement of pump and electronic equipment for the Marengo Station is many months out, the Town is coordinating efforts with our engineers in the development of a temporary water treatment system to be located at the Marengo site creating critical water system redundancy and capacity that will be needed in the coming months.
Engineers have also started to order replacement equipment for the Marengo site.
¡ Costs associated with this fire will be paid for by the Town's insurance carrier minimizing any use of local tax dollars.
With recent emergency planning efforts well underway, the Town is in a much better position than last week. Although there is no mandatory water conservation order at this time, we would appreciate any efforts from the community to voluntarily conserve water in the coming months.
We are optimistic this will be resolved without interruptions in water service. Please be rest-assured that the Town Commission and staff are working diligently to resolve this issue as quickly as possible.
We will keep the community informed with future Constant Contact communications and through updates to our website at www.stmichaelsmd.gov.
If you should have any questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact Town Administrator Rob Straebel at 410-745-9535.

title: Dorchester County Local Appointed To Commission On Indian Affairs
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub. Com
content:
Dorchester County Local Appointed To Commission On Indian Affairs

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub. Com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 406
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - Former Dorchester County Council Vice President and member of the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians Tom Bradshaw has been appointed to the Maryland Commission on Indian Affairs.Bradshaw said he was nominated for the position before the COVID-19 pandemic began.
"It was a whole myriad of things that just drew it out," he said. "So finally, with the new administration, everything got ironed out."
According to a news release from the Gov. Wes Moore's office, the appointments were made in partnership with tribal leaders and councils.
The news release states that Bradshaw has "lifelong ties to a range of cultural institutions and initiatives committed to supporting and promoting indigenous history."
Born in Cambridge, Bradshaw has spent his career in the agriculture, seafood and timber industries. He served on the Dorchester County Council, representing District 5, from 2014 through 2018. He served on the Maryland Heritage Areas Authority Board from 2016 to 2018.
Chief Donna Wolf Mother Abbott, of the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians, said that she, along with other members of the Nause-Waiwash, are excited to have Bradshaw representing them.
"He knows what our needs are and what our concerns are," Abbott said. "So we're happy to have him in that position."
When Bradshaw got the news of the appointment, Abbott was the first person he told.
"I'm a historian and I learned a lot of indigenous history from her predecessor," Bradshaw said.
In his new role, Bradshaw, along with eight other appointees, will be tasked with helping to obtain state and federal recognition for the state's indigenous tribes and communities, collecting data on the contributions of the Marylands's indigenous communities and promoting awareness of those contributions.
Bradshaw said that he looks forward to working with those in education "to teach them our history." He said he also looks forward to bringing attention to the needs of the tribal community.
"He will probably be working with different committees on hopefully getting the curriculum for the public schools system changed to include more of our history," Abbott said.
Bradshaw said he is excited to work with the other commissioners.
"I think we can accomplish some good things," he said.
"We've got a diverse representation of the tribal communities across the state."

title: 'Respect your neighbors' - Caroline Commission passes temporary moratorium on DAF storage
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
'Respect your neighbors' - Caroline Commission passes temporary moratorium on DAF storage

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 1013
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The Caroline County Commissioners upheld a resolution introduced at their Dec. 12 meeting, but only after revising some language in a temporary moratorium on DAF storage in the county.Following what was at times a contentious, nearly two-hour debate among local residents and poultry industry representatives from out of state, the three commissioners adjourned to go into closed session to further refine the resolution for another 90 minutes.
About 30 people attended the 9 a.m. meeting, and chairs had to be brought in to accommodate them in the small meeting room in the Caroline County Courthouse.
The commissioners adopted Resolution 2023-025 as a "temporary moratorium on certain use of land or structures for storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in Caroline County" for 60 days, starting Dec. 19.
However, the moratorium doesn't apply to structures or land used for storage of those residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023.
"In other words, we're not addressing the legality or not of such facilities," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said. "We are stating that future uses of land or structures are subject to the moratorium. So, this does not directly attack a preexisting facility." The poultry byproduct treatment system in question is dissolved air flotation, otherwise known as DAF.
A DAF pit is located on River Road outside Ridgely.
At the Dec. 12 Commission meeting, neighbors living near the pit reported the stench and flies emanating from the open-pit DAF were unlike manure since the DAF contains poultry processing byproducts.
Although it does not own that DAF storage tank, three representatives of the Arkansas-based Denali Corporation, "a specialty waste and environmental services company," according to its website, attended the meeting. They requested a 60-to 90-day delay in enacting the moratorium.
The company operates on Delmarva and "specialize (s) in repurposing DAF skimmings, transforming them into nutrient-rich soil amendments." Denali attorney Mark Cropper requested the delay, citing the holiday season and only having a few hours to review the resolution.
"I don't think there is an urgency that necessitates a moratorium," Cropper said.
"But I fully welcome and fully support the investigation you want to undertake." Several attendees who live on River Road, Cedar Lane and Peaviner Road alluded to the "one bad actor," whose River Road operation contains openair DAF holding tanks that produce a stench and flies, negatively affecting neighbors' quality of life.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked several times, "If there are ways to control the odor and the flies, why hasn't it been done?" Glenn Dowling, a senior environmental manager with Denali Water Solutions in Georgia, said Denali can respond to a problem when they are made aware of it. He said he would appreciate a "60-to 90-day reprieve" for "time to help create a solution that could become a model for the future." Barroll challenged the Denali representatives. "I'm a little curious that you're surprised by the complaints about odor and fly infestation, when Denali's been sued in multiple states in the last several years for exactly that. And you sit here telling us you didn't have any idea that that was happening here." The commissioners reiterated several times that their main concern was how DAF residuals from the Delmarva poultry industry are stored, not how they are applied.
They also reiterated their concern that materials are trucked into the county, stressing county road infrastructure.
They questioned why the poultry processing plants were not building DAF storage on the sites of their plants.
Dowling called the timing of the resolution "pretty curious." "Because it's being considered at the inception of the 2023-2024 winter nutrient application ban in Maryland and Delaware, it's difficult to accommodate when that storage of those materials is essential to the continuity of service of businesses," Dowling said. "It is allowed by the state (of Maryland) to store those materials specifically to protect natural resources and water resources on the Eastern Shore." The purpose of the temporary moratorium is to give the commissioners time to research the issue of DAF storage and "enact appropriate legislation." "I want to make it clear that I am pro-ag, but this needs to be cleaned up," Commission President Travis Breeding said.
Addressing his remarks to the poultry industry representatives, he said, "You need to carry that message back that we are not going to have this go on in our county. This does not mean that I'm not willing to vote to put a moratorium on the entire operation because, frankly, I am. But I think we need to sit down at the table.
It needs to be addressed, and we need to be a part of it. And the citizens of this county need to be a part of it, and they need to be heard by the producers, by the haulers and by the applicators." The Maryland Department of Agriculture "needs to be doing a better job, but they don't have to do a better job; if the applicators do a better job, then we don't have as many complaints," Breeding said. "So, stick to the regulations and make sure that they're enforced." The resolution also stated that county staff, Boards and Commissions are directed and requested to act in a manner consistent with the provisions of the moratorium." "We have directed staff to prioritize enforcement of our permitting process on non-permitted structures at this point," Breeding said.
"I'm ready to put the clamps on, so you guys need to come to the table," Commissioner Frank Bartz said.
"And respect your neighbors.
Respect this community," Breeding said.
A public hearing on the subject of the moratorium will be held 6 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 23, in Room 111 of the Health and Public Service Building (HAPS), 403 S. 7th St., Denton.
The Dec. 19 meeting can be viewed on the Caroline County website at carolinemd.org/667/Live-Meetings. Click on the County Commissioners Meeting link for Dec. 19 or click on the video link.

title: Easton to take next steps in approving new apartments - Town Council reaches consensus to move forward with more units for Elliott Road complex
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton to take next steps in approving new apartments - Town Council reaches consensus to move forward with more units for Elliott Road complex

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 535
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council reached a consensus to move forward with drafting an ordinance to approve a planned unit development amendment, which would add 16 units to an already-approved 120-unit apartment complex on Elliott Road.The apartment complex, first approved as a planned unit development by the council in March 2022, is now proposed to have 136 units in two four-story buildings and two three story buildings - a change from the original plan of four three-story buildings.
Parking requirements under the town's planned unit development overlay district were revised, which spurred the change in the proposal, said Brendan Mullaney, an attorney representing Mallard Construction Group Inc. and Elliott Road LLC, the project's developers.
Under current regulations, a minimum of one parking space per unit is required. The apartment complex is proposed to have 178 parking spaces, more than what's needed.
Though no additional changes are being made to the number of parking spaces, the developer was able to increase the number of units due to the revised regulations, Mullaney said.
Each three-story building is set to include 12 one-bedroom units, 12 two-bedroom units and six three-bedroom units. The four-story buildings will contain 16 one-bedroom units, 16 two-bedroom units and six three-bedroom units.
The new proposal eliminates a pool and adds a dog run and a pickleball court, Mullaney said.
Twenty-eight of the units will be designated as affordable. Those units will be identical to other units in the complex, said Victoria Hoffman of Mallard Construction Group.
Prices for all of the units available for rent have not been finalized, but rent for one-bedroom apartments in other Mallard Construction Group developments fall between $1,250 and $1,450 depending on their location, Hoffman said.
As for traffic, Mullaney said the impact of the 16 additional units would be "negligible" on traffic on Matthewstown Road and intersections in the area. A traffic study indicated a minor impact with the additional units.
Residents have previously raised concerns about extensive traffic congestion along Matthewstown Road. The State Highway Administration is currently studying a 1.6-mile corridor of the road. The study is expected to be completed by next spring.
Ward 2 Councilman Don Abbatiello, who drives down Matthewstown Road every day to go to work, disagreed on the impact being minor, saying he wasn't thrilled about the increase in traffic, but acknowledged the need for the project in town.
"But when we look at the fact that this is an apartment complex that is going to provide somewhat affordable housing for people in town it's worth the increase to provide some affordable, attainable housing in town for professionals," he said.
Ward 4 Councilman Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. agreed.
"I've never seen a traffic study give insight and foresight on the reality of sitting there for 10 to 15 minutes in my perception, but I'm like council member Don Abbatiello - I think it's worth the sacrifice involved to at least have an opportunity for individuals that work in the Town of Easton to live in the Town of Easton, and this is an opportunity for that," he said.
At the council's direction, the town attorney will draft an ordinance for approval at a future meeting.

title: Doverbrook Apartments redevelopment project begins
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Doverbrook Apartments redevelopment project begins

 December 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Work is underway at the Dover brook Apartments, located off Dover Street in Easton.Last week, the apartment complex officially closed its doors to residents for the redevelopment project to begin. When complete, the property's seven buildings will be torn down and replaced with five new buildings.
Although there will be two fewer buildings when complete, there will be an increase in 14 units, bringing the total to 64 units, confirmed Don Bibb, director of the Talbot Housing Commission.
"We're beginning the remediation," he said about where they are in the project.
"Probably in January they'll start tearing buildings down." Rather than a public housing program, the new units will be a part of a housing choice voucher program known as Section 8 housing.
"Both programs are structured such that a program participant pays no more than 30% of their adjusted household income toward the rent," Bibb said about the public housing and voucher programs.
Along with new, energy-efficient units, the redevelopment project will create a playground in the center of the community. Bibb said he believes the basketball court that is already on the property will stay there.
The Easton Housing Authority building located on the property will receive a facelift to create a better space for the community as well as new office space. An addition of 1,000 square feet will be constructed on the back of the building.
Bibb said that it was time for these renovations.
"I mean, this property's close to 51, 52 years old," he said. "It's been fairly well maintained, but it's outlived it's lifetime. So it's time to give something back to the community and the residents." The project, which will take about 14 months (barring any delays, Bibb said), is estimated to cost close to $25 million. Bibb said somewhere around $24 million has been raised so far.
Last year, the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council each voted to award the project $250,000 - totaling $500,000.
Last Wednesday, Gov. Wes Moore announced $63.7 million in awards through Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development programs, including $400,000 to the Dover brook Apartments project through the department's Community Legacy program.
"To win the decade, we must be intentional about building sustainable, vibrant communities that lift all Marylanders," Moore said in a news release. "These investments will support local and county leaders in their vital work to drive economic growth and create stronger pathways to prosperity in all parts of the state.
Together, we will continue to revitalize our communities and reveal Maryland's full potential." Bibb said the award from the state was great.
"We had that small gap (between cost and money raised), and that's why we applied to the state for that legacy," he said.
Since work on the apartments began last week, some residents have been moved to Housing-Commission-owned properties in St.
Michaels. Bibb said a few of the units in St. Michaels are still being worked on, and so some Doverbrook residents are being put up in a hotel until those renovations are finished.
The Housing Commission of Talbot hired a relocation specialty company to help find Doverbrook's residents relocation units. Bibb said that those who didn't get relocated to the Housing Commission's properties in St. Michaels were given vouchers for other properties.
"It's been tough with the relocation because the rental market is so tight," he said.
"But we did get everyone relocated." Those living at the apartments before renovations will have first right of refusal to come back.
Adding 14 more affordable housing units in Easton is significant, Bibb said.
"There's always a high demand for affordable housing," he said. "Nationwide, it's a problem I mean we could build another 200 (units), and it still wouldn't meet the need."

title: NEWS Rural council reflects on 2024 challenges - 'Pathways to Prosperity' Summit caps another successful year
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
NEWS Rural council reflects on 2024 challenges - 'Pathways to Prosperity' Summit caps another successful year

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 726
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS. When more than 200 rural community leaders and other stakeholders came together for the Rural Maryland Council's recent Pathways to Prosperity summit, there was one clear message. rural communities have an inherent ability to pivot, respond and recover during hard times.The breakout sessions focused on this ability to dig deep and come up with creative solutions, a quality that rural communities can share with its suburban and urban counterparts so that all of Maryland can tackle the tough issues and come out the other end more resilient and sustainable, the council said in a press release.
"Housing is an economic development issue," said Andy Bauer, vice president and Baltimore Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, during the lunch plenary. "The housing issue is something that's going to be with us for a while. It's going to take a lot of innovation in order to provide or make it easier for more supply to come online in either the form of greater density and more single family units." "It's going to have to be intentional," he added. "At the end of the day everybody in those communities are going to have to be onboard." Finding balance and leveraging challenges for the better was the message that Maryland Secretary of Agriculture Kevin Atticks delivered to summit attendees.
"Agriculture has to be profitable," he said. "Our farmers and our agricultural land are under so much pressure from development and from our clean energy goals." He didn't stop there, adding a message about resource conservation.
"We are farming in the context of the Bay. That's a pressure. We need to protect the land, preserve the land, and make sure the land is working for the Bay, not just being profitable," he said.
The summit closed with a message of hope and encouragement to tackle the challenges that lie ahead and to continue to break barriers from Maryland's first woman comptroller Brooke Lierman.
"We are focused on a new vision under our new leadership, and that is to be a partner in creating a state that is more equitable, more resilient and more prosperous so that every Marylander can reach their full potential," Lierman said. "There are still barriers to break, but by working together we can keep breaking them." The summit was just one of the key accomplishments for the Rural Maryland Council this year, the press release said. The Council received historic funding of the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund in the amount $9,050,000, along with the Maryland Agricultural Education and Rural Development Assistance Fund (MAERDAF), which received an additional $118,485. The funding enabled RMC to provide grants to the state's five rural regional councils as well as 84 RMPIF grants totaling $8,369,629 and 47 MAERDAF grants totaling $1,153,203.
Other 2023 RMC achievements include monitoring 135 bills, writing 60 position statements, passing three bills and hosting seven legislative committee meetings as well as co-hosting the 2023 Regional Rural Broadband Forum with the USDA Rural Development on June 21.
Looking to the coming year's legislative session, RMC has established several key priorities including: ¡ Level funding of $9 million in the fiscal year 2025 operating budget for Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund.
¡ Efforts to address affordable housing issues such as efforts to repair and weatherize homes to keep seniors aging in their homes as well as the creation of additional workforce housing units to serve public service and moderate income workers.
¡ $1,000,000 for the Wood Products Industry Equity Investment Fund to reach renewable energy goals and support upgrades in electric infrastructure.
¡ Establishing programs and policies to sustain and enhance agricultural production and agri-tourism and efforts to address food security.
"As we close this year, we'll take a moment to appreciate our successes, and then quickly roll up our sleeves as we know that the challenges facing our rural communities continue to be numerous and complex," RMC Chair Susan O'Neill said. "We encourage all our stakeholders to join us and draw on their resilience and ability to innovate so together we can build a stronger future for all Marylanders." Founded in 1994, the Rural Maryland Council operates under the direction of a 40-member executive board in a nonpartisan and nondiscriminatory manner.
For more information on the Rural Maryland Council or to get involved, visit rural. maryland.gov or contact RMC at 410-841-5772 or rmc.mda@maryland.gov.

 OXFORD - The Town of Oxford is seeking a person to fill its planning and zoning coordinator position.According to the job description, posted on the town website, the planning and zoning coordinator will be tasked with reviewing, verifying and approving permits for construction, subdivision and shoreline work; advising applicants, boards and commissions; coordinating review with other departments and agencies and providing assistance in support of commissions and boards, among other tasks.
Oxford's Commission President Tom Costigan said that in Oxford, improvements and maintenance are made to houses often.

author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
A spacious and welcoming place - Central branch reopens main floor following a year of renovations

 January 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 11 | Section: News

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Following a year of renovating and redesigning, the central branch of the Caroline County Public Library at 100 Market Street in the county seat reopened its first floor space Dec. 18.The soft reopening is designed to help staff fine tune details as they welcome patrons and visitors. A grand opening celebration is planned when the new elevator is finished in spring 2024.
New carpet, neutral walls, fresh shelving and new furniture create welcoming decor in the more open spaces of the library's main floor. The main desk is bigger and moved away from the wall, making it easier for staff members to see most of the library's interior.
Bennett said she wanted people to experience the library as "bright, open and inviting."
"This is perfect," customer Romont Fletcher of Denton said Dec. 20 as he set up his laptop on the desk attached to an upholstered chair. He had not been in the library for a year and was surprised when he walked in. "This is a great renovation," he said.
"This is good space, and it's flexible space," Executive Director Debby Bennett said. "It's a well-built library." Bennett, who has been with the library since 1983, will retire in June 2024.
"In 1983, people came in, got their books and checked them out and went home," Bennett said. "Now people come to stay, whether it's work on our computer, hang out with their friends in the Teen Zone, a family comes in and spends time looking for materials and just spending time here, small meetings in the study room, research in the Maryland room."
The $2.1 million renovation project began Jan. 2, 2023. Bennett, the Caroline County Board of Library Trustees and library staff met their goal of reopening the first floor to the public before Christmas.
The central branch has experienced many changes in its 62-year history. Card catalogs and hand-stamping due dates have been computerized. Circulating books are still a staple, but today library card holders can check out a Cricut machine, sewing machines and even fishing poles.
The central branch has 13,739 card holders who can check out materials, but visitors can obtain guest passes to use the public computers.
As if to illustrate the changes, two days after reopening, four teenaged young men checked out software to play games on library Xboxes in the Teen Zone.
The renovation was funded mainly by two "highly competitive" State Library Capital Grants, Bennett said.
In addition to replacing the roof slates on the library's 1995 addition, the building underwent extensive first floor renovations.
Phase 2 includes improving the elevator in 2024.
The Phase 1 grant in fiscal year 2023 financed 79%, or $917,000 of the project.
The library board provided the local match of $244,000 from their John Hargreaves fund.
This phase included replacing three HVAC units at the end of their useful life, improving lighting, upgrading the emergency fire alarm system and phone system, enhancing electrical capacity for increased technology, removing the wall dividing the two children's rooms, providing a family bathroom adjacent to the children's areas, increasing seating capacity, improving sight lines and creating quiet areas. The improvements brought the library into compliance with ADA requirements.
The cost didn't include shelving, furniture and other additional costs that were incurred throughout the renovation, about $335,236. The library paid for those costs, except for $78,000 raised by the Friends of the Library for shelving for the adult, young adult and Maryland Room collections.
Phase 2 is being funded by a fiscal year 2024 State Library Capital Grant that pays for 78%, or $467,000, of the project, with the remaining $132,000 provided by the Caroline County Commissioners.
This phase includes replacing the elevator, which is "at the end of its useful life," Bennett said.
The new elevator will comply with ADA requirements and current codes.
The phase also includes replacing the addition's 4,000 square foot roof with artificial slate, which had deteriorated and become a "serious safety hazard," Bennett said.
The elevator provides access to public space, administrative offices and the third floor attic storage area.
"The (two-sided) main service desk is going to work a lot better for staff to both answer basic questions and check out items, and also to be able to work with people with more complex reference questions," Bennett said. "And also we have so much better visibility of the other desks and more areas of library to see who might need help (and) for security."
"Back in 1995 when we renovated and added on, we didn't have cell phones and laptops and iPads," Bennett said, adding that the internet was fairly new then.
"The MakerSpace used to be our reference area in 1995 with 7-foot shelves of reference books. Now, all the reference materials are online."
More square footage not taken up by books "frees up more people space," she said.
There's a lot to figure out," Bennett said. "Half our staff are new and didn't work down here. And for all the staff, it's a new layout. So it's a matter of figuring out procedures and ironing out all the little extra things. So opening like this without a big fanfare - and this is a quiet time of the year anyway - is giving us time to figure a lot so that things go smoothly for staff and customers."
"I've seen a lot of changes, but this library has always been innovative," Bennett said. "It's always been forward-thinking and also thinking: What does the community need? What does community need that they don't even know they need?"

title: Easton Town Council approves changes to bicycle code
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council approves changes to bicycle code

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council unanimously passed legislation Tuesday updating the town's code on bicycles, skateboards and scooters.Ordinance 802, first introduced in November, deletes outdated provisions of the town code relating to bicycles, skateboards and scooters and updates language on prohibited riding areas and enforcement.
The most significant change to this part of the town code concerns who is allowed to ride bicycles on sidewalks within town limits.
Under the existing code, all residents are prohibited from riding bicycles on the sidewalks. A newly added exception, which will go into effect within three weeks, allows children under 13 years old to ride on the sidewalk.
Prior to the ordinance passing, Heather Grant, the executive director of Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit dedicated to promoting healthy and safe outdoor mobility within the county, requested a revision to allow for all those under 18 years old to ride on sidewalks.
"This age-appropriate exception allows schoolchildren to ride their bikes where they feel safest, whether on the sidewalk, a trail or a town street, and goes hand-in-hand with our organization's mission to get more kids on bikes and more kids riding them to school," she said.
An idea for a dismount district - an area where bike, skateboard and scooter riders would need to walk instead - in downtown Easton was initially floated around by Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry, but ultimately was not enacted.
Language on lawful bicycle riding was also updated in the new ordinance.
It includes provisions on maintaining safe operation and control of the bike, riders considering the safety of others, and yielding right of way to pedestrians.
The code update additionally makes riding skateboards and scooters on streets, sidewalks, parking lots and other public property lawful.
The use of both devices in those spaces was prohibited under a town ordinance passed in 1988.
Today, skaters can flex their skills at Easton's recently opened skate park and pump track in North Easton Park.
Language allowing roller skating was added to the code for the first time through the new ordinance.
Provisions of the bicycle ordinance will be enforced by the Easton Police Department. Violations are municipal infractions.
If police see a child operating a bicycle, skateboard or scooter in an unsafe or dangerous way, they can impound the vehicle, whether or not a citation is issued from the violation.
Grant called on police to also enforce existing laws, including the three-foot buffer between cyclists and cars and requiring cars to stop for pedestrians at all crosswalks.
Provisions on town bicycle inspections and licensing will be deleted through the new ordinance.

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council approved a supplemental growth allocation Tuesday to reclassify just over eight acres of land within the county's critical area on a lot at Talbot Commerce Park.The council granting the supplemental growth allocation is a step in redesignating the lot from a resource conservation area to an intensely developed area - a change in classification for land within the state's critical area, or land within 1,000 feet of tidal waters and tidal wetlands.
However, it is not approval for future development site plans.
Additional reviews will be done by the planning commission and town staff.
Applicant Thomas R. Cohee first requested the growth allocation for the two lots off of Mary's Court in 2020. The lots are zoned agricultural and business commercial, and office buildings already exist on one of the lots.
Several other developments, though residential, have gone through the supplemental growth allocation process since the state's critical area law was passed in 1984, including Easton Club, Cooke's Hope, Easton Village and Londonderry, said Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh.
After the critical area law passed, local jurisdictions, including Talbot County, established critical area programs.
The county provided a portion of its growth allocation to Easton, but the town has already used all of its 155 acres originally allotted, meaning that any new growth allocation must come from Talbot County.
Cohee's request was reviewed by both the town and county planning commissions.
Proposed development for the commerce park lots includes an addition to the existing office building, several new office buildings, a mixed use office and warehouse building and stormwater management infrastructure.
Although the property's stream buffer, non-tidal wetlands and wetland buffers are being designated as intensely developed areas with the allocation, no development activity will occur in those areas, said Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Cohee.
The project received a favorable recommendation from the town's planning commission, though its conditions included rezoning the critical area lot to a zoning district permitting the proposed uses.
