 EASTON — Voters across the state and on the Mid-Shore will have a full slate of candidates to vote for in this year's upcoming elections.Although 2024 will be marked nationally by a presidential election, Maryland residents will be casting their ballots for a U.S. senator and congressional representative. Locally, Mid-Shore residents will be voting for new county Board of Education members.
Maryland's primary election will be held on Tuesday, May 14, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Early primary voting will run from Thursday, May 2, to Thursday, May 9.
The general election is Tuesday, Nov. 5, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Early voting runs from Thursday, Oct. 24, to Thursday, Oct. 31.
U.S. Senate
The race for the next U.S. senator is a crowded one — 10 Democrats and eight Republicans have filed to run for the seat being vacated by current U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin. Three candidates not affiliated with either party have filed to run.
Several candidates are previous or current elected officials.
Congressional District 1Incumbent Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican, is seeking to maintain his position representing the 1st District. He's not without challengers, though — four others have filed in the hopes of winning the seat.
Blane Miller and Blessing T. Oluwadare, both Democrats from Harford County, filed to run against Harris. Fellow Harford County resident Chris Bruneau Sr. is running in the race as a Republican.
Caroline County resident Michael Scott Lemon, a Republican, is hoping to win the seat.
Talbot County Board of EducationSeven candidates have filed to run in this year's election for the three open seats in District 2, District 5 and District 6 on the Talbot County Board of Education.
In District 2, incumbent Board of Education member and current Vice president Candace Henry is running for reelection to her seat. Residents Connie Loveland and Ann C. O'Connor also filed to run for the seat.
In District 5, current Board of Education member Anna Howie is running for her first full term on the board. Howie was appointed to the District 5 seat last October after former Board President Susan Delean-Botkin vacated the district seat.
Trappe resident Karla Wieland-Cherry is Howie's sole challenger in the District 5 race.
The Board's District 6 seat will be the only one definitely seeing a new face after this year's election — incumbent board member Mary Wheeler did not file to run again.
Easton residents Kerry Gunshenan and Cynthia Marrah Jurrius will face off for the District 6 seat.
Dorchester County Board of EducationEight candidates filed for the three open seats on the Dorchester County Board of Education. Incumbents from each district are running to maintain their seats on the board.
In Councilmanic District 1, current board President Michael Diaz Sr. is running for reelection. Diaz is being challenged by Brandy Dawson Cumberland and Lucas Thorpe.
In Councilmanic District 3, current board Vice President Susan V. Morgan is vying for reelection. Cambridge resident Christine LaMonica is seeking the seat as well.
Chris Wheedleton, the incumbent Councilmanic District 5 board member who was appointed to his seat last year, is running for a full term on the board in this year's election. Candidates Jerome J. Harris and Michael Hartford also are running for the open seat.
Caroline County Board of EducationAlthough the terms of three members of the five-member Caroline County Board of Education are ending this year, only two are up for election by the public: the District 1 and District 2 seats.
A third seat opening up this year will be filled by gubernatorial appointment.
No candidates have filed to run for the District 1 seat.
In District 2, Stefanie D. Johnson is the sole candidate seeking the open seat.

title: Oxford votes on two items at Commissioners meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford votes on two items at Commissioners meeting

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 612
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — At a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, the Commissioners approved an ordinance that establishes zoning regulations for cannabis businesses as well as an application for FEMA technical assistance.CANNABIS BUSINESSES ZONING ORDINANCE
The Commissioners approved an ordinance on zoning regulations for cannabis businesses that would permit cannabis dispensaries and processing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's general commercial zoning districts (C-2).
The ordinance would also permit growing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's commercial industrial district.
A nine-month cannabis moratorium, which temporarily blocked applications, site plans, permits, construction, processing and approval for businesses looking to manufacture or sell recreational or medicinal cannabis in Oxford, will run its course at the end of month.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said that Oxford must establish reasonable zoning regulations for cannabis businesses and not be more burdensome than the town's regulations on similar businesses.
Under this ordinance, each applicant will have to come to the Board of Appeals to prove the business meets the criteria of a special exception, which includes the most appropriate use of land building and structure, adequate ingress and egress, and adequate utilities.
FEMA ASSISTSNCE
The Commissioners also voted to apply for the FEMA Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities Direct Technical Assistance application.
This program provides a wide range of non-financial support to communities that may not have the resources to begin climate resilience planning.It will deliver up to 36 months of technical assistance for the town.
Identified hazards for Oxford include erosion, flood, hurricane winds, rising sea levels and storm surge.
PUBLIC COMMENT
Transparency was a theme throughout public comment at the town meeting Tuesday. Residents asked questions about the town's stormwater management and how the town receives and uses grant monies.
At the beginning of public comment, resident Deborah Pulzone read a letter addressed to the Commissioners of Oxford and the town's citizens. In her letter, Pulzone said that for 2021 and 2022, there was only one Maryland Public Information Act filed. In contrast, from Jan. 1, 2023 to Jan. 30 of this year, Pulzone said 30 PIAs were filed.
"It is obvious that these PIAs have become weaponized," she said. "It appears they were made for the sole purpose of keeping our town employees preoccupied with busy paperwork, thereby making it extremely difficult to function in a productive and cost-effective manner."
After Pulzone received an applause from some residents for her comments, resident Jan Greenhawk said that although she has never written a PIA, the people who have filed them have done so for a reason.
"We don't have anything against our employees," she said. "In fact, our employees do a great job. But the problem is, when you don't have transparency, and when decisions are made that no one understands or knows about, then people will ask questions. And if they don't think they can get the answers, then they file PIAs."
Greenhawk said it is the right of town residents to ask questions.
While Greenhawk was speaking, a moment of tension between her and Pulzone caused Commission President Tom Costigan to say, "Please keep it civil."
Like Pulzone, Greenhawk also received an applause from some residents for her comments.
LIVING SHORELINE
During the meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said resident Jennifer Stanley will be installing a living shoreline to prevent erosion across the front of her property. Lewis said Stanley is willing to extend the living shoreline to include the end of First Street, which is owned by the town.
Lewis said Stanley knows the end of First Street is used to take out kayaks and other small boats, and so Stanley would incorporate that into the design.
Stanley is asking the commissioners if they would like her to extend the shoreline, Lewis said. This would not be a cost to the town.

title: County Council decisions on Lakeside resolutions delayed further
author: Natalie Jones
content:
County Council decisions on Lakeside resolutions delayed further

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: News 
 
 450
 Words

 EASTON — As happens every time the Lakeside at Trappe development is on the Talbot County Council agenda, the meeting room was packed Tuesday. They left without a deciding vote, which remains weeks away.Public hearings for all three pieces of legislation — Resolution 338, Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 — and their amendments were held, giving residents a chance to voice support or grievances.
But in spite of some support from the council and community members, no votes were taken as the council awaits recommendations from the Talbot County Planning Commission on two of the resolutions.
Most of the discussion centered on Resolution 338 and its amendment, which the Planning Commission deemed consistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan in December.
The legislation proposes amending the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit. Any expansion to the new plant would require a change to the plan and a certification of consistency from the Planning Commission.
Representatives from the Talbot Preservation Alliance and the Chesapeake Bay Foundation voiced support for the legislation requiring review by the county. An attorney representing the Town of Trappe maintained the town's opposition to it, saying it impedes the town's authority to control growth within its boundaries.
Council member Lynn Mielke, who championed Resolution 338 when it was first introduced nearly a year ago, emphasized that the legislation isn't solely about what Trappe wants or needs; it's about the whole county.
"The problem with Trappe is the infrastructure isn't like the other municipalities in the county," she said. "It's developing as this development is going on and that's a concern, and that's why we need to have a review at every stage."
Resolution 347 and Resolution 348 and their respective amendments drew less discussion, but some objections remained. Neither resolution has received a finding of consistency from the Planning Commission yet.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units at Lakeside across all six phases of the development. A second amendment to the resolution, which drew more scrutiny, would add language from the still-pending Resolution 338.
Attorneys for the Town of Trappe and Lakeside's developer expressed continued opposition to the second amendment, citing similar reasons to Resolution 338.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation that approved changes to water and sewer service status and a new wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside. An amendment clarified the purpose of Resolution 281.
Ryan Showalter, the attorney representing Trappe East Business Holdings Trust, which owns the development, said they did not object to the original resolution or its amendment.
The public record on all three pieces of legislation will remain open until the council meets in March.

title: Oxford town manager to retire at end of June
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford town manager to retire at end of June

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 710
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Cheryl Lewis, Oxford's town manager of more than a decade, will be retiring June 30.Lewis, who has worked for the town since 2012, made the announcement at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday.
Before making the announcement, Lewis discussed the town's progress in hiring four open positions in the town, including a planning and zoning coordinator, a clerk-treasurer and a police chief.
"As you can see, I'm kind of working through a transition of replacements," Lewis said.
Over the next several months, Lewis plans to get the town administration positions filled so that she can set up a "somewhat seamless" transition, where people have been hired and trained for their roles before she leaves.
ADMINISTRATIVE POSITIONS
During the meeting, Lewis said the planning and zoning coordinator position has been filled.
In an interview Wednesday, Lewis said Marilyn Williams from the Wicomico County Department of Planning, Zoning and Community Development has been hired for the job.
The position, which was previously held by Maria Brophy, Lewis' daughter, was posted on Dec. 28. Lewis said at the meeting Tuesday that Williams will begin working at the end of February.
The clerk-treasurer is a new position for the Town of Oxford.
At the meeting Tuesday, Lewis said she has recommended to the commissioners that the town try to hire clerk-treasurer by the end of February so that person can begin working by the end of March.
According to the job posting on the town's website, the new hire will be tasked with directing and managing the town's finances under the town manager's direction and implementing policy set by the Commissioners of Oxford. The clerk-treasurer will act as the chief financial officer of the town.
The creation of this position was talked about at a Jan. 11 Commissioners meeting, when Commissioner Katrina Greer said she wanted to discuss the possibility of hiring someone to take on the town's financial duties.
At the Jan. 11 meeting, Greer said this could address a material weakness detailed in the town's audit for the town's lack of internal controls. This has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
Once the town has brought in a planning and zoning coordinator and a clerk-treasurer, Lewis said she recommends the town advertise for a new town manager. At the meeting Tuesday, she said the town manager would "replace the remaining bits and pieces" of her job, which would be split up by having three town administration positions, not including an administrative assistant.
"I do believe, in order to seamlessly move forward, that you will need to bring in three people," she said. "You're going to have to disburse the workload. You can't just have a person come and replace me and pick up all three of these pieces."
Lewis said there have not been any discussions yet regarding the salary range for the town manager position, but she said it will be included in the job posting. According to the clerk-treasurer job posting, the estimated salary range for that position is $60,000 to $80,000 per year.
OTHER OPEN POSITIONS
The town is also in need of a new police chief and a new public works member.
Oxford Police Chief Eric Kellner stepped down from his position in January for "personal and professional reasons," but is staying with the police department as an officer. The department's Lieutenant Chris Phillips has stepped up as interim chief.
At the meeting Tuesday, Lewis said she planned to post the chief position online Wednesday and hopes the town can hire a new chief by mid-March so that person can begin working in April.
Mike McWilliams, will be leaving the town's Public Works Department. Public Works Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman said McWilliams came to work for Oxford from the City of Cambridge and is going back to the City of Cambridge.
Lewis said she hopes to get the job posting up for McWilliams' position in the next week or two.
Toward the end of the meeting, Greer thanked Lewis for the "well thought out" transition plans.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin said she had worked with Lewis for 12 years now.
"I've worked for a lot of people in my 50 years of business," she said. "And I have never met anyone as confident and as caring as you are to this town. Thank you. Thank you for this transition."
After Delean-Botkin spoke, the room erupted in applause.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners bid farewell to duPont, approve ordinances
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners bid farewell to duPont, approve ordinances

 February 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 573
 Words 

 Read News Document

 At the Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting Wednesday evening, leaders discussed Commissioner Thomas "Tad" duPont's resignation. The board also approved an ordinance establishing zoning regulations for cannabis businesses and approved the proposed contract with International Computer Services Incorporated for IT work.DUPONT RESIGNATIONCommission President David Breimhurst announced the resignation of Commissioner Thomas "Tad" duPont. Breimhurst stated that duPont's resignation was due to health reasons.
DuPont submitted a letter of resignation on Feb. 6 that Breimhurst read to those at Wednesday's meeting. In the letter, duPont recounted the "challenging" three years and nine months the board had while he was in office. Among the challenges duPont listed were navigating the pandemic, creating budgets and many other efforts.
"It has been a pleasure to serve, and (I) wish all continued success," stated duPont's letter.
DuPont was most recently elected to serve as a town commissioner in July 2020. He first served as a commissioner from 2010 until resigning in August 2013 over concerns with an ethics ordinance, according to prior Star Democrat reporting.
The vacancy on the town commission came three months shy of the town's upcoming election. Three seats, including duPont's, will be up for grabs on May 6.
But because duPont's resignation came within 90 days of the next regular election, the vacancy will remain unfilled until the election, according to the town's charter.
When Breimhurst finished reading the letter, he added a personal note on how grateful he was to serve alongside duPont.
"I thank Tad for his dedication and devotion to the town of St. Michaels. His love for the town is never ending," Breimhurst said.
CANNABIS BUSINESSES ZONINGThe Commissioners unanimously approved an ordinance changing zoning regulations for cannabis businesses that would permit cannabis dispensaries and processing facilities as a special exception in St. Michaels' general commercial zoning districts.
These changes would allow the zoning board to review each application based on factors such as noise, parking and compatibility with the neighborhood.
A nine-month cannabis moratorium, which temporarily blocked applications, site plans, permits, construction, processing and approval for businesses looking to manufacture or sell recreational or medicinal cannabis in St. Michaels will run its course at the end of the month.
ICSI CONTRACTThe Commissioners voted to renew St. Michaels' contract with International Computer Services Incorporated to assist with the town's IT services. ICSI is the town's current IT consultant and is under contract for another year and a half.
Town Manager Rob Straubel recommended the approval of the ICSI proposal because it will avoid issues with having multiple service providers and separate maintenance contracts.
OTHER TOWN BUSINESSMike Bibb, a member of the Talbot County Police Accountability Board, presented an annual review of actions taken by the Accountability Board, established in January 2023.
This board comprises two parts — the Policy and Procedure Committee and the Accountability and Charging Committee.
The Accountability and Charging Committee reviewed 50 complaints filed, and Bidd stated that no cases were made against law enforcement from St. Michael's.
The challenges faced by the Police Accountability Board included police recruiting and retention and new juvenile justice laws that make it more difficult to charge juveniles for crimes, Bidd said. He advocated for improved police training and changing laws regarding the statute of limitations for police misconduct charges.
The commissioners then discussed reviewing the town's ethics code.
Straubel recommended developing a board to review the code. The board will comprise five people: one to be a commissioner and four to be community members. The commission will post an announcement to the general public in ConstantContact for volunteers.

title: County must look at bigger picture for Lakeside
author: BRIAN SCHMIDT
content:
County must look at bigger picture for Lakeside

 February 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BRIAN SCHMIDT | Section: Columns 
 
 950
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Planning Commission, Public Works Advisory Board and the County Council are considering three resolutions that will determine the future of the Lakeside at Trappe development. In doing so, the county must continue to look at the bigger picture and not cave to the minority opposing the Lakeside development.Above all, the county must not adopt Resolution 338.
First, I want to state a basic fact regarding Lakeside: Resolution 281 was found consistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan by the Talbot County Planning Commission and the Talbot County Council in 2020.
Consistent with Resolution 281, the Maryland Department of the Environment issued a 540,000 gallons per day discharge permit, which it later modified to 100,000 gallons per day. The Town of Trappe and the owner of Lakeside will be required, at least four more times, to seek a major discharge permit modification at each 100,000 gallons per day increment.
This will require MDE to initiate public participation, including a public hearing. MDE will review the modification to confirm that the discharge meets or exceeds state ground water quality standards. This process will require review of the nutrient management plan and confirmation that the discharge permit effluent limitations are being met for nitrogen and phosphorus, among other nutrients.
Adopting Resolution 338 would require the town to seek a discharge permit modification from not only MDE, the entity equipped to review the permit, but also from the Talbot County Planning Commission and County Council. Such a requirement impedes the town's authority to control its own planning.
Those in support of Resolution 338 have noted concerns that the cost of expanding county resources will be passed on to other county residents. This is a misconception.
Lakeside residents will be paying county taxes to support county services, just as every other county resident. In addition, the county assesses an impact fee on new developments to fund public facilities and to offset the costs of capital improvements. Others have noted concern with the width of roads as a reason to support Resolution 338.
The roads and infrastructure within the Lakeside community are being built to town specifications and are independently inspected by the town's professional engineer, and, once completed, the town will maintain this infrastructure, not the county.
There are also plans and measures in place to ensure there are adequate public safety services to serve the county and the town, even with new growth. During a recent County Council meeting, a concern was raised that the sheriff's office will need to increase its staff to support the Lakeside development.
It is the town's intention to resume operation of a town police department when there is a large enough population to support another department. For background, pursuant to the Development Rights and Responsibilities Agreement, in the early phases of the Lakeside development, a town police department was established, and the developer was required to pay to support the police department for three years.
The developer went beyond their obligation, and continued to financially support the police department for a total duration of approximately eight years. Without the existing tax base to take over the financial support of the department, the town temporarily stopped operating the police department, and since that time, the sheriff's office has been patrolling the town.
The town expects and is prepared to resume operation of the town police department once the tax base is established from the anticipated growth in the Lakeside development.
With regard to other public safety services, there are provisions in the Development Rights and Responsibilities Agreement entered into between the town and the developer, requiring the developer to pay $450,000 and $100 per year per house in perpetuity to the Trappe Volunteer Fire Department for improvements to the Trappe firehouse.
Additional contributions to the town throughout the project include, among other things: payment to the Town Improvement Fund in the total amount of $3,375,000, with payment made at issuance of each building permit; construction of a new 3,000-square-foot town administrative building; dedication of a 4-acre park; dedication of a public works site and construction of a public works building; certain public works equipment; and water infrastructure improvements.
The town has acted diligently and in good faith and has gone through the proper channels with the county and the state in planning the Lakeside development. This process included a thorough review by the Trappe Planning Commission and Trappe council, with review and guidance from town consultants, before being sent to the county Planning Commission and County Council.
When Resolution 281 was adopted, it was reviewed by the Talbot County Public Works Advisory Board, the Talbot County Planning Commission and the County Council. Through this process, the plans for Lakeside have been found to be consistent with the town and county comprehensive plans. Resolution 338 would be taking steps backward in response to a minority of Talbot County residents who oppose the development.
The residents who oppose the Lakeside development argue that there has been a "tragic failure of planning mechanisms — of county officials' oversight and citizen input." Any failure conceived by this group is the result of their failure to put the same time and energy as our elected officials and staff have in educating themselves and remaining engaged during the entire planning process.
I commend the elected officials and staff who have put immeasurable time and energy into making informed decisions about this project. Resolution 338 would disavow years of effort and imply that the county government has failed in their duties to this point. The county must continue to look at the bigger picture and not cave to the minority opposing the Lakeside development. The county must not adopt Resolution 338.
Brian Schmidt is the acting president of the Trappe Town Council and a member of the Trappe Planning Commission.

title: Hope is a powerful force in our communities
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
Hope is a powerful force in our communities

 February 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 657
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Gov. Wes Moore came to Cambridge on Monday, Feb. 12, to speak about the ENOUGH Act that he has proposed. I had the opportunity to speak briefly prior to his comments and thought that I would share them with you here. Please see the relevant portion of them below.When I was asked to say something at this event, I decided to focus on the words "enough" and "hope." Enough is the acronym for this important and needed legislation that the governor has proposed. It has somewhat different meanings that, I think, are relevant to this legislation.
It can mean "as much or many of something as required" as in "you need to get enough of the right things to eat," and it can also mean that you are "unwilling to tolerate anything more of something that is undesirable" such as poverty or bad behavior. Both definitions are applicable to this legislation. We have not done the job that we could do to address systemically the challenges that the ENOUGH Act seeks to address.
While I understand that the legislation primarily focuses on the funding of the initiative and how the government must implement it, I know that the Moore-Miller Administration is also thinking about the communities the legislation is intended to serve and the need for people within the community to do much of the hard work. So local training, local collaboration in implementing this legislation, more effective local utilization of resources and the opportunity to lift up all of Maryland and its people are areas of focus.
This past summer I was able to attend the installation ceremony for Judge Gayle Carr as president of the National Council of Juvenile and Family Court Judges. I know Judge Carr from my time on the juvenile court bench in Virginia. The main focus of her speech was about "hope" and how it impacts children and families as well as all of the judges, child welfare workers, teachers, juvenile justice staff and others working with them.
I see these goals in the governor's proposed legislation. I see this legislation as the cornerstone of the kind of change that I have hoped to see since moving to Maryland almost 14 years ago. What I hope to see in supplementary laws or administrative requirements implemented by the Governor's Office for Children are the things that I think will give children, their families and communities the "Hope" that Judge Carr talked about in her speech.
She said:
"What are we without hope? Who here among us has not achieved without having hope? Why should it be any different for the children, youth, adults, and families we serve?
"The hope I speak of propels us to keep striving; to get up again when we fall. Hope is not wishful thinking but confident expectations.
"Research and science have proven Hope changes outcomes. Hope produces positive results. It changes the trajectory particularly for our children, our most vulnerable children — the ones we are responsible for in our work."
She concluded with these words. "You are optimistic if you think the future will be better than the past. You are hopeful if you believe the future will be better than the past, and you believe you have a role in making it so."
The hope that Judge Carr talked about is also needed by all of those people she mentioned who work with children and families. Just as the children and families need hope so do those who are working locally to help them. I have seen in my past work as a judge and consultant on child welfare what hope can do for a community, and it is a powerful force. I see Judge Carr's reference to hope as meaning "Help Out People Everywhere."
Gov. Moore, thank you for your leadership and your vision and for placing this first cornerstone for what will change Maryland for a better future for everyone. I look forward to helping however I can.
Stephen Rideout is mayor of Cambridge.

title: Water woes hit Federalsburg again
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Water woes hit Federalsburg again

 February 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — A downed tree behind Holland Drive uprooted a main water line, causing a "massive leak," according to town officials Tuesday, Feb. 20.Crews worked from mid-morning to late afternoon, trying to determine the cause and seal off the line at the break.
At mid-morning Tuesday, Feb. 20, town officials posted on the Town of Federalsburg Facebook page, "We have received reports of low/no water pressure and Public Works is currently investigating the cause. We will post more information as soon as it becomes available."
Shortly after 10 a.m., an update was posted: Public Works discovered an issue with Well 5 this morning. "Well 5 handles the capacity of all 3 of the other wells. It appears to be working properly now and pressure is returning, though it will take some time to fully return to normal. Staff is working to do everything possible to assist in this process."
In a 12:30 p.m. text message to The Star Democrat, Mayor Kim Abner said, "We were made aware of low water pressure early this morning and Public Works staff is working diligently to get it resolved."
"A Well Specialist has been called in to assist. Right now they are still troubleshooting. Town Manager Marshall is actively working the situation and we are hopeful it will be resolved as quickly as possible," Abner wrote.
Another update posted at 3:40 p.m. stated "the exact problem has not been determined." Bottled water was available at the town office until 6 p.m.
At 5:14 p.m., town officials announced, "Water pressure should now be back to normal. A massive leak was found in the woods behind Holland Drive where a tree came down and uprooted a main line. We turned off the line with the break which is restoring pressure to the rest of the system."
The town recently experienced problems with the system on Friday, Jan. 26, with a water shutdown that lasted until Tuesday evening, Jan. 30. Then a sinkhole developed Tuesday on Maple Avenue.
A power outage at the town's water and sewage plant in January caused the town's water pumps to fail, depleting the water in the system and leaving air in the lines.
The town's population is about 3,000, according to the 2020 census.

title: Easton considering 'conservative approach' to cannabis business regulation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Easton considering 'conservative approach' to cannabis business regulation

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 427
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During a Monday night public hearing, the Easton Town Council considered a conservative approach to regulating cannabis-related zoning ordinances.The discussed Ordinance Number 809 proposes amendments to revise the Town Code to regulate cannabis-related uses in light of the State of Maryland's approval of various recreational cannabis uses, which took effect July 1.
Town Planner Lynn Thomas presented the revised ordinance to the commission, characterizing it as having a "relatively conservative approach."
The revisions to the regulations are similar to those that are in place for medicinal cannabis. Thomas noted that there have been changes to the language, including changing some of the uses from special exceptions to outright permitted and vice versa.
Thomas made clear that the suggested conservative approach was recommended under the belief that further guidance and restrictions may come down from the state.
"So whatever we come up with, if we go too far, we might have to turn around and revise further or outright repeal," he said.
Following the guidance of the state of Maryland, Thomas stressed that the town must allow dispensary growing facilities and processing facilities in some place within the town. However, there is flexibility concerning the standards that the commission can apply.
Council members raised concerns about the need for parking requirements, odor regulations, hours of operation and other standards in the proposed ordinance. The commission considered adding stronger regulations and enforcement mechanisms for odor from growing facilities.
Council Member Rev. Elmer Neal Davis Jr. voiced his support for the conservative approach to the cannabis ordinance.
"If the state of Maryland wants this, they should give us more concrete direction," Davis said, "so we can be inside on the right side of the ball, not going back to court to defend what we're doing."
Easton's moratorium on cannabis businesses could end earlier than planned if the Town Council can agree on regulations promptly.
The Council passed the six-month moratorium in November for businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits.
The moratorium, introduced initially this summer as a nine-month ban on cannabis businesses, pauses applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for businesses that grow, process or sell cannabis within the Easton town limits.
If the Council approves the changes to Ordinance 892 before the moratorium expires May 9, they could consider simultaneously passing an ordinance that would end the moratorium early.
The Council ended the Feb. 19 meeting with a suggestion for proposed printed maps to better understand the areas that would potentially have growing facilities or dispensaries.
They are expected to continue discussion of the matter at their next meeting, March 4.

title: Solar energy discussed at Dorchester County Council meeting
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Solar energy discussed at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 721
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Solar energy systems were discussed more than once at a Dorchester County Council meeting on Feb. 6.During the meeting, the Council introduced legislation that would amend a part of the Dorchester County Code that deals with utility-scale solar energy systems.
Specifically, the legislation would put a cap on how many aggregate acres in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems. The legislation would also make it so that a 75-foot-wide alive and maintained vegetated buffer must surround the solar energy systems.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he thinks this legislation is not a move for or against solar, but a move against "bad solar."
"You know, when you go driving in your car, you hope you don't need a seatbelt, but you always put it on," he said. "We need that seatbelt there for (this)."
If this legislation is passed, up to 1,800 acres of land in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county could be used for utility-scale solar energy systems. County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said that currently, 1,574 acres are developed or being developed for these systems.
Webb said making sure the vegetated buffer is maintained and alive will be key.
"A 75-foot buffer that's alive, it's going to do its job as compared to a 100 or 200-foot (buffer) that's dead," she said. "So we just have to make sure that we're staying on it. And we will."
Webb said the requirement of a fence around these types of properties and adequate fire suppression devices on site are also in the proposed legislation. She said that any solar energy system that has not operated for a continuous period of 12 months would be considered unused and abandoned.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer asked Webb if this kind of legislation is something surrounding jurisdictions have tried to do.
Webb said it is very typical for jurisdictions to have a cap on aggregate acreage of solar energy systems. She said she understands the state has been looking into banning these caps.
"Right now, there's nothing in place," she said. "We're doing exactly like our neighbors."
PROPERTY TAX EXEMPTION
Also at the Feb. 6 meeting, Pfeffer brought up a bill that has been introduced in the Maryland Senate and Maryland House of Delegates.
The legislation, Senate Bill 783 and House Bill 1435, would make it so that nonresidential solar energy systems constructed on rooftops or parking facility canopies don't have to pay property taxes.
Personal property taxes would also be exempt for community solar energy systems that provide at least half of its energy to low or moderate-income customers at a lower cost than electric companies in the area, and are installed on a rooftop, brownfield, parking facility canopy, landfill or clean fill.
The legislation would also make it so that counties would receive $2,500 per megawatt when entering into an agreement with a solar facility owner to exempt real or personal property taxes for ground-mounted solar energy systems. This means that counties would no longer be able to negotiate individual payment in lieu of taxes, or pilot, agreements with solar developers.
Detmer said he disagrees with this legislation because he thinks the county should be able to negotiate pilot agreements.
"This is them taking away some of the scant leverage that we have," he said.
Pfeffer brought up that the negotiations the county has had with solar developers have, in some ways, set a standard.
"The pilots that we've done so far, we've set a standard, basically, on the amount of money on the megawatt-age," he said. "That's what everyone coming to us generally expects that we'll negotiate. ... So haven't we almost already set a price by doing that?"
County Attorney Chip MacLeod said he thinks every pilot agreement the county negotiates can be different.
MacLeod said he thinks this proposed legislation would result in less local control.
"I've personally been involved in many pilot agreements in various counties," he said. "And it is really one of the few (opportunities) that you get to sit face to face with these solar developers and say, 'This is what's important in my county.'"
Detmer said this isn't about banning solar.
"It's just we're trying to have some modicum of control over bad solar," he said.
Detmer said this makes the county's proposed solar legislation even more relevant.
"It just raises the stakes of us doing it now and doing it right," he said.

title: Approach is obfuscation
author: Staff Writer
content:
Approach is obfuscation

 February 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 395
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I appreciate Mr. Schmidt's column that no more restrictions should be placed on Lakeside development. I am sure I am one of many that wondered why there is resistance to further reviewing Lakeside.There are at least three things questionable in Mr. Schmidt's column. First, he uses a form of dialogue that defies refutation. Namely, he throws out so many "facts" that refutation will take 20 times the space to address.
It would good if he addressed just one major issue. Let the entire column be about wastewater treatment or about traffic. If discussing wastewater treatment, address total capacity for wastewater treatment in Trappe and Talbot County. Instead, Mr. Schmidt jumps from wastewater to roads to the fire department to the new administration building, then ends his column by professing the infallibility of prior government action.
This approach is obfuscation. As Nietzsche said, "They muddy their waters that they may appear deep."
Second, it is hard not to notice that every good-deed dollar from the Lakeside developer goes to the town of Trappe. Money for the town police, for the town fire house, money to the Town Improvement Fund, and to the town new administration building. And he falsely claims that property taxes paid by the new residents will fund all the remaining requirements from Talbot County. It will not fund new school buildings and adding other essential services.
Last, Mr. Schmidt fails to address the ethics of "the tragedy of the commons." To put it in local terms, no matter what we do as an individual, we cannot destroy the entire Chesapeake Bay fishery. I can harvest crabs 24/7, and there will still be enough for others. But if everyone makes that same rational decision, there will be no crabs. The commons of the Chesapeake will be destroyed.
I think Mr. Schmidt is making a similar kind of argument by ignoring what would happen if every town did what Trappe has done. He is saying that since everything remains in Trappe – the people, the wastewater, the cars – then the commons of Talbot County has nothing to complain about. As one specific example, Mr. Schmidt states that Trappe will take care of all roads in Lakeside. Wonderful if those thousands of new cars never leave Lakeside roads. And all the thousands of residents never send their kids to Talbot schools.
His column did not support denying additional review.
MICHAEL DAVIS
Easton

title: Caroline Commissioners enact DAF storage legislation
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners enact DAF storage legislation

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 838
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners voted unanimously to adopt four resolutions designed to give them time to study the issue of storing dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals and other materials in the county.About two dozen people attended a public hearing on the matter Tuesday, Feb. 27, at the Health and Public Services Building in Denton.
The commissioners considered four moratoria that had been reviewed, amended and approved by the Caroline County Planning Commission Feb. 14.
The five-member Planning Commission determined if each were in accordance with the county's comprehensive plan and water and sewer plan. The resolutions also were revised on the counsel of County Attorney Stewart Barroll.
The set of moratoria addresses issues the County Commissioners learned about in December, when residents complained of possible illegal storage of DAF residuals.
"This was totally going on without any knowledge or consent or permitting by the county at all," Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding, a member of the Planning Commission, said Feb. 14.
Breeding called the issue a "huge gaping hole in storage where it's unregulated." The new legislation, which is in effect until Nov. 1, gives the County Commissioners time to research and "generate local regulations to fill that hole," Breeding said.
The legislation comprises temporary moratoria prohibiting the use of land or structures for the discharge or storage of four types of materials.
Resolution 2024-004 deals with the storage of bio-solids, Resolution 2024-005 addresses the "vegetable processing waste/wastewater and other specified substances," Resolution 2024-006 focuses on the storage of "materials other than livestock manure" in a "structure designed and/or permitted for the storage of livestock manure" and Resolution 2023-007 deals with the storage of "food processing residual and/or DAF residual."
Two industry spokespersons who had voiced their concerns to the commissioners in previous settings again spoke.
Mark Cropper of Ocean City, representing Denali Water Solutions LLC, asked the commissioners to restore the commencement date of Jan. 1, 2023, a provision that had appeared in the original Resolution 2023-25, "and if you do that, then you will hear no complaints from Denali," he said.
"We are here to help if you want our help," Cropper said. "But we think it's imperative that you do try to distinguish between those that have been storing and land-applying DAF without concern to neighbors from those that do otherwise."
His concern was echoed by Holly Porter of Denton, who is executive director of Delmarva Chicken Association, "the trade association representing the backbone of Caroline County, and that is our chicken community here," she said.
She also requested that "This moratorium shall not apply to the use of structures or land which had been used for the storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023" be restored to Resolution 2024-007.
"We really just want to make sure that those 60 (or) 70 farmers throughout the state who have been using these food residuals properly and responsibly can continue to do so while we also have safeguards on those who are not," Porter said.
The commissioners did not restore that language.
County resident Russ Yates who, along with his wife, owns Holiday Park Campground near Greensboro, which now provides short-term rental units for 35 families, spoke up. He said he was "very upset" about the prospect of a neighboring former dairy farm's structures being used to store DAF, and the "adverse effect on our business."
Nick Carter, of Greensboro, also voiced his concerns about the defunct dairy operation. The receiving pits and structures "appear to have some materials in them," he said. He had recruited Choptank Riverkeeper Matt Pluta to take drone photos.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter called on Yates to answer additional questions.
Craig Yohn, nutrient management planning coordinator with University of Maryland Extension in Caroline County, arrived after Director Dr. Paul Rickert, asked him to provide his expertise if needed. Rickert had attended the commissioners' budget roundtable earlier.
Porter asked Yohn questions about the composition of DAF soil amendments and how they were tracked from point of origin to application.
Yohn said nutrient management plans, including those written by Denali and Synegro, both waste recycling companies, are confidential, prompting murmuring among the attendees.
Yohn told the commissioners that nutrient management plans are confidential, prompting those attending the hearing to murmur among themselves.
The commissioners voted on each resolution separately because each addresses "individual issues that have arisen," Breeding said.
"The goal to do them individually was so that they would stand on their own should we have to defend (them)," Breeding said Feb. 14. "It's much simpler. It seems convoluted, but you put all of this into one document, (and) it's really going to overwhelm us."
Each resolution explicitly highlighted health and quality of life concerns that were expressed at a previous public hearing that attracted hundreds of residents Jan. 23. Those concerns were "foul odors, insect infestation and adverse health effects in residential areas."
The resolution cited the commissioners' "power to adopt and enforce rules and regulations on any nuisance or cause of disease in the County" according to the Annotated Code of Maryland.
Each resolution was enacted unanimously by the commissioners.
The resolutions are available at carolinemd.org.

title: Local Lightning Rods: Social media, national partisan divisions, culture wars have changed tone and tenor of local politics
author: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor
content:
Local Lightning Rods: Social media, national partisan divisions, culture wars have changed tone and tenor of local politics

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor | Section: News 
 
 1445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Megan Cook, Russ Nelson and Ann Groves Lloyd are mayors of small towns in Maryland, Montana and Wisconsin.Nelson has been the mayor of Belgrade, Montana, for 20 years.
Karen Rose has been with Sarasota County Schools in Florida for more than three decades serving as a special education teacher, middle school principal and since 2020 on the local school board.
Over their tenures, the quartet and local officials across the country have seen the exponential growth of social media and its impacts on civil discourse, as well as the increasing intersections between divisive national politics and what's happening at the community level.
Rose, who became chair of the Sarasota County School Board in November, said she's worked for and with multiple superintendents — and times have definitely changed.
"We took great pride in no one knowing our political affiliation. We kept each other in check. It was a matter of pride," Rose said.
Now, Florida conservatives (including Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis) and progressives (including some outspoken teacher unions and Democratic-leaning school boards) clash locally over COVID and vaccine rules, controversial books in libraries, the state's so-called "Don't Say Gay" law restricting elementary school teachers from talking to young students about gender identity and sexual orientation and how to teach America's racial history.
Rose said she saw some previous superintendents let politics take away from the focus on academic achievement.
"Cultural wars were being let in and taking hold," she said.
Rose, a Republican, said the current superintendent, Terry Connor, (who was hired last year) has shown a focus on academic achievement and data-driven solutions.
But that's not stopping the politics at board meetings, she said.
"There is clearly an organized agenda that is political in the boardroom during public comment," Rose said. "It's very organized."
Rose said Democratic advocates will speak during the comment period, noting a recent hearing where 67 people spoke, with only three focused on academics.
Some of the recent comments have been geared toward Bridget Ziegler, who has served on the Sarasota school board since 2014 and was a co-founder of the lightning rod conservative education group Moms for Liberty, which has become a GOP political force.
Liberal activists and other critics have called for Ziegler to resign her post amid a police investigation of her husband, former Florida Republican Party Chairman Christian Ziegler, over an alleged sexual encounter with his wife and another woman. Christian Ziegler could face video voyeurism charges for allegedly videotaping the encounter. Bridget Ziegler has never faced any legal allegations in the episode. She did not respond to an interview request.
Rose said political advocates, as well as some media outlets, have focused on Florida controversies, including debates over controversial and mature content at libraries. Those debates, along with fights over drag shows at libraries, other public venues and local businesses, have been happening across the country.
"They continue to talk about book banning. This board has not banned one single book," she said.
Conservative and progressive advocates increasingly view local councils and school boards as venues to mobilize supporters and address issues of concern.
Carlos Guillermo Smith, senior policy adviser for Equality Florida (an LGBTQ rights group), said the group has "a long history" of mobilizing parents and community members to attend school board and council meetings when issues of concern arise.
"We have also had a regular presence at the Sarasota school board meetings, especially in the wake of recent Moms For Liberty/Ziegler scandals," he said.
Anti-war and pro-Palestinian activists have pushed liberal jurisdictions, including San Francisco, to approve resolutions condemning Israel's war in Gaza after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks and calling for a ceasefire. Other progressives advocated for spending cuts and shifting money away from police after the death of George Floyd in 2020.
Among conservatives, Mark Lee Dixson, a Christian pastor and anti-abortion rights advocate from Texas, has gotten 65 cities and seven counties in Texas, Nebraska, New Mexico and other states to pass Sanctuary Cities for the Unborn Initiatives. The measures aim to signal communities' oppositionto abortion rights and resistance to having abortion clinics in their jurisdictions.
'THAT'S MY TECHNOLOGY'
Frustrations with and more cautious approaches related to social media are common refrains from local officials wary of viral controversies and local rumor mills.
In small-town Montana, where Belgrade has a population approaching 13,000 people, Nelson avoids social media and its penchant for unpleasant and contentious discourse.
"I'm not on Facebook. I'm not on social media," said Nelson, who has been in office since 2003 and won reelection in November for a final term before his expected retirement. "You can call me, or if you need me, you can text me. That's my technology."
The more contentious nature of local politics — whether it comes from social media criticism or its mirroring of national fights over hot-button issues or former President Donald Trump — also can discourage potential candidates for local office and can lead to shorter tenures for some city, county and school district staff, Nelson said.
"Good people see how challenging it is and don't enter the game," he said.
Ann Groves Lloyd is the mayor of Lodi, Wisconsin, a town of just over 3,200 residents near Madison. Groves Lloyd describes herself as a "progressive feminist" and "small-town mayor" on her social media profile on X (formerly Twitter).
The progressive mayor is a vehement critic of former President Trump, is no fan of U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and is not sure she can find compromise or common ground with conservative adherents of alt-right media such as Alex Jones or those getting worked up about drag shows.
Groves Lloyd also said she saw already rough civil discourse get even rougher during the debates over COVID mask mandates, vaccines and shutdowns.
"It was pretty toxic," she said. "For me, personally, I took a giant step back from social media. I used to post a lot of mostly progressive things on Facebook."
Now, the Wisconsin mayor keeps her ideological posts to X, which has a national and international focus.
She also worries about social media rumor mills and rabbit holes leading constituents astray.
"From a city perspective, we just wish people would pick up the phone and call us. We are constantly fighting the rumor mill," she said.
Some activists counter that local governments and school boards are not always forthcoming with information or friendly with constituents who are less connected or come from opposing political camps.
Still, social media and live and replayed online broadcasts of meetings allow more residents and local businesses to engage with and keep tabs on local matters.
"The more information that we share with the public about what's happening in town, the better. We also have a live feed for all of our council, board and commission meetings. If residents aren't able to make it, they can always watch the recordings from our website," said Cook, mayor of Easton, on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
"The town is using social media as another way of sharing information with the community. It's a quick, easy and efficient way to share information," she said.
Even Nelson said social media helps drive interest and council meeting attendance on hot-button issues such as "dogs, fireworks and marijuana,"referring to city regulations and decisions on dispensaries after Montana voters legalized cannabis for recreational use in 2020.
PUTTING THE PARTISAN IN NONPARTISAN
While many local elected offices are nonpartisan, partisan politics has increasingly become part of local elections and governance.
In Montana, Nelson, a self-described moderate Republican, voiced frustration with the "far right" conservative agenda from the state legislature impacting and dictating policy paths to local entities.
Conservative state lawmakers have passed laws requiring local school districts to open their enrollments to out-of-district students, and looked to put limits on some municipal zoning powers, including efforts to develop more affordable and multifamily units statewide.
Back East, Easton, which has a population of close to 17,500, is part of Talbot County, which saw a contentious fight that drew national political and media attention over a Confederate statue in front of the county courthouse.
The Talbot Boys statue, erected in 1916, was relocated to a private memorial park in Virginia in 2022 after a vote by the county council. Cook said Easton has been able to avoid some of the wave of national divisiveness, but she has definitely seen a greater interest from Democratic and Republican groups in local races, as well as more questions from voters about her own party affiliation.
"In town elections, we don't run on a party system, which I love. It shouldn't matter what you're registered as, if you need assistance from the town we're going to be there," said Cook, a Democrat, who was elected mayor last year after serving as Town Council president.
"That being said, I was asked more during my last campaign what I was registered as than I have before and both Central Committees seemed to want to be involved."

title: Council introduces a new Lakeside resolution
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Council introduces a new Lakeside resolution

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words

 EASTON — Faced with a bewildering number of resolutions and amendments on the water and sewer plans for Lakeside at Trappe development, the Talbot County Council introduced a new resolution at its meeting Tuesday, Feb. 27.Resolution 353, which was introduced by council Vice President Pete Lesher and council member Lynn Meilke, "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas.
The resolution also changes the designation for water and sewer services from W-2/S-2 to W-3/S-3, essentially extending the time that the county would have to introduce future legislation on the project.
Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 are pending pieces of legislation that have been long discussed by county officials in an effort to clarify some aspects of Lakeside and ensure county oversight over the project and its impacts on the county as a whole.
Resolution 338 is meant to amend the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from the still-pending 338.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation that approved changes to water and sewer service status and a new wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside.
The resolutions were the subject of a joint work session between the county's Public Works Advisory Board and the county's Planning Commission on Feb. 7, which yielded no decisions.
The boards concluded more discussion on the resolutions was needed before they could offer recommendations or findings of consistency with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan, which would be necessary before the County Council could take the resolutions up for a vote.
"I directed council to draft (Resolution 353) in response to feedback from the Public Works Advisory Board for perceived flaws in Resolutions 347 and 348 from both their meeting and from the joint workshop between the Public Works Advisory Board and the Planning Commission," Lesher said.
The reclassification of W-2/S-2 portions of Lakeside to W-3/S-3 would allow for an extension to existing or potential construction of a new community, multi-use or shared sanitary facilities to progress within a six- to 10-year period rather than a three- to five-year period.
While this doesn't change the timeline of the construction of Lakeside, Lesher said in an interview that it does allow new legislation to be added prior to any construction, should the country determine it is needed.
Resolution 353 is scheduled for a public hearing on April 9 at 6:30 p.m.
"That will allow us to go to the Planning Commission before coming back for our public hearings," Lesher said.
The resolution will require the Planning Commission's finding of consistency with the county's comprehensive plan prior to the council being able to grant its approval.

title: Local lightning rods: Social media, national divisions changing local politics
author: Mike Sunnucks APG National enterprise editor
content:
Local lightning rods: Social media, national divisions changing local politics

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National enterprise editor | Section: News 
 
 449
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Megan Cook, Russ Nelson and Ann Groves Lloyd are mayors of small towns in Maryland, Montana and Wisconsin.Nelson has been the mayor of Belgrade, Montana, for 20 years.
Karen Rose has been with Sarasota County Schools in Florida for more than three decades serving as a special education teacher, middle school principal and since 2020 on the local school board.
Over their tenures, the quartet and local officials across the country have seen the exponential growth of social media and its impacts on civil discourse, as well as the increasing intersections between divisive national politics and what's happening at the community level.
School board, city council and county commission meetings have all become venues for fights over controversial curriculums and books, COVID rules, drag shows at public libraries and national issues with advocates from the left and right looking for local debates on immigration, abortion and Israel's war in Gaza.
Rose said public comments at school board meetings can be very political and very partisan. "It's very organized," Rose said.
Social media, with its expansive reach, along with online meetings allow more residents and businesses to engage with and keep tabs on local governments and schools. That can also help bring more transparency to city halls, local law enforcement and school districts.
"The more information that we share with the public about what's happening in town, the better. We also have a live feed for all of our council, board and commission meetings. If residents aren't able to make it, they can always watch the recordings from our website," said Cook, mayor of Easton.
But social media also magnifies broader contemporary distrust of the media, government, politicians and other institutions. It can also bring rumor mills and coarse discourse.
"From a city perspective, we just wish people would pick up the phone and call us. We are constantly fighting the rumor mill," said Groves Lloyd, mayor of Lodi, Wisconsin (a small town near Madison).
Groves Lloyd identifies herself as a "progressive feminist" and "small town mayor" on her X/Twitter account where she is no fan of former president Donald Trump. But the Wisconsin mayor said she's pulled back on her progressive posts, especially on Facebook, because of the atmosphere of social media.
In Montana, Nelson, the mayor of Belgrade (which has a population approaching 13,000 people), worries all the political tensions at the local level discourages candidates for office and shortens tenures for staff and officeholders. He avoids social media altogether.
"I'm not on Facebook. I'm not on social media," said Nelson. "You can call me, or if you need me, you can text me. That's my technology."
For a more expansive look at the issue check out our story online and in our national e-edition on Monday, March 11.

title: Lawmakers may derail dreams of high-speed transit
author: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service
content:
Lawmakers may derail dreams of high-speed transit

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LYDIA HURLEY Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 811
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland lawmakers this session are debating their possible role in funding a high-speed rail project from Washington, D.C. to New York City, with some convinced the answer is clear: the state shouldn't have any role at all.Those who back the project continue to push for the construction of the Northeast Maglev, a high-speed rail that would run through Maryland on its course through the northeast.
But some Maryland lawmakers vow they won't let the state pay for one inch of it. Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George's) sponsored the measure this year that would have prohibited any state funding for the project, even though none has yet been requested.
"I felt like this project should not be built with their taxpayer money," said Williams. "It's a funding issue. It's also an impact issue of the communities that it will traverse through."
Maglev supporters consider it silly to debate a bill that would outlaw funding that no one has asked for. Williams' no-funding bill is currently stalled in committee, leading some Maglev fans to conclude a majority of the Maryland General Assembly is supportive of their high-speed rail project.
"I think the fact that the bill has been turned down (several) times tells you that it's not something that the General Assembly supports," said Wayne Rogers, Chairman and CEO of the Northeast Maglev project. Similar measures have been introduced since 2021.
For years, the U.S. has debated the idea of a high-speed rail system like the Northeast Maglev that would travel from New York City to Washington D.C. in just an hour. Maryland's leg of the trip would allow passengers to travel between Washington DC and Baltimore in just fifteen minutes, as opposed to the hour it currently takes.
High-speed transit is a popular concept, in theory. Some 63% of Americans said they would use high-speed trains if they were available in the U.S., according to a 2015 study by the American Public Transportation Association.
However, decades since the idea was first proposed, little progress has been made in constructing these high-speed railways. Lawmakers and advocates disagree about what's preventing the project from making headway, though.
In the 1970s, Robert Embry, the former Baltimore Housing commissioner, was invited to Japan to study their new railroad technology known as magnetic levitation, a step up from bullet trains. Embry came back home and promoted the Maglev project in its earliest days.
"My view was that America's ground transportation was inadequate and too slow and that this was the new technology," Embry told Capital News Service.
Embry said that even today, this sort of high-speed rail could have a "significant benefit" to Maryland, encouraging tourism and commercial growth in Baltimore.
Connecting Washington and Baltimore via high-speed rail may not be so simple, though. First, getting federal funding requires an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS), said Embry. This comes from Maryland residents concerned with the project's alignment and whether it travels through their communities.
Funding issues aren't the sole reason the Maglev project hasn't broken ground yet, according to Rogers, the Maglev CEO. The project has to go through a "review and approval process with 30 federal, state and local agencies" before it can get permitted.
The Maglev project, which would run completely underground, would give commuters the opportunity to travel between Washington and Baltimore without the use of crowded roadways, Rogers said.
"We're not 10 years behind on our infrastructure, we're 50 years behind," he said. "If we don't do something, we're drowning in congestion. We're eliminating economic opportunities because we can't even connect two cities that are 30 miles apart."
As it stands, the Maglev project would not rely at all on state funding; it would be solely funded by Japanese private enterprise and U.S. government loan and grant programs. However, Maglev officials say they don't want to rule out the possibility if the project faces funding concerns in the future.
"While this project is not immediately requesting dollars from the state, the conversation is about the possibility of — in the future — the state supporting the project financially," said Maglev advocate Adrian Harpool of the Maryland Minority Business Counts Initiative.
Supporters of the project emphasized the need to keep improving transit options in Maryland.
"The bill would signal that the state is closed to innovative, future-oriented solutions to worsening transportation challenges," said Ian Rainey, senior vice president of the Baltimore-Washington Rapid Rail.
While a high-speed rail might be needed in some parts of the U.S., some question whether it's necessary in Maryland.
The sponsor of the Senate version of the bill, Sen. Alonzo T. Washington (D-Prince George's) said there are opportunities for high-speed rail elsewhere in the country, but he opposes the project in Maryland.
"It is not needed. We believe the MARC train is doing exactly what this project is trying to do," Washington said in the Senate bill hearing.
Williams said she plans to keep bringing up her no-funding bill until it passes. "I will continue to fight for this issue."

 QUEENSTOWN — The Wheatlands project adjacent to Route 50 is growing closer to fruition as the Queenstown Town Commissioners discussed developer rights and responsibilities for the proposed mixed use residential and commercial community development Feb. 28.A concept plan proposes 79 townhouse lots, 20 cottage court units and 77 single-family home lots for developers Waterman Family Limited Partnership to build Wheatlands on a 148-acre tract of land, directly across from the Queenstown Premium Outlets.
Queenstown Town Manager Amy Moore presented a development rights and responsibilities agreement draft for review including outlines of impact fees and donations to the local fire departments.

Waterman and Queenstown fought the reversal but ultimately lost in court, with the Maryland Court of Appeals enforcing a five-year stay on the zoning of the property.
When those five years were up in November 2019, the development proposal moved forward introducing concept plans and architectural guidelines in 2020.
The master concept plan approved by Queenstown in 2021, showed no strong opposition to it from local residents.
Public hearings were held after planning commission members found the master concept plan consistent with the town comprehensive plan.
During those hearings in 2021, Barry Waterman, the proprietor of Waterman Family Limited Partnership, the property owners, told the commissioners, homes will vary in size but will resemble the historic architecture of Queenstown.

title: Town Council leaves public hearing open for cannabis-related ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Town Council leaves public hearing open for cannabis-related ordinance

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 476
 Words

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council resumed and kept open a public hearing on a proposed zoning code amendment regarding cannabis businesses at its meeting Monday evening.Before continuing the public hearing, Town Planner Lynn Thomas spoke to the council about concerns regarding the ordinance that were raised at the previous council meeting on Feb. 19, including parking requirements, odors and state limitations and requirements.
Because Ward 3 council member David Montgomery was absent from the meeting, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council would leave the public hearing on this ordinance open. Gunsallus said Montgomery wanted to be able to vote on this legislation.
The proposed cannabis ordinance would revise the Town Code to regulate cannabis-related uses in light of the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses, which took effect July 1.
According to council documents, the ordinance would permit the use of dispensaries in the commercial general and commercial limited zoning districts and through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district.
It would also permit cannabis growing facilities and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and through special exception in the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments would be prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the proposed ordinance.
In November, the council passed a six-month moratorium on businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits. The moratorium will expire May 9.
Monday night, Thomas called the limitations and requirements at the state level "the biggest unknown."
"Some of this is being ironed out as we speak with proposals for additional clarification or refinement to the regulations, such as the question of how far we can go to regulate cannabis uses," he said. "Frankly, I'm not sure if they're making it clearer or less clear in some cases."
At a previous council meeting on Feb. 19, Thomas called the proposed town ordinance a "relatively conservative approach," making it clear that the suggested approach was recommended under the belief that further guidance and restrictions may come down from the state.
During the public hearing, resident Greg Zimmerman asked if the Easton Rails-to-Trails was considered a park, as the proposed ordinance does not permit dispensaries within 500 feet of a park.
Town Manager Donald Richardson said Easton's Parks and Recreation Department maintains it as a greenway trail but said it is not listed as a park on the town website.
Town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said that she would have to look, but thinks Rails-to-Trails is considered a park.
"It falls under park rules under the Parks and Rec Department," she said. "I think we consider it a park for our purposes, whether it's designated as a park or not."
Gunsallus said he thinks Rails-to-Trails is something that should be considered.
"Park or not, if we have a well-trafficked area for kids that walk to school, I think that's something that we should also factor into this zoning process," he said.
