 The Queenstown Town Commissioners discussed mandated state policies and projects at their March 12 meeting. Queenstown is currently investigating requirements as part of the state required Nuisance Flood Plan Development guidelines to address areas of flooding concern.While the state's nuisance flood plan development guidance includes an assessment that can help municipalities develop a local flooding plan, it does not have an exemption for towns with state roads, Town Manager Amy Moore said.
The commissioners noted the nuisance flood plan puts responsibility on them to make the public aware of flooding and discussed all the town can do on its part to spread awareness of road closings due to flooding.
The town does not have road staff on duty after 5 p.m. or on weekends unless called in for a special event or snow, Commission President Alton Hardee said.
Route 18 of Main Street Queenstown is the only road in town subject to flooding and as a state roadway, the town does not have the authority to close it in regular events, let alone during times of emergency flooding, Hardee further noted.
The council considered changing wording in its Nuisance Flood Plan to state Queenstown will request closing notifications from the state in the event of flooding.
Hardee suggested researching the town's specific liability on state road requirements.
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan also agreed to identify how the Town of Oxford addresses its plan, as Oxford Road is a state highway and experiences a significant amount of flooding.
In other business it was noted, Queenstown is currently reviewing and preparing for a state mandated investigation for lead service lines. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulations have mandated municipalities identify any lead piping locations within the community.
The council discussed a proposed agreement with the engineering firm Rauch Inc. of Easton, to perform the study. The engineers will utilize drones to assist with field investigation.
As the project includes strict inventory requirements deadlines, Ryan recommended additional wording in the engineering agreement to cover the town if timelines are not met to ensure the project stays moving along.
The council approved the engineering agreement with amendments to be sent to the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) for its approval before entering into an agreement with the engineer and beginning the project.
Queenstown has a total of 330 homes and inventory of town lead pipelines is required to be completed by October 2024, according to Moore.

title: Transparency in government
author: Staff Writer
content:
Transparency in government

 March 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 374
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The burden placed upon a free people who choose their own leaders is the responsibility to be vigilant stewards of the treasured liberties which were won for us by those who founded our country. This means we, the electorate, are duty-bound to make sure those to whom we have granted power are abusing neither power nor the public funds.It is necessary, therefore, to maintain a certain amount of transparency in the processes of government. As we know, in the last few years, many operations of our government, which we once took for granted as functioning on behalf of, and for the good of, the people, have become muddied, requiring extensive investigations while provoking both confusion and lack of confidence in the system.
It is good, therefore, to hear of SB 1052 sponsored by Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and cross-filed as HB 1222 by Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico). SB 1052/ HB 1222 will require the county boards of elections to publish and store all of the data, documents and reports generated in the administration of the official duties related to all elections. Such transparency should ensure fair and uncompromised elections.
Also to be commended is Sen. Benjamin Brooks (D-Baltimore County) who is sponsoring SB 1026, cross-filed with HB1115, called the "Transparency in Education Spending Act" because citizens have a right to know how their tax money is being spent. According to the Maryland General Assembly the "Transparency in Education Spending Act": "Requiring the State Board of Education to adopt a process for the uniform and timely reporting of certain county board of education budget information to a county governing body; requiring a county board to post certain information in a certain manner on the county board's website; requiring a certain transfer to be made only following the approval of the county commissioners or county council; providing for exemptions from certain requirements related to certain transfers; etc."
It is heartening to know that in Maryland we have elected officials on both sides of the aisle who are working for transparency in government. We are citizens, not serfs; we have not only the right to know but the duty to discover and observe how our country and our state are being run.
MARY-EILEEN RUSSELL
Claiborne

Make records available

 Regardless of who wins any election, confidence in the outcome is paramount, and should be so for every citizen and every elected official. In a recent survey 93% of all Americans polled, regardless of political party, agreed that there should be no fraud in our elections. Since at least the year 2000, there have been many people in each political party crying "foul" in our elections. We know, of course, that Donald Trump and his supporters have decried elections as rigged, but so have Hillary Clinton, Kamala Harris, Adam Schiff, Jerry Nadler, Maxine Waters, Elizabeth Warren and Stacy Abrams to name a few.Every single elected official and every single voter, no matter what party affiliation, should want to do all they can to ensure that our elections are legal, fair, and accurate, and do everything in their power to be transparent so no one can question the legitimacy of the elections from either party. Transparency is the answer.
The easiest way to prove or disprove the allegations of election fraud would be for the state of Maryland to publish and store all of the data, documents and reports generated in the administration of the official duties related to all elections. As the result of petitions from their constituents, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) is sponsoring SB 1052 while Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) has cross-filed and is sponsoring HB 1222.
The legislation is straightforward, simply asking for retention and access to what is already law. Full and total transparency would finally put to rest the concerns that "we the people" have that our elections may have been compromised.
SB 1052/ HB 1222 requires the county Boards of Elections to:
Follow existing Maryland lawMaintain accurate records and have them available for legal public inspection for the citizens of their county.
Please urge all of our elected officials to vote in support of transparency and trust, to vote "yes" on SB 1052/HB 1222.
SHARI WILCOXON
Easton

title: City manager's resignation a loss for Cambridge
author: Staff Writer
content:
City manager's resignation a loss for Cambridge

 March 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 1001
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I was sad to learn that Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll is leaving to take a similar position in Lexington, Virginia. This is a huge loss for Cambridge.In the two years Carroll has been in the position, much progress has been made in healing racial rifts that have divided the city. More work remains to be done.
"I love Cambridge and think it has so much potential," Carroll said in an interview Tuesday. "I think this community will benefit by getting very serious about structural racism that we have in this community."
Carroll plans to leave the city by May 17 at the latest. I wish him well.
In his resignation letter to the mayor and City Council, Carroll cited ongoing concerns with the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc's Cambridge Harbor project to develop space along the city's waterfront.
Responding to Carroll's comments, CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said Carroll's reasons for leaving are his reasons.
"I don't know what all the reasons are," Leonard said. "If that's the one he has chosen to promote, I'm sorry to see that. It doesn't make a lot of sense to me, but his reasons are his reasons."
Carroll said in a September interview that having spent 27 years in local governments and having been a part of two major economic development projects, he had concerns with the financial feasibility of CWDI's plan.
In an email to the Star Democrat this week, Carroll said he hopes that he is wrong and that Cambridge Harbor will "become a storybook success."
"But I fear that I will be correct in its lasting and long-term negative impacts for Cambridge unless it is fundamentally changed," he wrote. "I can no longer stand by while this project moves forward in its current form and with the current governance structure."
On the topic of the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., I am pleasantly surprised to see the organization become more open to the public since the start of the year. This has included regular newsletters about the progress of the project from the board's president and more openness in its meetings.
Readers may recall that the Star Democrat joined with WHCP radio and filed a complaint with the Maryland Open Meetings Compliance Board citing a November meeting with stakeholders — including the Cambridge City Council and the Dorchester County Council — was inappropriately closed to the public.
The open meetings board ruled in favor of the CWDI board, stating that the board did not meet the requirements to be considered a government agency subject to the open meeting laws. The CWDI board could have taken this as an invitation to become more closed to the public and more secretive.
I have seen that their reaction has been the opposite. The board seems to be taking steps to be more open and transparent in its meetings and discussions. That is good to see.
Yet it needs to be noted that the board went into closed session last week to discuss government relations, a topic that seems to be outside of the reasons to close a public meeting. This came just days after Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation.
Progress has been made, but there is more to be done.
On the topic of closed meetings, the Cambridge City Council went into a closed session where Tom Carroll delivered his resignation letter to the council. This, too, seems like something that should have been done in an open session.
In case you missed it, here are the Top 10 stories this week on the Star Democrat's website. If you missed any of them, go to StarDem.com to read them:
Ridgely suspends entire police department.
Sewage truck crash closes eastbound U.S. Route 50.
New owner hopes to be a 'steward' of Robert Morris Inn's history.
Motorcyclist killed in U.S. 50 Sunday morning crash.
Denton corn grower named state winner.
Meet the bikers who try — and fail — each year to erode Maryland's helmet law.
Cambridge city manager resigns over concerns with CWDI.
C-SD locked in for last dance in state basketball tournament.
Two die in 3-vehicle crash in Caroline County.
Town keeping watchful eye on Centreville mill.
A story that appeared in the Star Democrat Friday added another chapter of sadness to the story of a 10-year-old girl who died in a Christmas morning fire near Elkton.
The mother of the girl who was killed in the fire faces multiple charges — including involuntary manslaughter, child neglect and reckless endangerment — after investigators concluded that hoarding, overloaded electrical outlets and a lack of smoke detectors inside the dwelling were factors in the deadly blaze, according to Cecil County District Court records. For the same alleged reasons, the mother's live-in boyfriend is facing the same 23 criminal charges that have been filed against her, police reported.
Maryland State Police investigators arrested the suspects — Theresa Ann Moats, 40, and Kevin Neal Summerfield, 41 — on Friday, March 15, and charged each of them with involuntary manslaughter, neglect of a minor, reckless endangerment and 20 counts of animal cruelty, court records show.
A portion of the charging documents focus on horrid living conditions discovered inside their Willow Drive townhouse where, according to Moats' own admission, as many as 35 pets, mostly dogs and cats, were kept at the same time. In addition, court records allege that a "vast majority of the floor was covered in caked animal feces" and that the odor of animal urine and feces was pungent throughout the dwelling when Cecil County Department of Animal Services agents responded to that townhouse on Dec. 20 — five days before the fatal fire — after receiving a complaint.
Looking ahead, county councils and boards of education have some decisions ahead of them as funding to meet the Blueprint for Maryland's Future requirements for education programs comes up in budget talks.
It appears Eastern Shore councils are waiting to see what the Legislature does as this year's session winds to a close. Waiting may not help. It does not appear there will be much state assistance coming to fulfill those unfunded mandates on county and school governments.
Jim Johnson is executive editor of the Star Democrat

title: CWDI Board talks finances, hotel deal at board meeting
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI Board talks finances, hotel deal at board meeting

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 742
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge residents lined the conference room of at the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce for a Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors meeting Wednesday, March 20.The board addressed a variety of topics related to Cambridge Harbor — a project that will create public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River — before entering into closed session.
HOTEL DEAL
Board President Angie Hengst said CWDI is making progress on its agreement with a boutique hotel developer and hopes the signing of the agreement is imminent.
"There's just a little bit of back and forth with some final legalese with our lawyers," she said.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the board would meet with lawyers in the closed session portion of the meeting.
2023 AUDIT
Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr said the 2023 audit is currently underway. He gave a preview of what that report will look like when it is presented at the May board meeting.
Narr said CWDI has two separate entities when it comes to finances: CWDI Holdings, which is for real estate, and an operating entity.
In 2023, CWDI Holdings received a grant income of more than $2 million, Narr said. This income went toward pre-development costs including professional, design and consulting fees, he said.
CWDI Holdings had a net income of around $817,000, which Narr said is the cost of the Richardson Maritime Museum property that CWDI purchased in early 2023.
Narr said a lot of the operating entity's revenue for 2023 came through public sources, including a commitment from former Gov. Larry Hogan's administration and City of Cambridge American Rescue Plan Act funds. He said revenue also came through property leases and docking fees.
The operating entity had a net income of $24,000 in 2023. Narr said this would have been higher if CWDI had sold the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance, which it expected to do in 2023. He said CWDI now expects that sale to occur this year.
Narr said that other than an increase in legal fees "due to a couple issues we had to deal with here locally," costs to the operating entity stayed in line with what CWDI expected.
TAX INCREMENT FINANCING
Hengst said the Cambridge Harbor tax increment financing model looks "very stable," as a seventh run of the model was recently completed.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area due to development. The increased tax revenues are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area. CWDI's tax increment financing would cover the Cambridge Harbor development project area.
According to a CWDI presentation at a Dorchester County Council meeting in December, the net tax increment from the TIF is expected to be around $10 million each for the city and county.
"We continue to try to work with the city and the county to provide them all the information that we can on the TIF and to hold public meetings with them," Leonard said at the board meeting Wednesday. "We did have a couple with the county already. We're waiting for the city to agree to do that with us so we can move it forward."
OTHER NOTES
During public comment, some residents said they were unhappy with the look of the fence currently at Cambridge Harbor. Cathy Hanson called the fence "unsightly and industrial looking."
According to the meeting agenda, the board discussed government relations in closed session. This came just days after Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation. Carroll said he resigned over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.
Hengst said the board is still in need of one county-appointed member and is waiting for the county to put out a request for interest.
Hengst said CWDI is waiting for final approval on the plans for the promenade extension at Cambridge Harbor. CWDI expects to bid the project before May so it can break ground in July.
CWDI agreed to having the Girls on the Run 5K take place on its property on May 4. Leonard said 85 boards on the boardwalk were replaced to make it safe for the event.
The Rotary Club of Cambridge will place 40 to 50 flags on the Cambridge Harbor property for Memorial Day.
CWDI is planning a public update meeting where people can attend in person or virtually to get a detailed update with what is going on at Cambridge Harbor. Leonard said they plan to hold the meeting sometime in the second quarter of the year.

title: Talbot County Council discusses Golf Course renovation
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council discusses Golf Course renovation

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This report has been updated from an earlier version to correct information pertaining to the cost of the renovations.EASTON — The Talbot County Council's Thursday evening to discussion of the county's enterprise funds budgets for the upcoming fiscal year included a lengthy talk about the renovations of the Hog Neck Golf Course.
Rich Setter, general manager at Hog Neck Golf Course, came to the council with a plan for the future of this golf course.
The plan includes improvements such as driving range enhancements, venue operations and a new kitchen so the golf course can generate significantly higher revenues in the future.
Setter focused on the need for funds for kitchen improvements. This project would require $105,000, including items like a flat-top grill, oven, fryer and hood unit.
Setter provided financial projections to the council, showing that with the new projects, revenues could increase to around $3 million annually once the new facilities are open and fully operational.
The goal, Setter said, would be for the golf course, which is owned and operated by the county, to become more financially self-sufficient over time and generate enough revenue to pay for its capital projects and operations without needing as much subsidy from the Talbot County general fund.
"We're basically creating a whole new business," said Settler of the golf course's renovations, many of which are already underway.
The project will cost about $2.4 million as laid out in a previous meeting, not including Setter's $105,000 ask.
Council members Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp supported the changes to the golf course.
"I'm the only one that has seen one of these driving ranges and how popular and successful it is," Mielke said. "That makes an impact on me in terms of my view on proceeding on this and making an investment."
Council members Chuck Callahan, Keasha Haythe and Pete Lesher were more hesitant about investing further into the project.
Haythe said it was essential to treat this as a new business and take a more conservative approach to the revenue produced during its first fiscal year. Funds have already been provided for other capital projects, like the driving range enhancements.
Callahan suggested that they wait a bit longer before approving the decision. Haythe and Lesher agreed with this statement.
"It's a business decision that we have to make with the taxpayers' money," Callahan said. "I would feel a bit more comfortable waiting to see."
Stepp and Mielke protested.
"My theory on this is if we're going to do it, let's do it right," Stepp said. "Let's get everything in place because we're going to have an opportunity here for a lot of first impressions."
Setter stressed that revenue would drastically decrease if the business were unable to sell hot food, which ultimately changed the minds of Callahan, Haythe and Lesher. The council approved fully funding the kitchen improvements at the golf course.
If approved in FY2025 budget and advance funds are allocated. Setter said they hope to complete kitchen renovations before the "true grand opening" in 2025.

title: Oxford amends floodplain management ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford amends floodplain management ordinance

 March 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 430
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford unanimously passed an amendment at a meeting Tuesday that removes a section from an ordinance that deals with floodplain management.The section of the floodplain management ordinance that the commissioners voted to remove allows for certain equipment to be located below the elevation of the lowest floor of a building or structure if that equipment is designed and installed to prevent water from entering and "to resist hydrostatic and hydrodynamic loads and stresses," according to the ordinance.
Equipment listed in this section includes electrical systems, heating, ventilation, air conditioning, plumbing appliances and fixtures and duct systems.
By removing this section, the town will be able to maintain its Federal Emergency Management Agency Community Rating System classification of seven. If the commissioners had voted to keep the section in the ordinance, the town's classification would have changed to a nine.
Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the increase to a classification of nine would mean a loss in certain insurance benefits to residents. According to the FEMA website, class seven communities, a part of the FEMA Community Rating System, receive a 15% percent premium reduction on floodplain insurance.
Oxford Planning and Zoning Coordinator Marilyn Williams said the town would eventually need to make this ordinance change anyway due to the state's updated floodplain regulations. She said the town is due for an audit regarding these regulations.
"It has been out of FEMA regulations and the state's floodplain regulations for some time," she said about the exemption. "So it's not just because of the CRS (Community Rating System) component."
This was not the only agenda item at the meeting Tuesday that dealt with flooding. Brent Jett, an engineer, certified floodplain manager and climate change professional with the architecture and engineering firm George, Miles and Buhr, presented an engineering study on stormwater and tidal water mitigation for the greater Tilghman Street and South Morris Street areas.
Jett talked about high tides and increases in rainfall, and how these things are affecting the town's "antiquated" water systems. He also talked about what could be coming down the pike in the next 100 years.
The engineering firm proposes the town put in two pump stations, put a small pump in the wetlands area, replace its current tide gates and replace its stormwater piping. Jett estimated the cost of these changes to be between $350,000 and $400,000 total.
He said these changes could help the town land an even better FEMA Community Rating System classification in the future.
"Maybe it's just a little help," he said. "The cherry on top, potentially, to get you to the six (classification)," he said.

author: TOM MCCALL

Denton employees remember town attorney, begin process to fill role after his death

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News

 DENTON — Christopher Francis Drummond, who served as the Town of Denton's lawyer, died of a heart attack while cycling on March 16. He was 69.According to Scott Getchell, town administrator of The Town of Denton, Drummond will be missed by the people he worked with.
Getchell said, "Chris will be remembered fondly for his dedication to the town, his sharp wit and skilled abilities. He touched the lives of many in profound ways and leaves behind a legacy that will endure through cherished memories."
Drummond served as lawyer to several Eastern Shore towns starting in 1988. He was admitted into the Maryland Bar in 1980 and opened his legal practice in Centreville in 1983.
According to his Fellows, Helfenbein and Newnam Funeral Home obituary, "Throughout his legal career, Chris always did his best to remember that compromise and common sense produce the best results in difficult cases."
The obituary also said he was an avid boater, who sailed to Bermuda, traveled the Intracoastal Waterway and found most of the creeks and coves of the Chesapeake Bay.
The family asks that memorial gifts be given to BasenjiRescue.org or Queen Anne's County Animal Services.
Getchell said that the town has appointed an interim town attorney as they begin the process of filling the vacant role.
"We have appointed Ms. Lyndsey Ryan, ESQ, as interim town attorney," he said.
According to Ryan's website, she serves as town attorney for Oxford, Trappe, Queenstown, Greensboro and Federalsburg. She is also the attorney for Queen Anne's County Board of Appeals and the Talbot County Board of Elections.
She is a member of the Mayland Bar and joined Booth, Cropper and Marriner as an associate in 2016. She is a graduate of Roanoke College and went to University of Baltimore School of Law graduating in 2015.

title: Pier length changes could soon require variance
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Pier length changes could soon require variance

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 468
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Pier length proved to be a contentious topic during the Queen Anne's County Commissioner's public hearing on a conditional use ordinance on the same.If passed the new ordinance would require approval of a variance for new piers constructed in excess of 150 feet in length.
A variance is a departure from a minimum standard set forth in the Zoning Code and are most often affiliated with a bulk standard like a distance from property lines or the size of an accessory structure, according to Amy Moredock, planning director. Conditional uses are uses listed in each zoning district permitted under certain conditions of the Town Code.
Variances require more unique circumstance standards for the Board of Appeals to review than current conditional use permits, Moredock said.
At the March 12 public hearing, with concerns that longer piers can affect public use of waterways, residents spoke in favor of the ordinance to tighten up reviews for pier extension applications further than the normally allotted 150 feet.
Jay Falstad of the Queen Anne's Conservation Association noted property ownership stops at the shore line and it wasn't unreasonable to ask a landowner to have a higher burden when requesting longer piers.
The change to the ordinance would not automatically deny applications for a longer pier but "puts forth a little bit higher of a standard," he said.
If allowed to go unchecked, longer piers jetting into the water could create an eyesore, and larger boats can utilize marinas, he said.
Billy Benton, vice president of the Queen Anne's County Watermen's Association stated longer piers can impede on the working areas of crabbing and clamming.
On the other side, representing a client that has had a conditional use application in the works for months, Jeff Thompson of Thompson and Richard LLP requested the variance ordinance provide a grandfather condition.
Pier extension requests can be for a number of factors including water depth not just boat size, he said.
His client's request has been in the queue for months and Thompson was worried the variance bill approval would trump that.
It had not been the Board of Appeals' intention to "pull out the rug" from under current conditional use applicants with the proposed amendment, Moredock, said, noting it had not been realized that projects in the pipeline would be affected by the ordinance.
"Since 2002, we've had 45 conditional use applications for pier extensions greater than 150, all were approved. The greatest distance was 495," Long Range Principal Planner Stephanie Jones said.
Commissioner Jack Wilson requested additional information about the average pier length requested more than 150 feet.
Public comment will be open until the commissioners will return to discussion at its next meeting March 26.
In other business, the council approved a map amendment to upgrade the sewer and water services of the Foxx Farm property in Sudlersville to permit services on demand, calling it "long overdue."

title: St. Michaels commission apologizes for oversight regarding Makers Market
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels commission apologizes for oversight regarding Makers Market

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 399
 Words

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the St. Michaels commissioners apologized to the Markers Market and the St. Michaels Business Association for a previous oversight during a March 13 meeting.At that meeting, the commissioners voted to permit the Makers Market to host a vendor event at Muskrat Park, though the town code prohibits for-profit use of the park.
"We apologize that it was an oversight previously," Commission President David Breimhurst said. "And I can tell you that the staff is well aware of what the issue was. These permits will be thoroughly vetted in the future before they come to us."
During the March 13 meeting, Trish Payne and Mark Montoya, members of Talbot County's local art community, requested the use of the park every other Saturday or every second Sunday starting in April for a local art vendors event.
There was vocal opposition by members of the St. Michaels Business Association, who said that the vendor event could bring harm to local businesses.
After a heated discussion by members of the public, the commissioners approved the event on a trial run to begin in April to assess impacts to the local community.
During public comment at the March 27 meeting, Eric Bridges, a resident of St. Michaels, said that the town code prohibits for-profit events at Muskrat Park. He added that the town code prohibits tents on the park's grass to preserve the integrity of the grass.
Joan McNamara, a St. Michaels resident, said the commission should apologize for the oversight regarding the approval of the Makers Market hosting vendor events at Muskrat Park.
"The fact that no tents being erected in Muskrat Park was already in the code," McNamara said. "I would think that a public apology to two organizations, yes SBA (St. Michaels Business Association) and the Maker's Market, would be appropriate because there were some hard feelings."
Along with Breimhurst's apology, Rob Straebel, town administrator, apologized to the public and privately apologized to the event organization the previous week.
"I also apologize to the SBA for the oversight," Staebel said. "We have some new staff members, and ultimately, the buck stops with me, so I take full responsibility for that oversight. It won't happen again."
OTHER ACTIONS
The commissioners unanimously approved permits for the following events: Seaglass Festival, Taste of St. Michaels and the Charm City Running Festival 2024.
The commissioners approved R.L. Ewing Contractors's bid for $26,248 for milling and paving work on Fremont Street.

title: Talbot Council honors Judge Stephen Kehoe, Talbot Braves
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot Council honors Judge Stephen Kehoe, Talbot Braves

title: Cambridge establishes land bank authority
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge establishes land bank authority

 March 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 373
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council unanimously voted to establish the Land Bank Authority of Cambridge at a meeting March 25.With a land bank, the city hopes to advance its housing goals through taking an interventionist approach to the Cambridge housing market.
The land bank authority will have the power to take on, manage and sell vacant land in order to stabilize neighborhoods and encourage redevelopment.
The passing of this ordinance means the articles of incorporation for the land bank authority can now be filed.
The next steps to getting the land bank up and running will include deciding the structure of the board — including the number of representatives and how they are appointed — and searching for qualified residents to serve on the board.
In a Feb. 23 memo, Cambridge Program Specialist Gavin Woolford said city staff hopes to begin the search for residents who can serve on the board in the coming months.
At the meeting March 25, City Attorney Patrick Thomas said the ordinance identifies the mayor, city manager and himself by name as the incorporators for the original board before the actual board is selected.
"I would just ask that if there's a motion to pass the ordinance, that it just be clear that the articles should read the individuals holding those offices," he said.
Thomas said this is important due to Tom Carroll, the city manager having submitted his resignation. Carroll said his last day as city manager will be no later than May 17.
Commissioner Jameson Harrington made the motion to adopt the ordinance with a language amendment regarding the incorporators.
At a council meeting Feb. 26, Thomas said that to his knowledge, Cambridge would be the first municipality in the State of Maryland to establish a land bank.
He also said that because the land bank authority would be a corporation, it would be able to acquire and sell land "a little bit more nimbly" than the government because the authority wouldn't have to follow the same process outlined in Cambridge's charter.
Before the council voted unanimously to adopt the amended ordinance at the March 25 meeting, Harrington thanked Carroll and city staff for making the project happen.
"It's something I've pushed for since being elected," he said. "And it's really cool to see some progress."

title: Hundreds of children gather thousands of eggs on courthouse lawn
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Hundreds of children gather thousands of eggs on courthouse lawn

 March 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — About 150 children waited with anxious excitement on the Talbot County Courthouse lawn shortly before 10 a.m. Saturday for the arrival of a very famous rabbit and the start of the Easton Economic Development's annual egg hunt.There were lots of multi-generational families gathered.
Erica and Christian Mackendrick came with their 2-year-old son Noah.
"It is Noah's first time. We are going to see the bunny and the fire truck, hopefully get some eggs," Erica said. "It is fun to get out, see other kids and celebrate Easter and have a good weekend."
Dorothy Rudny came with her three grandchildren — Cooper, Charlotte and Magnolia.
"I am excited because I want candy," said Charlotte. "I just like picking up the eggs."
At 10 a.m. sharp, the Easter Bunny arrived in style aboard a red fire truck, with Donald "Bunky" Spies at the wheel. There was a palpable excitement in the air.
Then, the kids were off searching.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said, "It is so much fun seeing the community out and all the kids. It is a beautiful day. Easton Economic Development does a great job hosting the event. It is one of the things that makes Easton a great place to raise your family. We loved this event when my kids were little. It is like a big family reunion."
Holly Dakarske, executive director of Easton Economic Development, said that volunteers had set out more than 5,000 filled Easter eggs earlier Saturday morning.
They contained a mix of candies and trinkets, like erasers, tattoos and stickers, she said.
"We have done (the egg hunt) the last three years since we took it over, but I think it has been over a decade (since the town first started holding the event)," Dakarske said. "Every year it is the fire engine with the bunny and the mayor."
She seemed pleased with her team's effort to fill the lawn with thousands of eggs.
"It goes so fast. It the fastest event ever," Dakarske laughed. "The kids pick up the eggs in seconds, and it takes us an hour and half to put them out. It is cool to see all the families come out and the kids are dressed up for Easter and watch them take a picture with the bunny. It is wholesome, small town kind of stuff."
Val Dambrosio, Visitor Center coordinator for Easton Economic Development, said she had an "eggcellent" week stuffing eggs ahead of the event.
For Dambrosio, the best part of the event is seeing the creative Easter baskets that local children carry to collect eggs in. "I have yet to see two of the same," she said.
Whether they got a basketful or just a few eggs, everyone seemed happy. There was not one egg left on the green.

title: Resolutions face vote Tuesday
author: Staff Writer
content:
Resolutions face vote Tuesday

 March 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 289
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Tuesday, April 2, the Talbot County Planning Commission will at long last act on three resolutions (and also three amendments) all involving Lakeside.These matters include fixing the all-important sewer service map improperly approved by the county in 2020 that was the green-light for Lakeside.
A year ago, the Maryland Department of Environment recognized that the sewer service map was wrong, and instructed the county to correct it as the county deems necessary, "including Lakeside." And since then, the county engineer, the county attorney, and the Town of Trappe itself have all acknowledged on the record what MDE had come to understand: that prior to that 2020 approval, Lakeside had always been "unprogrammed" and, contrary to what was told to the Planning Commission and everyone else, had never been previously reviewed and slated for development by the county at all, ever.
The three resolutions before the Planning Commission (R347, R348 and R353) are all deeply flawed for reasons long discussed, and should all be found by the commission to be "not consistent" with the county's comprehensive plan — which is the question the commission must answer under Maryland law.
(The Public Works Advisory Board reviewed them in detail and unanimously recommended rejection of R347 and R348, standing alone and as amended; similarly, they did not recommend R353 as presently drafted.) The language of all three is about as confusing as possible, and misleading. R348 includes a starkly untrue recital. It and R347 are clearly designed not to "fix" the maps as they affect Lakeside, but to assure that that the developer's interests in that billion-dollar subdivision are not disturbed in any way.
The public hearing is scheduled for 9 a.m. on Tuesday, April 2, at the Bradley Room of the Courthouse.
DAN WATSON
Easton

title: Easton Town Council waits on Annapolis to vote on Cannabis ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council waits on Annapolis to vote on Cannabis ordinance

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council has still not voted on an ordinance that would revise the Town Code to regulate cannabis-related uses in light of the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses, which took effect July 1.At the meeting Monday, Town Planner Lynn Thomas gave an update on what is going on with related legislation in the State Senate and House of Delegates. He said the Senate has passed a bill that is different from the House of Delegates.
"As best (as) I can read it, the differences deal with a couple of the separation requirements," he said.
Thomas said the Senate version of the bill includes a 100-foot-separation between cannabis dispensaries and residentially zoned properties. He said the Senate version of the bill also allows for an increase to a half mile, or 2,640 feet, in the separation between dispensaries. He said that separation is 1,000 feet in the House version of the bill.
Thomas said a House of Delegates committee had "reviewed and recommended approval with amendments."
"Now I'm not sure if that is referring to the amendments that were in the Senate version or they themselves had proposed further amendments," he said. "But one way or another, it's still playing out."
According to council documents, the ordinance on the table in Easton would permit the use of dispensaries in the commercial general and commercial limited zoning districts and through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district. It would also permit cannabis growing facilities and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and through special exception in the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments would be prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the proposed ordinance.
Thomas said that considering the General Assembly adjourns next week, the town should have the information it needs to vote on this ordinance at the next Town Council meeting on March 15.
After Thomas spoke, Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council will leave the public hearing on this ordinance open until the next council meeting.
"Hopefully we'll have an update from Annapolis and we'll have some direction regarding what we are able to do," he said.

title: $150,000 to restore historic house tied up over landownership technicality
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
$150,000 to restore historic house tied up over landownership technicality

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Historical Society came to the Caroline County Commissioners last week to discuss funding for the Medford House Agricultural Interpretive Center project, which has been tied up due to a technicality with the property's ownership.The society had a bond bill from the state for $150,000, but because the society owns the Medford House building and the county owns the land that it sits on, the state would not, at first, release the money.
"We applied for a bond. We were awarded the funds, but we can't collect them as we are not the landowner. The county is. We own the building, but not the land," Mackel said. "Today I am here to request the commissioners' support of the Caroline County Historical Society that we move forward with the submission of the full application package to the Board of Public Works for their review and approval. They will in turn send you a form to be signed so that the bond is $150,000 requested. And that money will be used to complete the exterior elements."
Mackel had help from Maryland State Delegate Jeff Ghrist, Maryland Sen. Johnny Mautz and former Maryland Sen. Addie Eckardt in obtaining the funds.
"The Senator and the delegates put forth the request for the Historical Society, not the county," Mackel said.
Commissioner Larry Porter said that he has always liked the project but wanted to make sure the county was not going to be responsible if something goes wrong. He also said that The Caroline County Historical society will take on the fiscal responsibilities of taking care of the money.
The society has contracted with Shore Strategies, a consulting firm for nonprofits and government agencies, to guide them through the process of obtaining the funding.
Kat Stork Blaher of Shore Strategies said, "It is our understanding that the Caroline County Historical Society can be the direct recipient of the funding. The document will demonstrate that the Caroline County Commissioners is the beneficiary of the funds that are being invested in the building because it is seated on county property. But the administrative functions of processing those dollars, it appears to go directly to Caroline County Historical Society and does not need to pass through the county."
Porter responded with caution and said the county has been burned before.
"What does this obligate the county to do? Who is responsible for handling the money? What happens if the money is not handled properly?" Porter asked.
Mackel said the oversight will be done by the historical society and herself.
To be extra careful, the commissioners wanted to see the documents that verified they would not be on the hook for any of the dollars. Mackel said in a phone interview following the meeting that the historical society is "looking into getting bonded," which is a type of insurance that would further protect the county.
Mackel explained why the project is important.
"Caroline County is known for its agriculture. We do not have any agriculture center or really any information on that except what you can find in the Museum of Rural Life. In 2016 the Historical Society gained possession of a circa 1855 dwelling that was Capt. Medford's house," she said.

title: Easton Town Council discusses moving to exempt status for employees
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council discusses moving to exempt status for employees

 April 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 391
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Town Council discussed making the employment status of town employees exempt during a workshop that followed the council meeting Monday evening.Exempt status employees are employees that are paid a salary instead of an hourly wage, and are therefore not paid overtime.
During the workshop, Chief Human Resource Officer Rick Farr said all current town employees are non-exempt employees. This means they receive overtime pay.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, who has worked with Farr and Town Manager Donald Richardson to look at removing overtime from departments that have requested it, said that with the switch to exempt status, all employees would get a 3% pay increase. Although overtime pay would be taken off the table, those employees would be able to receive compensatory time, or overtime hours that can go toward time off from work.
Farr said he thinks this move is in the best interest of the town.
"As far as managing payroll, being able to align, as I said before, the knowledge, skills and abilities of the staff that are going to those exempt statuses," he said.
Ward 2 Council member Don Abbatiello said this idea has been talked about for years. He told Cook that he appreciated her moving forward on it.
Abbatiello said he had two concerns with the plan. One of his concerns is with the increase in salaries for the employees that are already on the high end of salary ranges.
He asked about what happens to compensatory time when a person retires and whether those individuals would be paid out for compensatory time. Cook said those employees would not be paid out for compensatory time when they retire.
Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. said exempt status employees should be given a fair market value salary and should not receive compensatory time.
"You can't have it both ways," he said.
Davis said exempt status will save the town money in the long term and said it is fiscally responsible.
Before the work session ended, Abbatiello said the council recognizes that there are a lot of town employees "who work their butts off."
"And I think that's important to point out," he said. "And we all realize that. We're not trying to take what they do for the town for granted in any way, shape or form. We are just trying to — as Rev. Davis said — be fiscally responsible."

 EASTON — Approximately 13 Town of Easton employees could receive exempt status in the new fiscal year.At an Easton Town Council workshop on exempt and non-exempt employment status Monday, the council discussed the possibility of switching some employee statuses from non-exempt to exempt.

"Our goal is to try to be fiscally responsible and not have to, for example, raise property tax rates in order to cover that," he said. "So we're trying to figure out a way to be as fiscally responsible as possible, while at the same time supporting the hard work that the town employees do."

title: Lakeside Resolution 353 gets Planning Commission's OK
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Lakeside Resolution 353 gets Planning Commission's OK

 April 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 1294
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Tuesday morning, the Talbot County Planning Commission approved, with some revisions, a pending resolution clarifying aspects of the often contentious Lakeside at Trappe development. This has been long awaited, and the process of developing and approving the resolution, Resolution 353, began over a year ago.The approval of Resolution 353 allows the Talbot County Council to vote on the measure at its April 9 meeting.
If approved by the council, this portion of the Lakeside development would finally complete the Maryland Department of Environment's requests for further information and correcting mapping errors, which had been roadblocks for the project.
Background
Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan has described Lakeside as a "complicated matter with a lengthy history."
This residential development project has been 20 years in the making and has been a hot topic for residents in Trappe and throughout the county. Lakeside is a planned 2,501-unit development spanning more than 850 acres off of U.S. Route 50.
According to Erin Braband, Trappe's town clerk, 114 building permits have been issued, and 109 connections have been made to the town's existing wastewater treatment plant.
Trappe's existing plant accommodates wastewater from the development's first 120 homes. Then the flow will eventually be diverted to a new wastewater treatment plant serving the development. The plant is expected to be operational by the beginning of June, according to Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Lakeside's developers who spoke to commissioners at the April 2 meeting.
Before the introduction of Resolution 353, attempts were made to amend Talbot County's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of the development's property for immediate priority for water and sewer service. The resolution created was called Resolution 281.
The MDE approved the resolution in November 2020. But a month later, the agency sent a letter stating that Resolution 281 did not provide the number of equivalent dwelling units for the different phases of Lakeside's construction — information needed for further development.
In December 2020, MDE issued a final wastewater discharge permit for Lakeside's new wastewater treatment plant, approving a flow of 540,000 gallons per day — the number the developer requested in its application.
There was a wave of public outcry over the development's environmental, pollution and water quality issues during a public hearing in October 2021. A month later, the issue was made more complicated when the Talbot County Planning Commission rescinded its approval of an amendment to Resolution 281, which split the property into two sections for differences in water and sewer classifications.
Lawsuits and petitions soon followed. In late October 2022, MDE issued a revised discharge permit for Lakeside, approving a significantly smaller wastewater treatment plant.
The revised permit allows for an average flow of 100,000 gallons per day — a sharp decrease from the 540,000 gallons per day initially requested by the developer. The limited flow will allow for only 400 residential units to be built, only a small portion of Lakeside's planned development. Any future expansion of the facility will require a significant permit modification.
Letters were sent by MDE seeking clarification on some specifics of the development. The agency re-emphasized the need for the county to provide the number of equivalent dwelling units in each phase of Lakeside to assess the adequacy of the water and sewer system to accommodate and serve the development.
The county debated the best way to address MDE's requests last summer, eventually settling on tackling them via comprehensive plan amendments via introduced resolutions 347, 348 and 338.
Resolution 338 would amend the county's comprehensive plan to be consistent with the provisions of Lakeside's wastewater discharge permit.
An amended version of Resolution 338 was found by the Talbot County Planning Commission to be consistent with the county's comprehensive plan in December, but the County Council has delayed voting on it, awaiting the Planning Commission's recommendations on 347, 348 and 353.
Resolution 348 addresses incorrect water and sewer classifications shown in two exhibits — maps displaying updates to Trappe's proposed water and sewer service areas — to Resolution 281.
Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units across all six phases of the Lakeside development's construction. A later amendment to 347 incorporates wording from the still-pending 338.
The original version of Resolution 347 provides the number of equivalent dwelling units — 2,874 in total across all six phases, with just over 1,200 designated for immediate water and sewer service.
It specified that the phases only represent land uses, not timing or sequence of development, and any changes in phasing or allocation will need to be included in amendments reclassifying any phase's water and sewer service.
Voting and a public hearing were delayed as the commissioners attempted to resolve any issues that may potentially arise from the resolutions being introduced.
Resolution 353
On April 2, the Talbot County Commission found Resolution 353 to be consistent with the Talbot comprehensive plan and will move it toward approval by the County Council.
Resolution 353, introduced by Council Vice President Pete Lesher and Council member Lynn Meilke at a Feb. 27 council meeting, "combines Resolutions 338, 347 and 348 into a single resolution," according to County Attorney Patrick Thomas.
Alone, Resolutions 347 and 348 were deemed by commissioners to be confusing, and 348 and 347 were voted to be inconsistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan at the April 2 meeting.
Resolution 353 stood out to many commissioners on the Planning Commission as an avenue to correct issues from Resolutions 338, 347 and 348.
The commission decided to revise aspects of Resolution 353 before finding it consistent with the comprehensive plan, fixing wording to make it compatible throughout the resolution. The revision also includes the removal of language pertaining to the initial flow for the units.
Resolution 353 specifies that 37,500 gallons will be used daily by the first 120 dwelling units. The commission decided to strike the language providing specific numbers and replace it with "the initial flow necessary to serve no more than 120 dwelling units and a community center and pool complex."
However, not everyone was in agreement. Commissioner William Boicourt said that the general confusion is why it should be labeled as non-consistent.
Talbot County Planning Commissioner Chip Councell said his biggest concern was the mapping of the southern portion of the Lakeside property. Resolution 353 changes the water and sewer services designation from W-2/S-2 to W-3/S-3, extending the amount of time the county would have to introduce future legislation on the project.
The reclassification of W-2/S-2 portions of Lakeside to W-3/S-3 would allow for an extension to existing or potential construction of a new community, multi-use or shared sanitary facilities to progress within a six- to 10-year period rather than a three- to five-year period.
The commission voted to find Resolution 353 to be consistent with the Talbot County Comprehensive Plan 4-1, with Boicourt voting against it.
Backlash
Though it is a feat to have a resolution approved by the Planning Commission, not everyone agrees with the resolution proposed.
During a lengthy public comment, several people expressed concerns surrounding potential harms to the environment and the oversight efforts by the county on Trappe.
Bob Flower, a Talbot County resident, said he is worried what Lakeside development would do to Talbot County's lakes, forests and air.
Lyndsey Ryan, attorney for the town of Trappe, said that the town of Trappe is opposed to the amendments on Resolution 347, 348 and 353.
"I think it treats Trappe differently than other municipalities in Talbot County to put this restriction on Trappe," Ryan said. "It sets a bad tone between the two entities … which is why Trappe is opposed to 353."
Under the amendment, any expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant would require a new change to the county's comprehensive plan.
Attorneys for Trappe and the developer opposed the requirement for the developer to come back before the county for future expansion.
Resolution 353 is scheduled for a public hearing during the Talbot County Council meeting on April 9 at 6:30 p.m.

 CENTREVILLE — With a lengthy process of workshops and public input still ahead, County Administrator Todd Mohn presented the first version of the proposed Fiscal Year 2025 County Administrator's Budget to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners March 26.In addition to the upcoming proposed FY25, Mohn presented information and highlights on the current FY24 budget and the previous FY23 budget for comparisons.
Total revenues for the proposed FY25 General Fund budget are $191.2 million, an increase of about $7.6 million from the previous year, he said.
Income tax and property tax make up 87.9 percent of total county revenue sources.
Recordation and transfer tax estimates are 6.5 percent lower than budgeted amounts, due to home sales tapering off, he said.
Investment income is estimated at $6.5 million compared to $4.8 million in FY23, according to Mohn.
Revenue highlights for FY25 includes a 4.1 percent growth from $183.6 million in FY 24 to a total of $191.2 million, he said.
Income tax revenue is projected to grow by 4.4 percent and property tax revenue is projected to grow by 9.1 percent from FY23 actuals, Mohn said.
New tax revenue coming in includes cannabis sales tax and short-term rental permitting programs for an increase of over $500,000, he noted.
County property tax rates are proposed to remain the same at 83 cents out of $100 of assessed value and the same income tax rate at 3.2 percent.
Queen Anne's County is proud of its real property tax rate, remaining the third lowest of the 2023 jurisdictions across the state, Mohn said.
The FY25 revenue budget includes funding for employee recruitment and retention actions and added compensation for a 3 percent cost of living and pay for performance adjustments
Just under $3 million "pay as you go" funding is slated for capital projects for FY25, he said.
FY25 General Fund expenditures are proposed at $191.1 million. The Board of Education receives the most allocation, with a total amount of $73.9 million slated for FY25, a $5 million increase over FY24, according to Mohn.
Debt funds for FY25 are $12.8 million, "which is pretty much flat from the current budget year," he said.
The county has included funding for seven new position requests for a total of $5.9 million in the FY25 proposed operations budget.
A $45 million Capital Budget is proposed for FY25 with $14.5 million proposed for the Board of Education, including the new central office currently under construction, and school district repairs and replacements. $9.4 million is allocated for the roads department capital projects including bridge maintenance and roadway rehabilitation.
Looking ahead, Mohn presented overall perspectives of the county's six year Capital Budget — $28.5 million is allocated for FY25 Capital projects and a total of $231.5 million is projected over the horizon — including funding for ongoing improvements to the 4-H Park, historic courthouse projects and the Cloverfields flood mitigation.
Budget work sessions are scheduled to continue driving deeper into details throughout April and a municipal tax differential hearing will be held April 9.
A budget work session to discuss programs with Chesapeake College will be April 18.
The final FY25 County Administrator's Budget is proposed to be released May 1 and public hearings will be held May 21 and 22 with final budget adoption scheduled for June 11.
The commissioners extended their appreciation to the department heads for their efforts on putting the numbers together.
In other business, the commissioners approved:
-Revisions and overdue updates to the Queen Anne's County Animal Control Ordinance, Chapter 9.
-An ordinance requiring approval of a variance for new piers constructed in excess of 150 feet in length. This variance included an amendment to grandfather in projects currently pending.
The Queen Anne's County Commissioners will next meet April 9 at 5:30 p.m.

 CHESTERTOWN — On Good Friday, Memorial Park in downtown Chestertown filled with Vietnam War Veterans, their families and residents, to honor the veterans for their sacrifice.The March 29 event, Kent County's third National War Veteran's Day, saw a turnout of 240.
Veteran and organizer Peter Sweetser said 35 veterans stepped forward to receive their pin, a handshake and verbal affirmation, thanking them for their service.
As Sweetser put it, soldiers in Vietnam had a unique experience compared to other war veterans being that when they returned from their tour they were mistreated.
Alongside Sweetser, Kent County Commissioners Ron Fithian, Albert Nickerson and John Price proclaimed March 29 as Vietnam Veteran's Day.
They, as well as Chestertown Mayor David Foster, recognized Gold Star family members and spouses who lost veterans after the war.
Keynote speaker Larry Wilkerson, retired army colonel and chief of staff for former U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell, put forth examples of bravery in the conflict.
He not only used examples of American soldiers enduring the pain and loneliness war created. He used examples of the opposition as well, how in tearful, emotional movements both sides came together, bonding over losses suffered.
Wilkerson then talked about a soldier who fought bravely, not just in Vietnam but also against pancreatic cancer.
"That's the Vietnam War for me. So many Americans, so many brave men and women, and so much pain and agony, for what," he said.
All veterans who stepped up were anonymous, with the exception of Sfc. Samuel Tiller, age 95, who had received a Bronze Star and a Purple Heart for his bravery in Vietnam from April 12 to 14, 1964.
Sweetser, who noted that this is a private ceremony between the Department of Defense and the veterans, was pleased with the results.
"It was a great day of celebration for veterans who served nearly 50 years ago, supported by a large crowd of family, friends, and Kent and Queen Anne's County residents. title: It's time to stop overtime pay for Easton town managers
author: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
It's time to stop overtime pay for Easton town managers

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Columns 
 
 875
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's about time.This past week, the Easton Town Council began discussing the way department heads and managers are paid. Currently all town employees are eligible for overtime, including highly paid department heads and managers. This is a discussion that has been a long time coming.
This is not how most governments and businesses operate. Top managers and executives in most organizations are paid a set salary and do not collect overtime, whether they work eight-hour days or 16-hour days.
The rules for paying employees are set in the federal Fair Labor and Standards Act, rules that date to the New Deal when it was first approved in 1938. Under the rules, employees are either exempt or non-exempt. Non-exempt employees are paid hourly and qualify for overtime.
FLSA rules clearly delineate executive functions for exempt employees — employees that do not qualify for overtime pay: "Job duties are exempt executive job duties if the employee regularly supervises two or more other employees, and also has management as the primary duty of the position, and also, has some genuine input into the job status of other employees (such as hiring, firing, promotions, or assignments)."
The Town of Easton's practice of making all employees non-exempt has cost taxpayers tens of thousands of dollars by paying executive and managerial employees overtime.
"There are some persons that got a lot of money in overtime," 4th Ward council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. said. "That is a fact."
The discussion before the Town Council came up during a budget work session on Monday. During the workshop, Chief Human Resource Officer Rick Farr said all current town employees are non-exempt employees. This means they all receive overtime pay.
During the discussion, no one came up with the answer to the question: How long has this been the case?
To her credit, Mayor Megan Cook tackled this thorny issue in the upcoming budget.
Ward 2 council member Don Abbatiello said this idea has been talked about for years. He told Cook that he appreciated her moving forward on it.
"I can't thank Mayor Cook enough for actually putting in the work to try and get this done," Abbatiello said.
But several council members, including Abbatiello, protested part of the plan which would provide compensatory time for extra hours worked by exempt employees. This time would be 1 to 1, if you work an extra hour, you get an hour off.
Cook said that the status change would affect about 13 town employees, mostly department heads.
Davis said exempt status will save the town money in the long term and said it is fiscally responsible.
All council members noted that town employees work hard and this discussion had nothing to do with the work performance.
"We are just talking about being fiscally responsible," Davis said.
"The way I see it, we have been living high on the hog," he said, "and now we have to pay the piper."
Taxpayers for too long — no one said for how long — have been footing the bill for this overtime practice that flies in the face of federal labor laws and best practices for businesses and governments.
Exempt employees should be paid a salary and not receive overtime or compensatory time off. There should be no adjustment of executive and managerial salaries to provide raises to employees who previously received overtime but will not in the future. Salary increases should be based on providing a fair salary for the work done as compared to similar positions in the public sector.
The current mayor and council are stepping up to fix this problem and return fiscal sanity to the Town of Easton's personnel policies.
It is about time they are doing this. Taxpayers owe them thanks for tackling the ongoing problem.
The NCAA Women's Basketball Tournament showdown this week between the University of Iowa and Louisiana State University, ended with the Hawkeye women celebrating their victory.
Yet the game itself was a celebration of the continuing growth of women's athletics and how the performance levels have risen over the years. It was a celebration of the aspirations of Title IX and the improvements seen since its passage in 1972.
The two stars of the game — Iowa's Caitlin Clark and LSU's Angel Reese — have legions of young girls who see in the fierce competitors a model for their own visions of the future, whether it is on an athletic court or in a career.
Those dreams are worth nurturing.

title: Returning Bay ferry servicey faces choppy waters
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Returning Bay ferry servicey faces choppy waters

 April 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 500
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On June 30, 1952, a ribbon-cutting in Anne Arundel County marked the beginning and the end of transportation options between Maryland's Eastern Shore and western shore. On that day, the first Chesapeake Bay Bridge opened for vehicular traffic. That same day, a ferry service that had carried 2 million passengers and 1 million vehicles on the Bay since being launched in 1930 ended.Conventional wisdom then was ferry service would never return to the Bay. Now an effort is underway to return ferry service that is very different from that which ended abruptly 72 years ago.
Currently nine Maryland counties — Queen Anne's, Anne Arundel, Calvert, Somerset, St. Mary's, Wicomico, Talbot, Kent, and Dorchester plus the city of Annapolis — are working with a consultant to study the feasibility of a new passenger only ferry service on the Bay. Their final report will include recommendations on next steps if the consultant's feasibility study concludes such a service is viable and sustainable. It is a work in progress. Routes may be added deleted or modified.
With all due respect to the supporters of this concept, I suggest there are two critical issues they need to consider if they have not done so already.
One issue is the ferry vessel under serious consideration for the proposed new service. It is the Candela P-12 all-electric ferry. It sells for approximately $2 million, does not carry vehicles, seats a maximum of 30 passengers, and has limited storage space for carry-ons such as bicycles, strollers and wheelchairs.
This vessel will not be a practical alternative for the huge number of tourists who use Route 50 when going to Ocean City ("downy shore").
Accordingly, this proposed new ferry service is not likely to generate significant support from Eastern Shore residents and public officials hoping for a solution to regular summer traffic jams on Route 50.
The second issue is the increasingly limited potential for state funding for this concept.
During the past several weeks in the General Assembly, there has been intense (and yet to be resolved) differences of opinion on how to address structural deficits in the state transportation trust fund and projected structural deficits in the state budget. Those deficits are almost certain to become worse based on the devastating impact on the state economy and state revenues from the tragic collapse of the Key Bridge in Baltimore.
Securing state funding for the launch and operation of a new ferry service on the Bay is not going to be a high priority in Annapolis in the foreseeable future.
I am not suggesting these are insurmountable obstacles or the only obstacles. I am suggesting they are very serious obstacles that cannot be ignored by the proponents of returning ferry service on the Bay.
One path forward may be securing private investment for this concept from investors with the resources to launch and operate it.
Otherwise, returning ferry service to the Chesapeake Bay may be an interesting idea whose time has not yet come.
David Reel is a public relations and public affairs consultant who lives in Easton.

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council is sending a letter of support for a United States Senate bill that would exempt seafood processors from the numerical limit on H-2B nonimmigrant visas.At a regular meeting April 2, the County Council voted unanimously to send the letter of support.
According to the U.S. Department of Labor, the H-2B program allows employers in the United States to temporarily hire nonimmigrants for nonagricultural labor or services.
Currently, there is a cap on how many H-2B visas can be issued every year. According to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Citizenship and Immigration Services, the cap is currently 66,000 H-2B visas per fiscal year.
If Senate Bill 3013 is passed, seafood processors would be exempt from this cap.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said at the meeting that it is important to emphasize in the letter the "huge impact" that the limit on H-2B visas issued has on crab picking houses in the county every year.
"Especially in the southern part of our county where everybody is working on the water or adjacent to them," he said.
Detmer said the letter should include the number of workers needed in the county to open all the local picking houses, "and maintain our heritage and our economic development." He said this number is a small one "compared to a larger pool."
Council President Lenny Pfeffer agreed and said that county staff could contact the Dorchester Seafood Heritage Association for those numbers.
"We can have good factual information put in our letter," he said.

author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com

Caroline Commissioners vote to keep proposed tax rates the same

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners unanimously voted to leave the county's proposed property tax rate unchanged for fiscal year 2025 at a meeting on Tuesday.The current tax rate, which would remain the same for the next fiscal year, is 98 cents per $100 of assessed valuation.
In an interview, County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said that rate hasn't changed since 2015.
The vote included the tax differential rates for towns in the county. Tax differentials are lower county property tax rates for properties within municipalities. At the meeting, Commission Vice President Larry Porter asked about Ridgely's tax differential.
"I would say that the logical question would be Ridgely," he said.
On March 13, the Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely Police Department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, according to a press release from the town.
At a County Commission meeting March 19, the commission said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Maryland State Police would divide responsibilities for providing law enforcement to the town.
At the meeting Tuesday, Fox said his current understanding is that Ridgely is discussing the possibility of continuing its contracted service with the the Caroline County Sheriff's Office at 140 hours per week.
"So if that holds true, I think they, by formula, would be entitled to the same differential," he said.
Fox said the hard part of this is that the town still has the opportunity to back out until a contract is signed and endorsed. He said Ridgely's differential is about a $60,000 reduction in property taxes.
"So that would be the number if the board chose not to do a differential," Fox said. "We would receive an additional property tax revenue."
Before making a motion to keep the tax rates the same, Commission President Travis Breeding said he was ok with keeping the rate the same.
"I'm ok with keeping it the same for the year and seeing where they end up," he said about Ridgely.
Caroline County will be holding a public budget hearing on May 7 at 6 p.m.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this article.

title: CWDI to hold public session this month to address concerns, questions

CWDI to hold public session this month to address concerns, questions

 CAMBRIDGE — Later this month, residents will have the opportunity to have their questions answered and hear more about the plans for Cambridge Harbor, a development project along the Choptank River.In a letter to the public, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board President Angie Hengst said people will be able to submit questions and get clarification on some of the topics "that have been circulating as of late." She said CWDI has been "the topic of conversation" over the past few weeks.
On March 18, Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said in a letter that his last day as city manager would be no later than May 17.
Carroll said he resigned over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project, a project that will create public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Cambridge waterfront.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard told the Star Democrat in March that Carroll's reasons for leaving are his reasons.
"I don't know what all the reasons are," Leonard said. "If that's the one he has chosen to promote, I'm sorry to see that. It doesn't make a lot of sense to me, but his reasons are his reasons."
In her April letter, Hengst said some of the recent conversations about Cambridge Harbor and CWDI have been inaccurate or a "mis-representation of the facts."
"I know many community members feel they are getting conflicting information from various sources and feel confused or unsure about what is really happening," she said.
The letter said CWDI will hold a public session on April 18. The session will be held at 6 p.m. at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center in Cambridge. It will also be live-streamed.
Hengst said that the public can always reach out to her at Angie.hengst@cwdimd.org, Leonard at matt.leonard@cwdimd.org or the other board members with questions or concerns.
At a Dorchester County Council meeting April 2, Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he had received an email from a constituent with questions about CWDI, including the status of the hotel and the possibility of the YMCA moving to Cambridge Harbor.
Detmer said he had a "great conversation" with Leonard, who answered the questions. Detmer said he will be following up with the constituent who sent the email.
Interim Dorchester County Manager Jeff Powell reminded the council at the meeting that a county-appointed seat needs to be filled on the CWDI board. The council voted to post the open position at the meeting.
Powell said he wanted to make it clear he will not be seeking the position when his role as interim county manager comes to an end in June.
