title: Dorchester County Council votes to add ballot measures for November election
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council votes to add ballot measures for November election

 July 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 657
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Come November, Dorchester County residents will decide whether or not to make changes to the county charter, including clarifying the county manager's responsibilities, adding language to ensure transparency and adjusting budget due dates.At a Dorchester County Council meeting on July 16, the council voted to approve six separate resolutions — which will be made into referendums on the November ballot. The council voted against approving one resolution that could have created a term limit for county council members.
The six resolutions, which were based on March recommendations by the Dorchester County Charter Review Committee, include:
Add language that solidifies the differences between the county manager's responsibilities and the council's responsibilities.Remove the residency requirement for the county manager.Remove the residency requirement for the director of finance.Require an administrative review to take place the first fiscal year of each new council.Change the due date for the proposed county budget from May 1 to May 15 and the due date for the adoption of the county budget from June 1 to June 15.Add language to ensure transparency.
Residents will not be able to vote on whether county council members should be limited to three consecutive four-year terms in November.
At the July 16 meeting, Council President Larry Pfeffer was the only council member to vote in favor of the resolution. He said he voted this way because the county charter says that the charter should be reviewed every decade by a commission, and this was one of the modifications to the charter that the commission recommended.
"So I felt it would be best to leave it up to the voters themselves to see if they felt the term limits were something that should be modified in the charter," he said.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he was voting against the resolution because he "philosophically opposes" these term limits. He said that every election is a term limit. Detmer also said that being a districted county rather than an at-large county limits the candidate pool.
"We want the best player available," he said. "And if that person should sit there for four terms or five terms, that should be the decision of the people."
Before voting to approve the resolution regarding county manager responsibilities, the council amended its language.
One amendment clarifies that the council has a right to direct the county manager. Another makes it clear that individual council members cannot give orders to employees.
Regarding the second amendment, Detmer said he took issue with phrasing in the resolution that says, "council shall deal with administrative and departmental and departmental services solely through the county manager."
"Does this mean I cannot even send an email to them?" he asked. "That's how it could be construed."
This part of the resolution goes on to say, "and neither the council nor any member thereof shall give orders to any subordinate employee, either publicly or privately."
Susan Dukes, who was on the County Charter Review Committee and is the mayor of Secretary, said the intention of this particular change to the charter was to make it clear that no one council member should be able to make requests to department heads or employees on their own.
"You're hiring a county manager to do that job," she said. "And that's what we felt like it should be because there has been past issues where that has become a problem. And we wanted to firm it up to make sure that you would act as a body and not as individuals."
The council voted to change the wording to make it clear that no individual council member should give orders to county staff.
Though the majority of the resolutions passed unanimously, council member William Nichols voted against the resolutions regarding county manager responsibilities and governmental transparency.
He said he voted against the resolution for county manager responsibilities because he doesn't think that an appointed individual should have more authority than five people who were elected. He said he voted against the transparency resolution "because it's already here now."

title: Trappe council considers uses for remaining ARPA funds
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Trappe council considers uses for remaining ARPA funds

 July 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 Words

 TRAPPE — Town leaders held a workshop on Wednesday afternoon to discuss potential ways to allocate outstanding funds from the American Rescue Plan Act in Trappe.The town has about $758,000 in ARPA funds that must be obligated by the end of 2024 and used by the end of 2026. While no formal decisions were made, the Trappe Town Council did agree to look into securing two new trucks for its public works department.
Town Administrator Erin Braband said that the town's current two trucks are "at their last leg." Council President Brian Schmidt estimated that the costs for two trucks could be around $150,000.
Braband also presented the idea of buying new water meters for the town since the current ones are about 20 years old. This would allow the city to directly receive reports, along with allowing residents to track hourly water usage and receive usage emails.
Council members were open to using ARPA funds for new meters and radio-read transmitters. Braband estimated the cost may be around $175,000.
Much of Wednesday's discussion centered around the town's roads. Town Attorney Lyndsey Jones Ryan warned the council about using ARPA funds to pave roads due to a lack of "clear guidance" at the federal level on whether it falls under allowed uses.
Though she said towns like Federalsburg have allocated ARPA money towards paving, she pointed out that there is a risk the town would end up responsible.
Council Member Jeremy Newnam also expressed concern about beginning work to pave roads before a lead lining initiative this October that may necessitate tearing up the roads for repair.
"I just really worry about paving roads and then possibly having to tear them all up in a couple months," Newnam said. Schmidt agreed, saying "it would be an awful shame" to have newly-paved roads and then tear and patch parts of the road.
Another workshop is planned for early August. No ARPA funds will be officially allocated until the council takes a vote at a council meeting.

title: Gov. Moore talks service, faith at Easton food pantry
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Gov. Moore talks service, faith at Easton food pantry

 562

 EASTON — Gov. Wes Moore hauled a large basket of food to the Society of St. Vincent de Paul's food pantry Wednesday evening, along with an even larger smile.The governor made his second public appearance on the Mid-Shore in as many months, speaking to local officials and volunteers of the Easton food pantry and thrift store.
"You all remind me of what it means to have hope," Moore said. "You all remind us that we live in a big and a beautiful and a bright world and that we all have a place in it."
He mentioned that St. Vincent de Paul's work to help county residents in need comes "at a time when we continue to allow political vitriol to create horrific images that we continue to see on our television screens."
Moore has denounced "political violence" in statements since an assassination attempt on Republican presidential candidate and former President Donald Trump less than a week ago. The shooting, which took place at a Trump rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, July 13, left one spectator dead and Trump with a minor injury.
The governor's Easton visit came in the midst of a push by some Democratic leaders for President Joe Biden to reconsider his candidacy in the upcoming November election.
Moore's name has been floated as a possible replacement for the president's atop the Democratic ticket. But the governor has been steadfast in his support of Biden.
Prior to speaking Wednesday evening, Moore explained his support for the president.
Moore pointed to the state's recovery in unemployment, a reduction in homicides and shootings, and the Port of Baltimore reopening — areas in which Biden's assistance has been crucial to Maryland, he said.
"Those things did not happen by accident," Moore said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "They required leadership, and they required partnership. And I'm just really thankful that we have the president as a partner."
Moore said the upcoming election between Biden and Donald Trump is a "binary choice."
"For me, the choice between Donald Trump and President Biden is an easy one," Moore said. "President Biden's consistently supported the people of our state, and I'm excited about thinking about what another four years of President Biden could be like."
Alex Handy, president of the Easton chapter of St. Vincent de Paul, said during the governor's visit that Moore is "one of the warmest people I've ever met."
"He (had a) big smile, came over, hugged people like crazy," Handy said.
It was the first time that Skip and Peggy Baraldi, volunteers at St. Vincent de Paul, saw the governor in person. Skip took notice of Moore's "outgoing" personality as he talked to the crowd for around 10 minutes.
Moore thanked volunteers at St. Vincent de Paul's Easton chapter, an organization he said acts as the "backbone of our social fabric" in an interview with The Star Democrat. Talking to the crowd, Moore emphasized his faith.
"I do want to be very, very clear: I am a child of God," Moore said during his speech. "I know who woke me up this morning. I know who will put me to bed tonight. … So when I say I'm thankful for you and I'm praying for you, I mean it."
"It's an honor to be your colleague, it's an honor to be your friend, it's an honor to be your neighbor, it's an honor to be your governor," Moore continued, drawing applause from the crowd.

title: Outage at Microsoft Closes Courts in Maryland

 EASTON — A massive technological meltdown affecting Microsoft users July 19 caused nationwide shutdowns, including several in Mid-Shore communities.No courts in Maryland are heard cases Friday while teams at Microsoft and other IT companies worked to piece together what happened.
Amanda Purnell, Talbot County Circuit Court administrator, said, "We are closed for the day. We do not have access to any of our court systems right now. They are working of a fix... We can't access our court system at all so we are not able to view anything within the cases."
A statement on the Maryland Judiciary website read, "Due to the worldwide Microsoft outage, all Maryland courts, offices, and facilities will be closed to the public today but will remain open for emergency matters. All clerks' offices are closed."
The culprit behind the outage was determined to be cybersecurity company CrowdStrike.
CrowdStrike said one of its software updates malfunctioned, causing some users' computers to go inert.
"CrowdStrike is actively working with customers impacted by a defect found in a single content update for Windows hosts," the company said in a statement Friday.
While national and state outages caused some closures on the Mid-Shore, the impacts to local technology were not felt quite as significantly.
Large corporate data bases were more at risk than smaller, local computer users, according to some IT professionals.
"Most of the outage is going to be a higher level corporate customer," said Jon Sharp, general manager of Jason's Computers in Easton. "We were worried this morning with the Microsoft stuff, but it hasn't seemed to trickle down to the residential customer."
Jeff Lankford, business and marketing coordinator for the Easton Airport, said the airport did not shut down operations Friday. Branch banker Amy McKenzie from PNC Bank in Easton said the bank had not had any problems.
CrowdStrike said that it had already implemented a solution to the bad code problem causing the outages Friday afternoon.

 EASTON — Bob Willey, Easton's former mayor, was honored Friday morning with a plaque describing his instrumental work in expanding Easton's Rails to Trails.The East-West section of the rail trail, which was dedicated to Willey, opened in April 2023. It connected the existing North-South trail to Port Street, the culmination of work by the town and the state.
Current Mayor Megan Cook said Willey carried the vision to expand the town's trails.
"Mayor Willey played an important role in turning the abandoned rail line into a thriving bike trail," Cook said. "Not only was he instrumental in the creation of the original North-South trail, but he recognized the benefits of extending the trail system throughout the community."
Town Manager Donald Richardson said expanding Rails to Trails became a priority of Willey's around 2016.
"It was a plan that had been sitting on a shelf for quite a long time," Richardson said. "And if any of you know Mayor Willey, he does not like plans to be sitting on the shelf. So we dusted it off, it already had some funding in place through Maryland State Highway Administration, and we went to work. By no means was this trail an easy endeavor."
Easton's North-South Rails to Trails path, completed in 1998, is nearly three miles long, connecting North Easton Park and Idlewild Park. It is a popular stretch for walkers, runners and bikers, as is the newer East-West path.
There is still about half a mile left to be finished of the East-West expansion. Cook said once completed, the East-West section will add 1.5 miles of additional trail for residents. She emphasized that the Rails to Trails project helps public health, recreation and the economy.
Willey and his family attended the ceremony on South Hanson Street, with more than 60 town employees and residents in attendance. The former mayor celebrated his retirement this past winter after more than 30 years of service to the town, which included his time as mayor from 2003 to 2023.
"You get electeds like myself that come up with these hair-brained ideas of a rail trail and all the other stuff that needs to be done," Willey said Friday morning to the crowd. "Then the engineers worry about how it's going to fit in. And then we have a very talented public works crew, that really guys, I haven't seen anything you haven't been able to do and do very well."

 EASTON — An ordinance that will crack down on the dumping and spillage of certain discharges in Easton is set to take effect in early August.The Easton Town Council unanimously passed an illicit discharge ordinance on Monday following discussions of the item at three public meetings. Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh worked to put the ordinance together, emphasizing that the only discharge that should end up in the street is rainwater.
"At the end of the day, the only thing allowed in the stormwater system is rainwater, so we need to do our best to keep everything else out," Van Emburgh said.
Due to EPA requirements that were passed down to the Maryland Department of the Environment, the town is required to restrict certain discharges. The restrictions come since Easton is in its sixth year of the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System program — a program that the state requires the town to follow.
The ordinance authorizes the town to perform inspections at sites where it has "reasonable cause" that an illicit discharge violation is occurring. The town may also fine violators.
However, Van Emburgh stated that the main goal is to make residents aware of the law and how to achieve "best practices" when disposing of substances.
"We're not going to come out and fine anybody," Van Emburgh said at the meeting. "We're just going to come out, and we'll have flyers."
Matt Pluta, the Choptank riverkeeper for ShoreRivers, expressed support for the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System program. Pluta said foreign material entering the stormwater system negatively impacts the Chesapeake Bay and local waterways. Grease from restaurants and concrete were two materials Pluta pointed out as harmful.
"Those storm drains along the street, those aren't treated," Pluta said. "The water that goes in there isn't treated, it's just a direct conveyance to our local waterways. Here in Easton, that waterway is the Tred Avon River right here at Easton Point."
PROHIBITED DISCHARGESThe town engineer noted some specific examples during Monday's Town Council meeting. Van Emburgh said the town is asking for leaves to be placed "behind the curb" for the public works crew to pick up. He also addressed the example of changing oil.
"We're not going to be out looking for people changing the oil in their cars," Van Emburgh said. "We're looking to make sure it's done in a responsible way, and if there is an accident, we use what's available to us to clean it up."
Some other prohibited discharges outlined in the ordinance include swimming pool water with chlorine levels beyond state regulations, new or used petroleum products, industrial waste and septic tank waste.
Chemicals put down drains in houses are fine, since those go to the sanitary sewer line and a wastewater treatment facility, Van Emburgh clarified at a previous Town Council meeting.
Exempt discharges include discharges from firefighting, irrigation water, dechlorinated swimming pool water in line with state regulations and residential car washing, among others.
While commercial car washers are not exempt, Van Emburgh said that car washing companies in town have proper recycling methods that will fall in line with the requirements of the ordinance.

title: Food processing residuals bill set for public hearing
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Food processing residuals bill set for public hearing

 July 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 671
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — New Caroline County legislation that aims to mitigate irresponsible storage of food processing residuals is set for a public hearing in early August.On July 9, the Caroline County Commissioners introduced an emergency bill that will create a permit process in order to store food processing residuals. It creates limitations on how residuals can be stored and permits the county to fine violators.
If passed, it would require closed-top storage tanks, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly. House Bill 991, which took effect July 1, created a state permitting process under the Maryland Department of Agriculture for the use, storing and hauling of the residuals.
"You should also bear in mind, MDA is not renowned for its enforcement," County Attorney Stewart Barroll, who drafted the bill, said at a July 10 Planning Commission meeting. "And this is a county. We can't enforce MDA regulations. We can enforce county ordinances. And so having it in here is belt and suspenders."
The Planning Commission, made up of five members including County Commissioner Travis Breeding, narrowly passed a favorable recommendation for the legislation on July 10. Breeding and Chair Jeff Jackson voted yes, Vice Chair Hannah Cawley voted no, and commission member Keith Bilbrough abstained. Member Roger McKnight was not present.
"In my personal opinion, the state has done an excellent job putting something together," Cawley said. "And if it were up to me … I'd like to see how far the state gets with theirs and then make amendments on the county level."
Bilbrough asked for more time and information, adding he wasn't "necessarily opposed."
After the favorable vote, the bill is set for a public hearing on Aug. 6 at 9:15 a.m. in the Denton Health & Public Services Building.
In that same building in January, the county commissioners heard from a record crowd of more than 150 people on the storage of dissolved air floatation residuals, a type of food processing residual. That and subsequent meetings led the county to place and later extend moratoriums on the storage of residuals. The moratoriums last until this fall but may be replaced by the permit bill at hand.
Three new amendments to the legislation were added during the July 10 Planning Commission meeting: food processing residuals cannot be mixed with other substances in storage containers, the county will no longer request an applicant's nutrient management plan, and language concerning temporary storage is adjusted to "mirror" state regulations.
The Planning Commission heard opposing views from local industry and environmental leaders.
Holly Porter, executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, asked the planning commission to not vote favorably. She believes the county bill is "25 pages of confusion" and will negatively impact farmers and businesses who responsibly store food processing residuals.
"I have repeatedly been told that Caroline County does not have the resources to enforce the bad actor that's out there, and yet now we have the resources to create a permitting scheme, that again, repeats and is more onerous than the state's," Porter said. "Caroline County has the ability to make text amendments right here with the zoning table of use regulations."
Matt Pluta, Choptank riverkeeper for ShoreRivers, and Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director of the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, each spoke in support of the bill.
"I don't think the size of the bill really matters," Pluta said. "I think it's how effective the bill is … I do think this bill does a really good job of making sure the county is taking control of what they are responsible for."
Girard questioned if the fines outlined in the legislation — $500 for a first offense and $1,000 for a subsequent one — were too relaxed.
While the planning commission was split on whether to recommend the amended bill, Breeding said the commissioners agree on the need to crack down on open-top storage tanks.
"The sentiment of the commissioners is it needs to be closed-top storage," Breeding said. "Because there's nowhere in this county that you're not going to store this stuff and have an adverse effect on a neighbor."

title: Council holds work session to discuss Route 662 closure
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Council holds work session to discuss Route 662 closure

 July 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 767
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council held a work session Tuesday afternoon to discuss the potential eight-month closure of Route 662 as construction for a new regional medical center commences.The University of Maryland Shore Regional Health is building the new hospital off Longwoods Road next to U.S. Route 50 and just north of the Easton Airport.
UM Shore Regional Health Attorney Ryan Showalter said that the hospital design has "changed slightly" from versions produced a decade ago, when discussions of the new hospital first began to gain momentum.
Current designs have portions of the hospital sitting in the middle of existing Route 662. To accommodate the plans, a stretch of the road will have to be relocated.
Under original county legislation allowing for the hospital's construction, the new road was required to be completed before portions of 662 were surrendered to Shore Regional Health.
"One of the reasons why we now have a conflict is that the elevation of the hospital will be higher than the existing bed of the road," Showalter said.
"Keeping 662 open to traffic until the new 662 is constructed would literally require not constructing one-third of the hospital, that arm of the hospital, because we can't pour the concrete for that and finish the building in stages," he added.
He said temporary closure of the road will prevent delays in construction of the hospital, which is slated to begin in spring 2025, with doors tentatively opening in summer 2028.
The legislation that Talbot County Council members will consider is an amendment to Bill 1231, which dates back to 2013. Its original form "conditions the transfer" of the old route to Shore Regional Health on the completion of the new road.
County Attorney Patrick Thomas explained that the amended bill would allow for that transfer before completion of the new stretch of 662 under three contingencies:
The State Highway Administration approves the closure from Oct. 1 to May 1.
A road transfer agreement amendment is executed to transfer the road from the state to the county before it's then transferred to Shore Health.
A road inspection and contribution agreement is executed.
The latter agreement would facilitate improvements to county roads that are expected to serve as unofficial detours for the closure — Hiners Lane, Hailem School Road, Goldsborough Neck Road and Airport Road. The State Highway Administration's official detour will be U.S. Route 50.
Council members previously voiced concerns for nearby county roads, especially if farm operators are forced to use them instead of Route 662. Showalter and Thomas both said Shore Health will contribute financially towards upgrading those roads, along with being responsible for the construction of the realigned Route 662.
Scott Saxman, division vice president at Whiting-Turner Contracting Company, said the company is "very confident" that the road's reconstruction will be done by May 1.
Thomas emphasized that the timeline for the legislation — which is set as an emergency bill — is tight, since the Maryland Board of Public Works is required to approve the transfer of the Route 662 land to the county.
Council Member Lynn Mielke pushed for Showalter to explain why the county was not involved in discussions sooner.
"I understand that this issue first arose in a meeting the hospital had back in February to consider this change," Mielke said. "And of course the county was not invited to that meeting or informed of that meeting to participate, is that correct?" Mielke asked Showalter.
"I don't remember. I know we've had discussions about how to get here," Showalter responded, adding that he's had multiple meetings every week since December.
Showalter said that all of the "core infrastructure" of the building design has stayed the same, and that "shifting the entire building to avoid the road requires redesign of the entire site" along with "substantial" impacts on cost.
"What is that cost?" Mielke asked.
"I don't know," Showalter said. He said he could request an estimate if needed.
"You haven't convinced me that this is an emergency," Mielke said of the impacts to the project if Route 662 is not temporarily closed. " … There's a possibility that this isn't really going to be completed by May, we may have another summer of diverted traffic."
Council Vice President Pete Lesher stated he's "fully behind this project," but said he wants to see the full project held true to timelines if Route 662 must be temporarily closed.
"There's this hiccup that we have, that we hadn't anticipated," he said. "The hazard and inconvenience of closing the route … I think we just want to be assured that this is absolutely necessary."
The legislation to amend Bill 1231 was introduced during Tuesday's County Council meeting. A public hearing is set for Aug. 27.

title: San Domingo Creek Park stirs controversy among St. Michaels commissioners
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
San Domingo Creek Park stirs controversy among St. Michaels commissioners

 July 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 679
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Tuesday evening, St. Michaels commissioners unanimously approved sending a letter to obtain a grant for a potential park in town, but not without tense discussion.The San Domingo Creek Park stirred controversy among the commissioners, who debated whether or not the five-acre land could serve a different purpose.
About a week ago, representatives from Open Space, a program of the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, encouraged the town to apply for a $1.7-million grant for the development of the park. Town Administrator Rob Straebel said the representatives would like to see a letter of information pertaining to the park within two weeks.
The commissioners, now faced with a tight deadline, held a special meeting Tuesday to vote on whether or not the town should apply for the grant.
Straebel, in his explanation of the grant, provided a tentative schedule of the buildout of the park, including estimated price points for the two phases of the park's development.
Phase 1 would take place in 2025 and be completed within three years, according to the documents provided by Straebel. Phase 2 would take about seven to 10 years with a completion date of 2033.
Straebel estimated the contribution to the park by the town would be about $3.7 million of the about $5.4 million total cost, though he emphasized that the town contribution may be lowered if funding is secured through other grants. Additionally, a group of residents are applying for a 501©(3) charitable organization designation, which would provide the opportunity for private fundraising for the park project.
Commissioner Alfred Mercier, showed favor for the timeline of the park and for the town to approve sending a letter to Open Space, describing it as the "first step."
Commissioner David Wojciechowski on the other hand said he was "struggling" with the idea of moving forward with the project due to the financial obligation the town, and potentially the residents, would have for it. Wojciechowski suggested the property could be sold.
"So is the park worth $3 million?" Wojciechowski asked. "I think that question should be presented to the public of the town, and we should let the public and the town people decide now that we have this new information and these alternatives."
Commissioner Alexis Roiter, also questioned the necessity of the park, stating the land could be used to help solve town problems.
"We have people who are going to the community center for food because they can't get to a grocery store, and then we're talking about a $3- or $4-million park, and I have to tell you honestly, my brain is having trouble with that," she said.
Straebel said if the commissioners voted to send the letter to Open Space, they would not be "committing to anything at this point." A decision on the grant would not happen for a few months, and during that time, if residents felt strongly, the town could decide to not take the grant money.
During the public comment period, residents of the town voiced favor for the potential park.
Dan Spiegel, a resident, expressed "disappointment" with the commissioners for considering not following through with the park project, stating there was a clear consensus with the residents for a park.
"I can't tell you how shocked and disappointed I am by this discussion, especially the views of Commissioner Wojciechowski and Commissioner Roiter," Spiegel said. "It was in the clear consensus of the residents of this town that one of the most important things that the government of this town did was acquire this open space to turn it into a park."
A 7.6 acre property at 201 Boundary Lane was purchased by the town for the park for $2.9 million last year.
The town plans to use the existing building on the property for a new town office. The remainder of the property will be a public park, complete with nature trails, expanded wetlands, a living shoreline, a fishing pier, a comfort station and associated parking, according to the town's plans.
After the public comment, the commissioners unanimously approved sending the letter, stating that they may have a future discussion to determine the fate of the park.

title: Tangier ferry captain retiring
author: MILES LAYTON APG Media
content:
Tangier ferry captain retiring

 July 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MILES LAYTON APG Media | Section: State News 
 
 500
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TANGIER, Va. — Townfolk came out to thank Capt. Mark Haynie, who is retiring after ferrying thousands of tourists between the Maryland Eastern Shore and Tangier Island for the past 15 years.July 19, the Tangier Volunteer Fire Department used a hose to spray water high in the air over Haynie's boat, Sharon Kay III, as it motored toward the town dock where a crowd awaited to congratulate the good captain for his service.
Mayor James "Ooker" Eskridge gave a short speech to mark the occasion of Haynie's last run to Tangier.
"Mark would always be willing to add special and emergency medical charters. At any time, day or night, Mark could be counted on, even in the dead of night, hauled out of bed for a medical emergency. Tonight marks his last official regular run. Fair winds are following seas as you enter retirement, Captain. Your rest is well earned and deserved. You will be sorely missed."
With a skilled hand behind the wheel, Haynie is comfortable piloting the Sharon Kay III, which holds up to 29 passengers, as he ferries tourists back and forth seven days a week across the Tangier Sound between the island where he grew up and Crisfield, Maryland.
"Yeah. I'm going to miss it," said Haynie, a native of Tangier Island. "I'll miss talking to people and dealing with people. I'm going to miss it."
Being a waterman comes naturally to Haynie, 71, who spent a lifetime crabbing and oystering on the Chesapeake Bay before turning his wheel toward the ferry service in 2008. The trip between the island and Crisfield takes about 45 minutes where folks can see Smith Island, Maryland, and other barrier islands.
Approaching Tangier, tourists revel at the iconic Swain Memorial Methodist Church or the water tower in the distance as the boat approaches the crab shanties bordering the harbor.
"The trip is pretty easy most of the time," Haynie said. "Most times, the weather's pretty good. Winter time, you have some bad trips. But yeah, I've enjoyed almost every minute of it."
Cruising the Chesapeake Bay can be a pleasant experience with smooth waters or a bit more animated crossing because strong winds and bad weather mean steering through rough waves.
"Well, we had one time that we had a funeral," Haynie said. "... Like when we got in Crisfield we had 60-65 mph winds, so that was too dangerous to be out in, but that hit us while we're out there. We made it in with 23 people."
A skilled waterman, Allen Parks, is taking over Haynie's route to bring tourists to Tangier and make other important runs as needed 12-13 miles away to Crisfield, Haynie said.
So what's next for Haynie? He's too skilled as a captain to sit on the dock of the bay wasting time as the Otis Redding song says.
"Well, I'd like to find something to do. I got a smaller boat. I could travel around in her and all. There's some fishing and crabbing, fishing," Haynie said.
Miles Layton is region editor for APG Ohio.

 GREENSBORO — Cleanup for a bat infestation in Town Hall is expected to cost about $12,000 for the town of Greensboro. Town Manager Tammy Kelledes said the town hopes to re-open the building Thursday.The town initially discovered multiple dead and alive bats in the Town Hall building on July 12. title: Cambridge City Council appoints next city manager
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council appoints next city manager

 July 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After more than two months without a permanent city manager, the Cambridge City Council has appointed someone to fill the position.At a council meeting on July 22, the Council voted unanimously to appoint W. Glenn Steckman as the next city manager. According to council documents, Steckman is expected to begin in early September. Acting Cambridge City Manager David Deutsch said Steckman is set to start the week after Labor Day.
Steckman is coming to Cambridge from Nome, Alaska, where he has served as city manager for about five years. Deutsch said Steckman has 25 years of experience in municipal government, which includes multiple city manager roles.
"So his experience certainly demonstrated that he had broad exposure to city issues in various types of municipalities," Deutsch said. "And he stood out as someone who could apply that experience here in Cambridge."
Though Steckman is traveling from across the country for this position, this isn't his first rodeo in Dorchester County. In the early 2000s, Steckman served as a circuit rider manager for smaller municipalities in the county, including Vienna, Deutsch said. As a circuit rider manager, Steckman would serve multiple small municipalities that might not be able to afford a full-time manager.
"That's real nuts and bolts experience," Deutsch said, laughing. "I know other folks that have done it, and it's a real juggling act."
Deutsch has been serving as Cambridge's acting city manager since May, following the resignation of former City Manager Tom Carroll. In March, Carroll announced he would be resigning from the city manager position due to concerns with Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront.
While serving as acting city manager, Deutsch has been leading recruitment for the permanent city manager position under a separate contract between the city and Mercer Group Associates, a consulting firm that Deutsch is a senior associate with.
Deutsch said the city received 15 applicants for the city manager position. He, along with a Citizen Search Committee, helped whittle the number of applicants down before the potential candidates were presented to the City Council.
Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout said he thinks Steckman has the skillset that will allow him to pick up where Carroll left off.
"He'll work long hours," Rideout said. "He'll take time to meet with people. He wants to meet with staff. ... All the things that, to me, is someone who, first of all, listens and learns from the community and the staff what's important and then puts his skills to use in making improvements."
Rideout said he thinks Steckman's skillset will be beneficial when it comes to the Cambridge Harbor project and CWDI. He said Steckman has experience dealing with development projects and tax increment financing.
With Steckman's appointment by the council and an employment agreement signed, Deutsch said the next step is just getting Steckman to Cambridge. Deutsch said Steckman has told him that he and his spouse are already looking at properties in the area.
"So that's great that they're jumping on it," Deutsch said. "(I) look forward to him establishing his residency here and becoming part of the community in that way, as well as the office."

title: Chestertown moves to change regulations in historic district
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Chestertown moves to change regulations in historic district

 July 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Chestertown council member, Meghan Efland, at their latest meeting with Mayor David Foster on July 22, called for a discussion with their Historic District Commission over regulations.The Historic District Commission regulations determines, for instance, what kinds of windows can be put on a historic building. They can decide what sort of materials may be used, or, for example, what siding can be implemented to maintain the historical authenticity of the neighborhood.
The council unanimously decided that although they cannot veto the Historic District Commission's decisions, nor desire to, they can change the rules and regulations to which they base their decisions.
Foster was adamant he is not in anyway looking to change something that has already been decided by the Historic District Commission.
But there are concerns he has with these current regulations.
For example, lead paint is a concern for him, especially on those old windows.
The regulations right now allow the homeowner to put in storm windows, but won't allow for brand new windows designed to look old, to be placed. Foster said there's a high level of difficulty if someone wanted to put in energy efficient windows in their historically old home.
Foster pointed out that shouldn't be, "I think it [new windows] would be a health and an energy benefit."
Efland added that roofing material has advanced as well since the regulations were written.
The council's not going to change the regulations in the dark of the night behind the Historic District Commission's back. Efland suggested they sit in on a meeting and talk to them about some of the changes they'd like to see.
Right now, an Historic District Commission ruling only gets appealed at the circuit court level.
Council member Tim O'Brien said that's not the way most counties operate. Most counties, he said, have an appeal process within the town structure.
O'Brien, consulting legal over this issue, said as long as the Chestertown Planning Commission and Historic District Commission appeal to the same entity, they wouldn't have to go through the circuit court any longer.
Right now, there is an Historic District Commission ruling over the Chestertown Armory that is being appealed in the circuit court.
The council does not want to interfere with cases like that. They all seemed to agree with Efland, expressing their aim is to make these regulations more readable to the community.
"I feel like it's a lot of responsibility for that group. To have what's modern and up-to-date and to see whatever other towns are doing, I think is important," she said.
O'Brien noted that Town Manager Larry DiRe, who was absent from the meeting, has found funding to make an internal Historic District Commission appeals process possible in the near future.
For residents interested in Historic District Commission rulings, regularly scheduled meetings are held the first Wednesday of each month at 4 p.m. in Town Hall unless otherwise announced. Their meetings are also online on the town website.

O'Brien noted that Town Manager Larry DiRe, who was absent from the meeting, has found funding to make an internal Historic District Commission appeals process possible in the near future.
For Chestertown residents interested in Historic District Commission rulings, regularly scheduled meetings are held the first Wednesday of each month at 4 p.m. in Town Hall unless otherwise announced. The meetings are also online on the town website.

title: County, state leaders break ground on St. Vincent de Paul expansion
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
County, state leaders break ground on St. Vincent de Paul expansion

 August 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 585
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — County and state leaders joined together Thursday morning to ceremonially break ground on the expansion and remodeling of St. Vincent de Paul, a nonprofit organization that provides food, shelter and clothing assistance to Talbot County residents in need.Though the project still needs a town permit to begin actual construction, stakeholders gathered to celebrate the progress the nonprofit has made toward growing its space and offerings.
The expansion and remodeling will increase the current 7,200-square-foot building on Canvasback Drive by 2,560 square feet. It will grow the organization's space for its food pantry, thrift store and advisory offices.
Alex Handy, president of the Easton Chapter of St. Vincent de Paul, spoke at the ceremony about the building's growth since he joined the organization.
"We have an incredible facility here," Handy said. "We're about to expand it even larger. And we have hundreds of volunteers. And all I can say (is) that God must've had a vision for where we were going, because I can tell you 22 years ago, we had no idea we'd be here today."
Willow Construction has designed a floor plan for the remodel, which attendees could look at on Thursday. St. Vincent de Paul Vice President John Plaskon says Willow Construction's general contracting service will cost about $898,000. Additional costs for engineering, plumbing and architecture may put the total mark over $1 million, Plaskon said.
To help with funding, St. Vincent de Paul is receiving a $625,000 grant from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development. The department's assistant secretary, Carol Gilbert, attended Thursday's ceremony.
"You guys are doing something right, I'm sure," Gilbert said. "I'm really impressed by the volume of support of services that you give to your community."
Talbot County Council Member Keasha Haythe also talked to the crowd about the organization's importance to Talbot County, calling it an "exciting day" for the county. Last month, the council allocated $100,000 in American Rescue Plan Act funds for the nonprofit's expansion project.
Plaskon said the project may take around eight to nine months once a permit is issued and work commences. He hopes that all sections of St. Vincent de Paul will remain operational for as much time as possible during construction.
Part of the added-on space will include a new food pantry. Plaskon said that if they can move the pantry from its old area to the new one between its normal Tuesday and Saturday distribution days, no services will be affected.
The thrift store, though, will have to close down for a short period.
"The thrift store generates half the revenue that we need to operate. The other half comes from donations," Plaskon said. "We want to minimize how long it's shut down. But there's no way around it, it's going to have to happen, it's just a matter of how many weeks."
In addition to a larger space for the pantry, thrift store and meeting rooms, Plaskon said the site's parking situation will be improved. Plaskon said the "parking lot gets really jammed up" on Saturday mornings when the pantry distributes and the thrift store and boutique are open.
During the ceremony, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) spoke to the crowd, emphasizing the current economic struggles residents are experiencing and thanking the St. Vincent de Paul volunteers.
"Being able to have this resource in the community is a life-saver for so many, so many that can't afford anything, and there's some that can afford some, but they still need some help," Mautz said. "And this has become just a critical part of the Mid-Shore community."

title: Port Street housing project nearing completion
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Port Street housing project nearing completion

 August 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 675
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nine affordable housing units and a new headquarters for a local nonprofit organization are nearing completion on Port Street. The Port Street Commons, a project led by The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, is slated to finish construction in October.The project includes nine apartments — seven two-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units — and approximately 10,000 square feet of space for The Arc's new regional headquarters, featuring offices and a behavioral health suite.
On Tuesday afternoon, Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc, gave a tour of the 24,000-square-foot space to Jake Day, Maryland's secretary of housing and community development.
Construction workers were in action on the site, and drywall and insulation was installed on the first and second floors of the three-story building. Day called it a "great looking building."
Rondeau pointed out the importance of bringing immediate assistance to those in need of housing in the Easton area, which is why his team has worked to aim for completion in under four years. The site was identified in July of 2021, and construction began last June. "We want to move quickly," Rondeau said.
$6.5 million of the project's approximate $11-million price tag has been raised, and The Arc is nearing the end of its capital campaign. Rondeau told Day that The Arc is financing the gap of around $4.5 million.
"If we wanted to raise the full $11 million, that would've taken us about eight years," Rondeau said.
Day was impressed with the pace of the Port Street project, asking Rondeau, "can we set you up with lots of other developers to help guide them through the process as speedily as The Arc has gotten through?"
A ribbon cutting is planned for Nov. 7. Rondeau said the first batch of tenants will move in Dec. 1, with a second batch coming in on Jan. 2. The Arc's headquarters will open in January.
Eight of the nine units will accept tenants based on a public lottery system. The ninth unit is designated to the Talbot Interfaith Shelter to house someone transitioning out of the shelter.
"Because of the site plan, all nine units are slightly different," Rondeau said, "which was not the most economical, but it was the only way we could maximize getting nine units into the available square footage."
All of the units will feature free Wi-Fi and appliances including a microwave, along with "solid surface countertops" and carpet in bedrooms to save money in the back end for property management. The units will be managed by Chesapeake Neighbors, a housing subsidiary of The Arc.
Rondeau said two of the units on the first floor are "universally designed," with accessible bathrooms and appliances meant to accommodate those with disabilities.
As Day and other members of the Department of Housing and Community Development toured the space, Rondeau pointed out how the office spaces will support The Arc's overarching goal of providing counseling and assistance to those with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
The headquarters are expected to add around 35 jobs to the area. Rondeau said employees at the Easton site will have health insurance. A full-time nurse will also be in the building.
"Three years ago, The Arc decided to self-insure our health insurance for our employees," he said. "And we have a partnership. We provide free urgent and primary care to all of our employees."
Rondeau is excited for The Arc's services to continue expanding outside of Anne Arundel County, which is where the organization was founded and has the largest presence.
"We've grown significantly over the last 25 years here in Easton," Rondeau said. "We wanted to have an Eastern Shore headquarters."
The project is the first building in Easton to fall under the town's mixed-use waterfront zoning district regulations, Rondeau said. Passed in 2019, the zoning code emphasizes connecting the Easton Point waterfront to the town's downtown area. Rondeau said The Arc made sure to have the front doors of the project facing Port Street as part of the zoning expectations.
After the tour, Day thanked Rondeau and expressed his support for The Arc's fast-moving efforts.
"It's an awesome project, it's an incredible project," Day said.

title: CWDI receives clean audit for 2023, talks lawsuit at board meeting
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI receives clean audit for 2023, talks lawsuit at board meeting

 August 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 584
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — On its 2023 audit, along with a clean opinion, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. received a note regarding its litigation with the City of Cambridge.The audit report, which was posted on CWDI's website under "financial data," mentions the CWDI's ongoing lawsuit under a paragraph titled, "emphasis of matter." Roy Geiser, a partner with the accounting firm UHY, said at a July 31 CWDI Board meeting that emphases of matter are added to audit reports when the auditor feels there is something in the financials that should be paid attention to.
CWDI, a nonprofit formed by Cambridge, Dorchester County and Maryland, has been tasked with planning and developing space along the Cambridge waterfront, known as Cambridge Harbor. In the last year, the city has repeatedly expressed its concerns with the project.
In May, the city filed a lawsuit against CWDI, CWDI Holdings and the Yacht Maintenance Company. The lawsuit alleges CWDI is in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. It seeks $75,000 in damages and requests temporary, preliminary and permanent injunctions stopping defendants from transferring any portion of the property in violation of the covenants of the 2021 transfer agreement.
Currently CWDI and the city are in mediation.
The emphasis of matter paragraph says that the full impact of the lawsuit on CWDI's operations and its ability to execute agreements is "unknown at this time."
"It doesn't change our opinion, but as a user to financials, you're going to want to know that," Geiser said.
A clean, or unmodified, opinion is the highest level of assurance an auditor can give, Geiser said.
"The opinion means that as these financials are presented, we feel that they are free of any material mistakes," Geiser said.
CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr called the clean opinion "the gold standard."
"So I hope this gives the public also some comfort knowing that we've used the funds as they were intended to be used and that we're good stewards of the dollars," he said.
After the audit, Narr presented on the organization's year-to-date financials, touching on the lawsuit's effects. He said CWDI is $200,000 over budget when it comes to legal expenses.
"It's the unfortunate result of litigation," he said. "It's an awful number."
Narr said that number is "strictly related to litigation." He said he hopes the city hasn't reached that same level when it comes to legal expenses.
"But that's the reality," he said. "And we really need to try to work through this and get to the other side quickly so we can move forward."
Narr also brought up the need for CWDI to sell property so that it can use that money to pay for other things. Since the lawsuit was filed, CWDI has not sold the piece of property it has been planning to sell to Yacht Maintenance. That property is part of the land that the city transferred to CWDI in 2021.
Narr said the organization has had to use some contingency funds to pay for design work because they haven't been able to sell property.
Board Vice President Shay Lewis-Sisco thanked Narr for highlighting "the detriment that we're in."
"It's definitely clear, as Frank has highlighted on our reports, that we need to sell property in order to continue operating," she said.
At the end of the meeting, Narr spoke directly to Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, who was in attendance.
"Mayor, know we need to work together to move this forward," he said. "We absolutely must. I mean there is just too much at stake. So please, whatever you need, let us know."

title: Oxford commissioners interview recruiting firms for open town manager position
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Oxford commissioners interview recruiting firms for open town manager position

 August 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — In an effort to move past the town's recent fruitless town manager hire, the Commissioners of Oxford held workshops Wednesday to interview two recruiting firms.This workshop was held a month after the town passed resolution requiring the hiring of a search firm for the town manager position as a result of controversy concerning the former town manager hire, Michael Calvert.
Calvert — who was previously a city administrator for Liberty, South Carolina — had been slated to get sworn in as Oxford's next town manager in July. But just three days after announcing the hire on June 24, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some community members expressed concerns about the town's candidate vetting process.
In an effort to move forward with finding a new candidate, Commissioner Katrina Greer introduced the resolution during a July 9 meeting, requiring the town to use a "professional search team that specializes in local government."
During the workshops Wednesday, separate interviews were held for the two firms, GovHRUSA and Berkley Group.
Each firm gave a presentation showing the goals, working timeline and outreach that could be done if they were hired. After each presentation, the commissioners asked questions of the firms.
Commissioner Katrina Greer requested a thorough understanding of the background checks each firm conducts on candidates.
Charlene Stevens, executive vice president for recruitment services at GovHRUSA, said her firm prides itself on ensuring well-researched candidates.
"We do media searches on candidates, to understand what is out there on them, as well as be able to have a conversation with them," Stevens said. "If there's media that is concerning, then … Mike (senior consultant) will review that information with you and make sure that you are comfortable moving forward with the candidate."
Kelsey Wong, chief operating officer for Berkley Group, said her firm uses a third-party background check to assess candidates but at the time could not remember the name of the company and said she could provide that information later.
Greer stated it was vital for the firm to come back with the company name since the background check was essential for hiring a new candidate.
"We had a problem with (background checks), and we would want criminal search to go back a number of years, do the credit check, do the civil check, etc. because people are handling money and purchases, etc.," Greer said. "And a national criminal check going back 23 years."
Each commissioner asked questions concerning issues of the timeline of hire, whether or not the firms have worked with communities with populations below 1,000, networking and how the firms involve the community in the hiring process.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the workshop was informative and helpful for the process of finding a new town manager.
"It's important to us because we're basically doing our due diligence to find the best possible candidate for our town manager position," Costigan said.
A decision will be made in the "next couple of weeks," and a follow up meeting with Berkley Group was requested to be scheduled to meet the rest of the team and to have a better understanding of the firm's background check process, according to Greer.

title: Longtime president and CEO of Delmarva Community Services retires
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Longtime president and CEO of Delmarva Community Services retires

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 633
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Forty-nine years ago, Santo Grande moved from Philadelphia to Maryland's Eastern Shore to take a job with the Dorchester Development Unit, an organization serving adults with developmental disabilities in Dorchester County.At that time, the organization, which had about 15 clients and three full-time staff members, was run out of the basement of a Baptist church on Locust Street in Cambridge.
Nearly five decades later, the organization — now called Delmarva Community Services — has grown to employ hundreds and offer a variety of services from day programs for those with developmental disabilities to senior services, childcare and transportation.
In that time, Grande has stayed with the nonprofit, helping grow it into what it is today. This summer, Grande retired from his long-held position of CEO and president, passing the torch to the former executive director of Upper Shore Aging, Andy Hollis.
Looking back on his career, Grande said he is most proud of how many people Delmarva Community Services has been able to serve.
"We always were serving people," he said. "Children, people with disabilities, seniors. We just continually wanted to provide service. We saw ourselves as a service provider to the community. And by doing that, we really became part of the fabric of the entire community."
Bill Batson, a former president and 16-year member of the organization's board, called Grande a visionary leader, adding that he always had a pulse on what was going on in the community.
"He has left his legacy on Dorchester County through that program," Batson said. "And I pray that it will continue for years and years. But it's all because of the solid foundation that he laid."
The opportunity to grow the organization is what kept Grande with Delmarva Community Services all these years. According to an Aug. 1 news release from Delmarva Community Services, the nonprofit assisted more than 6,000 residents and employed more than 250 people in 2023.
"I've never been one to rest on laurels," Grande said. "I just (felt) like there (were) needs in the community that (were) not being addressed, and we should be in the forefront with services."
When Grande noticed a need in the community, he made sure Delmarva Community Services looked into it.
"We kind of grew the services as the need was out there," he said.
This is how Delmarva Community Services expanded from serving only people with developmental disabilities to serving seniors, Medicaid recipients, children and more.
"So we started to be much more targeted in our services and taking the populations that were not being served as much as they could be served," he said.
Out of this, the organization's transit program, or Delmarva Community Transit, was born.
Grande grew up in Philadelphia, which has an extensive public transportation system he said his family used often. When he got to Dorchester County, there was no public transportation.
"And I thought, we need that here," Grande said. "We needed a public transit program."
Grande said he was able to build the Delmarva transportation program to what it is today: Around 100 vehicles that service residents in Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Talbot and Wicomico counties. He said the program made Delmarva Community Services better-known.
"It was really neat to watch it grow," he said.
As Delmarva Community Services transitions to its new leadership, that focus on continual growth isn't disappearing.
"Delmarva Community Services has a rich history in providing much-needed services to residents in the region," Hollis, the new president, said in an Aug. 1 news release. "Our goal moving forward is to continue to grow these services to meet the challenging times within which we live."
As Grande steps into retirement, he plans spend time with his family, write and possibly teach.
As for the organization that he invested five decades into, Grande has one simple hope.
"I just want them to be a community-oriented agency," he said. "Our goal is to serve the community."

title: Affordable housing dilemma at critical point in Easton
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Affordable housing dilemma at critical point in Easton

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1041
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Charlotte Brown has lived in Easton since 1996. The "peacefulness" of the town is one of many reasons she's been a longtime resident, but she's worried her time in Easton may end soon.Brown, 70, aims to downsize from her current two-bed, two-bathroom apartment once she retires. She knows she will likely have to move out of Easton to do so.
She points to a lack of affordable senior housing and extensive waitlists that make staying in the town unreasonable.
"I think that is such a disservice," Brown said of seniors having to wait years for housing units to open up.
The roadblocks seniors face to obtain affordable housing are only a portion of the town's current housing dilemma. Home prices are rising, and multiple potential housing developments have been met with pushback from residents.
Brown sees reason for concern not just for seniors, but low-income and middle-class people in search of housing.
"Everybody's not a doctor, everybody's not a nurse, everybody's not a lawyer," Brown said.
SENIOR WAITLISTSMultiple low-rent apartment complexes in town meant for seniors are at capacity. On Bay Street, the 93-unit St. Mark's Village has a waitlist of 262 people, which projects to be six-and-a-half years, director Wendy Dyott said.
"We've always had a waitlist," Dyott said. "It's never been this long. But it's been consistently, six, six-and-a-half years probably for the past three to four (years)."
Brown, who is on the waitlist, could envision herself living there. All of the 93 units are one-bedroom, one-bathroom, and tenants pay 30% of their income in monthly rent. All units used to be for seniors only, but Dyott noted that now the complex also serves those with a "handicap or disability."
Dyott said it's a popular place for seniors to downsize and in a prime location near downtown.
"I think one is affordability, and two is location," Dyott said of the two main factors that limit the options for seniors. " … Folks not only downsize their home, but then the next transition is they give up their driver's license. And (St. Mark's is) downtown pretty much, it's local, it's within walking distance to a bank, to a grocery store."
The 26-unit Asbury Place apartments off of Dover Road have a waitlist of two to three years, Don Bibb, the executive director of the Talbot County Housing Commission, said. Bibb said there's a lack of housing supply in Easton or single people and seniors, though "the demand is there."
Bibb, who serves on the Easton Attainable Housing Task Force, has attended international conference calls to discuss housing problems at a larger level. The struggles aren't just in Easton or the mid-Atlantic region, he said.
"Globally, we're all dealing with the same problem," Bibb said.
HOUSING INITIATIVESAt the local level, home prices in Talbot County are rising. According to the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors' second quarter report, the average home price in the county is just over $900,000, up 27% from the second quarter of 2023.
Realtors Property Resource data provided by Mid-Shore Board of Realtors shows the average estimated property value for single family homes, condos, apartments and townhomes in Easton is up 7.5% from one year ago. June data has shown the market is leaning towards sellers.
Jim Bent, a realtor at Benson & Mangold Real Estate, is working to address housing market problems as chair of Easton's Affordable Housing Board. Two affordable housing programs that he oversees have yielded different results.
The town's purchase program — meant to help provide affordable options for first-time home buyers — "just hasn't been feasible," Bent said. " ... There just isn't any property available to do anything significant," he added.
According to Bent, as of July 23, only six homes in Easton under $350,000 were listed for sale: three between $300,000 and $350,000, two between $250,000 and $300,000, and one under $250,000.
The town's renovation program has been more successful. Bent said there's been 38 renovations completed since 2014, and most of those have been for people that rely on social security as a main source of income.
COUNCIL MOVEMENTBent said of approximately 900 units under or nearing construction across Easton, he expects around 35 to be affordable. It's a reason he has supported potential projects brought to the Easton Town Council in recent weeks.
"A big part of moving this forward is education," Bent said, adding that many residents are often confused or misinformed on the goals of the Affordable Housing Board. Housing costs should not exceed approximately 30% of gross monthly income, Bent said, in order to be affordable.
A potential affordable multifamily housing development on the east side of Ocean Gateway moved forward last month, when the Easton Town Council approved an annexation request of around 17 acres of land between Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. The annexation agreement included language that 50% of the units must be "attainable." Developers have said they are committed to reaching the 100% mark.
With a lack of land available to be developed without annexation, Bent sees it as one of the town's best opportunities to add a significant number of affordable units.
The annexation was met with mixed feedback from the public, with worries about congestion, safety and whether the project developer would actually commit to the affordability aspect surfacing during town meetings and on social media.
Residents have also voiced concerns about a proposed 33-unit development at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street. Resident Charlotte Brown doesn't think 33 townhomes should be packed into that downtown spot, especially if they're not helping local residents in need. Thus far, there has been no commitment from developers to make any of the units affordable.
"What about those that are here?" Brown said. A public hearing on that proposal from Lane Engineering and Miller Development Corporation will continue at Monday's Town Council meeting.
Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello and Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis previously suggested that the council consider requiring the developers of that project make financial contributions to other affordable housing projects.
Brown hopes that push to require a sizable percent of affordable units is realized. She wants the town to prioritize projects that will help current residents in need rather than projects that are geared towards the upper-class.
"It's like playing Monopoly," Brown said of the town's housing outlook. "Turn a wheel and see who comes up." 

 © Copyright © 2024 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Bradshaw runs for Cambridge mayor against Lajan Cephas
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Bradshaw runs for Cambridge mayor against Lajan Cephas

 August 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw has thrown his hat in the ring for the city's mayoral election in October.Bradshaw, who served as mayor through 2021, resigned in January 2022 after being charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. In April 2022, Bradshaw pleaded guilty to five counts of distributing revenge porn.
Current Mayor Stephen Rideout, who is not seeking reelection, was elected to fill the remainder of Bradshaw's term.
Bradshaw will run against Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas, who served as the city's interim mayor after Bradshaw resigned and before Rideout took office.
Cephas also has faced legal issues. In 2022, she was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
As of Monday, Bradshaw and Cephas were the only two listed as approved candidates for the Oct. 19 mayoral election on the city's website. The deadline to file is Tuesday.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Bradshaw said he is running primarily due to an "outpouring of support" that he has received.
"And that was, I think, largely based on the background that I had when I was in office previously and our ability to move forward various parts of a broad-sweeping agenda that was aimed at improving Cambridge throughout the city," he said. "Not just in one neighborhood or in one aspect of the city's needs, but across all the various areas of need and geography in Cambridge."
Bradshaw wants to keep the focus of his campaign on where Cambridge is now and where it is going, rather than on his past legal issues. He said he thinks voters feel the same way.
"While I understand that there will be some thoughts and some attention given to those things, I think that where we stand now and where we can go in the future is really where I want to keep the focus," he said.
A news release from the Bradshaw for Cambridge Committee said during Bradshaw's time in office, the city started giving residential property tax credits for public safety officer recruitment, increased salaries for police officers, replaced and upgraded Cambridge Police Department and Public Services Department vehicles, expanded ethics reporting requirements for city representatives and began the planning and implementation of the Homeownership Works program, a state pilot program created to increase affordable homeownership opportunities.
Bradshaw said he thinks that as mayor, he served as a catalyst for the city council to move issues forward and work toward solving them.
"And I think the same will be true this time," he said. "That though there will be commissioners that have excellent ideas, that I'll be able to serve as a catalyst to get those ideas from the point of discussion to the point of decision."
Cephas, who has served on the city council since 2021, said in a text that being qualified for the position of mayor doesn't make you the best candidate. She said that after Bradshaw's resignation, she proved that she is capable and committed in the position of mayor.
"During (those) nine months with powers of mayor, we established the Gun Violence Task Force, resulting in 65% decrease in murder and decrease in violent crime in the city," she said.
Cephas said it's important for voters to believe in the legal system and "allow it to work."
She spoke about the importance of moving forward with a vision of a one Cambridge.
"We've notice Cambridge is divided on many platforms from policing, CWDI, businesses, race relations, community development and housing to name a few," she said. "We are divided in many ways in Cambridge, and (the) mayor should be the unifying agent bringing the city's business forward, not back."
Cephas said that if elected mayor, she will be committed to moving the city's business forward "with the spirit of ONE Cambridge."
Cambridge's city election will be held Oct. 19. All five Cambridge city council seats will be up for grabs, along with the mayor's seat.

title: Easton, town manager agree to 'part ways'
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton, town manager agree to 'part ways'

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Easton and Town Manager Donald "Don" Richardson have come to a "mutual agreement to part ways" effective Monday, according to a Tuesday press release from Mayor Megan Cook.Terms regarding the separation are still being considered by both parties.
"This difficult decision was made with the best interest and long-term health for the Town of Easton in mind, and the continued success and well-being of our employees and community as our top priority," Cook said in a statement. "Personally, I appreciate the work and support Don provided when I served on the council and again during my transition to the role of mayor."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Cook said she couldn't say why the decision was made and probably would not give any detail in the future, but she reiterated it was a mutual decision. Cook was in charge of the decision, she said, as the mayor has the power to hire and fire the town manager.
Richardson began his career with the Town of Easton in 2007, serving as a code official. He was instrumental in helping the Town of Easton Building Department become Maryland's first International Accreditation Service accredited building department. Richardson was then appointed to town manager by Mayor Bob Willey in September 2016 and was instrumental in overseeing the administration, operations and budget of multiple department.
During his tenure, Richardson was involved as a leader on numerous major projects, including Mistletoe Hall Commerce and Business Park, Housing on the Hill, Rails to Trails, Easton Point Park and stream restorations.
Richardson was not present at the Easton Town Council meeting on Monday.
Cook said the process to hire a new town manager has not yet begun but will as soon as possible. She said the town will advertise the position through the Maryland Municipal League, the Maryland Association of Counties and "all other avenues" they have used in the past for hiring other positions. A committee will be tasked with going through resumes, she said.
Once interviews have been held and the list of candidates has been narrowed down, Cook will make a recommendation to the Easton Town Council. The council will then either approve or deny the request.
Cook anticipates it will take about three to five months to hire a new town manager.
In the meantime, Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey will serve interim town manager. Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council voted unanimously to approve Lowrey as the interim town manager.
Lowrey said although he hasn't been a town manager before, and there's a lot for him to "come up to speed on," the Town of Easton already has a good team in place, which will make it easier to lead.
He said that while he is maintaining both roles of police chief and interim town manager, Deputy Chief Greg Wright is "well-capable" of keeping operations running at the police department.
Cook said she thinks Lowrey will be a good fit for the interim position.
"I really like his way of thinking," she said. "He has a very analytical mind and a good perspective."
Cook said that with Lowrey and Wright, the Easton Police Department has "two good leaders." She said she felt that "would offer an opportunity" for Lowrey to spend part of his time in the main office.
"I want to thank him for taking on this additional responsibility," Cook said in the news release. "Our focus is to ensure a smooth transition and maintain the excellent services we provide to our community."
