title: Town Council approves 33-unit housing project at former Safeway site
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Town Council approves 33-unit housing project at former Safeway site

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 620
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A proposal for a 33-unit housing development at the site of the former Safeway in downtown Easton was unanimously approved by the Easton Town Council on Monday evening.The proposal came from Lane Engineering on behalf of NAI Saturn Eastern and Safeway, along with Miller Development Corporation, the potential developers of the project. It includes 24 partially-connected townhomes and nine standalone units. The property, which has been vacant since 2017, sits at 139 N. Washington St.
The town's planning and historic district commissions reviewed the proposal before it landed on the Town Council's agenda this summer. On Monday, council members gave the green light to the project, which fell under the town's planned unit development infill subdistrict.
"I can assure you that we all thought long and hard about this," Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said before the vote. "This was not a quick decision. … This is going to be a decision that is going to outlive our tenures on the council."
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh discussed three conditions included in a findings of fact for the application prior to the vote.
The first condition requires developers to contribute $10,000 per unit to the town's affordable housing fund, with $5,000 due when the unit's building permit is issued and the other $5,000 due when the unit becomes occupied.
The second condition indicates the units "shall be privately maintained by a homeowners' association established for the community, which shall also provide private trash collection for all residences of the PUD District."
"They have to include that in their covenants," VanEmburgh said, "so there is notice to everyone who buys a piece of property there that it will be private trash pickup."
The final condition states if developers stray too much from the approved architecture of the homes, the project will have to return to the town's planning and historic district commissions for review.
While an Aug. 5 public hearing went by without resident input, many concerns were brought to the council at the project's previous public hearings in June and July. Abbatiello directly addressed those concerns prior to the vote Monday, including traffic, parking and the prospect of building a grocery store at the site.
"Traffic was another concern that was raised by many of my constituents," Abbatiello said, "and while the 33 units will add some traffic to the area, it will be significantly less than what was there when Safeway was open."
Abbatiello added that after following up on Town Council discussions about parking, he learned there are "over 550 parking spots, not including on-street parking, in the downtown area." Some residents' wishes that a grocery store replace Safeway "comes down to the fact that the current owner of the property is not going to sell it with the idea of developing another grocery store in that spot," he said.
Abbatiello's most difficult hurdle in fully supporting the project was the affordability aspect, he said.
"None of these units are going to be affordable," Abbatiello said. "We need housing for seniors, which was mentioned a lot. We need apartments that don't charge $1,600 for a one-bedroom. We do need those things. But when you look at the sale price for this property, there's no way a developer could purchase that and turn it into an affordable housing project."
Abbatiello thanked Robert Miller, the founder of Miller Development Corporation, for listening to council concerns and agreeing to "financially support an infrastructure project that's going to provide necessary workforce housing to town employees."
Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry echoed Abbatiello's statements and thanked developers.
"I could not have said it any better and I thank you for all the same reasons," Curry said. "And I appreciate the Miller (Development Corporation) stepping up and donating $10,000 per unit to our affordable housing fund."

title: Community newspaper recognized for 200 years

Community newspaper recognized for 200 years

 Words

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County newspaper Bay Times-Record Observer was lauded by state, county and local representatives for providing 200 years worth of community news at the Queen Anne's County Fair last Wednesday.With coverage spanning Queen Anne's County and beyond, Del. Steve Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) and Del. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) celebrated and voiced appreciation for the long serving publication. On behalf of the Queen Anne's County Commissioners, President Jim Moran presented a proclamation to commend the publication for its dedicated service and recognized its "distinguished efforts as a community partner for two centuries."
Centreville Town Council President Ashely Kaiser also presented a certificate of appreciation on behalf of the Town of Centreville, expressing gratitude for two centuries of gathering the news of the day and celebrating the residents, businesses and newsmakers that make communities on the Eastern Shore what they are.
Accepting the recognition on behalf of the publication, Executive Editor Jim Johnson noted the Bay Times Record Observer as a local newspaper, "It's not just the people who work there, it's our entire community," he said.
The Centreville Times (Centreville Observer) began reporting the news of Queen Anne's County in 1824 and merged with the Queen Anne's Record, creating the Queen Anne's Record-Observer in 1936.
Two decades later, in 1956, the Queenstown News began publishing under the Record-Observer masthead. In 2020, the Record-Observer and its sister newspaper The Kent Island Bay Times merged to form the Bay Times Record Observer.

title: CWDI, Cambridge City Council come to agreement in lawsuit
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CWDI, Cambridge City Council come to agreement in lawsuit

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 611
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., Yacht Maintenance Company and the Cambridge City Council have come to an agreement in a lawsuit filed by the city in May.According to Maryland court records, the case was closed on Wednesday. The suit was dismissed without prejudice, meaning that it could be refiled at a later date.
Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout said that the terms of the settlement include the ability for CWDI to transfer part of its property to Yacht Maintenance. Also a part of the settlement, the city and CWDI will enter into a memorandum of understanding to address issues between the city, county, state and CWDI that were not included in the lawsuit.
Rideout said the parties are currently working on developing the memorandum of understanding.
In May, the City Council filed a lawsuit against CWDI, the group spearheading the Cambridge Harbor project, and Yacht Maintenance, a boat service company. The lawsuit alleged CWDI was in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021.
The transfer agreement gave CWDI roughly 22 acres of land — including about 2.6 acres of land subject to a lease agreement between the city and Yacht Maintenance — for $5.
The city's lawsuit sought $75,000 in damages and requested temporary, preliminary and permanent injunctions stopping defendants from transferring any portion of the property in violation of the covenants of the 2021 transfer agreement.
In its lawsuit, the council argued that CWDI violated the agreement in March 2022 by transferring city-donated property to CWDI Holdings, a limited liability company also named in the suit.
Later that month, CWDI and CWDI Holdings filed a response to the lawsuit, alleging the city and CWDI agreed to CWDI creating CWDI Holdings to hold title to property named in the property transfer agreement.
With the settlement, the city and CWDI have entered into an agreement that allows CWDI to transfer property from the 2021 transfer agreement to Yacht Maintenance.
Rideout said the lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice for technical legal reasons.
"Something could come up in the future with regard to CWDI in the city or the county, and we didn't want to interfere or have this litigation be a roadblock to that litigation," he said.
'A FRESH START'CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said CWDI's Board of Directors is feeling great about the settlement.
"This just allows us to move forward," she said. "Hopefully we've opened up lines of communication with all of our partners, and hopefully this is a fresh new start as we move forward and just advance the Cambridge Harbor project."
Hengst said they are "eager" to move forward with the property transfer to Yacht Maintenance, which she hopes will happen in the next few weeks.
At the most recent CWDI Board meeting on July 31, the board talked about concerns with finances and the need for CWDI to sell property so that it can use that money to pay for other things. On Friday, Hengst told the Star Democrat that being able to sell property to Yacht Maintenance will help the organization's financial situation.
"We need the proceeds from selling property to contribute to our operating budget," she said.
The settlement follows almost three months of mediation between the city and CWDI before a retired judge.
Rideout said the city is still in discussion with CWDI "on a number of issues." He said he thinks they will be able to reach agreements on these issues to "help the future development go more smoothly."
Hengst hopes CWDI will be able to make some significant progress on Cambridge Harbor now that a settlement has been reached in litigation between CWDI and the city. She said CWDI hopes to break ground on its promenade expansion project soon.
This report will be updated.

Dorchester County creates Department of Water and Wastewater Services

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County is taking back control of its water and sewage systems.At a County Council meeting on Aug. 20, the council voted in favor of a bill that establishes the Dorchester County Department of Water and Wastewater Services and abolishes the Dorchester County Sanitary District and commission.
The bill also provides for the establishment of an advisory board for the Department of Water and Wastewater Services.
Under the bill, the county council will take on powers and duties related to the new department.
For decades, a volunteer six-member Sanitary District Commission has governed the Dorchester County Sanitary District, which includes the county's water and sewage systems. The commission has been appointed by the County Council to six-year terms.
The county has worked for the past year to take control of the sanitary district, arguing the county has more resources to manage the services.
At a council meeting in April, two residents came to speak about issues relating to water and sewers, and County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the sanitary district had grown too large for a voluntary board of members to handle.
Pfeffer asked for the residents' patience, saying that the county was in the process of taking back control of the water and sewage systems.
At the Aug. 20 meeting, the council voted unanimously to approve the bill that establishes the new department. Council member William Nichols was not present at the meeting and therefore did not vote.

title: Residents get update on Cambridge flood mitigation project
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Residents get update on Cambridge flood mitigation project

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge held the first of what it says will be multiple "periodic" public meetings to share progress and get feedback on its flood mitigation project along the shore of the Choptank River.The city's Make Cambridge Resilient Flood Mitigation Project Manager Larry White said the city will continue to reach out to the public throughout the entire design process of the project.
"This is the kickoff," he said. "There'll be other meetings where we get you up to date on what's transpired and what's come out of our studies."
The presentation, which was held at the Cambridge branch of the Dorchester County Public Library on Aug. 21, brought many residents who had questions about how the project, which will stretch from Gerry Boyle Park at Great Marsh to the mouth of Cambridge Creek, will affect their properties and the city in general.
The plan for the project includes three main elements: a living shoreline, earth and rock embankments and stormwater management to alleviate flooding.
The city is funding the two-phase project through the grants from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, a grant from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the Resilient Maryland Revolving Loan Fund and city budget funds. In June, it announced that the FEMA had awarded the city $1.7 million for the first phase of the project.
The city said FEMA is also reserving $16 million for the second phase of the project. The total $17.7 million in grant money is being awarded through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Assistance grant.
During the meeting, representatives from the city, the state, the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science at Horn Point, and BayLand Consultants and Designers spoke about climate change, flooding and the project itself.
Maryland Secretary of Emergency Management Russell Strickland talked about the importance of mitigating disasters prior to them occurring. He said mitigation cuts down on the need for response and on the costs associated with recovery.
"So this would be what I would call a transformative mitigation project for the city," he said. "And it's important that it be projects like that because that will have a greater result and a greater benefit for more people."
Horn Point Lab professor Ming Li talked about sea level rise across the Chesapeake Bay and increases in flooding. He said working with nature can be better than fighting with it.
"So that's why there's a lot of interest in a lot of places all around the world to look at nature-based solutions," he said.
Megan Barniea, a BayLand senior project engineer, said no design decisions have been made yet, but the plan is to build upon those three main project elements of a living shoreline, embankments and stormwater management.
Horn Point Lab, which is supporting the project, will help to optimize the living shoreline design, assess flood risk reduction, monitor living shoreline performance and evaluate ecological co-benefits of the project.
Barniea said the project partners will be coming back to the public to get feedback on a 30% design plan. The plan, which she expects will be ready to show in early 2025, will include the footprint of proposed features, elevations and dimensions, and a construction cost estimate.
After the presentation, residents asked questions about the project, including how the project will affect private docks and public access to the waterfront.
White said the city and its partners will work with each property owner, and residents will keep access to their docks. He said there will be some public access to the living shoreline.
"I mean it can't be everywhere, but there will be access," he said.

title: Commissioners discuss landfill agreement, upcoming detours
author: Tom McCall

Commissioners discuss landfill agreement, upcoming detours

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 429

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners met on Aug. 20 and discussed a wide range of topics, including a River Road detour, an agreement pertaining to the waste transfer station and the tabling of the food processing residual storage bill.RESIDUALS BILLThe commissioners decided to hold off on the third reading of a Food Processing Residuals Storage bill that has garnered a large amount of public comment during previous hearings.
Commissioners stated this was so they could have a full board present to vote on the bill. Commissioner Frank Bartz was absent from the Aug. 20 meeting.
The bill requires the use of closed-top storage tanks for food processing residuals, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly.
The commissioners decided to hold the third reading until their next meeting, which will be Sept. 3.
RIVER ROAD DETOURThe commissioners discussed the upcoming replacement of the culvert pipe on River Road in Ridgely and traffic problems that may ensue. Central Avenue and Holly Road will be covered by the Sheriff's Office to keep traffic moving.
Through Oct. 1, Holly Road will be closed between Central Avenue and Route 404 between 2:40 and 3:15 p.m., which will reroute the traffic of North Caroline High School. Traffic will be directed north of Central Avenue up to north of 480 to access 404.
LANDFILL AGREEMENTCounty Administrator Kathleen Freeman brought up the County Administrator's report on the landfill agreement between several Mid-Shore counties, which was signed by all jurisdictions.
Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill, located in Caroline County, is governed by a four-county agreement between Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot and Caroline counties.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, the partnering counties have agreed to allow the landfill to stay in Caroline County for 12 years longer than initially planned.
"We are not expanding it. We are filling it to its full capacity," Travis Breeding said.
DETENTION CENTER REPAIRSThe Regional Detention Center has a leaky roof that is jeopardizing electric operations, according to county officials who spoke at the Aug. 20 meeting. An emergency repair was requested at the detention center for the leak.
A bid from Dynamic Roofing was $67,000 to fix it. The commissioners will take the money out of remaining American Rescue Plan Act funds. The commissioners voted to approve the purchase order to fix the roof.
"The money for this is not in the capital budget. We are still spending down some of the ARPA funding," said Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox.

title: Pinnacle Hospitality Group hopes to build hotel on Cambridge Harbor
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Pinnacle Hospitality Group hopes to build hotel on Cambridge Harbor

 August 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 600
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Less than a week after the city and Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. settled a lawsuit regarding the ability to transfer certain land, members of the CWDI Board of Directors sat in the front row of an Aug. 26 Cambridge City Council meeting.With them: a hotel developer interested in building a hotel on Cambridge Harbor, the project led by CWDI to develop Cambridge's waterfront.
The first half of the meeting, the developer, Tauhid Islam, spoke about why he would like to build a hotel on Cambridge Harbor and what he would like that hotel to look like.
No deal has yet been made with Islam to develop on Cambridge Harbor. On Aug. 23, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst told the Star Democrat that CWDI will be working with the city and county to identify the appropriate time to sign a deal after "various details" have been worked through.
Islam, the founder of Eastern-Shore-based Pinnacle Hospitality Group who started his own venture in 2016 after spending two decades with Choice Hotels, has been in talks with CWDI for the past year. Islam said that in the past eight years, his group has built seven hotels, including a Cambria Hotel and a Hampton Inn & Suites, both in Ocean City.
Islam said in an oceanfront hotel room, when you turn off the lights, all you can see from the balcony at night is darkness. By contrast, in a hotel room "on the tip of the bridge," it's not just darkness, he said.
"The rumbling of the bridge, the beauty of the dolphins swimming by and the moon actually glistening on the water," he said. "That's what attracted me to Cambridge."
Islam sees this venture as an opportunity to embrace a working waterfront. He said it's an opportunity for the younger generations to learn about a "forgotten art."
"Things that our children and their children may not have the opportunity to see first hand," he said, mentioning boat repair. "I think Cambridge does bring that and it will resonate with people who are just trying to get away from the city. ... I want to create something that will make them stop."
Islam said his plans include a rooftop restaurant and a conference center. He said he wants to bring in a franchise that doesn't exist in Cambridge.
During the meeting, Islam and his team unveiled an initial rendering that shows the project concept. The rendering included balconies that overlook the Choptank River and a pool steps away from the river.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), who sat in the front row of the meeting along with two CWDI board members, acknowledged that this hotel would take a few years to build and open if a deal is made.
"But boy, we have a great vision, and I think this is a great restart of Cambridge Harbor," he said.
Over the past year, tensions between the city and CWDI over the Cambridge Harbor project have received significant attention. With the lawsuit settlement — which includes both parties entering into a memorandum of understanding to address certain issues — representatives from both the city and CWDI Board have expressed hope about their relationship moving forward.
At the meeting, multiple City Council members thanked Islam for the presentation and shared their excitement for his approach to the project.
"There's an old adage that says a home without a heart is nothing but walls, roof and floor," Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said. "And its nice to hear you speak of the buildings, that they have heart in them as well. I think that's something we definitely want to have moving forward in our projects in Cambridge."

title: Trappe Planning Commission approves changes to Lakeside plans

Trappe Planning Commission approves changes to Lakeside plans

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 TRAPPE — Last Tuesday evening, Trappe's Planning Commission approved the changing of three lots set aside for spray irrigation into one parcel for the Lakeside Wastewater Treatment Plant. This change will help the plan meet requirements from the Talbot County Health Department.Ryan Showalter, Lakeside's attorney, said new representatives of the Health Department had waited to provide comments on the preliminary and final plans for Lakeside until they receive approval from the Maryland Department of the Environment.
MDE requested two changes to the final plan. The first relates to the Health Department's signature approval block. The approval block before referenced the parcels that are associated with the treatment plan. According to Showalter it basically said they're approved as lots for development purposes.
The second change pertains to the lots for the spray irrigation field. According to Showalter, there were three lots for the spray field, which was everything north of the treatment plant, the storage lagoon and the reserve spray field was a lot.
MDE is requesting all the lots to be on a single parcel, essentially erasing boundary lines on the plan.
"And so that's the only change, is to remove those internal division lines so that what was three lots is now Lot C."
According to Robert Rauch, this change in no way alters the boundaries or acreage of the parcels.
"We had three parcels associated with the spray field they wanted to incorporate into a single parcel," he said. "Didn't change any of the boundaries. Didn't change every acreage, but we had to switch them to a single parcel instead of three separate ones."
The planning commission unanimously approved a motion to authorize Commission President Edgar to sign the revised plats when they are approved by the Health Department and MDE.
Rauch shared with the commission that the wastewater treatment plant is now meeting effluent requirements and the Health Department and MDE approved that the treatment plant can start discharging to the lagoon starting last week.

title: Parking in Easton garners mixed opinions
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Parking in Easton garners mixed opinions

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 747
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As Easton fields housing proposals, some residents and officials are questioning whether the town has adequate parking.At multiple town meetings, Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry has expressed a keenness to dig deeper into the town's parking systems and availability. Curry, who has served on the council from 2003 to 2008 and since 2023, believes a parking analysis should be completed.
"Twenty years ago, I was sitting in the same seat, talking about the same thing, that we need parking downtown," Curry said at a June 17 meeting. "But now it's critical."
While Curry and others have been adamant about needs to improve parking access and availability, a range of differing opinions have been raised regarding parking in Easton. And some believe the parking problem is sometimes more perceived than it is real.
'PERCEIVED' OR REAL?Since moving to Easton in 1997, resident and restaurant owner Steve Mangasarian is used to hearing calls for increased parking. When concerns were raised during discussions of housing proposals at Easton Town Council, he decided to take an inventory of spaces in town.
Mangasarian said he spent three weekdays earlier this summer assessing available parking, all at different times of the day. On average, he found anywhere from 180 to 250 empty spots, not counting street parking and dedicated spots for businesses.
"It's completely overblown," Mangasarian said of demands for additional parking.
Scott Messick, the town's IT director, has led efforts in the town's parking kiosks and mobile parking app, Easton Park Smart. As he attended parking conferences and learned about the industry, he developed a similar stance on parking in town.
"It is a perceived problem. And part of the perception is I want what I want, where I want it, when I want it," Messick said.
Messick said free on-street parking and low per-hour rates hurt the availability of premium parking near businesses, which is often what residents and visitors seek.
However, with more than 500 spots in lots across town, Messick argues additional parking isn't a dire need. Around 100 of those spots are 50 cents per hour and around 150 spots are 25 cents per hour, with more than 300 free of charge.
Curry's view is that as the town grows and adds new residents, those residents will need to be accommodated. On Aug. 19, the Easton Town Council passed proposal for a 33-unit housing development at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street.
Currently, the lot has around 50 parking spaces that are used, which will be taken away once construction begins. Curry says it's "incumbent upon us as the Town Council" to push for a parking study before that construction.
"We're not the same town center that we were 20-plus years ago," Curry said. "We're ever changing. We definitely need to take a look at it."
KIOSKS AND APPTwo downtown paid parking lots have kiosks where drivers can pay with credit or cash, Lot 1 at the corner of Glenwood Avenue and South Harrison Street, and Lot 5 between Washington Street and Harrison Street.
Holly DeKarske, executive director of the Easton Economic Development Corporation, says tourists often come to the Easton Visitor Center after struggling with the downtown parking kiosks.
"I'm frustrated about this kiosk parking," Curry said in an interview. "And I want to see a solution to that because I don't think that's working. … They're not user-friendly to begin with, in my opinion."
Messick said it's a "mixed bag" with drivers understanding the technology. "There are people who think it's the greatest thing since sliced bread, and there are people who want that meter back," he said.
The meters, though, aren't a viable option since parts are hard to find if one breaks and the price per hour cannot be changed, Messick noted.
The town's mobile parking app, Park Smart, allows users to register a vehicle and choose a payment method. The app will automatically draw from an initial balance so users can simply park and walk away.
Both Curry and Messick pointed out that parking enforcement is a challenge with only two meter enforcement officers in town. Thus, many hours during the week go without meter enforcement on duty.
Along with a lack of enforcement, education and expert help remain at the forefront of Curry's vision.
"We need a comprehensive parking solution. … I don't claim to have the answers, I just want to go find them," Curry said. "And I want to find somebody that can help us get to the next level so that we can be more welcoming to our citizens and our visitors."

title: New Dorchester County manager says he is ready for the role
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
New Dorchester County manager says he is ready for the role

 August 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The day that now-Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones was sworn into office as Maryland State Police superintendent, then-Gov. Larry Hogan grabbed him and told him they needed to go to a press conference about COVID-19.It was March 2020, the month that the World Health Organization would declare COVID-19 a pandemic.
"We went through a lot of things nationally on the law enforcement level that was very challenging, COVID being one of them," Jones said. "But we had a bunch of other things going on. Some of the unrest that was going on in the country with law enforcement-related issues. So that was very challenging."
When he retired at the end of 2022, Jones needed a break. He had heard about the open Dorchester County manager position, but he wasn't ready for it.
"I knew this was going to be a lot of work, which I don't mind, but I just wasn't there then," he said.
Jones said that during his period of retirement, people would suggest the county manager job to him.
"It took a while to get there, but it just seemed like it made sense," he said about eventually applying for the job.
It was his love for the county he's spent his whole life in and seeing that county through his 2-year-old granddaughter Emma's eyes that made Jones realize this was the job for him.
"We forget I think, when we live here our whole lives, how beautiful this county is," Jones said.
Carrying Emma around, Jones noticed her amazement with the water and boats in the county.
"And I thought, maybe I can help ensure her future," he said. "That she has all this."
COMMUNICATION IS KEYSince taking on the role in May, improving communication has been a focus for Jones.
"I see opportunity here to create a more efficient, more professional government," he said.
Jones wants to ensure that when citizens calls the county, they get answers.
"I never want people wondering," he said. "If you've got a question, please ask. And if we don't have an answer, we'll get it for you. Because that's the kind of service people expect and deserve."
Communication with other agencies is also important to Jones. The county is working to develop its relationship with the City of Cambridge again, Jones said. Every few weeks, he meets with Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson.
Jones' experience at the state level benefits the county when it comes to communication with outside agencies. County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said Jones knows a lot of people at high levels of state government.
"So when he has a problem in our county relating to those agencies, he has been able to get on the phone and make some great connections with the people he already knew or the people that have taken over during the Moore-Miller administration," Pfeffer said.
Pfeffer said that Jones — who he called "a very good fit" for the county — jumped into the manager position "with both feet." Pfeffer talked about Jones' efforts in updating county policies so they "fit everybody fairly."
"He has a lot of experience on personnel policies and procedures and applying them to large organizations," Pfeffer said.
With some of the challenges the county is facing — from falling behind on submitting audits to staff turnover over the past few years to tight budgets — Jones recognizes the job he has taken on isn't an easy one. But he has hope.
"With a lot of the things that the county is working through right now," he said, "I think there's a lot of opportunity to be hopeful."
Jones hopes that along with being good stewards of what they have — so that his granddaughter can enjoy those things through her life — the county is "standing shoulder to shoulder" with its partners and helping them when they need it.
"Because we all win," he said.

title: Cambridge City Council moves toward creating TIF policy
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council moves toward creating TIF policy

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council voted at a meeting on Aug. 26 to direct its attorney to prepare a resolution creating a tax increment financing, or TIF, policy.During the meeting, Acting City Manager David Deutsch recommended the council make this move. He brought up the Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop Cambridge's waterfront. Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., the group spearheading the project, has been looking into using tax incremented financing to help fund the project.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area due to development. The increased tax revenues are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area.
CWDI's proposed TIF would cover the Cambridge Harbor development project area. The TIF would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30 million bonds taken out by the city and county. According to a CWDI presentation at a Dorchester County Council meeting in December, the net tax increment from the TIF is expected to be around $10 million each for the city and county.
In March, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said they had completed a seventh run of a TIF model and it looked "very stable."
At the council meeting on Aug. 26, Deutsch said that a TIF project is different from a general obligation bond issued from a municipality.
"This is a method of financing that is unique to a specific project," he said. "And in order to position the city to be able to seriously consider that, we need to have a policy document in place."
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE POLICYIn an Aug. 22 memo to the City Council, Deutsch pointed out parts of TIF policies used in other Maryland jurisdictions that he said were "worth noting." These include creating an application process, using an outside financial advisor, requiring analysis of a test that demonstrates whether there is a need for the TIF and requiring developers to pay for fees and expenses of the city's consultants.
In creating a report with recommendations, city staff looked at TIF policies in six jurisdictions in the state. According to the report, staff recommend that the city use Bowie's policy and application, adding select practices and language from Frederick and Howard counties.
Deutsch said that if a policy is approved by the Cambridge City Council, the city would be ready with an application process in the event that a developer requests a TIF.
"And then we can sit with them and make sure that all the various elements are proper and in place so that the folks on city staff and our advisors can advise mayor and council properly," he said.
Before the council voted unanimously to direct the city attorney to prepare a resolution creating a TIF policy, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he thought the policy was an excellent idea.
"I'm delighted that we're moving in that direction," he said. "Not only will it help the city and the commissioners, but it will help a developer understand what they're going to have to go through in terms of making the application and what they're going to have to produce."

title: Talbot County considering raising hotel tax rates for visitors
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County considering raising hotel tax rates for visitors

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 482
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Tourism Board is asking county officials to consider raising its accommodations tax rates from 4% to 6%.The Talbot County Council held a work session Tuesday to discuss the possibility of raising its accommodations tax, or hotel tax, on visitors to the county. The county has the lowest hotel tax rate in the state at 4%, which has been in place since 2005.
Around $2 million was collected throughout the county in accommodation taxes in fiscal year 2024. If the rate had been 6%, that total would have increased to just above the $3 million mark.
Harold Klinger, a member of the tourism board since its inception, relayed the history of the county's hotel tax rate to council members. He noted that the law was first passed in 1986, updated once in 2005 and has remained flat at 4% since.
"The person who pays an accommodation tax are visitors when they come to Talbot County, it's not the residents who pay the accommodation tax," Klinger told the council.
Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of economic development and tourism, said the portion of the accommodations tax the county collects goes towards tourism marketing and economic development.
"I think we can all agree that the cost of serving our visitors has increased," Vanhooser said. "The cost of policing, the cost of roads, sidewalks, trash collection, all of that. An accommodations tax is merely asking your visitor … to help offset the costs."
The towns of Easton, St. Michaels and Oxford collect the 4% tax on all hotels and short-term rentals within respective town limits or within a mile of those limits. The county collects the tax from lodgings that don't fall in or within a mile of town limits.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said the county would need to be prepared to ask state delegates this October to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year.
"What has to happen on our part between now and Oct. 1 to make this happen?" Lesher asked.
Vanhooser said the three towns would need to be on board for the spike and added that there needs to be public meetings and votes in each town.
Klinger said the county attempted to raise the accommodations tax in 2021, but St. Michaels was not on board. Vanhooser said she has already presented the proposed change to the three towns.
If approved by the towns and county, the tax rate could be introduced at the upcoming legislative session and take effect Jan. 1, 2026, upon approval from the state.
"It's not a guarantee that it'll pass when it gets to the state legislature," Vanhooser said. "Worcester (County) raised their accommodations tax in the last legislative session, but the previous one they failed, in spectacular fashion. We will have to do quite a bit of work to make sure that we have laid all the groundwork at the state legislature once it leaves our hands."

title: Oxford tables plastic bag ban ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford tables plastic bag ban ordinance

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 521
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Following a nearly 30-minute public hearing, the Commissioners of Oxford tabled an ordinance that would ban retail establishments in town from giving out single-use, disposable plastic bags.At a town meeting on Aug. 27, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said the ban would apply to retail establishments including grocery stores, convenience stores, shops, department stores and service stations. The ordinance would not apply to restaurants and food service establishments.
Ryan said while the ordinance would apply to the Oxford Market, it would not apply to the deli within the market.
"So the sandwiches, subs, things like that that would be wrapped in plastic would continue to be in plastic," she said.
During the public hearing, some local business owners and employees expressed their concerns with the proposed ordinance. Graham Norbury, the general manager at Safe Harbor Oxford, said that while this may be a national issue, he doesn't observe plastic bags being littered often in Oxford.
"Why is restricting a retailer's right to choose the best delivery mechanism for their products, why is that something that the commissioners feel necessary?" he asked.
Oxford Vintage & Trade owner Barbara Ranson said in her six years of being in business in Oxford, she has always used paper bags. She said she doesn't understand why the commissioners are looking at this legislation when "it may or may not target three very small businesses."
"So it seems to me (like) legislation looking for a problem, and I don't understand why we would spend one minute on this," she said, receiving some applause from residents in the audience.
Ranson also brought up a part of the ordinance that would require retail establishments to charge a 10 cent fee — which the retail establishment would keep — for each paper bag it hands out to customers. She said that having to charge and keep track of that would take up time and labor and would just be another thing that the town needs to enforce.
"And who's going to do that?" she asked. "Because we already have ordinances that are not enforced because we don't have anybody to do them."
Resident David Donovan, who is in support of the ordinance, acknowledged that it won't solve the global problem.
"But if every one of us in every little town stands up and does their share, you do solve a problem," he said.
Resident Rose Donovan said she considers this to be a "common sense ordinance." She said this is a way to stop using plastic bags "where we can."
Commissioner Katrina Greer said she feels passionately about banning plastic, but Oxford is facing a lot of other important issues right now.
"So I would like to find a way forward with this. But perhaps just not now," she said, adding that there is more commissioners should consider regarding the ordinance.
Before the commissioners voted unanimously to table the ordinance, Ryan brought up the idea of giving retail establishments an incentive to not use plastic bags, rather than banning them. She said the commissioners could consider a tax incentive, among other possible incentives.
Commission President Norm Bell said they should bring all of these ideas to the table before they make a decision.

title: Council approves bill that may lead to 8-month closure of Route 662
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Council approves bill that may lead to 8-month closure of Route 662

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 819
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An emergency bill facilitating an eight-month closure of a portion of Route 662 was passed by the Talbot County Council on Tuesday.A stretch of the road will need to be relocated to accommodate The University of Maryland Shore Regional Health's new hospital off Longwoods Road next to U.S. Route 50, just north of the Easton Airport. Designs have a corner of the hospital sitting in the middle of existing Route 662.
Bill 1577 amends Bill 1231, the latter of which dated back to 2013 and conditioned the transfer of current Route 662 to Shore Regional Health upon the construction of a new route. Now amended, the current road can be transferred to Shore Regional before the relocated road is complete.
"The emergency bill for the Route 662 relocation is essential to keep the project's timeline and minimize the impact of the road relocation on seasonal travelers," Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel told the council. "We accept responsibility for the need for urgency."
The road is expected to close this October and reopen in May. Kozel said the hospital is projected to open in the summer of 2028.
Council Member Lynn Mielke expressed opposition to the bill and questioned whether passing the legislation should be considered an emergency. She asked that the vote be delayed, though the rest of the council elected to move forward with approving the bill.
"In my mind, if one person (is) seriously injured or killed because of this detour that you're proposing, closing the road, … I don't want it on my conscience," Mielke said.
The state's official detour for the closure is expected to be U.S. Route 50, though council members have raised concerns about local farmers and residents using county roads as unofficial detours instead of the highway.
County Secretary Susan Moran stated 68 residents wrote the county in opposition to the closure. No residents spoke in person during Tuesday's public hearing.
As part of the amendment to the bill passed Tuesday, a road inspection and contribution agreement will require Shore Regional Health to contribute to road work preparing Hiners Lane, Hailem School Road, Goldsborough Neck Road and Airport Road for increased traffic.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said a traffic safety committee will be meeting to assess safety concerns stemming from the closure.
"At the end of the day, it's an inconvenience, but I don't see it as being a huge safety issue," Gamble said.
Mielke, though, pushed for a delay to the vote. "This upcoming meeting is a reason why we should postpone the vote for tonight and have it at the next meeting, so I can get all the information," Mielke said.
"I beg to differ with Councilwoman Mielke," Council Member Keasha Haythe responded, asking for the bill to be moved to third read prior to a vote. " … We've heard that there's no safety issue."
A 4-1 favorable vote moved the bill to its third read before the council passed the bill by the same vote count, with Mielke opposing both times.
FAA REPORTDuring Tuesday's meeting, Kozel said Shore Regional Health received a report from the Federal Aviation Administration indicating that "a corner of the penthouse on the roof is eight feet too high," Kozel said.
"Despite all other reviews indicating our building height met standards, we will need to work with the FAA to address their assessment before the spring when we will seek construction permits to build the building," Kozel said.
Mielke argued that the need for a redesign of the roof could bring the possibility of redesigning the part of the hospital sitting on Route 662. Ryan Showalter, an attorney for Shore Regional Health, said addressing the FAA issue includes vertical adjustments and not the horizontal adjustments needed to avoid the road.
"With respect to the FAA issue, there's no scenario in which the building would be shifted to come into compliance," Showalter said. " … If there was a shift in the hospital to avoid that issue, the hospital would actually shift to the north, onto 662, not away."
Avoiding Route 662 "would require a shift to the hospital by approximately 150 feet," Showalter said, due in part to grading and road circulation work that will be done during construction.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher pointed out any delay in hospital construction has significant financial burdens.
"Council's in a tough position," Lesher said. "We've heard from 60-some residents who will be inconvenienced by this, who have concerns about this. This is a change in the plan. We didn't want to have to close this road in order to make this happen."
" … This council does not want to be responsible for creating barriers to the construction, either in schedule or costs," Lesher added.
While the bill approved by the county on Tuesday facilitates the transfer of the road to Shore Regional Health, the Maryland Board of Public Works first must approve the transfer of the land from the state to the county. That board's next meeting is Sept. 11.

 EASTON — Town employees and representatives gathered at the Easton Town Office on Aug. 22 for a presentation of Easton's economic potency for land use planning.Joe Minicozzi, the principal and founder of Urban3, an urban finance consulting group, spoke during the presentation regarding Easton's potential to up its economic potency. He compared the growth of the town to the trajectory of one's DNA.
"Cities all have those moments," Minicozzi said. "They all have a DNA baked into them through their infrastructure, their growth patterns, that will have effects into the future."
Miguel Salinas, the town's director of planning and zoning, helped organize the partnership with Urban3 and last week's presentation.
"We hired Urban3 to model the potential revenue implications of various development scenarios based on different types of land use, … how we build out, … and at what densities," Salinas said.
Minicozzi pointed out the success of Easton's core downtown area. His presentation provided hypothetical examples of how much certain residential developments, businesses and homes could deliver in property taxes per acre.
"As Talbot County taxpayers, you take up 3% of the county's footprint, you're producing 26% of the county's property taxes," Minicozzi said of the town. He encouraged the town to find "opportunities for infill" and "neighborhood growth areas."
Urban3's analysis noted there was a potential $637,000 in property tax revenue from a Poplar Hill housing proposal that never came to fruition.
In August 2023, an application from a developer to build 456 residential units between Easton Bypass and Oxford Road was rescinded. A 119-unit plan was approved by the Easton Planning Commission in September 2023, but this February, Talbot County bought the 120-acre Poplar Hill Farm property.
"That was an opportunity lost," Minicozzi said. "Make sure that you account for that or find a way to learn from this and do it in another place. Maybe that's not the right place, that's cool, your decision. But don't just avoid that."
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who attended the meeting, said he felt it was "inappropriate" for the presentation to mention the canceled Poplar Hill proposal given that it was a "democratically led and made decision."
"The data are perfectly useful in their own way," Montgomery said of the presentation as a whole, "but I was disturbed by the way the presentation made it seem like the only objective we should have … is how we can maximize the amount of tax revenue we can take in. And that's just wrong. There are so many other things that matter, starting with how we preserve the character of the town and maintain our rural character, maintain our open spaces."
During the presentation, Minicozzi raised the topic of sea level rise. He noted Maryland Department of Planning projections that predict Talbot County will lose $817 million in property value due to sea level rise by the year 2100, with $8.1 million of that coming in Easton.
Minicozzi also encouraged the town to ensure underrepresented groups of people — such as those under 45 and the town's non-white population — should be heard in conversations of economic potency.
"Those folks get pushed out of the community and take on more burden in transportation to get here," Minicozzi said, "which is even more painful financially."
Salinas said the analysis and presentation brought information that can serve the town's planning and zoning department moving forward.
"This information can be important for us to add another tool to the toolbox," Salinas said.

title: Cambridge City Council members talk CWDI after lawsuit settlement
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge City Council members talk CWDI after lawsuit settlement

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 557

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Harbor project was the overwhelming focus of a Cambridge City Council meeting on Aug. 26.Along with a presentation from a hotel developer interested in building on Cambridge Harbor and a decision to move forward with creating a tax increment financing policy — a financing method Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. has been looking into using for the Cambridge Harbor project — council members shared their thoughts on the project and the city's relationship with CWDI.
Tensions between the two have been bubbling to the surface for the past year.
In October, the city wrote a letter to CWDI expressing concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project. In March, then-City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said he was resigning over concerns with the project.
On Aug. 21, the city and CWDI settled a lawsuit, which was filed by the city in May alleging CWDI was in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021.
After the settlement, both Mayor Stephen Rideout and CWDI Board President Angie Hengst expressed hopes for a stronger relationship between Cambridge and CWDI moving forward. Part of the settlement involves both parties entering into a memorandum of understanding to address issues between the city, county, state and CWDI that were not included in the lawsuit.
At the council meeting on Aug. 26, Commission President Lajan Cephas reminded everyone that CWDI's board is made up of volunteers. She said that the hotel presentation is an example of what CWDI can do.
"If we just give them just a little more faith, I know we can work together to make the project moved forward," she said.
Commissioner Brian Roche said he is excited to see the project move forward "despite the ups and downs."
"I think the progress — however uncomfortable it's been made — with the Yacht Maintenance expansion, the working waterfront, things that have been in our comprehensive plan, thank god we're moving that forward," he said.
Cephas asked about city spending on litigation with CWDI. She said the city has spent $34,000 and asked when it will stop. She said it looks like the project is moving in the right direction, and the money that has been going toward litigation should be saved.
"I'm hoping that maybe the next meeting, the next couple meetings, we can have a plan in place for how we can end that that process," she said.
Acting City Manager David Deutsch said the city would provide a report on the matter.
In July, CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr said CWDI was $200,000 over budget on legal expenses so far this year. He said the number was "strictly related to litigation."
Commissioner Jameson Harrington shared feelings on CWDI at the Aug. 26 meeting that contrasted Cephas and Roche's.
"I'll start off by saying not running for election again means I'm free to speak my mind, which also means I'm not going to sit here and falsely praise CWDI and give them thanks that they're not due," he said. "I've sat here, and over the past year, they have been unhelpful at best, antagonistic at worst."
Harrington said that it took a third party to get to this point in the relationship between the city and CWDI.
"And I'm not going to sit up here and pretend that didn't happen," he said. "So to sit here and praise them? No, that's not going to happen."

title: Proposed software to streamline septic, well permitting in Caroline County
author: Tom McCall
content:
Proposed software to streamline septic, well permitting in Caroline County

 September 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 395
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Sept. 3, three public health officials announced that they are looking to streamline the Caroline County Health Department's website's functionality. They want it to be easier to use, have more internal efficiency and feature enhanced collaboration.The system being considered by the department is called the LAMA System, an integrated local government interface. The Health Department plans to use the system to streamline the county's septic and well permitting process. According to the department representatives at the meeting, the system could be employed at no cost to the county.
"We are here to request approval for Caroline County Health Department's well and septic permitting to be added to the current Caroline County Planning Code LAMA system," said Robin Cahall, Caroline County health officer. "It is used to manage permits, licences, planning projects and code enforcement."
It can review environmental health services permits, planning reviews and code enforcement. County residents could pay fees through a portal and check the status of well and septic, and water and sewer.
The system even allows for mobile inspections and sends the inspection in for real-time reviews.
The department officials said it would take time to deploy the system and train the staff to use it. They hope to have it in place by the next fiscal year, which begins in July 2025.
"You are going from paper files to actually being able to utilize a tablet or smartphone to complete things... We want to start out small and then push it out to the public that this is what is going to happen," Cahall said.
Josh Parker, director of the Environmental Health Division, said, "The transition on our side is when, as Robin said, there is double work that is a big bottle neck in our office. On site, in the field approvals is really going to alleviate a lot of paperwork on our side and an immense amount of time scanning, uploading, verifying. It just won't need to be done anymore."
She said the department is committed to doing a mini campaign to let residents know the process is changing. The commissioners agreed that anything to make the process more efficient is welcome.
After lots of discussion about the potential efficiency of LAMA, the commissioners gave it the OK.
"It sounds good. I think we are good to move forward with this. Good luck," Commission President Travis Breeding said.

title: Easton Town Council divided over proposal to remove 10-cent paper bag fee
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council divided over proposal to remove 10-cent paper bag fee

 September 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 789
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A proposal to remove a 10-cent fee on paper bags in town was brought to the Easton Town Council Tuesday night, drawing mixed opinions from council members and residents.In September 2022, the council passed an ordinance prohibiting retailers from giving customers single-use plastic bags. The law, which went into effect in April of 2023, required retailers to charge customers a fee of at least 10 cents for each paper bag used, encouraging shoppers to bring reusable bags.
Ordinance 829, introduced at Tuesday's meeting, would alter the original ordinance and allow businesses to provide paper bags free of charge.
"The reason for the proposal to remove this fee comes directly from the voices of many Easton residents who are feeling its impact," said Council President Frank Gunsallus, "especially those in lower-income brackets who are already stretching every dollar to make ends meet."
Gunsallus and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery both said they've talked to residents who do not support the current 10-cent fee. The rest of the council, though, stated otherwise.
"I have heard from many people the exact opposite, that the ban is working and that the 10 cents is not onerous in any way, shape or form," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello and Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis stated the fee has incentivized people to bring their own reusable bags. Abbatiello said, "the reason for that (fee) is because paper bags pollute just as much as plastic bags do."
"I'm just not quite sure why we're even diving into all of this," Davis said, asking that the paper bag fee remain in place. "It blows my mind."
Gunsallus asked that a public hearing on the ordinance be added to the council's agenda for the next meeting so residents affected by the paper bag fee have the time to "plan ahead" and attend.
Davis asked that the discussion not be extended to a future meeting, pointing out the large crowd in attendance, most of whom were in support of keeping the 10-cent fee.
"So you're saying you want to hold this over because there's some people that need to be here?" Davis asked Gunsallus.
"(They) should be able to voice their concerns over the public hearing," Gunsallus responded. "That is a routine part of the process."
"Not everyone is privileged enough to have a salary where 10 cents is a negligible fee," Gunsallus later said, after Curry asked audience members in support of the fee to raise their hands.
Abbatiello stated that while he will vote against the proposed ordinance to remove the fee, he's willing to have the issue go to a public hearing.
"I still think that everybody should have an opportunity to speak," he said. "I think that's important. So if we hold this over until the next meeting, I'm fine with that."
Curry made a motion to dismiss the proposed ordinance and not discuss it at the town's next meeting. Davis seconded that motion, but it failed, as Abbatiello, Montgomery and Gunsallus voted against it. Gunsallus stated a public hearing on the paper bag fee ordinance will be held Sept. 16.
PUBLIC INPUTNearly all of the residents in attendance at Tuesday's meeting spoke in disapproval of the proposed ordinance to remove paper bag fees. Some brought reusable bags to display, and others brought signs that read, "KEEP THE 10 CENT FEE."
Many members of Plastic-Free Easton, a group that lobbied for the plastic bag ban in 2022, spoke on Tuesday.
"We didn't want to go from free plastic bags to free paper bags, effectively going from one type of environmental problem to another," member Elaine Tama said. "We need a more livable climate for our children and grandchildren's future."
Sarah Price spoke on behalf of the Maryland Retailers Alliance, indicating the group recommends council to maintain the original ordinance so that businesses aren't forced to drop the fee and subsequently increase grocery prices.
"If you remove the mandated fee, businesses will likely have to reduce or completely remove the fee to remain competitive with one another, and you will see your prices go up in all likelihood," Price said.
Easton resident Shari Wilcoxon held a different stance, questioning why the businesses are forced to charge the 10-cent fee.
"I don't know why people are afraid of freedom of choice," Wilcoxon said. "Why don't you let the merchants decide if they want to charge or not, what's wrong with that?"
Following a lengthy public comment section, Gunsallus emphasized the proposed ordinance is not meant to bring plastic bags back. He said it was brought to the table to address the struggles of "people who are having a hard time (making) ends meet."
"That is why this has been introduced, that's why it's being discussed, that's why it's being revisited," Gunsallus said. "However the pieces fall, so be it."

title: Town short on funding for Port Street infrastructure project
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Town short on funding for Port Street infrastructure project

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 777
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council learned at Tuesday's meeting that the town is well short of necessary funds to complete an infrastructure project on Port Street, leading to a lengthy back-and-forth between councilmembers and town employees.Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh and Mayor Megan Cook presented Ordinance 828 to the council, which would reallocate four separate amounts of fiscal year 2025 carry forward capital funds.
Two of the proposed reallocations involve removing $1.1 million in funding from the second phase of the Port Street project. The project, which leads down to the Tred Avon River, involves digging trenches and putting conduit pipes underground, running them on the side of the road. It's part of the town's efforts to revitalize the Port Street waterfront area and the nearby Easton Point Park.
It has an estimated cost of around $3.1 million.
"The money that we have that was carried forward equals $1.1 million," Van Emburgh said, "so we're $2 million short of having the money needed to complete that project."
The ordinance proposes $862,000 to be reallocated to Easton Woodland Park improvements, $50,000 for accessibility upgrades at the Easton Visitor Center and $225,000 for rails-to-trails work.
That $225,000 comes from American Rescue Plan Act funding, which must be obligated by the end of 2024 and used by the end of 2026.
Tuesday's discussion honed in on the funds proposed to go towards Woodland Park, a 200-acre property off Oxford Road near Cooke's Hope. Proposed amenities at the park include a 35-space parking lot, walking trails, a restroom facility and reforestation on 10 acres.
"We have 60% drawings completed to do improvements to the road and the small parking lot for that park," Van Emburgh said. " … These funds could be used for that project to bring that project to completion. That's not saying that we wouldn't ever do the Port Street project, we just don't have the funds. We're just kind of stuck in the middle, where we have some funds but not nearly enough funds to do that project."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry asked if the town is abandoning the Port Street project. Cook said it isn't, adding that the town can start on the Easton Woodlands project while searching for funding for Port Street.
"By reallocating the just over $800,000, we can actually start getting people to this park and utilize the 200 acres of parkland," Cook said. The town acquired the woodlands property last year using a $5 million state grant.
COUNCIL CRITICISMCouncil President Frank Gunsallus, along with other councilmembers, questioned why the reallocation proposal wasn't brought up sooner. "When was it determined that there wasn't enough for the underground project?" he asked.
"As the project grew, we knew that we just couldn't afford it," Cook responded.
"I just ask because we spent several months going through the budget process, and it seems like the perfect kind of thing that should have been discussed," Gunsallus said. The town passed its FY25 budget in June.
"It was probably overlooked at the time," Cook said.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis also asked why the council was not made aware of the insufficient funding for the Port Street project until Tuesday. Van Emburgh said carry forward funding is a "piece of the budget (that) needs to get more attention." He added, "I know we got to do better on the next round."
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery took issue with the fact that the Woodland Park project was placed above "high priority items" that the town wasn't able to fund last year.
Cook said moving the money to Woodland Park is "keeping in the spirit of pedestrian access and parkland," since the original "theory behind the funds was to extend pedestrian access to Easton Point Park."
"And that's more important to you than continuing to fix our stormwater management system where it's failing or acquisitions that we know we're going to have to make for failing equipment?" Montgomery asked the mayor.
"Not necessarily, but this is the start of the conversation," Cook answered. "That's why it's in the ordinance."
Montgomery pushed for a "budgetary argument" of why the money was proposed to fund Woodland Park improvements compared to other projects. "No rationale for that?" he asked.
"No rationale then," Cook said.
Councilmembers pushed for a workshop on the carry forward fund ordinance, which Cook agreed to. They asked for the workshop to include a list of potential projects in addition to the Easton Woodland Park that could use funding, along with a breakdown of American Rescue Plan Act funds that must be obligated by the end of December.
"Please bring your budgetary argument or strategy," Davis said during the end of the discussion. A workshop is scheduled for Sept. 16 before the Town Council's next meeting.

title: Washington College court win confirms partial demolition of armory will proceed
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Washington College court win confirms partial demolition of armory will proceed

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Chestertown Historic District Commission's May 1 decision to grant an application to Washington College to partially demolish the John H. Newnam Armory will most likely stand following a judge's ruling Wednesday.Over the summer, the college hit a speed bump in its plan to build a boutique hotel and conference center on the property that once headquartered the National Guard.
After the Historic District Commission's decision, there was a citizen's appeal made to the circuit court by residents Barbara Jorgenson, Tom Kocubinski and Steve Mitchell. They were opposed to the college's plan, favoring restoration over partial demolition.
But on Wednesday, with local Judge Harris Murphy recusing himself, visiting Judge Sidney Campen sided with the college.
Campen's decision came on the grounds that the petitioners didn't have legal standing to make their appeal.
In his opening argument, Collin Wojciechowski, an attorney representing the college, brought up a case he said was similar to this one.
Ray v. Mayor and Maryland City Council of Baltimore, he said, had "striking parallels in this matter."
In that case, citizens lived within 1,000 feet of the property, but the city still moved to dismiss the case, a move with which the Maryland Supreme Court agreed.
Unlike in that case, the petitioners, Wojciechowski claimed, can't argue by proximity since none of them live within 1,000 feet of the applicant property.
He said other than proximity, the burden of proof for the petitioners is to prove their "personal or property rights are adversely affected in a way different than the rest of the public."
"... Petitioners can't show that here. None of the history of the individuals is unique from their neighbors. That uniqueness is needed and Maryland courts have never found it to exist," Wojciechowski said.
Nelson rebutted, saying this case was indeed unique.
"There's no appellate authority that addresses the question of standing in the historic district," Nelson said.
Furthermore, he said he had actually worked the case referenced by the defense, arguing it in every stage of litigation.
That issue, he said, was a zoning decision over a 200,000-square-foot Walmart, not an historic district decision of a building constructed in 1931 in a small town.
He firmly disagreed with Wojciechowski. Residents within the Chestertown historical district are the exception, he said, because demolishing and rebuilding will affect the petitioners' taxes, property values and insurance.
Then pointing to the Historic District Commission guidelines, he read, "If an owner within the historic district allows a building to fall in disrepair, that adversely affects the character of the district."
And again in the guidelines, "The loss of any contributing historic building diminishes the district and can never be replaced."
Nelson said in this situation, the college allowed the building to go into disrepair. Additionally the Historic District Commission then violated guidelines by not issuing a written statement summarizing their decision on May 1, he said.
Combined with the written testimonies from the petitioners, it proves they should have standing, he said.
Wojciechowski countered, stating this is straightforward case, and the arguments about the Historic District Commission were merit questions, not about standing.
He said if the judge allowed this, it would set a precedent encouraging the appeal of Historic District Commission decisions.
After both sides presented their arguments, the judge agreed with Wojciechowski, dismissing the petitioner's claim.
He said Nelson did not present enough evidence or case law to show the petitioners would be adversely affected differently than any other resident in the district.
Mike Sosulski, president of the college, said he was satisfied with the judge's decision. "I think's it's the right result," he said. "While we appreciate our neighbor's position, we're pleased that the project's going forward."

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Chief of Staff Donna Lane was thanked at her final County Council meeting as a county employee.During the meeting, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced that Lane has taken a job with the state. In her 18 years and nine months as a county employee, Lane served a variety of positions, from administrative assistant to acting county manager.
Pfeffer, who called the news "bittersweet," thanked Lane for being a valuable resource in the county, as well as a friend.
"Even before I was elected, when I would sit in the audience and I'd have questions about how the county works, I'd come to you, and you would give me answers, and I greatly appreciate that," he said to her.
Council Member William Nichols teared up as he recounted Lane's first day as a county employee.
"I wish you could stay," he said, later adding, "you're doing what you have to do to make you happy, to make your family happy. And that's the main thing."
During public comment, Derek Griffin, who is on the county's Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee, said Lane has "provided exceptionally outstanding support" to the boards he is on.
"So I would appeal to the county officials, please, with enhanced urgency, please make sure that we have the adequate and appropriate support that we need to maintain our programs on both boards," he said.
Pfeffer thanked Griffin for his comments and said the reason they asked Lane to provide support to those boards is because of her attention to detail.
"She knows how the programs work," Pfeffer said. "She knows how the legal system works with us. Donna, I can't say enough about all that you do here, so thank you again."
Before the meeting ended, County Attorney Chip MacLeod said that over the years, he's always copied Lane on emails.
"Knowing that whatever happens, if Donna knows I've sent this email, there's going to be a record and we'll figure something out," he said.
MacLeod joked that with Lane leaving, he is going to have more to do.
"I think I'm going to have to pay attention a little more (to) what's happening at these meetings," he said, laughing. "Thank you."
At the end of the meeting, Lane said that it has been a pleasure working with county staff, the County Council, and previous councils.
"I'm honored to be able to do that and also focus on the best that we could do for our citizens of the county," she said. "And I know that'll be continued with this council and staff."

title: Easton council supportive of potential spike in hotel tax rate
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton council supportive of potential spike in hotel tax rate

 September 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A plan to increase the accommodation tax rate in Talbot County was presented to the Easton Town Council at Tuesday night's meeting.Cassandra Vanhooser, the county's director of economic development and tourism, recommended the increase to the council. It would raise the accommodation tax, or hotel tax, from 4% to 6% in the county.
"Anybody who's renting a room to someone for less than four months who's considered a 'transient' would be required to collect accommodations tax," Vanhooser said.
Vanhooser pointed out that Talbot County's rate is the lowest in the state. Around $2 million was collected throughout the county in accommodation taxes in fiscal year 2024. If the rate had been 6%, that total would have increased to just above the $3 million mark.
She noted the success of the county in the tourism industry. Despite the rate remaining stagnant since 2004, Talbot County has more than doubled its accommodation tax revenue.
"We consider this as an indicator of our success as a tourism destination," Vanhooser said. "We know people are coming here. We know we're commanding a premium price, and people are willing to pay that."
In order to raise the rate, the county needs to ask state delegates this October to bring the proposed change to the General Assembly next year. The county is looking for support from three towns, including Easton, in order to move forward.
The towns of Easton, St. Michaels and Oxford collect revenues from the 4% tax on all hotels and short-term rentals within respective town limits or within a mile of those limits. The county collects the tax from lodgings that don't fall in or within a mile of town limits.
"The county would like to hear a vote from you on whether you would support this or not, because obviously, we don't want to go to the state legislature and ask for something that you do not support," Vanhooser said.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello asked if the county reached out to hotels in the area for feedback on the spike. Vanhooser said the county's tourism board has hotel representation, adding that the county is aiming to reach out to all hotels as a courtesy.
After a short discussion, the council voiced support for the proposed increase, unanimously voting in favor. No formal resolution was required for the agenda item.
"Talbot County obviously is not unique," Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said. "But we have attractions that are not matched by our neighbors, and for that reason, I fully support raising this to 6%."
