title: Remarkable events, development top 2024 Mid-Shore headlines
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Remarkable events, development top 2024 Mid-Shore headlines

 January 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Holiday 
 
 1941
 Words 

 Read News Document

 2024 brought countless stories, ranging from changes in local politics to historic celebrations.As we reflect on 2024, the Star Democrat would like to thank all our readers for their stories, their support and for being actively involved in the community.
GROUND BROKEN FOR NEW HOSPITALOfficials and stakeholders joined together at the Talbot County Community Center in October to celebrate the groundbreaking of a long-awaited regional medical center.
The University of Maryland Shore Regional Health's project is estimated to cost around $550 million.
Shore Regional Health first applied for a certificate of need to relocate its Easton hospital on Sept. 7, 2012. Industry changes, fiscal concerns and shifting project plans delayed the timeline.
In January, the Maryland Health Care Commission finally approved the certificate of need application.
The hospital will be built on around 230 acres just north of the Easton Airport and across from the Talbot County Community Center. It is replacing the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center in downtown Easton.
Site preparation construction is currently underway, with the bulk of construction beginning in the spring of 2025. The medical center is expected to be completed in the summer of 2028.
The new hospital will serve as the primary inpatient hospital for Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties.
STAR DEMOCRAT TURNS 225The Star Democrat celebrated its 225th anniversary in August. In celebration of the landmark anniversary of continuous news coverage of Maryland, the newspaper held a party at the Avalon Theatre in Easton on Oct. 3 to celebrate the milestone.
The Star Democrat traces its history to the Republican Star, founded in August 1799 by Smith as the Jeffersonian rival to The Maryland Herald, Easton's Federalist newspaper. John Adams was president at the time. The paper has been published during every president's term since, making it one of the oldest newspapers in the country.
In 1799, The Star stood for the principles of individual liberty, local autonomy and limited central government. As it continues in its mission to inform the public about important local issues and happenings, these doctrines still apply.
For the anniversary, leaders from senators to local officials gathered in October to celebrate the years of work the paper has done for the community and will continue to do.
LAKESIDE WASTEWATER PLANT COMPLETEDIn June, the Lakeside wastewater treatment plant was completed in Trappe. This controversial project, an essential step in moving forward with the Lakeside at Trappe housing development, faced lawsuits, petitions and an array of public outcry over environmental concerns over several years.
First proposed over 20 years ago, the planned 2,501-unit housing development spans more than 850 acres off of U.S. Route 50. The development is slated to include a mix of single-family homes, townhouses and apartments, and commercial and retail spaces.
Trappe's existing plant had the capacity to take on wastewater from the development's first 120 homes. That flow will eventually be diverted to the new wastewater treatment plant serving the development, a plan approved by county legislation and a Maryland Department of Environment wastewater discharge permit.
During a June Trappe Town Council meeting, two Lakeside transfer agreements were presented. These agreements were the first steps in eventually passing ownership of the new wastewater treatment plant to the Town of Trappe.
ELECTIONS SHAKE UP LOCAL GOVERNMENTMajor changes were set during the 2024 election cycle. Three new members were elected to the Talbot County Board of Education in November.
Cynthia Marrah Jurrius, Karla Wieland-Cherry and Ann O'Connor won seats for their districts. Wieland-Cherry and O'Connor defeated incumbents to win their spots on the board.
St. Michaels and Cambridge councils also had significant turnover. During the Commissioners of St. Michaels election held in May, the town had three of the five commissioner positions up for vote.
Jay Hudson, David Wojciechowski and Alexis Roiter were elected to fill three seats up for grabs during a townwide election. They defeated four other candidates for the office, including two incumbents — David Breimhurst and Joyce Harrod.
In Cambridge, a close election stirred controversies as Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas was elected the city's mayor.
From past criminal charges to residency requirements to campaigning practices, the race gave voters a lot to talk about. Former Mayor Andrew Bradshaw's bid for the office came up short. Bradshaw resigned from the position after he was charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit 2½ years ago.
RIDGELY POLICE DEPARTMENT DISBANDEDThe Town of Ridgely was hit with big news in March, when the town lost the service of the Ridgely Police Department due to a state investigation into the town's police chief, Jeff Eckrich. Ridgely's commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department on March 12.
The town entered a short-term agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide police coverage in place of the suspended officers. When the Ridgely officers were officially laid off at the start of the fiscal year on July 1, the town entered into a new agreement with the sheriff's office for fiscal year 2025.
The town of Ridgely has since sold seven vehicles and three firearms once belonging to the Ridgely Police Department, according to records obtained by the Star Democrat. In August, the state announced that the investigation into Eckrich had been closed, citing that "sufficient evidence" of allegations made against him was not found.
C-SD TRACK WINS TITLECambridge-South Dorchester High's track and field teams held big wins in 2024.
The girls track team picked up a fifth title when Kassidy Young won the shot put with a heave of 33-1, and also got big points from Al'Janae Jackson, who was runner-up in the 100 meters (13.06) and 200 (27.27) and the pole vault (7-9).
Led by Jayden Smith, Tori Willis Jr., and Tekai Drummond, Cambridge-SD won the 1A boys title with 155½ points, easily outdistancing second-place Perryville (94½).
CAMBRIDGE SUES CWDIIn July, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., Yacht Maintenance Company and the Cambridge City Council reached agreement in a lawsuit filed by the city in May.
The City Council filed a lawsuit against CWDI, the group spearheading the Cambridge Harbor project, and Yacht Maintenance, a boat service company. The lawsuit alleged CWDI was in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021.
The transfer agreement gave CWDI roughly 22 acres of land — including about 2.6 acres of land subject to a lease agreement between the city and Yacht Maintenance — for $5.
The city's lawsuit sought $75,000 in damages and requested temporary, preliminary and permanent injunctions stopping defendants from transferring any portion of the property in violation of the covenants of the 2021 transfer agreement.
When the lawsuit was settled after months of mediation, all parties voiced a desire to move the Cambridge Harbor project forward.
In August, Matt Leonard, CWDI's former executive director, left the position, leaving Frank Narr to serve in the role in the interim.
In December, CWDI and the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Cambridge Harbor promenade.
PRIDE BANNERS, FESTIVAL STIR DISCUSSIONIn January, Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery voted against issuing the permit to hold the annual Pride Festival event. The festival permit was approved in a 3-2 vote, eliciting strong reactions from many town residents in the following months.
At a May 20 meeting, Gunsallus said that the Pride flag is "antithetical to America" and questioned whether the town should use funds to support such flags and banners, voicing his opposition to Easton funding and displaying celebratory banners for Pride in June. Montgomery supported Gunsallus' statements about the flags and doubled down during following meetings.
Montgomery said the country is being "torn apart by identity politics." He went on to call out the transgender community's involvement in the LGBTQ+ movement specifically, which was met with boos and some attendees leaving the chamber.
Gunsallus' and Montgomery's comments were met with support and opposition from many town residents and other elected officials.
In November, Gunsallus initiated the motion to approve the festival permit for 2025, which this time was passed with no back-and-forth council discussion. Montgomery was not present for the vote, though he told the Star Democrat that if he was present he would have once again voted against approving the permit.
FEDERALSBUG SETTLES HISTORIC LAWSUITA historic lawsuit against the Town of Federalsburg ended in a $260,000 settlement that includes an apology to the town's Black residents and other requirements memorializing the case.
The April 1 settlement includes a sweeping array of measures aimed at providing reconciliation after Federalsburg's previous at-large election system was determined to have prevented Black residents from electing their chosen representatives.
The town's Black population has grown steadily over the years, with Black residents now accounting for about 43% of the roughly 2,800-resident population.
But until last September, the town had never had Black representatives on the Town Council in its 200-year history. Two Black women were elected to the Town Council during Federalsburg's 2023 election — Darlene Pitt Hammond and Brandy James.
The settlement came just over a year after the plaintiffs filed suit in federal court in Baltimore under the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Through months of charter amendments, legislation and federal court rulings, the town's previous at-large election system was changed to a two-district system to ensure more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents.
GROUND BROKEN FOR TRAINING FACILITYIn December, first responders, along with local and state officials, broke ground on a state-of-the-art emergency services training facility in Easton.
The A. James Clark Emergency Services Training Campus is being constructed on Mistletoe Drive. The 7,200-square-foot facility is intended to allow for cross-training between emergency responders and reduce long commutes for first responders in training.
The campus will have a public safety building and an educational building with classrooms, as well as a 1,500-square-foot concrete pad for car fire and extrication training. Hostage rescues, ladder climbs and traffic safety situations are other ways in which the facilities will be used.
TOWN MANAGERS Easton, Cambridge and Oxford all lost town managers last year.
For Easton, the vacancy is the result of a "mutual agreement to part ways" between the town and former Town Manager Donald "Don" Richardson in August. Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey has been serving as town manager in the interim.
The Town of Easton has secured the services of the professional recruitment agency Sumter Local Government Consulting.
For Oxford, former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis retired in June. The town of Oxford was in the midst of controversy due to a previous hire of Michael Calvert, the town's would-be town manager.
Calvert — who was previously a city administrator for Liberty, South Carolina — had been slated to get sworn in as Oxford's next town manager. But just three days after announcing the hire, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some community members expressed concerns. Oxford resident Scott Rensberger said it was "shocking" the town didn't vet Calvert more because it took him a short time to find out "there were a lot of problems" in the town he was leaving.
In December, Oxford announced the hire of Holly Wahl, who announced her resignation as Chesapeake Beach's town administrator on Dec. 4 amid some turmoil in the western shore town, largely dealing with increasing water and sewer bills.
Tom Carroll, Cambridge's city manager of two years, submitted his resignation in March. In a letter addressed to the mayor and commissioners, Carroll said his last day as city manager would be no later than May 17.
"This was a hard decision for me to reach, but I do know it is the right decision to make," he wrote in an email to the Star Democrat. The reason for this decision, he said, was his concerns with Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.'s Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront.
Glenn Steckman was appointed as Cambridge's city manager in July.

 EASTON — Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello announced his candidacy for Easton Town Council President Tuesday.Abbatiello, a public school teacher in Wicomico County and a longtime member of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, has filed to run for council president in the town's election this May.
"My motivation to run is feeling that we're starting to face more and more challenges here in town," Abbatiello said in an interview with The Star Democrat. Current Town Council President Frank Gunsallus announced his intention to run for reelection last month. Gunsallus has served as president since September of 2023.

"I feel like the challenges that we're facing are big enough that it's worth the risk to not be on the council in exchange for the possibility of being president on the council," Abbatiello said.
Abbatiello has served on the town's Affordable Housing Board and noted he hopes to make housing a focus of his if elected president. He added that financial transparency and responsibility are important.
"I think that's one of the things that I've been most proud of over the last six years and one of the things that, if I was president of the council, I'd continue to work with the mayor and the other members of the council to make sure that we're spending the people's tax money wisely," he said.
Gunsallus and Abbatiello each told The Star Democrat that they plan for the race and their campaigns to be positive.
"Don and I spoke this morning and we agreed that it will be a positive race and the voters will decide in May," Gunsallus said in a statement.

title: Maryland legislators kick off 447th General Assembly
author: Konner Metz
content:
Maryland legislators kick off 447th General Assembly

 January 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 670
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — With snow piled up around the Statehouse, Maryland lawmakers returned to downtown Annapolis for the 447th General Assembly on Wednesday.More than 560 bills were prefiled in either the House of Delegates or Senate prior to the opening session. While both chambers began introducing bills Wednesday, the focus largely remained on the state's looming budget deficit that will be tackled in the coming weeks.
The state is predicted to face a $2.7 billion budget deficit in fiscal year 2026. Gov. Wes Moore (D), who some Republicans have criticized for his fiscal decisions, must submit his balanced budget proposal by next Wednesday.
Leadership in the House and Senate acknowledged the deficit will be center stage but spoke optimistically about what's ahead.
House Speaker Adrienne Jones, a Democrat from Baltimore County, said the House, which reviews the budget first, will "use it to reflect our values."
"As we begin this session, I know there has been a lot of talk about our financial limitations. And there should be," Jones said. "We can't deny our difficult fiscal reality. But instead of talking about what our budget can't do, I'd like to talk about what it can do. Most importantly, our budget has the power to protect the most vulnerable Marylanders."
Jones noted health care and transportation as areas that will continue to be prioritized, as well as the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's expansive education initiative.
"We don't want to talk about cuts and prioritizing programs, but we have to," Jones said. "We don't want to talk about high-energy costs, but we have to. And we have to talk about protecting the investment we made for our students and teachers in The Blueprint."
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Baltimore Democrat beginning his sixth year in the role, said the General Assembly's efforts to fund and facilitate reconstruction of the Francis Scott Key Bridge last year showed the aptitude of Maryland's lawmakers.
"This institution showed exactly who it is," Ferguson said. "Within days, we had put together legislation working with our House counterparts, with the governor, setting up the PORT Act in a bipartisan way to find ways to put resources immediately to use, to set the state up for success in the midst of crisis."
Ferguson said the budget deficit is the General Assembly's next significant challenge.
"I've been thinking about it a little bit differently recently, in that yes it is a challenge, but really, it's an opportunity for us in this body," Ferguson said. " … What do we want our future to look like? How do we take this challenge and have the hard conversations about what do we prioritize to invest in people and to build communities in a way that everyone has the opportunity to thrive."
The Senate president offered positivity through the fact that the state came in under budget and ahead of schedule on a significant project just outside of the Statehouse — the Maryland Department of Legislative Services building. A ribbon-cutting ceremony will be held tomorrow, he said.
"What emerged was everything that the state of Maryland should look like," Ferguson said of the new building that he called "beautiful."
Leadership in both chambers remained the same Wednesday. Ferguson and Senate President Pro Tem Malcolm Augustine, a Democrat from Prince George's County, were unanimously nominated to their positions.
In the House, Speaker Pro Tem Dana Stein, a Baltimore County Democrat, was nominated and approved for a second consecutive year. Jones begins her sixth full term as speaker.
On Wednesday, the House Speaker reflected on the fact that her first job in public service was made possible by the Comprehensive Employment and Training Act, legislation the late President Jimmy Carter extended during his time in office.
"I know that we all love public service," Jones said. "And when I think about public service, I think about the late President Jimmy Carter. As it turns out, I owe a lot to President Carter."
Jones said those are the ways in which "government can do powerful things for regular people."

title: New restrictions on historic vacation cottages in St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
New restrictions on historic vacation cottages in St. Michaels

 January 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the St. Michaels commissioners unanimously approved an ordinance to permanently bar historic cottages from obtaining new short-term rental permits in historic districts.The ordinance focuses on homes in the R-2 District, which encompases areas within Chestnut Street and Mill Street including Water Street and St. Mary's Square.
Short-term rentals that have been lawfully operating as of Jan. 8 will be allowed to continue under the new ordinance, but no new rentals will be allowed to operate.
Rob Straebel, town administrator, said there are approximately 11 approved short term rentals in the assigned district that will be grandfathered into the new regulations.
Commissioners were presented with findings from the resolution that was passed in September.
During the public hearing, Commissioner David Wojciechowski asked logistical questions on the short-term rental permits that are grandfathered in, including whether or not short-term rental permits could be transferred with new ownership.
Straebel said as long as the new owners file proper paperwork for permits, the homes can continue to operate as short-term rentals.
"I think all of the areas that have approvals are within the area we would like to see them," Straebel said. "And if (short-term rental properties) do run with the land and the legal background on special exceptions are that they can continue with the change into the ownership as long as it's the same location."
The restrictions were first introduced as a resolution during a Sep. 18 commissioners meeting as a moratorium on new zoning permits or licenses for historic vacation cottages in the R-2 District for a period of six months.
The town's Planning Commission reviewed the regulations at a Nov. 7 meeting, where they supported the moratorium because "regulations have been successful in promoting historic preservation of older and smaller houses in the Historic District," according to an opinion the commission.
Additionally, the Planning Commission said the intention was to concentrate renovations in the Carpenter Street and Locust Street area and should not be promoted to expand this use elsewhere.
In the ordinance it states that a lawful vacation cottage used for short-term rentals in the R-2 District that existed as of Jan. 8, 2025 may be continued provided the use remains otherwise lawful and meets the provisions already embodied in town.
After a quiet public comment, the commissioners moved to vote on the ordinance. It was unanimously approved by all commissioners.
The ordinance will take effect Jan. 28.

title: Wind causes snow drifts on Mid-Shore, make clearing roads more difficult
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Wind causes snow drifts on Mid-Shore, make clearing roads more difficult

 January 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Thursday afternoon, Grand Rental Station of Easton employee Zach Kilmon sat atop a green tractor and cleared snow off the facility's driveway.It was not the first time Kilmon had been out to clear snow in front of the building that day. With strong winds blowing through the Mid-Shore, snow has been drifting into the roads, making conditions difficult on drivers and on public works departments.
With the next bout of snow expected Friday night, public works departments on the Mid-Shore are trying to address those snow drifts.
Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones said they have plowed every road in the county.
"Every road in the county has been touched multiple times," he said. "But with this prevailing, strong, 20-plus mile-per-hour northwest wind, you can go through and them a half hour later, there's drifts again."
According to the National Weather Service, wind gusts Friday night were anticipated to reach as high as 29 miles per hour in Cambridge and 30 miles per hour in Easton.
Talbot County Manager Clay Stamp said snow drifts are having a significant effect on the county's back roads.
"We're working hard with our road crews to address that," he said. "And we've activated our farm community to join our county resources to try to address the re-drifting of these roads. And it's just an uphill battle until the wind decreases."
Stamp said the rural community has been very helpful with clearing roads using tractors, which has freed up county resources.
"As a rural community, we're very proud of our farm community for stepping up when the community is in need with that heavy equipment," he said.
Jones said that in Dorchester County, a lot of contractors have offered assistance in clearing roads.
"And we have certainly welcomed their offers and gotten them into the queue to try to help us manage these roadways," he said.
Kilmon said Grand Rental Station of Easton has rented out tractors to "a good few" people interested in clearing snow. He said he witnessed a few cars get stuck in ditches Thursday in front of his workplace on Centreville Road.
As they try to address snow drifts, both Talbot and Dorchester counties are preparing for the predicted snowfall Friday evening. According to the National Weather Service Thursday, about an inch of accumulation is possible in Easton and two inches of accumulation is possible in Cambridge.
Stamp said Talbot County's crews are prepared for the additional snow. He said the county wants to stress to the community that it's better for drivers to stay off the roads if they're able to and allow road crews to clear snow. He said drivers should also avoid the snow drifts if possible.
"I think our roads crew (members) are often unsung heroes," Stamp said. "They work well into the night, day in and day out, to try to get these roads open. We appreciate the public's patience."
Jones said Dorchester County's road crews are working as much as they can and the county is monitoring potential precipitation on Friday.
"We've got a lot of road here," Jones said. "I think it's 570-some miles that we're responsible for. So we're certainly doing the best we can to get that all done. And we're certainly working with State Highway (Administration) in trying to leverage that relationship as well where we can. I think right now, we just need mother nature to ease up on us and give us a break so we can get on top of it and get it cleared up."

title: Freedom Caucus chair says officials who resist Trump may pay a price
author: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service
content:
Freedom Caucus chair says officials who resist Trump may pay a price

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 723
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland) said Tuesday he expects President-elect Donald Trump will withhold federal dollars from those who don't comply with mass deportation and other policies — potentially even in Harris' home state of Maryland."After having discussions with incoming members of the Trump administration, they're not going to look favorably upon jurisdictions that, with one hand, ask for federal dollars and, with the other hand, pass it out to illegal immigrants, including protecting them from the reach of federal law, including deportation law," Harris said.
"The fact of the matter is that, when the jurisdiction of Maryland says we're not going to cooperate with deportation policies, why, with the other hand, are they reaching out for federal benefits?" Harris said.
"I think what you're going to see, as part of our efforts to control federal spending," Harris went on, is that "one of the first things we're going to do is go to those jurisdictions that don't cooperate with the federal government and attempt to achieve savings there."
Harris' comments came during a press conference in Annapolis to debut the Maryland House of Delegates' Freedom Caucus, a bloc of half a dozen conservative state delegates modeled after the U.S. House caucus of the same name. Harris, whose district includes Maryland's Eastern Shore, was reelected chair of the House Freedom Caucus last month and is a Trump-friendly member of the House Appropriations Committee.
His prediction on Tuesday echoes similar signals from a handful of Trump's current and former advisers, including Steve Bannon and Newt Gingrich, about suspension of federal funding for jurisdictions that plan not to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. Harris also made similar comments to WBFF-TV Baltimore last week.
Many Democratic officials across the country have expressed concern about mass deportation in their states. But days before Trump is due to be sworn in, most are currently emphasizing their plans to find ways to cooperate with the new president.
Lawmakers in the state's new Freedom Caucus suggested that Harris' ties to the Trump administration could result in the use of federal funding as leverage to boost other state-level priorities. This could potentially give the small group an outsize voice in the General Assembly.
Del. Matt Morgan, a Republican who represents St. Mary's County, is chair of the Maryland General Assembly's Freedom Caucus. At the press conference, he rattled off a list of Republican priorities he hopes will receive a boost from the incoming administration. This would include rolling back some of the General Assembly's recent criminal justice reform efforts, he said.
He also expressed optimism that the Trump administration could shut down the construction of light rail projects that Republicans oppose.
Mass transit projects are draining the transportation trust fund, Morgan said, and "right now they're canceling local projects all across the state for roads and bridges, and overwhelmingly, the people that pay into that fund are motorists."
"We believe there's been a void in conservative leadership in this state for quite some time," Morgan said, "and we're going to fill that void."
The group is small, said Del. Ryan Nawrocki, a Republican from Baltimore County and caucus spokesperson, but that's how the Freedom Caucus in the U.S. House of Representatives got its start.
"You start out with a core group of people that are committed to an ideal," said Nawrocki, "and you demonstrate success, and that's how you grow any group."
Robert Ehrlich, the former Republican governor, also appeared at Monday's press conference, speaking to the assembled crowd alongside members of the group.
"In difficult times, people are challenged, and that means leaders emerge," Ehrlich said, as he stood at the microphone before the news cameras. "Folks behind me are clearly leaders that are emerging in Maryland today."
The new caucus's model is to "equip conservatives to win on issues across the country," according to Rachel Ullmann, communications and community outreach director for the legislature's District 7 delegates.
"We stand firmly with the National Network's policy of 'fighting federal overreach and standing firm against those in both parties who prioritize seizing political power over representing constituents,'" she wrote in an email to Capital News Service.
Maryland's Freedom Caucus has not yet sought formal recognition from their party's House and Senate chamber leaders, Nawrocki told reporters.
"There's a possibility that we might do so," Nawrocki said. House Minority Leader Del. Jason Buckel, a Republican representing Allegany County, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Commissioners of Oxford swear in new town manager
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford swear in new town manager

 January 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 499
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — New Town Manager Holly Wahl was sworn into office in an uncharacteristically short Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, bringing hope for calmer seas after half a year of rough water in the town."I think I speak for the three of us. It gives us great, incredible pleasure to swear Holly in," Commission President Norm Bell said before giving Wahl the oath of office in front of a full audience that included Wahl's parents.
Wahl was previously the town administrator for Chesapeake Beach, a town on the western shore. Her arrival marks the end of a nearly six-month period in Oxford where there was no town manager.
In late June, Michael Calvert — a former city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina — was hired to fill the role of town manager, which former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis was retiring from. But just three days after the commissioners announced the hire, they announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
The commission never commented on why the decision was made. Former Liberty City Council Member Peggy Edwards said that when Calvert was in his position in Liberty, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
The situation led to Oxford's commissioners choosing a search firm to assist in its search for the next town manager, which led to Wahl's hiring.
After getting sworn in Tuesday evening, Wahl told residents that it's "great" to be in Oxford and said they should feel free to stop by the town office or reach out to her with any questions or concerns.
"It's been a wonderful start coming here in a major snow storm and watching commissioners climb through a treatment plant and truly be engaged to understand what staff needs," she said.
In the 30 minute meeting, from the swearing in to conversations about updating the town's website and creating a searchable town code in an effort to increase transparency, no disagreement was voiced aloud from residents nor commissioners.
In an interview with The Star Democrat, Bell said there hasn't been any contention at the "last several meetings."
Many Oxford residents have said that since former Oxford Police Chief Patrick Maxwell's abrupt retirement in February 2023 — for which the town never provided a reason — community involvement in town government has heightened. This has led to some tense meetings with significant debate.
Bell said he hopes that with Wahl's entrance, Oxford is entering a new chapter. But he said time will determine if this change in meeting culture is a "definite trend."
He said there is a lot the town can accomplish with Wahl and he is excited for the town.
At the end of the meeting on Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer said the commissioners are "delighted" to have Wahl in Oxford.
"And we look forward to a smooth process and great business management," Greer said.
On Thursday evening, the town will host a meet and greet with Wahl from 5:30 to 7:00 p.m. at the Oxford Community Center.
This report has been updated to include comment from Norm Bell.

 DENTON — The Greensboro Library's 30-year lease is coming to an end, and the intention is to renew the lease, but the Caroline County Commissioners want some changes before signing.The lease expires on March 31 and has to be renewed within 60 days of the expiration date.
The Maryland Rural Development Corporation, which holds the lease, is between administrators. The corporation has selected a person to be administrator but has not confirmed the new hire, which is holding up the lease extension.
The commissioners' concern was with Section 2.3 of the lease, which does not direct any part of the lease payments into a fund for library maintenance. The county wants to structure a fund that will handle the library's maintenance but doesn't want to fund a property they don't own.
The library's maintenance has been a problem, according to Jonah Owens, executive director of the Caroline County Public Library. He said the HVAC system has not been working properly the past two months. Sometimes employees can come into work and see temperatures of 40-50 degrees on the thermostat.
The county commissioners want to establish a good working relationship with the library and the Maryland Rural Development Corporation. The first step, they said, is fixing the HVAC system.
"I'm no longer prepared to accept the building not being heated and cool," Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "I mean, that's just a standard when you lease a space. It's your responsibility to make sure everything works properly, so we need to resolve that."
To establish a good working relationship with all three parties, the plan is to renew the 30-year lease so the library can stay open and work on a new lease that allows some money to flow to a fund to upkeep the library.
The process of reworking a new lease will be derailed until the corporation appoints a new administrator.
The county commissioners made a motion to sign the lease with the intention to rework the lease at a later date.
ALCOHOL, CANNABIS TAXThe Caroline County Commissioners passed the emergency bill establishing the Caroline County Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund.
The tax sales of alcoholic beverages and cannabis will go to the fund, which will benefit low-income communities in Caroline County.
The emergency bill was proposed by the county to comply with the Maryland Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, which allows the sales tax of these items to be used for the county's benefit. The state mandated each county create its own version of this fund.

title: A public hearing will come for potential regional detention center
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
A public hearing will come for potential regional detention center

 January 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 449
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County wants to hear the public's opinion before making any big decisions on the potential regional detention center agreement with Kent and Queen Anne's counties.The Caroline County Commissioners discussed the draft agreement for the potential facility for the second week in a row at their weekly meeting Tuesday.
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman and County Attorney Stewart Barroll attended a meeting with Queen Anne's County officials about the draft agreement for the detention center Monday, bringing with them a list of concerns from the commissioners.
Freeman was not in attendance for Tuesday's commissioners meeting, but Barrol and Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox presented an update on what was discussed in the meeting Monday.
Last week the commissioners' concerns largely dealt with the power Queen Anne's County would have over the regional detention center, and Queen Anne's County ability to throw Kent or Caroline County out of the agreement with no warning.
The majority of the authority over the center will be in Queen Anne's County hands, according to the draft. All decisions and disagreement must go through Queen Anne's County Commissioners, and if they may have a disagreement it will be mediated.
Under the draft, Queens Anne's County could decide after a certain amount of time to remove Caroline or Kent county from agreement, regardless of the amount of money that was put up. To remove one or both of the other counties from the agreement, according to the draft, Queen Anne's County must give the other county a two-year notice to take all their prisoners and house them somewhere else.
Those issues were discussed at the meeting on Monday, but Queen Anne's county has yet to send back the new revised draft bill.
Queen Anne's County was not receptive to all of Caroline County's requests at the Monday meeting, Barrol said, particularly a proposal to create a three-county authority to oversee the facility.
"I finally got it out of them that no, Queen Anne's will never part with any part of the title to the campus," Barrol said.
But Queen Anne's County verbally agreed to draft the agreement so that it can no longer exit the deal or force Caroline or Kent county out of the deal.
In addition, Caroline and Kent county will have the right to exit the deal if they please.
Another proposed change from Caroline County is allowing Caroline County employees positions at the regional detention center as opposed to having staff provided by just Queen Anne's County.
"From what I gather, from talking with Kathleen, that has pretty much been resolved that our employees would be able to be absorbed into the workforce," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said.
A date for a public hearing on the agreement has not yet been set.

title: Dorchester Burial Sites Preservation Board gets another chance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester Burial Sites Preservation Board gets another chance

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 717
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A board designed to help preserve grave sites in Dorchester County has one year to prove it is able to accomplish its mission or it will face dissolution.After holding a public hearing about repealing a chapter of the county code regarding burial sites preservation, the Dorchester County Council agreed Jan. 21 to keep the chapter — which includes the Burial Sites Preservation Board established within it — for a test period.
"A one-year test from today to see what you can accomplish and see if it is a worthy board to have within this county," Council Member Ricky Travers said before making the motion.
Throughout the public hearing and following discussion, council members brought up concerns of past problems with the board's participation and its ability to work cohesively. Council President Lenny Pfeffer said that in the one-year test period, the board would need to prove it can fill its seats and provide a quorum at its meetings.
Travers said board members would need to work together, not against each other as has been the case in the past.
"As passionate as people might be about grave sites, ... we cannot have this controversy," Travers said. "So whomever comes on that board needs to be willing and ready to work side-by-side."
County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said the Maryland Historical Trust is the state's enforcing entity regarding burial sites preservation.
"And we were basically duplicating the effort," she said. "While this may be a good board for a nonprofit, being under the county's umbrella, I don't think it's working out."
Dorothy Samonisky, the chair of the Burial Sites Preservation Board, said the Maryland Historical Trust only gives guidance and does not "act as an arm of the law" like the county can.
"So right now, this burial site preservation is the only thing that gives you as county members anything to stand on if there is an incident with a grave site."
Pfeffer clarified that the board is an advisory group to the council.
Samonisky said people have been buried in Dorchester County since 1669, and many of those burial sites are on private property. She said the policy in county code gives the county the authority to "act upon destruction of those cemeteries."
Ashley Samonisky, who also spoke during public comment, said the board can guide council actions and help with outreach and education. She said there needs to be something in the code that addresses what happens if a person "maliciously destroy(s) a property or (tries) to hide the fact that it was there," in order to build a beach house, for example.
"There needs to be fines," she said. "There needs to be penalties up to and including the cost of restoring it to the pre-demolition stage. These are just a few ideas that this body can help with."
Dorothy Samonisky acknowledged that there were "internal conflicts" between several board members at one point. She said she also was out due to two major surgeries in 2024.
"We had met up through '23 and had things on the agenda and topics to discuss," she said.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer, who ultimately voted in favor of the board having a one-year test period, said he thinks the board has value, but would function better if not affiliated with the county.
"It being a law and having to be constituted a certain way and done a certain way is holding an effort to preserve burial sites back," he said, later adding, "I think it could be more flexible and more dynamic as a stand-alone."
Detmer said as long as he is on the council, if someone comes to the council with "a salient point" about something in the county, it will get attention. That doesn't require a board, he said.
Before the council unanimously agreed to give the board a test period, Travers said the board had previously gone through an "extremely adversary" time that got to the point where some board members felt unsafe coming to the meetings. He said the county practically had to act as a referee.
"And that's not what we need on our boards," he said.
Pfeffer warned the this can't happen again.
"The last board that was assembled ... had brought things to this chamber," he said. "Had brought thoughts of slander. Had brought disagreements. I will not allow that to happen during these meetings."

title: Easton planners: amid affordable housing shortage, inclusionary zoning may be useful
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton planners: amid affordable housing shortage, inclusionary zoning may be useful

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1134
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Through her work at the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, Daisy Aguilar interacts with many prospective first-time homebuyers. Of the many challenges they face, housing prices in Easton and Talbot County are at the top of the list."The houses, they're not affordable right now," Aguilar, the center's housing coordinator, said. "And most people that are buying, they're buying in Dorchester County because it's more affordable than it is in Talbot County."
An inclusionary zoning ordinance in the works could pave the way for more affordable homeownership and rental opportunities in Easton. It would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable, defined separately for ownership and rental.
Inclusionary units in ownership developments would need to meet an affordable price for households making up to 100% of area median income, while rental developments would need to meet prices affordable for households making up to 60% of area median income.
According to Jim Bent, chair of the Affordable Housing Board, Easton's area median income was around $98,000 last year.
While similar legislation has faced hurdles in the past, town leaders and affordable housing proponents are hopeful the time is now for inclusionary zoning to be implemented.
EASTON'S WORKFORCEEaston Mayor Megan Cook is well aware of the fact many can't afford to live in town, including essential workers, town employees and police officers.
"When you're sworn to protect and serve a community, yet you can't even live in the community that you're dedicating your life to, that says something," Cook said. "That's not quite the message we should be sending people."
According to the draft ordinance, Census data shows that 42% of around 17,000 Talbot County workers commute into the county. Cook and others are hoping the ordinance can lower that percentage.
"A lot of the people who work in those fields earn wages where they have been priced out of the Easton market, and so their only option is to find housing in adjacent counties," said Miguel Salinas, Easton's director of planning and zoning.
For homebuyers, the local market is a significant challenge. According to the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors, the average home price in Talbot County in 2024 was $856,000.
Town staff's calculation of the maximum affordable home price for a family of four making the area median income is $292,000.
"There was a time, a couple years, not too long ago, that houses were affordable," Aguilar said. "I mean, they were selling fast, but they were affordable. And at least you had the possibility of actually getting a house."
THE ORDINANCESalinas, who has led the town's efforts to create the ordinance, recognizes it is just one piece of the puzzle. But it's a critical step, he said.
"This is one tool in the toolbox. And it's been discussed for 20-plus years," Salinas said.
Since it was initially presented in February 2023, Salinas said the ordinance has endured many revisions, along with being viewed by the town's Affordable Housing Board, Attainable Housing Task Force and an outside contractor.
Town planners looked at similar provisions in jurisdictions such as Queen Anne's County, Annapolis and Frederick when drafting the ordinance.
A draft version of the inclusionary housing ordinance was passed 4-1 by the town's Planning Commission last November.
Planning Commission member Michael Ports, speaking for himself and not the commission, said the inclusionary zoning ordinance would do two things particularly well. It would push the "cost burden predominantly away from existing residents" and incentivize developers to build inclusionary units.
In addition to the requirement that 15% of units fit the inclusionary definitions, the ordinance would grant developers that provide inclusionary units on the same site as market-rate units with a 20% density bonus.
Such aspects of the ordinance encourage mixed-income projects, which town leaders believe can help to reduce housing inequities.
"Housing segregation opens the door to other types of segregation, and you can certainly see that in many, many communities," Salinas said. "But not just racial and ethnic, but also age."
Tom Klein, the Planning Commission's sole vote against the ordinance, says he is a proponent of more affordable and workforce housing. He believes inclusionary zoning is not "necessary nor a cost-effective way" to achieve that goal.
"For the past two years that I have been on the Planning Commission, just about every new development proposal has come with a component of affordable/workforce housing," Klein wrote in an email.
Recent developments that provide the town with affordable housing include projects from The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, such as Port Street Commons, a multi-use property with nine affordable apartment units that opened in December, and Silo Square, a mixed-income housing project greenlit in October.
Revitalization of the Doverbrook Apartments complex in Easton is underway and will feature an additional 14 affordable units on top of 50 existing ones. On Elliott Road, more than 100 apartments are under construction, a portion of those affordable.
Last July, the town approved the annexation of 17 acres of land for a housing project on the east side of Route 50. In the annexation agreement, developers agreed at least 50% of the project's apartment units will be affordable.
Given the number of ongoing projects, Klein says he feels inclusionary zoning would not "provide a significant number" of additional affordable units.
But Ports believes the ordinance will ensure that the limited supply of undeveloped land in the town is being used properly.
"It's really the biggest asset any community has," Ports said. "If we want to allow someone to potentially change it forever, we need to make sure that they're investing in the community in some way."
REGULATIONAt the November Planning Commission meeting, Klein and other commission members expressed concerns of overregulation prior to voting on the ordinance.
"I think that the market's taking care of it," Klein said. "I think that we're putting a lot of regulation here. Like I said, I think there could be a lot of unintended consequences that come out of that and a lot of cost for what we get out of it."
Salinas and Bent both said the market hasn't been able to address ballooning home and rental costs in recent years.
Bent said he's heard from planning commissioners in the past that a "tool" is needed to point developers toward what the town wants in terms of affordability.
While proponents of inclusionary zoning are confident it can be this tool, they recognize the housing problem in Easton is complex.
"If we got into this hole of housing deficiency over the course of decades, it's impossible to fix that in one year, let alone even 10 years," Ports said. "It will be a game of playing catch-up."
Cook hopes Easton residents, along with the Town Council, see affordable housing as a top challenge to tackle.
"I do hope that they see the importance of this issue, and I also hope that the community itself sees the importance of the issue," Cook said. "For the longevity and the vibrancy of the Town of Easton, it's an important issue."

title: Caroline County commissioners offer legislative session updates
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub
content:
Caroline County commissioners offer legislative session updates

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub | Section: News 
 
 458
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday, officials discussed bills working their way through the General Assembly.Commission Vice President Larry Porter led the discussion about the legislative session. He highlighted two proposed bills that the county commissioners are concerned about.
Senate Bill 0189 prohibits counties and the state from taking preserved farm or conservation land via eminent domain and Senate Bill 0724 would mandate seatbelts on all school buses.
SCHOOL BUS SEATBELTSThis isn't the first time seatbelt requirements on school busses has been proposed in the General Assembly. Similar bills have been filed for many years and have not passed, with counties largely complaining about the cost of implementation.
This year's bill would mandate that every school bus made, brought or built after 2027 must have a seatbelt installed on every seat.
The county commissioners said they would have a conversation with Caroline County Public Schools about the bill, but they expressed concerns about the potential cost of enacting it.
"I don't think I'm interested in testifying," Larry Porter said about a request he received to oppose the legislation. "But I think we could probably reach out to the superintendent because there were some concerns from their transportation department about it."
The concerns for the County Commissioners have been the same every time this measure has been proposed — the cost of installing seat belts on every school bus, who is liable if the kids don't put seatbelts on and how the school bus drivers will enforce seatbelt wearing.
"We have the same concerns that we had before," Porter said at the Tuesday meeting.
In an interview, Commission President Travis Breeding mentioned but he believes the design of the seats on the bus helps keep students safe without seatbelts.
EMINENT DOMAINThe county is more receptive to eminent domain bill, but they want to see some revisions before it's passed.
"The eminent domain bill was prohibiting the state or county from taking land by eminent domain in areas that were preservation areas," Porter said. "In the beginning, that sounds like that's something we would absolutely support."
The county recently had a situation at Long Swamp Bridge that made the commissioners feel revisions needed to be made to the measure. The county needed more space for the construction of a new bridge at the site, and it brought some preserved land from a owner to make more space.
If the eminent domain bill was enacted it would have been way more trouble for the county to go through that process of buying the land, Breeding said. It could have caused a lane closure.
"We didn't use eminent domain, but because (of) the landowner. It was in preservation land, and he negotiated," Breeding said.
They commissioners suggest maybe revising the bill to make it easier to work out future land preservation problems.

title: St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board holds first meeting
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board holds first meeting

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 538
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of controversy surrounding its creation, the St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board held its first meeting at the Boy Scout Cabin in St. Michaels Thursday morning.During this meeting, members of the board, the St. Michaels Business Association and residents of the town came together to discuss the future and current condition of the tourism industry.
The board discussed potential budgets, marketing and branding strategies including combining various websites, and getting a better understanding of the tourists who are visiting and the tourists the board would like to bring to St. Michaels.
Timothy Law, the representative of retail businesses on the board, said as a business owner he is really excited for the work the board will produce.
"I love St. Michaels, and today was a huge stride forward to really understanding tourism and promoting our spectacular destination. I think it's a great group of people and we've got a great diversity of thought and diversity of background. It was just a very positive first step."
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during a commissioners candidate forum hosted by the St. Michaels Business Association last April, when representatives of the Business Associations stated a need for marketing assistance due to a decrease in revenues within the last year.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
The board has seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership includes residents not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
The members of the board were elected by the Commissioners of St. Michaels and include:
Brian Ball, managing director for the Wildset Hotel, to represent lodging.
Chris Agharabi, chief executive officer of Ava's Hospitality Group, to represent restaurants.
Katie Blaha, advancement manager of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, to represent nonprofits/museums.
Michael Morgan, owner and president of St. Michaels Marina LLC, to represent marinas.
Timothy Law, owner of American Holiday Shop, to represent retail.
Craig Bertolett, chief operating officer of COLUMBIA Technologies, and Michael McMillan, associate clinical professor of accounting at the University of Maryland, as two representatives for the residents of St. Michaels.
Included in the board is St. Michaels Commissioner Katrina Whittington as acting representative for the commission.
On Thursday, the board discussed the importance of a unified marketing message and the potential benefits of public Wi-Fi for data collection. Board members emphasized the need for a clear target audience and suggested a short-term plan to focus on digital marketing.
Ball said it's important for people to understand how tourism effects all aspects of the town's economy.
"St. Michaels is very much a tourism-based economy and it really affects everything we do from local government to all the businesses and all the restaurants and hotels," Ball said. "I think that this (board) is a very valuable economic tool to use to help the town grow."
Plans were made for the next meeting to include presentations on budget allocation and marketing strategies. The next meeting will be held on Jan. 30.

 EASTON — During Tuesday's meeting, the Easton Town Council approved four-way stops at two different intersections on Brookletts Avenue.Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh recommended the stop signs be added at the intersection of Brookletts Avenue and South Harrison Street, as well as the intersection of Brookletts Avenue and Hanson Street.

title: Easton leaders split on property tax breaks for first responders, veterans
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton leaders split on property tax breaks for first responders, veterans

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 559
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Tuesday's meeting, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus suggested the town should consider property tax breaks — and potential removals — for emergency responders and veterans."One idea to explore is the reduction or removal of property taxes for our emergency responders, as well as for our active duty military (and) veterans," Gunsallus said immediately before the meeting adjourned. "Such an initiative could help us attract more volunteers to our fire department, ensuring it remains a volunteer-driven organization."
Gunsallus encouraged the council to consider his proposal. Councilmembers have offered mixed opinions.
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said while an "immense debt" is owed to all veterans, he thinks "broad-based" tax relief for veterans is likely not the way to go.
"I could not see offering property tax reductions to all veterans," Montgomery said in an interview. "I don't think we could afford it. I think there are other ways that we can express our appreciation."
At the state level, disabled veterans and surviving spouses can apply for property tax exemptions.
According to Easton's budget ordinance from last year's budget cycle, it was estimated the town would bring in $13.4 million in revenue from real property taxes.
The town's current property tax rate is 0.52 cents per assessed $100 of value. Last year, the council voted unanimously to keep it at that rate, a mark that hasn't been increased in nearly two decades.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who is running against Gunsallus to be council president, said property tax removals for all veterans would create a budget shortfall and impact the town's funding toward its police, fire and public works departments.
"As a result residents will either do with reduced services in town or other residents will have to pay higher taxes to make up for the loss of revenue," Abbatiello wrote in an emailed statement.
In an email, Gunsallus stated he hopes to explore the possibility of property tax breaks this budget season. He emphasized any consideration of property tax relief should be balanced with fiscal responsibility.
"I fully appreciate, understand, and share the concerns regarding potential impacts on our budget," Gunsallus wrote. "My ardor for this initiative is tempered by financial stewardship."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said in an interview that she would rather see the council look toward assisting first responders in buying homes, noting the town's affordable housing shortage.
"It's really not our property taxes that are the problem, it's the cost of buying a home that's a problem," Curry said.
Abbatiello, a member of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, added that former Mayor Bob Willey spearheaded a tax relief program for Easton firefighters that is still in place. Life members or volunteers who go on at least 100 calls in a year receive a $500 tax incentive, he said.
Abbatiello, who announced his campaign for Town Council president earlier this month, alluded to the town's upcoming election in his statement.
"Volunteer Firefighters and Veterans have not been asking for a tax cut," Abbatiello wrote. "But they do expect responsible government. Proposing a massive change to the tax base without truly examining its effects because it's an election year is not being fiscally responsible."
Gunsallus says he's heard from first responders and veterans regarding potential tax reductions.
"Through numerous conversations, I've gathered that there is interest for this form of financial relief," Gunsallus wrote. "While these requests have not been formal, the sentiment is clear and merits our attention."

title: Southern Dorchester County residents push for a seat at the table
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Southern Dorchester County residents push for a seat at the table

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1121
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TODDVILLE — Around a big wooden table in the back corner of Elijah's General Store in Toddville Wednesday, three generations of south Dorchester County residents outlined a plan to save their home.Dick Dawson, a lifelong resident of Bishops Head, has watched over the years as areas in the southern part of Dorchester County turn from woods to swamp. He's seen land where cattle used to graze become water holes and mud holes that would take a boat to get through.
"The ground is sinking, there's no doubt about that," he said.
Sea level rise has become a significant issue in Dorchester County over the years, particularly in the southern part of the county. Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said the area has faced environmental challenges "as the relationship between the land and the water changes."
"There's massive erosion, there is saltwater intrusion and just a variety of other really relentless environmental challenges," he said.
In an effort to protect these communities in southern Dorchester from disappearing, three men are working to incorporate Blackwater, a new town, giving the communities that call this area home a seat at the table and a chance for survival.
The communities included in the plan for Blackwater are Andrews, Robbins, Wesley, Lakesville, Crapo, Wingate, Toddville, Bishops Head and Crocheron.
Each community would still exist within the new town, the planners said. But incorporating would give the communities a voice, said Drew Dawson, Dick Dawson's 17-year-old grandson.
"Because on our own, the communities aren't large enough to incorporate," he said.
David Beverley, who owns Elijah's General Store, said that by incorporating, the communities would have a better chance of receiving funding from government agencies.
"As you can tell when you're driving down here, it's beautiful landscape," he said. "But unfortunately, regulations and all kinds of things have made it really hard to fix properties here."
Beverley, who owns Elijah's General Store, sees a direct correlation between critical area regulations and deteriorating roads and houses in the area. According to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the state's critical areas include land within 1,000 feet of tidal waters, wetlands, and the Bay and its tributaries.
"If you buy a property down here, if you put so much money into it based on the tax assessed value, you have to raise it," Beverley said. "And the people don't have the money to raise it. ... Why are we even going to raise it if you aren't going to put the money into the roads because of the population decrease? And would you consider a priority road fix? So it's a whole circle of problems."
Beverley and the Dawsons — who make up the organizing committee to create the town — see incorporation as the path to being able to apply for state and federal grants so residents can do things like raise their homes.
Dick Dawson said the area is in need of a good road that doesn't flood "just because the tide comes up" and drainage so that when the tide does come up, it can go back down.
The effort to incorporate isn't "a move against the county," Drew Dawson said.
"We understand that the population is very low and a lot of times it doesn't make sense for them to do everything that really needs to get done," he said. "The idea is just to do what the county can't, not necessarily drill the county for what they're not doing."
PULLING UP A CHAIRA drafted charter for the proposed Town of Blackwater sat in the center of the table where the trio sat Wednesday.
Under the charter, the town would be able to elect five members to a council for a term of four years. The commissioner with the most votes would be named mayor, and the commissioner with the second-most votes would be named deputy mayor. The town would not impose new taxes.
"The idea is to give more power to the people of the area, not add an unnecessary level of government," Drew Dawson said.
It took a couple weeks for Drew Dawson — who is a dual enrollment high school student at Chesapeake College — to write the charter. His initiative in creating it is something his grandfather is proud of him for.
"Drew has written the majority of this," Dick Dawson said.
Drew said he used other charters, mainly Eldorado's, to create Blackwater's charter. "But a lot of it was also written myself," he said. "It's nearly double the size of the charter of Eldorado."
Once they can get enough signatures on their petition, the three plan to go to the county to submit the charter for review. If the county accepts the charter, the decision will go to the registered voters within the area that Blackwater would encompass.
If those residents vote in favor of creating the town, Blackwater will become Dorchester County's newest incorporated town.
As the group moves forward with the process to become a town, other residents are getting involved. Drew Dawson said "public sentiment is positive" among residents they've spoken to so far. Dick Dawson said they plan to host a public meeting to explain the idea and what incorporating a town could do for residents.
"We're interested in their comments as well," Beverley said.
Drew Dawson said the length of time it could take for Blackwater to become a town is "hard to tell" because of all of the smaller steps necessary in the process.
"The hope is to get it done by the end of this year," he said.
Detmer said that although he doesn't know how his fellow councilmen feel about the idea to create Blackwater, the chance for residents to make a decision at the ballot box has his "full personal support."
"The best thing about their initiative, to me, is not just that it's looking to the future and the picture of how business is done with local, state and federal government, but the real advantage of their initiative is they are actually going to give the residents of the area a chance for their voice to be heard about whether or not they want to do it," he said.
If Blackwater becomes a town, both Dick and Drew Dawson are interested in serving as commissioners.
"I am one of the older people that is down here," Dick Dawson said. "And I have seen a lot of changes. And not many of them have been for the good. I'd like to be here to help get this thing started."
Drew Dawson said he encourages everyone to read the drafted charter to understand what incorporating would mean for the area.
"If we continue to do nothing, the land and the roads will continue to sink, and the land will erode away," he said. "We'll lose more and more residents and they'll just keep creating regulations until it becomes nearly impossible to live here."

title: Cronan sworn in as Talbot County Circuit Court judge
author: Konner Metz
content:
Cronan sworn in as Talbot County Circuit Court judge

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 508
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With hundreds in attendance at the Talbot County Courthouse, Philip Cronan was sworn in as the new judge of the Talbot County Circuit Court Friday afternoon.Cronan, appointed by Gov. Wes Moore last month, assumed the seat from acting Administrative Judge Broughton Earnest. Earnest had been serving since March 2024, when previous Judge Stephen Kehoe was appointed to the Appellate Court of Maryland.
"You can put your stamp on the system of justice here," Earnest said during Friday's ceremony to Cronan. "You're the face of justice, at least in the Circuit Court. There are things you can do not only to perpetuate this system, but to enhance it."
In an interview Friday, Cronan said he's excited to begin as the Circuit Court's administrative judge.
"This is a very humbling experience, and it's just an incredible honor to have the opportunity to serve Talbot County in this capacity," Cronan said. "I look forward to it."
Cronan received his law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law. He served as an assistant state's attorney in Caroline County before beginning his own private practice in Easton.
The new Circuit Court judge is a founding principal of the Easton-based Hollis, Cronan & Fronk law firm. Over the years, his practice has taken a broad path, including domestic litigation, civil litigation, criminal defense and family law.
He said the application and appointment process for the Circuit Court seat was extremely detailed and thorough. Once a judicial nominating commission selected Cronan and two other finalists for the role, they each met with the governor.
It was right before Christmas when Cronan received a call from Moore congratulating him for his appointment.
"I was super excited," Cronan recalled. "I was in court, I was in District Court in Dorchester County when he called. He's such a charismatic, energetic figure, even on the phone. He just makes you feel good."
Cronan says in a one-judge county like Talbot, a judge is "integral" in fairly administering justice.
"I hope to operate in a way that really makes people feel that they are heard, and that they have an opportunity to be heard," Cronan said. "And that they find the process to be fair, even when it doesn't go their way — that they're not steamrolled by the court, so to speak.
"We need to make sure that our citizens find the court a place where they can find justice. If they don't feel heard, if they feel slighted in any way, then we're going to fail. We need to really focus on that."
Cronan previously served as a law clerk for former Talbot County Circuit Court Judge William Horne. He noted Horne held high respect for the institution of the court, something Cronan says was "very powerful."
The longtime Easton attorney aims to channel what he's learned from judges across the state into his work in the Talbot County Circuit Court.
"I've had the benefit of watching so many other judges and how they handle it," Cronan said. "The incredible importance to have a good temperament, to have respect for everybody there, to treat people with dignity."

title: Cambridge City Council hears plans for Harriet Tubman mural area
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge City Council hears plans for Harriet Tubman mural area

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge mayor and commissioners spent a significant portion of their three-hour meeting Monday learning about Alpha Genesis Community Development Corporation's plans to revitalize the area surrounding the Harriet Tubman mural behind 424 Race St.Adrian Holmes, president and program director of Alpha Genesis, said the second phase project will help extend the stay of tourists in Cambridge.
"Right now, most people who go back there stay no longer than five or ten minutes because there's nowhere to sit, it's hot, it's just not really appealing," she said. "So this is what we want to do to help the people who come to the mural extend their stay. And when they extend their stay, they'll spend more money ... and they'll just have a better experience."
The plan, which extends into Cannery Way off Race Street, is to add two retail spaces adjacent the mural. One of the spaces will be a souvenir shop, Holmes said. The building itself will also include Alpha Genesis' headquarters, three other retail spaces that face Race Street and an exhibition deck.
In front of the mural will be the Harriet Tubman Pavilion, which will shield viewers from inclement weather. Near the pavilion, there will be a community garden.
"We affectionately call this project the North Star Village, a tribute in honor of Harriet Tubman," Holmes said.
Alpha Genesis has been working with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, the Maryland Historical Trust, the Rural Maryland Council, state legislators and the City of Cambridge to make enhancements to the space. Alpha Genesis is still raising funds for the second phase of the project, which will cost around $1.5 million. The project has received funding from the Maryland General Assembly and the city.
"And then we have a couple grant opportunities that can cover the rest of it," Holmes said.
According to council meeting documents, the proximity of Alpha Genesis' property to city property has made the project a "joint venture" between the two. One document from Alpha Genesis states the city will improve Cannery Way and the adjacent parking lot, and Alpha Genesis will focus on 428 through 432 Race St.
Alpha Genesis is asking the city for the installation of public restrooms, the repositioning of the brick wall on Cannery Way and the addition of a replica of the Ben Ross Cabin on the Cannery Way property.
Holmes said restrooms would benefit tourists who come from far distances to see the mural. Alpha Genesis' proposal is to construct a "North Star Station" that includes two all-gender bathrooms, a 135-square-foot public meeting room and a small lobby space with digital kiosks that have information about the city.
RESTROOM DISCUSSIONCommissioners asked a variety of questions about Alpha Genesis' plans. Multiple questions focused on the restroom proposal.
Commissioner Brian Roche shared his concern with the North Star Station blocking the view of the water from Cannery Way. Holmes said a possible change to the proposal could be to remove the meeting room from the station to make it smaller.
Commission President Sputty Cephas asked who would be responsible for maintaining the public restrooms. Alpha Genesis Executive Director Jermaine Anderson said he thinks it would be a good idea to form a youth or recidivism program where those in the program would be tasked with maintaining areas around the mural.
"Now's the time," he said. "Let's get real creative. Let's continue planning, continue talking, developing relationships. ... I think we can find the solutions we need."
During public comment, Chuck McFadden said he supports revitalizing the area, but the city should be careful about how much it commits. McFadden also cautioned that bringing youth in to clean the public restrooms might not be an easy feat.
After council discussion, the City Council unanimously voted to have city staff work closely with Alpha Genesis on its proposal and make sure it gets through the Historic Preservation Commission and the Planning and Zoning Commission. The vote, which Cephas motioned, also called for a presentation on the fiscal impact of the proposal and made sure Roche and any other interested commissioners can work with city staff on the matter.
