title: Caroline County Courthouse needs a new door
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Courthouse needs a new door

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Greensboro Historic Society President Charles Dean has a vision for the Caroline County Courthouse's new door. The vision dates back to 1797, when the first version of the courthouse was built."The county was gaveled into existence by commissioners meeting March 15, 1774," Dean said. "About a month after that, there was an architect by the name of William Buckland, and he presented designs for the very first Caroline County Courthouse."
The County Commissioners have been having conversations about a new courthouse door since December, when security concerns at the facility were brought to their attention. The conversation came up after Circuit Court Judge Heather Price said she had been receiving death threats. Price declined to comment further on the matter at this time.
The county approved the budget for installing new windows at the building in December but tabled the conversation about the door, raising concerns with historical accuracy.
The Caroline County Courthouse is a historical site in Denton. According to the Greensboro Historical Society, the courthouse was first built in 1797 and then was rebuilt in 1895. The courthouse was redesigned in 1965 to what it looks like today.
Dean sent an email to Caroline County Commissioners explaining the history of the courthouse. He believes that the county is not going back far enough in time with its research for the new door.
"My email to the commissioners basically reiterated these facts," Dean said. "I'm not sure that they have ever seen pictures of the original courthouse door or the second courthouse door. They're going for a replica of the current courthouse door. So if they wanted to be historically accurate, they could go back much further than 1965."
Caroline County shares the courthouse with several state departments, and certain security protocols need to be followed. The county commissioners are committed to keeping the courthouse's historic design, as long as this is in keeping with state mandates.
"Let's see what Mr. Dean has," Commission President Travis Breeding said at the commissioners' Tuesday meeting. "If its a picture or a design."
The grant cycle has passed for the county to get funding for the door, but the commissioners decided Tuesdays that the door can be paid for with county funds.
"We will find someone to get the information and give it to facilities and look at the historic door," Breeding said. "If we don't like the historic door, we will get the door replaced."

title: Centreville Planning Commission tables cannabis expansion
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Centreville Planning Commission tables cannabis expansion

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 660
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Centreville cannabis dispensary Green Thumb Industries request for major site plan approval for a two-acre expansion was tabled Jan. 15 by the Centreville Planning Commission to address additional comments.The original facility final site plan was approved in 2021 with two-acres of outdoor growth, and Green Thumb is now requesting amended final minor site plan to expand with an additional two acres and include a new irrigation shed and incorporate drying trailers to enclose order, according to attorney Kevin Shearon, DMS Associates on behalf of the applicant.
The expansion is a permitted use and meets town requirements, he said.
Public comment was split on the expansion.
Several emails from citizens presented to the planning commission voiced support, citing Green Thumb as a job creator and revenue source for the town, as well as cannabis fitting into the expanding definition of agriculture.
In-person public comment largely played a different tune however, mainly residents of Symphony Village speaking against the odor.
Over the summer odors were described as minimal or not as noticeable, but during September to December of the harvest and drying time, residents claimed the order as "pungent" and "almost daily."
In operation in Centreville for a year and a half, Green Thumb has undergone major odor mitigations following previous community feedback, spending over $100,000 assessing, identifying and installing technology, according to Rebecca Brown, of Green Thumb's government affairs department.
Green Thumb has invested over $40 million in the building, she said.
The location had been vacant for eight years before Green Thumb moved in, Brown said. The location was chosen for the Green Thumb's ability to grow as expansion is a key component of the business model and needed to stay competitive, she said.
Green Thumb is considered one of the largest private employers in town and in the county, employing over 200 at the Comet Drive location, Brown said.
Byers Scientific performs the testing samples both indoor and outdoor for Green Thumb twice a year previously in June, Brown said.
While odor hasn't completely gone away, Green Thumb was doing everything it could to diminish odors, "and we're not going to stop doing that," according to Brown.
Smells have been identified as coming from harvesting and processing, not just budding outside, Green Thumb officials said, and mitigation has been applied where odors have been noted to be the most prevalent including the extraction lab, and the indoor kitchen hood, where edible products are created.
Green Thumb previously utilized a cost-prohibited hemp dryer, while moving forward, seeks to use fully enclosed drying containers with charcoal odor mitigation built in, according to officials.
Scrubbing the air, the 40-foot long, eight-foot wide containers perform roughly 42 air changes per hour and filters are swapped out every two weeks, officials said.
The same odor mitigation technology already employed will be utilized on a broader scale, she said.
Brown claimed with the expansion, twice that outdoor growing area would not double the odor, "It's sort of like when you bake two apple pies versus you bake four apple pies, you're not going to smell any additional pies, you're already smelling it."
Acknowledging she was not in the marijuana industry, planning commission member Wendy Emerson disagreed with the pie analogy, stating herself as a baker, and that "four pies will in fact provide more scent."
Emerson sought information regarding the industry's standards that she claimed should have been shared with the planning commission prior, including what was the odor level previously, where is it today, and what is the intended increase.
Noting existing technology to detect other odors such as carbon monoxide monitors, Emerson sought exploring technology to monitor cannabis odors and Brown said Green Thumb could look into technology as part of the expansion's approval.
The planning commission also noted the plan's public works agreement and tree canopy requirements need addressing.
Tabling a vote, the planning commission determined there was not enough information and sought additional comments to be addressed including testing data from other Green Thumb sites during the fall months and submission of the most recent Jan. 20 test results.

title: Caroline County Commissioners offer legislative session update
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Commissioners offer legislative session update

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 513
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County Sheriff Donald Baker and County Commission Vice President Larry Porter agree that Senate Bill 292 would not be good for Caroline County.Concerns with the proposed state legislation were brought to the Caroline County Commissioners' Tuesday meeting by the sheriff, who detailed how the bill would impact traffic stops.
The proposed bill, which includes several measures related to traffic stops, would turn some primary enforcement offenses into secondary enforcement offenses. A primary offense is a reason for an officer to pull someone over and give a citation. A secondary offense requires a primary offense to occur first in order to be enforced.
The changes outlined in the bill could cause some evidence to be inadmissible, the sheriff's office argues.
"If it comes to find out if that a stop was in fact supposed to be a secondary violation and the officer stops them on primary violation, any evidence after the fact would be inadmissible in court," Chief Deputy Capt. Rodney 'RJ' Helmer said.
For example, some primary violations that would be moved to secondary violations include driving an unregistered vehicle; improper display of registration plates or tags; and driving, standing or parking a vehicle in dedicated bus lane.
If an officers pulls over a vehicle for one of these reasons as a primary violation, any evidence discovered thereafter will be inadmissible in court.
"So, for example, if a car was riding with their headlights off at night time to avoid detection and you stop that vehicle and its supposed to be a secondary stop and not a primary stop, and their is evidence of rape, sexual assault, or an armed robbery in the car, that evidence would not be admissible in court," Baker said.
The county plans to send in a letter opposing the proposed bill.
Other proposed billsAt Tuesday's meeting, Porter mentioned multiple other proposed bills from the Maryland General Assembly and the county's stances on them.
Proposed Senate Bill 478 would prohibit the Public Service Commission from approving a solar energy generating station unless they receive written approval from the county. The county is in favor of the bill, with Porter saying, "obviously that's a support for us."
Proposed House Bill 487 and Senate Bill 484 would ban a local legislative body from prohibiting the placement of a certain manufactured homes in certain residential zoning districts under certain circumstances. The county will oppose the bills.
"This basically means someone can come pitch a tent and live on the courthouse greens, and it will be nothing we can do about it, and if we do they can sue us," Porter said. "We had a long discussion about this last night, and we will have a big discussion about it tomorrow. This is something we should oppose."
Proposed Senate Bill 481 prohibits the Maryland Department of Health from limiting the amount of revenue the holder of an on-farm home processing license may derive from food processed under the license. This is another bill the county will oppose.
"This is for people the grow produce and sell it, Porter said. "I don't think we should be involved in limiting the revenue they make."

title: Tunis Mills bridge replacement project moves forward
author: Konner Metz
content:
Tunis Mills bridge replacement project moves forward

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TUNIS MILLS — A beloved bridge in the Tunis Mills community is moving toward reconstruction after months of resident input into the bridge's redesign.In recent years, the 345-foot-long Leeds Creeks Bridge and its wood planks have deteriorated. County engineers consider the bridge structurally deficient, necessitating a replacement.
Tuesday, the Talbot County Council agreed to move forward with the bridge replacement project. County Engineer Ray Clarke recommended the county work toward finalizing rights-of-way acquisitions and necessary permits so construction can be pursued later this year.
As proposed, the replacement would include a wooden deck and a timber wearing surface. The structures below the bridge supporting it, known as piles, would consist of concrete and steel materials.
Clarke told council members that in order to use federal funding for the project, the bridge replacement project cannot use timber piles per the State Highway Administration. He added that trying to build an all-timber replacement will cause significant delays and costs.
"The big disadvantage we have is that if we don't get the federal aid, we're probably going to need to request the council for additional funding for the project, local funding," Clarke said. " … This could be a $3 or $4 million ask."
The project costs around $6.5 million, with $1.5 million coming from the county. The rest is federally funded.
Advocates of a 100% wooden replacement have been in dialogue with the county, including at an August public meeting. Susan McDermott and John Tabori, two of those advocates, have lived in Tunis Mills next to the bridge for four years.
McDermott says the original proposal to rebuild the bridge many years ago "was just unacceptable to the community." The county's recent proposal matches more of what she and some other neighbors had hoped for.
"We're very pleased that the council has shown as much flexibility toward community views as it has," McDermott said.
Residents like McDermott previously expressed concerns that an asphalt wearing surface would encourage speeding across the bridge. The county's plans now include a timber wearing surface. Clarke said that change will amount to around a $250,000 increase.
The other main change based on community feedback is a reduction in the height of the safety railing from 42 to 36 inches.
McDermott, who leads a small group of neighbors called the Tunis Mills All-Timber Bridge Alliance, hopes to find answers to whether an exception can be made for the requirement that piles not be timber.
She adds that the bridge is an integral part of the community.
"I think the town feels that the wooden bridge of Tunis Mills — one of the last wooden-deck bridges in the county — is very much part of the community," McDermott said. "It's not just a bridge that occasional traffic goes across. We've got a lot of walkers in this neighborhood, a lot of kids and people just use that bridge as a foot path."
After a video of the bridge was shown during the meeting, Talbot County Council Member Lynn Mielke said it seems the replacement "needs to be done sooner rather than later."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher thanked Clarke and his team for their efforts to advance the replacement project.
"I appreciate the homework that you've done to investigate the alternatives as requested and appreciate that we really can't sacrifice the federal aid," Lesher said. "The economics of this project dictate that we absolutely need to go with the recommended steel concrete pilings and concrete cap."
Lesher motioned to approve the project as presented, and the rest of the council unanimously agreed. Lesher added that he hopes the federal funding for the project comes through, referencing President Donald Trump's temporary pause on federal grants and loans announced earlier this week and rescinded Wednesday.
"And we'll just hope that any suspension of federal grant aid for transportation projects is very short-lived," Lesher said Tuesday.

title: Caroline Cares connects community with services at Resource Day
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Cares connects community with services at Resource Day

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Multiple vendors at Caroline Cares Community Resource Day Wednesday were reminded how amazing it is to do community work and help others.His Hope Ministries Youth Director Desiree Jefferson distributed winter clothes at the event. She was one of many vendors who had previously attended the event not to distribute resources, but to receive them.
"It's really refreshing to be able to give back," Jefferson said. "Just a couple years ago, I was somebody that was coming through the doors and receiving services myself, so it's good to see that we can help families in need."
The Caroline Cares Community Resource Day featured around 40 vendors providing information, help and food to the community.
"This is what it's all about," said Stephanie Johnson, His Hope Ministries' executive director and board member for Resources Day. "Just getting all the resources in one building so that it can be kind of an easily accessible for those who need them the most. Being able to bring those providers under one roof, on a specific day, to get those services out to everybody who needs them is huge."
One of the main focuses for Resource Day is providing many different types of help for many different people.
Some attendees face expenses they can't afford or are just in a bad financial situation, and some people are homeless. Resources Day helped with a variety of situations.
Directors expect 100 to 150 county residents experiencing homelessness to attend Resources Day every year, and they have a plan to make sure homeless residents can find shelter.
"With this particular event, they have access to walk around, talk to the vendors and see what exactly what their services are that they provide," Johnson said. "However, like when it comes to those who are actually experiencing homelessness, we have a separate room set aside for them to really dig into what their needs are and see how we can connect them with services."
Caroline County Public Schools officials attended, providing information for children on enrollment in school and many different resources for mental and physical health. United4Caroline provided free diapers for families with infants.
Chesapeake College's nursing program provided free blood pressure checks for all people in attendance. Nursing students gained experience and enjoyed serving the community.
"Oh, I love this, and I'm actually from Denton myself, so to give back to the community is amazing," Katie Reuwer, an assistant professor at Chesapeake College, said. "It's a great experience for the students to really learn about community service and helping others. I've already had some really good feedback from the students about how much they enjoy it."
Staff from Studio 107 Hair Salon in Kent Island and Edwards All Star Barbershop in Denton enjoyed providing free haircuts and styles at Resource Day, something both shops provide every year.
"There's no better feeling," Lisa Milligan, owner of Studio 107, said. "You're helping people that are maybe down on their luck or they're just getting out of jail or they're just going for jobs. It's every aspect, older people that can't afford to get their hair cut especially in this economy. So it's great to give back."

title: Cambridge to receive more than $1 million from state for revitalization
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Cambridge to receive more than $1 million from state for revitalization

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge has been awarded $1.15 million from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development for four of the city's revitalization projects.Projects receiving grant monies include the Mace's Lane Community Center, the 444-448 Race Street development project, the old City Hall renovation and Cambridge's façade improvement program, according to a news release from the city.
Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman said in an interview with The Star Democrat on Friday that the grants were awarded about a month ago.
"I think this shows that city staff is working very hard to create a good first impression for people visiting our community," he said. "And that they see Cambridge as a happening place and not a sleepy backwater."
The Mace's Lane Community Center has been awarded $500,000 to complete construction and renovation at the former Cambridge high school. Founded by The Good Shepherd Association and the Mace's Lane High School Alumni Association, the community center will offer a variety of programs — including sports, arts and education programs — to support Cambridge's youth.
In November, about about $8 million had been raised for the community center and $4.5 million was still needed. The $500,000 in grant money is from the Strategic Demolition Fund, which is a state program that aims to activate local economic development and create jobs.
In order to complete the third phase of the 444-448 Race Street development project, the state has awarded the city $500,000 from the Community Legacy program. The third phase of the Race Street project includes creating three retail spaces and nine apartments.
Community Legacy grants are awarded to projects in Maryland's "sustainable communities," a designation that Cambridge received in December 2023.
A total of $100,000 from the Community Legacy program was awarded to the "Old City Hall" renovation project on Gay Street. The grant money is for the creation of a community room in the building. Renovating and preserving the old city hall is a priority for the city.
The city was also awarded $50,000 to go toward improving the city's commercial building façades. The grant is through the Maryland Façade Improvement Program. Steckman said he expects this grant to benefit the city's downtown area.
"The City is grateful for these generous awards from the State of Maryland, which demonstrate its ongoing support of Cambridge's work to improve its buildings and economy for the betterment of the lives of all our residents," Steckman said in a news release. "We look forward to the continued improvements these projects will bring to the City of Cambridge over the next year."
Along with the city's awards, the Packing House received two awards totaling $550,000 from Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development programs, according to the city. The grants, from the Community Legacy program and the Strategic Demolition Fund, will be used to furnish the building's shared commercial kitchen and to complete the building's interior and exterior event space.
Margaret Norfleet-Neff, the development manager overseeing the Packing House renovation, said the Packing House appreciates the support from the state.
"The Packing House is most appreciative of the ongoing support from DHCD and looks forward to unveiling the completed interior and exterior spaces for the benefit of the community and public use," she said.

title: Oxford moves forward with website update
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford moves forward with website update

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 318
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford is getting a major update to its website.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, the commissioners awarded a contract to CivicPlus to develop an updated website that includes a direct resident messaging platform.
Commissioner Katrina Greer called the move "exciting."
"It'll be much easier to use," she said. "The old WordPress site was really clunky and difficult to use, so this will be drag-and-drop technology."
Greer said with the new site, users should be able to get where they need to go within two clicks, "which is simply not true right now."
Town Manager Holly Wahl said with this update, the town will be able to forward its current website to a government domain. She said with a direct resident messaging platform, the town will no longer have to use Constant Contact, an online platform it has been using to get information out to residents.
Wahl said all of the messages the town sends out will also populate on the updated website.
Residents who have been using Constant Contact will not have to do anything to stay in the loop. Wahl said all of the users subscribed via Constant Contact can be uploaded as subscribers to the new website. She said those who were not previously using Constant Contact will be able to subscribe to town updates from the updated website.
The mobile-friendly and ADA-compliant website will cost the town $3,598 to initiate. This price is approximately 50% less than the original quote the town received. Wahl said that cost will be covered in the town's existing fiscal year 2025 budget.
Wahl said she hopes to have the updated website up and running within the next two months.
"I'm aiming for six to eight weeks to get a base site set up so that agendas can be clear, meeting minutes are easy to locate (and) all of the boards and commissions have a page that's easy to navigate," she said.

 DENTON — The Caroline County Historical Society wants to rebuild a working relationship with the County Commissioners so they can get some help funding for different projects to help bring tourist to the town."We have in and around Preston a five-mile radius the most significant components of the Underground Railroad in the United States," lifetime member of the historical society Mick McCrea said.
The Linchester Mill historical sight offers many trials and buildings to where Harriet Tubman and other prominent individuals lived.
"We have actual buildings you can literally walk in the footsteps of people where they stayed in the homes where they got freedom from," McCrea said.
Another suggestion made by historical society board member David "Gene" Harris that the Linchester Mill pond be restored for many reasons.

Potential Regional Detention Center updateThe potential Regional Detention Center came up in discussion again for the commissioners.
The center would be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill and would house detainees from Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties. It aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
The commissioners said they still have not received exact numbers for how much everything will cost and how much the county will save by joining the agreement with the other counties.
Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested that the county should do an independent evaluation of the operating cost.
"This decision is going to depend on the operational cost and I'm talking long range operational cost," Porter said. "Would it make sense for us to engage someone to do an independent evaluation of these operating cost?"

title: Sen. Van Hollen talks federal grants pause with Eastern Shore legislators
author: Konner Metz
content:
Sen. Van Hollen talks federal grants pause with Eastern Shore legislators

 February 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 758
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While speaking with Eastern Shore legislators Friday morning, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said a short-lived pause of federal funding earlier this week had impacts on local organizations such as fire stations and law enforcement agencies.Monday, President Donald Trump's budget office issued a memorandum ordering a pause on federal grants and loans. A U.S. district judge temporarily blocked the pause Tuesday before the White House rescinded the memo the following day.
"Because of the public outcry, they did pull back on this overall freeze," Van Hollen said. "But there's still a whole lot of uncertainty and confusion. So if you are hearing from folks on the Eastern Shore that are recipients of federal programs that are being disrupted, please let us know."
At the weekly Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, Del. Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) asked Van Hollen to elaborate on his perspective of what happened.
Van Hollen said the memo from the Office of Management and Budget brought forth confusion for government agencies. The senator heard from thousands that were impacted, he said in an email newsletter.
"It was very broadly worded and very ambiguous," Van Hollen said. "Federal agencies interpreted this based on what it said. Essentially, they did freeze a lot of ongoing payments to organizations that do important community work."
Arentz said some of the spending that was paused could be viewed as "questionable" in the first place.
"I think that's the point that was being made about that," Arentz said. "I keep getting questions on it, because it does look like when you portray it in one way, it looks bad, but in the other way, you look at some spending that people would have questions on. And I think that's part of the explanation I try to give."
"The way the memo was worded and the reason it was retracted was because it was so broad that it appeared to impact everybody," Van Hollen responded.
Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) also attended Friday's Eastern Shore Delegation meeting. She explained to state senators and delegates her line of thinking when voting to confirm recent political appointees, emphasizing that she is prepared to vote on "qualified" candidates across party lines.
"My primary interest and sole interest, really, is making sure that I protect the interests of Maryland," Alsobrooks said.
SUPERINTENDENTSEastern Shore superintendents gathered at the meeting Friday to provide legislative requests and recommendations.
Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons, president of the Eastern Shore of Maryland Educational Consortium superintendents' group, framed Friday's discussion around The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education funding initiative.
It comes as Gov. Wes Moore (D) and the state legislature attempt to balance a $3 billion state deficit, in part by making cuts to education funding.
Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson explained the importance for districts to attract a diverse and qualified teacher workforce. However, state requirements, such as teacher salary minimums, sometimes bring about challenges.
"It is not good for a district, especially like mine, since we don't have the funding that other districts have," Thompson said.
Queen Anne's County Public Schools Superintendent Patty Saelens said the Eastern Shore superintendents don't support Moore's proposed funding cuts to teacher collaborative time (out-of-classroom time to grade and plan) and community school initiatives.
"Our number one priority right now that we just can't support is literal cuts to our budget, specifically as it relates to the collaborative time and the community schools," Saelens said. "Those are two major things that will negatively impact our overall state support."
EDUCATIONRepresentatives from colleges and universities attended Friday's meeting, including Chesapeake College President Clifford Coppersmith and Washington College President Mike Sosulski.
Sosulski provided an update on Washington College's Innovation Plant Project, which is a project the institution is collaborating with Chesapeake College on.
"In the year-and-a-half of its development, it's already garnered $3 million in public and private funding to support it," Sosulski said.
Sosulski added that he hopes the Maryland Sellinger Grant Program, which provides independent colleges and universities with state funding, isn't slashed.
"I can't tell you how important Sellinger has been to making a Washington College education affordable and accessible to all Maryland residents," he said. "It is really, and quite literally, the difference for many, many of our students and their ability to achieve the kind of education that we can provide."
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) asked about whether universities are considering raising tuition due to potential state funding cuts.
"We fully understand the need for the governor to cut the budget," said University of Maryland Eastern Shore President Heidi Anderson. "We will not be looking at increasing tuition for our students, and we will abide by that."

title: Easton Postal Service short staffing causes late mail deliveries

Easton Postal Service short staffing causes late mail deliveries

 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton resident Bart Pelstring has experienced late mail delivery for about two months now, and he believes his neighbors and other Easton residents have experienced the same issue.Pelstring said that he has consistently received his mail between 1 and 3 p.m. But for the past few months, Pelstring said delivery times have been "unacceptable."
"I noticed that there were times when no mail was delivered," Pelstring said. "I have neighbors that said the same thing, and then we noticed that mail was being delivered at seven or eight o'clock at night, and sometimes later than that."
Pelstring called the Post Office to speak to the post master and the response he got alarmed him, he said.
"I called to speak to the postmaster, and they told me he was out delivering mail," Pelstring said. "The girl I talked to, she said, 'well we're short staffed, we don't have enough people anymore, and we don't have backup people.'"
Mark Wahl, a strategic communications specialist for the postal service in Washington, D.C., Maryland and Virginia, detailed the Easton location's recent challenges.
"We recently experienced challenges with employee availability that did impact mail deliveries," he said. "We have taken specific actions to continue service to our valued customers."
The actions Easton Post Office plans to take include:
Authorizing overtime to allow employees to work the time necessary to deliver mail.Expanding mail deliveries to earlier in the morning and later in the evening.And using additional carriers from nearby offices to maintain mail deliveries.
"We appreciate customers' patience and understanding and expect staffing to be restored to normal levels soon," Wahl said. "With our carriers delivering later in the evening, often when it's dark, we kindly ask customers to keep porch lights on for our employees' safety."

title: Dorchester County braces for budget season, asks residents to participate
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County braces for budget season, asks residents to participate

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a County Council meeting Feb. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said that based on preliminary numbers, the county is in need of an estimated $3.5 to $4 million to balance its budget for next fiscal year.With significant concerns, the County Council is encouraging residents to participate in the budget process and reach out to elected officials.
Pfeffer said there is no fat left to trim, and so it is searching for ideas on how to balance the budget. "All of our departments are cut down to bare bones," he said.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer called the county's preliminary budget numbers "extraordinarily drastic."
"There's no cutting, in my view," he said. "There's no navigating through it. There's no weathering the storm. ... This is a breaking point type of moment."
Pfeffer said Blueprint for Maryland's Future mandates are the reason for these shortfalls. The Dorchester County Board of Education is facing a $10.19 million deficit going into fiscal year 2026.
"We don't want to put the kids at risk here," he said. "We just can't afford this Blueprint program that exceeds our revenues by drastic numbers."
Detmer said tough decisions might need to be made this year and residents should be paying attention to the budget process.
He brought up a June 2024 Board of Education decision — which was ultimately reversed — to remove media specialists from libraries, redistributing them to other positions in the school system. The move, which did not have to do with Blueprint requirements, would have saved the district more than $313,000 this school year.
"What else do you think might be on the chopping block for them to be able to balance?" Detmer asked.
Pfeffer said not paying for the Blueprint is not an option. He said the state will withhold the county's income tax revenues if it doesn't pay.
"It keeps all of us up at night trying to figure out ways to fix this," Pfeffer said, "and we just don't have all the answers. So, please, help us think of ideas. Send us emails."
During public comment, resident Sharon Smith said the county needs to "inundate" Gov. Wes Moore (D) and other state leaders with emails and phone calls. She suggested the County Council take out ads in local newspapers that ask residents to do the same.
Resident Morgan Tolley asked the county to post contact information for state legislators and leaders on social media so that residents can reach out. "Because this is a dire situation," Tolley said.
Detmer said although residents might be hesitant to reach out to their representatives because they don't want to complain, it is helpful when they do.
"You're not chewing them out," he said. "To me, you're arming them with evidence that their voters feel a certain way."
Resident Bucky Jackson said the county is cutting "pennies on the dollar" and recommended it look at the number of schools in the district. He said the district has too many schools considering its number of students.
Detmer said Jackson was right about his "pennies on the dollar" comment, adding that if the county were to eliminate its Economic Development, Tourism and Recreation and Parks departments, it would only save about $1 million.
The county will host its first budget work session on Feb. 25 at 6 p.m. The budget adoption schedule can be found on the county's website.

title: Eastern Shore stakeholders gather in Annapolis
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Eastern Shore stakeholders gather in Annapolis

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Stakeholders from throughout Districts 36 and 37 gathered in Annapolis Monday, bringing with them concerns and comments for the Maryland General Assembly.Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) hosted the event, which was attended by Mid-Shore residents, business owners, nonprofit representatives and other elected officials.
"We do this every year," Mautz said. "It's an opportunity for anyone to come and meet their legislators, people who are in government work and just concerned citizens.
"It's great opportunity talk to everyone, find out whats going on, and we had a great turnout tonight."
According to Mautz, the most important part of representation at District 36 and 37 event is building unity to help fight proposed budget items and bills that will not help the community.
"We've got a bipartisan delegation, and we work hand-in-glove on all these issues on behalf of our district because usually it's us against the western shore delegations and things like that," he said. "It's great to have everybody together."
Budget Concern
Stakeholders voiced concerns about the state's proposed budget the $3 billion deficit state lawmakers face.
Del. Christopher Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) believes citizens are concerned with state spending and the cost of their taxes.
"Citizens want investment," Adams said at the event. "They like seeing the state spend money wisely. Citizens that I'm hearing from are saying, 'we're worried because not only should we not be talking about tax increases, tell me why the budget went up $3 billion in one year, what are the additional things that we're getting for that tax dollar?'"
Funds for many different groups, organizations and services are at stake as lawmakers work to balance the state's budget.
For All Seasons, an organization from Easton that offers free mental health services, came out to meet with lawmakers in Annapolis. Representatives of the nonprofit wanted to make sure they advocated for mental health services on the Eastern Shore.
"We serve a community that is rural," said Beth Ann Doorman, For All Seasons' president and CEO. "For All Seasons serves as an agency that is serving people regardless of their ability to pay, so being able to access mental health and rape crisis services with no wait lists.
"Mental health issues impact every single one of us, and to know that the delegation is paying attention is huge."
Lauren Kay Weber, For All Seasons' vice president of strategy and development, said they wanted to make sure their services and other services don't get lost in the shuffle of a tough budget year.
Energy crisis
Maryland stakeholders are working to decrease energy prices in Maryland. Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) believes the proposed plan for the energy crisis was "underwhelming."
"Higher energy prices are not just common to the Eastern Shore residents, we're seeing that across the state," Hershey said. "The Democrat leadership introduced three bills today that they believe are going to try to address the energy crisis. Frankly, I was underwhelmed by them.
"I didn't think that they were anything that was going to fix any type of immediate problems that we're having, and that's what people want."
Hershey believes to see energy prices go down, the state must take control of the energy problem and not depend on other states.
"Maryland is a net importer of energy. We don't create enough energy within the state to satisfy our demands," Hershey said. "I think that we need to change that. A cost effective way to do that is probably through gas generation and seeing if we can get some quickly, get some power plants online that take natural gas, turn that into electricity and see if that will help drive down our energy costs."

title: As new Oxford town manager, Holly Wahl wants to focus on people
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
As new Oxford town manager, Holly Wahl wants to focus on people

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 627
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — For Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl, it's all about ensuring the success of town staff and making sure residents have the information and clarity they need."My first goal is people," Wahl said in an interview with The Star Democrat Tuesday.
Wahl — who has been in the position for nearly a month — wants to make sure town employees, whose jobs have a direct impact on citizens, have the resources they need to be successful.
Staff redundancy, or making sure more than one person has the training and licensure to do a job, has been a focus. For example, Wahl said the town's nutrient removal treatment plant only has one licensed operator, who also serves as the plant's superintendent. She said the town is working on getting additional training so there is more than one licensed operator in town.
Along with supporting staff, Wahl is also focused on government transparency and streamlining communication for residents. She sees upping the town's communication game as a way to build residents' trust in Oxford town government, which has been a concern over the past two years.
During the most recent Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Jan. 28, the commissioners approved a contract with a company to develop an updated website that includes a direct resident messaging platform. Wahl said updating the website was a priority for her because it will streamline communications and address residents' frustrations with not being able to find information.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said the new website will include a searchable town code so that residents won't have to "wade through an out of date PDF" to find what they're looking for.
Wahl is also trying to address concerns about the town's budget by sharing updated fiscal information at town meetings.
"There've been a lot of comments about budgeting and making sure citizens can understand the budget, understand what's within the budget," she said. "So (we're) working on providing clarity in that."
The town's record system is another area Wahl is setting her sights on improving. Currently, the town has a paper record system. She would like to digitize it so that individual records can be found more easily and the town can respond more efficiently to public information requests.
As she settles into the Oxford Town Office, Wahl is working on obtaining a doctorate in public administration and public policy from George Washington University. She is currently finishing up her dissertation, which focuses on how town managers respond in the complexities of local government.
"It's really centered on how we can be more inclusive (and) engage further so that, ultimately, we're solving problems with better decision making models," Wahl said.
All three Commissioners of Oxford agree that Wahl is a great fit for the job.
"She seems to have picked everything up without missing a step," Commissioner Tom Costigan said.
Greer and Commission President Norm Bell both noted Wahl's significant experience and qualifications. Greer said Wahl is the ideal person for the job.
"What you want for this job is someone who's committed to the profession of public administration," Greer said.
A month into the job, Wahl is looking for housing on the Eastern Shore and getting used to the pace of things on this side of the Bay Bridge. Although she hasn't had much time in the last few years, she would love to get back into doing water sports, like kayaking and paddle boarding. She is excited to explore all the Eastern Shore has to offer.
Looking to the future, Wahl hopes that 10 years from now, Oxford will have "more avenues for engagement" so more perspectives are brought to the table.
"I think everyone should feel comfortable giving their feedback," she said. "They might not want to do it in a town meeting, but there might be other ways that we provide them opportunities to do that."

title: Easton leaders at odds over affordable housing ordinance's next step
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton leaders at odds over affordable housing ordinance's next step

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town leaders held a tense discussion Monday regarding inclusionary zoning, debating how quickly the town should move forward with an ordinance meant to address affordable housing shortages.At Monday's meeting, the Town Council was asked to schedule a workshop to review the draft of an inclusionary zoning ordinance that's been in the works for two years.
In November, the Planning Commission approved the ordinance by a 4-1 vote. It would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable.
Initially, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus made a motion for the town to seek out a firm and delay the workshop. The motion was immediately seconded by Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, but a lengthy discussion followed before the motion was eventually rescinded.
"It's clear from studies in other jurisdictions that the impacts have varied but that they have included a serious slow down in building because this is essentially a tax on builders," Montgomery said of inclusionary zoning. "They've included higher housing costs to the extent that it's been possible to pass those on."
Gunsallus proposed the town find an independent firm to conduct a study "over the next nine to 12 months." The firm would provide "an objective analysis" of the positive and negative effects an inclusionary zoning ordinance may have, he said.
Montgomery said in his experience, the town could be "looking at $50,000 at a minimum" for such a study.
Mayor Megan Cook disagreed with the proposal to hire an outside firm for a long-term study. She emphasized that town planners, staff, and the Planning Commission have already spent a significant amount of time drafting the ordinance and considering its potential effects.
Town planners worked with an advisory firm, David Paul Rosen & Associates, to help revise the legislation last summer.
"What information are you looking to gain that has not already been looked at?" Cook asked Gunsallus. "And by the way, we don't have $50,000 in this year's budget."
"I beg to differ," Gunsallus responded. "I read the budget thoroughly, I would actually very much beg to differ on that."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said she'd like to "see the scope of work" before the town commits funds toward a study. Curry asked who would select the firm. Gunsallus said the council would be in charge.
"Why? Why would the council be choosing?" Cook asked.
"Because we're the ones tasked with needing to make a decision on this," Gunsallus said. "The town has already spent a significant amount of money into drafting it. Because the responsibility ends right here, that's why."
Gunsallus later added that based on studies he's read, there are "serious doubts" about whether inclusionary zoning will lead to the number of affordable units the town is seeking.
"But there's equal research out there that shows that it will," Cook said.
Councilmembers Don Abbatiello and the Rev. Elmer Davis said they'd like to have the workshop before making a decision on a study. Council agreed to a March 3 workshop for the Attainable Housing Task Force to provide a report related to the ordinance.
Gunsallus maintained that he appreciates the hard work of town staff. He said it's the council's "responsibility to carefully evaluate what has worked elsewhere before determining the best course of action for Easton."
"There is a serious housing issue with the Town of Easton," Cook said toward the end of the discussion. "We can't even employ a police officer, hire a new police officer, and have them be able to live in the town that they have been sworn to serve. That is a real issue."
"We are talking this to death," Cook added. "And that is inaction by constant conversation."
This story has been updated.

title: Assessments and taxation discussion at Caroline County meeting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Assessments and taxation discussion at Caroline County meeting

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 485
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — In anticipation of changes to the division of costs for property assessment, the Caroline County Commissioners asked questions of Keith Bobbick, Caroline County supervisor of assessments and taxation, about some general operation of the department.A part of Gov. Wes Moore's proposed budget is a shift of more expenses for property assessment services to the county.
Counties will be responsible for 90% of operational costs for their assessment offices if the budget is passed as written, according to Commission President Travis Breeding. Currently, the county and the state split the cost of operation evenly.
The commissioners' questions dealt with how things were assessed and the process of assessment. In particular, the commissioners wanted to know what the process looked like for having agricultural properties reassessed for commercial uses.
The tax money paid for a property goes up when agricultural properties turn into commercial properties, making the taxes more expensive for the land owner and generating further revenue for the county and other taxing agencies.
"That happens once a year," Bobbick said. "It's usually in July, and it happens whenever the change actual starts from agricultural use to some other use."
By law, the towns and counties are supposed to provide permits about new operations in their area. A problem the assessment office faces is not receiving information on properties from the towns in a timely manner.
If the properties are not reported by the town, the assessments office will have no knowledge of the property, which could cause the reassessment to be delayed until after the July deadline, limiting the taxes that can be collected.
The county suggested the assessment office make a list of the towns it is having trouble with so the commissioners could encourage them to remain on top of reporting new developments.
Another big concern from the county is that a lot of taxpayers are showing up in the county tax office with assessment questions. The taxpayers are saying that the voicemail of Caroline County Assessment Office is directing them there.
"When you call our main line, it does have a bit in that in there," Bobbick said. "It says 'if you have a question about your tax bill, call the tax office.' When people come into our office, we try to help them as much as we can. If they have a question about their tax bill, we're gonna try to help them."
Commissioner Frank Bartz also questioned the assessment office's hybrid work schedule.
By state law, the assessment office employees are only required to work from the office three days a week.
Commissioner Frank Bartz questioned whether when the staff is working from home, they can accomplish all the necessary tasks.
"Anything we can do in the office, we can do from home," Bobbick said. Bartz responded, "expect answer the phone."
Bobbick informed Bartz that there is always someone in the office to answer the phone.
The county commissioners suggested that the language in the voicemail be changed to not confuse taxpayers.

title: Solar energy should not trample town's master plan
author: STEVE KLINE
content:
Solar energy should not trample town's master plan

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEVE KLINE | Section: Columns 
 
 871
 Words 

 Read News Document

 My love for the Chesapeake's Eastern Shore started in Chestertown.I used to visit each fall for the Chestertown Wildlife Exhibition and Sale, and it was one of my favorite weekends of the year — skeins of migrating Canada geese passing noisily overhead, a little bit of autumn in the air. That celebration of wildlife art was a fixture on Chestertown's fall calendar from 1965 to 2012, and it was my first exposure to the magic of Chestertown.
As with so many Eastern Shore towns, that magic comes from the close interplay of vista and village. Just a stone's throw from your favorite bookstore, you can enjoy the rural countryside in full by paddling Radcliffe Creek, cycling a scenic byway or photographing combines as they bring in the harvest.
Around the same time I was making those trips to Chestertown, not quite 20 years ago, the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy was working with Chestertown, Kent County and a professional planning firm to create the Chestertown Greenbelt Master Plan. The master plan was meant to encompass the future of the Clarke-Hopewell Farm, described by Chestertown Mayor David Foster as "our only real opportunity for expansion of Chestertown."
The nearly 500-acre farm, northeast of Chestertown's historic downtown, is one of the last remaining sizeable undeveloped tracts within the town's planning boundary.
This was just before the Great Recession. Real estate was booming, and there were plenty of questions about how development would shape the future of Chestertown and the entire Eastern Shore. Hence the master plan, developed with strong input from the community, to ensure that future development of the Clarke-Hopewell Farm would be an "organic extension of the historic fabric of the town," an effort to replicate in Chestertown's future what had worked so well in its past.
One of the questions asked at the inevitable community workshops during the process: "What defines the character of Chestertown and should be reflected in this new part of town?"
Responses included: "historic … small town feeling … neighborhood feel … walkable … life on a human scale." Those words do a nice job describing what works about Chestertown. The master plan hews closely to these ideas, providing a flexible and iterative development program designed to "accommodate much of the growth of the town and the county over the next 50–100 years." The plan includes hamlets and villages, each of which incorporates mixed-use buildings, civic uses and neighborhood greens.
But instead of human-scale hamlets and mixed-use neighborhoods, what now seems poised to occupy the Clarke-Hopewell Farm is a 45-megawatt utility-scale solar array. The array will send power straight to the grid, keeping lights on and computers buzzing in homes and businesses and data centers as far away as Illinois. And all of this has been planned despite clear and formal opposition from Chestertown and Kent County.
This change came about because the solar developer, a subsidiary of a massive Canadian-based asset management company, petitioned for and was granted a certificate of public convenience and need from the state of Maryland. What does that mean? Well, it's essentially a permission slip from the state, allowing the solar developer to simply ignore time-tested and well-understood local land use decisions.
This "preemption," as it's called, is being done in the spirit of addressing the challenge of climate change head-on, for which the state has adopted aggressive renewable energy generation goals. But in its rush to site solar power, the state has tilted the playing field. Parcels close to our towns and designated growth areas deserve careful attention, responsible land use and close examination.
In Chestertown's case, the state is trampling the town's best-laid plans and taking off the table a parcel that was meant to accommodate well-planned growth for the next 50 years or more. Instead of public parks, community orchards, apartments that young people can afford and easily bike from — instead of trees, a café, playgrounds, gardens, a barbershop or cottages — we'll have solar panel, solar panel, solar panel. More than 140,000 modules.
Solar panels do not need fertile soil. They do not need to have their hair cut and they do not bike to class in the morning. There are many other places solar fields can go. Where else is Chestertown supposed to go? There are not many other spaces the rest of Chestertown can grow into. At least not without contributing to what the Greenbelt Master Plan describes as the Eastern Shore's "auto-oriented suburban sprawl, which threatens to erode its rural character."
In the race to site solar power as quickly as possible, the Eastern Shore looks increasingly attractive. But we must have balance, a level playing field, some way to say, "Here or here, but not there."
Many of our open acres are best at producing food, and they should remain in agriculture. Other acres, located nearest our towns, are best suited for new neighborhoods. Some spots are well-suited for solar generation. But when we write a new set of rules that favor solar energy over all other land uses, there is no balance.
Rather than allowing Chestertown to "grow harmoniously … slowly and methodically as to maximize the efficiency of its land use," as the Greenbelt Master Plan so eloquently states, we will allow our land to be "rapidly digested." The Eastern Shore will lose.

title: Local lawmakers press energy company on rising utility bills, seek solutions for state power generation
author: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com
content:
Local lawmakers press energy company on rising utility bills, seek solutions for state power generation

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 563
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — With constituents facing soaring utility bills, Maryland lawmakers pressed energy company representatives for answers during a Zoom meeting with the Eastern Shore delegation Friday. The discussion centered on rate hikes, energy generation and ongoing efforts to educate customers on conservation methods.Representatives from Pepco Holdings, a subsidiary of Exelon, and Delmarva Power addressed concerns from state delegates, many of whom have been inundated with complaints from residents whose electricity bills have doubled or tripled.
Marcus Beal, regional vice president and director of external affairs for Delmarva Power, emphasized that the company does not generate electricity but serves as a delivery provider. Beal said regulatory processes govern rate changes, and any increase must go through formal approval channels.
"We will continue to be front and center for our customers," Beal said, noting they can't change rates without going through the formal regulatory process.
Del. Wayne Hartman (R-Wicomic, Worcester) challenged company officials to explain why rates have risen so dramatically, particularly in comparison to member-owned cooperative utilities.
Beal attributed the bulk of the increase to higher energy usage during extreme weather, inflation-driven material costs and regulatory expenses.
He also explained that colder temperatures, especially when dropping below 32 degrees, significantly impact the efficiency of heat pumps, leading to substantial spikes in usage.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) questioned the accuracy of mailers warning residents of yet another impending rate hike. Beal responded that some of these campaigns are not necessarily organic, though he did not specify their origin.
Another major topic of discussion was the potential for Maryland to reintroduce energy production within the state. Del. Teresa Rilley (R-Cecil, Harford) is sponsoring legislation that would authorize investor-owned electric companies to construct and operate their own generating facilities, including natural gas and nuclear energy sources. The bill, which has gained support from several Republican delegates, is currently in the House Economic Matters Committee.
Beal acknowledged increasing energy generation within Maryland could help reduce costs for consumers. "The more generation we have, the more affordable that energy becomes," he said.
Eastern Shore Delegation Chair Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) emphasized the urgency of the issue, arguing that Maryland's energy struggles stem from a lack of local generation. Adams pointed to the shutdown of the Vienna power plant as an example of the state's declining capacity to produce its own electricity.
Beyond legislative measures, Delmarva Power representatives highlighted ongoing efforts to assist customers.
The company recently expanded its Saturday customer service hours and is hosting a workshop Wednesday, Feb. 12 from 3 to 7 p.m. the Kent Island Library to educate residents on conservation strategies, including weatherizing homes and optimizing thermostat settings. Beal encouraged customers to bring their bills to these sessions to receive personalized assistance.
Public frustration over rising bills has sparked grassroots activism, including the creation of the "Delmarva Power Victims" Facebook group, which has grown to 3,600 members, and a petition with approximately 10,000 signatures demanding action against what critics call excessive charges.
Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Wicomico, Worcester) requested a response from Delmarva Power regarding these movements and shared concerns from Delmarva Chicken Industries, which relies heavily on affordable electricity for poultry farming operations.
As lawmakers continue to evaluate solutions, Adams stressed the importance of addressing Maryland's energy generation shortfall. "Once you get past the budget, the number one issue we're going to have to deal with in session is electricity," Adams said. "We can't be silent on the matter of energy generation."

title: Easton councilmembers ask for more say in approving housing projects
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton councilmembers ask for more say in approving housing projects

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With 1,000 units in the town's residential pipeline, some Easton councilmembers are asking whether the Town Council should be granted a larger role in approving housing developments."Many people are pretty upset about the rate of growth we've been experiencing," Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said during a workshop Monday. "So I guess I'm just really trying to understand how we got here and why perhaps there aren't tighter checklists when things go in front of the Planning Commission."
According to numbers from Easton's planning and zoning department, 1,004 housing units are approved for construction by the town as of Feb. 3. While some are built or have permits, nearly 800 of those units are waiting to be permitted.
Most projects received a final thumbs up from the Planning Commission or Board of Zoning Appeals and never make it before the Town Council. The Town Council greenlit 369, or 36.8%, of the approved units.
Those 369 units make up three projects that went through a planned unit development application, requiring council permission. They are a 136-apartment complex on Elliott Road, a 200 single-family home development on Matthewstown Road and a 33-townhome project at the site of the former Safeway on North Washington Street.
Projects under the planned redevelopment overlay district are typically in industrial areas or older, dilapidated areas of town. They do not go in front of the council and instead seek final approval from the Planning Commission.
Recently, Silo Square, a 28-unit townhome development on Needwood Avenue, went through that process. Easton Crossing, a 123-unit mixed-income development at the site of former Perdue properties in town, is expected to be on the Planning Commission's Feb. 20 agenda.
Following a discussion regarding priority areas for annexation as the town aims to add to its housing stock, councilmembers chimed in on the projects that are proposed within town limits.
"I'm struggling with the fact that we're approving all of this stuff, and I feel like we're doing it sort of in a hole," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said. "And we're not taking everything into the full picture."
Miguel Salinas, Easton's planning and zoning director, said Curry's concerns were fair. He said given council feedback, the town should look at whether the planned redevelopment process is appropriate given the town's current needs.
"Do we still need that for the Town of Easton? A lot of the redevelopment areas have now redeveloped," said Salinas. "And certainly other ones could come forward in the future. But is that really needed?"
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery suggested the council eliminate the overlay district. In response, Salinas suggested the planning department could come back to the council with multiple options to consider.
"Any proposal we would provide you would include any potential changes to criteria the Planning Commission looks at," Salinas added.
At the end of the workshop, Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said there's not enough communication between the Planning Commission and the Town Council.
"It goes to the Planning Commission, and we get phone calls like no tomorrow about things that went through the Planning Commission that we as elected officials really had no oversight over," Davis said.
Salinas said the commission could look at doing a couple joint workshops each year as well as an annual report to the Town Council detailing housing pipeline data.

title: From crushes to banning cell phones — Maryland lawmakers propose new legislation covering range of issues
author: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com
content:
From crushes to banning cell phones — Maryland lawmakers propose new legislation covering range of issues

 February 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 654

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland state senators and delegates have introduced a variety of bills in the 2024 legislative session, addressing issues ranging from state symbols and education mandates to law enforcement policy and budget concerns.State Symbols and Utility RegulationsState Sen. Steve Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) has introduced Senate Bill 562, which would designate the original Maryland Orange Crush as the state cocktail. The bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester).
Hershey also sponsored Senate Bill 561, which, along with House Bill 227 sponsored by Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), would allow electric cooperatives to use unclaimed funds only to assist cooperative members or donate to nonprofit organizations, rather than treating them as abandoned property.
Additionally, Hershey introduced Senate Bill 355, seeking to delay the implementation of the Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program by two years.
Energy and Education LegislationDel. Jeff Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) is behind two bills on solar energy regulation: House Bill 739 (cross-filed as Senate Bill 478) and House Bill 742. One bill would prohibit the use of eminent domain for solar siting, while the other would return control over solar development to county governments.
Ghrist also introduced House Bill 736, which seeks to remove the mandate requiring local school systems to offer pre-kindergarten for three-year-olds. Another provision in the bill would increase state funding to help Kent County construct a new middle school.
On law enforcement, Ghrist is supporting a bill — potentially House Bill 122 — that would require the removal of unfounded complaints from police personnel files.
Nursing, Historic Preservation, and Cemetery ProtectionsDel. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) has proposed House Bill 602 (cross-filed as Senate Bill 407), directing the State Board of Nursing to negotiate reciprocity agreements with neighboring states for advanced practice nursing licensure. Another measure, House Bill 616 (cross-filed as Senate Bill 421), would extend the statute of limitations for crimes related to cemetery destruction and prohibit damaging cemetery landscaping. The bill is co-sponsored by Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico).
Hutchinson is also behind House Bill 760, which would establish a local appeals process for Maryland Historic Trust decisions.
Budget Deficit Shifts to CountiesGov. Wes Moore's proposed budget shifts some of the state's structural deficit onto county governments. Ghrist criticized the move, stating that counties did not contribute to the deficit but are now being forced to compensate for state overspending.
"For my district, $720,000 will be shifted to Caroline County on top of an additional $1.8 million more that the county will have to add to education under Kirwan mandates," Ghrist stated. He cited similar financial burdens for other Eastern Shore counties, including Cecil, Kent, and Queen Anne's.
"This will stifle economic growth because people will be sending more of their hard-earned money to the government rather than spending it in their local economies," Ghrist added.
Law Enforcement and Traffic StopsA controversial proposal, Senate Bill 292, has drawn strong opposition from law enforcement officials, including Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker. The bill would reclassify certain primary traffic offenses as secondary offenses, preventing law enforcement from stopping drivers solely for those violations.
"These minor traffic violations could actually lead to catching suspects that have committed serious felonies, recovering firearms, and stopping drug-related crimes," Baker said. A hearing on the bill is scheduled before the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee.
Other Bills of Local InterestHouse Bill 28, sponsored by Del. Josh Bouchat (R-Carroll, Frederick), proposes a constitutional amendment requiring all Maryland counties to adopt a charter government structure.
House Bill 278, also from Bouchat, would provide an income tax subtraction modification for enhanced agricultural management equipment to support sustainable farming practices.
House Bill 192, introduced by Del. Nino Mangione (R-Baltimore County), aims to curb student cell phone use in schools under the proposed "No Distracted Learning Act."
As these bills move through the legislature, local officials and residents will have the opportunity to voice their support or concerns during committee hearings and public forums.

title: Caroline County Commissioners discus multiple solar issues
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Commissioners discus multiple solar issues

 February 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 486
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their meeting Tuesday, The Caroline County Commissioners discussed a solar application issue that led to the county intervening.An application for a 3.0 milliwatt solar facility near Federalsburg, filed by Chaberton Solar Pahar LLC, does not meet requirements laid out by the county, County Attorney Stewart Barroll said at the meeting. The company has requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area where such developments are prohibited by the county, the commissioners said.
Barroll said the applicant had been informed by the county prior to submitting the application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, Barroll said.
But other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
Barroll said the Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
"So the department of natural resources came in and over said a project that we said wasn't complete was complete," Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said.
"We're getting steam rolled by the state," Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding added.
Next steps in the application process will include public hearings, which the commissioners have been invited to, Barroll said.
The Caroline County commissioners are concerned about the precedent this case may set for future solar applications, the commissioners said Tuesday.
"We have to draw the line somewhere," Porter said.
At the meeting, the commissioners also discussed another solar application in which they will be intervening.
An approximately 40-acre solar facility to be constructed on a farm near Greensboro does not meet a new setback regulation the county implemented, requiring a 200-foot setback from adjoining properties. The commissioners said they would not oppose the project, which meets all other county requirements, should that issue be remedied.
Along with the state's role in solar applications, the commissioner voiced anxieties about legislation making its way through the General Assembly.
The county also has concern about proposed Senate Bill 931, which would prohibit a county from enacting zoning laws or adopting regulations restricting or prohibiting the construction or operation of ground-mounted solar systems or facilities.
The county currently has a 2,000 acre moratorium in place for solar development, which is being neared but has not yet been met.
This proposed bill would put the county in another situation where legislation the county has enacted, including an acreage moratorium on solar development, could be overruled by state agencies, the commissioners said.
"We're gonna have to fight every application. We're gonna spend time and money fighting every application, and we're probably gonna get steam rolled every time, that's the way its looking," Breeding said.
