title: Ink spot: Tattoo shop coming to Delaware college town after decades-long prohibition
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Ink spot: Tattoo shop coming to Delaware college town after decades-long prohibition

 February 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 620
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The city of Newark, which is home to the University of Delaware, soon will be getting its first-ever tattoo shop.On Monday, city council granted a special-use permit to tattoo artist Brittnie Lopez, ending a decades-long prohibition on tattoo shops.
"I'm glad we're on the same page, and it's going to be a fun journey," Lopez said.
Lopez plans to move her business, B13 Tattoos, from Wilmington to a basement storefront at 170 E. Main St., the building that also houses Frolic, Oishii Ocean and Occupy Studio.
She said most of her clients are University of Delaware students, so moving the business to Newark makes sense.
"They can walk to their appointment if they wanted to; they don't have to schedule around their work schedule and get a ride and all that," Lopez said. "I'm trying to just be more convenient for everybody."
A Glasgow High School graduate, Lopez enjoys spending time on Main Street and patronizing the downtown businesses.
"I'm familiar with the area. I love the people," she said. "I mean, you can't beat a college town."
Lopez has been trying to relocate to Newark for several months, but first she needed city council to amend the zoning code.
On Monday, city council added body art establishments — a term that encompasses both tattoo and piercing shops — as an allowable use in certain commercial zoning districts.
Each body art establishment requires a special-use permit, meaning that the business owner needs permission from city council to open a tattoo or piercing shop. The permit can be denied or revoked if council determines that the business would be a detriment to the community.
The law requires that a body art establishment be located at least 300 feet from another body art establishment and at least 200 feet from an elementary, middle or high school.
Another requirement is that body art establishments must operate on an appointment-only basis to avoid the shops turning into a hangout spot and to eliminate spur-of-the-moment tattoo decisions.
Though some council members had expressed reservations about allowing tattoo shops during a previous discussion in November, both the zoning change and Lopez's special-use permit were approved 6-0 on Monday.
Lopez is currently renovating the Main Street shop and hopes to open in March.
She said her business has always operated on an appointment-only basis, which helps her customers feel comfortable. Most of her clients are women, and she works hard to make her shop a safe space.
"The traditional way of a tattoo shop, you walk in there and there's big, muscular men with needles and covered in tattoos, you know, the typical stereotype," she said. "Honestly, we're just girls. We just want something cute, something dainty, something to remember our college years by."
Attitudes toward tattoos are modernizing and for younger generations, they can be a form of therapy, Lopez said.
"I look at it as a meditation, a soothing getaway without booking a flight or getting on a cruise ship,"she said. "It's our mini vacation that we kind of just carry with us wherever we go."
Tattoos are a way of remembering something you're going through, or a way to distract yourself from it, she added.
"It's a different kind of pain, and it's a pain that we pay for, and we keep coming back," Lopez said. "It's kind of crazy, but we love it."
Lopez has been a tattoo artist for seven years.
"I'm covered in tattoos, and that's how I learned, by tattooing myself," she said. "Anything that I can reach on my body, I've tattooed."
Lopez specializes in small tattoos, often floral designs or handwriting.
"It's quick, easy, you're never in my shop longer than an hour, max," she said. "Tattoos are impulsive, and we want a whole bunch of them. So the small ones are easier for people that want a little getaway."

title: Former Cambridge elected officials, outstanding residents receive recognition
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Former Cambridge elected officials, outstanding residents receive recognition

 February 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — From Charles Cornish to Shirley Jackson, a number of impactful Cambridge residents were recognized during a Cambridge City Council meeting Feb. 10."I think it's important for us to acknowledge our local history here in Cambridge," Mayor Lajan Cephas said.
During the meeting, Cephas read a proclamation that makes the first Saturday of February Commission President Charles Cornish Day. Cornish served as a commissioner and commission president of the Cambridge City Council for decades, beginning in the 1940s. He was the first Black person to serve as commission president.
Cephas said she hopes Commission President Charles Cornish Day will be a day where the city can come together and reflect on its history.
"Because African American history is history," she said.
In celebration of Black History Month, Cornish and seven other Black former Cambridge elected officials were recognized with citations honoring them. The eight elected officials who received citations are:
Victoria Jackson-StanleyLa-Shon FosterGilbert CephasDonald SydnorEdward WatkinsOctavene SaundersHerbert St. ClairCharles Cornish
"Without leaders such as President Charles Cornish, there would be no me, there would be no Shay Sisco, there would be no Commission President Sputty Cephas," Lajan Cephas said. "So It's always important to keep in mind those who have paved the way, those who have showed us what excellent looks like."
A proclamation was also read to honor former Maryland Sen. Rich Colburn, who died on Dec. 27. Colburn — who served as a state delegate before representing Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot and Wicomico counties as a state senator — became the longest serving Republican senator in the Maryland Senate. He served as a senator for four terms.
Colburn, who was a member of the American Legion Post 91 in Cambridge, was known for his kindness and leadership, the proclamation read. Colburn's wife Alma Colburn accepted the proclamation during the meeting.
SHIRLEY JACKSON HONORARY STREET SIGNLater in the meeting, the commissioners unanimously approved an application to place an honorary street sign at the corner of Rigby Avenue and Stiles Circle.
The sign, which will have "Jackson Way" printed in white white lettering on a black background, will honor Shirley Jackson for her many years of service to the Cambridge community. The sign will not change the name of the street, but will be placed above the current signage, Commission President Sputty Cephas said.
Jackson, who died in 2022, volunteered with a number of local organizations and served as a trustee for the Nanticoke Historic Preservation Alliance. In her lifetime, she was recognized by the state multiple times for her service and was awarded the 2019 Gloria Richardson Award.
"Anyone that new Ms. Shirley knew that she embodied the gift of help," Sputty Cephas said during the meeting.

title: Greensboro suspends Zoom meetings after 'vulgar' meeting interruption Monday
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro suspends Zoom meetings after 'vulgar' meeting interruption Monday

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 322
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Greensboro's special meeting stream on Monday was cut short.The Zoom meeting was a victim of a "disturbing experience," which led the town to continue the meeting without the live stream.
"We were just having a normal meeting, and next thing we know, there's an interruption with vulgar racial language and pornographic video," Town Manager Tammy Kelledes said. "It was stopped within a minute or less than that."
After the meeting, the town put out a statement via Facebook stating all future Zoom meetings for the town would be suspended.
"Last night, during the Council meeting, an individual or individuals hijacked the Zoom feed. There is an active investigation to identify the individual(s) responsible for what appeared to be an intentional transmission of obscene materials over the internet," Town of Greensboro said in a statement.
"Council will take all necessary steps to prevent such incidents from happening in the future, including the suspension of all Zoom meetings," Town of Greensboro said in a statement."
The town later clarified that Zoom meetings would be suspended while the incident is investigated by the FBI, not indefinitely.
"The suspension is like a school suspension, Kelledes said. "It's not a permanent thing. It will be evaluated as the investigation goes forward and council is able to talk and decide what they want to do."
Greensboro will still be uploading the meeting minutes for residents to check and see what was discussed, the town said.
"They can always get a copy of the of the meeting minutes. There's certainly, there are plenty of people that attend that put the content out on social media," Kelledes said.
The town of Greensboro's plan is to have another form of video up after the investigation has been conducted and they receive recommendations on what software is good to use to conduct meetings without interruption.
"We're just trying to get through the investigation and see what the FBI tells us and what they recommend," Kelledes said.

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 EASTON — The National Weather Service recorded nine inches of snow in Easton on Wednesday, which was more than expected six to eight inches forecasted earlier this week.The weather service recorded 8.5 inches of snow in Denton and eight inches of snow in Cambridge.
As a result of heavy snow, conditions on roads throughout the Mid-Shore were expected to be bad. After having battled another large snowfall just a month prior, road crews and first responders were prepared.
Caroline, Talbot and Dorchester counties responded to the snow fast and were able to clear roads in a timely manner, allowing many government offices to open Wednesday.
"Our Public Works team was ready for the winter weather that hit Tuesday afternoon," Kathleen Freeman, Caroline County administrator, said. "Crews came in at 4 p.m., and with the rising temperatures, they quickly cleared the roads and made sure all county buildings were accessible."
"By 10 a.m. Wednesday, everything was set for a delayed start," she said. "I want to thank our road crews and all essential staff for their hard work in making this event go as smoothly as possible. Their quick response kept everything running with minimal disruption for our community."
Caroline County opened their offices at 10 a.m. Wednesday morning, as did Talbot County and the towns of Easton and Denton.
Talbot County could not be reached for comment, but the county decided to open up their offices at 10 a.m. Wednesday morning.
Dorchester County's offices were open during regular business hours Wednesday, though non-essential employees were given the option to work from home if they could, according to a Facebook post from the county government.
"We had a great night. Snow slacked up earlier than expected. It was great experience," Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones said. "Folks stayed off the road. It was good Mother Nature is helping us. The window was bigger (than with the last snow) to get everything. Emergency responders were great as well."
Schools decided to keep campuses closed Wednesday because of the snowfall, but several districts had students attend class virtually.
Talbot County Public Schools conducted its first virtual learning day since 2020, and district officials were pleased with the results, according to TCPS Directer of Communications Debbie Gardner.
"The feedback from school principals has been positive," Gardner said Wednesday afternoon. "Student attendance has been better than we anticipated, and our teachers have done a fantastic job."
Dorchester County Public Schools conducted a virtual learning day as well, but could not be reached for comment.
Caroline County Public Schools did not have students attend class virtually, but the district plans to open on time Thursday.

title: Centreville considers sidewalk repair and RV parking
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Centreville considers sidewalk repair and RV parking

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Noting trip hazards on town sidewalks, Public Works Supervisor Clifford "Kip" Matthews sought feedback from the Centreville Town Council in developing a sidewalk replacement program Feb 6.Precision Concrete Cutting preformed an evaluation on sidewalks at the northeast portion of town in 2021, as requested by previous council members to review the conditions and costs, Matthews said.
The assessment identified a total of 917 trip hazards with 845 that could be corrected by the contractor trimming misaligned joint areas, according to Matthews.
The estimated cost to fix all trip hazards is estimated at more than $234,000 and the estimated replacement cost to be more than $213,000, he said.
With the upcoming budget, Matthews sought the council to consider tentative questions such as where should priorities lay and how will the project be continually funded.
Looking to avoid a "squeaky wheel situation" in which only those who complain to town hall would receive fixes, council President Ashley Kaiser suggested a policy on how sidewalks repair is prioritized.
The council reached a consensus for the public works department to consider ways to triage repairs and provide a rough estimate of spending before the budget process is completed.
In other business, seeking to address unattended mobile homes parked on the street, Centreville Town Council presented the first reading for a proposed ordinance update Feb. 6.
The town's current ordinance regarding unattended trailers has faced frustrations in admonition and enforcing, and expansions aim to specifically addresses motor homes and occupiable RV trailers, according to council member Jim Beauchamp, an RV owner himself.
Situations have come up in which trailers were "subverting the zoning ordinance," he said, and the proposed ordinance will give more teeth for enforcement.
The current town code states the trailer must be attached to its beast of burden if parked on the street; while the new ordinance will not allow street parking at all.
The town attorney will consult on language of the proposed ordinance and a public hearing is anticipated for March 6.
It was also noted, the Queen Anne's County Chamber of Commerce recognized the Town of Centreville for 230 years of business.
The Centreville Town Council will next meet Feb 20. at 7 p.m.

title: 'Just not here': Solar project tests small town's growth plans
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'Just not here': Solar project tests small town's growth plans

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 334
 Words

 A proposed 30-acre solar facility is sparking concerns in Betterton, an Eastern Shore town of 287 residents, where local officials worry the project could hamper future development.Halo Betterton Solar LLC has submitted a nearly 300-page application for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity to the Maryland Public Service Commission, despite objections from town leadership.
"We're not opposed to alternative forms of energy, just not in Betterton," said council member Gerry Werner. "Especially not in the only area that could be zoned residential and commercial for our future expansion."
The project, planned for property owned by Schirmer Family Farms LLC along Route 292 and Howell Point Road, would be visible from all town entrances. Town officials have sent their concerns to the solar company and await a response.
The local fire company has also raised safety issues, noting the project would use land currently serving as overflow parking and an emergency helicopter landing area.
The Betterton project is one of seven solar facilities either pending approval or in pre-submission process in Kent County, as solar companies leverage Maryland state preemption laws that limit local control over such developments. The push aligns with Gov. Wes Moore's initiative to reduce greenhouse emissions 60% below 2006 levels by 2031.
In nearby Chestertown, officials faced similar challenges when the Public Service Commission approved a 245-acre solar system on Morgnec Road, despite opposition from both town and county governments.
"If there is well-expressed public sentiment against building this here, maybe the power company will cut their losses," Werner said. He is researching what rights, if any, the town has in the matter.
Meanwhile, Millington is further along in its solar facility process. A second public hearing is scheduled for Feb. 17 regarding the KE51 project, which would occupy part of a 199-acre property. That project, designated as a Community Solar Energy Generating System, would deliver power to subscribers via the Delmarva Power electric distribution grid.
The Public Service Commission maintains final authority over solar facility approvals, though it must consider local jurisdiction input in its decisions.

title: At Daysprings Townhomes, poor housing conditions persist
author: Konner Metz
content:
At Daysprings Townhomes, poor housing conditions persist

 February 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1351
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Phillip Gibson often walks around the complex where he lives, checking in on his neighbors at the Dayspring Townhomes. He's recognizable and trusted by neighbors, many of whom call him "Pappy."Last October, the retired maintenance worker walked around the complex and into some of his neighbors' units, pointing out what looked like mold above the shower of a second-floor bathroom.
He repeated one word that encapsulates how he and many others view the living conditions at the low-income complex: "Unacceptable."
"I've only been living out here for eight months," Gibson said in October. "This is what I'm seeing. This is crazy. This is crazy, and I've been a maintenance man for 40 years."
Gibson isn't alone, as other residents of the Caroline County-owned complex have voiced similar concerns.
During recent months, dialogue surrounding the 46-unit operation has picked up among housing and social activists, disgruntled tenants and Caroline County officials. Property management has sought to collect unpaid rents while many tenants point to poor housing conditions and unresponsive maintenance requests.
Owned by the county, the property is run by East Coast Property Management, a Delaware-based company. In November, the Dayspring Townhomes filed 23 complaints against residents for failure to pay rent.
Shore Legal Access and Maryland Legal Aid took on cases for residents that accepted their legal services. Some cases were dismissed, while others were ruled in favor of the landlord. A number of tenants agreed to rent payment agreements.
County officials say only around half of the units are currently occupied and collecting rent. Some of the vacated units have extensive damage stemming from evicted tenants, Caroline County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said at a Feb. 4 county meeting.
While the county explores the possibility of selling the property to a qualified nonprofit, some residents remain confused and frustrated with lacking maintenance and communication.
Gibson said he wants the units fixed up, and that at times, property management has been putting "a Band-Aid on a little sore" when it comes to addressing issues.
"I can't let these people live like this," he said.
LIVING CONDITIONS
The Dayspring Townhomes complex is located just outside Ridgely on School Street. The initial property was built in 1994 by Interfaith Housing Development, a former local nonprofit that worked with the county, according to Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter.
That nonprofit ceased operations a handful of years ago, leaving the low-income housing complex in the hands of its owners, Caroline County, and the contracted property management company, East Coast.
In October, Caroline County paid for First State Inspection Agency, based in Milford, Delaware, to perform unit-by-unit inspections.
Of the complex's 46 units, inspection records showed common damages in a number of units: cracked window surfaces, doors off their frames and damaged outlets or light switch covers. Some apartments had damaged or worn stairs.
None of the units had smoke detectors in the bedrooms, which Caroline County and property management remedied in the days after inspection.
Manizh Brown, a former tenant, lived at Dayspring for more than a year with her two children. In her townhome, an electrical outlet was faulty, closet doors were broken and the ceiling leaked where the second-floor bathtub sits.
"Everybody else got similar … problems. Especially this," Brown said while standing in her then-apartment, pointing to the leaks. "This is really getting me."
Brown said many of the issues with her townhome existed when she moved in. Aside from her floor, which she said was upgraded, Brown said there weren't sufficient improvements.
"The health situation right here, the water and everything else. F. F-minus," Brown said. "Ain't no way I should move in, and there's mold already on my window sill."
Caroline County officials have labeled the Dayspring Townhomes as high priority, facilitating the inspections last fall and consistently checking in with property management and the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development.
"We want those units to be in good shape," said Porter, the Caroline commissioner. During recent meetings, the county has focused on facilitating renovation of heavily damaged units.
Some residents hold concerns about physical safety, as well. A non-fatal shooting outside of the complex last August intensified those worries. The county purchased security cameras, which were placed at the front of the complex.
Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker has remained in contact with Bridge Maryland Inc., a Baltimore County nonprofit that's held meetings for residents to air concerns and is assisting tenants with the court process.
Some tenants and nearby homeowners participate in neighborhood association meetings, during which they discuss their concerns about violence, drug use and large parties in or outside of the Dayspring Townhomes.
In October, resident Trina Ewell said the shooting was still affecting her peace of mind, and her son's as well.
"You're just at your own risk," Ewell said. "And I do know that my son has increased with panic attacks because of the shooting."
PROPERTY MANAGEMENT
East Coast Property Management, which manages the Dayspring complex, has more than 50 rental properties across Delaware, Maryland and Virginia, according to its website.
Despite repeated attempts to reach the property manager or a company representative, East Coast Property Management did not respond to The Star Democrat's requests for an interview or comment.
Residents have raised concerns about a lack of communication with property management, the property manager and maintenance workers.
"We have not heard from anybody, letters, emails," Ewell said last fall.
Brown said in order to place maintenance requests, she called the "maintenance man" or the property manager, as there was no standard maintenance order procedure.
"You ain't got to do no type of papers, no work (order), just tell them," Brown said. Often, she considered doing some of the maintenance fixes herself.
Rachel Wolpert, a chief attorney at Maryland Legal Aid who has worked with landlord and tenant issues since 2008, says it's an "incredibly relationship-based business."
Wolpert acknowledged it's a difficult task to be a property manager at any apartment or multifamily complex. She notes, though, that clear communication and follow-through from property management are critical.
"I see successes when the on-site manager is accessible and responsive to tenants," Wolpert said. "And then you see real troubles where tenants feel like the on-site manager is not accessible, not responsive."
Recently, tenants were notified monthly rent rates would increase. Porter said since there are no rent subsidies, but also an income threshold tenants must be below, a tight window exists of those who qualify but can still meet rent payments.
Bridge Maryland Board of Directors President the Rev. Angelique Mason said in an interview that rent payments and fear of eviction both play a role in how outspoken residents feel they can be.
"We do know that some of them are not being vocal because they might be behind in their rent," Mason said. "They had this idea that they might be evicted if they speak up. And that's really why Bridge is being the voice for the people, because some of them do have fear of eviction."
WHAT'S NEXT?
While Caroline County owns the property, the option for that to change is up in the air.
"Our position at this point that we're going to express is the possibility of selling that property to a qualified nonprofit organization," Porter said at a November county meeting. "The question we need to have answered is the mortgage amount."
Porter calls it a "tough situation" because of that mortgage conundrum. The state has involvement with the property, he said, binding the county to have at least a portion of ownership and the apartments to be low-income in order for the mortgage to remain deferred.
As the county has been in consistent dialogue with Maryland Housing and Community Development, many tenants faced court proceedings at the end of 2024.
Bridge Maryland organizer Hannah Freeman, who has facilitated community meetings, assisted many tenants during the court process. She said while some owed thousands in rent, others owed less than property management alleged.
Freeman says she remains focused on helping those who need it most.
"There's people just out homes," Freeman said. " … These are people with kids, with legitimate complaints about management."
Ewell acknowledged that amid her concerns regarding safety and the complex's living conditions, there isn't always another option.
"You got to live somewhere," Ewell said. "Right now, during this time with everything, you have to. You have to live somewhere." 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Six months into the job, Cambridge city manager says he'r ready to tackle city's challenges
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Six months into the job, Cambridge city manager says he'r ready to tackle city's challenges

 February 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 624
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman likes a challenge."I've dealt with cities on the verge of bankruptcy and cities going into bankruptcy," he said.
Although Cambridge is not on the verge of bankruptcy, the city does face challenges when it comes to housing, communication and certain delayed projects, Steckman said, mentioning the Cambridge Harbor project and the old city hall renovation project.
"That's sat vacant now for almost 18 years," he said about the old city hall, "and the cost of the project has doubled in those 18 years."
Nearly six months into the job, Steckman is working with his team to tackle these issues, which he knows can't be solved in a day.
"It's a process," he said. "No community gets into facing their challenge in a year, and it takes years to address a community challenge."
Ten years from now, Steckman would like to see better housing for residents, general improvements made that the city can afford to maintain and the Cambridge Harbor project at or near completion.
When it comes to housing, Steckman said improvements are already being made, but it's going to take time.
"But I also think there are a lot of people that I have interacted with that are committed to that," he said. "And I would like to see stronger collaboration with the area organizations so we're all rowing in the same direction."
Collaboration is important to Steckman, although he acknowledges it's not always easy.
"I think the challenge in any community is sometimes there are personalities and people who may have felt excluded, people that might have been hurt," he said. "How do we speak with them and look at their conditions and address them. But in any community, there are some very strong personalities, and Cambridge is no different."
Steckman said it's not realistic to ask for everyone to "sing by the same song sheet."
"But how do we work better together?" he asked.
Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said Steckman has made an effort to work with the many different communities within Cambridge, from the Black community to the Hispanic community to the senior community to different neighborhoods.
"When you seek different perspectives, it always gives the best outcome," Cephas said. "Even myself as a Black woman. If I just go about my day every day from the perspective of a Black woman, I'm going to miss some things. So that's why it's always important to have a diverse staff, a diverse group of people that you can rely on to get information from."
Starting this Saturday, Feb. 15, Steckman will be at City Hall from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. one or two Saturdays per month to speak with any residents who aren't able to see him during the normal week day. Steckman has also made it easier for residents to come to City Hall by making it so they don't need to be buzzed in at the door. The city has also put in a railing and an automatic door opener for accessibility at City Hall.
"Because I try to maintain an open door policy," he said about the changes. "But I want to talk with people. ... I'm not a huge fan of just emails back and forth."
Born and raised in Baltimore, with experience serving on the Ocean City Council and a career spent managing cities as far away as Alaska, Steckman is no stranger to Maryland nor city management. In his free time, along with spending time with his wife and their two dogs, Steckman enjoys reading.
He said it's important to read about what's going on not only in his community, but in surrounding communities.
"We are not some little isolated community," he said. "And sometimes people in other communities have very good ideas that maybe we can export here or modify what they're doing."

title: Maryland considers shake-up in how judges are picked
author: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service
content:
Maryland considers shake-up in how judges are picked

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 1253
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland lawmakers are weighing two bills this year that would shake up how the state chooses circuit court judges.The proposals are at odds with one another. One bill aims to adjust the existing contested election process for circuit court judges by opening primaries to all Maryland voters. The other would eliminate contested circuit court elections altogether — a shift that would require a constitutional amendment.
The proposals represent two sides of a decades-long debate in the Maryland General Assembly about the value of contested circuit court elections.
Some members of Maryland's judiciary argue doing away with judicial elections entirely would shield judges from the ethical and practical challenges involved in competitive political campaigns.
"The job of a judge is, or at least should be, inherently apolitical," said Maryland Supreme Court Chief Justice Matthew J. Fader.
Others stand by Maryland's approach to filling circuit court benches, arguing that contested elections are a valuable opportunity for voters to shape their judiciary.
Circuit court judges are currently the only Maryland court to run in contested elections. All other state courts fill their benches with judges appointed by the governor, giving voters a say in whether those judges hold their seats in retention elections every 10 years. But the judges run unopposed and, at least according to some of the state's leading legal experts, no Maryland judge has been ousted in a retention election in living memory.
While the governor appoints judges to fill vacancies on circuit courts, the state constitution requires those judges stand for reelection every 15 years — elections in which they, unlike any other Maryland judge, can face a challenger.
The conversation about the system's merits has restarted among Maryland lawmakers, with Fader and other prominent Maryland legal figures backing a bill that would change circuit courts' process for filling benches to match the rest of Maryland courts.
The proposal arose from a work group formed by the Maryland Judicial Conference three years ago to review the issue. The work group released its final report — which argued that Maryland should move away from contested circuit court elections — last year.
"We believe that this is the best solution to maintain public trust and confidence in the court and in its ability to have judges who are fully qualified to take office in all cases," Fader told members of the House Judiciary Committee in a preliminary hearing on the bill.
Proponents of the bill assert that contested elections for circuit court positions open the bench to candidates who are unqualified for the role.
"Our system allows individuals with little to no judicial experience to challenge sitting judges," said Prince George's County Circuit Court Judge Cheri Simpkins. That means some judges who were initially appointed to their seat "must run against opponents who only meet the minimum qualifications of being a licensed person residing in the county for five years and paying a nominal filing fee," she added.
Maryland State Bar Association President Raphael Santini pointed to former Prince George's County Circuit Court Judge April Ademiluyi, who won her seat in a contested election in 2020 and whose "egregious" violations of judicial ethics prompted the Maryland Supreme Court to remove her from the bench in 2024.
Appointed judges, Santini told Capital News Service, have passed through a rigorous vetting process run by a judicial nominating commission and more than a dozen committees within the state's bar association. That vetting is done by fellow attorneys from a variety of legal fields who are well-equipped to review a candidate's legal and personal record, he added.
Elizabeth Hewlett, an attorney in Prince George's County and supporter of the proposal, said that voter participation in circuit court races is vastly lower than participation in better-publicized races, in large part because judges' schedules and ethics code leave them poorly positioned to campaign.
Campaigning in competitive elections, said Kelly Hughes Iverson, co-chair of the Maryland State Bar Association's laws committee, can place judges in ethically compromising positions.
"When the courts are fundraising, the appearance of sitting judges accepting campaign donations from contributors, which includes attorneys and litigants who have cases before them, undermines the public trust in an independent judiciary, and may discourage candidates from applying for the bench at all," Iverson said.
Attorneys are more engaged in judicial elections than the general public, Santini said, and more likely to contribute to a judge's campaign.
Backers also argue that judges, who routinely receive threats from those impacted by their decisions, put their safety at risk when campaigning for reelection.
But not all members of the judiciary are on board with the proposed changes.
"All it does is remove any opportunity for anyone to challenge the person that is named by the governor," said Carroll County Circuit Court Judge Maria Oesterreicher, who won her seat in a 2018 contested election and served on the judicial workgroup that put forward the bill.
Critics like Oesterreicher argue while circuit court elections are imperfect, they are also a rare opportunity for voters to play a larger role in shaping Maryland's judiciary.
If lawmakers are concerned about the qualifications of judicial candidates, she argued, they could require candidates to go through the same vetting process as applicants for appointed seats.
"That's an easy solution, but we've jumped right to the extreme," Oesterreicher said. "I think taking the rights out of the voters' hands is not the right way to fix the problem of judges campaigning if that's the problem that people want to fix."
Skeptics asserted that the appointment process is far from perfect, in large part because it relies on a relatively small group of attorneys to review and recommend candidates. Those attorneys, critics argue, may choose favorites based on politics or personal relationships rather than qualifications.
"It is clubby," said Claudia Barber, who ran unsuccessfully for an Anne Arundel Circuit Court seat last year. "It is also political … which is why, oftentimes, the best is not always chosen."
"I ran against someone who was the third member of the same law firm to be on the bench that only has four seats," Oesterreicher said of her 2018 campaign. The appointment process can favor well-connected attorneys over those with equal or greater qualifications, she argued.
Del. Robin Grammer Jr., a Republican representing Baltimore County, offered harsher criticisms. He argued that the proposal to end contested circuit court elections would primarily benefit the judges, not the public.
"Elections are hard," he told CNS. "You don't get to exempt yourself out of the system and have, frankly, what ends up being a lifetime appointment just because you think it's hard … When is the last time a judge has lost a retention election, like, ever?"
Grammer also contended that judges could avoid ethical concerns about campaign contributions from attorneys by finding alternative fundraising options.
Lawmakers skeptical of eliminating contested circuit court elections have another option this year: expanding voters' input in circuit court primaries.
Del. Chao Wu, a Democrat representing Howard and Montgomery County, is the sponsor of a bill that would replace Maryland's closed partisan primaries for circuit court elections with open, nonpartisan primaries. Closed primaries leave unaffiliated voters — who make up nearly a quarter of the state's electorate — without a voice in key local races, Wu said.
"I think a lot of unaffiliated voters feel they're really disenfranchised," Wu told CNS. "They're not able to vote in (primaries for) one of the most important positions in the state."
Wu's bill received no pushback from members of the House Judiciary Committee, but lawmakers have yet to act on either bill.
If the proposal to end contested circuit court elections passes this session, the question will appear on Maryland voters' ballots in November 2026.

title: Caroline County Commissioners will grapple with shortfall to balance budget
author: Konner Metz
content:
Caroline County Commissioners will grapple with shortfall to balance budget

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 509
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — A draft of the fiscal year 2026 budget presented Tuesday shows Caroline County could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.Caroline County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox presented projected operating requests and revenues for the upcoming fiscal year during Tuesday's Caroline County Commissioners meeting.
Fox noted while the entire budget is fluid, the current requests total $79.7 million and the revenues total $78.8 million, up from the fiscal year 2024 operating budget, which was balanced at $72.3 million.
"This is where we're at currently today," Fox said. "Obviously there's a lot of items still not set in stone."
Some of those fluid items include income tax cuts proposed by Gov. Wes Moore and potential cuts to The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education funding initiative.
Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter expressed concerns about expected cost shifts from the state to local governments.
"I don't even know where to start on this because every indication we have is that it's worse than this," Porter said about finding a way to balance the budget. "The state shifts are going to be worse than this. I think at this point, I'm going to be looking at this as a zero budget."
Porter said he views it as a lack of leadership in Annapolis. Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding concurred.
"Nobody's going to tell the solar lobby or the teachers' union no," Breeding said.
"All your work that you've done is great, but I'm not sure at this point where we go," Porter told Fox.
In terms of revenue, Fox noted there are increases projected in income and property taxes, respectively, though Moore's plan to cut income taxes for many Marylanders may reduce that number if his proposals are passed by legislators.
Breeding said income tax reduction for Caroline County may be $1.4 million. He added he's not looking to raise the county's property tax rate, since increased property values are already hiking up those taxes.
"People cannot sustain a property tax increase, not with the way the assessments have gone through the roof," Breeding said. " … I'm not entertaining raising property taxes."
Breeding said given the tight fiscal situation, the commissioners will be pushing county department heads on why requested funds are absolutely necessary.
"It's not that we enjoy asking the hard questions or scrutinizing everything," Breeding said. " … But they need to be prepared for tough questions because I think we're going to have to scrutinize everything."
Fox presented a list of capital requests to the commissioners Tuesday. Those projects came from departments and agencies including Chesapeake College, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Public Works Department, among others.
The requests totaled just over $11 million. Fox said around $7.3 million is currently available for capital projects, leaving a $3.7 million gap.
"Do know that this is fluid, so if there needs to be more money transferred out of operating to fund capital and vice versa … you can do so," Fox said.
Porter asked how this year's capital requests compare to previous years.
"It's high," Fox said. "This is probably the largest capital budget request we've had."

title: Legislators, local officials differ on unhoused individuals bill
author: Konner Metz
content:
Legislators, local officials differ on unhoused individuals bill

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A bill filed in Annapolis to enshrine rights for homeless individuals is drawing differing opinions from advocates and local officials.House Bill 487, and its paired Senate Bill 484, would protect the ability of homeless individuals to partake in "life-sustaining activities" such as sleeping, eating or drinking, in public places so long as traffic is not obstructed.
If passed, any civil or criminal punishment against an unhoused individual who is on public land without an "adequate alternative indoor" space would be considered cruel and unusual punishment.
According to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's most recent data, Maryland's homeless population in 2023 was 5,865 individuals, both sheltered and unsheltered.
Del. Bernice Mireku North (D-Montgomery), the bill's sponsor, and other advocates say the proposed legislation comes in response to a Supreme Court decision last June that ruled it was not cruel and unusual punishment for local governments to civilly and criminally penalize homeless people for setting up encampments on public land.
Mireku-North wrote in a statement to The Star Democrat that the proposed bill has "brought to light the heart-led efforts" of local governments to support unhoused individuals. An emphasis of the bill is to prevent immediate arrests, she said.
"At a minimum, we are asking law enforcement to prioritize inquiring whether an alternative indoor space exists for unhoused people engaging in life-sustaining activities before resorting to arrest," Mireku-North wrote.
The delegate said legislators are "committed" to working with local officials and stakeholders on the bill.
Allie Post, director of development and communications for The Women's Law Center of Maryland, said the bill would be a measure in which the state "(stands) up for folks proactively" following the June Supreme Court ruling.
"Especially for survivors (of domestic violence) and survivors of color, homelessness is often a price of leaving an abuser," Post said. "And folks who have less financial means and less flexibility in those means are really put between a rock and a hard place, and this is an opportunity for Maryland to step up and start taking seriously the homelessness problem that we have."
While advocates say it's a needed step forward in the path to address Maryland's homelessness crisis, some Easton and Talbot County officials say the bill is endangering the efforts already being taken.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and the Sheriff's Office released a video on Facebook last month depicting what they believe a potential encounter could look like with a homeless individual if the bill is passed.
"If these were to pass, we could have homeless encampments in Idlewild Park, (the) courthouse," Gamble said in a separate video the department shared. " … You literally could set up a tent on the 50-yard-line at Easton High School before an Easton football game and call it your home, and we would not be able to move those people."
Gamble said the homelessness issue is serious in Talbot County and that he's not against addressing it. However, he believes the bill as written will strip away authority of locally elected officials.
"They will not be able to follow the zoning laws that they've put into place to make downtown Easton the place it is, or downtown St. Michaels or downtown Oxford to be those nice places that people want to come to visit and spend their hard-earned money," Gamble said in an interview. "They will have absolutely no control over it."
Easton Mayor Megan Cook addressed the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee in a Feb. 5 letter opposing the bill.
Cook wrote that the bill "would supersede local ordinance and policies that have been carefully crafted to address the needs of both unhoused individuals and the broader community."
"By prohibiting local and state officials from enforcing reasonable regulations on the use of public spaces, the bill could lead to unintended consequences that compromise public safety, hinder economic development, and create significant enforcement challenges," Cook wrote.
In her letter, Cook asked legislators to instead focus on policies that would provide funding for housing assistance, mental health and job programs.
"Our community is committed to addressing homelessness with dignity and care—through outreach, support services, and housing initiatives—while also ensuring that public spaces remain accessible and safe for all," Cook wrote.

title: Demolition begins as developers wait for Easton Crossing project approval
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Demolition begins as developers wait for Easton Crossing project approval

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 442
 Words

 EASTON — Demolition of the abandoned silos and storage buildings on Brookletts Avenue is underway.The tearing down of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation is one step in The Arc Central Chesapeake Region's plan to build Easton Crossing, a mixed-use development, on about 6.29 acres between Brookletts Avenue and South Street.
Ross Benincasa, who is senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said the demolition will take six months. He said some of the material from the silos will be salvaged for potential future use.
Although demolition has begun, the project still requires site plan approval from the Easton Planning Commission. It is scheduled to go before the Planning Commission on Thursday. Following site plan approval, the project will need standard grading and building permits.
Easton resident Maury Schlesinger was walking his dog Monday when he noticed demolition was underway. Although he has some concerns with future plans for the site, Schlesinger said he thinks the demolition is "appropriate."
"Something has to happen there," he said.
According to the draft site plan for Easton Crossing, if approved, the development would create 123 multi-family units, including 29 affordable apartments priced below the market rate. It would also bring parking, stormwater management and landscaping to the property.
The property would have six buildings, with some buildings that include commercial spaces. The first building, which would have 15 units, is expected to open in December 2027 if the plan is approved.
Benincasa said project plans "emphasize public green spaces."
"We want the community as well as our tenants to enjoy the space, which is why nearly 30% of the property will be open public space," he said.
According to Planning Commission documents, town staff would like the developers to address scale and consistency concerns with one of the proposed buildings.
Schlesinger also has concerns with that building. He said it would bring too much density to one area of the property.
"I think it needs to be relooked at," he said.
Schlesinger brought up concerns with traffic and the need for traffic improvements.
"I'm not opposed to a redevelopment project on that site, and I think that there's some really good stuff they're trying to do here," he said. "It just could be moved from being a good project to a really great project that the town could be really proud of and could show off as good, small-town urban redevelopment."
Benincasa said community feedback has been helpful. He said feedback helped the developers define what types of units are wanted in the area as well as determine which materials are "more reflective" of the town's historic architecture.
Schlesinger said he hopes the Planning Commission "does the right thing."

title: Easton OKs outdoor party at Hummingbird Inn for Pride Festival weekend
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton OKs outdoor party at Hummingbird Inn for Pride Festival weekend

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 627
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town Council approved its first extension of Easton's new noise ordinance, granting the Hummingbird Inn permission to host an outdoor dance party the night after the Delmarva Pride Festival this summer.A zoning certificate was passed by councilmembers in a 3-1 vote during a Monday meeting. Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry was absent from the meeting.
The exception will allow the Hummingbird Inn to host a party June 14 until 11:30 p.m., a 90-minute extension of the town's normal limit for outdoor music.
The 10 p.m. cutoff was established last July following resident concerns of music at night. The council instituted a noise ordinance, which required businesses or groups seek special approval to play amplified outdoor music past 10 p.m.
Eric Levinson, owner of the Hummingbird Inn, said he was happy and relieved when the council approved the inn's zoning certificate.
"What I appreciated was the fact that they didn't just assume it was going to be a problem and deny it," Levinson said in an interview, "and that they said, 'Let's see how it goes. And then if there's a problem, then we'll deal with it at that time.'"
Before Monday's Town Council meeting, Levinson gained signatures from surrounding neighbors in support of the extended dance party. Last year, around 70 people attended. Easton police noted no complaints were made.
Levinson expects 100 to 120 people at the event this year. The later end time will allow for a better atmosphere, he said.
"The problem was at that time of year it doesn't really get dark until later, so we had people hanging around and stuff, but nobody was actually doing anything until it was dark," Levinson said of 2024's party. "It just didn't set the right mood."
Monday, councilmembers thanked Levinson for reaching out to neighbors well in advance. However, Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery voted against the extension.
Montgomery said approving the request would set a "very dangerous precedent," and that there are many other one-time events that could seek similar exemptions.
"I don't see how to differentiate this request for a special exemption from one that might come from the Tidewater Inn if they have a couple with 100 guests, a man and woman who are being married and they want to have Christian gospel music until 11:30 at night," Montgomery said. "I think we would have to approve that request equally well."
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who voted in favor, acknowledged Montgomery's concerns as valid. But he said the dance party being an annual event versus a weekly one made a difference in his opinion.
"I was going to give them the benefit of the doubt with the idea that if there are complaints … then I'm fine with not approving it in the future," Abbatiello added.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said he's not "overly concerned," though this approval will set a precedent and that the town will be monitoring if complaints are made.
Levinson said Town Council President Frank Gunsallus helped the business navigate the request for the extension, a first for the town as well. Gunsallus made the motion for its approval Monday.
"Given everything that you've done to go through this the right way and do your due diligence, and the fact that this is a once-a-year thing, I think that it is completely acceptable," Gunsallus said.
Considering tense discussions and split votes surrounding the Delmarva Pride Festival and its place in Easton in recent years, Levinson says he's glad the town is following through on its promises to be both inclusive and neighborly.
"It is good to see that they're following that, standing by that, and putting their own personal preferences or opinions aside," Levinson said. "Because that's the way it should be. It's not based on what they like or dislike. It's what's good for the community."

title: ESLC talks land values at Dorchester County Council meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
ESLC talks land values at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 608
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — When it comes to acreage and land value, Dorchester County is expected to be one of the most affected counties by sea level rise and storm surge in the year 2100, according to the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy.During a Dorchester County Council meeting Feb. 18, Eastern Shore Land Conservancy Land Use and Policy Director Owen Bailey presented data on land value throughout the Eastern Shore. Bailey said the data was acquired with the help of Urban3.
The land trust estimates that an average of three feet of sea level rise in 2100 would mean the loss of 270,000 acres of the Eastern Shore and $2 billion in property tax values.
"And then when you add in storm surge, then that really puts into perspective the financial distress that our communities are going to face in the future with the loss of properties and property tax revenues," Bailey said.
After Bailey showed a map that accounted for storm surge in 2100, County Council President Lenny Pfeffer pointed out that more than half of Dorchester County's land is projected to be gone.
Bailey said Cambridge alone is projected to lose 280 acres and $63 million in value by 2100.
Throughout his presentation, Bailey advocated for concentrated development on the Shore to increase property value. At the same time, he spoke about the importance of maintaining the value that could be loss to sea level rise.
Bailey said the efficiency of land use can be measured by looking at value per acre.
"You take the appraised value of each parcel and you divide it by how many acres it sits on," he said.
When the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy applied this to the Eastern Shore, it noticed historic downtowns are "much more productive than the more suburban, car-focused development" that has been popular since the 1950s. This means that those downtowns, which often are more vulnerable to sea level rise, bring in more property tax revenue per acre than more sprawling areas of the Eastern Shore.
Bailey said that before the Bay Bridge was built in 1952, only 10,000 acres of land — valued at approximately $560,000 per acre — had been developed on the Shore. An additional 163,000 has been developed at less than half of that value since.
With the additional developed land, there has been a need for more sprawling infrastructure, he said.
"So we've built all this infrastructure," Bailey said. "But we haven't really built the value to help us with the maintenance of that infrastructure, which is why a lot of our jurisdictions, pretty much all of our jurisdictions, are struggling with how to keep up with that kind of maintenance."
Bailey said many historic communities on the Shore, which bring more value per acre, are built on waterfronts, meaning sea level rise will most likely affect them.
"So we're encouraging every town to think about how are you going to account for that," he said. "How can you either move that property, protect it or replace that value somewhere else in our community?"
Along with concentrating development, Bailey recommended the county look at zoning restricting the county from allowing value to grow.
"This is something we're encouraging every jurisdiction to take a look at," he said. "It's not our job to tell you what to do. We just want to provide the data and perspective. ... Use your land wisely."
At the end of the presentation Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer asked if the land trust had any recommendations specific to Dorchester County zoning ordinances.
Bailey said they have been focusing on municipalities, looking at zoning in historic districts.
"And how can we ease up on that zoning just to allow that historic pattern to continue," he said.

title: Planning Commission approves majority of 123-unit Easton Crossing development
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning Commission approves majority of 123-unit Easton Crossing development

 February 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A mixed-use project on Brookletts Avenue at the site of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation received a stamp of approval, though not a full one.The Easton Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve 67 of the 123 units planned for Easton Crossing, a joint commercial and residential development. But Building 409, the project's largest structure, and the 56 units that come along with it are still under consideration.
Commission members and residents alike expressed concerns about the five-story building that includes around 10,000 square feet of retail space. Developers from The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, the project's developer, agreed to work on alternative options for the unapproved building and return to the commission at a future date.
Largely, the commission applauded developers for their advanced outreach to the community, as well as what they called an attractive project aimed at addressing Easton's lack of affordable housing.
"I love the project," commission chair Philip Toussaint said. "I think the positive aspects of it far outweigh any negative aspects. We have to take that into account when we're making a decision."
Toussaint joined vice chair Michael Ports, William Ryall and Victoria McAndrews in approving the project with the exception of Building 409. Thomas Klein was the sole vote against, citing his concerns that the plan's 217 off-street parking spots won't suffice once the units are occupied and commercial tenants move in.
The proposal noted 49 on-street parking spaces along Brookletts Avenue are mostly unused right now and would provide additional parking once renters and businesses move into Easton Crossing.
Klein said only 217 dedicated spaces for a 229-bedroom development did not seem sufficient, particularly if the backup plan is parking on Brookletts.
"If people from the development start to go and park in those areas, the tenants that live there now are not going to have any place to park," Klein said.
Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of Chesapeake Community Development, presented the site plan at Thursday's meeting. It calls for 30% of the rental units to be affordably priced, with others at workforce and market-rate levels.
Demolition of the Perdue grain bins and storage buildings currently on the lot began this month. Apartments are expected to be available beginning in 2027.
Speaking to the commission Thursday, Benincasa said the nonprofit developers felt a "necessary duty" to make a dent in Easton's affordable housing crisis with the infill project.
"We really felt kind of a need to make sure that if this was going to be developed, that we thought of it more inclusively," Benincasa said, "and more geared around making sure there was housing provided for all income levels, including people with disabilities."
BLENDING INWhile many complimented the project's cohesion with the intersecting Rails to Trails, worries centered around the fact that the structures don't integrate into the neighboring historic community.
Talbot County Council Member Lynn Mielke, speaking for herself and not the council, said the project is "incompatible" and its architecture ignores the nearby residential buildings.
Toussaint pushed Benincasa on if it was appropriate for the project to face away from The Hill, one of the first free African American neighborhoods in the country. The commission chair said that's been a significant source of public input.
"It appears to me that you've turned your back on the existing community, The Hill district," Toussaint said. "And you focus on Rails to Trails, and did a wonderful job of that."
Benincasa said The Arc doesn't own a lot of land in The Hill community to be able to integrate with it and that he disagrees with sentiments that the project doesn't fit into the surrounding fabric.
"We are not necessarily in that community here, and I would go as far to say as I think that doing duplexes here or mimicking that in some way would kind of really negatively offset what we could do in terms of usable units," Benincasa said. "It's never been a serious consideration."

title: Tensions rise as Cambridge City Council discusses HR position
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Tensions rise as Cambridge City Council discusses HR position

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A motion to adopt a job description for the addition of a human resource generalist position to City of Cambridge staff resulted in significant discussion and caused some tension at a Cambridge City Council meeting Feb. 24.During the meeting, City Manager Glenn Steckman recommended creating the additional staff position. He said there is currently only one employee in the department who has "a tremendous amount of responsibility under her job title."
Steckman said that the city advertised for the position in house and currently has a candidate within city staff. The position would require a budget amendment and could be discussed further at an upcoming meeting, he said.
Commission President Sputty Cephas said he would like to see the process started sooner rather than later and made a motion to adopt a job description for the role.
The motion was ultimately voted down, with Cephas voting for it, Commissioner Shay Lewis-Sisco abstaining from the vote and the three remaining commissioners voting against the motion.
During discussion, Lewis-Sisco said she had concerns with the city's hiring process. At the end of the meeting she said she abstained from the vote not because she doesn't understand why the council needed to take an action when the city seems to have started the hiring process.
Commissioner Brian Roche, who voted against the motion, said he didn't think the city's vision moving forward was "articulated well." He said he thinks the city needs a more comprehensive view of how human resources should function and should look for ways to set the director of administrative services up for better success.
Commissioner Frank Stout said he voted against the motion because he wasn't prepared to make a decision. He said his vote was not because he was opposed to the idea.
"I was just a little taken back, I think, for something that does require a budget amendment of this nature," he said.
During discussion, Steckman said the budget amendment would only be for three and a half months of salary and said he expects the city will have a "substantial" surplus this fiscal year.
Cephas, who said the request had been five years in the making, said by voting no, a commissioner is saying they are against the idea. He called for the commissioners to display more support of city departments.
"If (city staff) presents something to us, we have a responsibility to support them as long as it makes sense," he said. "And to not support this tonight, yeah, that's a problem."
As commissioners made comments on the issue at the end of the meeting, Steckman interjected to say his intention was to introduce the position. He said he was planning on bringing a formal resolution to a later meeting.
"A little discussion kind of got a little out of control tonight," he said. "There is a process that I have, and we will continue that process forward."
Mayor Lajan Cephas cut discussion short, saying it was already approaching 8:46 p.m. and talking about the issue "over and over again" wasn't getting the council anywhere. When Commissioner Frank Stout tried to talk, she said she had closed discussion and the commissioners would need to take a vote.
"It's getting late, right?" Cephas said. "If this fails and you have additional questions, you can make an appointment with the city manager and go to the city manager's office."
Before the meeting was adjourned, Lajan Cephas asked that everyone be patient as the new group of commissioners settles in and finds its stride. The commissioners were sworn into their seats in January. Two of the five commissioners have no prior experience on the council, and one commissioner, Stout, served as a Cambridge commissioner from 2008 through 2012.

title: Caroline County holds first FY26 budget workshop
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County holds first FY26 budget workshop

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 480
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners held their fiscal year 2026 budget roundtable with all internal and external county agencies.While agencies need more money for salary raises and equipment repairs and replacements, the commissioners are facing tight budget constraints.
At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting last week, the draft FY 2026 budget presented showed Caroline County could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.
Caroline County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox presented projected operating requests and revenues for the upcoming fiscal year during the last week's meeting.
Fox acknowledged while the entire budget is fluid, the current requests total $79.7 million and the revenues total $78.8 million, up from the fiscal year 2024 operating budget, which was balanced at $72.3 million.
Some of those fluid items include income tax cuts proposed by Gov. Wes Moore and potential cuts to The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education funding initiative.
The County Commissioners are concerned that the Blueprint cuts will leave the county in a bad financial predicament.
"There is no leadership at the top. There no leadership in the state," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said Tuesday. "We don't have anyone who is willing to stand up and say this Blueprint policy is a mistake."
On Tuesday, all internal and external county agencies presented their FY26 budget requests.
"We just want to take input from from all the agencies that are asking here straight from them," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "Learn what their priorities are ... to help us educate ourselves and make informed decisions on what they need."
The majority of the agencies experienced some of the same issues. Their fiscal year budgets were rising for multiple reasons.
Employee pay, overtime, and general equipment and technology updates were needed for many agencies.
"One of biggest challenges is hiring and retaining employees. It's getting increasingly difficult for us," Executive Director of Caroline County Public Library Jonah Owens said. "Queen Anne's County typically offers salaries 20 to 25% above ours, Anne Arundel County sometimes 50 to 100% higher salaries than what we offer for similar positions. We have become a farm team, as have all our agencies have."
For many agencies, every five to 10 years, equipment needs upgrades. Some upgrades fall on this fiscal year. Others will come in the following years.
But facing a budget shortfall, the commissioners are aware of potential cuts they will have to make and how honoring these requests from agencies will be difficult.
"We can't go out and and find any more money," Breeding said. "Our tax rates are as high, I think, as as we feel comfortable having them. I don't want to entertain any rate increases.
"I think the only thing we can do is search for efficiencies inside our existing budget and make sure we spend it as efficiently as we can, and prioritize spending in the areas that actually need additional funding."
Star Democrat Reporter Konner Metz contributed to this report.

 DENTON — On Del. "Right now, the event venues would have to hire a alcohol catering company," Breeding said, "which would come in and cater the event essentially. We don't have anybody that I'm aware of, or we don't have many in-county businesses that provide that service, so this would be an opportunity to allow local businesses to fill that that role, give them another revenue stream to help make their business ventures viable and more profitable."

title: Oxford residents share thoughts on who should be allowed to vote in town elections
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford residents share thoughts on who should be allowed to vote in town elections

 February 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 731
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — At a Commissioners of Oxford public hearing Tuesday evening, it all boiled down to the question of who should have the right to vote in town elections.The public hearing was held for a resolution that would amend the town's charter to clarify a person must register with the Talbot County Board of Elections to qualify as a voter in the town. This means a resident would not be able to vote in Oxford town elections if they aren't registered with the county board.
The commissioners opted not to vote on the resolution during the meeting.
"Listening to this conversation, it seems like we're putting the cart before the horse," Resident Warren Davis said during the public hearing. "What we really want to do is figure out who we want to vote in our elections."
Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said registering with the Talbot County Board of Elections means an Oxford resident is declaring their home in Oxford as their domicile, or primary residence. She said that when a person registers in Talbot County, they are removed from any voting registry they may have been on elsewhere.
Currently, the town charter states a person should register in the town office. The charter says it is the duty of Oxford's Election Board to keep registration lists up to date.
When it comes to eligibility, the charter states a person is able to vote if they are a U.S. citizen, are at least 18 and have resided in the town for at least 30 days prior to any town election.
At the outset of the public hearing, Ryan said the commissioners could choose to take a different path than the resolution presented.
Commissioner Katrina Greer brought up her concern that the list of registered voters in Talbot County is not always updated.
"As residents in a very small town, I know who lives here, I know who died this year," she said. "And so it's much easier for our own board of elections to clean up those voter logs."
Residents who spoke at the public hearing brought up scenarios and shared thoughts on who should and shouldn't be able to vote in town elections.
After confirming Oxford commissioners serve all proprietors and renters in town, Dan Kordell said anyone who owns or rents property in town should have a say in who is serving them.
"It's about representation," he said.
Jim Wilcox asked the commissioners to focus on who should vote based on "who has skin in the game." He said property owners and people with leases for more than 30 days should be able to vote in town elections.
"I would say somebody who has maybe a six-month lease," he said. "Something that shows a substantial term commitment to Oxford rather than just landing here for 30 days."
Warren Davis brought up that there are multiple residents in town with more than one residence. He included himself in the category, saying he usually goes to Maine in the summer.
"Should I be allowed to vote in Oxford because I'm not here for 30 days before the election?" he asked.
Multiple residents spoke to the issue of whether residents away at college should be able to vote in town elections. David Donovan said he doesn't think these students should be able to vote in town elections.
"They don't have any skin in the game," he said. "They don't have any intention to move back here. ... So I don't think those people should be allowed to vote here."
Chris Maynard said that could be considered disenfranchisement.
"We should keep in mind that 18-year-olds, we're referring to them as children, but they're really adults," she said, later adding, "It's not that the parents drive them over to the voting place and tell them what to do."
Donovan said he has an alternative to the town's proposed resolution. He proposed the town instead amend the voting eligibility section in the charter to say that voters should be physically present in their Oxford residence 30 days prior to the election unless they are absent due to vacation or circumstances beyond their control.
He said residents absent from town for those 30 days due to "voluntary enrollment in any education program" should not be considered eligible to vote.
Donovan said the town should add an application for absentee voting that requires absentee voters to affirm they are eligible to vote.
After the public hearing, the commissioners agreed to schedule a work session to discuss the issue further.

title: Oxford hires full-time town clerk, seeks treasurer
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford hires full-time town clerk, seeks treasurer

 February 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 362
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has a new full-time employee.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Holly Wahl announced the addition of Ashley Samonisky as town clerk. Wahl said Samonisky has worked with the town on a temporary basis since November, "a time when the town was significantly backlogged on permit applications," Wahl said.
"And she's done a great job of cleaning up that process and helping support those on the Planning Commission and the Historic Commission," she said. "And she's also worked very closely with me as a town manager in terms of working through the town's operational processes."
Samonisky will now serve in the town clerk position full time.
"In this capacity, Ashley will continue to coordinate permit applications, she will continue to provide support to the Historic Commission and the Planning Commission, and she will now also provide support to the commissioners," Wahl said.
In the announcement, Wahl said Samonisky has more than 10 years of experience at the federal, state and local level — as well as with private and nonprofit agencies — in continuity of operations, hazard mitigation, emergency management, stakeholder engagement, communications, social media and public outreach.
"So we're very, very happy to have Ashley," Wahl said.
With the move to hire Samonisky as town clerk, the town is separating the previous position of clerk-treasurer in two. Later in the meeting, the commissioners voted unanimously to post a job description for the role of town treasurer.
During a meeting on Feb. 19, Commission President Norm Bell said Vickie Sharp, who had been the town's clerk-treasurer since April, was "no longer employed" by the town "due to violations of some policies."
Sharp told the Star Democrat on Feb. 20 that she did not wish to comment, and Wahl told the Star Democrat the same day that she could not provide more information about why the position was open.
Tuesday, Wahl called the commissioners' move to separate the clerk and treasurer functions "really important."
"They are two very separate functions," she said. "And so we need to be sure that we're tracking our record keeping properly. And Ashley will do that as the clerk in support of all the governmental functions of the town."
