title: 'A milestone': Demolition of Talbot County Business Center a big step for Easton Airport
author: Konner Metz
content:
'A milestone': Demolition of Talbot County Business Center a big step for Easton Airport

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Words

 EASTON — Wednesday morning, the Town of Easton granted Reynolds Excavating Inc. a demolition permit to begin work on the former Talbot County Business Center.Later that day, demolition had already begun.
The clearing of the property is part of the second phase of Easton Airport's airfield modernization project, a long-term effort to improve the airport's safety and operations.
Micah Risher, Easton Airport's manager, said the demolition is a major step in the modernization efforts, which began in 2006.
"This is a milestone," Risher said. "We've been waiting for 20 years to get to this point."
Once cleared, the site will become a runway protection zone, meant to improve safety in case of an aircraft crash or extended landing.
The business center, previously a Black & Decker facility, saw its tenants move out in 2023 and 2024, all of whom successfully relocated.
Thursday, significant work on the building's southwest end nearest to Glebe Road was underway. The building's exterior and roof were in the process of being torn down.
Risher noted that an environmental report was completed to ensure demolition is handled properly. Testing and mitigation measures were taken to abide by state and federal regulations.
Risher said the site will mostly be made up of open, green space, along with airfield lighting.
"It's a big environmental improvement project," Risher said.
Additionally, scrap materials from the building will be reused, Risher said. Asphalt and concrete will be crushed and repurposed for the new airfield, while aluminum will be recycled by Reynolds Excavating.
Easton Airport will continue operations during demolition. The building is expected to be mostly demolished later this spring, with site work and recycling continuing throughout the year.
Risher expressed excitement that the demolition is underway. He said it's a step forward in swapping one economic driver, the former business center, for a new one, the runway zone and overall airfield upgrade.
"The reality is it's being transformed," Risher said.

 In the struggle between historic sidewalks in Port Deposit and the Americans with Disabilities Act, the ADA wins, according to the Maryland State Highway Administration.SHA has two projects in progress in Port Deposit; one to remediate flooding and the second to make stretches of sidewalk handicapped accessible. title: Federal layoffs come home to Oxford
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Federal layoffs come home to Oxford

 March 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 926
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Marine scientist Sierra Hildebrandt had about 30 minutes on Feb. 27 before her government computer and access to her email were revoked at the Cooperative Oxford Laboratory.Hildebrandt had just learned that she'd been terminated from her dream job with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
"I cried," she said about learning the news.
Hildebrandt was one of two NOAA scientists fired from the Oxford lab that day. The two represented a 15% reduction of the lab's total workforce, both state and federal.
"We're already a small lab," Hildebrandt said. She said with the two terminations, there are only two remaining federal employees and one federal government contractor at the Oxford lab who do field work.
Hildebrandt and environmental scientist Jake Shaner, who also was fired from his position at the Oxford lab, were not alone. At least 800 employees across NOAA have lost their jobs since Feb. 27, part of the Trump administration's move to reduce the size of the government. According to the Associated Press, President Donald Trump has called the size of the federal government "bloated."
In an email to The Star Democrat, NOAA public affairs specialist Jasmine Blackwell said she could not discuss "internal personnel and management matters." She said NOAA remains dedicated to its mission of "providing timely information, research and resources that serve the American public and ensure our nation's environmental and economic resilience."
THE IMPACT ON OXFORDAlthough NOAA is known for gathering weather data, the agency does more than that.
At the Cooperative Oxford Laboratory, scientists monitor water quality, tides and the presence of vibrio, which can cause fatal food poisonings, in oyster populations. The lab — which is Oxford's largest employer — works on an array of projects, from oyster restoration to evaluating nature-based solutions like living shorelines.
At the time that Hildebrandt and Shaner were let go, they were implementing a water quality monitoring station in Oxford with another scientist. Shaner said the monitoring station gathers tide data, helping Oxford determine when flooding is likely.
"So that falls off immediately," Shaner said, explaining that leaving one scientist to maintain the station alone would be difficult.
Hildebrandt and Shaner were the only two scientists at the lab working with the Town of Oxford to evaluate the Strand Beach project, a project to create a living shoreline on Oxford's waterfront. Hildebrandt said their job was to understand how the already implemented shoreline was providing coastal protection and additional ecosystem benefits.
Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said the loss of Shaner and Hildebrandt from the lab is having an impact on the completion of that project. She said the lab is engrained in the town and surrounding areas.
"When we have the largest employer in town facing terminations, I think that directly will absolutely impact the town from an economic standpoint," Wahl said. "As well as just the economic standpoint of having that innovation and research directly accessible to the town to continue to make improvements to protect property, to protect vital critical resources that we're providing to citizens."
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said this situation shows Oxford and the Eastern Shore are not isolated from the rest of the country.
"We're really starting to grapple with what do we do longer term so that we can survive as sea levels rise (and) storm water levels rise," he said.
Bell said the work Hildebrandt and Shaner were doing in Oxford was helping the town address those water-related concerns.
THE BIG PICTUREShaner had been working at the Cooperative Oxford Laboratory — which is utilized by NOAA, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and the U.S. Coast Guard — since 2016. Although Shaner had about nine years under his belt at the lab, eight of them were spent as a state employee. At the time of his termination, Shaner was considered a probationary federal employee.
St. Michaels resident and deep-sea ecologist Andrew Thaler works with NOAA scientists and uses the agency's data. He said that when employees are hired, they are put on a period of probation before they can receive tenure. He said the probation period repeats when someone switches jobs within the federal government.
"So if you get promoted to a management level position, your probation block starts over," he said. "So many people were fired who were senior in the administration."
At the U.S. Department of Agriculture, more than 5,000 probationary employees were temporarily reinstated to their positions via a federal board ruling Wednesday after the employees had been terminated in February. The ruling was determined based on "reasonable grounds" to believe the agency "committed a prohibited personnel practice."
According to the Congressional Research Service, factors that should be taken into account with reductions in force include tenure of employment, military preference, length of service and efficiency or performance ratings. The service states agencies are "generally required" to provide written notice to affected employees 60 days in advance of the date of release.
Hildebrandt said she understands layoffs occur, but she said her and Shaner were well-performing employees.
"I think I wouldn't be as heartbroken if this was done the correct way," she said. "And if both of us were not performing very well in our jobs."
WHAT'S NEXT?"A NOAA job is a dream job for a lot of marine scientists," Thaler said.
Both Hildebrandt and Shaner have filled out forms to volunteer at the lab so they can continue to work on the projects they had been working on in a volunteer capacity.
Shaner said the terminations at the Oxford lab are a resource lost for the community.
"You're losing skilled people that live here, care about the Eastern Shore and the Chesapeake Bay and want to fix problems," he said.

title: After heated meeting, Talbot County retains DEI statement by 3-2 vote
author: Konner Metz
content:
After heated meeting, Talbot County retains DEI statement by 3-2 vote

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 995
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During a charged meeting that saw council members exchange remarks and three members of the public asked to leave for speaking out of turn, the Talbot County Council rejected a resolution to repeal the county's DEI statement.Although tensions eased by the meeting's end Tuesday night, council members had heated back-and-forth before voting 3-2 against the resolution sponsored by Dave Stepp.
Council President Chuck Callahan joined Stepp in favoring the resolution. Vice President Pete Lesher and council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke opposed.
Stepp contends the resolution will protect Talbot County's federal funding after a Jan. 20 executive order from the Trump administration to end all diversity, equity and inclusion policies and programs in the federal government.
Stepp said he's heard from many county employees that want the diversity statement repealed. He called it a "political stunt" for the measure to be voted down.
"You simply choose to go against the oath of office you took when you took this office," Stepp said of the three council members who voted against.
Haythe, Lesher and Mielke contested Stepp's claims.
"We really were not going to go there tonight because all five of us have agreed to sit here and tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth," Haythe said. "And in some of those statements, the truth was not told."
She said she hasn't heard from any county employees who want the statement removed.
"What we are not going to do as this council is stand here and accept the lies that are pushed down from the federal government to our local community," Haythe said. "We are not doing that."
The failed resolution would have repealed two 2020 resolutions — the first developed the county's diversity statement found in the employee handbook, and the second implemented an annual report of diversity training offered to staff.
Stepp said that an email to the council from Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble, a Republican, stated a grant for police work in Trappe is at risk due to the county's DEI statement.
Lesher disagreed, stating that Trump's executive order "does not deprive federal funds for our airport modernization, for rural development or for policing."
"Those funds are not in peril," Lesher said.
"So you're saying the sheriff is lying?" Stepp responded.
Prior to the vote, Haythe added her support for diversity training, saying it helps people identify their underlying biases, including herself.
"Council members should go through diversity training as well," Haythe said. "We all should, because there is bias. There's bias on this council. I've received it."
SPLIT PUBLIC
At the council's Feb. 26 meeting during which the matter was tabled, more than 100 residents attended, most speaking against Stepp's resolution. Tuesday, public opinion was split.
At one point, Stepp motioned to move public comment so it occurred before the council's vote. Callahan seconded, but the rest of the council disagreed.
Some residents expressed displeasure the vote would be held before their comments. Stepp said "the three council members didn't want those to speak in the audience."
Haythe responded, pointing out that the council did not move up public comment at its last meeting.
"We had public comment in the same order at our last meeting, and we did not move anything to the front," Haythe said.
Many residents opposing DEI attended Tuesday's meeting. Lori Stepp, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee and Dave Stepp's wife, said the DEI statement including equity and inclusion doesn't line up with the original 2020 resolution that only mentioned diversity in its text.
"That's not what the original council voted on," she said in an interview. "So unfortunately, I'm not sure how the equity and inclusion piece got thrown in there for the county employees."
Easton resident Brandi Whiting said DEI is "here for a reason" and that she's seen it make a positive impact in her experiences hiring for different companies.
"If you want to sell your morals for money, you go right ahead," Whiting said during public comment. "But I'm glad that at least three of our council people did not."
Resident Shari Wilcoxon called out Haythe, Lesher and Mielke for voting against Stepp's resolution.
"If we do indeed lose these funds that you have now put in jeopardy, it is on the three of you ... who rolled the dice for all Talbot County citizens," Wilcoxon said.
Following her comments, Wilcoxon and another resident expressed disagreement from their seats with Haythe while Callahan and a third resident went back and forth. "You've been a problem all night," Callahan told the third resident.
After Callahan initially requested only the third resident leave the room, Haythe said to him that the others who spoke from their seats out of turn should be asked to leave as well.
Callahan then asked the other two residents to leave. While deputies escorted the third resident out, the other two left on their own.
MOVING ON
Rhetoric toned down once public comment closed, as council members ensured they will continue to work together in the future.
"I don't think any minds got changed, but I appreciate the public engagement," Lesher said.
Stepp said he still wished public comment was moved up. "But I thank those who did stick around to make sure that those comments, you were able to get them out," he said.
Haythe and Callahan said the council will move on as a unified group.
"Once we take a vote, we're done and we move on. That's it," Haythe said. "And we still continue to be friends."
Callahan thanked county staff for supporting the council during the controversial last two weeks and expressed appreciation for fellow council members.
"I really appreciate you putting your thoughts together," Callahan told Stepp. "It takes a lot of bravery to do that. It really, really does. And Keasha, the same way with you.
"But at the end of the day, it's over, we've made a decision and we all move on."
This story has been updated to clarify that three residents were asked to leave during the public comment portion of the meeting for speaking out of turn. Police escorted one person while the other two left on their own.

title: Cambridge shares progress on Douglas Street houses
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge shares progress on Douglas Street houses

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 592
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Those walking down Douglas Street this summer might see new homeowners sitting on spacious porches, looking out onto Cornish Park as kids run around and play.A city project to build four homes on Douglas Street in Cambridge's historic Pine Street neighborhood has been underway since September. Cambridge Housing Program Manager Ed Crosby said the city expects construction on all four houses to be complete by June 30.
These custom houses will be energy efficient and have features that make them feel like home, from oak staircases to crown molding.
"We wanted folks to take a sense of pride," Crosby said.
This project is one way the city is improving its housing stock, uplifting the community and fostering a culture where residents want to stay in Cambridge.
The houses on Douglas Street will be sold at 80% of area median income to people who qualify based on income and standards by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. Crosby said prospective buyers will have to complete homebuyer education training.
Three of the four homes getting built on Douglas Street will have three bedrooms. The fourth home will have four bedrooms and follow accessibility guidelines from the Americans with Disabilities Act, including having a ramp.
In all of the houses, features include electric fireplaces and washer and dryer units. Each house will have backyard space with a shed.
Crosby said the homes will be listed in the low $200,000s, with the most expensive home possibly reaching $250,000 in price. In February, the median selling price for homes in Cambridge was $276,000, according to Realtor.com.
On March 4, those working on the houses were putting up drywall. Gregory Beard, the general contractor for the project, said the next steps will be painting, putting in flooring, installing trim and bringing in subcontractors to install fixtures, hardware and plumbing.
"Things are coming together great," Beard said. "Fantastic build. It's a fun project."
Crosby hopes the city will have the property listed online this month.
"There's an excitement brewing that we're just ready to move forward with this," he said.
Although the properties could be purchased by people who don't live in Cambridge, Crosby said the city has made an "intentional effort" to market the homes to city residents before listing them. He said there are at least 30 Cambridge residents who have shown interest in the homes and have applied to buy one.
In late February, the city gave tours to show the construction progress to the Cambridge City Council and the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development. Crosby said the tours gave attendees an opportunity to learn more about the project from the developer, architect, engineers and contractors.
During the tours, some commissioners gave the city ideas on how to ensure the homes are not flipped or purchased by landlords to turn into rentals, Crosby said.
"You can actually write that into the deed where there's a requirement that the city could get what is called the right of first sale," he said. "So if it comes to a point and the homeowner's interested in selling, the city would have the opportunity to actually purchase the property back and then keep it under that 80% of AMI program so that we can continue to have it available as affordable housing."
After the city finishes building the Douglas Street houses, it plans to build at least 10 more homes on Chesapeake Court and School House Lane. Crosby said this project will help inform the city on how to go about building more houses.
"And from this blueprint, we'll learn how the next set of homes will be," he said.

title: Emergency cannabis bill discussed at Caroline commissioners meeting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Emergency cannabis bill discussed at Caroline commissioners meeting

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 522
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held the first reading of an emergency cannabis legislative bill and the introduction of permit zoning on property legislative bill at Tuesday's meeting.The emergency cannabis bill is proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
The adjustments are being made as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 bill that established zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates that cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches.
At last week's meeting, Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter suggested a zoning map be created to show the zoning locations for the proposed emergency cannabis bill.
While Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds is still working on the zoning map, Porter made a suggestion on increasing the distance for dispensaries from schools.
"My concern is the dispensaries, I don't think 500 feet is enough," Porter said. "Im particularly concerned about the schools."
The 500 feet distance of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches is mandated by the state.
While dispensaries will only be allowed to be located in C1 and C2 commercial zoning districts, some schools in Caroline County are close to commercial zoning districts.
"I don't think we will ever run into a situation where a dispensary is that close to a school," County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said, "but to Commissioner Porter's point, 500 feet is not enough."
The county could be at legal liability if they decide to mandate that the buffer between cannabis businesses and schools will be bigger.
"So what will happen if you enact an ordinance with a greater distance and someone applies within the 500 feet and they are denied, it would be an appeal by the judge to rule in favor of the applicant," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said. "Or somebody can file suit against the county stating their ordinance is invalid."
The officials will discuss all avenues of the proposed bills and make some revisions before making a final decision.
The county commissioners also discussed a new section to denials of a zoning legislative bill. The new section will allow the Department of Planning and Codes to deny applications if an applicant is not within code or zoning compliance of the county on that same property.
"If you had a violation on your property, let's say you put a pool in without a permit and it's unresolved," Batts said, "now you come in and you want to seek a permit for something else, we would not grant that permit until you updated or gotten your proper permits for the other structure."
If a resident comes into fix a violation, the county will permit to allow the resolution of the violation.
Also covered in the proposed bill if an applicant has multiple properties they can apply for permits on one property and not be denied because of a violation on another property.
Both proposed bills will move on for the first and second reading.

title: Rally held in Cambridge demanding Harris hold town hall

 CAMBRIDGE — Chants of "Where is Andy?" and "AWOL Andy" sounded outside the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina Thursday evening as people lined the sidewalks with signs.Cambridge Indivisible — a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders — held a rally outside the entrance of the Hyatt to demand Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md. 1st) hold a town hall.
The rally was held before Harris was set to take the stage at the Hyatt as the keynote speaker for the 79th annual Dorchester Chamber of Commerce Business Meeting and Dinner.
Cambridge Indivisible Founder and Chair Michelle Fowle said Harris' constituents "just want answers."
"Andy Harris refuses to meet with us for a town hall," she said. "He's locked us out of his office. He won't talk to us."
Myra Orme Frost, who held a sign on the sidewalk as cars honked their horns, said her concern is that Harris' agenda is more aligned with Department of Government Efficiency head Elon Musk than with his constituents.
Those at the rally voiced concerns over veterans affairs and mass firings of federal workers.
Charles Breitschwerdt, a Republican, had not participated in political rallies before this year. He expressed concerns with the information coming from the Trump administration, calling it lies.
This is not the first rally that has been held on the Mid-Shore this month to criticize Harris. Last week, hundreds lined Dover and Harrison streets in Easton protesting Harris and the Trump administration outside a fundraiser hosted by Harris at the Tidewater Inn.
Fowle said Harris' "inaction" will only increase their action.
"They're just waiting for us to throw up our hands and say there's nothing that we can do," she said. "But there's a lot that we can do. And it's to show up, it's to call him out, it's to speak truth to power. And we are not going to stop until all of this ends."
Before the rally, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said the Cambridge Police Department was aware of plans for the rally and were in communication with the Hyatt. Todd said the department wanted to ensure everyone's safety, including those attending the rally and those attending the Dorchester Chamber event.
Speaking to members of the media after the chamber dinner, Harris said he didn't believe many of the people at the rally were his constituents. He said he believed the protesters were paid and brought in by buses.
Harris said he will be holding a virtual town hall on March 25 so he can communicate with constituents from all over his district.
"If these protesters want to call in, if they want to get on my town hall, I will answer that question on my town hall," he said. "But I'm not going to hold a town hall for 100 people when I could hold a town hall and reach out to 5,000 people who don't have to leave their homes, get bused in by some entity paying for that bus."

title: Commissioners of Oxford hear plans for portable pump stations
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford hear plans for portable pump stations

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — In an effort to address flooding caused by rainy day events, Oxford is looking into setting up portable stormwater pump stations across town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, engineer Wayne Newton presented plans to install four temporary, portable pump stations in three locations in town: Two stations near the causeway, one station at Bank Street and one station at Mill Street.
Newton is the president of Messick & Associates, an engineering firm the town has a contract with. He said he expects the pump stations will relieve moderate flooding, which he defined as anything less than storm surge.
"A storm surge comes in, it comes over the bulkhead, it comes over the causeway, that's not what we're planning for here," he said. "We're just planning for rainy day events."
Oxford Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman, who has been working closely with Newton, said the pumps will allow the town to drain water faster.
"It's the plan of moving the water where it's not going to take us days, it'll be hours," Ozman said.
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said the town is trying to take a step back, look at what it would like to see in the future and determine what is needed today in order to build toward that.
"So this is more of a holistic viewpoint than what we've been looking at previously," he said.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the portable pump stations are more flexible than permanent pump stations in the ground.
"You can take our solution and move it to where the problem is instead of having a problem and saying, 'Oh, well we've got this really neat pump station eight blocks away,'" he said.
Along with placing portable pump stations in the low-lying areas Newton identified, Newton also outlined plans to address the existing drain system on Mill Street that runs through the marina. He said he would like to re-grade and rebuild some of the drain system so water drains toward the water tower and the pump station can be moved to that area.
"We'd prefer (the pump station) to be down there," Newton said about the area where the water tower is. "There's more room for it down there."
Newton said over the next month, his office plans to work on designs and cost estimates for the project that he can bring back to the commissioners for review. He said his goal is to have the project complete by the end of 2025.
The project will be funded using American Rescue Plan Act funds.
Ozman considers this project to be laying the foundation when it comes to addressing flooding issues. He said the town can hone in on these three areas first, then address flooding in other areas.
"We're trying to do the best that we can with the money that's available at the time without having to spend millions on something that can't be moved, can't be touched, can't be retrofitted," he said.

Caroline public hearing revivals bigger shortfall and property tax talk

 DENTON — On Tuesday evening, the Caroline County Commissioners held the first public hearing for the county's fiscal year 2026 budget.At the workshop, agencies presented their needs for more money for salary raises and equipment repairs and replacements. But the commissioners are facing tight budget constraints.
"We just want to take input from from all the agencies that are asking here straight from them," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "Learn what their priorities are ... to help us educate ourselves and make informed decisions on what they need."
At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting in February, the draft FY 2026 budget presented showed the county could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.
After the first FY26 budget roundtable, that number has increased. The county is expected to bring in $77 million in revenue, while the proposed fiscal year budget is projected to be $79 million, leaving a $2 million shortfall.
"We gotta find $2 million in cuts somewhere basically," Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "We still have tough decisions to make, well evaluate everyone's testimony and well do what we think is best."
While majority of the public comment Tuesday was thanking the commissioners for their work, the commissioners offered some insight on property tax rates.
"I don't think the property tax rate has been raised in nine years," Larry Porter Caroline County Commissioners Vice President said. "For the people who say my taxes go up every year, your taxes go up because of the assessment, we don't control assessments."
"The only number we control up here is the property tax rate and we have held the line for nine years, and my guess is we will hold it this year."
Residents may still have to pay more in property taxes regardless if the rate remains the same because if the assessment values have risen the rate is applied to those values.
While the property tax rate may not go up the commissioners understand that many changes must be made to keep up with the states requirements for the counties.
"Sooner or later I don't know if its reasonable to think planning, budgeting and looking at cost is gonna be enough, if the state keeps shoving expenses and cost down the line to us," Porter said.

title: Commissioners of Oxford table voting resolution
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford table voting resolution

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Although at the start of a Commissioners of Oxford discussion Tuesday Commission President Norm Bell recommended the commissioners vote that evening on a resolution to clarify the town's voting registration requirements, the commissioners tabled the resolution in a two to one vote."In order to get this right, I think we need more time," Commissioner Katrina Greer said. "I think it would be better to do nothing and write some rules for the election committee, which we can do without a charter change."
The now tabled resolution would amend the town's charter to clarify a person must register with the Talbot County Board of Elections to qualify as a voter in the town. This means a resident would not be able to vote in Oxford town elections if they aren't registered with the county board.
Before the vote was taken, Bell expressed concern that if the resolution is not voted on at the meeting, it could be delayed to the point where, if the resolution is passed, it is not in effect for the town's upcoming election in June when Commissioner Tom Costigan's term is set to expire.
But Bell, who ultimately voted in favor of tabling the resolution, acknowledged the commissioners should not rush into making amendments to the charter regarding voting.
At a public hearing for the resolution Feb. 25, residents shared thoughts on who should and shouldn't be considered eligible to vote in town elections. The discussion, which opened the doors to potential additional charter amendments, led commissioners to hold a work session March 5.
Greer said the work session brought a lot of input, and she said there were still a lot of questions.
"I do not want to pass this in a rush tonight," she said Tuesday.
Costigan, the only commissioner to vote against tabling the resolution, said he felt the resolution addressed a "flaw" in the charter's verbiage.
"All that it did was recognize that the Talbot County system was the most logical way to assure that people are eligible and can vote," he said, adding that the concerns around who is eligible to vote would need to be addressed in another section of the charter.
After the resolution was tabled, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan suggested the commissioners write rules for the Oxford Election Board regarding registration, absentee ballots and poll watching.
"The last election we had a livestream for individuals to watch," she said. "If you're going to follow that process again, we should have something established."
Greer said they should hold a work session on the matter, and Bell agreed that a work session should be scheduled.

 ELKTON — The Elkton Colored School Museum project has been put on hold after the Maryland Board of Architects issued a $20,000 fine against Dale Glenwood Green, the project's architect, for falsely representing himself as a licensed architect for at least 17 years. The board said that his claims have led to Green stealing opportunities from qualified architects, such as the museum project.The ECS Museum project had been working in partnership with an architecture firm that Green was a part of, during which partnership Green gave a tour of the ECS building to Gov. Moore during his visit last year to Cecil County. Due to the fine against Green and his lack of licensing, the project has been put on hold.
"We are on pause right now because we can't move forward until we find out what is going to be done architecturally for the benefit of the group and the benefit of putting the building in place where it's supposed to be," said Town of Elkton Commissioner Charles Givens, an ECS alumni who has been heavily involved in the museum project. "We're dependent upon grants and other finances to move forward…we aren't going to get funds until the mess that we have right now is cleared up."
Green is known for working to preserve the oldest Black communities in Maryland, and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore appointed him to the board of directors for the Maryland African American Museum Corporation.
Green also claimed to have a Ph.D in architecture and historic preservation from the University of Missouri, but the school has no record of his enrollment according to an article by the Baltimore Banner.
Until being fired recently, Green had taught architecture and historic preservation at Morgan State University since 2008, where he earned his undergraduate degree in architecture. Baltimore architect Jerryn McCray was teaching as an adjunct professor at Morgan State when he met Green as an undergraduate nearly 20 years ago.
"He was the best salesman I think I've ever met, but his work was just awful," McCray said.
McCray acted as a mentor for Green in one class, but said "his ego would never allow him to see himself as a mentee. He took the position as if he was already a professional. He dressed the part, wore a bow tie, the suit, the whole get up that he still carries."
Shortly after graduating from Morgan State, Green started a company and listed himself as the principal project architect on the website. McCray recalled confronting him for marketing himself as an architect, and proceeded to file a complaint with the state against Green in 2008 when the website went unchanged.
However, the state did not have a record of the initial complaint and nothing came of it, till now.
McCray said that Green has continued to cause problems for himself and other architects in the community since then.
"He's persisted to find different ways to promote himself as an architect," McCray said. "It had gotten to the point where it was affecting my company, the local economy, my family, my relationships…I had to make it stop."
According to McCray, because of the way Green presented himself and played the part, he became connected with a lot of people in the industry, which took away opportunities from legitimately licensed architects like McCray.
"It's been more of an obstacle dealing with Dale, in terms of my business, than it's been being Black and being an architect," McCray said.
McCray recalled telling several architects who partnered with Green that he is not licensed or trustworthy.
"They look at me like I'm the issue, and it's ruined those relationships for 20 years, and I've persisted to speak the truth. I know that Dale is a con artist," McCray said.
McCray filed a second complaint when a national architectural firm was reviewing Green's application for a renovation project and upon reviewing his credentials, found mismatched fonts and a license that seemed fraudulent. The project manager reached out to McCray, who proceeded to look up Green's license number, which was associated with a woman living in Georgia. After speaking with her, both filed complaints which led to a state investigation on Green.
The investigation into Green began in the spring of 2023, culminating in a final order issued by the board in December of 2024. The board increased the fine from $15,000 to $20,000, insisting on the maximum penalty for each violation because of Green's "incessant bad faith" which persisted for at least 17 years.
The Maryland Board of Architects determined that Green did in fact forge a license to practice architecture, and even created a fake email chain blaming one of his former students for the fraudulent license.
The fine is the largest issued by the Maryland Board of Architects since 2012.
A main focus of the case was on the testimony of Stanford Britt, the president of Sulton Campbell Britt & Associates, that he had hired Green to manage the firm's website and help with technological aspects of the company, a firm at which Green had been claiming to be a vice president and partner.
Britt testified that he never promoted Green to a partner of the firm. Currently, the firm website lists Green as vice president and partner, with Britt the only other listed employee. Britt said that his architecture license had expired three years prior to the trial and he was now working as a teacher in Virginia.
According to Givens, Green reached out to the Elkton Colored School Museum team to set up a meeting and discuss next steps in the upcoming weeks.
"It's thrown a wrench in the plan because he was one of the architects for the company and right now we are at a stand still," Givens said.
Givens compared the situation to buying a Mercedes that breaks down on your way home, unexpected and disappointing.
Green and his firm did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Harris speaks to Dorchester Chamber after rally calling for town hall
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Harris speaks to Dorchester Chamber after rally calling for town hall

 March 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 748
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Hours after a rally was held questioning Rep. Andy Harris' (R-Md. 1st) loyalty to his constituents, Harris told Dorchester Chamber of Commerce members inside the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina that his office is here to help them."We can make your business run easier," he said during his keynote speech for the chamber's 79th annual business meeting and dinner. "We can work through the bureaucracy. Please get in touch with my office. We're more than happy to help you."
Earlier that evening, protesters lined the sidewalks of U.S. Route 50 outside the Hyatt, calling on Harris to hold a town hall and questioning whether Harris' allegiance is to his constituents or to Elon Musk and the Trump administration. The rally was organized by Cambridge Indivisible, a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders.
Speaking to members of the media after the chamber dinner, Harris said he didn't believe many of the people at the rally were his constituents.
"They're brought in by buses," he said. "I don't know where those buses come from. And we know that the national Indivisibles are involved. So we believe that a lot of those people aren't even constituents."
Harris said he heard from a Washington, D.C., organization's leader "who knows what's going on" that people at the rally were getting paid to be there. He said he would not name who told him that.
"This is astroturf," he said. "This is not grassroots."
Cambridge Indivisible Founder and Chair Michelle Fowle said many of those at the rally were her neighbors who live in Cambridge.
"He's just a liar," she said about Harris.
Harris said he will be holding a virtual town hall on March 25 so he can communicate with constituents from all over his district.
"If these protesters want to call in, if they want to get on my town hall, I will answer that question on my town hall," he said. "But I'm not going to hold a town hall for 100 people when I could hold a town hall and reach out to 5,000 people who don't have to leave their homes, get bused in by some entity paying for that bus."
Harris said he is "laser focused" on working for his constituents and advancing the Trump administration's agenda.
"Who also won the district with high numbers," he said about President Donald Trump (R) getting elected in November.
In Dorchester County, Trump won 55.99% of the vote, according to the Maryland State Board of Elections.
During the rally before the chamber dinner, protesters brought up concerns with recent mass firings of federal workers. Suzanne Sullivan said she has concerns about what the firings will do for the local economy. Sullivan, who lives in Dorchester County, is the wife of environmental scientist Jake Shaner, who was recently fired from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Harris told media after the dinner that most companies layoff employees every three to five years. He said that with federal tax cuts, the federal government will grow the economy so there are "plenty of jobs for every American."
"Look, do I feel for everybody who's laid off?" he asked. "Absolutely. Private industry, public government. It's a personal family setback. That's exactly why we have unemployment insurance and we have the social net until these individuals find another job."
HARRIS' KEYNOTE SPEECH
During his keynote speech, Harris touched on a number of issues relevant to Dorchester County and the Eastern Shore. He spoke about the importance of the agriculture industry, low-cost energy and the H-2B visa program.
Harris also brought up the need for blue catfish processing centers to help reduce the population of the invasive species in the Chesapeake Bay. He said federal funding will be available to entrepreneurs who want to build processing plants so the catfish can be considered a commercially viable seafood product.
Harris said two things the county should focus on are addressing drug and alcohol addiction and making sure every child is reading on grade level.
"And we can certainly provide help from the federal government," he said. "But I'll tell you, some of the best solutions are at the local level."
Harris, who lives in Cambridge, said it is a pleasure to represent the people of the Eastern Shore. He said he lives a "blessed life" where he can be at Mar-a-Lago one night and eating at Cindy's Kitchen in Cambridge the next morning.
"It's like the best of both worlds," he said. "And to be honest with you, I like Cindy's better. But don't tell the president that."

title: Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts
author: Konner Metz
content:
Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council sent a letter this week to the Maryland General Assembly expressing its concerns regarding more than $1 million in county money impacted by the state's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act."The proposal to shift costs onto counties by sending invoices simply places the State's fiscal problem into other hands and threatens local services," reads the letter, which was unanimously approved by the council Tuesday.
Cost shifts are expected as the state aims to balance a budget with a nearly $3 billion deficit. Specific costs include contributions to teacher pensions and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said it's "simply a poor and inappropriate strategy for resolving the very real state budget crisis."
Lesher noted Tuesday that Talbot County isn't seeing the worst of the cost shifts — Dorchester County may be looking at more than $3 million affected, he said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he testified at a Senate budget committee meeting in Annapolis and talked with members of the governor's staff.
Pfeffer says Department of Legislative Services recommendations to double the costs for counties to pay toward teacher pensions is particularly alarming. For Dorchester, it would cost $1.1 million compared to the previously estimated $550,000.
Gov. Wes Moore has said solving the budget crisis is an "enormous task" only made more difficult by constraints from the federal government. At a Feb. 28 Senate budget committee hearing, he emphasized that the budget bill is nowhere near final.
"While I still remain locked in on the destination, I come in moving in partnership to be flexible on the journey," Moore said.
Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the county may lose $1.1 million in income tax revenue if Moore's tax cut plan is approved.
Moore has maintained that giving middle-class families tax relief is a critical component to the budget and state's economic growth plan.
"Marylanders are being squeezed. They're being squeezed by rising prices," Moore said Feb. 28. "They're being squeezed by the rising cost of groceries, they're being squeezed by the rising cost of energy."
As session continues, Breeding says Caroline County has representatives in Annapolis fighting for relief from the potential cost shifts.
"We have a lot of heartburn with the proposed budget," Breeding said.

title: Qualities we can hold onto
author: Staff Writer
content:
Qualities we can hold onto

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 326
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's hard to believe five years have passed since the beginning of the pandemic and the loss of John Ford, my husband and then president of the Easton Town Council in 2020—and how much has changed since then. This past February, on the anniversary of his death, I found myself smiling as I remembered watching "John Ford TV" as our family jokingly called Easton Town Council meeting nights, broadcast on the local cable channel. I recalled, with fondness, his kindness and attentiveness as he actively listened to the voices of our citizens.Looking back at the February 2020 articles in the Star Democrat and the Talbot Spy about John gave me hope. Pete Lesher worked with John at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum and later served alongside him on the Easton Town Council. Lesher said, "He coached me and provided a compassionate model of supervising people."
Lesher shared that Ford's leadership was rooted in three principles: "He thought everyone deserved respect, deserved to be heard, and deserved to be given straight answers."
Rich Scofield, who also worked with John at the museum, said, "He was extremely important to the Town of Easton. His integrity, his honesty, his ability to listen and to make a measured decision — those are rare qualities."
Ron Engle, who served with John on the Town Council, said Ford had a unique ability to foster cooperation and compromise. As the Talbot Spy wrote, Ford inspired friendship and respect. He was a thoughtful listener. His decisions were deliberative and sensible. As a public official navigating diverse opinions and complex issues, he had a rare talent for building consensus. In his quiet, reserved way, he was remarkably effective.
In these tumultuous times, when everything seems to be shifting, these are qualities we can hold onto and practice every day: show respect, listen well, pause, and respond rather than react.
I have hope that soon we will see more of this spirit in our town and in our nation.
PEGGY FORD
Easton

title: Angela Alsobrooks talks with Eastern Shore Municipalities about concerns
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Angela Alsobrooks talks with Eastern Shore Municipalities about concerns

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 545
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D) met with multiple municipal leaders from across the Eastern Shore to discuss issues they face.In addition to meeting with multiple municipalities, Alsobrooks visited Eastern Shore agricultural leaders and participated in a tour of Chesapeake College. She met with higher education leaders during her stop at the college.
Alsobrooks heard concerns of municipal officials including the freezing and cutting of Federal Emergency Management Agency funds and how U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on the Eastern Shore can affect the agricultural economy and area families.
"It's so important today to be here and to have conversations," Alsobrooks said. "We spent the day here very intentionally to hear from farmers, to hear from business owners, to hear from municipal leaders, who are primarily sharing the impact of some of the federal cuts that we've seen and that we've seen in some of the freezing of funds."
Multiple municipalities voiced their concerns about the freezing and cuts of federal funding. One big project on the Eastern Shore is the Ocean City beach replenishment project.
According to Ocean City officials, the beach replenishment project was first started in 1989 and is a partnership between the federal government, the state of Maryland, Worcester County and Ocean City.
The project was built to protect the shoreline along the Ocean City coastline. It consists of building a dune system, a seawall and pumping sand on the beach to provide protection from storms.
The project has estimated to save $1 billion in property damage since its completion in 1991. Every year in the winter, Ocean City conducts the project, but the federal funding for this winter project has not been received.
Another concern brought to Alsobrooks was the funding freeze for the Shore Resiliency program by FEMA.
According to Cambridge officials, the plan for the project includes three main elements: a living shoreline, earth and rock embankments and stormwater management to alleviate flooding.
Almost 30% of the design for the Cambridge program is done, but the funds for that project has been frozen.
Another concern brought to Alsobrooks was helping kids who experience immigrant enforcement with their parents and how immigrant enforcement will effect the economy on the Eastern Shore.
Salisbury officials mentioned two men on work visas with families who were picked up by ICE and that have already been shipped to New Orleans. The officials are concerned about how the agricultural economy can be affected.
Another story mentioned was about two daughters a 5- and 7-year-old whose parents were picked up by ICE. The children lived at home for two days without mentioning anything to school officials.
Alsobrooks listened to all concerns and what what she plans to do and how important their concerns are to the state.
"I'm going to be working to make sure that I really do what I can to to get those funds unfrozen and to continue to stay in communication with leaders and community of members to help our state be successful," she said.
Officials voiced appreciation for Alsobrooks listening and her promise to continue to communicate with leaders on the Eastern Shore.
"It's really important that the senator hears from small communities here in the Eastern Shore," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook. "It feels like she's really taking our concerns seriously into heart, and she's going to find the answers to our questions."

title: Oxford election set for June 17
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford election set for June 17

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 247
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With Oxford Commissioner Tom Costigan's term set to expire in July, the town's voters will get the opportunity to decide who should be sitting at the commissioners' table during town meetings for the next three years.Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said the election to fill Costigan's seat will be held June 17. Those interested in running for the position must file for candidacy by May 19.
Wahl said that in order to file, prospective candidates will need to submit an application for the town's Election Board to review.
"We are going to post the applications on our town website," she said on Monday.
According to Oxford's town charter, to be a commissioner, you must be an Oxford resident who has been a resident for at least one year prior to the election and must be qualified to vote in town elections.
Wahl told the Star Democrat on Monday that the town office had not yet received any candidate filings.
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Costigan said he is considering whether he will run for reelection. He said he will probably announce his decision in the first week of April.
Costigan said he has not heard of anyone else who is interested in filing, but he said anyone who considers filing should know this is not a position where you just show up for two meetings each month.
"It's quite a commitment," he said. "I hope anyone who steps up to the plate understands what a commitment it truly is."

title: Caroline County conduct first FY26 budget workshop
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County conduct first FY26 budget workshop

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 635
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Caroline County Commissioners, Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox and grant coordinator Stacy Seward, who helps with the budget annually, tackled the first workshop for fiscal year 2026 budget at the county commissioners meeting on Tuesday.While the budget is a work in progress, Caroline County Commissioner President Travis Breeding cautioned that the work done at Tuesday's meeting is fluid and could be changed as discussions continue.
"I should point out that a lot of this is fluid and still up in the air," Breeding said, adding that the pending state budget could change things. "We still don't have a clear picture of what kind of fiscal situation were going to be in when they strike the budget."
The county is expected to bring in $77 million in revenue, while the proposed fiscal year expenditures are currently $79 million, leaving a $2 million shortfall.
For capital funding the county has $7.3 million allocated for capital funding. The requested amount for capital funding in FY26 is $10.4 million, leaving a shortfall of $3.1 million.
Both budgets need to be in balance when they are presented at a public hearing in May.
The commissioners discussed both the operating and capital budgets to account for the shortfalls in both budgets.
CAPITAL BUDGET
A number of items were discussed in the capital budget.
The Department of Corrections control panel for $120,00 is already being worked on but the requested new van is still in question. While the van is damaged the county took into account the mileage on the van is only 22,330.
"I think we should get the van looked at and evaluated," County Commissioner Frank Bartz said.
The Department of Emergency Services could receive funding for the 14 cardiac monitor replacement, but the commissioners discussed waiting one more year for purchasing a number of requested trucks.
Facilities requested a long list of items which the county commissioners discussed to fund the first seven and will discuss the rest as the budget workshop sessions continue.
The county commissioners discussed potentially cutting capital funds for these organizations.
All Circuit Court request for $272,000.DES $180,000 for EMS lieutenant and EMS division chief.Facilities proposal to receive $498,000 of requested $1,477,000.All Public Works requests except a six-wheel dump truck and a Husqvarna Zero Turn mower for $1,203,500.All Rec and Parks requests except a Skag 72-inch Zero Turn mower for $136,000All 4-H Park requests for $90,000.All Human Society requests for $85,000.
OPERATING BUDGET
While the operating budget has a $2 million deficit, the county must find cuts in many different areas. Companies in the expenditure category gave the commissioners the most discussion at the county commissioners' first workshop.
"I appreciate everything these volunteers organizations do," County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "There is a lot of other volunteers organizations and nonprofits in the county that we don't give money to, our job is public safety. My position is the same as its been the last two years, I don't think we should fund any of them."
While Breeding thinks they could potentially save funding here, Commissioners Porter and Bartz said that some nonprofits should be allocated some funds.
"I looked at some of the budgets to see whether the $5,000 will impact their budgets or not, some I thought I felt we could contribute to, some I struck off," Bartz said.
The commissioners also discussed the fire companies that requested a 10% increase in allocation, and a property tax credit. Breeding landed on a 5% increase, Porter at 10% and Bartz at 7.5%.
"Enter our different numbers I don't think we will come to a consensus today, we have one more public hearing," Breeding said.
The commissioners will discuss more requests. Here are the numbers for the potential expenditure category:
Expenditure Category: Breeding allocated $6,300 for non-profit organizations.Porter allocated $5,000 to Positive striders.Bartz allocated money to all nonprofit organizations.Porter gave $50,000 for a property tax credit, Bartz and Breeding $0.All commissioners have different numbers for allocations.

title: Cambridge amends paving contract to address ADA requirements
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge amends paving contract to address ADA requirements

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 324
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a Cambridge City Council meeting March 18, the council voted unanimously to amend a paving contract to include updating intersections so they are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act.In September, the City Council awarded David A. Bramble Inc. with a $447,150 contract to resurface three miles of roads at various locations in the city. City Manager Glenn Steckman said the contract was approved before city staff was made aware that if the city paves through intersections that are not up to standard with Americans with Disabilities Act, it has to update those intersections.
"So to pave through the intersection, you have to improve the intersection," Steckman said.
During the council meeting, Steckman told commissioners the city could either spend approximately $125,000 more to address the intersections as the city paves the three miles or reduce the scope of the project and pave less road in order to address the intersections with the money already budgeted in the contract.
Steckman said the city is estimating intersection updates would cost about $6,000 per intersection. He recommended the council vote to spend additional money to complete the three miles of paving. He said the city had originally budgeted $600,000 for the project.
Before the council took a vote, commissioners asked questions about prioritizing certain streets and areas for paving.
According to City Council documents, the city used a 2018 pavement condition study for the project to determine which streets are in most need of being repaved. Commissioner Brian Roche said it would be a waste of money to ignore the study.
"You have to be careful because we could end up having roads that fall further into disrepair just because someone thinks that their road is in worse shape when in fact an engineering analysis has determined where (is in worse shape)," he said.
After discussion, the council voted to increase the cost of the contract to include updates to the intersections without reducing the scope of the project.

title: How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore

 March 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Delegate Jay Jacobs, who represents Maryland's District 36 — encompassing Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline counties — has seen the region through economic peaks and valleys. But the COVID-19 pandemic presented a crisis unlike any other.At the same time, it brought a rare opportunity.
Through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), Maryland received $3.7 billion in federal relief funds. Jacobs estimated that roughly $88 million of that flowed into his district over the past five years.
"The money gave counties and municipalities a chance to get things done when they normally might not have had that opportunity," Jacobs said.
Across the district, more than 200 projects were funded through ARPA, aimed at bolstering local infrastructure, supporting nonprofits and modernizing essential services.
Rock Hall to Queen Anne's: Local Needs, Local SolutionsEach town took a unique approach, reflecting ARPA's flexible framework.
In Rock Hall, the town's aging wastewater system was a priority. Mayor James Cook said of the $1.3 million received, $300,000 went toward replacing the headworks at the sewer plant — a key filter that removes debris such as grease and rags from wastewater.
Chestertown formed a task force led by Ward 2 Council member Tom Herz to ensure transparency and community input. Of the $4.25 million allocated, local nonprofits were invited to align funding requests with the town's comprehensive plan.
In Galena, $570,000 supported road improvements designed to make parks more accessible and attract visitors.
Betterton directed its $311,000 toward modernizing its website to be ADA-compliant, enabling online payments, purchasing an air purifying unit, and upgrading pump stations with generators for resilience.
Millington received $504,821, though specific projects were not detailed.
Queen Anne's County saw one of the largest allocations: $16.3 million. Projects included installing 3,300 feet of water line at the Old Towne Shopping Center, investing $900,000 to upgrade affordable housing units, and expanding broadband access with $1.5 million. Six new consoles were also added to the county's 911 backup center, and cell phone boosters were installed in public schools to strengthen communication in rural areas.
Countywide Efforts and Broadband ExpansionIn Cecil County, where municipalities received a greater share of ARPA funds than the county itself, a major initiative focused on expanding high-speed internet. A $16.2 million broadband project combined $12.8 million in state funds, $2.5 million from internet service providers, and $900,000 in ARPA funds contributed by the county.
According to county officials, additional ARPA investments went toward two emergency medical services paramedic stations and a new training center for the Cecil County Sheriff's Office.
Rising Sun used $2,300 for infrastructure repairs, while the Town of North East applied its share to enhance police department operations.
In Caroline County, which received just under $6.5 million, part of the funding was used for infrastructure, while a portion supported reentry programs and post-release case management for individuals leaving the Ordnance Road Detention Facility.
Jacobs noted that ARPA's flexibility was one of its most valuable aspects.
"It was not one size fits all," he said. "Municipalities could use the money to meet their specific needs — with the only caveat being it must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026."
As ARPA Winds Down, Financial Pressure MountsNow, with the funding window closing, local governments are bracing for its absence. Jacobs said the drying up of ARPA funds is intensifying pressure on the state as the General Assembly works to pass the FY 2026 budget — which currently faces a $3.5 billion shortfall.
"Certain services were being relied on and now are cut off," Jacobs said. "ARPA funds possibly would have kept some of these programs afloat."
A notable cut is the reduction in senior care funding by the Maryland Department of Aging. Jacobs said the proposed $2.5 million budget — an 18% reduction — could translate to about $28,000 less per county. He warned this could destabilize staffing and services for vulnerable seniors, such as in-home care, transportation and meal delivery.
"These cuts will be felt, not by the lawmakers, but by ordinary hardworking folks who have to make decisions about affording food or putting gas in the car," he said.
Talbot County: Planning for LongevityTalbot County took a strategic approach. Officials distributed surveys to identify community priorities, which included broadband access, public health, and household assistance.
According to Cassandra Vanhooser, director of Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism, the county received about $7.2 million in ARPA funds. The goal, she said, was to ensure that projects wouldn't falter once federal dollars were gone.
"These are largely capital items, these are one-time items... a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," said then Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher. "We need to be very careful about how this is done."
Among Talbot's allocations:
- $1.75 million to Easton Utilities' Connect Talbot project to expand broadband to rural residents.
- $105,000 to the Chesapeake Center in Easton to replace a failing septic system and connect to county sewer.
- $500,000 in grants for volunteer fire company equipment upgrades.
"People recognize that this is transformational money," Vanhooser said at the time of the funding discussion, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be a driving force for change and to impact the lives of our citizens."
Looking AheadAs the Dec. 31, 2024 obligation deadline nears, and the Dec. 31, 2026 expenditure deadline looms, local leaders are focused on maximizing remaining funds while grappling with what comes next.
Jacobs is urging urgency from lawmakers.
"With less than 20 days in session," he said, "the Assembly needs to come up with solutions — and fast."

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council will consider raising its 911 fee more after passing legislation to increase it by 50 cents earlier this month.On March 4, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. During a County Council meeting March 18, the council voted to introduce legislation to further increase the fee to $4.25.
Currently, the county is going through the process of preparing its budget for fiscal year 2026. At a budget work session Feb. 28, County Manager Jerry Jones said the county is facing a deficit of $6.2 million, with $87.7 million in estimated revenue and $93.9 million in estimated expenditures.
At the council meeting March 18, Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he wanted to introduce the legislation to increase the 911 fee because he thinks it is necessary.
"Unfortunately, because of the budgetary mandates that have been passed down to us and the need for us, as we discussed, to look to other sources to raise revenue, unfortunately I believe it's my duty to introduce another increase from $2 to $4.25," he said.
Detmer said the county's Emergency Communications Division has a budget of about $1.9 million. He said the $1.50 fee raised about $660,000 for the county last year.
"If we increase it out of necessity to $4.25 per line per month, it would bring fees to a total of $1.8 million, which would be a large part for funding that budget," he said.
The council will need to hold a public hearing before it can vote. Detmer said he thinks it's the county's duty to consider the bill and hear residents' opinions on the matter.
"I would love to be having a discussion about how we lower these things," he said. "That's not the world that we're living in right now. Certainly not the state we're living in."

title: CWDI board hears presentation about using brokerage firm

 525

 CAMBRIDGE — During the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors meeting Wednesday, the board heard a presentation on the benefits of hiring a brokerage firm to market the Cambridge Harbor site.Cambridge Commissioner Brett Summers, who said he came to the board as a resident and not as a commissioner, presented on why he thinks hiring a national brokerage firm would help move forward the Cambridge Harbor project, which is a project to develop land along the Choptank River in Cambridge.
"I came to appreciate the value a brokerage firm can bring to a development site," Summers said after describing his 40 years of commercial real estate experience.
During his presentation, Summers told the board a brokerage firm would act as the marketing arm to help attract developers to the different sites at Cambridge Harbor.
"You have a mixed-use project here," he said. "And all these brokerage firms have different expertise. They have industrial brokers, they have retail brokers, they have office brokers, they have multi-family (brokers), restaurant (brokers). You need to find a brokerage firm that has those different expertise."
Summers said the brokerage firm could disseminate information about Cambridge Harbor to local and national developers.
During the presentation, the CWDI board brought up a city requirement that CWDI must use a request for proposals process to select developers to develop land conveyed to CWDI from the city. CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr said he was unsure if using a brokerage firm could serve as a replacement to the request for proposal process.
Narr asked Summers how CWDI could ensure the process of obtaining developers for the site stays public if CWDI uses a brokerage firm.
"Because I think that was always the intent," he said. "That this was a public process."
Summers said a brokerage firm can be "very public." He said the firm could come to CWDI board meetings and give updates.
CWDI board member Tim Crosby said the time to decide whether to hire a brokerage firm is now. Summers agreed, saying the sooner, the better.
"You've got a good concept," Summers said. "You've just got to get it out in the world and let people know about the opportunity with the math to back it up."
Summers said he expects it would take CWDI about three months to choose a brokerage firm. From there, he said CWDI would sign a listing agreement with the brokerage firm and the firm would begin putting together an offering memorandum, which includes detailed information about the property for the brokers to market it.
Later in the meeting, Cambridge resident Mary Ann McNamara thanked Summers for his presentation.
"Because I think that's what's needed," she said about his idea to involve a brokerage firm. "Something to get the project moving forward."
McNamara asked how the board plans to proceed. CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said the board will discuss the idea further and make a decision.
Doug Schuetz said he's "all for" Summers' idea, but said there should be a "sunset" on CWDI and the Cambridge Harbor project if CWDI can't get the ball rolling.
"Let's have a time frame," he said. "If these guys can't get it together in a year, let's start with the idea of a park."

He brought up recent actions taken by President Donald Trump and the the Department of Government Efficiency. He said he is trying to "stop this savage assault on American democracy."
"They're not opponents of corruption," Raskin said. "They're agents of corruption."

title: Greensboro meeting frenzy caused by potential movement of town agencies
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com

 GREENSBORO — The potential shuffling of town agencies' offices sent Greensboro residents and officials into a frenzy at town hall meeting.Town officials discussed potentially moving the Greensboro Historical Society out of the Weaver Building to allow the food pantry Aaron's Place to occupy a bigger location. The officials also discussed potentially moving the Greensboro Police Department into another space inside the town building.
Discussions, led by Mayor David Spencer and then Town Manager Tammy Kelledes, took a turn when Commissioner Joe Noon voiced his frustration about how residents treat town representatives and the confusion taking root with town officials.
"I've have never been on a more dysfunctional, I don't know what's going on here," Noon said. "But I can promise you we are going to get this straight. I can promise you I will back this council. I will back every person up here on this council, and I will back my employees on this."
"... The disrespect that comes from the citizen since the way you talk to our staff is terrible, and it makes me upset. We do this because we love our town. We don't do this because we have to do this. We work full-time jobs. How are we ever going to come together we don't work as one?"
Spencer reiterated to the public that the town is not trying to kick the Greensboro Historical Society out of its home, but he said all options are on the table to help accommodate the town's needs for space.
"I know that it's going to be difficult for us not to utilize the historical society. That's terrible," Spencer said. "I'm a lifelong resident of Greensboro. I want to do everything, I want to do whatever I can to help, but we need that space."
There was confusion among the town officials and Community Programs Coordinator Amanda Weaver on whether the town had already decided to put the food pantry in the Weaver Building or just had discussed moving them into the building.
Spencer was out of town during this discussion at the town's Feb. 22 working session, so he declined to comment on whether a decision was made or not.
During the public comment period, Weaver wanted to make it clear to residents and officials that she did not come up with the idea of moving the historical society. She said it was brought to her by the commissioners.
"I would like the record to show that commissioners brought this idea to me," she said.
Spencer hit his gavel to let Weaver know she was out of order, but Weaver rebutted, "That's OK. I'm going to leave now, but the commissioners brought this to me, I didn't ask to take over the historical society."
Charles Dean, president of the Greensboro Historical Society, and other members of the historical society offered a presentation during the public comment period of the meeting stating why the society should stay in its building.
"You can imagine my shock and dismay after I heard from the February meeting that the displacement of the historical society was being considered," Dean said.
Dean and town officials discussed how they could move the historical society artifacts without damaging them. Town officials are willing to help with that move if the price doesn't exceed a $5,000 threshold.
Dean assured moving and safely storing the historical society artifacts would cost more than $5,000.
During the public comment period, residents offered many different solutions to historical society and food pantry dilemma. All were listened to by town officials.
Town officials suggested that the historical society and some town officials would meet to discuss what would be the best course of action.
