title: Proposed resolution sets off tense discussion at Cambridge meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Proposed resolution sets off tense discussion at Cambridge meeting

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Tensions flared at the April 14 Cambridge City Council meeting over a proposed resolution directing the city manager to analyze the city's human resources capabilities and follow a specific process when hiring staff.The resolution was ultimately tabled.
Commissioner Frank Stout, who brought the resolution to the council, said he saw the resolution as a way to standardize the hiring process and ensure the city completes a broad search for job candidates, citing previous meeting discussions on the topic.
City Manager Glenn Steckman said he was not consulted about the resolution before it was sent to him. He said much of what is outlined in the resolution is already part of the city's process.
"I will tell you, I'm not real happy about this," he said. "It has bothered me through the weekend. And I appreciate the commissioners that hired me. They know about my experience."
Steckman was hired prior to the city's November election, after which several new faces were added to the council.
Bringing up part of the resolution that encourages the city manager to "expand recruitment efforts beyond internal applicants to include external candidates," Steckman said he's heard from city staff that they think the council wants to take opportunities away from them.
He said with most organizations, including the city, there is a five-day window where employees can apply to a job posting before the posting is made public. After the five days, management can make a decision about whether to expand the search externally, Steckman said.
"I'm not exactly sure why I need a resolution to tell me what I already know how to do," he said.
Stout said he sees the resolution as a way to "put words around" what the council had discussed in previous meetings.
"I don't want there to be anything misconstrued that I don't have full faith and confidence in city staff," he said.
Commissioner Brian Roche agreed with Stout's resolution, saying none of the language was "detrimental" and it just put into words what the council said it wanted to see.
Before calling on the commissioners to make a motion to table the resolution indefinitely, Mayor Lajan Cephas cut off discussion and spoke about the value of city employees.
As she spoke, Stout asked her to "please" not "steer" the discussion "in a different direction," and Cephas responded, "I didn't interrupt you when you were speaking, so can you please provide me the same respect?"
After talking about the importance of having opportunities for promotion in a workplace, Cephas said although she doesn't have a vote in council matters, she has a voice.
"I'm going to stand up for city employees every single time," she said.
Not long after Cephas' comments, the council opted in a 3-2 vote to table the resolution until after June 30, which will mark the end of the budget process. Stout and Roche voted against the motion.

title: Talbot County introduces $161M budget with a focus on conservatism
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County introduces $161M budget with a focus on conservatism

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County officials introduced a $161 million budget proposal Tuesday, emphasizing their intention to flatten spending after multiple years of significant increases.Tuesday's proposal is balanced at around $2 million below last year's total budget.
"This year, you are introducing a budget that is flat from last year at this point in time, which was a hard task, and I commend you for doing that," County Manager Clay Stamp told County Council members.
Three fiscal years ago, the county's budget was $112 million before it rose to $128 million one year later and $163 million last year. The county is continuing to focus on building a stable fund reserve, an effort that has peaked in the last three years, Stamp said.
In addition to smoothing out recent hikes, Stamp said this year's budget considers threats it faces from federal and state government spending cuts.
"There's some severe federal policy shifts going on right now," Stamp said. "The state of Maryland is passing funding obligations down to (county) governments."
One obligation Talbot County will assume, pending an amendment to the proposed budget, is $440,000 in teachers' pension payments. Finance Director Martha Sparks noted the county worked with state legislators to add language to the law "in the eleventh hour" during this year's General Assembly.
Talbot County would cover that $440,000 through an education supplement tax. The supplement to the property tax would be less than half a cent per $100 of assessed value.
Overall, the real property tax rate is proposed at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, nearly even with last year's total rate. The tax bill on a home valued at $300,000 would increase by $4.80 from last year, county officials said.
The county will bring in a projected $67 million in property tax revenue in fiscal year 2026, up from $60 million last year (not including the education supplement tax). That's a 12.3% increase, which stems from rising property value reassessments.
"As undesirable as it is to raise taxes, our tax increases by our charter's design are moderate increases and are reflected in our standing as the county with the lowest property tax rate in the state of Maryland," Sparks said.
The proposed budget includes $55 million in funding for Talbot County Public Schools, a mark required by the state's funding plans in its expansive education initiative, The Blueprint for Maryland's Future.
The county did not include the district's request for $5.7 million in additional funding to help with teacher salary increases and new positions, among other requests. Vice President Pete Lesher urged the council to do so at a previous workshop, but the rest of the council opted to hold off. The budget ordinance could be amended to include some or all of that request.
Stamp said despite the flattened budget, capital upgrades aren't stalling. He pointed to projects such as the St. Michaels library branch upgrade, moving the county's public safety complex and continuing renovations at Chapel District Elementary School.
Sparks noted the county is in a "healthy financial position" thanks to fiscal year 2025 revenues exceeding projections by around $8 million. The added revenue is largely due to income tax distributions from the state coming in higher than expected, Sparks said.
A similar situation with the income tax revenue isn't a guarantee for next fiscal year, she said.
Tax hikes to the state's most wealthy, part of Gov. Wes Moore's plan to close an over $3 billion state budget deficit, were enacted by the General Assembly this month. Those increases could drive wealthy residents out of Talbot County to surrounding states and reduce income tax revenue, county officials say.
"The last time this type of tax was implemented, Talbot County's income tax revenues decreased by 40% within one year," Sparks said.
Amid looming uncertainty, County Council members thanked Stamp and the financial staff for their work to present a balanced budget ordinance Tuesday.
"Clearly we've still got some storm clouds on the horizon, both from the federal and state budgets (and) impacts on local budgeting." Lesher said. "… We're going into this, as you outlined, in a strong position. I think that this is a sound approach."
Public budget hearings will be held May 6 at 2 p.m. in the Talbot County Courthouse Bradley Meeting Room and 7 p.m. in the Easton High School Cafeteria. The final budget is expected to be passed by the County Council May 27.

title: FRANK GUNSALLUS

1. Why are you running for Easton Town Council president?
My core reason for seeking reelection as Easton Town Council president is my inherent and unwavering dedication to serving the community. I believe service to one's fellow citizens is an exceptionally important calling and a fundamental responsibility to make a positive difference.
I am running for reelection because Easton is at a critical point. We are facing serious decisions about housing, growth, infrastructure and public safety that will impact our town's future. I've served the council with a focus on results, not rhetoric. I will continue to provide steady, common-sense leadership that respects the taxpayer, protects our neighborhoods and moves Easton forward.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
I will prioritize four primary issues: defeating the proposed inclusionary zoning ordinance, enhancing public safety, improving infrastructure and increasing government transparency.
The inclusionary zoning ordinance would drive up costs for home builders, discourage investment in our community and negatively impact home values.
I will ensure the police and fire departments receive the necessary funding and support to effectively serve the community.
As we see more development, we need to consider investing in areas like roads, utilities and stormwater management to improve infrastructure.
We must ensure Easton's residents have an in-depth understanding of issues and proposals and why decisions are reached. I will strongly encourage more direct community engagement.
3. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
Inclusionary zoning is not the answer. It restricts supply and raises costs for builders and homebuyers through the redistribution of losses imposed on market-rate units to offset the cost of below-market rate requirements.
Over time this type of legislation can create a deflationary effect, reducing the market value of comparable homes. The town should instead encourage workforce housing by streamlining permitting, offering targeted incentives and considering the removal or deferral of upfront costs when specific housing products are being delivered. I served on the Attainable Housing Task Force, and there are more effective ways to expand workforce housing by collaborating with private and nonprofit partners — without penalizing those who already live here.
4. The town has seen increased development in its downtown core as well as on Route 50. How should the town prepare for the impacts of such growth?
We need to get ahead of the growth, not react to it after the fact. That starts with infrastructure: roads, traffic flow, sewer capacity and stormwater systems all need investment. We also need to be clear-eyed about the fiscal impact of development and make sure projects pay their fair share toward the infrastructure they require. Growth must be managed, which includes enforcing our comprehensive plan and making sure development fits the character and capacity of the area.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
Public safety is non-negotiable. As Easton grows, the demands on our police and volunteer fire departments grow too. We need to ensure these departments are fully staffed, have modern equipment and receive the training they need. I support data-driven policing and community-based approaches, but that only works if the departments are adequately resourced.
I will lead efforts to explore various options to support our first responders financially, including improving retirement benefits for our public safety personnel by increasing contribution percentages or by exploring enrollment in alternative programs such as Law Enforcement Officers' Pension System, which could strengthen lateral recruitment efforts.
6. What have you accomplished during your time on the council thus far? How will you seek to continue those efforts?
I've supported freedom, family values, public safety, key infrastructure investments and capital improvements. I've worked to improve communication between the town and residents. I've advocated for fiscal responsibility and accountability. I led the effort for the council to formally oppose a bill that would restrict the abilities of law enforcement agencies. I testified publicly in Annapolis against tax increases. I took the initiative to rewrite the council's rules and procedures.
I'll continue asking questions, doing research and making decisions based on what's best for Easton. My primary focus remains on the four items I have prioritized herein and on delivering the best results for the people of Easton.

Completing the town's comprehensive plan is critical for smart growth, and I will focus on enhancing community engagement to ensure that every voice is heard in shaping our future. Together, we can build a stronger, more inclusive Easton.
3. What changes would you make to the town's budget, and what budget items should not be cut?
The proposed budget is balanced. I believe some areas require better adjustment to support our community. I would prioritize increasing funding for our first responders, ensuring they have the resources to serve and protect us effectively. Their safety and well-being directly impact our community's security. As for budget cuts, this year's proposal leaves little room for reductions without compromising essential services. However, I would carefully review discretionary spending to identify any inefficiencies or non-essential items that could be trimmed, allowing the Town Council to reallocate those funds to critical areas that enhance public safety and community well-being.
4. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
To address the challenge of affordable housing in Easton, the town should consider purchasing land designated for this purpose. Partnering with organizations like Habitat for Humanity can be an effective strategy to develop affordable housing options. Collaborating with such organizations allows us to leverage their expertise and resources, ensuring homes are built efficiently and sustainably. These proactive steps can create more inclusive housing opportunities, ensuring all residents can access safe and affordable homes in Easton.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
My plans for enhancing public safety in Easton focus on proactive community engagement and support for our police department. I believe in the importance of transportation safety initiatives and continued proactive neighborhood patrols to foster a sense of security. While recruitment efforts have improved, we must prioritize officer retention by developing a suitable retirement plan that benefits current officers and those nearing retirement. This will ensure younger officers gain valuable experience before advancing to command staff positions. Investing in our officers and fostering community relationships can create a safer, more resilient Easton for everyone.
6. In addition to serving the Town of Easton as a whole, what are your plans to improve your ward specifically?
To improve Ward 4 specifically, I will focus on fostering a strong sense of community through partnership, respect, integrity, dedication and empowerment. By actively engaging with residents, I aim to understand their needs and aspirations, ensuring that our initiatives reflect our shared values. Together, we can address local concerns, enhance public spaces and promote community events that strengthen our bonds. I invite the constituents of Ward 4 to join me on this journey, working hand in hand to build a vibrant and inclusive community that not only uplifts our ward but also contributes to the overall progress of Easton.

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners discussed their Capital Transportation Priorities list and drafted a letter to send to the state at their April 15 meeting.The priority list is presented to the state every year to receive funding for road work projects within the county that the commissioners and town officials believes are a priority.
The state will ultimately determine which projects it funds.
PRIORITY A
Priority A for Caroline County is maintaining and improving existing infrastructure. The county asked for a comprehensive resurfacing of Route 313 from Route 404 to Federalsburg, including repairs to pavement, shoulders and stormwater infrastructure.
Next is the completion of the resurfacing project on Route 16 from Lake Drive to Route 404.
Lastly, Caroline County asked for general resurfacing, shoulder repair, drainage improvement and signage upgrades across Caroline County's state road network. Timely investment in these areas will help avoid further deterioration, reduce maintenance costs and significantly improve travel conditions for our residents and businesses, the county said.
PRIORITY B
The county requested Route 404 be widened from Harmony Road to Route 16 East.
Previous phases of this project have led to improved traffic flow and reduced accidents, demonstrating the importance of completing the corridor, the county said in its priorities list.
PRIORITY CCaroline County requested help with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 454 (Crownstone Road) from Marydel to Templeville.
Route 454 is a vital connector for residents in the western part of the county and serves as a gateway to Queen Anne's County. This route has seen substantial wear and requires resurfacing and structural upgrades to ensure safe and dependable travel, the county said.
PRIORITY DThe county requested state assistance with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 313 from Greensboro to Goldsboro.
This is a major north-south route within the county and is essential for local mobility and emergency response, the county said. It added resurfacing and drainage improvements are necessary to restore safe travel conditions and extend the life of the corridor.
PRIORITY ERounding out the county's priority list is an effort to restripe Route 317 and add a right turn lane.
"We propose restriping MD 317 (Burnsville Road) at the intersection of MD 313 to add a right turn lane. This improvement will help enhance traffic flow and improve safety for all drivers," the county said.

title: ROBERT RANKIN

ROBERT RANKIN

 Name: Robert Jeremiah RankinEmail: robertjrankin@gmail.com
Age: 46
Family: Caddie (wife), Lucy (daughter, 16), Thomas (son, 14)
Education: B.A. in public policy studies, Duke University
Occupation: Consultant (self-employed)
Previous political experience: None
1. Why are you running for the Ward 2 seat on the Easton Town Council?
I am running to serve the Town of Easton and all its residents. I have followed local politics since moving here in 2012 and have always thought I could bring my skills to the council and enhance its work.
When I learned the Ward 2 seat was coming open, I decided now is the time to step up and exercise my civic duty. I believe the council should be addressing the most important issues facing our town in an inclusive way while ensuring Easton remains a great place to live, work and play.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
I will prioritize strategic development, continued support for first responders and fiscal responsibility. Easton is special, and I want it to remain a thriving, vibrant and welcoming community for all residents. This requires a strategic approach to ensure we are developing the right way, focusing on key issues like affordable housing and keeping a pace that maintains our small-town feel.
Easton is very safe thanks to our police department and first responders, and it is vital that our police and fire departments are properly staffed and outfitted. We need to be good stewards of taxpayer dollars by prioritizing the most important work.
3. What changes would you make to the town's budget, and what budget items should not be cut?
Not being on the council currently, I don't have full visibility of the budget and all town expenses. However, I believe the budget should prioritize public safety, infrastructure, sanitation and community services. We should maintain and expand possible resources for the police and fire departments.
I don't know of anything that I think should be cut, but to ensure we are being fiscally responsible I would support looking at whether certain programs can be made more efficient or streamlined. The goal is to maintain essential services and ensure every tax dollar is used wisely.
4. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
I'm hearing from many residents who are concerned about the potential impacts of all the new residential development on traffic, parking, schools and public safety. I would like to see how these current projects address demand, then take a more strategic approach to approving future work.
Affordable housing is huge, especially for younger professionals and families, and it is unacceptable that we have first responders who can't afford to live in town. We need to work together to find solutions, such as building more townhouses and apartments and redeveloping existing properties through a combination of residential and commercial.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
The Easton Police Department and the Town of Easton do a great job keeping our residents safe, and it is important that both are resourced properly. In terms of improvements, I think the town can do more to help EPD and the fire department recruit and retain top talent.
I think more sidewalks and crosswalks, particularly along Route 50 and the Easton Parkway, would support pedestrian safety and better connect the east and west sides of town to downtown. I'm open to exploring how we can divert or slow traffic in parts of downtown to prevent accidents.
6. In addition to serving the Town of Easton as a whole, what are your plans to improve your ward specifically?
The west side of Ward 2 is well-connected with easy access to downtown and recreational areas. With several new housing projects happening on the east side of the ward, which will add more cars to Route 328 and increase traffic on surrounding streets, we need more sidewalks and crosswalks to support pedestrian safety.
We also need to ensure traffic can flow on the east side so people can get to Route 50 and shopping areas. I think more recreational areas on the east side, such as a multi-modal trail alongside Route 328, would provide residents more options closer to home.

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held the third reading for emergency bills on wastewater treatment and term limits at their Tuesday meeting. Both emergency bills were enacted.The emergency bill on wastewater treatment adds a definition of what a wastewater treatment facility must be, a facility that must be for treatment, storage and disposal of certain wastes.
The past definition suggested a facility could be for treatment, storage or disposal of wastes.
While commission President Travis Breeding discussed leaving the definition at "or" instead of "and," the commissioners decided to change the definition to "and" to ensure a facility accomplishes all of these tasks.
The second emergency bill eliminated term limits for members of the Board of Zoning Appeals and potentially eliminated term limits for members of the Planning Commission.
The bill was proposed because the Board of Zoning Appeals believes by the time its members gain knowledge of all county zoning rules, they have termed out.
While the enacted emergency bill is exclusively for the Board of Zoning Appeals, Crystal Dadds, county director of planning and codes, discussed with the Planning Commission about similarly eliminating the commission's term limits.

title: Dorchester County proposes tax increases to balance FY26 budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County proposes tax increases to balance FY26 budget

 April 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 633
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, the Dorchester County Council introduced a draft fiscal year 2026 budget that raised taxes.The $91.96 million proposed operating budget presented Tuesday includes proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
The council will consider these proposals through the remainder of the budget process, which concludes May 20.
The balanced draft budget comes after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million operating budget deficit, which the county has said was brought on by cost shifts from the state.
"These are painful decisions," County Manager Jerry Jones said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "But at the end of the day, given the climate and what's being pushed down from the state for us to absorb, sadly it's one of those things we have to do."
GETTING INTO THE NUMBERS
In the draft operating budget, the county is proposing an increase of the real property tax by 3 cents so county residents would pay a rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
The proposal to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for municipalities would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full tax rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county $0.9267 per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay $0.9179 per $100 of assessed value.
On properties with a semi-annual tax payment option, the proposal would add a service charge based on a rate of 0.02% applied to unpaid real property taxes due in December.
With the proposed property tax changes to the budget, the county expects to bring in an additional $2.15 million.
The proposed budget would raise the county's income tax rate from 3.2% to 3.3%, generating $600,000 more in revenue.
In another effort to increase revenue, the county voted April 15 to increase its 911 fee to $4.25 per month. This is the second time the rate has been raised this year.
In early March, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. Council Vice President Mike Detmer said in March that he introduced the legislation to increase the fee to $4.25 as a potential way to reduce a budget deficit.
To alleviate the tax and fee increases' impact on seniors, the county is considering expanding its senior tax credit, which offers a 5% deduction on the county tax bill for those who are at least 70 years old and receive the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit. If passed, the expansion would increase that deduction to 10% and expand eligibility to Homeowners' Property Tax Credit recipients who are at least 67 years old.
Proposed expenditure increases include 3% salary increases for airport, solid waste, water and wastewater, courthouse maintenance, courthouse security and Eastern Shore Innovation Center personnel and an increase in spending on the county's 14 volunteer fire companies. The proposed $35,000 total increase to fire companies would add to the county's $1.22 million expenditure on fire companies and advanced life support services.
Proposed cuts to expenditures include the delaying or eliminating funding to nonprofits that request money from the county.
According to the draft grants budget, the county expects to receive a total of $9.78 million in state and federal grants.
At the end of the council meeting April 15, Detmer encouraged residents to come to council meetings or reach out to council members and make their voices and concerns about the budget heard. He said he is available to discuss the budget or just listen.
"It's your budget too," he said.
The first public budget hearing, as well as a meeting with municipalities, will be held May 6.

title: Easton Planning Commission approves Zaxbys on Route 50
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton Planning Commission approves Zaxbys on Route 50

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 493
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Planning Commission approved a plan to build a Zaxbys restaurant on Route 50 Thursday.Developers for the restaurant largely quelled concerns expressed last month when commission members tabled architectural approval. Those concerns centered on the bright red and blue colors in design renderings.
Thursday, franchise co-owner and Delmarva Real Estate Management Group attorney Curtis Snyder presented colored renderings of an updated design, which includes additional brick around the 2,000-square-foot building. The new renderings were less "cartoonish" in color and more accurately reflect what the building will look like, Snyder said.
Most commission members felt the updated design was an improvement.
"There are some existing businesses that have blues that are much brighter than this," commission member Laurie Forster said. "… I don't think it's unacceptable, and I do think it could be a great addition to the restaurant scene."
The Georgia-based franchise has hundreds of restaurants nationwide and is known for its chicken fingers, wings and signature sauces.
Commission member Tom Klein said the Easton Zaxbys will bring jobs to town and serve as an upgrade to the "eyesore" that is the empty Wendy's building.
"If this went down in flames, I don't know how long it would be before something else came along," Klein said. "So it could be sitting for quite some time like a lot of other empty lots on 50."
Snyder said the Zaxbys building will be smaller than the former Wendy's, allowing for two drive-thru lanes that can accommodate 26 cars at once. "We're confident in getting people in and out," Snyder said in response to a question of whether lines may spill onto the highway.
PUSHBACK
During Thursday's meeting, member Victoria McAndrews criticized the design, saying it's "very garish" compared to other Zaxbys restaurants in the country.
"I'm just not looking at this as an improvement over what was not satisfactory to begin with," McAndrews said.
Snyder said corporate isn't willing to budge on the blue and red colors, part of the company's branding efforts.
McAndrews said the commission is not doing its job by accepting designs pushed down from the corporate level.
"That's in direct conflict with what the (comprehensive) plan says for Easton that we're supposed to strive for, which is not making it look like Anywhere, USA," she said.
"I'm still getting blowback from corporate over this design," Snyder responded. "They do not want this brick on their building. … This is an extreme deviation in their mind."
Following Forster and Klein's comments, commission Chair Philip Toussaint and member William Ryall indicated their satisfaction with the updated Zaxbys application. Ryall made the motion for approval, and McAndrews joined the rest of the commission in voting yes despite her concerns.
"I think it's an improvement," Ryall said. "It's not perfect, but nothing ever is."
The Easton Zaxbys is one of three locations developers are pursuing as part of the restaurant's Maryland debut, with the others in Cambridge and Berlin.
The Easton location is projected to open in late 2025 or early 2026, Snyder told The Star Democrat last month.

title: Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.During the meeting, which was held at the college's main campus in Queen Anne's County, the five counties approved a total $9.02 million budget request made by the college for fiscal year 2026. The school's budget is $1.31 million higher than its fiscal year 2025 budget.
Part of the $9.02 million budget request included a $952,560 request for the design of a new technical building. Chesapeake College Vice President for Administrative Services Karen Smith said the new building will have areas for a variety of programs, including agriculture, electrical, welding and fabrication, construction trades and advanced manufacturing. She said the cost for the design phase could be lower depending on state approval.
Although the five counties approved the request for funding for the design, the decision came with a shift in contributions toward the project.
Dorchester County's share of costs for the design phase will be taken on by Queen Anne's County. This means Queen Anne's County's responsibility for the project will jump from 28.9%, or an estimated $275,290, to 47.8%, or an estimated $455,324.
During the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer outlined their council's concerns regarding paying for the project.
Although other counties hope to use the new technical building for career and technical education at the high school level, Dorchester County has a career and technology center it is still paying off, they said.
Through its budget process, Dorchester County has struggled to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
Pfeffer said Dorchester County takes in about $45 million in property and income taxes and will have to give Dorchester County Public Schools $26.6 million for fiscal year 2026.
"So we're trying to run the rest of the county on half of that," he said. "So while in conceptual context, we believe in the project, fiscally our citizens and our staff are saying we don't know how we're going to be able to participate."
At the Chesapeake College meeting, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. shared his county's decision to cover Dorchester County for the project design costs.
"We all know what happens if we let this money go back to the state," Wilson said. "It's going to go somewhere else in this state, and it's not going to be here. We got this far. And Lenny, listen, I feel for you guys. I know what you're going through. But I think we just need to keep it on the rails at least through the design phase and see what the state's going to help with."
According to documents from the meeting, the state will support 75% of project costs, and the counties will support the remaining 25%.
After the counties voted to approve the amended capital budget, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said he understands the position Dorchester County is in, mentioning the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and "unfunded mandates" by the state.
"I think we all understand any one of us could be in your same position very easily," Fithian told the Dorchester County Council members.

 Bay Bridge Cove residents took to the streets in Stevensville to protest a potential Royal Farms development before a Queen Anne's County Planning and Zoning technical meeting April 16.On April 14 and 15 preceding the meeting, about a dozen residents each day from the 55-and-older community demonstrated outside their neighborhood to oppose the project, said coordinator Teresa Tamburrino.
Traffic in the area is "already contentious," she said.
A county Staff Technical Advisory Committee meeting brought together local and state agencies to discuss technical aspects of the development proposal, including representatives from the Departments of Public Works and Parks and Recreation and the State Highway Administration.
The applicant is proposing to combine three parcels at 336 Romancoke Road (Route 8) in Stevensville for a 5,154-square-foot convenience store, six gasoline fuel islands with 12 fueling positions, and a 1,248-square-foot car wash located at the rear of the convenience store.
The Queen Anne's County Planning Commission previously tabled a decision on the concept plan for another Royal Farms convenience store on Kent Island in December 2022.
The county received extensive public input regarding the project, according to Planning Director Amy Moredock. The room was packed with concerned citizens and surrounding business owners Wednesday.
Major concerns the board continued to address with the developers included traffic impact on Maryland Route 8, entrance and exit access, and architectural issues.
The proposal is not before the County Commissioners for a vote, and due to subsequent comments from the planning commission that must be addressed, the Royal Farms project is not expected to be placed on an agenda for some time, Moredock said.
Bay Bridge Cove residents and members of the Homeowners Association there plan to seek information about a potential county ordinance to prevent gas stations within 500 feet of a day care center, Tamburrino said.
Residents are also compiling data and crash statistics to prepare for the next meeting, according to Tamburrino.
More information and updates can be found on the Planning and Zoning Department section of the county website at qac.org.

 DENTON — Kids enjoyed fun and special prizes at Denton Elementary Thursday for Caroline County Parks and Recreation's flashlight Easter egg hunt.Although the event was postponed from the week prior due to rain, Parks and Recreation program specialist Lynn Davis doesn't think the attendance was affected. Seventy kids aged 3 to 10 participated in the egg hunt, which Caroline County has been hosting the past 10 years.
"We love this. This is what we do it for," Davis said about having kids out for the event.
While traditional Easter egg hunts take place in the daylight, the Caroline County event has an added obstacle for egg hunters — darkness. The annual hunt takes place at dusk, and children use flashlights to help locate eggs on the elementary school's lawn.
Each age group had a special egg to look for. For ages 3 and 4, it was a soccer egg. For ages 5 to 7, it was a camouflage egg, and for ages 8 to 10, it was a football egg.
Each group had a separate time slot to capture the most eggs they could and go after the special egg. When a child found the special egg, they received a special prize, an Easter basket.
The event is fun for the children, but Parks and Recreation employees have fun as well.
"I found different patches of taller grass, leaves, branches and twigs," Parks and Recreations employee Liam Wallace said about hiding the eggs. "I kind of just hid it within those."
"It was just crazy. I wanted to see how happy they were out here, no elbows, no shoving, so safe fun," Halie Readores, another employee, said.
Lynn Zepp, a mother of two, brought her son, Weston, and daughter, Willow, to the egg hunt for their first year of participation.
"It was exciting," Lynn Zepp said. "We just got done with a baseball game, and we rushed over here because we wanted to try out the flashlight egg hunt."
When Weston and Willow were asked if they enjoyed the event, they said they had fun.

title: Easton council rejects Gunsallus' proposal to delay introduction of campaign finance law
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council rejects Gunsallus' proposal to delay introduction of campaign finance law

 April 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 784
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town Council members held a heated discussion Monday on a proposed ordinance mandating campaign finance reporting in town elections.Before the opening Pledge of Allegiance and prayer, council President Frank Gunsallus moved to remove the campaign finance law's introduction from Monday's meeting agenda.
Gunsallus said the law shouldn't be introduced due to current conflicts of interest existing with the town's upcoming election.
Mayor Megan Cook and Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery announced their sponsorship of the ordinance last week. It comes as the town's May 6 election nears, with Gunsallus facing off against current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello in an increasingly heated race. Montgomery, along with Ward 1's Maureen Curry, have publicly endorsed Abbatiello.
On Monday, Gunsallus read a letter he sent to the Attorney General's Office, requesting guidance for how to proceed with the ordinance that he called "retroactive."
Montgomery and town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh, who drafted the ordinance, said the ordinance would not retroactively apply to the May 6 election.
"This won't apply to this election," VanEmburgh said. "If you're thinking about a conflict, there will always be a conflict for all five of you because you will all at some point potentially be running for reelection. This is for a future election."
Gunsallus said he didn't feel comfortable discussing the ordinance without clarification from the attorney general. VanEmburgh said the attorney general has no authority over the town election, later adding it's unlikely the attorney general will offer an official opinion to Gunsallus' request.
When Gunsallus said he would not entertain the ordinance as an agenda item, Montgomery moved to overrule him and was joined by the remaining three council members.
"All we're saying is that we want to move forward with (the ordinance) at a first reading," Curry said.
THE ORDINANCE
As drafted, the ordinance would require candidates to have a treasurer file campaign contribution reports to the town before and after the election. It would also set a maximum $250 contribution limit for all individuals, businesses and organizations, excluding the candidate and their spouse or partner.
Councilmembers shared mixed thoughts.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said it's a "good starting point" but emphasized it needs to use "inclusive language."
Curry said, "not everyone has a spouse" and asked if the limits would apply to other family members. VanEmburgh said as written, other family members would need to adhere to the $250 cap.
Council members agreed to further discuss the ordinance at a workshop May 19. Residents, though, were more steadfast in their concerns during a heated public comment session.
Resident Daniel McBride said the $250 limit "seems a bit arbitrary" and "serves as a barrier to free expression of town voters." McBride and other residents said it would put grassroots or less wealthy candidates at a disadvantage.
Residents also questioned Montgomery and Cook for introducing the ordinance so soon before next month's election, with some labeling it election interference and an attack on Gunsallus' campaign.
"I believe it was done to try to destroy one of the members of the council," Catherine Nobles said.
CAMPAIGN DONATIONS
At the onset of Monday's meeting, Gunsallus asked the council to "follow my lead by disclosing your campaign finances ... with the state." He has been reporting online through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System each January since he was elected.
In the system, the most recent filing from the Friends of Frank Gunsallus shows campaign finances from Jan. 11, 2024 through Jan. 8, 2025.
Montgomery encouraged Gunsallus to report finances from his ongoing campaign.
"I do not understand how you can claim that you have revealed your campaign expenditures in the state when there's nothing there," Montgomery said.
Gunsallus said Monday that transparency is "paramount" and he will continue reporting through the state next January. Tuesday, Gunsallus told The Star Democrat that he's received approximately $16,000 in campaign contributions from 34 donors.
Abbatiello sent a log of campaign donations to the town office Monday.
From Dec. 29, 2024, through Monday, Abbatiello has brought in just over $13,000. More than 70 individual donors are listed, though Abbatiello said he's not releasing their specific donation amounts since "many people donated believing their names and donations would not end up on a list or scrutinized by the public."
"I also think that what's more important than the dollar amount, is that with only a few exceptions, the donors live in Easton," Abbatiello wrote in an email to The Star Democrat. "I'm also not taking any money from a political party or any group with a special interest in town."
In an interview with The Star Democrat's editorial board Tuesday, Gunsallus said the proposed campaign finance ordinance is "nonsensical" and that the town could instead fall in line with state law regarding campaign finance disclosures.
"We don't have to have political theater as we witnessed last night," Gunsallus said.

 CAMBRIDGE — Over the past four months, an atmosphere of concern, frustration and, at times, despair has colored budget meetings in Dorchester County.In mid-April, the Dorchester County Council introduced a $91.96 million proposed operating budget for fiscal year 2026 with proposals to increase taxes. The introduction came after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
At the same time, Dorchester County Public Schools has been working to eliminate a multi-million dollar deficit of its own. At an April budget work session, DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said the district is still $5.59 million in the hole. The district hopes to eliminate the deficit by the Board of Education's May meeting.
To balance and pass these budgets, difficult decisions — like the school district canceling summer school for 2025 and the county increasing 911 fees from $1.50 to $4.25 — have already been made.
"We hate to have to put any of this on the backs of our citizens, but these are state laws that are being passed down as a bandaid for us to pay," County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "And unfortunately we're having to pass it down onto our citizens because we have no other revenue to pay these bills."
WHAT MAKES FY26 DIFFERENT
Dorchester County's proposed operating budget is $10 million more than the fiscal year 2025 budget passed last May. County Manager Jerry Jones said the increases are in part due to new education requirements from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education plan.
Jones said another reason the county has had to increase spending include cost shifts from the state to the county for things like teacher pensions.
In an effort to lessen budget costs, the county sought a waiver for the maintenance of effort for education, which is a law that requires counties to provide as much funding per pupil as was provided in the previous fiscal year. But with a narrow window between the state passing a budget and the waiver's due date, the county had to ask for an extension, which was denied.
"It's disappointing," Jones said. "But at the end of the day, we've got to keep moving forward."
Thompson said Blueprint requirements, like increasing teacher starting salaries, are part of the reason why the school district's budget — which is separate from the county's — has been difficult to balance this year. He said inflation and recurring program costs have also hindered the process.
"No decision is easy," he said. "But I think we're all trying to make the best decision for our students."
Both Jones and Thompson said they don't see the annual budget process getting easier any time soon. Jones said he doesn't see things getting easier unless change is made at the state level.
"I don't see (the budget) easing up in years to come unless some big changes are considered at the general assembly and future sessions," he said. "We'll see how it plays out."
TAX DIFFERENTIALS
One of the proposed changes to balance the county's budget is to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for Cambridge and Hurlock. This would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full property tax rate.
Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said although the county is trying its best to balance the budget, she believes this measure is unfair to Cambridge residents. She said the tax differential essentially returns money to tax payers for "duplicated" services.
Cephas also said Cambridge is growing, which will increase the tax base and bring in more revenue for the county. She said the county should instead look into raising taxes in unincorporated areas that are "a little bit better off."
Jones said he doesn't know what the final budget will look like, but said the council welcomes input.
"We want people to come forward and contribute to this conversation," he said.
Adoption of Dorchester County's budget is slated for May 20. The county's first public budget hearing will be held May 6.
Thompson said the Dorchester County Board of Education has to pass the budget by the end of June, but he hopes the board will pass the budget in May to give staff time to make necessary preparations.

title: Easton introduces proposed $28M budget for FY26
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton introduces proposed $28M budget for FY26

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 367
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Mayor Megan Cook said Easton's fiscal year 2026 budget focuses on transitioning the town out of an era of one-time funding sources and pandemic-related dollars."That period of growth positioned us well, but now we shift our focus to the responsibility of maintaining what we built," Cook said. "This year's budget is lean, focused on sustaining our progress by investing in the essentials."
At Monday's Town Council meeting, Cook presented a balanced draft budget with $28 million in general funds, nearly even with last year's mark. The capital fund budget came in just above $1 million.
Easton's property tax rate will remain the same as it has been since 2008 — 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. The town is projected to bring in around $13.6 million in real property taxes, according to the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, slightly up from last year.
"When you compare tax rates across the region, Easton stands out," Cook said. "We have the second lowest municipal property tax rate among surrounding towns, but we're also the largest community and provide the most comprehensive range of services."
The budget aims to equip town government departments with the necessary tools and training to do their jobs, Cook said. While "it's not exciting as building new things," she said, it's an important focus.
In the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, just above $1 million is allocated for transfer to capital work. That's down from the around $2.2 million mark in fiscal year 2025.
Cook added that areas of government improvement will include adding safety features to town hall, providing leadership training to Easton employees and hiring a new town manager. The town has been without a permanent employee in that role since last August.
Expenditure categories in the draft general fund budget include:
Public safety (police, fire, code enforcement, etc.): $11.5 million.
Public works: $7.1 million.
General government (financial administration, IT, HR, planning and zoning, executive functions, etc): $5.3 million.
Economic development: $503,000.
Recreation: $192,000.
"This year's budget reflects a shift: from growth driven by outside funding to careful maintenance, steady service and smart planning for what comes next," Cook said Monday.
A budget hearing is scheduled for the Town Council's next meeting on May 5. The budget can be accessed online at eastonmd.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=53.

title: Strand Beach project not yet approved for completion
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Strand Beach project not yet approved for completion

 April 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 678
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Small grasses, planted this month, mark something of a turning point for Oxford's Strand Beach, which many residents say has been an eyesore in town since 2023.The new plants are the result of a push by the town for the Strand Beach project's contractor, Underwood and Associates, to finish the job of creating a living shoreline that would prevent erosion and flooding.
Although new grasses have been planted, Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said the town has not yet signed off on final completion of the project, which Underwood and Associates was required to finish by April 19.
"We are analyzing all of the work, and we are working with our regulating agencies, the Army Corps of Engineers and the State of Maryland," Wahl said. "They are assessing it as well and making an evaluation."
The grasses were one part of the contractor's job. Other tasks included lowering the islands on the beach, removing temporary access to the islands and installing a grassy strip along the road to prevent sand from flowing into the road.
The work this month comes after Oxford's previous town manager signed off on the project's completion in June 2024.
At a town meeting in December, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the project had not been completed to the specifications Underwood and Associates originally presented. Commissioner Katrina Greer said she had brought together the Maryland Department of the Environment, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Underwood and Associates and the organizations that funded the project to ensure Underwood and Associates would address the town's concerns.
Wahl said there are a "few concerns" that Underwood and Associate's work this month did not fully bring the project into compliance with the project permit. She said she is working with regulating agencies to complete a list of those concerns.
Although the project is still being evaluated to determine everything was completed, Wahl said the town is looking forward to having this phase of the project complete.
"We're doing everything we can to make sure that its purpose of providing stability on that coastal shoreline is adhered to," she said.
CONCERNS FROM RESIDENTS
The Strand Beach project, which was approved in 2021, has stirred up questions and concerns from residents over the years.
Wahl said she has been meeting with residents on the beach to update them on progress. She said residents have raised concerns about the proximity of the dunes and evergreens to the road.
She said she has made a request to relocate the evergreens out of concern they are too close to the road. Regarding the dunes, Wahl said the town is preparing to install sand fencing to stabilize the area.
For resident Mac Sommerlatte, who lives next to the beach, a significant issue with the project remains.
"This is partially completed," he said.
Sommerlatte, who has been involved with the project since before 2021, said he has a contract with the town, which includes that the bulkhead on his property will be fixed as part of the project. He said only some of the bulkhead has been fixed.
Wahl told The Star Democrat the town's engineer examined the bulkhead on Sommerlatte's area and determined the "whole area has been armored.
"And so there is no concern at all about stability of that location," she said.
Sommerlatte said he and his lawyer are reviewing information and considering filing a lawsuit against the town.
"It's not that I'm railing against anyone," he said. "That's not what I'm trying to do. I just want them to complete the work that they agreed to before they started the project."
Wahl said she had no comment on the potential lawsuit.
THE NEXT PHASE
The town sees the shoreline project as the first phase in addressing the Strand. Wahl said once the town has signed off on the completion of the shoreline project, it plans to move on to raising the road and building a water retention area where the parking lot is.
"We definitely have to do some work to address the stormwater that is pooling on the roadway," Wahl said. "So those are additional phases that the commissioners will be talking about here soon in a public meeting."

St. Michaels commissioners pass ordinance on leaf blowers

 ST. MICHAELS — After a five-year discussion on leaf blowers, the Commissioners of St. Michaels passed an ordinance limiting contractors' use of leaf blowers to certain times and days.Contractors can use leaf blowers from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Mondays through Fridays. The use of leaf blowers on Saturdays, Sundays and federal holidays is now prohibited for contractors.
The ordinance does not apply to residents of St. Michaels. Homeowners working on their own property are allowed to use leaf blowers and other loud equipment from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Friday and 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday and Sunday under town code.
"I'm really happy that the commercial contractors as well as the residents were able to come up with the resolution," Alfred Mercier, commission president, said.
The discussion around leaf blowers has reared its head several times since 2020. It was brought up for consideration in 2023 and again on Jan. 22 of this year.
The discussion Jan. 22 was about whether the town should only allow electric leaf blowers, which make less noise than gasoline-powered leaf blowers. The commissioners ultimately decided not to include language on gas or electric leaf blowers in the ordinance passed Wednesday.
Contractors and St. Michaels public works officials argued gas leaf blowers make their jobs easier. Electric or battery-powered leaf blowers must be charged, which takes time. They also argued that gas-powered leaf blowers are more powerful and help them accomplish their jobs faster.
"We thought it was a very tremendous burden for contractors to go totally out to electric leaf blowers," Mercier said. "So instead of doing that, we put time limitations and also the fact that they will not be able to do any work on weekends now.
"During the week, we lessened the time by an hour each day," he continued. "So we're hoping that will appease a lot of the residents and obviously create a more quiet neighborhood for them, especially on the weekends."

title: Commissioners discuss potential water and sewer issues in Caroline County
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Commissioners discuss potential water and sewer issues in Caroline County

 April 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 609
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the April 15 Caroline County Commissioners meeting, Kia Pierce spoke about her mother's property in Ridgley."My mom's property started flooding with the rain, and she is on a septic, and it's been drained three weeks ago," Pierce said. "But the flooding is causing her septic lines to back up to the point where we cannot flush the toilet, and it's coming through the sinks now."
The discussion prompted the county to consider options for the future of northern Caroline County's water and wastewater infrastructure.
Commission President Travis Breeding said Tuesday that the county has set up a meeting to walk through the neighborhood and look at the drainage on that road.
Breeding also reported he had met with North County Water Authority, the entity behind an agreement for the northern towns in the county established more than a decade ago.
The agreement, which aimed to end the use of failing septic systems in the county's four northernmost municipalities — Goldsboro, Henderson, Marydel and Templeville — established a new sewer system.
Eventually, Greensboro built a new sewage treatment plant because the existing plant was flooding. Greensboro's plant began to serve Goldsboro residents after the upgrade.
Rates for Greensboro's waste water treatment have been rising rapidly, commissioners said, and residents of Goldsboro have had issues with the rates.
"Essentially under the the current agreement, those municipalities really don't have any say in the operation of the plant," Breeding said. "The rates that they pay or any real input into the maintenance operation and they're kind of just silent re-payers."
Tuesday, the county weighed whether to continue to have Greensboro's plant serve residents of other towns or whether to set up a county-run wastewater treatment plant at the north end of the county.
"We discussed each individual town having their own system or plant, which we believe is probably cost prohibitive, and we put them in a situation where they would all be competing with operators or competing to find an operator to operate the plant for them," Breeding said. "We also discussed option where there was one plant to service all three towns, Henderson, Marydell and Templeville. And what that would look like would either be the establishment of an authority or the county potentially stepping in and managing the plant for them."
While all options are on the table, Breeding presented this to the commissioners not expecting a definitive response.
"My question is just throwing this all out there for you guys to think about. I guess we don't need an answer right now, but is it time that Caroline County got into the water and sewer business or start to investigate that?" Breeding asked.
The commissioners concluded that if they were to consider an agreement with the towns to run their own water and sewage facility, the commissioners would need to go through multiple hurdles to do so.
"I'm certainly willing to talk about it," Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "My concern is if we want to talk about an exponential jump in costs and start operating a wastewater treatment plant, that's a whole different ballgame."
"The only way I would entertain it is if the people connected covered the cost to operate it," Breeding said. "If it's not a cost-effective, if there's not enough grant money that can be obtained, then it's tough to go. But I wouldn't want to subsidize it with any money from the rest of the county."
The commissioners plan to reach out to the Greensboro Town Council and see if the town is willing to push its wastewater treatment out of town limits. If the town is not willing, Henderson, Marydel and Templeville will need some sort of plant to service those residents.

title: Easton election: Gunsallus, Abbatiello weigh in on housing, growth and more
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton election: Gunsallus, Abbatiello weigh in on housing, growth and more

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town Council president candidates Frank Gunsallus and Don Abbatiello both recognize the need to monitor and manage Easton's growth, but they each indicated different strategies on how to do so in editorial board interviews with The Star Democrat this week.Gunsallus, the incumbent, is being challenged by Abbatiello, the current Ward 2 councilmember. Voters head to the polls May 6 to decide the council's next leader, as well as representatives for the second and fourth wards.
During the interviews, both candidates were asked how to tackle Easton's affordable housing issue.
Gunsallus noted one of his priorities is to vote down an inclusionary zoning ordinance town leaders have expressed mixed opinions on. Instead, he said methods like removing impact fees or marking down land should be considered.
"It's a lot simpler than it's being made out to be," Gunsallus said. "Those are very straightforward, simple ways that can be done very soon to make that happen."
Abbatiello said the main issue with the lack of affordable homes is the rising price of land. He said incentivizing developers to build "middle housing" options is a solution.
"How do you get that price of land out of the equation? You have townhouses," Abbatiello said. "And townhouses become your starter home for people."
The current Ward 2 representative added that his vote against the Gannon Range project on Matthewstown Road in 2022 stemmed from the high prices of those homes.
"It was bringing us $450,000, $500,000 homes, which is not something that we needed," he said.
Gunsallus pointed out he's asked for the Town Council to have more say in approving housing projects. At a February workshop, Gunsallus and others led a discussion of how the council has only approved 37% of the town's 1,000 housing units in the pipeline at the time.
ENVISIONING THE FUTURE
The town is in the early process of revising its comprehensive plan for the first time in 15 years. The Planning Commission is currently reviewing drafts of the new plan, which lays out a vision for how the town should prioritize its growth.
Abbatiello said that in 2010, Easton was aiming to draw developers into town, but now the focus has changed.
"Tap the brakes, we need to slow down," he said of the current thought process.
The town's current comprehensive plan calls for 1% year-to-year growth. Gunsallus says he's "of the school of thought that that 1% is the ceiling, and we should not be exceeding that."
"When I graduated high school here in 2006, the town was literally half the size population-wise that it is now," he said. "So if we continue that same rate of growth, in 20 years, we'll have almost 40,000 people here."
REPRESENTING RESIDENTS
Candidates were asked questions concerning constituent representation. Gunsallus said he's given underrepresented groups a voice since being elected, such as when he voted to remove a 10-cent paper bag fee, a measure that narrowly fell short.
"That stemmed directly from a conversation with a room full of people about, 'I count my pennies when I go shopping so I can buy bags because my food stamps don't cover the cost of bags,'" Gunsallus said.
Abbatiello said if elected, he would push for each ward to have quarterly meetings. He said follow-up is critical, such as when he helped Ward 2 residents who raised concerns about safely walking to Walmart and Giant.
"I was annoying in saying, 'There needs to be a sidewalk on Elliott Road,'" Abbatiello said.
LEADERSHIP
With an election cycle that's become increasingly heated, both candidates offered thoughts on the responsibility of the council president and the disagreements that come with serving on the council.
"You can be the most amazing council president in the world, but if you can't get there with the rest of the council members, then you're going to lose every single vote that comes up," Abbatiello said.
"Sometimes you are not even part of the issue, but you still have to mediate or at least navigate the conversation," Gunsallus said. " ... Let's find common ground and go from there."
Gunsallus said it's been an honor to serve in the role since 2023.
"I'm happy with what has occurred under my administration, and I am looking forward to continuing the good work for another four years," Gunsallus said.
Abbatiello acknowledged serving on the council isn't an easy job, but he said it's an enjoyable one.
"You wonder if you're making the right decision," Abbatiello said. "But at the same time, I am still glad that over the last six years I've had the opportunity to make those decisions. And I wouldn't trade it for anything."

title: EDITORIAL: Our pick for Town Council president: Don Abbatiello
author: Staff Writer
content:
EDITORIAL: Our pick for Town Council president: Don Abbatiello

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 698
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the two-person race for Easton Town Council president, the Star Democrat recommends a vote for Don Abbatiello. We believe his leadership style is more conducive to getting things done within the give-and-take framework of the council.This was not an easy decision for our editorial board to make. Both candidates have strengths. We think the Town Council will accomplish more in the coming four years with Abbatiello at the helm than we would see if his opponent, Frank Gunsallus, is elected. Abbatello has shown signs of a more balanced leadership approach, critical in the current climate.
In his answers to questions that the Star Democrat submitted to all candidates, Abbatiello captured why he is our pick.
"Good leadership is about teamwork," Abbatiello said. "No matter how strong your ideas are, they won't move forward without support from your fellow council members."
In the past year and a half Gunsallus has shown signs he needs a broader approach to the Town Council decision-making. He has repeatedly alienated his fellow council members with an autocratic leadership style, pointed out here in previous editorials. Each time we suggested he learn from his experience.
We believe the problem with Gunsallus is how he goes about leading meetings. In a recent council meeting, he attempted to change the agenda prior to the start of the meeting. The item legitimately could have been discussed and tabled if proper protocol and order were followed. Instead, Gunsallus gaveled the meeting to order and announced he was removing the item from the agenda until he received an opinion from the state attorney general's office. It came before the standing item to approve the agenda when such requests are considered. It caused unnecessary discord and distraction.
The result: The council members unanimously overruled the decision by the council president. This is highly unusual on such a procedural issue and one example of what concerns us about Gunsallus' leadership style.
Time and time again we have seen Gunsallus advance an idea but fail to move it forward. The Town Council president needs to be a more of a leader. Leaders get people to follow, allow for dissension and are about motivating others to pursue an objective. There have been numerous times when Gunsallus has his say and then attempts to cut off other council members when they attempt to voice their opinions. This leadership style needs improvement.
In another example early in his tenure as president, Gunsallus attempted to push a delay on a moratorium of cannabis dispensaries in Easton. His methods sparked heated exchanges with council members. Ward 4 Councilman Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. voiced worry with how the situation was handled.
"... We have never had such a dialogue that we had tonight regarding issues and concerns," he said. "That dialogue — I'm quite concerned about things that have been said, I've never seen this on this council in all my days."
Voters in the May 6 election have seen the contrasting styles of the two candidates. So let's get to the reasons why we are supporting Abbatiello. His top issues: smart development, public safety and fiscal responsibility. Abbatiello was the candidate who offered more specific plans — targeted incentives to developers — to create more houses in the $250,000 to $350,000 price range, which are desperately needed in Easton.
He talked about updating the 15-year-old city comprehensive plan that sets the priorities guiding development in Easton.
One thing we wanted to hear candidates talk about was reducing the property tax rate on homeowners. Both candidates boasted that the tax rate for Easton has not increased in more than 15 years. They both acknowledged that soaring property values puts more and more money in the city coffers. Yet neither suggested in our interviews reducing the property tax rate. That's what we wanted to hear. We suggest either winner consider this option.
We want to see progress in Easton. We want to see the status quo challenged and a recognition of lingering issues of equity for all residents of the city. We want a cohesive town council that allows disagreement while making progress on issues. We think Don Abbatiello is the candidate to deliver a better future for the town. We urge voters to elect him on May 6.

title: Challenge to Oxford candidates
author: Staff Writer
content:
Challenge to Oxford candidates

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 361
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I applaud the joint actions being proposed by Easton's Mayor Cook and Councilmember Montgomery to address the need for developing campaign finance disclosure guidelines. In fact, in the interest of transparency, it's a matter which I feel needs to be addressed to benefit our citizens here in Oxford.In June 2022, following about 12 years of service on Oxford's Historic District Commission, I campaigned for the position of commissioner and was elected. My only expense was the production of a two-sided flyer (total cost of $238.36 with tax), which I personally distributed door to door.
How times have changed. What brought this campaign finance issue to light for me was what I observed during our recent elections, and that troubled me greatly. The proliferation of campaign signs that were displayed along the Oxford Road on the approach into town reminded me of the signage along 1-95 advertising South of the Border. And I recall someone who described the sequential rhyming signs as being reminiscent of Burma-Shave highway ads along Route 66.
In addition to the elaborate signage throughout our town, additional expenses such as customized glossy flyers, brochures, website design and even a pre-election private event at a local restaurant are now a part of the Oxford election fabric. Doesn't all of this beg the question: How many tens of thousands of dollars were spent, and where did that money come from?
Here's some food for thought:
Should a commissioner's seat be influenced by the highest bidder?Should a candidate who fails to disclose their supporters' contributions merit the privilege of trust?
In my opinion, the answer to both of these questions is an emphatic "no," and I believe other readers will wholeheartedly agree.
I have placed my name in nomination for our upcoming town election on the June 17, hoping to continue my service to our citizens. My plan is to continue with a grassroots approach. Even though it's not a current requirement, I will be maintaining a list of expenditures and contributions (to include in-kind donations), which I'll be glad to share in the interest of full disclosure. If any other candidates decide to run for this seat, I challenge them to do the same.
TOM COSTIGAN
Oxford

 EASTON — Childlene Brooks and Kenley Timms were honored Friday for their outstanding community service.During a Talbot Day ceremony, an annual celebration for the county's April 25 birthday, the county presented Brooks with the Lifetime Service Award and Timms with the Ripple Effect Award.
Brooks is manager of the Brookletts Place Senior Center, and Timms serves as commander of VFW Post 5118.
Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Keasha Haythe spoke on the impact of the winners' work in the Talbot County community.
"Childlene's name is synonymous with service to Talbot County," Mielke said. "Through her leadership at Brookletts Place, her tireless volunteerism, she's guided, mentored and uplifted generations. Her service has not only filled gaps, but has built bridges."
"A Vietnam veteran and longtime VFW commander, Kenley's legacy is one of action and compassion," Haythe said. "Whether organizing welcome-home parades, helping homeless veterans, supporting first responders, or simply showing up for those in need, Kenley leads with heart. His efforts have not only made a difference, they've inspired movement."
Brooks volunteers for nonprofit organizations along with leading the Brookletts Place in its mission to serve the county's growing senior population. Timms recently organized a Welcome Home parade for Vietnam veterans and families, an event that brought hundreds to the streets of Easton.
A 1983 proclamation originally declared April 25 as the county's birthday. The County Council led a charge to reinvigorate Talbot Day by signing a new proclamation to create the holiday in 2023.
In all, the county recognized 17 nominees for community service, part of the new tradition.
Haythe noted that the county created the award ceremony to continue the tradition of a now-defunct state program dating back to the 1980s, which honored community service leaders.
"Although the statewide program ended in 2022, the Talbot County Council chose to carry the tradition forward," Haythe said. "We renamed it the Talbot Citizen and Service Awards, continuing its legacy of recognizing those who give their time and heart to our community."
Talbot Day also brought around 100 residents to the lawn of the Talbot County Courthouse to celebrate the county's history. Mike Mielke, a local farmer, waterman and historian, served as Friday's guest speaker.
Mielke said a range of local organizations, schools and volunteer groups make Talbot County a special place to live. He pointed out towns such as Oxford, St. Michaels and Easton for bringing a unique way of life to the Eastern Shore as well as being a "mecca for weddings."
And for unincorporated areas such as Tilghman Island or Neavitt, Mielke said it's a neat mix of residents.
"The people do get along, the newcomers and watermen and stuff," Mielke said. "They get along pretty darn well."
"It's still the land of pleasant living," Mielke said of Talbot County. "Talbot's my home, and I love it."
