title: Cambridge City Council calls on county for tax differential
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge City Council calls on county for tax differential

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Following the introduction of Dorchester County's draft fiscal year 2026 budget, the Cambridge City Council is requesting a more equitable approach to taxes.In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials, or lower property tax rate, for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
During the meeting, Cambridge Commissioner Brian Roche said the council understands the county is facing budget problems that have been brought on by "unfunded mandates" from the state.
"We're sympathetic to those challenges," Roche said. "However, the solution cannot be to place an even greater burden on Cambridge."
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
Roche said the tax differential is essentially the county acknowledging Cambridge and Hurlock pay for many of their own services — like public safety and water and sewer — so the county doesn't have to.
Roche estimated that with the county's budget proposals — which include an increase of 3 cents to the real property tax for all county residents — Cambridge residents would face a 11.15% increase on their county tax bill. He said Hurlock would face an increase of about 12%.
Roche said county residents who do not live in Cambridge or Hurlock would face a 3% increase.
"It's not equitable to ask for us to take a bigger slice of this pie when there's other areas they're not asking for them to do their share," Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said.
Before the City Council voted to adopt the resolution, Commissioner Brett Summers said he has been talking about the tax differential since his campaign. He said he has been advocating for the hiring of a consultant to determine what the "right" tax rate is.
"And I think what that'll result in doing is reduce the tax rate that city residents pay but ... increase the tax rate that county residents pay," he said, "... because we're not trying to reduce the revenue coming into the county, we're just trying to have a fair and equitable allocation of taxes bases on services provided."
Commission President Sputty Cephas agreed with Roche and Lajan Cephas, saying that he understands the county's situation, but the city is providing services that would otherwise fall on the county's plate. He said there needs to be a "fair and equitable" solution.
"So how we get there, I'm open to it," he said. "But as of right now, I'm in support of (the resolution)."

title: Federalsburg council member: misuse of town funds brought to state prosecutor
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg council member: misuse of town funds brought to state prosecutor

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 429

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Town of Federalsburg announced on Facebook Tuesday morning it had investigated allegations of misappropriation of town funds.The investigation was conducted by the mayor and the council. They learned of town funds being used to purchase personal items, financial errors costing the town to spend money, personnel policies that were not followed, inappropriate purchases and employees engaging in inappropriate discussions in the workplace, the post said.
"The Town was reimbursed for the personal and inappropriate purchases and the interim town manager is working to rectify and improve personnel and financial management of the town," the town said.
While the internal investigation was completed, District 1 Councilwoman Brandy James said she reported the investigation findings to the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, where she said the investigation is ongoing.
"It was only me who went to the office of the state prosecutor and said, 'Hey, this is what's going on in the town and has been historically happening,' So, they got involved, and they started to investigate like toward the end of February into March. It's to my knowledge they're still investigating," James said.
James said the fiscal year budget of 2024 brought attention to some of these issues.
"So a lot of what's going on is historical misuse of funds, it's historical stuff," James said. "Since I have gotten there, it has always been a rush to pass the budget. There was things in the budget that just did not add up. There was line items to pay somebody to cut grass for a crazy amount of money."
According to James, toward the end of November 2024 she received a complaint from a individual about misuse of funds in the town office and the alleged individual wanted the complainant fired.
James said she immediately reached out to town leadership and suggested they call a meeting to discuss the allegations further.
"Everybody on the dias said, 'Oh, we have holiday plans, we have this.' I was put off again. So we never got around to addressing the allegations until we had a meeting in January," she said.
Through closed session meetings that followed, the town ultimately decided to let go a member of the town staff, James said.
"While we feel it is important that our citizens are aware of the issues the Town faces, we have decided to not release the specific complaints received at this time to avoid the risk of liability for releasing confidential personnel information," the Town said in the Facebook statement.

"Everybody's doing all their great things in their towns, but we don't always reach over to the next town, and I don't know why that is. So as chamber director that serves the whole county, my goal is to try to build that communication."
The chamber and county representatives participated in a speed-dating-like event Tuesday. For 10 to 15 minutes, a group of representatives would sit with chamber members and discuss their positions and what they offer to their town or to the county.
After hearing from all sitting at the table, representatives would ask different questions to each other on what they could improve and how to help each other.
Multiple business cards were passed around, and connections were made.
"It's giving those businesses more resources," Snyder said. "It's also giving the businesses more resources within our county that they may not know exist. So that's really what it's all about.
"I feel like the chamber is a conduit. That's really our role. We connect others together through networking, marketing and things like this."
Multiple county representatives attended the event and enjoyed the conversation and feedback that was given about the work in the county.
"I mean it's good to interact with the community and the towns to get feedback from them," said county Commissioner Frank Bartz. "The department head directors communicating what they do on a day-to-day basis, which they might not know, and they get to put a face with somebody they haven't met yet. So, that gives them a little bit of a one-on-one to where they can feel free to contact them. They don't feel like, 'Oh, I don't want to bother anybody.' So, that's good on that end of that."

title: Cambridge city manager presents balanced draft budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge city manager presents balanced draft budget

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A few sentences into introducing Cambridge's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget, City Manager Glenn Steckman told those at a Cambridge City Council meeting April 28 that the city is financially stable."And I think that's very important," he said. "That does not mean that challenging times may not be in the city's future. However, we should look at the glass as half full."
During the meeting, Steckman detailed the city's proposed balanced $18 million general fund budget and discussed the city's four enterprise funds, which include sewer, marina, water and special projects funds.
Steckman called the fiscal year 2026 budget a "transitional budget" as COVID-19 relief funding through the American Rescue Plan Act comes to an end.
"This year's budget preparation included transitioning away from the ARPA funds," Steckman said. "These are once-in-a-generation funds that allow the city to pay salaries, support capital projects and fund nonprofit donations."
GENERAL FUND
According to the draft general fund budget, the city expects to bring in $9.84 million in taxes at the same tax rate it did last year, 80 cents per $100 of assessed value. With no plans to raise taxes, the city's budget stands in contrast with the county's.
In mid-April, the Dorchester County Council introduced a $91.96 million proposed operating budget for fiscal year 2026 with proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
In Cambridge, the proposed general fund budget includes a 3% raise for all city employees except Steckman and additional $3,000 raises for those in the police department so the positions stay competitive in the marketplace.
Steckman said the budget includes four new positions: a public information officer, code officer, housing adviser and GIS technician.
Steckman said the housing adviser will act as an advocate for renters in Cambridge.
CAPITAL PROJECTS
Although the city is not facing the same kinds of budget concerns the county is facing, Steckman said the city has $23 million in capital needs. He said the city will seek grants to help address this but that probably won't be enough.
Currently, the city has budgeted $2.1 million for capital projects in fiscal year 2026.
Steckman said the mayor and commissioners will "seriously" have to look into borrowing or obtaining a bond of $1.5 million to replace the HVAC system at the city's public safety complex on Washington Street and at least $8 million to renovate the historic city hall on Gay Street.
"We cannot get grants or anywhere enough grants to offset these costs," Steckman said. "And these costs are only rising each year that we don't address them."
Steckman said the city will begin setting times to meet with City Council about the budget.

title: Groundbreaking ceremony held for Tides at River Marsh housing project in Cambridge
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Groundbreaking ceremony held for Tides at River Marsh housing project in Cambridge

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 547
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Local and state leaders mingled on the lawn in front of the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina Tuesday for a long-awaited groundbreaking ceremony.A gentle breeze blew over those gathered, a contrast to the headwinds the project has faced in recent years.
"This has been a long haul, but we've done it," Fairchild Properties President Charlie Fairchild said about Tides at River Marsh.
Fairchild Properties is the developer behind Tides at River Marsh, a residential community located on the Hyatt property that is expected to bring 619 new townhomes, villas and single-family homes to Cambridge.
Mentioning rising interest rates, Fairchild said it took three "long" years to get a shovel in the ground for this project. Hyatt General Manager Shane Nicolopoulos said the addition of these homes to the Hyatt property has been in the works for decades.
"And how awesome is this?" he asked. "We are so excited, and I'm sure you felt it driving into the resort and seeing the progress that has taken place so quickly."
Although the groundbreaking ceremony was held April 29, the developers and builders started work on the project Dec. 30, Fairchild said. Currently, 75 homes are under construction with a plan to build 150 homes in the first phase and another 150 homes in the second phase.
In an interview, Fairchild said he expects in the next four months, about 80% to 90% of the first phase of homes should be built. He said they plan to begin the second phase in about two months.
Once complete, the first two phases of the project are expected to bring in roughly $2.5 million in property taxes for the city, county and state. Fairchild said the city is projected to bring in $1 million on the 300 homes, the county is projected to bring in $1.2 million and the state is expected to bring in $300,000.
This increase to the tax base is particularly significant for Dorchester County as it faces a difficult budget process.
"One of the biggest problems we have with Dorchester County is our failure to increase the tax the base, which is shown this year with us having to increase the tax rates," Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said. "And that's just what we need."
Fairchild said he expects the entire project of 619 houses to be completed in five years and be worth $300 million. He said approximately 40 houses have been sold so far, with the highest sale coming in at $580,000. Listing prices start in the low $300,000s for townhomes, at $400,000 for villas and at $450,000 and up for single-family homes.
The groundbreaking ceremony brought local and state officials to the Hyatt, including Maryland Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas.
Day said he is excited for families to move into these new homes, invest in the community and contribute to the economy.
"It's an incredible thing, and it's precisely what we need to be doing in every corner of this state," he said.
Hutchinson said his mantra as a state delegate is "to make a beautiful place to live even better."
"Oh my, have you made a beautiful place to live even better," he said to the developers and builders. "Congratulations."

title: Easton Town Council candidates make their cases at town hall
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton Town Council candidates make their cases at town hall

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 756
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With the election less than a week away, voters had the chance Tuesday to ask Town Council candidates a number of questions about issues facing Easton, including fiscal responsibility and housing.During a town hall hosted by The Talbot Spy and the Avalon Foundation Tuesday night, all seven candidates for three spots on the council made their pitches to voters.
For the council president seat, incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello will square off.
With Abbatiello opting to run for president, a new resident will assume the Ward 2 seat. In that race, Lynnette Keefe and Robert Rankin will face off.
The Ward 4 race will present voters with three options: incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, who has served in the seat since 2020; Moonyene Jackson-Amis, previously Ward 4's representative from 2001 to 2008; and newcomer Cameron Keefe.
Gunsallus and Abbatiello, along with other candidates, spoke about the town's budgetary outlook. The town's proposed budget for fiscal year 2026 is $28 million and includes a real property tax rate of 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. That mark hasn't changed since 2008.
One resident asked whether the candidates would consider a property tax rate cut given increasing property values, which have caused residents' tax bills go up.
Gunsallus said he would consider it and that it has been discussed by the council. He said the town could work on increasing the number of business to bring in more commercial tax revenue.
He added that since joining the council in 2023, he's pushed for detailed reviews of the town's budget.
"Through my direction, this council has done something that it hasn't done in at least 30 years," Gunsallus said, "and that is go line by line, every single line, in the $28 million budget to be just that: responsible stewards of the town's money."
Abbatiello said during this year's budget discussions, he was against a property tax rate hike. He said a tax break is dependent upon the town's fiscal need.
"If we can afford to reduce taxes, great. I'm all in favor of that," Abbatiello said. "I don't think we should just automatically say we're cutting taxes. We need to also look at other revenue sources."
Abbatiello said he's focused on keeping the Easton Volunteer Fire Department a volunteer organization — since a shift to paid would be "one of the biggest tax increases this town will ever see."
Ward 4's Cameron Keefe advocated for the town to continue funding its police department at a high level. He said he's "absolutely immovable" on fiscal transparency.
"I would like to — and I might be shooting myself in the foot — strike fear into the hearts of our representatives and let them know, the money we're spending is not ours," Keefe said. "We have to have the people of Easton's best interests in mind."
HOUSING
During both the moderated and open question portions of the town hall, the need for more affordably priced homes was mentioned. Candidates offered different ideas to tackle the dilemma.
Jackson-Amis said the town should "hold the developers responsible" by requiring a percentage of units be affordable. She vouched for smart growth, and said the Town Council should have more say in approving housing projects.
"We need to be very strategic in what it is we desire, and then how that can be implemented," Jackson-Amis said. "But the council is accountable for that. We're responsible. It's not the Planning Commission."
Davis has lobbied for that same increase in council involvement. Tuesday, he told residents the town should buy land and partner with a housing developer or nonprofit.
"So, therefore, the people who work at Wawas can get a house that's around $200,000 because the town has purchased property," Davis said. "I think we need to make that kind of investment for affordable housing in the Town of Easton, and we will meet the needs of the individuals in the community."
Ward 2 candidate Lynn Keefe emphasized the town should be thinking "outside of the box" when it comes to addressing housing and infrastructure problems.
"I really feel like we need to work on our green space here," she said. "We need to look at different parts of housing, not just affordable housing through the government, but also sustainable neighborhoods."
Rankin, Lynn Keefe's opponent, said development is the most common issue he hears from residents. Rankin said it's important to attract health care professionals and young people to Easton while also keeping an eye on growth.
"It's really important that we properly manage these developments that are coming on to make sure that those potential concerns are mitigated," Rankin said.

title: Ward 4 candidates talk property taxes, housing
author: Konner Metz
content:
Ward 4 candidates talk property taxes, housing

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 734
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Candidates for the Ward 4 seat on the Easton Town Council have offered varying opinions on the town's property tax rate.Incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, Moonyene Jackson-Amis and Cameron Keefe are squaring off in the town's election May 6. Each discussed their views on property taxes, housing and more in interviews with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week.
Currently, the town levies a tax on real property at 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. That mark hasn't changed since 2008. It's higher than Talbot County's other towns, but relatively low compared to Eastern Shore towns such as Cambridge, Denton and Salisbury.
Property values, though, have increased significantly in recent years. The state's 2025 reassessments showed the value of Group 1 residential and commercial properties in Talbot County increased by 22.1% from 2022. The town's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget projects $13.6 million in real property tax revenue, slightly up from last year. It was a tight and "lean" budget, Mayor Megan Cook has said.
Davis, who's been on the council since 2020, said the property tax rate should be increased.
"I think the mayor's playing around a little bit. … They're not fiscally responsible," Davis said. "We have not raised taxes, and here's the problem. We got that COVID money. We've been living high on the hog, and now we have to pay the piper."
Jackson-Amis, Ward 4's representative from 2001 to 2008, says the Town Council should have conversations with professionals about potential tax breaks.
"I think the property tax is a little steep," Jackson-Amis said. "It seems like the idea is to get, to have a money funnel. A funnel as opposed to exacting what's necessary to support the budget."
Keefe in his interview emphasized fiscal responsibility, while adding he understands new initiatives cost money.
"They make a lot of decisions that don't affect their wealth, but it affects everybody else's wealth," Keefe said of the council. " ... We need to dismantle this ivory tower thing."
HOUSING
The Ward 4 hopefuls each touched on plans to improve Easton's affordable housing stock. Keefe said "we need to make Easton not just survivable, but livable."
"We can say all the buzz words we want, but I would love to see specifically starter homes in Easton, things that draw young families here," Keefe said.
He said he hopes to sit down with town planners to discuss their proposed inclusionary zoning ordinance that would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable.
Jackson-Amis says she's "all for inclusionary zoning." She hopes to revisit the requirement that developers include 25% low or middle-income units in projects, an effort she supported in her prior stint on the council.
"If you're getting a benefit from the town, we need to be able to exact a benefit from you," Jackson-Amis said. "If you're creating housing, we ought to know what our housing needs are, and that it shouldn't just be for the financial gain of wealthy people."
Davis said he's "not 100% sure" current housing legislation in the works will answer all of Easton's housing needs. He advocated for the town to buy a piece of land and work with nonprofits.
"The town should buy a piece of land," Davis said. "And the town should partner with Habitat (for Humanity) or some other organization to … ensure that we deal holistically with the person and the property."
EXPERIENCE
The Ward 4 candidates bring different experience levels to the table.
Davis, 58, said he focused on constituent representation during his time on the council, such as when he supported a seafood odor ordinance last year.
"I'm in the position as the council member because of the people," he said. "I represent those individuals in my ward. I'm not the end-all, be-all. So if my constituents say that this is what they want, then I represent them well."
Jackson-Amis, 77, said "we should look toward wisdom."
"Right now you need people with some seasoned ability to ferret out issues and help bring solutions to problems," she said. "So I don't think age really should be that important, but I think the experience is what should matter."
Keefe, 25, said he wants more youth involvement in the town.
"I know I'm young. That is by no means any reason to take this lightly," Keefe said. "I think this is important. I think there's a lot of potential for good that can happen from this. And above all of those things, I want to be a representative who listens."

title: Keefe, Rankin discuss growth, businesses and more ahead of Ward 2 election
author: Konner Metz
content:
Keefe, Rankin discuss growth, businesses and more ahead of Ward 2 election

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — May 6, residents in Easton's 2nd ward will head to the polls to choose a new representative. Current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello is running for Town Council president.Lynn Keefe and Robert Rankin are running for the open seat. In interviews with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week, Keefe and Rankin discussed a need to control growth in Easton.
Keefe said the town's pipeline of approved projects — which recently included around 1,000 housing units — could negatively impacts schools and infrastructure.
"Apartments and apartments and apartments — lots of them coming, without really taking into consideration schooling, and roads and things like that that are really going to be affected," Keefe said.
Keefe said it is possible to address housing needs while managing growth. She worries the influx of apartment projects may result in a large number of unoccupied units.
"It's going to come back to bite you," she said.
In regards to the town's comprehensive plan, which lays out a vision for how the town should prioritize its growth, Rankin said he prefers "slower growth."
The current plan, which hasn't been updated since 2010, calls for 1% year-to-year growth. It is in the draft stages of being revised by the town's planning department and commission.
Rankin said he doesn't see annexation — which has been used by the town to facilitate future housing developments — as an "apparent" need.
"I am pretty comfortable with the footprint of Easton currently, and I think we have enough space within the town for redevelopment purposes, for refurbishing, to meet the needs of immediate future development," Rankin said.
BUSINESSES
Both candidates offered thoughts on how to support local businesses.
Keefe, who owned a small business in Virginia for 18 years, said Easton has less red tape than where she operated her business. But she says Easton can still reduce some obstacles to help business owners.
"We need to make it a little bit easier for people. So many hoops," she said.
Meanwhile, Rankin said it's important to improve pedestrian safety and prevent potential accidents in order for residents to feel comfortable walking to downtown businesses.
"I think there is an opportunity in Easton to have some more pedestrian-friendly interventions to make it easier for folks to feel comfortable walking around, and crossing streets and walking among traffic," Rankin said.
PROPERTY TAXES
While Easton's real property tax rate has remained even at 52 cents per $100 of assessed value since 2008, property values have significantly increased.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook proposed a fiscal year 2026 budget last month that would keep the property tax rate the same. The budget projects $13.6 million in real property tax revenue, slightly up from FY25.
Keefe and Rankin were asked their takes on the property tax dilemma.
Keefe said the town should keep spending under control and be cognizant of the potential impacts of tax hikes.
"You don't want to tax your people to death where they have to move," Keefe said. "I have an elderly couple at church, they're concerned. They're living on social security. They're concerned about if it gets too much higher, 'We're going to have to move.' And I think that's a travesty."
Rankin said due to this year's tight budget, a property tax increase is a "real topic" of conversation.
"While we don't want to just raise taxes unnecessarily, if we want to deliver the services that residents want and need, that is a serious consideration we're going to have to make," Rankin said.

title: Stronger together: Rebuilding Together wraps up Rebuilding Month with appreciation lunch
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Stronger together: Rebuilding Together wraps up Rebuilding Month with appreciation lunch

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Wrapping up National Rebuilding Month and celebrating its first appreciation lunch following its merger, Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore recognized volunteers and supporters at the Centreville United Methodist Church April 26.Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore provides free, critical home repairs for income eligible homeowners in Kent and Queen Anne's counties the whole month of April kicked projects into high gear to provide vital repair needs across the area, completing six projects including fresh off of two that very Saturday, said co-President Larisa Thomas.
Providing more resources and personnel to help more residents, the recent merge of the Kent and Queen Anne's counties departments has made Rebuilding Together even stronger together, Thomas said.
Thomas started as a volunteer swinging a hammer 15 years ago and credited the non-profit as making a difference in local lives.
Before rebranding, Rebuilding Together originated nationally as Christmas in April in 1973 and started in Queen Anne's County in 1994 and in Kent Count in 2004, according to Executive Director Genevieve Croker in a presentation to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners April 22.
Keeping the human aspect along with the housing aspect, Rebuilding Together recognizes everyone has the right to live comfortably, and works to repair homes, revitalize communities, and rebuild lives, Croker said.
All work is done at no cost to the homeowners who meet the income limits and other criteria. Typical projects can include painting, installing ramps and grab bars, repairing floors, plumbing, electrical, and other areas needed to ensure safe and healthy housing for homeowners.
"We say what we're going to do," Community Service Coordinator Cory Palmer said.
Rebuilding Together seeks to establish safe homes and communities for all and addresses the housing crisis by improving property values and preserving affordable housing stock, noting it is often cheaper to repair a home than build a new one and help aging homeowners age in place, Croker said.
Helen Fisher, of Crumpton, was one such homeowner utilizing volunteer services including smoke detector installation, outside lighting installation, and improved home skirting. At the appreciation luncheon, Fisher credited volunteers as professionals who get the job done.
Rebuilding Together welcomes volunteers of all calibers, whether with repairs or behind the scenes fundraising. "There is a role available for you," Thomas said.
Palmer encouraged anyone struggling with home repair costs to apply for services, noting income requirements and guidelines can change.
Volunteer Dan Hercher, of Church Hill, recently celebrated his first completed project with Rebuilding Together. Experienced with repair work, he said he loved seeing the change made to the homes and what it means to the homeowners.
"Some people don't have the tools or resources, so it's nice to help," he said.
More information about Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore can be found at rebuildingtogethereasternshore.org.

title: In visit to Easton, Secretary Day commends county's broadband efforts
author: Konner Metz
content:
In visit to Easton, Secretary Day commends county's broadband efforts

 May 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County's mission to extend broadband to 100% of residents is within reach.During a roundtable discussion Wednesday with Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day, county and broadband leaders said the Connect Talbot broadband initiative has the funding it needs.
"The Connect Talbot project is proof. It's proof that partnerships work," Easton Utilities President and CEO John Horner said. "We're here to say that at this point in time, Talbot County is the first county to be fully funded with enough grant funding to provide service to everyone in the county that does not have service."
Horner said the broadband effort is a "legacy project" and that it is within a year-and-a-half from completion.
Day spoke highly of the county and nonprofit utility company's efforts to connect rural residents with high-speed broadband access.
Day has visited several Eastern Shore counties in recent weeks to tour towns and discuss funding opportunities. Thursday, Day confirmed to Maryland Matters that he's raising money for an "exploratory effort" to challenge U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) in the 1st District that stretches the length of the Eastern Shore.
In Easton Wednesday, Day presented county and Easton Utilities leaders with a $1.1 million check of the grant the department awarded to the project last summer.
"We have been working our tail off to be your partner, to make sure that from Tilghman to Queen Anne to Trappe to Cordova, there is high-speed broadband," Day said. " ... We will make sure you've got the last money you need to get 100%."
According to the Department of Housing and Community Development, Maryland's Office of Statewide Broadband has facilitated $11.1 million in investments for Talbot County.
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, who has been a longtime proponent for broadband infrastructure, said he's heard the calls from residents to focus on increasing internet access.
"I have colleagues and constituents who live not too many miles from here, who told me when I was running for office, you need to pay attention to this issue," Lesher said.
As of March, Easton Utilities and its Easton Velocity service had reached 1,900 subscribers since 2021, according to Easton Utilities communications director Kelly Simonsen.
Horner said the county helped the project get off its feet, and a U.S. Department of Agriculture program was an "enormous stepping stone" to begin serving two-thirds of Talbot County residents.
Five grants from the state helped the project forge ahead, Horner said.

title: Political mailers stir discourse; mayor says Gunsallus claims are 'flat-out false'
author: Konner Metz
content:
Political mailers stir discourse; mayor says Gunsallus claims are 'flat-out false'

 May 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two political mailers from Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and the local Republican committee are stirring discourse, including from Mayor Megan Cook, who said claims made on the flyers are "flat-out false" and insulting.The mailers, which many residents received Thursday, list the Talbot County Republican Central Committee on the authority line. The committee has endorsed Gunsallus in his race against Don Abbatiello for president, as well as candidates Lynn and Cameron Keefe in the Ward 2 and Ward 4 races, respectively.
Both Gunsallus flyers call out the mayor, one stating, "Don't let our out-of-town Mayor and her supporters change the character of Easton." They home in on draft inclusionary zoning legislation — which Cook and town planners have advocated for and Gunsallus opposes — that has not yet been introduced as an ordinance.
Cook told The Star Democrat Friday that multiple statements made by the Gunsallus campaign are false, including the claim Cook recruited three candidates to run in Tuesday's election. Cook said she did not recruit anyone.
"I just think all the claims are ridiculous," Cook said. "They're all misleading or flat-out false."
One sentence states that Cook "and her staff quietly usher in new developments—with little to no public input." The mayor disputed that assertion.
"It's an insult to our staff, who are excellent, and the many volunteers that we have serving on boards and commissions," she said.
Neither Gunsallus nor the Republican Central Committee responded to The Star Democrat's requests for interviews.
This year's council president race is the second in a row during which mailers were sent to residents. In 2023, during a four-person race for the seat, mailers targeted former mayor and then-candidate Bob Willey.
Flyers during that campaign were paid for by Scott R. Wagner, a former Pennsylvania state senator and Talbot County business owner. One featured an image of a diaper and said both politicians and diapers need to be changed.
In an interview Thursday, Abbatiello said this year's flyers are "full of misstatements."
"They are meant to instill fear in residents," Abbatiello said. "They are meant to divide the community. All so that they can win an election."
INCLUSIONARY ZONING
In Thursday's flyers — as well as flyers sent to Ward 4 mail boxes this week by Cameron Keefe and the Republican committee — inclusionary zoning is prominent.
Presented to the Town Council at a February workshop, draft legislation would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable. For ownership developments, the legislation would require inclusionary units meet an affordable price for households making up to 100% of area median income.
The legislation would grant developers that provide inclusionary units on the same site as market-rate units with a 20% density bonus. But the ordinance hasn't been formally introduced. Its next step is a potential recommendation to the council from the town's housing task force.
In an interview earlier this week before the flyers were received, Republican Central Committee Vice Chair Shari Wilcoxon said inclusionary zoning is the "number one thing in this whole race." She said if passed, it could hurt property values.
"In my opinion, every single person who owns property in this town, Republican or Democrat, ought to be concerned," she said.
"I am of the full belief that the mayor, it's her bill," Wilcoxon said. "She tried to get it through before, but didn't have the votes, so it somehow got tabled until after the election."
Gunsallus has made clear his opposition to inclusionary zoning. In an interview with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week, he said defeating inclusionary zoning is one of his top three priorities.
Regarding the legislation, a Gunsallus mailer reads: "I am the only Councilmember who has vocally opposed the current Inclusionary Zoning bill, which will allow (and effectively require) high-density housing in each and every neighborhood."
In a fact check post on the town's website Friday afternoon, the town clarified the bill would only affect new developments or redeveloped properties with seven or more residential units. It also addressed other claims made by candidates during this election cycle.
Councilmember David Montgomery has also expressed his opposition publicly. Montgomery has endorsed Abbatiello and cited Abbatiello's concerns over the legislation as a reason for supporting him.
"I think neither of us sees the inclusive zoning ordinance as the best way of going out and providing affordable housing," Montgomery said last month.
Abbatiello, who was questioned at a candidate town hall Tuesday about his unclear stance on inclusionary zoning, said Thursday he doesn't think it's the answer.
"I think there's other things that we can do, and I've said that repeatedly," he said. "But again, I wasn't going to make a decision without hearing all the information."

title: Poor judgment, lack of transparency

 If one needed further proof of Frank Gunsallus' lack of fitness for reelection to the presidency of the Town Council, view online his performance at the April 21 council meeting.I'm referring to his handling of a vote for discussion of a draft ordinance regarding future campaign finance regulations. He refused adding it the agenda because of his unfounded belief that it would affect this year's election, even though the town attorney had repeatedly corrected him. While publishing such information is voluntary, contrast this with Mr. Abbatiello who has provided a list of donors to town authorities to make it available to the public.
You can determine how to characterize this behavior, but to me it illustrates, poor judgment, lack of transparency and manipulation or misstatement of facts. Not the character of a person we need to lead the Easton Town Council.

title: Rankin and Davis: The Star Democrat's picks for Wards 2 and 4
author: Staff Writer
content:
Rankin and Davis: The Star Democrat's picks for Wards 2 and 4

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Star Democrat recommends votes for Robert Rankin in the Ward 2 Easton Town Council Election and for the Rev. Elmer Davis in Ward 4.ROBERT RANKIN
Robert Rankin is a newcomer to Easton politics, yet he displayed a firm grasp of the issues facing the town.
We liked his stands on issues, and most importantly, we liked that he admitted when he needed more information before voicing a conclusive opinion on issues we asked about.
Rankin's professionalism was evident. He called for a multi-faceted approach to increasing affordable housing in Easton, stressing the need to get more housing that is affordable for young families. His suggestions included working with developers to provide incentives, looking for more projects with townhomes and apartments, and redeveloping existing properties. It was a thoughtful answer.
Rankin also talked about his concerns on how new residential developments impact traffic, parking, schools and public safety. He wants an emphasis on a more strategic approach to approving future projects.
He wants to see more pedestrian-friendly and traffic calming features throughout the town. One suggestion included more crosswalks and sidewalks to better support pedestrian safety.
He was the only candidate to talk about increasing recreational opportunities on the east side of Route 50 where the majority of Ward 2 is located.
He suggested looking at retirement packages to assist in recruiting and retaining police officers in Easton.
One last note: Rankin has managed trade associations during his career. He knows what it is like to build consensus among many competing interests. Those will be valuable skills on the council.
THE REV. ELMER DAVIS
The Rev. Elmer Davis has long been a voice for people in the 4th Ward. He is also a voice of reason in the city during council meetings. Davis is not afraid to speak his mind, but his background as a preacher and pastor helps him look for common ground.
Davis noted his position on the Town Council dais. As the Ward 4 council member, he is the last one called to voice an opinion on discussion topics. This gives him a chance to hear all of the other council members. Often his message is one of finding consensus in disparate views.
"I aim to continue bridging the gap between the council and the people I represent, ensuring every voice is heard and valued," he said.
Davis was prophetic when he asked the question in our interview: "What do we want Easton to be?"
His multi-part answer is a walkable community with sufficient traffic infrastructure to keep the town moving. He suggested a bus service from hotels to downtown to get visitors to the shops that make Easton special. He was solution oriented.
Davis called for ensuring that first responders have the equipment and resources to respond to any incident.
He offered the best option we have heard for building affordable housing in the community — having the town purchase land and then partnering with organizations such as Habitat for Humanity to build the homes, involving the future homeowner in the process.
He said the town needs affordable housing "that people working at WaWa and McDonald's can afford."
He wants the council involved in approving housing projects in Easton. The Planning Commission, he said, should be making recommendations, not granting approvals.
One of his two opponents, Moonyene Jackson-Amis, would be our pick if Davis had not been doing such a fine job during his five years on the council. She is a former council member, an attorney and a community leader with multiple college degrees. She spoke passionately in our conversations about underrepresented communities in Easton. She continues to be a foundational rock in our town.
But Davis is our pick to continue his work on the council. He has done well these past five years, and he has become the face of Ward 4 with deep connections throughout the community.
Davis has experience, civility and strong ties to the community. He talks about his close-knit connection to his roots in the community shaping his values.
"I believe there is still much work to be done to enhance the quality of life for our residents," Davis said. We agree, and the reverend is the person to do that.

title: Easton election cycle has been charged, political in nature
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton election cycle has been charged, political in nature

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 869
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton saw a heated election the last time the council president seat was up for grabs. This year's race is no different.Since campaigns for the three open Town Council seats began this winter, there have been stolen and vandalized campaign signs, tense debates on campaign finance transparency and, most recently, political mailers from Republican-endorsed candidates calling out Mayor Megan Cook.
The tenor of the election cycle — which culminates with voting Tuesday — is largely influenced by the race for Town Council president between incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello.
At a town hall Tuesday, both candidates offered thoughts on civility.
"In the past two years, the council members overall, have been almost always conducting themselves in a civil manner," said Gunsallus. "There are times where debate may get heated. That is the nature of democracy."
"Arguing is fine, I get it. Disagreements occur," Abbatiello said. "But it needs to be done in a respectful manner."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry, who has endorsed Abbatiello, said the charged nature of this election isn't normal for Easton. And it's hurting the town, she says.
"Anytime you create an environment based on animosity, it becomes counterproductive, fairly quickly," Curry said. "And I think that's sort of where we are today."
Talbot County Republican Central Committee vice chair Shari Wilcoxon believes a reason the race is so intense is that it's a fight to preserve Easton's charm.
"People love our little town. It's a jewel," she said. "And we had a lot of people move here during COVID because they wanted to get out of the crud to come to this little town. A lot of us want to preserve that."
ENDORSEMENTS
As Gunsallus and Abbatiello square off, they have racked up endorsements from local politicians and even fellow council members.
Abbatiello received endorsements from Curry and, in a surprise to some, Ward 3's David Montgomery, who had sided with Gunsallus on several contentious matters discussed by the council in the past year.
"It would be very hard for us to move forward productively for the next four years under that kind of leadership," Montgomery said of Gunsallus.
Curry says Abbatiello's experience and knowledge make him the best candidate. "He has the right temperament," she said.
Meanwhile, Gunsallus' main endorsements come from Republican leaders — the Republican Central Committee, Sheriff Joe Gamble, Sen. Johnny Mautz and Dels. Chris Adams and Tom Hutchinson.
Wilcoxon said the committee looked at values — not necessarily party affiliation — when endorsing Gunsallus and mother-and-son newcomers Lynn and Cameron Keefe, who are running in Wards 2 and 4, respectively.
"To me he's a phenomenal leader," Wilcoxon said of Gunsallus, citing his thoughtfulness and transparency.
"He's not afraid to ask questions," Mautz said. " ... Sometimes, the questions may seem silly. And other times, they may reveal things that most people aren't aware of."
Abbatiello and his supporters have denounced the involvement of political parties in the town's election, which is nonpartisan and doesn't list candidates alongside a party.
"I do not think that the Republican Party platform has anything to do with the issues that we face here in Easton, and so I don't understand why the party has decided to intervene so strongly in a local election," Montgomery, a Republican, said.
Mautz said while the election is performed as nonpartisan, it is political in nature. "Every election has got politics baked into it," he said.
"I think that everybody fools themselves if they say it's nonpartisan," Wilcoxon said. "Everybody knows. Everybody knows everybody's party. We can just cut the pretending, right?"
Flavio Hickel, an associate professor of political science at Washington College, sees both sides of the argument.
"Broadly speaking, I don't think it's a good idea to allow for local party endorsements or to make nonpartisan elections partisan, because you are allowing partisanship to interfere in local town government," Hickel said.
However, Hickel said knowing which parties candidates align with is informative for voters, especially at a local level.
"Most voters probably aren't familiar with the candidates running," he said. " ... What party identity does at all levels of elections is it provides a very quick information shortcut for voters."
Curry and Montgomery's endorsements have raised questions, too.
Wilcoxon said she views Montgomery's opposition to Gunsallus as personal and said she believes Montgomery and Cook's sponsorship of a campaign finance ordinance was "100%" an attack on Gunsallus' campaign.
At the town hall Tuesday, Gunsallus spoke of council endorsements: "I would not want an endorsement from a fellow council member because I believe that that is out of bounds," he said. Then he made a remark seemingly concerning Montgomery.
"And especially one of them, I would not accept it."
Montgomery disputed that claim, telling The Star Democrat Friday that Gunsallus asked for his endorsement a few months ago, but that he declined.
Curry said she hadn't before made an endorsement as a sitting council member, but that she gave a "great deal of thought" in endorsing Abbatiello.
In her eyes, the discourse around endorsements and political sides are making the campaign heated, instead of what she'd rather the election be centered on: issues such as growth and housing.
"There's too much of the 'he said,' 'he said,' and he's backed by this guy and he's backed by this guy," Curry said. "The issues have taken a back seat, and that's wrong."

title: Gunsallus campaign flyer is misleading, outright false
author: MEGAN COOK
content:
Gunsallus campaign flyer is misleading, outright false

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MEGAN COOK | Section: Columns 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As someone who has worked hard to serve this community with honesty and transparency, I've always believed that facts should guide our public conversations, especially during an election. That's why I feel compelled to address several misleading and outright false claims circulating in recent campaign materials.When falsehoods are left unchallenged, it risks becoming accepted as fact. Our community deserves better. These tactics are part of an effort not to inform or unite us but to stir fear and falsely influence voters. That's not who we are in the Town of Easton, and it's not how we should conduct ourselves.
One candidate, Frank Gunsallus, has claimed he is the only council member in 30 years to have gone "line by line" through the town budget. That statement isn't just misleading, it's false and is a disservice to the many council members, past and present, who have worked diligently every year to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent wisely. Every budget season involves careful review, discussion and difficult decisions. Suggesting otherwise dismisses the thoughtful and responsible work of others who have taken that duty seriously, including myself when I served on the council from 2009-2023.
The inclusionary zoning bill is still a work in progress, and no final version has been drafted. Since 2022, there have been numerous meetings and workshops with both the Town Council and Planning Commission. A dedicated task force, made up of volunteers who spent countless hours reviewing Easton's housing needs, was appointed to offer thoughtful recommendations. That group is still finalizing its report.
To claim the bill mandates high-density housing in every neighborhood is simply false and undermines the work of dozens of people trying in good faith to address a real challenge. The goal is simple: to make it possible for teachers, nurses, police officers and others who serve our town to actually live here. If an officer has sworn to protect and serve our town, they ought to be able to call it home.
The same flyer accuses the mayor and staff of quietly ushering in development with little or no public input. That's not only untrue, it's an insult to the hardworking staff, Planning Commission and community members involved in every step of our public planning process. Nothing is being "snuck in." Transparency and community input are cornerstones of how we operate. Claims to the contrary are simply false.
It's also been claimed that I "recruited" three pro-mayor, pro-development candidates to run for Town Council. That's false. Two of the implied candidates are already serving on the council. One of them is running against Mr. Gunsallus not because of ideology, but out of concern over how meetings are managed, the lack of respect shown and civility and communication breakdowns among council members.
Mischaracterizing the motives of individuals who Mr. Gunsallus opposes is unfair and misleading. Voters should look for leadership that is respectful, collaborative and able to work with others, especially when navigating difficult issues. That's the kind of leadership Easton deserves.
It's also been suggested that because I wasn't born in Easton, I somehow care less or am less committed to this community. That's not only wrong, it's also deeply disrespectful. My husband and I moved to Easton 22 years ago for his job as a pediatrician and to be closer to his family. My work as mayor, as a former council member and my involvement in projects like Project Idlewild, CarePacks, coaching sports and serving on local boards and clubs, has always been about giving back to the place my husband and I chose to raise our family.
And I'm far from alone. Many of the people who make meaningful contributions to Easton each day weren't born here. What matters is not where someone started, but the heart and effort they bring to serving this town.
Easton is a town worth fighting for, not with fear or falsehoods, but with integrity, respect and a commitment to the truth. Elections should be about ideas, accountability, and the future we want to build together, not personal attacks or misleading claims. I will continue to stand up for the facts, for our hardworking staff and volunteers and for a community where we listen to each other even when we disagree. I encourage every voter to look past the lies, ask thoughtful questions and choose leaders who value collaboration, honesty and real public service.

title: Two potential dispensaries compete to open in Easton
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Two potential dispensaries compete to open in Easton

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 295
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two potential cannabis dispensaries are racing to secure final approvals from the Easton planners, but only one will be able to be built, at least in the location the business plans.Both potential locations sit near each other in the former bank locations near the Giant and Walmart on Elliott Road. State law will require one of the two dispensaries to find another spot.
"It was described at our hearing as something of a race to the finish at this point," said Lynn Thomas, town planner, in an interview. "The one issue that is at play for both of them is part of the state law requires minimum separation between other cannabis dispensaries.
"They obviously are right across the street from one another, so whoever gets their final approval first is going to prevent the other from opening at that location."
According to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, dispensaries are required to be 1,000 feet away from each other.
The applicant for 8223 Elliott Road is BGFY LLC and the applicant for 8171 Elliott Road is Driller Ventures LLC, Thomas said in an email.
Both business were approved for special exception by the town on different dates.
According to the town planner, BGFY LLC received its special exception on Dec. 17. A subdivision application for this property is currently under review, which would create a new parking lot surrounding the dispensary. Following the completion of the subdivision, the business will also need to submit applications for building permits.
According to Thomas, Driller Ventures LLC received a special exception on Jan. 25. The business' next step in the process is to apply for building permits.
The town planner states, "to my knowledge, we have not yet received any such applications."
The Star Democrat could not reach Driller Ventures LLC or BGFY LLC for comment.

title: Critical component of democracy

Critical component of democracy

 On May 6, Easton residents will decide who they want to represent them on the Town Council for the next four years.Participation in local government is a critical component of democracy and a responsibility that should not be taken lightly.
Town elections are smaller than state and national elections and typically candidates are known within the community absent of political party. Town issues are also very different from federal and state issues and impact a larger percentage of the electorate.
As a result, town elections should be nonpartisan and focus on individual candidates and their ideas for the future.
Running for local office is not easy. It requires time, commitment and resources to be successful. Serving is no less difficult and demands the ability to research issues, gather input from a wide range of stakeholders and make decisions that are in the best interest of the whole.
Good leaders listen, build consensus and look to unite, not divide. This cannot happen when political parties exert influence on local elections through contributions and slanderous talking points.
As the campaigns wind down, it is now time for the voters to decide who they want representing them. I continue to pledge to serve Easton and all of its residents through honesty, hard work, integrity and respect.
I call on all residents to be engaged, seek the truth and hold your leaders accountable for their actions. And I humbly ask for your vote on May 6.

title: Easton hires town manager
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Easton hires town manager

 May 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 501
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Andrew "Andy" Kitzrow has been named the Easton town manager.The appointment by the mayor was announced at the Town Council meeting Monday evening.
Kitzrow comes to Easton after serving as the Salisbury city administrator since 2023 and as the deputy city administrator since 2017.
As Easton town manager, he will be responsible for overseeing all town operations, acting as a leader to personnel and serving as a key point of contact for the mayor, town leadership, Town Council and residents of Easton.
"I'm looking forward to working alongside you to make Easton the best place on the Eastern Shore," Kitzrow told council members and residents Monday.
Kitzrow brings a wealth of experience and knowledge to the role with 19 years in local government, including seven years in executive leadership roles.
After obtaining his bachelor's degree at University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 2005, Kitzrow began a career in community administration by serving as a recreation program director and later a recreation superintendent for Wicomico County before landing his role as deputy city administrator for the Salisbury in 2017.
In his roles as Salisbury deputy city administrator and city administrator, Kitzrow championed many projects and initiatives, including:
The establishment of the Arts, Business and Culture Department, promoting tourism, revitalization and economic growth.The introduction of THRIVE, an employee health and wellness plan designed to holistically improve the physical, mental and emotional well-being of city staff.The launching of two youth community centers, which now serve hundreds of youths while fostering growth and community engagement.The recruitment of top talent in numerous critical roles throughout the organization, including police chief and fire chief.Overseeing teams that secured over $25 million in state and federal grants.
Mayor Megan Cook said the town partnered with a local government consulting firm during the hiring process, which began last fall. Around 50 applicants were narrowed to 10 semifinalists and then four finalists, she said.
The four finalists participated in full-day, in-person interviews and met with council members.
"Andy brings with him a deep understanding of municipal operations and brings a steady, informed perspective to the role," Cook said. She added that Kitzrow has strong budgeting and capital improvement planning experience.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey has been filling in as acting town manager since the town parted ways with former town manager Don Richardson in August 2024. Cook and council members thanked Lowrey for stepping up and serving in the important role.
"We've been lucky to have his leadership and his guidance — and his sense of humor — the last several months," Cook said.
Kitzrow's appointment was made by Cook and approved by the Town Council at its meeting on Monday. He is scheduled to begin serving as Easton town manager on July 7.
"Every new beginning comes from the courage to let go of the familiar," Kitzrow said in a news release from the town. "As I step into the role of town manager for Easton, I do so with great excitement for the opportunities that lie ahead."
This story has been updated with details from the Monday night council meeting.

title: Over 3,000 residents vote in Easton election, setting new record
author: Konner Metz
content:
Over 3,000 residents vote in Easton election, setting new record

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 625
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A record number of residents voted in Easton's election Tuesday.There are 3,001 votes and counting in the council president race, which saw Don Abbatiello defeat incumbent Frank Gunsallus. Tuesday night, Abbatiello held a decisive 2,025- to 976-vote lead.
The previous record for voter turnout in a municipal election came in the 2023 mayoral contest, according to town officials. In that election, 2,578 residents cast a vote in the competitive mayoral race, which was won by current Mayor Megan Cook.
Around 230 absentee ballots remain to be counted Wednesday, election supervisor Ed Forte said.
In Ward 2, Robert Rankin won the seat being vacated by Abbatiello. Rankin earned 493 votes Tuesday, a decisive lead over opponent Lynn Keefe's 228.
In Ward 4, incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis has a sizable lead. Davis has 253 votes, with Cameron Keefe in second with 128 and Moonyene Jackson-Amis third with 103.
Residents began coming out to the Easton Volunteer Fire Department once polls opened at 7 a.m, and the steady pace continued through much of the day.
The town's Board of Canvassers will tally absentee ballots Wednesday and then formally certify the election.
Both in the morning and afternoon, the line for residents from Ward 3 stretched to outside the voting hall.
At one point early Tuesday afternoon, the line for voters went past the indoor lobby all the way to the outside doors of the building.
Tuesday evening, the turnout continued to be steady as many residents navigated a crowded parking lot to perform their civic duty.
Inside the fire hall, Forte and election judges swiftly assisted voters who were unsure of which wards they live in. Election judge Mariana Lesher called it a "crazy" good turnout.
All seven candidates were at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department Tuesday to speak with voters.
Abbatiello, Davis and Rankin stood next to one another under a tent in the lawn outside the fire hall. Gunsallus was set up with his own tent next to them.
Jackson-Amis had a table and chair set up next to the tents on the lawn. Lynn and Cameron Keefe, mother and son, stood next to cars in the parking lot to greet voters as they entered and exited.
Lynn Keefe said the campaign has been a great experience and that she's thankful for all who came out to vote. She said no matter who wins, it's important to be respectful.
"It's been a whirlwind," she said of the recent weeks campaigning.
Since it began, the election cycle has seen stolen and vandalized campaign signs, tense debates on campaign finance transparency and, most recently, political mailers from Republican-endorsed candidates calling out Mayor Megan Cook.
Resident Carolyn Coon voted Tuesday morning. She said the importance of this election brought her to the polls. Coon said Easton "needs civility back in place."
"I think the council's been disjointed," Coon said. She added that misinformation during the campaign cycle — coming from "one side," she said — has hurt and divided the town.
"I think it's been really sleazy," Coon said.
Jason Bell stood at the corner of Leonard Rieck Drive and North Aurora Street Tuesday morning, where vehicles turned into the parking lot. He held a large American flag and a Gunsallus sign.
Bell said he was optimistic about the voter turnout and hoped everyone would come out and vote.
"I'm supporting America," Bell said of his support for Gunsallus.
Across from the main entrance, fire department volunteers mingled among themselves. Former fire chief Sonny Jones said he believes the high turnout can be attributed to residents being "fed up with partisan politics."
Endorsements from the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, as well as within the Town Council itself, have come under scrutiny in recent weeks.
Jones is a supporter of Abbatiello, saying his fellow firefighter "brings common sense" and civility to town government.
"He's an all-around, genuinely decent guy," Jones said.

title: Residents soon will move in to renovated Doverbrook Apartments
author: Konner Metz
content:
Residents soon will move in to renovated Doverbrook Apartments

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The revitalized Doverbrook Apartments were shown off to state, county and town leaders last week as final touches are completed before residents move in.Don Bibb, executive director of the Housing Commission of Talbot, said the 64-unit redevelopment project will benefit the community.
"You can see the tremendous improvement this has made to the community and the opportunity for much improved, long-term sustainable housing for the program participants that we have that are going to be living here," Bibb said April 30 during a tour of the complex.
Bibb said Thursday that move-in for returning residents is imminent and is likely to begin within seven to 10 days.
The commission and construction company Pennrose began redevelopment of the Doverbrook Apartments in late 2023. The $26 million project replaced the apartment complex's seven old buildings with five new buildings, adding 14 units to its original 50-unit setup.
"It's good utilization of open space that provides the opportunity for the growth to add more units in," Bibb said.
Located on Dover Street, the complex will accommodate households earning between 30% and 80% of the area median income, or between $21,000 and $58,000 for one-person households.
It includes one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom apartments. Project leaders said the complex was designed to bring original residents — who were assisted in finding temporary housing during construction — back once completed.
Bibb said of the original 50 tenants, around 30 will return — a relatively high percentage for a redevelopment project during which residents move elsewhere temporarily.
Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day toured the apartment complex April 30. He applauded the redevelopment efforts and lightheartedly pointed out how close residents will be to Rise Up Coffee across the street.
"Do your marketing materials for the remaining (units) talk about how many steps it is to the Rise Up?" Day said with a smile.
Bibb praised the public-private aspect of the project, which included state and local funding and low-income housing tax credits for the 14 new units.
"It was well worth the blood, sweat and tears," Bibb said.

title: Program Open Space bill is 'a success,' county says

Program Open Space bill is 'a success,' county says

 DENTON — Bruce Bereano and Steve Wise, Caroline County's lobbyists, presented their 2025 legislative session wrap-up at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday.Bereano and Wise spoke about House Bill 717, a bill that was passed this session regarding Program Open Space, a state program that allocates funding from transfer tax collections.
"This was a success," Wise said. "We were able to get all counties in the state to use that capital money for operating, upgrades and improvements."
House Bill 717 originally started as a departmental bill, spearheaded by the Department of Natural Resources. Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding testified on a panel to support the bill with Secretary of the Department of Natural Resources Josh Kurtz.
Breeding originally sent a request to Maryland Association of Counties and the counties' lobbyist to have Program Open Space changed to allow the counties to use acquisition funds for park improvements, he said.
The association then suggested "instead of making the bill a standalone bill let's see if Secretary Kurtz is willing to include it in their department bill," Breeding said. Kurtz agreed and then included it in DNR's bill.
The bill states, "altering and repealing certain provisions of law regarding the use of Program Open Space local funding"
"We got it put in, and it made its way through the legislature and passed. It hasn't been signed yet," Breeding said. "What it's going to do, it'll allow Caroline County to use 25% of the money it gets in Program Open Space and additional 25 towards building park infrastructure. Whereas before, roughly 25% of the money allocated to the county from the state had to be used to purchase property."
According to Breeding, projects like the Sharp Road Park project and the North County Park project could see improvements from this bill.
"It does make more money available for us to do the improvements at Sharp Road Park and North County Park and various other parks around the county," Breeding said. "So, it does give us more state funds to work with to make improvements."
The county's lobbyists credit Kurtz for help with getting the Program Open Space into the bill.
"Really very thankful to the secretary for being so flexible, and open-minded and accepting, and throughout all of it, he was very insistent on having that as a part of the bill," Bereano said.

title: Piscataway Conoy Tribe receives land donation
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Piscataway Conoy Tribe receives land donation

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 581
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After a long process, it's official — a property on Country Lane in Waldorf will be donated to the Piscataway Conoy Tribe.The donation did not come easily, as tensions rose between a split tribe, with a number coming out to oppose it.
Charles County first received notification about the land donation request in January 2020 and sent correspondence about the process on Feb. 5, 2020.
On July 29, 2020, the county sent the first of four lease renewal documents between then and March 16, 2022. Despite several attempts at communication between the county and the tribe, the two sides were unable to come to a formal agreement.
A letter said the plot of land had been a center for indigenous culture with biannual pow-wows from 1982 through 2014, as well as school field trips and other public events.
The letter also stated that the Cedarville Band was required to jump through "numerous bureaucratic hoops," including paying $10,000 for a land survey.
The American Civil Liberties Union requested the county stop a planned eviction and work toward a long-term solution to donate the land to the Cedarville Band of Piscataway Indians.
"Returning the land would affirmatively recognize and show appreciation for the people who have been preserving American history and Indigenous American culture on this land," the ACLU letter stated.
The site is divided with approximately 9.5 acres in Charles County and 7 acres in Prince George's County.
"The property being proposed for transfer is located in both Prince George's and Charles counties. The property is owned entirely by Charles County, and so there is no approval needed from Prince George's County in order to complete the transfer," Danielle Mitchell, an attorney with Charles County government, told Southern Maryland News earlier this year.
During a public hearing last month, a large number of the Piscataway were split on what to do with the land.
From the 1950s through the 1970s, the property was owned by the U.S. Army and used as a Nike Battery site.
Rosanna Swann, the first speaker of the hearing, said at the time she opposed the land donation because of a court case between Jesse James Swann Jr. and Francis Gray, who both lead different portions of the Piscataway people.
Rosanna Swann also pointed to the site as a potential "environmental disaster" due to its military history and said that the area was contaminated and could cost anywhere from $4 to $10 million to clean up.
Gray, the chairman of the Piscataway Conoy Tribe, said, "We the Piscataway Conoy people welcome this opportunity as it will finally provide a much needed home base. … It runs deeper than that. It will provide a means for the preservation of our identity."
Later in the night, Acting County Administrator Deborah Hall said that the federal government covers the cleanup of the contaminated land.
Many others came up and supported the donation, citing the importance of giving the Piscataway people a land base so other tribes can find them.
County attorneys reported that there were well over 200 written comments on the matter, and that sentiments were very split on if the land should be donated.
On May 6, it was time to put it to a vote.
Commissioner Gilbert "BJ" Bowling (D) told tribe members in attendance that he would be abstaining from the vote.
"I don't feel it's appropriate for me to get in the middle of it," Bowling said, citing disagreement between sects of the tribe and the ongoing legal dispute.
The other four commissioners voted yes, passing the resolution and giving the tribe a land base.
