 GREENSBORO — With the mayor acting as the tiebreaker vote, the Greensboro Town Council voted to support the Board of Appeals in its fight against Halo Greensboro Property LLC, a proposed solar facility on Sunset Avenue.The Town of Greensboro Board of Appeals held a public hearing March 10, during which it consider an application filed by Halo Greensboro Property LLC for special exception approval to permit a private utility facility and major utility facility with capacity to produce 1.2 megawatts AC power with related equipment, transmission lines, utility poles, access areas, fencing and similar features.
The application was denied by the board. As a result, Halo Greensboro filed an appeal to the Caroline County Circuit Court. The Board of Appeals will be fighting the solar appeal.
Lindsey Ryan, town attorney, brought forward to the town council the option to support the Board of Appeals in the case or allow the court proceed with the case at hand.
Councilmember Joe Noon, who voted for the courts to proceed with the case without the council's support, emailed his decision to Ryan earlier in the week but wanted the public to know why he decided to make that decision.
"Just so the public knows, I do care about the solar panels, don't get me wrong. But I'm looking at everything else. I'm looking at the big picture too," Noon said. "Like the sale of the house, what we're going to use the money for... I'm looking at the big picture also. I'm not against fighting for the solar panels, but I'm looking at our bank. So, I'm not against fighting for our town to keep the solar panels out. I'm just trying to look at how we're going to pay for everything."
Councilmember Bob Harrison, who also voted in favor of letting the court make a decision without council input, agreed with Noon about saving money for the town.
"I agree with Joe," Harrison said. "Just let it go. How much money do we want to spend? If it's going to cost us more money, just let the judge make the decision."
Councilmembers Pete Brelia and Christina Robinson both voted to support the Board of Appeals in the fight. Brelia's explanation for support brought applause from the residents in attendance of the meeting.
"The Board of Appeals had a hearing, and they opposed it. These people are filing an an appeal, and I think we should do whatever takes to back our Board of Appeals," Brelia said. "... To have the Board of Appeals have to hearing, go through this and then all of a sudden us just say, 'Well, let's just see what the courts do. Just sit here and tread water waiting.' That's not very supportive. Those people come out of out of their homes, they took a lot of time, they listened to everything, and they're acting in our best interest. I think that we should support them."
Brelia made the motion to support the Board of Appeals, which Robinson seconded. Harrison and Noon opposed the motion, which meant the decision needed to be made by the mayor.
"Let's vote to fight it," Mayor David Spencer said.
According to a press release, a virtual public hearing for Halo Solar case will take place on Tuesday, June 10, at 6:30 p.m. To sign up to speak on the public hearing, residents can go to psc.state.md.us.

title: Claims misleading, false
author: Staff Writer
content:
Claims misleading, false

 May 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 386
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last weekend, you published an article under the headline of "Legislators reflect on this year's wins and losses." The legislators were all three local Republicans (Messrs. Mautz, Adams, Hutchinson) and they spoke before what was probably a friendly audience, a local Chamber of Commerce.Your article quoted them making extraordinary claims that were misleading and patently false.
For starters, they ignored context. Mr. Mautz announced Moody dropped their rating of Maryland's general obligation debt for the first time since 1973. I'm certainly not going to argue that is good. But Mautz apparently did not say that the other major national rating service, Fitch, reaffirmed Maryland's GO rating as AAA. (Your article included that, but not as a quote from the speakers.) One out of two rating agencies lowered it. Not good, but not a financial disaster.
To put it in a greater context, a few days after these legislators blamed Democrats for the rating downgrade, Moody downgraded the U.S. government's credit rating. This makes the U.S. the first major economy in history to lose its top credit rating from all three major rating agencies. A unique accomplishment under Trump and Republicans. I'd guess these legislators like Trump and Congress despite crashing credit ratings.
Mr. Mautz also made a statement that is astonishing false. He said that a budget is not a partisan issue; it is either fiscally in control or fiscally questionable. If these three legislators produced a budget for Maryland, it must be balanced. Just as the budget passed by the state legislature.
What would be the difference between these balanced budgets? As a thought experiment, consider if the representatives' budget abolishes public education and the Democrats' budget does not. Which budget is in control and which is questionable? Good luck answering that without being partisan.
I'd love to go into the entire history of government budgeting that began in Mesopotamia in 2300 BCE. I'd bet in the 4,300 years since, no one has said with a straight face that budget issues are nonpartisan.
I would like to see these three gentlemen team up with Andy Harris and hold an open town hall where anyone, in person, can ask questions. All four share Trump's values and eagerness to impose them on Marylanders. I think that would be far more enlightening than a cozy chat with a Chamber of Commerce.
MICHAEL K. DAVIS
Easton

title: Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery decked out with flag display to honor soldiers
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery decked out with flag display to honor soldiers

 May 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Around 100 volunteers placed thousands of flags on graves at the Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery Saturday morning just outside Hurlock.When the gates opened at 8 a.m., volunteers made quick work of the flag display, cemetery Superintendent Dean Arcoraci said. American flags whipped in the wind along with many Military Order of the Purple Heart flags honoring those killed or wounded in action.
"There's a lot of tradition here," Arcoraci said of the annual flag display.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery is one of five official veterans cemeteries in the state and the only one on the Eastern Shore. Arcoraci noted it was the first ever Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families cemetery, opening in 1976.
Civil War veteran John Henry Blades was the first person to be buried at the cemetery. Today, there are around 8,000 burials and there's room for thousands more, Arcoraci said. He said the state also recently relaxed its residency requirements, allowing some families from nearby Delaware to place veterans at the Hurlock cemetery.
The cemetery features a unique design, with the burial sites forming curves facing the American flag in the middle of the cemetery.
Once the flags were placed, Mary Alice Jones and her son Bill Jones took some time to visit the graves of relatives, including Korean War U.S. Army veteran Joseph Horenstein.
Mary Alice Jones said it's important to remember and honor veterans no matter the time of year.
While Memorial Day was widely celebrated Monday, the Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery commemorates Memorial Day later this week with an annual program.
At 1:30 p.m. Friday, the cemetery will host a Memorial Day program open to the public. It will include remarks from American Legion members and guest speaker Ross Cohen, acting secretary of the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families.
Memorial Day was originally observed on May 30 in the years after the Civil War. That tradition continued through much of the 20th century before a federal act moved it to the last Monday in May.
Arcoraci said the cemetery and its committee continues the May 30 program because of tradition. "I'm expecting quite a crowd," he added.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery partners with a number of local veteran groups and organizations, including local American Legions.
"This cemetery's about community involvement," he said.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery is located at 6827 E New Market Ellwood Road, Hurlock, MD, 21643.

title: Talbot County OKs $161 million budget
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County OKs $161 million budget

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 685
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County made good on its promise to deliver a flat, conservative budget for fiscal year 2026. The County Council unanimously passed a $161.1 million spending plan Tuesday.It comes in at nearly $3 million under last year's budget amid what County Manager Clay Stamp calls "uncharted waters."
"The economic landscape out there is a bumpy ride right now," Stamp said. "This year, we knew that we needed to flatten the budget out, we needed to live within our means."
Stamp and other officials have emphasized Talbot County's continued financial commitments toward public safety, whether through capital projects such as an EMS station in Cordova or support for correctional officers.
In a draft version of the budget that only received a few adjustments Tuesday, the council is expected to allocate the following funds for public safety:
$11.5 million for emergency medical services.$10.5 million for the Talbot County Sheriff's Office.$7.6 million for the Department of Corrections.$5.4 million for emergency management.$3.3 million for volunteer fire departments.
Council members thanked Stamp, Finance Director Martha Sparks and Assistant Finance Director Kaitlin Foster-Clark for their work during the budget process.
"This was the most challenging budget that I've ever sat through," council member Keasha Haythe said. "The decisions were very hard on some items."
"It was definitely a heavy lift this year, but everyone bucked down, and we made it happen here," council member Dave Stepp said.
The county's property tax rate will remain largely steady at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, though residents will see a supplemental tax of just over 1 cent per $100 of value on their tax bills.
EDUCATION FUNDING
That supplement stems from education funding OK'd by the county. While most line items were ironed out through deliberations, workshops and meetings, Tuesday's discussion centered on funding amendments for Talbot County Public Schools.
The budget already included $55 million in education funding as required by The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's initiative to fund and improve education. County Council members were left to consider how much the county would contribute above that mark.
In a 4-1 vote Tuesday, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding for schools, aimed at filling nine positions, including multilingual and special education roles. Council member Lynn Mielke was the sole no vote.
The approved budget change came after an amendment to fulfill the district's entire $1.1 million request — which had been scaled back from $5.5 million earlier this budget cycle — failed narrowly. Vice President Pete Lesher and Haythe favored the $1.1 million, but President Chuck Callahan, Stepp and Mielke did not.
Lesher argued it is "short-sighted" to not fund the full request. He said it'd be prudent for the county to gradually increase its education funding as even higher Blueprint projections loom in future fiscal years.
"This would be a small step in that direction," Lesher said. "And frankly, it will make next year, an election year, a lot easier for all of us up here."
"I think we should be going farther," he said of the $600,000 mark. "But this goes some distance."
Callahan sponsored the amendment to partially OK the district's request, citing the significant need for teachers. The $500,000 not approved by the council was requested by the district to increase teacher and instructional assistant salaries.
"I would ask that the school board use the money that we give you for (hiring) teachers," Callahan said. "I would like to see that, and not for something else."
Mielke said she was initially on board with Callahan's amendment. But she said she needs "more security" that the district will put the $600,000 toward the nine positions.
"I'm not advised that it necessarily would be," Mielke said. "So for that reason I couldn't support it."

"We are grateful for their support for educators' pensions and for the additional staff needed to serve our students," the statement read.

title: Idlewild Park's tile wall to be removed Monday

Idlewild Park's tile wall to be removed Monday

 EASTON — Residents only have a few more days to visit a cherished tile wall at Idlewild Park before the town removes the collection on Monday.Hundreds of hand-painted tiles create a winding wall next to the playground at Idlewild Park. The tile display is as old as the park itself, which opened in the summer of 2007.
Many of the nearly two-decade-old tiles include handprints, names or school classes. However, they are significantly worn and at the end of their lifespan, town officials say.
Easton officials delayed the initial plan to remove the walkway in October following substantial community feedback. In a Facebook post last week announcing the June 2 removal date, the town stated it will remove the tiles and resurface and paint the wall. Tiles will not be retrievable.
"As there is no way to remove the tiles without damaging them and neighboring tiles, individual tiles can not be salvaged from this process," the town wrote.
Last fall, community members spoke of memories they had from the tiles and the park overall. Many suggested a community art project replace the wall.
Easton resident Michael McCormack said last fall he remembered painting his tile when he was 8 years old.
"You can see the weather, you can see the time has taken its toll on those things for sure," McCormack said at the time. "So you can see why they need to be taken down. It's just one of those things that I don't think people in the town really appreciated until they realized it was going to be gone."
The town has posted a gallery of the Idlewild Park tile wall on its website. The town's parks and recreation department is open to hearing suggestions on how the space should be used in the future.
To reach the town, email parksrec@eastonmd.gov.

title: Oxford commissioners approve budget items
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford commissioners approve budget items

 May 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Town commissioners approved eight budget requests during Tuesday evening's meeting, including employment posting for a new police officer position in Oxford.Before the approvals, resident Jim Wilcox began the open session by expressing concerns over hiring a new police officer. "I wanted the commissioners to seriously consider whether we could exist with two police officers rather than three," he said.
Wilcox said he's concerned it's expensive to hire a third officer and said there's no need to because there's no crime in Oxford other than the occasional speeding incident.
Town commissioner Tom Costigan said in an interview that it's true that there is very little crime in Oxford and hiring a third police officer will make sure it stays that way. "Or even even improve it, you know, if we can get to zero (crimes), then we're doing great," he said.
The other seven approvals included:
Awarding the Gordon Graves Community Service scholarship(s) of $1,000.Authorization for the town manager to submit an application to the Department of Natural Resources to license offshore blinds within municipal limits.Approval to contract with Capital Coatings to refinish the exterior of Town Hall.Approval of the purchase and installation of a ultraviolet index sensor at the water reclamation treatment plant, requiring a budget amendment.Approval of the purchase of a Wapro 14-inch valve for the causeway inlet check valve to improve wastewater management.Approval of the purchase of an emergency water reclamation treatment plant pump.Approval of the Avery Hall auto-renewal for employee health care benefits effective June 1 through May 31, 2026.
The meeting agenda also proposed an authorization to transfer more than $1 million from a maturing Bay Vanguard Bank Certificate of Deposit account to the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool for potentially higher returns. The Bay Vanguard account offers a fixed-term investment with a fixed interest rate, while the investment pool is designed to grow local government investments at a competitive rate.
Commissioner Katrina Greer proposed amending this item to include funds currently in Shore United Bank that are no longer maturing.
Commission President Norm Bell and Costigan asked to table this item to speak about it in a closed session among themselves. Residents began to murmur and did not seem pleased with this response.
"Didn't we go through this with a bank a couple of years ago about keeping the bank here and if we took the money out?" said Oxford resident Deborah Pulzone. Bell and Greer confirmed there have been several iterations of the same conversation over the past couple of years.
The current budget proposal for fiscal year 2026 is balanced, leaving little wiggle room. The budget will be adopted during the commissioners' next meeting on June 10 at 6 p.m.

title: Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'
author: WILL BONTRAGER
content:
Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER | Section: Life 
 
 560
 Words 

 Read News Document

 High Street in Chestertown was clear Memorial Day of many tourists following a successful Tea Party weekend, but the streets remained filled with locals honoring veterans during an annual parade, a longstanding tradition in the area.First responders from all Kent municipalities, local businesses, organizations, vintage vehicles and marching bands, symbolized the community's appreciation to the fallen. A crowd of approximately 500 lined the sunny streets, shouting well-wishes and flag waving.
After the festive Memorial Day parade, keynote speaker, veteran and board member of Sumner Hall, Aubrey Sarvis, spoke about his time serving during the Korean War, a conflict that started on June 25, 1950 — July 27, 1953.
Sarvis' message was simple yet strong — to never forget.
As a member of the U.S. Army 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division from 1961-1962, he talked about that war, dubbed the "forgotten war" because it was overshadowed from World War II and Vietnam.
But for those who experienced the conflict, there was no way of forgetting it.
Sarvis said while on guard duty in the 38th parallel, separating North Korea and South Korea, he knew two things about his fellow soldiers: they were afraid and they did not want to die.
Surrounded by veterans, he provided sobering statistics of those who were killed in action or severely wounded, starting from World War I to the wars in the Middle East following Sept. 11, 2001.
He talked about those who died on the Western Front, France and Belgium, buried under poppy fields. He spoke of those 23,613 killed in action in Korea and the 58,220 who deployed in Vietnam and came home in a fresh casket with brand new American flags.
Thinking about his fallen comrades in every conflict, he recited the poem: "In Flanders Fields," by John McCrae, written in World War I. The poem beckons the hearers to remember the dead buried under poppy fields or those living would never be free.
President of Sumner Hall, Vanessa Isaacs Ringgold also remembers the sacrifices of these soldiers and stated how Sumner Hall is one of two existing African American Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) buildings still standing in the country.
She said that in 1868, founder of the Grand Army of the Republic Colonel John A. Logan issued a general order to 7,000 post members to decorate the graves of fallen comrades.
Sumner Hall aims to carry on that tradition of honoring and remembering. She said fraternity, charity and loyalty, is what they strive for, and will continue the legacy of the Parker White American Legion #143, formerly led by by the late Calvin Frasier. It was founded in 1919 and was the first Post in Kent County Maryland started by African Americans.
After the speakers, veterans gathered around the memorial and held a moment of silence for the lost, followed by "Taps" played by trumpeter Brad Holloman.
Ringgold said she was honored to be a part of this ceremony. She added whereas in former years, Sumner Hall has done something separate for Memorial Day, this year, two groups came together, and she hopes they will continue planning the Memorial Day Parade together.
She thanked Katy Weddell, Ellen Uzelac and everyone on the planning commission for their hard work, starting around February.
Sumner Hall encourages veterans to reach out to them, young and old. They hosts monthly events and meetings and is open to the community as an event venue. For information, visit sumnerhall.org.

title: Idlewild Park tile wall comes down
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Idlewild Park tile wall comes down

 June 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 556
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After months of delay, the tile wall at Idlewild Park has been taken down.The beloved wall has been covered with hundreds of hand-painted tiles since the park's construction in 2007. Some showcase artwork or footprints, while others display names or ages, unique designs representing the kids, families or town residents who painted them.
Tyrone Pinder, a maintenance worker from Easton, spent the day Monday taking down the tiles. Despite not growing up in Easton, Pinder was aware of the memories attached to the tiles.
"We got a couple of our bosses that had some on here," Pinder said. "We saw one of his, and it was all broken down and stuff."
Pinder said the removal of the tile wall was a part of the town's efforts to increase safety and make the park look neater. Gabriella Alvarez from Federalsburg said she understands the safety hazard after watching her daughter glide her hands against the chipped tiles.
"If it's gonna upgrade the park and for the children's safety, I'm okay with it," Alvarez said.
Despite the safety concern, Alvarez has appreciated the colorful presence of the tiles in the park.
"I thought it was really cute," Alvarez said. "While my daughter was playing, I would observe each one of them."
The construction of the park was a community effort, and the tiles helped represent that. The construction was completed with the help of around 500 volunteers, according to Mayor Megan Cook, who helped organize the creation of the park in 2006.
Cook said the tiles were created as part of a fundraising effort for the park's construction.
"Families could go in and paint a tile, and then the cost helped cover Kiln Born's or Clay Baker's portion, and then the rest went to help fund the construction," Cook said.
After nearly twenty years, the tiles were falling apart. While some only had minor chipping, others were almost entirely defaced, leaving little to see of the original artwork.
"Some of them have lasted the test of time, and a lot of them have succumbed to the weather and damage," Cook said. "It was time to kind of make a clean slate there."
After the town first announced in September that the tile wall would be removed, many residents wondered whether they would be able to retrieve their tiles. However, in a Facebook post last month, Easton officials shared that no tiles would be salvaged during the removal process as removing them would cause significant damage.
"I think it was definitely a memory," Alvarez said. "I feel bad for the kids if their art was displayed, and they can't refurbish it or come back and get it."
Adalea Ringgold from Caroline County is among the park visitors who were surprised to see the removed tiles.
"It was my favorite part," Ringgold said. "It is really cute to see all the little kids throughout the years and their beautiful little tile marks."
With the tile wall officially removed from the park, its memory will be commemorated on the town's website with a gallery of all the tiles.
Ringgold suggested that the tile wall could be replaced with handprints or an updated wall with art created by the new generation of kids. The town of Easton invites residents to submit their suggestions for replacing the wall and will come up with a plan moving forward, according to Cook.
Residents can reach the town by emailing parksrec@eastonmd.gov.

title: Easton council members hesitant to change seafood odor ordinance
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council members hesitant to change seafood odor ordinance

 June 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Town Council members indicated Monday that they were leaning toward rejecting a debated amendment to the town's seafood odor ordinance, though there was no vote to put the issue to bed.The council's final vote on the amendment could take place at its June 16 meeting, ending months of discussion on the matter.
Passed by the Easton Town Council in December, the ordinance came after repeated odor complaints from residents living near Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a wholesale crab processor on Maryland Avenue. The law is set to take effect July 1.
The legislation requires that the business install odor control technology and do so "in such a manner that no odor ... can be detected" — or, in other words, "effectively eliminate outdoor odors."
Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner Mitch Hughes and his attorney requested the amendment to the ordinance, citing the "no odor" requirement as unachievable per industry experts.
Last month, the Planning Commission voted against Chesapeake Brand's proposed amendment. But the commission wasn't sold on the council's original ordinance, either. In a formal recommendation, commission members advised the council to find a more enforceable and achievable standard.
On Monday, the Town Council discussed but didn't take official action on that recommendation. Council members largely leaned away from changing the soon-to-be effective ordinance.
"If we move this to something else, then we're not going to get anything resolved," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
Davis represents many of the neighboring residents and has consistently advocated for the placement of odor requirements on the business. He said Monday the issue "needs to be dealt with yesterday."
Ward 2 representative Robert Rankin said he understands Chesapeake Brand — which opened in 2019 under a town permit — is simply a business trying to operate. But he said it's "unclear" if the business is ready to address its odor issue.
"I don't see a reason to change what's in place at this point," Rankin said.
Hughes has said he's ready to install odor control technology but is holding off since he doesn't want to foot monthly costs if the odor system won't end up meeting the ordinance's requirements.
"They all said we can install a system and get your odor down," Hughes said in an interview last month. "But there's no way you can reach zero odor."
The Planning Commission specifically recommended the Town Council alter language in the ordinance so it requires the business to "effectively mitigate" odors instead of "effectively eliminate" them. Town planners say it's consistent with odor reduction language used by the Environmental Protection Agency.
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he didn't like the proposed change to "mitigate."
"It simply introduces a more ambiguous word for a clear one," he said.
The ordinance has brought mixed public reaction. A handful of residents and some seafood industry leaders spoke at the recent Planning Commission meeting, urging the town not to drive Chesapeake Brand away.
"Mitch got a permit," Donna Bramble said May 15. "He did not hide what kind of business he was having. He told you what it was going to be. It's a signed, legal document, and now the town is trying to take that away."
Meanwhile, neighbors concerned with the odors appealed Monday for the council to retain the legislation as passed.
"This is law," Peter Maloney said, adding concerns about the proposed amendment. "Are we allowing businesses to write law for us? That whole piece of this irks me."
After public comment, Ward 1 representative Maureen Curry said the council won't leave residents hanging.
"You guys (are) worth a lot more to us than Chesapeake Brand," Curry said. "And you've been there longer, and all we want is for him to be a good neighbor. And we're going to hold his feet to the fire."
Though the Planning Commission recommended against the seafood odor amendment, the council still has final say. A public hearing will take place before the potential vote June 16.

title: Greensboro will not bring northern towns onto wastewater system
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro will not bring northern towns onto wastewater system

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Caroline County is creating a plan to address septic system concerns in Henderson, Marydel and Templeville by building a wastewater treatment facility, but there is still a long way to go, officials say.The county has been brainstorming ideas since the May 6 commissioners meeting, where Commission President Travis Breeding announced the town of Greensboro would not take the towns onto its wastewater treatment system.
Greensboro Mayor David Spencer said the Greensboro Town Council came to that decision because of the wear and tear the facility would take by adding three new towns.
"I don't know that the council had absolutely said that they didn't want to be involved in the process. I think that they preferred not to be because of the additional responsibilities and potential expenses that may incur on our residents," Spencer said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Monday.
"I know that they were going to come back and give some more numbers... I don't know that the door has been absolutely closed, but I don't think the council had any appetite to try to move forward at this time," Spencer said.
The discussion arises after multiple north county residents complained about problems with their septic tanks. One resident brought their concerns to the county commissioners in April.
"My mom's property started flooding with the rain, and she is on a septic, and it's been drained three weeks ago," Kia Pierce said at an April meeting. "But the flooding is causing her septic lines to back up to the point where we cannot flush the toilet, and it's coming through the sinks now."
The commissioners are working on a plan, Breeding said, but it all depends on government permits and funding.
"We're talking to Maryland Department of Environment about other options, whether it be individual plants for each town, which we don't think is feasible, or one new plant in a centralized location that all three towns, Templeville, Henderson and Marydale, could connect to," Breeding said.
"We are looking at options as far as locations of a potential plant and what kind of discharge permit MDE would be willing to give us... Then also we're looking at what kind of funding MDE or (U.S. Department of Agriculture) may have available to help us construct a new plant up there."
While the county is working with MDE and USDA, Breeding said there is no time table for when the county will have a solidified plan.
"It's all pretty much funding-dependent, and one thing I've learned in the two years I've been in the office, it takes a lot longer than you think it's going to take," Breeding said. "So, we're working through it."

title: Short-term rentals come under scrutiny in Talbot County with proposed regulations
author: Konner Metz
content:
Short-term rentals come under scrutiny in Talbot County with proposed regulations

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 720
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As a proposal to increase regulations on short-term rentals in Talbot County draws sharp criticism from rental owners and companies, some residents are pushing back in support of the legislation.Leslie Steen, of Tilghman Island, says there are four short-term rental properties within 1,000 feet of her home. She's worried it'll become a domino effect for the "tight-knit" community if more rentals pop up.
"The more houses we lose, the less of a community we have," Steen said. "And that's not healthy."
Regulations proposed last month by County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher would introduce stricter rules on short-term rental operations and the licenses they receive. The proposal elicited divided opinions at a county meeting last month, and there's no clear middle ground as county planners prepare to meet with the council Tuesday for a workshop on the legislation.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license. Most license requests are granted.
Proposed are measures that some rental owners argue go too far, including a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, an increase from the current three-night requirement.
Lesher says the seven-day minimum isn't a huge change — he says short-term rentals are "by and large a weekend business."
"It's really, how often can it be rented?" Lesher added, saying an increase from three to seven days still leaves 52 weeks a year on the table.
Michelle Hoyle, owner of the rental company Tidewater Vacations, says renters won't be likely to pay for seven days if they can only stay for less than a week. She says shorter stays have become more common since many of her renters have gone back to in-person work in Washington, D.C.
"This will shut me down," Hoyle said. "Three-day is hard enough. We understand the three-day."
Hoyle says the possibility of the change is already leading her to seek out homes in nearby counties. Currently, Tidewater Vacations operates seven short-term properties, all in Talbot County.
"It's something I don't want to do because I truly do love this county," Hoyle said. "But I don't have an option."
ADDED RESTRICTIONS
Draft legislation would amend the county's current short-term rental rules, which property owners largely say they understand and accept.
Along with the seven-day stay requirement, some of the proposed rule additions that have received divided reactions include:
Licenses would split into two classes — one for properties that are the applicant's primary residence and the other for non-primary residences. The latter class would limit one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on zoning district.Landlines would have to be installed in all short-term rentals.Short Term Rental Review Board members would only be eligible for one immediate reappointment.Renewal applications would require logs of when the rental was occupied by tenants, family members and the owner.
The ask to provide more detailed logging hasn't sat well with Easton residents Kevin and Angeline Hartmann, who often rent out a second home on the Miles River.
"To me, that's a total overreach," Kevin Hartmann said. "I still can't believe that lawmakers and the county attorney would put that in the legislation."
Keith Watts is chair of the review board and owns two short-term rental properties himself. He says the new restrictions would only add more stress on county planners tasked with reviewing and tracking licenses and applications.
"The amount of time that planning and zoning spends on short-term rentals is astronomical," Watts said.
Residents supportive of the regulations view them as an improvement from the current rules that they feel are "one size fits all." They hope the class distinction could help prevent clusters of short-term rentals from popping up in St. Michaels neighborhoods like Bentley Hay or on smaller residential roads in areas such as Tilghman Island.
"You may not need the same kind of restrictions for 10-acre lots as you do for houses that have 10-foot setbacks," St. Michaels resident Monica Otte said.
The revisions are still far from a potential vote. The commission and council will hold a joint workshop Tuesday at 2:30 p.m. Lesher said in an interview that he's listening to critics of the legislation, especially those who have specific objections.
Residents like Otte say they aren't looking for legislation to completely kill short-term rentals, but instead something to provide more balance.
"What we're looking for is a better balance, a more fair balance between Talbot residents and short-term rental owners," Otte said.

title: As Easton works on storm drains, future needs could present challenges
author: Konner Metz
content:
As Easton works on storm drains, future needs could present challenges

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 594
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Engineers in Easton are aiming to take a proactive approach to the town's storm drain infrastructure as they look to address flooding in susceptible areas.At an Easton Town Council meeting last month, Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh and Engineering Director Kody Cario said the town is currently performing video analysis on its storm drains on an as-needed basis. That leaves them in a reactionary position, Cario said.
"We don't know what we don't know right now, and that's concerning to us," he said at the May 19 meeting. "Because we don't know what the next problem could be."
Cario and Van Emburgh explained the town's ongoing storm drain projects and outlined proposals for how to fund future storm drain repair needs. The update to the council comes as experts say storms are putting more of a strain on drain systems.
Easton saw nearly two inches of rain on May 16. Engineers say some storm drain systems were "overwhelmed."
"When we have nights like we did last Friday night (May 16), you see how important it is to make sure that our storm drains are maintained," Van Emburgh said.
Environmental experts say this type of rain event may become more common in coming years.
"That sort of high intensity is what is expected as climate change impacts continue," said ShoreRivers Choptank Riverkeeper Matt Pluta in an interview. "Those storms are different from what we were used to 50 years ago, where a sprinkle or a moderate rain was common."
Pluta said storm drains can't always handle heavy rains and hail.
BEING PROACTIVE
Easton has 351,000 linear feet of storm drain pipe, or around 66 miles. Most of it is concrete, though the town also has plastic, metal, clay and brick pipes. Some of the older infrastructure dates back decades and could present road or water safety challenges according to town officials. But without video analysis done in advance, it's difficult for the town to know what needs to be replaced until it fails.
In hopes of gaining a more complete understanding of the condition of Easton's storm drains, Cario noted a few rough proposals from the engineering department: $500,000 for an emergency storm drain repair fund, $300,000 over six years to assess the town's other watersheds and $25,000 annually for storm drain analysis.
"Eventually we'd like to perform, yearly, a video analysis of our storm drain so that we can start checking through and seeing what the condition of our storm drains are," Cario said at the May meeting.
The proactiveness in video analysis could prevent the town from having to assume unexpected costs when emergency storm drain damages occur. The emergency repair fund would cover "what might be a catastrophic repair on the street," Cario said.
As considerations of future funding are put forward, some of Easton's storm drain systems are receiving attention this summer. Thanks to American Rescue Plan Act federal funding, Easton is forging ahead on two storm drain projects that fall within the Tanyard Branch watershed, a 900-acre area that drains into the Tred Avon River.
First is the mostly-completed Harrison Street effort. The town replaced a lot of brick pipe with reinforced concrete pipe, or RCP, Cario said in an interview. RCP generally has a longer service life compared to clay and brick pipes.
Crews worked Wednesday to repave Harrison Street as part of the project's final touches. Cario said the town appreciates the patience of residents through the multi-month process, which has included road closures.
In a few weeks, the town will embark on its East Avenue project, which is especially meant to address storm drain and flooding issues on August Street.

title: Oxford town commissioner election Q&As
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford town commissioner election Q&As

 June 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 1203
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — On June 17, the Town of Oxford will choose someone to fill one of three town commissioner seats. The race is between incumbent Tom Costigan and resident Dave Donovan. The winner will serve a three-year term.The Star Democrat sent a questionnaire to candidates running in the election to allow them to share their perspectives on various town issues in their own words.
Tom CostiganAge: 67.
Family: Married 39 years.
Occupation: Oxford Town Commissioner; retired realtor.
Political Experience: Three years as Oxford Town Commissioner.
Why are you running for office?
I am now, and have been for many years, dedicated to the town of Oxford. I devoted 12 years serving on our Historic District Commission (10 of those as chair) in the interest of preserving and protecting our architectural and cultural heritage. I've also spent countless hours volunteering within our community.
We're in the midst of progressing on many important challenges and projects, and I am determined to see them through. The institutional knowledge I've acquired in service to our town covers every facet of our government.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are to fully staff and equip our police department; attract, retain and support our town staff; complete Oxford's comprehensive plan (our road map to the future); continue our progress on flood and stormwater control (pumps and check valves); complete our infrastructure projects (water upgrades, shoreline protection); hold the line on property taxes and water/sewer fees; limit the growth trajectory of short-term rental properties; explore new technologies to defray escalating utility costs; support our local businesses and civic organizations and help them thrive; continue to resist Oxford Road development/sprawl; and ensure that Oxford's future is determined by full-time residents.
How should Oxford address the flooding and infrastructure concerns in the town?
We are addressing these issues. I have personally visited other coastal jurisdictions, where they shared their knowledge, challenges and solutions. Here in Oxford, we have successfully installed check valves and tide gates to limit tidal inundation in vulnerable areas. We have procured ARPA funding, which will allow us to purchase mobile pumps. I will continue to lobby the state government to resolve flooding issues at the Causeway (a choke point that can cut our town off from emergency services). In addition, I'll continue to seek new solutions such as cisterns to collect stormwater and appropriate plantings to further mitigate flooding.
How would you as an Oxford commissioner ease tensions between residents and the commission?
It all starts with effective communication. One recent example relates to our FY2025/26 budget planning, where we hosted citizen workshops to explain our financial projections and to garner the public's input. During my tenure, I've initiated live streaming of all town meetings. I instituted the Constant Contact platform to inform residents of helpful messages relating to meeting agendas, board openings, weather alerts, events, etc. In addition, we've implemented a new, more user-friendly website for ease of locating information. I will always welcome and respect new voices and ideas to enhance transparency.
What is your vision for the Strand Beach project?
Most importantly, I want to see the Strand project succeed. When the next major storm hits, I want to provide the most resilient protection possible. Did you know that the east end of the Strand was once an island? This project, which has been discussed in public workshops and presentations since 2010, is being done with grant funding, not costing local taxpayers a single dollar. As for the logs, discussions should continue as to their disposition — It's a question of aesthetics vs. ecological benefit. Bottom line: the project is working, the beach area is expanding and plantings are taking root.
Dave DonovanAge: 67 years old in June.
Family: I have been married to my wife Rose for 44 years this August. We have three children and two grandchildren.
Occupation: I retired at the end of 2018 from my partnership in a large law firm in Washington, D.C.
Political Experience: I have not previously sought to hold any public elective office or played any role in a political campaign other than as a low-level volunteer.
Why are you running for office?
For the past three years, the town has made needless mistakes that have created and exacerbated deep frustration among our residents. These errors include mishandling the termination of a long-time police chief; appointing a candidate to fill the balance of the term of a resigning commissioner rather than holding an election as the voters demanded; failing to manage completion of the Strand project; and utterly botching the hiring of the previous Town Manager last summer. We have serious issues that need to be addressed. I have the experience to help us make needed improvements, minimize damage already done and avoid repeating errors.
What are your priorities if elected?
We need to correct and complete the Strand project and get it behind us. Sound financial management is also a top priority. We need sensible management of our substantial cash reserves. I also will prioritize open and candid communications about all our issues, engaging the community to discuss potential solutions, and leveraging the incredible reservoir of talent and expertise we have in Oxford. We need to take advantage of the skills and experience of our residents and not shut them out, as has happened far too often in the last three years.
How should Oxford address the flooding and infrastructure concerns in the town?
We have had a plan in place for nine years to address flooding and infrastructure and done next to nothing to implement it. Addressing the Strand was the lowest priority in that plan, yet it has almost completely swallowed our attention. We need to work with our engineers and our residents to confirm our priorities, restart stalled initiatives, and identify and execute work that is in line with the priorities in that plan. With federal grants now drying up and our own tight budget, our options are limited, but we can still make meaningful progress.
How would you as an Oxford commissioner ease tensions between residents and the commission?
Rebuilding trust is essential, and it starts by electing new leadership that is not tied to and responsible for past mistakes. Much of our tension is due to poor communication by the commissioners. We need more open and candid discussions by the commissioners about matters that come before them so that residents can understand what the commissioners are thinking and why (and vice versa). Commissioners need to provide actual answers to questions that are asked. Too often, questions are acknowledged but never answered. With new leadership and better communication, we can rebuild the trust between our residents and the commissioners.
What is your vision for the Strand Beach project?
We must get this project behind us. We don't have the money to redesign or rebuild it, and it appears we waived many of our legal rights when the commissioners prematurely signed off on its completion last year. The only course now is to figure out what needs to be done to finish it, including restoring public and ADA access and minimizing the hazards created by the "natural" features in the islands. We should never again embark on a project of this magnitude just because we found a funding source, especially one for which there was no clear design at the outset.
Candidate responses may be edited for length and clarity.

title: Greensboro Council votes historical society out with 120 day notice
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro Council votes historical society out with 120 day notice

 June 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 508
 Words

 GREENSBORO — After months of discussion, the Greensboro Town Council voted to give the Greensboro Historical Society 120 days to vacate the Weaver Building.The 3-1 vote took place at the council's Thursday meeting. Councilwoman Christina Robinson did not vote because she is a member and on the board of of the Historical Society.
The Historical Society was first told about a potential move out of the Weaver Building in March, when officials raised the need for more space to house town agencies. The town determined the building could be used to house either the police department or the town employees office, but the council has leaned toward moving the police department.
The decision Thursday came after the public comment period, in which the Historical Society members asked the town to give them 90-120 days to vacate the premises.
"I would also like to request that we have some assistance from you to help us with the move and the items as well," Historical Society Vice President and Acting President Robert Moser said Thursday. "If you have any resources available to us like public works or even if it's to borrow a truck or something, or maybe have some people to volunteer to help."
Mayor David Spencer told Moser the town wants to help, but there are some legal hurdles they must go through in order to do so.
"I think that as much as we want to help you, with our vehicles and equipment and people, I think we need to talk to our lawyer to see if we need to have a liability release signed by you in the event that something is damaged in the move," Spencer said. "We don't want to be liable and have to to pay for any historic items."
Now that the Historical Society knows it must vacate the building, Moser and the Historical Society have plans for two potential alternative locations.
"One is actually in Greensboro," Moser said. The second option involves a reintegration with the Caroline County Historical Society, which Greensboro Historical Society was a chapter of at one time. "So, that was another option we kind of kept on our back pocket," Moser said.
"However, the leadership and the entire historical society membership wanted to keep it in Greensboro, which I would agree with."
Other changes Moser plans to make include changes of the group's bylaws and fundraising.
"We're actually doing a complete review of our bylaws and so forth like that because everything needs to be updated. That's something that should be completed at least on an annual basis. I mean, things need to change," Moser said.
"We have a golf tournament that's going to be coming up Sept. 19 at the Caroline County Golf Course. We're excited about that. "... Things that we're doing for fundraisers and so forth and that's going to be something that's really I'm going to be key to our success too, especially moving because we're not going around free now. So, we're going to have to be able to generate funds, funds to be able to maintain the facility and so forth."

title: Talbot County to revisit removing DEI statement with airport's federal funding at risk
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County to revisit removing DEI statement with airport's federal funding at risk

 June 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 635
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council will revisit the prospect of removing its diversity, equity and inclusion statement amid concerns for Easton Airport's federal funding.Though voted down in March, a resolution to remove the diversity statement found in the county's employee handbook is on the agenda for Tuesday's council meeting. Its reappearance is fueled by a directive from U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that could put millions of dollars for an ongoing Easton Airport project at risk, council members say.
The diversity statement — created after the passage of a 2020 resolution — defines diversity, equity and inclusion, explains its purpose and details the county's approach to ensuring diversity. It also outlines how employees can report discrimination.
In an April 24 letter, Duffy outlined the department's interpretation of federal law, including regarding DEI.
"Whether or not described in neutral terms, any policy, program, or activity that is premised on a prohibited classification, including discriminatory policies or practices designed to achieve socalled 'diversity, equity, and inclusion,' or 'DEI,' goals, presumptively violates Federal law," Duffy wrote.
Duffy wrote that noncompliance with federal law or "failure to cooperate" with federal agencies "could lead to a loss of Federal funding from DOT."
Easton Airport's ongoing modernization project — which will relocate and expand the airport's main runway — is 90% funded by the Federal Aviation Administration, an organization within DOT. The airport is owned and operated by Talbot County.
The resolution to remove Talbot County's DEI statement was initially proposed by council member Dave Stepp in February. It elicited strong resident opposition, stirred two heated council meetings and split the five-member council.
The council rejected the statement's removal in March by a 3-2 vote: President Chuck Callahan joined Stepp, while Vice President Pete Lesher and council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke opposed.
But now, Stepp and Lesher are sponsoring the resolution's reappearance after working together to tweak it given the recent DOT directive. Lesher said he supports it "without enthusiasm."
"The two of us came together, knowing that we are coming at this from different points of view," Lesher said in an interview Monday.
They both say passing the resolution will protect essential federal funds for the Easton Airport's modernization project. Stepp said $46.8 million is at risk.
"I think that folks didn't think this was real prior," Stepp said of the funding risks. "And they certainly will now."
Lesher said he's confident the county isn't violating what the Trump administration and DOT are targeting. But merely having the DEI statement, he said, could lead to blowback from what he called a "capriciously" acting administration.
"Does this feel like extortion? Yes," Lesher said. "We have to choose our battles. And I believe that what we are giving up here is important for appearances, but it is not substantive. We are not changing any policies in Talbot County by issuing this new administrative resolution."
The two sponsors of Tuesday's resolution offered slightly different interpretations of what it will do if passed.
Lesher said it would supersede the 2020 resolution and either lead to the removal or revision of the DEI statement so that it doesn't "presumptively violate" Duffy's directive.
Council can't "un-direct" staff to create the statement, Lesher said. Instead, he said, the resolution serves as "fresh direction."
Stepp, meanwhile, indicated the measure would completely repeal the 2020 resolution and remove the DEI statement, which is how the resolution was initially presented when it failed.
"It was fiscal responsibility then, and it's fiscal responsibility now," Stepp said.
The updated resolution will be read aloud Tuesday and potentially voted on. Lesher and Stepp both say they expect it to pass.
"We cannot afford to put the airport funding at risk," Lesher said. "It just would leave us in the middle of a project. It would really leave us in a lurch."
The Talbot County Council meets at 5 p.m. Tuesday in the Talbot County Courthouse Bradley Meeting Room.

title: Talbot County removes DEI statement amid funding concerns for airport
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County removes DEI statement amid funding concerns for airport

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 752
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council voted Tuesday to remove the diversity, equity and inclusion statement from the county's employee handbook, reversing course from March, when the council upheld the diversity statement.Tuesday's decision came amid concerns for millions of dollars in federal funding for an ongoing Easton Airport project. Those worries stem from an April directive from U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy outlining the Trump administration's view that DEI programs violate federal law.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher and council member Dave Stepp sponsored Tuesday's resolution, which passed 4-1 with council member Keasha Haythe opposing. Haythe, Lesher and council member Lynn Mielke had voted down Stepp's attempt to remove the DEI statement in March.
Lesher, a Democrat, said it was a difficult decision, noting he changed his tune on the measure due to a "vindictive and maleficent federal administration."
"The risk is that some incompetent political appointee will read only the title of our statement, misconstrue it as an illegal policy and deny a federal grant on that basis," Lesher said. "In an event like that, even if we win on appeal, it could leave us in a state of construction limbo for an unacceptably long time."
Lesher added, "We simply need to ensure that we are using none of the language that could trigger some snowflake in Washington."
Mielke, a Republican, said she agreed with Lesher and that Talbot County has always been a merit-based employer.
Stepp, a Republican, said council members "fell short" and put the county in a vulnerable spot when they rejected his original proposal in March.
"It's very frustrating that we even need to be discussing this here today. It should've been dealt with months ago," Stepp said. "This matter has been highly politicized and turned into something it is not."
"Today's action is fiscal in nature," he added.
Council President Chuck Callahan, a Republican, voted to remove the statement in March and did so again Tuesday. He said the controversial topic — which garnered strong resident opposition and led to two heated meetings — has been "tough on council."
"I know we all have our own beliefs, one way or the other with the DEI stuff," Callahan said. "But at this time I think we've made the right decision and the right statement."
Haythe, the council's only non-white member and a Democrat, asked county attorney Patrick Thomas about an opinion letter he provided on the DEI statement and Duffy's directive. Duffy's directive to all DOT funding recipients referenced the U.S. Supreme Court's 2023 rejection of affirmative action programs at Harvard University.
"I do not believe that the statement is discriminatory, and I do not believe that the Supreme Court (case) being referenced in the secretary of transportation letter applies to that statement," Thomas said.
Tuesday's resolution, effectively immediately, voids Talbot County's DEI statement. Two 2020 diversity resolutions are also "of no further force and effect," according to the newly approved resolution.
Those resolutions had facilitated the creation of the diversity statement and required the county manager to provide an annual diversity training report to the council, respectively.
The new resolution states nothing in it "shall be construed as a repudiation of the intent and desire" of the county to ensure a "welcoming workplace" in which employees are treated fairly based on race, sex, national origin, etc.
Lesher asked county staff to work on a "replacement welcoming statement" for the county's employee handbook.
AIRPORT PROJECT
Easton Airport's ongoing modernization project — which will relocate and expand the airport's main runway — is 90% funded by the Federal Aviation Administration, an organization within the Department of Transportation. The airport is owned and operated by Talbot County.
Airport Manager Micah Risher said he consulted with county staff after the April DOT letter. In an interview Tuesday, Risher said he has "absolute faith" in the council's support of the airport. Risher added that the airport ensures it is always abiding by federal and state laws.
"To have Easton Airport have any sort of funding at jeopardy, it's a bigger deal than the average person may think," Risher said, citing the airport's large economic impact on the community.
According to Risher, the airport received around $17 million from the FAA for the first two phases of the project. Estimates on the remaining federal funding for the rest of the project aren't available since bids are out, he said, but over $30 million of work remains.
"We're up here against our greatest milestone that is really going to ensure that we have a viable airport, and this great economic engine, succeed here in Talbot County for another 80-plus years," he said.

title: Caroline County passes fiscal year 2026 budget
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County passes fiscal year 2026 budget

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 413
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners adopted the county's fiscal year 2026 operating and capital budgets at a meeting Tuesday.The commissioners and county employees have been working on the budget for about six months and have balanced a $2 million shortfall. The revenue total for the county sits at $79,208,471.
Allocations to some departments and agencies dropped compared to years prior. Some organizations and nonprofits completely lost county funding in this year's budget. Among those organizations are the Human Service Council, His Hope Ministries and Big Brothers Big Sisters of the Eastern Shore.
While Commissioners President Travis Breeding wanted to cut all nonprofit funding to avoid picking and choosing organizations, Commissioners Larry Porter and Frank Bartz chose to give to certain nonprofits.
"My thought process was that that there are a lot of good nonprofits in the county, and we don't have the funding ability to support them all," Breeding said. "So, I didn't really want to get in a situation where we were picking and choosing which ones. I advocate for people to donate to all of those nonprofits, but it just didn't feel like a core responsibility of Caroline County to provide funding there."
During the end of the budget process, changes from the state impacted the proposed budget. In the income tax line item, the county's original $1 million loss due to the state allocating more cost to the county went down to only a $200,000 loss. In the disparity grant section, the legislators passed a bill to make the disparity grant gap cover 90% instead of the normal 75%.
The county decided to add money to the tar and chip fund in the infrastructure line item of the capital budget. This move left over $1 million for the county to allocate in the capital budget.
The county put $100,000 to Public Works for tree trimming and $980,994 toward a fund to purchase radios for emergency services.
In addition to the budget being passed, the county S&P grade has increased from an "AA minus" grade to an "AA." This grade is what allows the county to bond or borrow money.
The commissioners thanked county employees, Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox and Grant Coordinator Stacy Seward for their hard work balancing the budget and the grade upgrade.
"In an environment where a lot of government agencies are seeing reduced credit ratings, we have managed to see an increase here. I think its a testament to staff, tight budgeting and managing every dollar to make sure its used appropriately," Breeding said.

title: Oxford candidate forum draws large crowd
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford candidate forum draws large crowd

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 672
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — All the seats were full at the Oxford Community Center on Monday evening as town commissioner candidates Tom Costigan and Dave Donovan responded to residents' questions.With a week until the election for one of the town's three commissioner seats, the League of Women Voters of Mid-Shore, in tandem with citizens of Oxford, held a candidate forum to create dialogue between residents and candidates.
League of Women Voters Co-President Glenna Heckathorn moderated the event, and members handed out index cards and golf pencils for residents to write down questions.
Appointed timekeepers in the front row held green, yellow and red cardboard circles to indicate to the candidates one minute remaining, thirty seconds remaining and time complete. Each candidate had two minutes for their opening remarks and one minute and 30 seconds to answer each question.
Common themes of discussion included concerns over government transparency, local budget and federal grants, and flooding and wastewater management.
Transparency
Oxford residents have raised concerns about government transparency for several years. Donovan said Monday that many residents have raised these issues with him.
Because of the open meetings act, which requires commissioners to hold any meetings and or discussions of town matters in public, Donovan thinks it's particularly important to have tough, candid conversations during open sessions.
"The commissioners need to look at each other and have conversations out loud in front of whoever's there, or whoever's watching the video," he said. Donovan continued saying commissioners shouldn't fear getting caught in a "gotcha moment."
Costigan said he isn't afraid of a "gotcha moment" and that he has done more than any other commissioner in terms of boosting transparency, citing his efforts to have town hall meetings live streamed.
Residents expressed concerns over public information act requests going unanswered. Costigan said this was due to the volume of requests. Last year, over 40 of 73 total requests were submitted by the same four people on the same topic, he said.
Donovan said he's been satisfied with the PIA situation since Holly Wahl was hired as town manager in January. "I do think she was met with a mountain of work, and I also hope that as we move forward, we can increase the level of trust between the commission and the public and get fewer of these requests," Donovan said.
Flooding and Wastewater Management
Oxford currently deals with flooding retroactively with pumps. Donovan said Monday he wants to see a proactive plan in place so the town doesn't have to react every time it floods.
Donovan suggests taking another look at the storm water management plan from nine years ago and bringing in an outside consultant to advise the commission on how to proceed and how they can afford it.
Costigan said the town's been working on this for years through a federal ARPA grant they received as pandemic relief. He said he has also been working with public works officials in North Beach and Cambridge to see how they have been addressing the issue.
"There's additional equipment that we need to buy, that we are going to buy with the money that we have through ARPA, and I think that would go a long way towards fixing a lot of our flooding problems," Costigan said.
Budget and Grants
The Town of Oxford is currently reviewing its fiscal year 2025-2026 budget which is balanced. With the budget being perfectly balanced, there is little wiggle room for extra expenditures.
"There's money in there for various civic organizations, there's money in there for stormwater, there's money in there for various things that we want to get done in this town and that I know you all want to get done too," Costigan said.
Costigan said the budget will hopefully be approved at the Tuesday, June 10.
Donovan would like to see Oxford's excess funds divested from the local bank and invested in the Maryland Local Government Investment Plan, where it can grow at a higher interest rate.
Both candidates expressed concern over the future of federal grants.
The Oxford Town Commission election will be held on June 17 from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the Oxford Community Services Building.

 ST. MICHAELS — St. Michaels commissioners announced live Zoom meetings for the town government would be "discontinued for the foreseeable future" after second security incident in 2025.Both incidents involved disruptions caused by meeting attendees, town officials said.
"Both the February and June incidents were the same or similar with intentions of disrupting the open format forum," Town Manager Don Richardson said in a email to the Star Democrat on Tuesday. title: Floating solar panels could power Chestertown’s future
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Floating solar panels could power Chestertown’s future

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — A quiet corner of Chestertown may soon become home to a cutting-edge floating solar array, thanks to a newly approved lease agreement between the town and Third Pillar Solar, a renewable energy company working on a large-scale project atop the town's wastewater lagoon.The site, located off John Hanson Road, already houses the town's wastewater treatment plant and serves as a popular birding location, with more than 160 species reported.
The Town of Chestertown is working with Tom Dietz, the environmental committee's energy adviser, on the project, which is still in the design phase.
If constructed, the solar array would feature 7 megawatts of floating solar panels anchored to the lagoon and connected to Delmarva Power. The system would be built and operated by Third Pillar Solar, a U.S.-based company specializing in floating solar arrays on municipal and industrial water bodies.
At its June 3 meeting, the Chestertown Council approved a lease agreement allowing Third Pillar to proceed with development. The same night, Dietz's plan to begin project design was approved.
Project developer Michaela Hunt Hess attended the meeting to answer questions, though council members and Mayor David Foster had few, having already heard from Third Pillar Vice President of Development Ned Horneffer at previous meetings.
At the May 5 meeting, Horneffer presented a detailed overview of the project. He said the company, now about 20 employees strong, has grown rapidly, attracting professionals from major firms and securing backing from Glentra Capital, a private investment firm committed to fully funding the project.
Horneffer said the project has two phases: development and construction.
During development, Third Pillar will work with Delmarva Power to identify an interconnection point. In this phase, the company will pay the town $15,000 annually in rent, with increases of $3,000 per year.
If Delmarva determines the project is viable, Third Pillar will move into construction. At that point, the company will seek a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Maryland Public Service Commission, a process Horneffer said typically takes about a year.
Once construction begins and energy production is confirmed, the rent paid by the company will increase to approximately $81,000 annually, based on $12,000 per megawatt.
Third Pillar will cover the cost of any infrastructure upgrades required by Delmarva, estimated between $1 million and $3 million.
A decommissioning bond will be issued to the town as insurance in case the project becomes obsolete or is not completed.
Town Manager Larry DiRe asked whether the town would receive solar energy credits. Horneffer said no, but noted Chestertown could benefit by becoming an anchor subscriber to the energy output.
Foster raised questions about environmental impact and bird activity. Horneffer said that birds are often drawn to the floating panels and that the company may install deterrents, such as washers, to manage that.
Foster noted that the project involves a 42-year lease agreement — a long-term commitment for the town.
Before construction can begin, the next step will be approval of a transmission easement to run cables from the site. Horneffer said he would return to the council for that authorization.
He emphasized that Third Pillar would assume all project risk — owning, operating and maintaining the system, and subcontracting construction and maintenance to Maryland-based companies.
Floating solar arrays have gained support in Maryland as an alternative to projects that use farmland. Horneffer said Third Pillar is developing similar projects across Maryland, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, and hopes to add Chestertown to that list soon.
"We look forward to working with you all going forward," he told the council.

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council adopted its fiscal year 2026 budget Monday night after a contentious discussion over whether or not they would hold a vote or defer the budget adoption.After hearing public comments, council members considered whether or not they needed to make further amendments or deletions that would require deferring the vote.
Council member Brett Summers suggested deferring the vote because council member Brian Roche was not in attendance.
"I just want to remind you all, we're here to do the city's budget not to make sure commissioners have their camera time," said Mayor Lajan Cephas in response.
Council President Sputty Cephas pointed out that two council members will be absent at the next meeting and that deferring budget approval again would push the budget adoption very close to the start of the fiscal year on July 1.
The discussion of whether council members' schedules aligned and if they would discuss budget approval continued for several minutes.
"I just want to make you all aware, I'm very disappointed right now," said Lajan Cephas, who is not able to vote on council matters except in the event a tiebreaker vote is necessary. "I know my opinion doesn't matter, but we're here to do the city's business, and that should always matter."
Summers made a motion to defer the vote, and council member Frank Stout seconded. Sputty Cephas was joined by council member Shay Sisco-Lewis in opposition the motion. Lajan Cephas broke the tie, also voting in opposition of the motion. The council then began discussing the proposed budget.
Eventually, council members approved the budget unanimously.
The council also passed an ordinance establishing a maintenance reserve fund, which transferred $500,000 from the general fund to the maintenance reserve. Steckman and Director of Finance Perry Peregoy will maintain the reserve and deposit a minimum of $50,000 each fiscal year. No money will be withdrawn from the maintenance reserve fund until July 1, 2036.
The FY26 budget established the property tax rate of $1.69 per $100 of all assessed value, the same tax rate as the previous year.
The City Council was presented with a comically large check from representatives of Chesapeake Employers Insurance totaling $174,000 from a 2022 dividend. Steckman said the city has been working with Chesapeake Employers to help control workplace accidents and that the money will go into the general fund.
The city's FY2026 budget will go into effect on July 1.

 Historically, those living down long lanes and private roads in Dorchester County have struggled to get broadband access. The Maryland Homestretch — Difficult To Serve Properties Program is administered by the Maryland Office of State Broadband and provides funding for internet installation in areas where it can be particularly expensive. The program is also referred to as the Long Driveway Internet Program.
Williams referred to the program as "ever changing," saying the state modified the grant program as recently as this spring.
This came in handy when the amount initially awarded to the county was not enough to cover projected costs for the project.
Initially, the county was granted $1.1 million, but the project is estimated to cost $2,422,493. The county was recently awarded with a higher grant after Williams advocated for more homes to be covered.
However, The grant still will not cover all of the 299 homes approved to be serviced, so energy companies Bay Country and Choptank Electric are investing in the county to ensure access, Williams said.
Choptank Electric spokesperson Valerie Connelly and Williams requested two action items from the Cambridge County Council at the June 3 County Council meeting.
The first item is accepting the higher grant award of $1,217,852. The second is having the county sign a memorandum of understanding with Choptank Electric and Bay Country. The Commissioners unanimously agreed, with County Commissioner Ricky Travers leading the motion.
According to Connelly, broadband will be installed at no cost to the homeowners and all construction must be completed by Dec. 31, per the grant.
