title: Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Planning Commission members are largely skeptical of proposals to increase regulations on short-term rentals in the county.During a joint workshop with the County Council on Tuesday, the commission reviewed legislation sponsored by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher. Planning Commission members said they struggled to understand why stricter rules for short-term rentals were necessary.
Commission Member Chip Councell said some of the proposed items are more of a "hindrance" than an improvement to the county's existing rules.
"I would almost support an easing of some of the restrictions more so than getting more stringent," Councell said. "I'm struggling to see this as a balance."
Mielke has previously said the legislation was drafted amid a "proliferation" of short-term rentals in Talbot County, noting her concerns for St. Michaels village communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista.
Mielke said Tuesday that in village zones, some communities don't have covenants or restrictions on the temporary rentals. County attorney Patrick Thomas, who helped draft the legislation, noted it can be "tricky" to change covenants since many require 75 to 80% of homeowners to agree.
"They can be overwhelmed by short-term rentals, so the idea was to sort of make a distinction," Mielke said.
Mielke added that an increasing number of short-term rentals are "being scooped up by investors," which she says is hurting the county's affordable housing stock. Planning Commission members disagreed.
"I don't see where this is a proliferation," Councell said, citing that the number of licensed short-term rentals hasn't significantly increased or reached 200 in the last few years.
"They're taking them from subpar to show pieces for people to come down and enjoy," said commission chair James Corson. " … I don't think the majority of these are even in that range of affordable housing."
Some of the new restrictions if the legislation is passed would include: mandatory landlines; more detailed stay logs for license renewals; a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts; and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
The proposals have drawn support from a number of residents around the county but sharp criticism from short-term rental property agents and owners who view them as government overreach.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license to operate a short-term rental. Most license requests are granted.
Corson raised qualms with how the proposed seven-night minimum stay could deter tourists from attending weekend events such as the Waterfowl Festival. Lesher acknowledged it's "largely a weekend business" and said he's comfortable keeping the current three-day minimum in place.
County Council member Dave Stepp weighed in against proposals for more detailed logs and required landlines.
"To have that legislation in there, it just doesn't make any sense," he said of the landlines.
No official changes were made to the draft regulations Tuesday. The commission will hold a public hearing and discuss the legislation at its July 2 meeting. A recommendation will then be made to the council, likely with significant revisions to the original proposals.
Planning Commission vice chair Michael Strannahan said the issue comes down to preserving the balance between economic benefits and maintaining the county's complexion.
"It's the old growth versus character thing we face all the time," Strannahan said.

title: Easton council maintains seafood odor ordinance, rejects amendment
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council maintains seafood odor ordinance, rejects amendment

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 678
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council on Monday rejected a proposal to relax language in a seafood odor ordinance that has been a topic of contention between residents and a local business for much of the last year.In a 4-1 decision, with council member Maureen Curry the lone yes, the council voted down an amendment proposed to change the wording of the odor law that takes effect July 1.
The town's ordinance, passed back in December, is meant to address resident complaints of odor from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue, a crab processing facility near many homes. Per the ordinance, the business must install odor control technology and do so "in such a manner that no odor ... can be detected."
While attorney Zach Smith said Monday that an odor control system was recently installed, he appealed to the council to accept the amendment. Smith and Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner Mitch Hughes have said the "no odor" standard is unachievable, citing industry experts. They've expressed concern that once the ordinance goes into effect, further complaints could leave them out of compliance and force them to close the business.
Ward 2 representative Robert Rankin visited the business last week and said on one hand, he's "optimistic and hopeful" the new odor system will address the residents' complaints.
"On the other hand, it just being installed over the weekend, it doesn't give a lot of time to measure success," Rankin said.
Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis said it's a "wait-and-see" approach. "We may have to look at our (original ordinance) and make sure that it has teeth," he said.
Ward 3's David Montgomery said he wished there was a more obvious correct decision. He said the focus will turn to town code enforcement on how future complaints or violations are dealt with.
During more than 40 minutes of public comment on the topic, multiple residents said the smell hasn't gone away since the system was installed. A Chesapeake Brand employee noted the system may take some time to be fully dialed in.
Those who spoke included family and friends of Hughes or local watermen. Some criticized the town for issuing the restrictions targeted toward Chesapeake Brand, a business that was legally permitted by the town and opened in 2019.
"There's been a negative portrayal of my cousin in the paper and on social media when in fact it should be the town that is to blame for all of this drama," said Kim Gibbons-Neff, Hughes' cousin.
"The town should have nipped this in the bud after the initial complaints and told the residents that the business is in compliance and they are doing nothing wrong," she added.
Local business owner Donna Bramble said the town could be losing trust with small businesses.
"As a business owner, how can small businesses trust the Town of Easton if you issue a permit, they put the expense in of starting their business, and then because there's a complaint, you force them to move?" Bramble asked. "And that's really what's happening. You're going to force Mitch to close up and move."
Peter Maloney, one of the residents who's led calls for reduced odor from the business, said residents don't have anything against Hughes or small businesses.
"They got a legal permit to be there. And that is a question you all need to ask, as to why that legal permit was given," Maloney said toward the council. "But that doesn't mean that they should be there."
Smith, the attorney, warned the council that its "authority here is not limitless."
"While the town can certainly adopt new standards to some extent, you can't adopt standards that are going to preclude him from continuing to operate his business," Smith said.
Following the public hearing and vote, council President Don Abbatiello said people on both sides made valid points and that it wasn't an easy decision to reject the business' amendment.
"But at the end, at least for myself, it's responsibility to represent the residents," Abbatiello said. "And my hope is that going forward, this mitigation process will work, and the facility will be able to stay there and be successful."

title: Donovan wins Oxford commissioner seat
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Donovan wins Oxford commissioner seat

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 518
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Dave Donovan won the Oxford town commissioner election by 44 votes Tuesday after a sometimes tense race.Residents cast their ballots for either Donovan or incumbent Tom Costigan between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. or by absentee ballot. On Tuesday, 326 voters showed up, and 71 voters cast absentee ballots.
"It's quite gratifying," Donovan said after hearing the results. He said it was hard to tell if the news was good when he initially received the phone call from Oxford's Board of Elections Supervisors Tuesday night. "They're very matter of fact. They have a form they read to you, so you don't really know what the punch line is until the end."
Donovan will serve a three-year term as an Oxford commissioner.
The town's elections took a new shape this year, with the Board of Elections overseeing the process after residents voiced concerns over transparency.
The board instituted two new rules that chair Debbie Krolicki said went smoothly during Tuesday's voting process. Krolicki said residents now have to bring proof of domicile and identification, measures taken in order to prevent "temporary residents" who do not live in the town year-round from voting.
"About 95% of our voters have brought their IDs," Krolicki said. "They're very happy about our new process, but it's a new process."
According to Costigan, the past three elections have become increasingly "ugly" and contentious. "People should treat each other with a little bit of respect and a little bit of courtesy, you know?" he said Tuesday afternoon.
Donovan and Costigan both referenced separate "smear campaigns" that have spread throughout the town during campaigning.
"I was surprised that they waited until the last minute when they knew there was no opportunity for me to address it, which I thought was underhanded," Donovan said in reference to emails sent to town residents Sunday questioning Donovan's motivations.
Though tension was building between candidates, the atmosphere on Election Day was relatively light. The Board of Elections livestreamed the vote count inside the Oxford Community Services Building.
Resident Carol Griggs said she came out to vote in this election because of pressing issues at hand, particularly town finances and the Strand Beach project.
"You know, we need a little change here," she said. "We need things to move forward."
Griggs said this election has drawn more community attention than previous elections due to all the "hot button issues" at hand like town finances and the Strand project.
Costigan said he was disappointed with the results of the election and in some ways disappointed with the people of Oxford. "I've served in this town for 15 years, and they decided to bring on somebody new. I understand that, that's their choice," Costigan said.
Donovan will be sworn in as the new town commissioner on July 3. "Honest to God, I think this is a win for everybody in Oxford," he said. "There's still a small number of people that may be upset by this, but I also believe that those people are just as important to the outcome as anybody else in town, and I will represent them as if they voted for me. I hope that I can earn their trust."

title: Cambridge steps up code enforcement
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge steps up code enforcement

 June 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News

 CAMBRIDGE — City Manager Glenn Steckman said Cambridge is stepping up its code enforcement as trash cans are increasingly left on the sidewalk, grass is going uncut and cars are parked in the wrong direction."There seems to be a lack of lawnmowers in our community because the grass and grass height has been an ongoing issue in the town, and we're having to send violation notices out," Steckman said.
Code enforcement is a process used by local governments to enforce state and local laws, codes or ordinances regarding housing, building and health standards. The city's stepped-up code enforcement efforts became a topic of discussion at the Cambridge City County's meeting Monday after a resident raised concerns and confusion.
Cambridge resident Sharon Wilson was fined $200 due to a partially knocked down brick wall on her property. Wilson presented images of the fallen wall to the City Council, saying she feels zoning codes are being enforced unfairly.
Wilson said a city staff member stopped by her property asking her to clean up the bricks.
"They told me I had to clean it up, and he said, 'You cleaned it, but you didn't clean it up enough.' OK, so what is enough for you?" Wilson said.
She continued to address the council asking if this is something they do for all city residents.
"I said that's a lie. You're not fair," Wilson said. "Because if you're being fair you'd be going to the city limits checking all the properties."
Wilson said she "was shocked" when she drove around the city to look at the properties and saw many that were "more of hazard" than hers.
"We want to make sure she understands that she is not being picked on," Steckman said. "That this is not just her issue, this is a Cambridge issue."
He said that the city has received a growing number of code-related complaints, which is why the city is sending out more citations than in previous years.
Steckman said the city has sent out a notice to residents outlining the city's code standards and plans to send another one soon.

title: Dorchester County Council to submit five legislative initiatives
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Dorchester County Council to submit five legislative initiatives

 June 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Dorchester County Council Members are planning to submit five recommendations for the Maryland Association of County's 2026 legislative initiatives.MACo will select four initiatives based on feedback and suggestions from Maryland's county jurisdictions and Baltimore City to prioritize during the state's General Assembly beginning in January.
MACo's 2025 initiatives focused on local revenue structures, infrastructural funding, the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and clean energy. Dorchester County's recommendations for 2026 do not differ too much.
The Dorchester County Council's five recommendations are:
To consider a pause or suspension of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future education plan to allow counties to catch up financially.To rethink or review existing rules or policies that override local control over solar energy regulations.To improve infrastructure related to transportation and water drainage in Dorchester County.To introduce an initiative regarding safety concerns of solar battery storage and concerns regarding the sufficiency of the decommissioning bond that covers the cost of removing solar infrastructure once it's no longer in use.To continue to reform juvenile justice. This recommendation came after a 15-year-old resident shot and killed another resident in the 900 block of Cornelia Street on June 8.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said juvenile justice laws need serious reformation to make Dorchester County a safer place.
"Whether you're below 18 or over 18, you have to get some feedback for your actions," Detmer said. "Your terrible actions aren't in a vacuum; we all live here."
The purpose of MACo's recommended initiatives is to address problems counties are facing with state legislators. County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the organization collects concerns and information from counties to assist them in navigating the legislative process at the General Assembly.
Detmer said that these initiatives don't always align with Dorchester County due to the county's unique set of problems, and this misalignment has caused some tension with the state. "You know, things are complicated," he said. "I would say the tension really stems from the policies and laws that the state is enacting."
Elected officials from Maryland's 23 counties and Baltimore City can submit legislative proposal initiatives on behalf of the county as an elected body, generally at an open meeting or via a voting process, or not on behalf of the county, but as an individual.
Nominations can be submitted online through June 27 on the MACo website.

title: 'Proven leader': Easton will soon welcome Kitzrow as new town manager
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Proven leader': Easton will soon welcome Kitzrow as new town manager

 June 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After nearly a year without a permanent town manager, Easton will welcome Andy Kitzrow next month.Kitzrow, the current Salisbury city administrator, was tapped by Mayor Megan Cook to assume the post from Police Chief Alan Lowrey, the interim town manager since August. Kitzrow begins July 7.
During an interview in Salisbury last week, Kitzrow said he instantly noticed opportunity in Easton.
"The more I looked at Easton, the more I started to fall in love with where they're going," Kitzrow said.
The new town manager is Cook's most major appointment in her two years as mayor. Kitzrow will oversee town operations, lead department heads and town staff, and be a point of contact with the mayor and Town Council members.
After whittling down a list of around 12 semifinalists, the town conducted full-day interviews with four finalists. It was an intensive but worthwhile process, Cook said.
She felt Kitzrow rose above the others, as he was up to speed on what's happening in Easton and meshed well with her and with town employees.
"(Staff) really thought of the candidates, he could get up and running the fastest because he had the background of Maryland politics," Cook said.
Kitzrow, 42, served as Wicomico County recreation superintendent before becoming Salisbury's deputy city administrator in 2017 and city administrator in 2023.
In Salisbury, Kitzrow worked under three different mayors, including Jake Day, now the Department of Housing and Community Development secretary. Day noted Kitzrow's oversight of city permit and procurement operations as especially impactful.
"It's not easy work, but he's a proven leader," Day said of Kitzrow. "Somebody who can do it."
Cook says while the Day connection didn't factor into her decision, it will benefit Easton as the town tackles its own housing challenges and initiatives.
"Having that relationship, I think, is great. It's key," Kitzrow said. "A lot of this is about relationships, whether they are elected officials or state officials."
A BETTER FIT
Working under three different mayors, Kitzrow says he's experienced three very different visions.
In early 2023, Day left Salisbury with then-city administrator Julia Glanz to head up the state's housing and community development efforts. Jack Heath served as mayor until current Mayor Randy Taylor won an election later that year.
During Day's tenure, Salisbury undertook a number of efforts to redevelop its downtown through programs providing tax incentives to developers, such as "Here is Home" and HORIZON — the latter aimed at bringing multifamily residential and hotel units, an initiative which Kitzrow championed.
"(He was) the mastermind behind the HORIZON legislation that we passed locally," Glanz said.
Taylor and developers have clashed in recent months over the stalling of downtown projects, some of which were approved by former mayors and councils. In April, DelmarvaNow.com reported that developers of a downtown project filed a $40 million lawsuit against Salisbury and Taylor.
While Kitzrow believes the change in vision is OK and can be solved through compromise, he acknowledges it factored into his choice to accept the Easton post. Neither Taylor nor Heath could be reached for an interview.
"Professionally and personally, the town that Megan wants to run and her goals align more with what I value and what I want to be part of," Kitzrow said.
GOALS IN EASTON
Salisbury's population is nearly double Easton's, but Kitzrow sees similar challenges and opportunities in the two areas.
He said he wants to "move projects forward in a smart way." In Salisbury, he's dealt with a housing pipeline of around 5,000 units and led a focus on building "from the inside out." Easton's pipeline has recently hovered around 1,000 units.
Kitzrow is hoping to bring a focus to Easton's Rails to Trails network, given his parks and recreation background, as well as get "under the hood" in the human resources department.
Cook said she's excited to bring on a consistent leader during what she says has been a year full of change in town. "I'm looking forward to a steady ship ... and some calm seas ahead," Cook said.
Working for the mayor, Kitzrow emphasized that strong relationships with the Town Council will be crucial in completing the work that will make Easton a better place.
"We are working together, not against each other, and I think that's important," Kitzrow said.
Kitzrow will remain living in Salisbury with his wife and kids. He owns Escape Salisbury, a downtown escape room business.
But he's looking to learn as much about Easton as possible. He said he's especially excited to meet business owners, nonprofit leaders and community members in his first 60 days on the job.

title: Unaffiliated voters should vote in all elections
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Unaffiliated voters should vote in all elections

 June 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Under current Maryland election law, political parties have the power to decide whether or not to hold closed primary elections.For example, with closed primary elections, only voters registered with the Republican Party can vote in Republican primary elections and only voters registered with the Democratic Party can vote in Democratic primary elections.
Unaffiliated voters and voters registered with other parties can vote in post primary general elections, nonpartisan municipal elections, local judicial elections and school board elections.
When most Maryland voters were registered as Republican or as Democratic voters this was not widely viewed as an issue requiring review or attention.
That could change based in large part on unaffiliated voter registration numbers.
Currently, 907,638 of Maryland voters are registered as unaffiliated in contrast to 1,007,000 voters who are registered Republican and 2,211,316 voters who are registered Democrat.
Currently, 123,324 of Congressional District 1 (which includes all of the Eastern Shore) voters are registered as unaffiliated in contrast to 242,659 voters who are registered Republican and 185,754 voters who are registered Democrat.
Currently, 5,905 of Talbot County voters are registered as unaffiliated in contrast to 11,597 who are registered as Republican and 10,534 who are registered as Democrat.
The unaffiliated voter registrations numbers in Maryland have been noticed by the Open Primaries Foundation. This national organization advocates for open primary elections in America and should not be confused with the Open Society Foundation founded and funded by George Soros.
An Open Primaries Foundation spokesperson recently said, "The Open Primaries Foundation is dedicated to closing closed primary elections around the country. Maryland is just the beginning."
Another foundation spokesperson recently said, "Nearly a million Maryland voters shut out of voting is a crisis. Independent voters are the fastest growing group of voters in America, but they are treated as second-class citizens in Maryland and across the country. We cannot continue to publicly fund and administer elections that shut these voters out if we want to continue to call ourselves a democracy."
The Open Primaries Foundation is now collaborating with a Maryland law firm and five Maryland voters on a lawsuit challenging state funding of closed primaries.
All five voters are registered unaffiliated voters and were barred from voting in the partisan 2022 and 2024 primary elections in Anne Arundel County.
The lawsuit claims that state election officials are violating Article 1, Section 1 of the state constitution, which guarantees that every qualified U.S. citizen who is a resident of Maryland shall be entitled to vote in the ward or election district in which the citizen resides at all elections to be held in this State. The suit also maintains state election officials are violating Articles 7 and 24 of Maryland's Declaration of Rights.
The lead attorney for this lawsuit is former Maryland Lt. Gov. Boyd Rutherford.
Recently, Rutherford has said the following regarding the lawsuit:
"The constitution says all elections. Nowhere in the constitution does it state anything about primaries or political parties or anything of that notion.
"It [the lawsuit] is not an attack on the parties. It does not require the political parties to allow unaffiliated voters to vote in partisan party elections. This action is to prevent the state from funding these primaries that unconstitutionally exclude unaffiliated voters.
"Requiring party affiliation to vote creates a barrier of partisan primaries that the state endorses and supports and funds, which is contrary to the plain reading of the state constitution and the Declaration of Rights."
Some suggest this issue could be and should be addressed in the General Assembly. While that is always possible, it is not probable, at least in the near future.
In 2023, two open primary bills in the General Assembly were never voted out of a committee.
Rutherford has said "I don't think the legislature sees it in their interest, even though they should, because it is a question of voting rights. We think the courts need to take it up, just like the Voting Rights Act or Brown v. Board of Education. The legislature alone is not going to do it."
I agree and suggest that lack of legislative action on this issue affirms Niccolo Machiavelli's timeless observation on change:
"It must be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to plan, more doubtful of success, nor more dangerous to manage, than introducing new ways of doing things. For the initiator has the enmity of all who would profit by the preservation of the old ways of doing things and merely lukewarm defenders in those who would gain by the new ones."
That said, I optimistically predict that eventually the legal challenge will succeed, and the General Assembly will approve changes to the current law to allow for some form of open primaries in Maryland.
Until then, Maryland's unaffiliated voters will continue to be observers of, rather than participants in partisan primary elections.

title: 'Ride on, dear friend'
author: BOB FORD Special to the Star Democrat
content:
'Ride on, dear friend'

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BOB FORD Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Ride On Dear Friend 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — An unusually large rockfish was landed in Rock Hall on June 20 when a new striped bass-inspired bike rack was installed on Main Street to honor the memory of Ken McLaughlin, whose tireless work for the community is sorely missed.The rack, created by Greg Jetton of Gunsmoke Fabrication, calls to mind McLaughlin's fondness for pedaling around his adopted town, often doing favors or making deliveries, or dropping in to aid various non-profit organizations with their websites.
McLaughlin, who died suddenly last September at the age of 65 in the Main Street home he shared with his partner, Carol Sutera, was a retired website designer. He volunteered his expertise to help with the Friends of Eastern Neck, the Lions Club, the Mainstay, Main Street Rock Hall, as well as events including Rock Hall FallFest and Pirates & Wenches.
"This is a great addition to our town. It really speaks a lot about this community. It is very Rock Hall," said Mayor James Cook at the unveiling ceremony. "It helps the community, and that's a testament to our friend, Ken. He was active day-in and day-out to improve the lives of others. This speaks to that and his spirit lives on."
The rack was funded with help from the Kent Cultural Alliance, the Lions Club and Rock Hall Main Street. It rests on a bed of oyster shells that came from the backyard of Kent County Commission President and Rock Hall native Ron Fithian.
"And I shucked every one of them," Fithian said.
When Jetton was commissioned to build the rack, he knew what he had in mind before he found it.
"My intention was to have something like a crab or a rockfish to really make it Rock Hall," Jetton said. "It took some time, but I finally found a design I liked that would work."
The rack, located on a corner of Durocher's lot on the west side of Main Street, is made from half-inch and quarter-inch welded steel and weighs a sturdy 350 pounds.
Steve Leonard, the pastor of Raum Chapel UME on Skinner's Neck, is also co-operator of the new Rock Hall Brewing Company, which is located directly across the street from the bike rack. The brewpub hosted a small reception for those who attended the ceremony, which also served as a soft opening for the business.
"We just got the fire marshal's approval today," Leonard said. "To be part of this is an honor and it is amazing."
"Ken would have had a blast here tonight," Sutera said, as she looked around the gathering. "He'd be a little embarrassed by the attention, because he was so humble. He never made it about himself. He loved Rock Hall. We bought the house here three years ago and I was still going back and forth to Pennsylvania for work. It didn't take very long for Ken to say, 'I'm staying here. I'll see you when you get back.' He fell in love with the town."
The town returned the affection, and now his place in its memories is matched by a special spot on Main Street, with a dedication plaque that ends with these words: "Ride on, dear friend. Ride on."

title: Caroline County employees and residents voice concerns about Chaberton Solar
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County employees and residents voice concerns about Chaberton Solar

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Caroline County's latest battle against solar development took place during a public hearing for Chaberton Solar in Federalsburg on June 12 at Caroline County Public Library.The hearing was held amid an ongoing court battle between the county and the development company. Multiple county residents voiced their concerns for bringing Chaberton Solar into Federalsburg, citing housing options that could replace the proposed solar array.
"Well, I think it's good," Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said about residents coming forward. "The main reason that we were opposing this one was because it was in the R1 (residential) zoning district and we just felt that it was not in compliance with our comprehensive plan and we feel that the town could grow with the availability of water and sewer and that land would be better used for potentially for housing."
Late last year, Chaberton Solar Pahar applied with the county to construct a 3.0 MW solar facility in Federalsburg. The application was denied because it did not meet zoning requirements laid out by the county.
The company requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area, where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting the application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, according to County Attorney Stewart Barroll.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
According to Lauren Barchi, community engagement manager for Chaberton Solar, the proposed solar facility will cover 42 acres parcel, and 20 acres will be used for the placement of solar panels. Chaberton also plans to create an access road off the project location. The project's access to the site will be controlled via a locked gate with a seven-foot agricultural style fence around the perimeter.
While dates and locations have not been set, there will be more informational sessions on Chaberton Solar, according to county officials.

title: Caroline commissioners weigh potential locations for new Lockerman Middle
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline commissioners weigh potential locations for new Lockerman Middle

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During the Caroline County Commissioners' open comment report Tuesday morning, Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter brought up the discussion on Lockerman Middle School's proposed locations.Porter said he preferred that the new middle school go on the North Caroline High School property, one of two locations being considered during the design processes for the building begin. The other location, near the county sheriff's office on Double Hills Road, presents several challenges, Porter said.
"I think at this point I would like to say that I am in favor of the North Carolina location as opposed to being built in town," Porter said.
Commissioners Frank Bartz agreed with Porter and cited traffic and safety concerns on Route 404.
The commissioners also had discussions about the school's location at their meeting two weeks ago.
At that meeting, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman presented the two location options. Commissioners President Travis Breeding sparked a conversation about how much sway the commissioners have over the school's location.
"How much influence do the commissioners actually have over where the school gets constructed?" Breeding asked two weeks ago. "As part of the funding of this, other than a survey, we haven't really been consulted."
Breeding then explained the issues they would run into with each potential location.
"From what I gather, it seemed like a lot of people really preferred the Double Hills location. But, with Double Hills, we've got to work out a ton of details with the Town of Denton as far as sewer, water allocation for that to work, potentially pump station upgrades," Breeding said.
He then mentioned traffic issues on Route 404 with beach traffic towards the end of the school year and students from northern county towns like Marydale, who would have to take the bus a long distance to the potential Double Hills location.
Porter, said he didn't recall that "the county did not have a lot of input" on the design of new county buildings in the past.
Freeman assured Breeding that the county will be involved with the full feasibility study for both sites to determine which site makes the most sense.
Breeding also brought forward discussion of how much influence the commissioners will have for the design of the school.
"Then also, how much input do we have over the the design?" Breeding asked. "I mean, we don't want a situation where we're building something that's way more expensive than it needs to be or making it as functional as we can and keeping the cost as low as we can."
Bartz raised an issue where if the county has to build a new detention center, a school on the Double Hills Road site would cause a problem. The Caroline County Sheriff's Office is located near that Double Hills Road site, making the location logical for a detention center, he said.
The county is in talks with Queen Anne's County about a new 388-bed regional detention center that would house all Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent county prisoners. After conversations about control and cost of the center, discussions between the three counties have slowed down.
Lockerman name
Porter pointed out conversation that are being had about the Lockerman's name staying at the location of the current building instead of being attached to the new school.
Though the existing building will no longer be used as a school when the new school is built, Porter said he was in favor of keeping the Lockerman name attached to the facility in the interest of honoring its history.
"I think it's going to be important that the history of the school and the name of Lockerman be retained," he said. "I don't know what the future use is going to be for that building, but it's important, I think, from the alumni standpoint, from the community standpoint, that the history be be kept there for whatever use is going to be done in the future."
Breeding suggested drafting a letter of intent to the Caroline County Board of Education stating that it would be the commissioners' intention to retain the name of the building.

title: Water park renovation cost, timeline, vex council
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Water park renovation cost, timeline, vex council

 June 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 411
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Another summer of water park dormancy in Chesapeake Beach could stretch into year three if the price isn't right.On June 12 the mayor and town council received a second presentation from a consultant about how to improve the 30-year-old facility, which was closed in 2023 by the previous administration.
"We know it needs to be done, we are trying to find the most efficient way to do it," Mark Wilkerson of Paddock Pool Company told the town council during the presentation.
In April the council allocated $60,000 for the consultant to explore the feasibility of bringing the facility back to life.
Wilkerson said a design team was hired and geo-technology engineers examined the pilings on which the park is located.
"The intent is to use the existing piling system," Wilkerson said.
The consultant provided town officials with two concepts.
Wilkerson said the Concept A is "basically, the park as it is now, with some changes that came from the waterpark committee, from public works, other interested parties and my team as well."
The changes would include a new slide and what Wilkerson described as improved park circulation.
Wilkerson described many of the components of Concept B as being friendlier to the area's aging population, with more shade, underwater benches, increased deck space and speed control for the park's "lazy river."
Wilkerson said of potential changes to the facility, "It will never be perfect because I can't make the ground any bigger." He said the town will "make the best use of the space we have."
The uncertain price tag of the renovation project prompted one council member to speak up.
"I think it would be irresponsible for this council to continue with additional funding without knowing what this project costs," Councilman Eric Reinhardt said. "We need to know what it's going to cost up front before we're dumping additional money into it. The water park has never been a profitable enterprise."
Reinhardt added that while he understood the water park is part of Chesapeake Beach's "DNA, the best path is not going as fast as we can."
Councilman Jamey Shuls said the town does need to do something.
"We know the water park is not repairable," Shuls said, adding that to do nothing would leave a park "rotting in front of our eyes."
Councilwoman Laura Blackwelder said she would prefer the recommended demolition be part of the contract for any renovation project, rather than possibly working with two separate contractors.
Wilkerson said he would return to the council for their July meeting and provide cost estimates.

title: Planners not sold on 365-unit development near new Easton hospital
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planners not sold on 365-unit development near new Easton hospital

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 739
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An application for a 365-unit residential development near the in-construction regional medical center in Easton has been submitted to the town's Planning Commission for review, though it's drawing criticism from some town and county officials.The project, Fox Chase Estates, is proposed on 112 acres of land off of Airport Road nestled within the Easton Technology Center. Developers are seeking town approval through Easton's planned unit development process, which would allow the homes to be built on the commercial-zoned land.
The developers are Easton Sunrise Partners LLC and Scott Wagner, a Talbot County businessman and a former Republican member of the Pennsylvania State Senate. They previously aimed to build warehouses on the site, but in recent years plans shifted to residential — an effort that Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel supports, according to Wagner's attorney, Lawrence Scott.
"We are trying to build a residential community that meets the need of the hospital," Scott said Tuesday, noting that Wagner and Kozel have met to discuss the project.
In a statement Wednesday, Kozel said affordable housing availability is "essential" to recruit and retain health care workers in a rural community like Easton. The hospital is not legally or financially involved with the proposed development, Scott said.
At an hours long meeting Tuesday, Planning Commission members were nowhere near ready to provide a positive recommendation on the proposal.
"It feels like we're being the Planning Commission for the hospital and not for the town," said member William Ryall. "And that gives me a lot of concern."
Victoria McAndrews said the plans are "overwhelmingly suburban." Michael Ports, the commission's vice chair, said a lack of connectivity from the proposed development — which sits at the northernmost part of town limits — to Easton's core is a "non-starter."
Philip Toussaint, commission chair, said parts of the plan significantly fall short of meeting Easton's comprehensive plan, which sets the framework for how the town facilitates growth. That comprehensive plan is undergoing an update currently, and McAndrews said such a large project should wait for that update.
Scott said Tuesday that developers have met individually with Town Council members and Mayor Megan Cook multiple times and that the 365-unit project meets affordable housing needs that the town and its residents are asking for.
THE UNITS
Application documents show that developers are planning for a variety of units, including single-family homes, three-story townhomes and multifamily buildings, along with two commercial buildings.
The 365 units are broken down as follows: 108 single-family detached homes, 137 three-story townhomes and 120 multifamily units, the latter of which are contained in four four-story buildings.
The density is well below the maximum permitted by the town's planned unit development standards. According to developers, 185 of the 365 units would be affordably priced.
"We're doing that without even the statutory forcing of us to do it," Scott said, adding that developers have a "bidding war" from home building companies to take on the project. "The market is working on its own."
APPROVAL PROCESS
Fox Chase Estates still has a handful of steps before it is approved by Easton officials. With significant pushback already, it's likely to be a lengthy process.
In staff analysis of the application, concerns were raised about the site plan, which only includes one main vehicle access point to the 365-unit development. An emergency exit stretching west to Goldsborough Neck Road did not satisfy town staff. Scott said developers would prefer not to add that as a main access point but will consider it.
"We really want two access points to any project like this," said Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh.
Talbot County Engineer Ray Clarke criticized the project and the lack of communication between developers and the county. Clarke said it'll put an undue stress on Airport and Goldsborough Neck Roads and added concerns that the homes will be in the runway protection zone for Easton Airport.
"We need to be very, very careful when we're looking at these types of development," Clarke said. "This was general commercial as originally planned. We were told three or four years ago it was going to be warehouses."
On Tuesday, the Planning Commission opted to place a pin in the matter and revisit it on July 17. Commission members may then provide a recommendation.
Once the commission makes its recommendation, council members will consider the application and hold a public hearing before any decision. While the council may take the commission's decision into account, the five council members have the final say, with a majority required for approval.

Remaining units at Easton Crossing receive OK from Planning Commission

 EASTON — The Easton Planning Commission on Tuesday approved the remaining portion of a residential project on Brookletts Avenue at the site of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation.Developers from Fello, formerly The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, are aiming to build Easton Crossing, a mixed-use project with commercial space and significant open space in the center of the residential buildings.
In February, the commission OK'd 67 units but balked on Building 409, the project's largest structure, which was originally proposed to stand five stories tall and house 56 units.
Tuesday, developers returned with a smaller Building 409, down to four stories and 38 units. A previously approved building, Building 411, was increased in the adjusted site plan to account for some of those lost units. The entire project, though, is still down from its original 123-unit plan to 116.
Commission members were largely pleased with the new Building 409. Developers and architects moved the large structure to the north of the project site, creating a larger lawn in the middle of the buildings.
Chair Philip Toussaint said he needed to be "sold a little bit more about" the center lawn after the building's move.
Ross Benincasa, Fello's vice president of community development, said it will help address a lack of public open space between John Ford Park and Idlewild Park.
"We have to make this more of a focal point so that people know this is open for them to use," he said.
Commission member William Ryall said he was first unhappy with the decision to move the building but warmed up to the idea after hearing Benincasa's explanation.
Some of Tuesday's discussion involved concerns over the lack of a landscaping plan, which had been approved in February. Commission members felt like it should be resubmitted in more detail given the significant changes to the project.
"I think it's an incomplete submission if you haven't updated the landscape plan," Toussaint said.
"The landscape plan could mitigate a lot of the concerns people have about the project," commission member Victoria McAndrews said.
Despite those qualms, the commission — which applauded developers in February for an attractive project with proper community outreach — was on board with the revised plans.
In a 4-1 vote, the revised Easton Crossing site plan was approved with conditions, one of them being a return by developers to present a landscaping plan. The votes fell the same way as they did in February, with Tom Klein being the sole no vote.
Klein, who cited a lack of parking on site as a reason for voting down the project in February, did so again Tuesday. He said competition for nearby on-street parking spaces will occur once tenants move in.
"I like a lot about this project," he said. "But I still am not going to be able to vote yes because I'm still not comfortable with the off-street parking."
Apartments are expected to be available beginning in 2027. At least 30% of the rental units are planned to be affordably priced — between 30% to 80% of the area median income. Other units will be at workforce and market-rate levels.

 OXFORD — Residents were growing increasingly concerned over the past few weeks that there would be no Fourth of July fireworks in Oxford, but with little over a week to spare, commissioners approved a request for $12,500 to the Tred-Avon Yacht Club to ensure the display would go on.The $12,500 will be taken out of the town's fiscal year 2025 general fund.
Oxford Town Commissioner Katrina Greer said there would always have been fireworks this Fourth of July and that rumors that there may not were misinformation. However, town funding for the display in future years is likely to be rolled back, according to discussion between the commissioners at a meeting Wednesday.
Town commissioners have communicated to yacht club staff that next year, they will decrease funding. The following year, they may not fund the display at all.
According to Tred-Avon Yacht Club manager Ashley Wheeler, the firework display has been a longstanding tradition in the town and has been held at the yacht club for as long as she can remember.
Wheeler said she had never heard of town funding for the fireworks being an issue until this year.
"I don't know what prompted that decision or why they made that decision to take the funding away," Wheeler said.
The decision to shift future funding came from months of commissioners deliberating with staff, residents and each other on how to approach the town budget in future fiscal years.
"We are looking at cutting it possibly next year," Oxford Town Commissioner Katrina Greer said. "We need to establish reserves."
Greer said the town will split its general reserve into three separate funds to look more attractive to federal funding opportunities. Those three funds are are a general fund, an enterprise fund and a Stormwater Management Shoreline Protection Fund.
Wheeler said she is excited for everyone to come out to the yacht club to enjoy the fireworks and "celebrate America's birthday eve."
The firework display will occur on July 3, with a rain date of July 5.

title: Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 976
 Words 

 Read News Document

 City officials in Newark, Delaware are in the early stages of evaluating whether a transitional housing village of small cabins could be a solution to local homelessness.Council members John Suchanec and Corinth Ford visited such a village in Georgetown, Delaware and suggested that a similar idea could be implemented here.
"We truly felt the experience was transformative," Suchanec said. "The approach that Georgetown has taken is starting to shape up to be a model for how you would deal with homeless sheltering."
Georgetown's Pallet Village was built in 2023 by the nonprofit Springboard Delaware. It consists of 40 small one-bedroom cabins, as well as shared bathhouses. It's become known as the Pallet Village because the cabins are produced by a company called Pallet.
"Our goal is to get unsheltered people out of the woods, get the help they need and move on to permanent housing or some form of self-independence," said Judson Malone, executive director of Springboard Delaware.
Malone said there are many reasons that people stay in the woods rather than go into traditional homeless shelters. Maybe they don't feel safe in a group shelter, they can't be with their partner, they can't bring their pet or they can't bring all their possessions.
"The most impactful thing you will do for them immediately is a lockable door with heat and air conditioning in a secure community, and that's exactly what we provided," Malone said. "Within two weeks, you'll see a difference in their demeanor simply because of the trauma that they experienced in the woods."
The Pallet Village does not require residents to be sober.
"We do not allow substance use on site, but best practices have shown that when people are in a safe space where they're accepted as they are, they can then begin to process the other issues in their life, including deciding whether or not to get treatment," Malone said. "We have a very high success rate of people voluntarily choosing to go to treatment."
Within a week of opening, the Georgetown shelter was 100 percent occupied and has remained so.
"People see a value in being there," Malone said. "They want to be there, and they want to get help and support."
Springboard Delaware works with 30 different support organizations to provide medical, mental heath, banking, employment and other services to people living at the Pallet Village.
"While people are unsheltered and in the woods, they almost never want those services," Malone said. "They really don't care about getting clean or sober, because getting high is how they survive a traumatic life."
The average length of stay is approximately three months, and then many residents of the Pallet Village move on to more permanent housing.
The Pallet Village cost approximately $1.5 million to build, money that came from the American Rescue Plan Act. Ongoing funds for operation has been harder to come by, however. Last year, Springboard Delaware had to lay off staff when a grant fell through and leaders were scrambling to piece together state money and private grants to keep the village open, according to reporting from Spotlight Delaware.
Malone said he is still working with the state to develop sustainable longterm funding.
Springboard Delaware has another $1.4 million in ARPA money to build a second Pallet Village somewhere else in the state.
"We've got the money in hand to do it," Malone said. "We just need a location."
If a Pallet Village were built in Newark, it would not require funding from the city, Malone said.
Ultimately, Springboard Delaware envisions building five to seven Pallet Villages around the state by the end of the decade.
"We have a vision, and we believe that homelessness is solvable," Malone said. "This is not the whole solution, but it's a huge part of it."
During a city council meeting last month, several council members expressed skepticism.
"Obviously, we all want to be compassionate, we all want to be empathetic, and we all want to help solve this problem," Mayor Travis McDermott said. "But we have realistic hurdles that we would have to overcome, and even with our best intentions, we can't escape it."
One big question, he said, is where would a Pallet Village be located.
"People are not going to want you to use the land behind their house to build this," McDermott said. "That's just a simple fact."
Councilman Jay Bancroft expressed similar thoughts.
"I hope we'll be very sensitive to local opposition that is likely to be an issue," Bancroft said. "I think this idea of making it look suitable to the neighbors is important for this education campaign, for us to take steps that we've been talking about for a long time"
Councilman Jason Lawhorn noted that the Georgetown Pallet Village was built near where there was already a large established homeless encampment. He said it's important to understand the scale of homelessness in Newark to better understand whether a Pallet Village would be utilized here.
He added that city staffers are already overworked and questioned whether the city should have a role in creating a Pallet Village.
"I love the program," he said. "I have reservations about how we execute it in Newark."
Suchanec asked his colleagues to direct City Manager Tom Coleman to prepare a report on whether there are any city-owned properties that could potentially be used for a Pallet Village. He suggested looking at underutilized parks as well as a piece of land the city recently purchased off Paper Mill Road, between the city's electric substation and White Clay Creek.
Ultimately, the council decided that in order to not burden city employees, each council member will compile of list of possible locations in their district for further study.
"You can find so many reasons to say no for something," Suchanec said. "The easy thing is to say no or to convince yourself this is something not worth doing. All I'm saying is take a baby step. Find out if we have any locations in this city where something like this could happen."

title: Oxford splits general fund into three new funds
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford splits general fund into three new funds

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 385
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has undergone a series of changes over the past year with a new election process, live-streamed town halls and a new town manager, Holly Wahl, who plans on streamlining more of the town's processes.Historically, the town has kept its finances in one general fund and allocated from there. But with the uncertainty of future federal funding, Oxford Town Commissioners, with the guidance of Wahl, and town staff have split the general fund into three separate funds: a general fund, an enterprise fund and the shore maintenance and protection fund.
"We had one budget that was adopted by commissioners each year," Wahl said. "And so the act this year was separating and having an ordinance for each fund being the general fund is one and then the two additional enterprise funds."
According to Wahl, the separation of funds is intended to improve transparency, finance stability and long-term planning for infrastructure projects like the Strand Beach project.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said part of the reasoning behind this decision was to appeal to federal and state grant opportunities, especially at a time when federal funding is uncertain. "Because you're showing that you can support yourself," Greer said. "You're managing the money and you're managing your expenses."
Wahl said commissioners and staff have created five- and 10-year capital improvement plans so the town can prioritize its budgetary needs.
"There may be some movement between fiscal years, but at least if we can prioritize and think about what those expenses are and plug them into a fiscal year so that staff can also prioritize their actions and work towards those projects and seek proposals," Wahl said.
Greer said that throughout the year, the town will start to allocate funds to build up reserves, look at capital and develop a capital plan. "So that means, look at all your infrastructure and all the things you want to do, have a five- or a 10-year plan, and then start to build our revenues accordingly," she said.
The new budget structure allows for proactive rather than reactive management of infrastructure needs, especially for critical systems like water and sewer which require preventative maintenance, Town Commissioners said.
Wahl said there is no plan to further restructure the budget at this time and the town will focus on effective project prioritization and adapting to funding uncertainties.

title: Queen Anne's County eyes solar soil development fees
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Queen Anne's County eyes solar soil development fees

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In response to the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, Queen Anne's County Commissioners considered an emergency ordinance to give a semblance of control back to the county and try to reap soil development fees. It is a tactic no other jurisdiction has yet tried.On May 20, the General Assembly put forward and Gov. Wes Moore approved Senate Bill 931/Renewable Energy Certainty Act that address specific state siting requirements of solar energy generating systems, community solar energy generating systems, establishes siting and standards, and energy storage devices.
Taking effect July 1, this Senate bill establishes a (new, higher) 5% limit to the total acreage of the combined number of solar energy generating stations that may be approved for construction in the priority preservation areas.
It also gives the Public Service Commission the power to approve solar and energy storage projects that meet specific conditions, even if local jurisdictions object; aims to expedite the permitting process for solar projects; addresses the use of agricultural land for solar development, including provisions for priority preservation areas; and also includes some minor provisions for local (county) input on project design and implementation.
While complying with the new rules in Senate Bill 931, Queen Anne's County is now pushing the envelope to try and recoup money from the state permitting solar to be placed on county Class 1 soils, Commissioner Jack Wilson said.
According to Wilson, Queen Anne's County is seeking to impose an impact fee on soils used for development of solar through a per-acre financial contribution to be made to the county when solar energy generating stations and storage devices are developed on Class 1 soils.
The fee will be based on the rates used in the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation (MALPF) process, which is recognized by the state, according to Wilson.
"It's like if you were going to collect this and pay this for this land, we should be reimbursed at the same level," Wilson said.
With concerns for the Maryland Ag Land Preservation Fund not being supported by the state over the next few years, the proposed impact fee or Compensatory Preservation Contribution on solar generating systems and storage sites is a way to recoup money for further land preservation, Wilson said.
The contribution or soil impact fee will be based upon 50% of the fair market value appraisal as determined by the annual amount, according to Amy Moredock county planning and zoning director, and directed to the county Farmland Preservation Fund.
Senate Bill 931 differs from similar recent cannabis legislation because it doesn't let counties create additional use standards, Moredock said. This means the county must remove all existing utility-scale solar standards and definitions and apply new standards instead.
The Senate bill addresses community solar, which the county's ordinance did not have specific provisions for and also requires the county address energy storage siting, Moredock said.
Solar is permitted in Queen Anne's countryside, agricultural, and industrial zoning districts, according to Moredock.
The county code has kept solar out of mixed use zoning districts, and high and medium density residential zoning districts, she said.
In accordance with the law, Queen Anne's County was also able to prohibit solar in Tier One and Tier Two growth areas and surrounding growth areas often zoned agriculture. This would prohibit siting within areas that are slated for development and municipal growth, she said.
Donna Landis-Smith and Joe Pippin of Queen Anne's County Soil Conservation helped solidify a compensatory preservation contribution, a payment into the dedicated farmland preservation fund to assist with obtaining easements, Moredock said.
The law is written that the 5% applies to the definite article Priority Preservation Area and does not have a caveat as to when that calculation begins, Moredock said.
Easements already preserved are not included in the total Priority Preservation Area numbers, she said.
As listed in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan, the county has approximately 109,000 acres available for the 5% designated for solar, according to Moredock.
Of the 238,000 acres in the county, approximately 88% of it is zoned agricultural and ag use, according to Landis-Smith. At the time of the previous comprehensive plan, there were 83,684 acres preserved and since the adoption of the 2022 Comprehensive Plan, the county has preserved an additional almost 8,000 acres, Landis-Smith said.
The county currently has 1,100 acres in solar.
The commissioners have noted there is a good chance the impact fee proposal would get challenged, Wilson said.
Moredock credited the expertise of Queen Anne's County Geographical Information Systems Coordinators Sam Stanton and Tyler Pease for their understanding of land use to be able to present clear statistics.
The introduction of the ordinance will move forward to the planning commission for more discussion and a public hearing scheduled in two weeks.
The Queen Anne's County Commissioners will next meet July 8 at 5:30 p.m.

title: Dominoes have started to fall
author: Staff Writer
content:
Dominoes have started to fall

 July 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I moved to Tilghman to enjoy the beauty of the water and sky. I stayed because of the community. Tilghman is a village of people who care about each other and the well being of the community. I would guess that we have more nonprofits and volunteers than any other part of the county. Three examples:When it appeared that the county would shut down the school due to budgetary reasons, everyone rolled up their sleeves and saved it. It is the pride and joy of the community.Some 15 years ago when our recently 98-year-old neighbor lost his wife of 67 years, our neighborhood started rallying round and supporting him with daily visits and all types of support.Community members created and run Healthy Tilghman, a community outreach program bringing resources and healthy activities such as mental health resources and the 5K/1K run/walk to Tilghman.
Community like this doesn't happen when the houses are owned by investors and rented to short-term renters, the "ins and outs" as we call them in Tilghman. The ins and outs don't have time to become neighbors. They don't invest in relationships. Sure, their money pays to mow the lawn, paint the house and plant the flowers, as does the money of the full-time residents. Unfortunately, the money of the ins and outs does not pay for a lot of year-round jobs.
Parts of Tilghman are protected by homeowner associations, but the older neighborhoods are not. Tilghman, and other parts of the county with small lots often on waterfront with small side yard setbacks need protection. When we lose permanent residents and replace them with ins and outs we lose a lot. We lose our volunteers, our voters, our neighborhood serving businesses. We lose the glue that holds us together. We become neighborhoods of strangers.
Homes rented by principal homeowners, as Easton allows, is OK. One well-behaved investor-owned short-term rental is OK, but what happens next? There is a domino effect. Who wants to live next to a short-term rental with constantly changing strangers next door, looking into your house? If one becomes a short-term rental, the next one will as well until there is no community left.
The dominos have begun to fall. There are clusters within the county. The cracks in our neighborhood are happening. The in and outs are showing up. We need to keep our neighborhoods and communities.
LESLIE STEEN
Tilghman

title: Let's be neighbors, smile more
author: Staff Writer
content:
Let's be neighbors, smile more

 July 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 390
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Gosh, I miss Rick Kollinger. I can only imagine his spot on wit lampooning in cartoon form the downright laughable issue currently clogging the Talbot County political landscape that is "Short-Term Rentals." I envision an Eastern Shoreman standing bewildered in a sea of yard signs reading "Came Here's" vs. "Been Here's," "From 'Round Here's" vs. "Come Down Here's," all with directional arrows pointing every which way, a political compass gone rogue. The ol' bait and switch, alive and well.Folks, there is no issue of concern relating to STRs, not to be confused with STDs, but surprisingly similar in their effect on a community. Reminds me of a brief stint I spent in Florida, living in a community complex of all ages. There was a newsletter sharing the happenings of the neighborhood, a must-read. Almost monthly there was a "noise complaint" from Ms. Unhappy with the world. This went on for what seemed like forever. It turned out the plaintiff kept hearing kids playing in the pool. It disturbed her peaceful existence, I was told. I said to myself, what, for real? Then, the tables turned.
We had a good old-fashioned BBQ with most participating. A great time was being had. Lo and behold, a well-dressed lady arrived and eased into the crowd. It was soon obvious she was the one and only Ms. Unhappy. The crowd seemed off for a bit when a young girl ran over and gave a tug on her dress and handed her a brownie. We tried not to notice, but you couldn't help yourself. She then gave Ms. Unhappy a hug and the world changed in front of our eyes. Our neighbor of discontent smiled and said, "Thank you, darlin'." It took a few minutes to soak it all in, but I think she just wanted to, well, feel included. A simple random act of kindness by, god forbid, a child – go figure. It worked magic. No more noise complaint letters appeared in our cherished gossip monthly.
Moral of the story, give this a try: Let's be neighbors again, solve our own perceived problems, and smile a little more – "It makes people wonder what your thinkin' about." Leave the heavy lifting to our chosen political friends, they have a lot to do. And let's just make and share some brownies. Just be kind!
ROO WOOD
Easton

title: Talbot Council discusses a senior citizens task force
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Council discusses a senior citizens task force

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council is set to consider creating a senior citizens task force to address the needs of the county's older residents, including those without stable housing.Council member Lynn Mielke asked for the council to approve the task force by way of a resolution last week, but council members largely preferred holding off until a work session is held.
"We do have a growing problem with homeless senior citizens," Mielke said at the July 1 council meeting. "They are in need of services, particularly in the Easton area but throughout the county."
Council President Chuck Callahan said he liked the idea.
"But the first thing that came to my mind was, do we get these groups and we have a work session and kind of get a game plan," he said.
The council introduced Mielke's resolution but did not approve it, opting instead to hold the work session with local senior care leaders.
As Talbot County's average age grows, nonprofit organizations like Upper Shore Aging and groups like the health department's senior care program aim to address senior housing and health needs. The county has a Commission on Aging which meets monthly; Mielke is the council's liaison to that commission.
According to census data, people 65 and older account for 30% of Talbot County's total population. The county's average age was 50.9 in 2023 and has slightly increased each year since 2020. The national average is just under 39 years old.
The task force, if created, would provide recommendations to the County Council on how to implement services for homeless senior citizens in the county.
Mielke said after talking to leaders at Upper Shore Aging, the Talbot Interfaith Shelter and the aging commission, it's clear homelessness is a problem for seniors. She said the groups are aware of 52 seniors in the area dealing with homelessness.
"I think it's extremely important that we form this task force and move forward to address those special needs," Mielke said.
Council member Keasha Haythe said a work session could be a "starting point" so the entire council can gather information and data from senior care experts.
Mielke reluctantly agreed to a work session but said it'd be "redundant."
"So because, I guess, they're senior citizens, you're putting another level of delay by having a work session rather than moving forward with the task force," Mielke said. "I hear you."
All five council members introduced the resolution, though a vote to approve was not held at the meeting. As currently written, the task force would include: a Commission on Aging member; a board member each from Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center; a person working in Talbot County Health Department's senior care program; an Easton Town Council member; and a Talbot County Council member.
A work session to discuss the potential senior citizens task force has not yet been scheduled.

title: Superintendent and commissioners discuss Lockerman
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com

Superintendent and commissioners discuss Lockerman

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons discussed Lockerman Middle School at the County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday.At the last commissioners meeting, the commissioners discussed their role, responsibilities and preferred location for the new Lockerman Middle School.
The superintendent came to the commissioners meeting to discuss the approval of its fiscal year 2026 budget. After the discussion the commissioners talked about Lockerman Middle School and the next steps.
"I think it'd be good for us to say that we are working together on the Lockerman Middle School construction," Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "We were asking questions about what role the commissioners officially play in siting and construction, they were just questions that we were asking. It wasn't like the Board of Ed's going to run all over us and make crazy stupid decisions and we're going to be stuck with it. It was just what influence do we have over the process."
Breeding explained the consensus the commissioners have come to on their personal choice for the new school location.
"I think we talked about it, and our consensus is that the most logical place to put it is probably next to North Carolina High School for us," Breeding said. "We understand that there's a whole process that has to be going through, fact finding, the Board of Ed will review that and make their decisions based off of that. But we were just saying that that questioning what influence we actually had over the process."
Simmons clarified they understand the commissioners wanting understanding of their role and told the commissioners how the process will go.
"Board of Education selects the site," Simmons said. "The feasibility study, which was presented to the board on July 1st, indicated North Caroline High School was the better of the two locations. We did review the two sites that we were asked to review that were basically the county-owned, which is cost efficient way to do it.
Simmons said the board received the feasibility study that night and should be making its decision on a site at the August meeting. He added the site selection does not include picking what the design of the building will be.
After looking over potential designs for the new Lockerman Middle School, Breeding suggested having athletic facilities have their own location and not sharing fields.
"One of the major things that stuck out with me was, relocating the athletic facilities around there," Breeding said. "If we can get dedicated facilities so we're not sharing space like we have been doing forever, where lacrosse or soccer is using the outfield of the softball and the baseball field, if we can actually get dedicated space, that would be a priority of mine."
He noted that facilities in surrounding counties should be studied.
"We've got one bite at the apple here, let's get it right," Breeding said.
