 CHESTERTOWN — The Kent County commissioners talked about not "releasing the hounds," but gave consideration to licensing their kennel, at their regularly scheduled meeting on June 24.Due to recent legislative changes, the commissioners now sit as the Fox Hunting Club Dog Kennel Licensing board.
Their first applicant was The Wicomico Hunt Club, a club in existence since the 1920s, seeking to preserve a rich history of safely hunting red foxes on horseback with hounds along fields, forest and wetlands beside rivers and tributaries of the Bay.
Approval of the application would enable the club to build the kennel for the hounds on the 20 acre Worton farm that until recently, was prohibited from housing more than five dogs since it is located in a Resource Conservation District.
Director of Planning, Housing and Zoning Bill Mackey explained that last year the club sought to change that law with an application for a text amendment.
Attorney Genevieve Macfarlane acting as counsel to the club, said the text amendment sought to create a definition for kennels specific to organized fox hunting clubs, and to amend the Zoning Ordinance to permit such kennels within the RCD zone.
However, while in that process, during a meeting with the Planning Commission, some public outcry arose concerning potential noise and safety issues over the hounds. The planning staff then recommended the commissioners hold certain licensing requirements to protect both the club and the public.
This past year, the hunt club has worked with the County to address those concerns and a text amendment was approved to allow hounds in the RCD zone on the condition a Fox Hunting Kennel Licensing Board and licensing scheme be put in place.
The county commissioners act as the oversight board and are responsible for implementing a regulatory framework specific to the licensing of such facilities.
"We've been called worse than that," Commission President Ron Fithian quipped when they were deemed the Fox Hunting Club Dog Kennel Licensing Board.
At the June 24 meeting, Deputy Director of Planning, Housing and Zoning Carla Gerber submitted the club's application for a kennel license as well as permission to build a temporary kennel to house 30 fox hunting hounds at Worton.
Gerber said the application met all the requirements as outlined in the new chapter 64 under Animals, article 62.
At these proceedings, Club Huntsman Eden Kloetzli was accompanied by supporters of the club, Attorney Genevieve Macfarlane lending counsel, Master of Fox Hounds Ed Fry, and member Dan O'Toole. Together they responded to concerns about potential noise and safety issues.
O' Toole, huntsman with Mount Carmel Hounds, stated he has been housing hounds on his Baltimore County property for 65 years. Although the area is far less rural than Kent, he has not had any issues so far. It relies on good communication with neighbors.
O' Toole has been helping design the club's kennel and suggested using mass-loaded vinyl on the fencing for effective sound proofing.
Kloetzli added that elevation changes on the property, the surrounding woods, the acoustic panelling on the fence and the natural isolation of the area, will help cut down on noise. They plan on growing a sound barrier with cedar trees as well.
Kloetzli assured them that the previous property owners of the farm had a working septic system used for cattle which would suit their purposes. Waste gets pumped out and disposed of properly and there will be no smell since they sanitize everyday.
Previously the hounds were housed at Tolchester and although challenging, Kloetzli learned from that experience, O'Toole pointed out.
Kloetzli said if the hounds are limited to what they see, they will be happy and not prone to bark as much.
Since many of these regulations are similar to the requirements they adhere to in Baltimore County, O'Toole applauded the County's process.
The club is the only recognized one on the Eastern Shore, Fry said, one of 142 clubs around the country. They adhere to Master Fox Hounds Association where they follow a strict code of how operations are run, the sanitary condition of the kennels and updated vaccinations.
The hounds all have their shots and are microchipped and soon will be wearing identifiable collars, Kloetzli pointed out.
Commission President Ron Fithian stated being a board member for dog kennel licensing is a new experience for them but by being so, if any complaints arise, they now have a system to address it.
With no voiced opposition to building the kennels during the hearing, Commissioner John Price moved to close it out. The application will be considered for a vote on July 8.
The club is cherished by many on the Eastern Shore and today, is the only remaining hunt sanctioned by the Masters of Foxhounds Association on the Delmarva Peninsula.

title: Oxford commissioners test the dignity index
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford commissioners test the dignity index

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 266
 Words

 OXFORD — Oxford Town Commissioners are discussing implementing a new system of dignity and respect among the council members called the Dignity Index.The Dignity Index is a scale from 1-8 that aims to ease divisions, prevent violence and solve problems, according to the website.
One is the lowest end of the dignity scale and states: "they're not even human. It's our moral duty to destroy them before they destroy us." Eight is the highest end and states: "each of us is born with inherent worth, so we treat everyone with dignity — no matter what."
The index was introduced to commissioners at the Maryland Municipal League summer conference in mid June.
"Holly, Katrina and I heard about it at MML, and all three of us said, 'That's a ... good idea,'" Commissioner Norm Bell said.
The goal of the index is to build better communication skills and maintain respect during disagreements. To build these skills and go from a one to an eight, the index provides ways to have "dignified disagreements."
To have dignified disagreements, the index suggests the following:
To build up rather than tear down.Acknowledge others' points.To challenge ideas without attacking people.By listening to understand rather than listening to respond.By regulating your emotions before a debate.To approach disagreements with curiosity and language that opens dialogue.
"Norm and I want to talk about doing what Holly does, which is treating everyone with dignity and explaining things," Commission President Katrina Greer said.
Bell said commissioners are discussing implementing the system among themselves first, and if that is successful, they will implement it with town staff as well.
"And then maybe beyond that," Bell said.

title: When Easton needed him, Alan Lowrey stepped up as interim town manager
author: Konner Metz
content:
When Easton needed him, Alan Lowrey stepped up as interim town manager

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 861
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — It was shaping up to be a normal council meeting early last August for Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey, until the mayor suddenly asked him a big question before the meeting started.The town had parted ways with former Town Manager Don Richardson on Aug. 5, 2024, and a stand-in was needed while the town conducted a search to find a permanent replacement. Mayor Megan Cook asked Lowrey if he would step in.
Back in his police uniform in his office on Thursday, Lowrey recalled knowing that if he assumed the interim role, it wouldn't just be a transition for the town and the police department. Things would change at home, too, with the high demands of both roles.
Lowrey talked to his wife, Michelle, before agreeing to become interim town manager. They have four kids, ages 15 to 19. Their love and respect for Easton — where they've lived since 2011 — played a role in saying yes.
"The town is really important to us," Lowrey said.
In the 11 months since, Lowrey was Easton's acting town manager, trading out his uniform for a suit and tie at council meetings. And even as new Town Manager Andy Kitzrow, who started Monday, takes over, Lowrey's helping with the transition process.
The police chief said it's been humbling to learn so much from the town's different departments. Whether it was absorbing new knowledge about stormwater management or crafting a $28 million budget, Lowrey said the job allowed him to grow closer with the department heads who carry out the town's important duties.
"We all want the same thing, a great Town of Easton," Lowrey said. "And to do that, it's helpful when we all pull together."
'TRUE PUBLIC SERVANT'
Easton's government has had its fair share of hot-button topics since last August. The town had to obligate its remaining pandemic-era funds by the end of 2024; a debate between a seafood processor and neighboring residents persisted for months; and Easton residents elected a new council president in a heated and politically contentious election cycle.
Cook said Lowrey was the perfect person for the interim role during such a busy time. She said he's capable of working with anyone.
"He's so calm," the mayor said in an interview last month. "He's genuine, he's sincere, he's easygoing. I can't say enough good things about him."
One of the most challenging tasks, Lowrey said, was creating a budget, a six-month process. He and Finance Officer Carol Callahan spearheaded efforts to execute the mayor's vision in creating the town's fiscal year 2026 budget.
The budget, touted by town leaders as "lean" amid the culmination of pandemic-era federal funding, was nearly even with the previous year, and it didn't raise property tax rates. Council unanimously approved the budget in May.
"It was a huge commitment. I know it took a toll on the police department, his family," Cook said of Lowrey. "It was a true sacrifice. What a public servant. True public servant."
EPD FORGES AHEAD
As Lowrey took on new responsibilities, so too did Deputy Chief Greg Wright, who became Easton's acting police chief as Lowrey shifted his focus to town government.
Wright had already served as interim chief for two months between former Chief David Spencer's retirement and Lowrey's appointment in 2022.
"I've always felt comfortable making the decisions that need to be made," said Wright, a nearly 40-year veteran of the department.
For Lowrey, since joining the Easton force as chief in 2022, Wright hasn't just been his deputy chief but a mentor and trusted colleague. Lowrey said the confidence in Wright to lead the police department made it easier to accept the temporary town manager job.
Wright, who began to sit in on town meetings as EPD's lead contact, said he now has a greater appreciation for town operations and the hard work of department heads and town employees. The solid relationship between the Town of Easton and the police department is better off, too, he noted.
"I think it makes us stronger," Wright said.
Cook said that when asking Lowrey to step in, she knew the strong leadership of Wright and other officers would come in handy.
"(Lowrey) has tremendous staff in the police department that would help carry the load of the department in his absence," Cook said.
"They both knew that it was for the betterment of the town," Town Council President Don Abbatiello said of the two police leaders. "... The town owes a debt of gratitude to the both of them."
Easton Town Council members thanked Lowrey on Monday for stepping up when the town needed it.
"You have just done an absolutely spectacular job, as well as keeping on top of your police force," Ward 3 representative David Montgomery said.
Abbatiello said in an interview Friday that Lowrey's leadership abilities were key.
"He's phenomenal at bringing people together to tackle challenges," Abbatiello said.
The town will be in good hands with Kitzrow, Lowrey said, emphasizing that the former Salisbury city administrator brings a "fresh perspective" that can be beneficial.
"He knows more about being a town manager than I will ever know," Lowrey said.
And for Lowrey himself, he's excited to be back at the Easton Police Department full-time, surrounded by the police officers and staff he loves.
"This is where my heart is," Lowrey said.

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners are moving to discuss building a new YMCA in Caroline County."I just make a comment, the YMCA, there's been a lot of discussion about the YMCA building a facility in Caroline County, and I think we need to start having a serious discussion with them about why they haven't," commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "I mean, they've built them all around us, and I think it's time to have have that discussion with Robbie Gill."
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman responded saying that she had talked to Gill, the CEO of the YMCA of the Chesapeake, the day before the meeting.
Freeman said that she and Gill discussed restarting conversations about bringing a new YMCA to Caroline County and they will continue to have discussions to make sure that it happens.
On Friday, Gill told the Star Democrat that the YMCA of Chesapeake has always had "a desire to build a full facility YMCA in Caroline County," conversations sizzled out after COVID-19 hit in 2020.
"Since then we've been blessed and fortunate enough to have opened new facilities in St. Michaels, Centerville and Chestertown," Gill said. "Even with all those wonderful things that have happened and tens of thousands of people that have benefited from it, Caroline County has still been a priority for us. We just haven't quite been able to put the pieces to the puzzle together, and so I'm excited that Kathleen and the commissioners have an interest in beginning those conversations again."
The current YMCA facility is an 11,000-square-foot storefront facility that is in Denton just off of state Route 404 in a shopping center. While the facility provides service to Caroline County residents a new facility would potentially look something like the new facilities built around the Mid-Shore.
"if you look at the YMCA that just opened at Centerville, it's a 70,000-square-foot facility serving a little over 7,000 people," Gill said. "...They're really built specifically to meet specific community needs."
The new facilities around the Mid-Shore have congregate meals daily for older residents in the community. To service the elderly, the YMCA partners with multiple groups around the community.
The new facilities include a six-lane pool with a shallow depth entry, allowing chances for swim classes for kids and adults. Another feature included is a double gymnasium with an indoor walking track, giving residents options for physical activity on cold and hot days.
Two other features includes multiple program open spaces and after-school care programs that will be beneficial for Caroline County Public Schools.
While their is no timeline on a new YMCA, Gill is happy that conversations have started again.

title: What they do doesn't always match what they say
author: DAVID REEL
content:
What they do doesn't always match what they say

 July 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 784
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Following Richard Nixon's election as president in 1968, John Mitchell, Nixon's campaign manager, was asked by the media what to expect when Nixon assumed office.Mitchell said prophetically long before Watergate, "Watch what we do, not what we say."
Those words apply to many candidates for public office today.
The are at least two recent examples in Maryland.
Prior to leaving office after two terms, Republican Gov. Larry Hogan proclaimed he had no interest in running for an open U.S. Senate seat in Maryland formerly held by Ben Cardin.
Hogan went as far as saying his experience as a business executive and eight years serving as governor, left him reluctant to serve in a deeply divided legislative body marked by lengthy and often bitterly partisan dialogue and decision making.
Then in February 2024 Hogan entered the Senate race where he easily won the Republican nomination in a primary election but lost in the general election with 42.8% of votes cast.
In 2022, Wes Moore was elected as Hogan's Democratic successor with 64.5% of votes cast.
Almost immediately following his election Moore was widely viewed by political pundits in Maryland, Washington, D.C., and nationally as a potential presidential candidate in 2028.
To date, Moore has said early and often regularly he is not pursuing that goal.
Despite saying that, it has been most interesting watching media reports of what Moore has done in the political arena during his first term as governor.
Moore ...
Spoke at the 2024 Democratic National Convention.Campaigned for Kamala Harris in Pennsylvania, North Carolina and Michigan.Campaigned for Democratic candidates in Virginia.Appeared on The View where Joyce Behar told him he looked "very presidential."Interviewed with CNN following his college commencement speech in southeastern Pennsylvania.Attended an Aspen Colorado fundraiser hosted by Damian O'Doherty, a Maryland political operative and co-founder of Baltimore based KO Public Affairs.Shared his thoughts on "bold, purposeful leadership" on a podcast with the NBA's Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr and CBS Evening News co-anchor John Dickerson.Delivered a keynote speech at the South Carolina Democratic Blue Palmetto Dinner.Attended a fish fry hosted by Congressman Jim Clyburn who is widely credited for a Joe Biden 2020 primary campaign resurgence when that campaign was stalled.Met with former political advisers to Barack Obama and Joe Biden to discuss a presidential path to the White House through South Carolina.Spoke to hundreds of political insiders in South Carolina about his personal biography and on his record as Maryland governor.Spoke at an NAACP "Fight for Freedom" dinner in Detroit, Michigan.Spoke at the Virginia Democratic Party's Blue Commonwealth Gala.Will attend The Sun Valley Conference in Idaho sponsored by private investment firm Allen & Company, which is branded by Fortune magazine as an annual "billionaire summer camp," that brings together business executives, social media titans, traditional news figures and elected officials who aspire to become president.
Ultimately, all this travel and schmoozing by Moore may be for naught.
Next year, Moore must win a Democratic primary election and a general election in Maryland.
Conventional wisdom that he will win both is far from a given.
In polling done earlier this year, Moore's job performance approval fell to 55% from 61% from polling done in the prior month.
These poll results occurred before Moore signed into law a wide range of tax increases, new taxes, fee increases and new fees that were approved in the 2025 general assembly session.
As I write this, Moore has an opponent in the 2026 Democratic primary and three potential opponents seeking a gubernatorial nomination in the 2026 Republican primary. He will have a Green Party candidate in the 2026 general election.
In the Democratic and Republican primaries there may be more candidates deciding to run.
One wild card in the Republican primary is former Governor Hogan.
Despite his failed U.S. Senate run, a survey done after Hogan's two terms as governor, showed he had a 77% job approval rating that included an 81% approval rating with Democratic voters.
Hogan has not yet announced his decision on seeking a third term which the state constitution allows since it would not be a third successive term.
Assuming Moore is the successful Democratic candidate for governor, there is also the hard political reality that not meeting expected vote totals in elections that any candidate is expected to win can be an insurmountable roadblock on a journey to the White House.
Preeminent Maryland political analyst Len Foxwell has observed: "What we have seen in the past where prospective gubernatorial candidates and prospective presidential candidates have been derailed because of weaker than expected showings back home."
Regardless of who is elected Maryland governor in 2026, voters in that election cycle and every election cycle in Maryland would be best served if there was no longer a regular mismatch between what some candidates of every party affiliation do and what they say.

title: Here's the difference between a king and a president
author: JIM BRUCE
content:
Here's the difference between a king and a president

 July 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM BRUCE | Section: Columns 
 
 724
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On June 10, Talbot County learned firsthand the difference between a president and a would-be king. The county sought to improve our airport with the federal government providing 90% of the cost, typical for smaller airports. All was set until U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy wrote on April 24 to the effect that Talbot County and every other county would not receive airport or other federal funding, unless they removed from their policies anything labeled "diversity, equity, and inclusion," because they are discriminatory and "presumptively violate(s) federal law." In short, our county council could choose between policies labeled DEI or expanding our airport.In 2020, the County Council unanimously approved a diversity, equity, and inclusion statement that was noncontroversial and merely aspirational. They also adopted unanimously a resolution on diversity, saying county employees should understand the diversity of county residents to serve the public better. In two council sessions in early 2025, many residents testified to defend these policies against two Republicans' (Dave Stepp and Chuck Callahan) call for repeal, which the council rejected, an embarrassing Republican defeat.
Yet this month, June 10, the council, under the threat of losing federal funding for the airport, repealed the diversity resolution and DEI statement, which were adopted unanimously in 2020.
Every Talbot resident should understand what happened here. It shows the difference between a president and a would-be king, between a Constitutional democracy under the rule of law and an autocracy.
On Jan. 20, President Trump issued his Executive Order 14151, "Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferences." He declared programs labeled DEI presumptively discriminatory, therefore illegal and directed all federal agencies to ferret out these programs and dismantle them. With no statute behind it, no due process (notice and comment) to determine if a DEI program is in fact discriminatory, no rule-making and no hearings, President Trump made illegal anything labeled DEI.
First, no president before Trump has so broadly asserted that his 161 executive orders signed in 2025 are the equivalent of laws. Our Constitution says only the Congress makes laws. In contrast, absolute kings are not limited by legislatures, nor by due process, notice and comment procedures with which presidents must comply.
Second, the president unilaterally decreed, like a king, that his executive order would apply not just to federal agencies but to states and counties having DEI policies. A king's rule extends to all his realm including every county and village. In contrast, the 10th Amendment of the Constitution limits the reach of the federal government over states and local government. No president before Trump tried to dictate, without clear Congressional backing and due process, the policies adopted by state and local government.
Third, Trump, like a monarch, would enforce his executive order by denying federal grants to any state or local government having DEI-labeled policies. Absolute kings, not the legislature, control their nation's purse. Under our Constitution, Congress controls the spending power. No president before has so broadly used federal funding to local government as a cudgel to enforce his views on federally funded projects.
Predictably, several counties and other entities, including in Maryland, promptly sued the president for denying federal grants to entities with DEI policies. The cases cite the lack of a statutory basis, absence of notice and rule-making, violation of free speech and unconstitutional vagueness. Federal judges, one in Maryland, issued temporary restraining orders, but the litigation is ongoing.
The actions of Stepp and Callahan deserve attention here.
The county attorney stated he thought the county's DEI policies are in fact nondiscriminatory, and Duffy's letter deficient in legal reasoning. Ignoring this, the two Republicans pressed Trump's royal edict on the council on June 10, insisting that the council repeal what the council had earlier adopted unanimously and defended twice.
Like envoys from the royal court, Stepp and Callahan played their trump card, the Duffy letter, proclaiming the very specific threat of loss of the airport funding if the Council did not repeal the DEI and diversity measures. The rest of the council, except for Councilwoman Keisha Haythe (D), buckled in the face of this likely illegal and draconian threat.
The tide is turning though. On June 14, more than 500 people in Talbot County protested for "No Kings," joined by 5 million others nationwide.
When the courts finally overrule Trump's unconstitutional overreach, the County Council should reinstate what they repealed on June 10. Long live Constitutional democracy.

title: Cambridge commissioners remove solar cap
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge commissioners remove solar cap

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 483
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge City Commissioners adopted an ordinance at last week evening's meeting to amend the city's unified development code to exempt medium, large and community solar energy projects from the town's current 350-acre cap.The move essentially removes the cap, which was implemented in 2014, paving the way for a community solar project from Pivot Energy, a Denver-based renewable energy provider and independent power producer. Commissioners unanimously voted in favor of the ordinance to remove the cap.
The plan for community solar was first introduced to commissioners in December, 2024, when Pivot Energy's lawyer Anthony Kupersmith said getting rid of the cap would be critical to the project's success.
Cambridge City Planner Brian Hermann presented Pivot Energy's community solar proposal to commissioners again last week. "The community solar projects are designed to provide opportunities for residents of the community who don't own their house, or are living in the woods and have shade, or don't want to look at solar panels," Hermann said.
Community solar is a way for multiple individuals to share in the benefits of a single solar installation, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. "The term refers to the pooling of resources to develop a community-scale solar energy project that provides the benefits of solar energy to a group or neighborhood," the USDE website states.
After around an hour of questions from commissioners, Mayor Lajan Cephas thanked the gentlemen from Pivot Energy and attempted to move on to the next agenda item, but Commissioner Roche had one more question he 'demanded' be answered before voting on the ordinance.
"So at the end of the day, how do we know, and how does the state know that this power is actually for its intended purpose, which is to lower the utility rates of, in many cases, income constrained individuals, or the community, where it's located?" Roche asked.
Kupersmith told Roche this word isn't neutral and lends authority to regulatory oversight from the Public Service Commission through an application, bonding, subscriber certification and annual reporting to ensure benefits, especially for low- and moderate-income customers.
Hermann and Pivot Energy representatives were uncertain of how many acres they will need for the new community solar project, but it will exceed the current cap. Kupersmith and Pivot Energy Development Project Manager John Shields made it clear that if the city does not remove the cap, Pivot Energy is willing to go to the state, which can supersede the city's code.
Commissioners asked if there were decommissioning protocols for the end of the project's life or in case of damage. The decommissioning plan and bond would follow the city's existing zoning rules and Public Service Commission standards.
When it comes to what exactly the community solar project will look like, Pivot Energy is keeping its options open.
Shields said at the current moment, there is not a drawn-up project plan. "We'd rather kind of look at it more holistically if we can," Shields said.

title: Fate of Talbot's short-term rental proposals still up in the air
author: Konner Metz
content:
Fate of Talbot's short-term rental proposals still up in the air

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The future of short-term rental legislation in Talbot County remains uncertain as the county's planning commission and elected officials have yet to find a middle ground.In an ongoing debate since May, Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher are aiming to further regulate short-term rental properties in the county. But agents, owners and now county planners have indicated opposition to the proposals.
At its July 2 meeting, the Talbot County Planning Commission reviewed draft legislation line-by-line. Commission members delivered mixed thoughts on some of the rules, but for the most part, they provided negative reviews on changes they described as "onerous" and unnecessary.
And on a couple specifics, they discussed relaxing requirements instead of increasing them.
In an interview Tuesday, Mielke said it's clear the commission is "100% on the side of short-term rentals."
"Anybody who is affected negatively by short-term rentals doesn't have a voice," she said. "And those who are profiting from short-term rentals control."
The Planning Commission left written comment open on July 2, and it's unclear exactly when that body's amended version of the legislation will be officially sent to the council.
The commission's recommendation is likely to gut a number of the proposed regulations; however, the commission is only a recommending body in the matter, leaving the County Council with final say.
PROPOSED RULES
Proponents of the legislation, such as Mielke and some county residents, argue a proliferation of short-term rentals is hurting local communities, especially village zones. Opponents say the number of rentals hasn't significantly increased in the last few years and that changes aren't needed given a lack of formal complaints from neighbors.
As currently set up, property owners obtain short-term rental licenses from a review board. Once an initial license is approved, they must obtain renewal from the board one year later, then every two years.
Some of the new proposed restrictions include mandatory landlines, more detailed stay logs for license renewals, a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
Commission member Paul Spies said the class split is a "hard sell."
"I think the law as it is is fine," he said. "Two licenses, to me, doesn't make sense."
"It seems onerous on staff," Commission Chair James Corson said.
For renewal applicants, the proposed legislation lays out new logging requirements. Property owners would need to submit specific stay logs, including when the property was occupied by the owner or family members.
"I think that's a little bit too much of an overreach," Chip Councell said.
Mielke said the concerns around how much work will be put on staff and what would be asked of rental owners aren't totally valid. She said wording for the draft regulations was derived from Prince George's County.
"It had a basis," Mielke said, adding that for tax purposes, rental owners should already be documenting information that the new proposals would ask for.
The commission at times voiced that Talbot County's current short-term rental rules could be relaxed. Commission members said the council should make rental licenses transferable. Currently, new applications must be submitted if ownership of a property is transferred.
"The use hasn't changed. Zoning follows a land, it does not follow the owner," Councell said. "So it would seem to me that there would be a way that makes sense.
"I would say that a short-term rental license should be transferable" with conditions, he added.
Lesher and Mielke disagree.
"That's something that I don't support," Lesher said in an interview. "I think that who is running one of these matters, and that should not be automatic in the transfer and renewal."
Lesher said the council does pay attention to the commission's recommendation, and that with positive reviews of some smaller aspects of the proposals, there will be an update to the code no matter where some of the more major pieces land.
"I do think that something should pass here," Lesher said.
It's still unclear whether Mielke and Lesher's proposals will garner majority support from the council. Dave Stepp and Keasha Haythe both said they are waiting for the commission's official recommendation and further discussion.
Council President Chuck Callahan says he hopes to take the recommendations into account while coming "to a compromise" with all council members.

title: Talbot County considering new cannabis legislation
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County considering new cannabis legislation

 July 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 523
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County is reviewing regulations on cannabis operations, but drafted legislation drew concerns from prospective business owners at a recent meeting.As drafted, legislation would bar cannabis growing and processing operations from locating within 500 feet of residential properties. That mark could be reduced for a specific project only if all property owners within that radius agree.
At a County Council meeting on July 8, a public hearing on the legislation was opened, during which two state license holders raised concerns. Discussion centered on changing the 500-foot setback to 200 feet.
Dave Ferraris, winner of a cannabis-processing license from the Maryland Cannabis Administration, which are awarded via a lottery, said the proposed restrictions would be "detrimental."
"It's not the wild west," Ferraris said of cannabis operations. "It's agriculture with oversight."
Easton resident Lori Yates received a license for cultivation. She said on July 8 that passage of the county legislation would hinder her progress toward acquiring a property in Cordova, the now-closed Triple Creek Winery.
"It really would pull the rug out from us trying to work with the current owners," Yates said.
On the prospect of a 200-foot setback, Yates said she feels it would still allow for proper space "to have it off of the public access road."
Brennan Tarleton, the county's planning and zoning director, noted that in the original draft legislation, there's already a written-in opportunity to reduce the setback to 200 feet if the affected property owners agree. But he said moving the starting point down from 500 feet is a possibility.
"Two hundred feet isn't a pie-in-the-sky idea for a setback," Tarleton said.
If passed, the legislation would require processors and growers to obtain site plan approval from the county and operate on a lot of at least 20 acres. Additionally, operators must procure professional testimony that cannabis odor is not "detectible from adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Ferraris voiced opposition to the "no odors" regulation, citing it is too extreme of a rule.
"Talbot County will realistically and effectively be disqualified from participating in cannabis processing and growing endeavors," Ferraris said.
He added that prospective cannabis operators aren't looking to exploit the county. "We're not asking for a blank check. We're just asking for a fair chance," he said.
Tarleton noted the county mostly mirrored Easton's cannabis ordinance in regard to the odor requirement. He said Easton restricted to just indoor growing operations, though. Tarleton said council could consider exempting open-air growing operations from the "no odors" rule.
Talbot's draft cannabis legislation also lays out standards for cannabis dispensaries to follow, largely falling in line with the state's recent legislation effective in July, 2024.
Dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care centers, playgrounds, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or places of worship. They also can't locate within 1,000 feet of one another; that standard is present in Easton town limits, too, and in one case created competition between businesses.
While Talbot County's potential regulations stick with the state, local jurisdictions are permitted under state law to change those distance requirements.
The county's cannabis legislation wasn't eligible for a vote on July 8. It may return to the council at its July 22 meeting or later in August.

 CAMBRIDGE — A car sized sink hole swallowed part of Cedar Street on Tuesday, July 8, the result of a failing storm drain pipe.Sink holes are not a new phenomenon in Cambridge, according to Public Works Director Wayne Suggs, who has been in this position for two years.
Suggs said during his time with the town, it's experienced about half a dozen small "ankle twisters" but nothing of this magnitude.
"You know, your foot might go in, but not your car," he said.
Suggs said the repair job has been a complicated process because crews had to dig 11 feet deep to avoid a 27-inch sewer line and a tightly packed bundle of Verizon cables. Public Works needed a specially made trench box to do it safely.

Residents can expect Cedar Street to remain closed over the weekend and should plan accordingly. Cedar Street will fully reopen by Tuesday morning.
"We can see light at the end of the tunnel now," Suggs said.

title: Federalsburg sets town hall meeting to answer questions
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg sets town hall meeting to answer questions

 1054
 Words

 FEDERALSBURG — Misappropriation of funds, resignations and now $5 million of debt have riddled the town of Federalsburg in the last year.Now town officials want to set the record straight.
The Federalsburg Town Council will be holding what town officials are calling a "state of Federalsburg address" Monday at 6 p.m. at the Federalsburg Elementary School gym.
"I'm encouraging the public to come out because what we have planned is full transparency, full answers to questions," council member Brandy James said. "We do have an agenda where we're going to go down and we're going to lay out the length of whatever it is."
At this meeting, officials said issues like the town's high employee turnover rate and budget concerns would come up. When the Star Democrat reached out to Federalsburg town officials, they all refused to answer questions about these issues prior to the meeting.
The forum, they said, would make things more clear.
Federalsburg council members confirmed to the Star Democrat on Monday the town is $5 million in debt, accumulated over multiple years from loans.
On top of the debt, the town of Federalsburg passed an unbalanced budget at its June 17 meeting. The budget shows planned expenditures at $5,382,649.28 while the anticipated revenues sit at $4,931,594.74, leaving a shortfall of $451,054.54.
Multiple water pump problems and insufficient revenues with the wastewater treatment facility were cited as a big reason the town could not present a balanced budget.
On top of the debt and unbalanced budget, the town has experienced employment turnover with multiple town positions. This has caused lack of consistent work and confusion for the town.
Now the town of Federalsburg town hall building has been closed for mold remediation.
"We're addressing everything, everything from town hall, wastewater, treatment plant, maintenance, police, anything that is Federalsburg is the purpose of that meeting," James said.
Debt
$5 million worth of debt towers over Federalsburg. Council members plan to be fully transparent about how the debt was accumulated and how the town plans to go about paying off the debt.
"It's no hiding, and we are going to go into full detail about where the debt came from, how the debt was accumulated, who's responsible for the debt, all of that stuff will be addressed there," James said.
Councilman Ian Furgeson thinks solving all of the issues with the debt will help the town solve other issues the town faces.
"The debt is probably the biggest thing," Furgeson said. "Because if you don't have the means of getting that debt taken care of, you're going to have issues with how do you go forward with the police. How do you go forward with the wastewater treatment plant? The debt is one of the bigger things."
Police Department
The Federalsburg Police Department will be a topic of discussion next week. At the July 7 town meeting, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner announced Police Chief Joseph Gasser resigned from his position on June 25.
Mayor Kim Abner said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would take over leadership of the Federalsburg Police Department to give the mayor and council time to figure out police department leadership.
The sheriff's office and the town of Federalsburg are in the early stages of conversations about the sheriff's office taking over police coverage for Federalsburg. Sheriff Donnie Baker believes all options are on the table for the Federalsburg Police Department, including an memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office that could disband the police department.
Gasser was appointed as interim police chief in October 2024 and announced as the police chief in January.
On Oct. 14, the Town of Federalsburg posted on Facebook about an unspecified incident requiring the town to have a third-party investigate the department.
"The Town of Federalsburg received a complaint about an incident involving the Federalsburg Police Department that occurred on October 9, 2024. We are engaging an independent third party to investigate this incident," the post said.
Gasser confirmed the October incident was a consideration in his appointment.
"But that's as far as I'll go with it," he said.
Worker turnover
In the last year, Federalsburg has experienced high turnover. The town has been through two police chiefs, a town treasurer, a town manager and a new council member.
Former Police Chief Michael McDermott started with an official announcement of resignation in January. Following McDermott, former Town Manager Kristy Marshall, resigned in February and according to the town, former Town Treasurer Debbie Lawler was laid off in February.
Also announced in February, former council member Torbert Williamson II resigned because he moved out of town.
"The town has lacked structure on many levels, including employment," James said. "That's not any secret to anyone who's ever worked there. There's not been that stable structure there for employees. So we have reformatted the way we're doing things.
While town issues have continued to grow throughout the year, according to town council members, consistent town employees have helped shape where the town can improve on issues. Implementing new training programs and policies will help the town, council members say.
"We are creating new policies and procedures and structures to make sure staff feel supported and to make sure they're getting the adequate training that they need by making sure the employee handbook is there to be a guide for not just the town but for town employees as well," James said.
Wastewater facility
According to conversations during previous meetings, Federalsburg's wastewater treatment facility has been a drain of money.
"From what I can gather and understand is that the wastewater treatment plant should pay for itself," council member Furgeson said. "Our water bills should pay for it, and it's not going to make a profit, but it certainly should not lose money. What we're finding is that we are spending more money on it than we are bringing in."
According to discussions at the June 17 meeting, raising the water rates still would not cover the almost $500,000 shortfall in the budget. The wastewater treatment plant is operating with a significant deficit.
Furgeson said the age of the facility leads to issues.
"Part of it is the age, there's certain things that need to get fixed and that's what we got to figure out, where we can shore that up," Furgeson said.
The agenda for the public forum includes a welcome with a meeting rules reminder. Next the town plans to discuss a finance update, wastewater treatment plant update, public works update, police department update and last a public comment and questions portion.

title: Planning Commission recommends against housing project
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning Commission recommends against housing project

 July 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 832
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Planning Commission didn't budge Thursday on its staunch opposition to a proposed 365-unit housing development near the under-construction hospital and Easton Airport.The body unanimously agreed to send a negative recommendation to the Town Council on an application from developers looking to build the Fox Chase Estates on 112 acres of land off of Airport Road.
As they did last month, commission members cited the lack of connectivity, segregation between housing types and an already large pipeline of other housing projects as reasons for their disapproval.
Commission member Victoria McAndrews said OK'ing the Fox Chase homes would be a "hasty" decision. She said the town should let other projects build before adding more units to the pipeline.
"I'm feeling like it's the wrong place, wrong time," McAndrews said.
Easton Sunrise Partners LLC and Scott Wagner, a Talbot County businessman and a former Republican member of the Pennsylvania State Senate, are the developers. They previously aimed to build warehouses on the site but in recent years shifted to residential.
Wagner was seeking approval through Easton's planned unit development process, which would allow the homes to be built on the commercial-zoned land. It's near what will be Easton's new hospital on Longwoods Road, which is expected to open in 2028. University of Maryland Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel has voiced support for the housing development, hoping it would help retain and attract health care workers.
Wagner's attorney Lawrence Scott defended the project on Thursday. He focused on the argument that Fox Chase meet the standards of Easton's comprehensive plan, which is the basis the commission uses when deciding whether to recommend a development.
"This land has been in the town for over 25 years," Scott said. "This is not an annexation to do residential building. This is not someone trying to grow the town."
But Scott's appeals didn't quell the commission's concerns nor the public's. Many residents spoke against the proposal during public comment.
"When I first saw this project, I had to reach for an oxygen bottle because it took my breath away," resident Bruce Harrington said.
Easton resident Barbara Lane shared concerns about the homes causing more traffic on Airport and Goldsborough Neck roads, as well as how far the development would be away from Easton's other residential areas.
"There's no connectivity to other neighborhoods," Lane said.
THURSDAY'S DEBATE
Developers on Thursday agreed to fixing a number of items flagged by town and county officials in June, including the lack of a second vehicle access point to the neighborhood. But largely, the site plan remained as originally submitted.
Of the 365 proposed units, 108 are single-family detached homes, 137 are three-story townhomes and 120 are multifamily units. Developers say 185 of the units will be affordably priced. Those units would enjoy the same access to the neighborhood's commercial buildings and open space, though they're largely grouped by type on the site plan.
Commission Vice Chair Michael Ports took issue with that aspect.
"We are making several different neighborhoods where it is very clear that there are different housing types and different income levels within them, and I don't believe that's in the spirit of the comp plan," Ports said.
Meanwhile, commission members echoed resident concerns that the development wouldn't be connected enough to the rest of town, citing that as a core tenet of Easton's current comprehensive plan.
Approved in 2010, the comprehensive plan is undergoing a major update. The Planning Commission and town staff are drafting an updated plan, which will lay out objectives for growth in town and may offer more clarity on what town planners envision for the northernmost part of town around the new hospital.
As the commission's negative views on the project became clear Thursday, Scott contested that some reasons for disapproval were "beyond the scope of what we're here today to do."
"Making us wait for the next comprehensive plan is not part of today's deliberation," Scott said.
"The alternative here is we go back to giant warehouses and the Amazons of the world and 1,000 trucks a day," he added. "At the end of the day, the property owner has a right to make use of his property."
Developers have said they've met multiple times with council members and Mayor Megan Cook to discuss the need for affordable housing, although it remains unclear where council members will land if the project goes to them for a vote. Council has final say as the commission is only a recommending body.
"We're here because we met with council members, and they said, 'We need for-sale, affordable homes,'" Scott said Thursday.
Commission Chair Philip Toussaint said his body's letter to the Town Council will lead with why the project isn't in line with the comprehensive plan. He noted the project brings about health worries and strays from the plan's future land use map, in addition to not meeting connectivity and integrated housing standards.
Some residents expressed worries the development would damage Easton's small-town character. McAndrews acknowledged the "anywhere USA" concerns.
"There's a lot of suburban sprawl outside Easton, and that's what we're trying to control," Toussaint said.

title: Not the time for Fox Chase

Not the time for Fox Chase

 Fox Chase Estates? The name of this proposed 365-home development should cause us to raise an eyebrow. What does such a development have to do with the historic nature of small town Easton? Sounds like a suburban subdivision to me, especially located separately at the north end of town and not connected to any other Easton neighborhoods.And why do we need 365 additional dwelling units with 1,200 units currently under construction or approved and waiting to start right now. One of the major issues cited by citizens during the election for Easton Town Council president was too much residential growth and the unacceptable traffic it causes. What will these 1,200 units plus 365 in this proposal do to traffic, already excessive now, in the near future?
Besides the location being basically separate from residential Easton, the plan requires rezoning the property from commercial to residential designation. Commercial businesses pay more taxes to the town. So why would we not save that property for such businesses that would increase Easton's revenue and also provide jobs.
An important additional concern is proximity to the airport runways where it creates a potentially dangerous situation. This is a location where there was a recent plane crash. Proximity to the airport will also create noise levels that would be unacceptable to homeowners.
Finally, and really most important, the Easton Comprehensive Plan is now under review. This huge development should be considered when the Comprehensive Plan is completed, so it will fit with Easton's vision of the future. There is no compelling reason for approval now. Now is not the time for the Planning Commission to approve this development.

title: Federalsburg officials address town's mounting issues at public forum
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg officials address town's mounting issues at public forum

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Federalsburg Town Council hosted hundreds of residents for a public forum at Federalsburg Elementary School Monday evening.Town officials wanted to set the record straight about town rumors, addressing issues like misappropriation of town funds, employee resignations, $5 million of debt, wastewater treatment issues and police department cost.
A 50-minute explanation by the council members explained the root of these issues and the options and plans to solve them.
Debt and staff accountability
Council members revealed the town's $5 million of debt dates back to 1995.
"We did not get into a over $5 million debt overnight, but here we are and we're trying to clean it up piece by piece," council member Brandy James said. "When I came on council, the math just didn't add up. So, looking into things, some of this debt goes back to 1995.
"The town has had a very historic past of one not paying bills on time, two robbing Peter to pay Paul, and three in order to get anything done instead of doing the right thing and figuring out how to better utilize the funds that were coming in, they would just take out loans or they would take out grants. Some grants were grants that the town wasn't even qualified for, but that's what they would do."
James said the town must pay back grants to grant providers because the grant providers have discovered that the town wasn't eligible to receive the grants. She said the town has lost grants because of not having audits done since fiscal year 2023.
Federalsburg officials plan to establish a plan to pay off debt within 12 months using money from the town's general fund. The town has frozen spending and committed to a hiring freeze, except for a part-time code enforcement officer.
After the hiring freeze, James said that the town will shift its employment focus to hiring staff who are qualified for their positions, no longer hiring employees based off relationships.
Wastewater and water issues
Council member Darlene Hammond led the discussion on the fire department water usage. She said the town will not charge the fire department for water used to fight fires, but the fire house will be metered for non-emergency uses, which it previously has not been.
The town will install meters on hydrants to help track and detect leaks and start billing churches and other town serving companies for water and sewer usage.
Town officials acknowledged past issues with inconsistent billing and old meters. They plan to take steps to clear billing statements and update account balances. They will explore tools for online payments and text alerts when bills are due.
The town's wastewater treatment plant was also discussed at the meeting. The facility was built to support a housing development in the town that was never constructed, making it outsized to the town's needs.
Mayor Kim Abner said the facility is built to handle 750,000 gallons a day, more than double the current usage of 350,000 gallons per day.
The town has many issues with taking care of the facility due to cost and improper usage.
"It costs a lot of money to fix the water main. It costs a lot of money to maintain the wastewater treatment plant," Abner said. "There are state mandates that we have to deal with. We also need a new sludge press because the sludge press presses the water out, and if you don't press all the water out, you're paying more at the landfill. So, the wastewater treatment plant's a lot. It's a big investment. It's a lot of money, but we have to do it for safe drinking water and safe toilets."
Police Department
Council member Ian Ferguson talked about the cost of the town's police department.
If the town were to sign a memorandum of understanding with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide policing services, it would save the town between $300,000 and $500,000, he said.
The town currently pays $1.146 million for the Federalsburg Police Department.
Sheriff Donald Baker told residents that the his would hire Federalsburg's police officers if it were to assume policing duties for the town.
According to the Town Council, the current police station could be used as a substation for the Sheriff's Office if the town signs a memorandum of understanding.
The town plans to continue to have quarterly public meetings to keep the town informed on all issues and improvements.

title: Caroline commissioners hoping to nail down site for new YMCA
author: Konner Metz
content:
Caroline commissioners hoping to nail down site for new YMCA

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County and YMCA leaders are restarting efforts to build a new YMCA facility after discussions fizzled out in recent years.At a county meeting Tuesday, YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill told county commissioners that the organization has always wanted to build a full facility in Caroline County. The biggest step to moving forward is choosing a location, he said.
"The goal is still to build a YMCA that can be a hub for community," Gill said. "We just haven't solved the first piece of the puzzle, which is the right site and getting everybody on board."
During Tuesday's talks, stakeholders didn't land on one location in particular, though commissioners indicated three potential considerations: land on Double Hills Road off of Route 404, the old Southern States property at Gay and Market streets in Denton, or near Denton Elementary School.
"It's probably time for us to, as you said, pick a site and start telling a story," Commission Vice President Larry Porter told Gill.
Gill briefed the commissioners on the YMCA's recent expansions on the Eastern Shore, including in St. Michaels and Centreville. A new facility serving Caroline County residents would need to be around 60,000 square feet or more, Gill said. The project could fall in the $20 million range.
The YMCA of the Chesapeake currently operates an 11,000-square-foot facility nestled in the Denton Plaza shopping center off of Route 404. Gill said it serves around 3,000 people. A full-fledged building could more than double that mark.
PAST ROADBLOCKS
Past efforts to expand the YMCA's presence in Caroline County have been met with roadblocks. Porter, a commissioner since 2010, said it's time to get the ball rolling.
"The thing that's frustrating for me is it seems like we've had this conversation several times, and we are still in the same spot we were," Porter said.
In 2018, the county and YMCA signed an agreement in which the county would donate 15 acres of land on Double Hills Road to the YMCA. It was conditioned on the project beginning by July 1, 2023.
Talks stalled, and the project didn't begin before the deadline.
Gill said on Tuesday that there "wasn't support from a (county) administrative standpoint" at the time. Other concerns, such as the fact that the Town of Denton didn't own the land, parking meters and, eventually, the pandemic, hindered efforts, he noted.
In 2022, the YMCA of the Chesapeake returned a $2.5 million donation from a New Jersey donor that was meant to go toward the Caroline County endeavor.
"We really didn't see a pathway forward," Gill said.
But now, as talks resurface, there's renewed interest in delivering a new YMCA.
Commission President Travis Breeding said it may be challenging to locate the YMCA next to a school, though he said near Denton Elementary on the south end of town could be a consideration.
When commissioners raised the idea of considering the current and soon-to-be moved Lockerman Middle School on the north end of town, Gill expressed some reservation.
"With the school going away there, and if you demo'd that and built (a YMCA) there, it's kind of tucked away," he said.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the county will look at some potential sites and put together a list. Gill said the nonprofit organization can conduct market assessments on potential sites to determine viability.
The CEO said it "hurts my heart that we still haven't solved this one," but expressed confidence that pursuing a larger YMCA facility in Caroline County is a benefit to residents and local businesses.
"There's an economic engine behind the Y as well because it gives you kind of that third place in your community to connect to people," Gill said.

title: Residents want Federalsburg to keep promises of transparency
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Residents want Federalsburg to keep promises of transparency

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — After a 50-minute explanation from town officials about mounting issues in Federalsburg, the community spent over an hour and a half voicing concerns.The town addressed issues like misappropriation of town funds, employee resignations, $5 million of debt, water and wastewater treatment issues and police department cost, offering transparency that residents have said was lacking.
Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner hopes this community forum is a step in the right direction for the town.
"I think that it went well," Abner said about the meeting. "I mean, it went as good as it can be expected. The problem is that a lot of stuff gets posted on Facebook that isn't true. We were trying to set the record straight about some other things that have happened. We're trying to be more transparent about what is going on down at Town Hall, and we want the public to be engaged."
During Monday's meeting, residents voiced multiple times that the town needed to maintain more open communication with the public.
Eric Padgett, business owner and owner of multiple properties in Federalsburg, spoke passionately about the town's issues and about the good in the town.
"I've been walking around town. I watch everything that's going on. Nobody is held accountable for nothing," Padgett said. "Count the town managers, every ... one of them have never walked around, drove around, asked anybody any questions about nothing. … The town needs to open up at 7 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. so these people who have a problem can go in there and do something about it."
A proposal to have the Caroline County Sheriff's Office take over policing duties for the town garnered a lot of back-and-forth among residents.
Former Police Chief Donald Nagel spoke on the topic by asking how important police protection was to the residents by show of hands. All residents raised their hand indicating it was important.
"I worked in this town 24 years or whatever, and it was rough, and we had to bring it back, and we brought it back," Nagel said. "I'm not here for any accolades or anything. I just know this town by word. You're not going to get the same service by having the sheriff's department in here that you have now. People know you're police officers, so please, don't do away with the police."
Multiple residents thought differently about the police department. Some indicated the Sheriff's Office could offer better coverage to the town.
Residents who spoke agreed on that property tax prices, wastewater problems and lack of transparency from the town government were pressing issues.
Resident Danielle Brodka acknowledged the town's efforts to be transparent, but without work, she doesn't believe the town residents' anger will change.
"Is it a wonder that everyone in this building is angry because there is so much that has been addressed?" Brodka said.
"I don't want you to think that I'm saying it's each one of you individuals," she said to town officials. "You all have different tenure, you all have different goals. But is it any wonder that everybody in this building is upset because there is a lot going on."
Brodka and many other residents in the room expressed their support of the town's plan to hold quarterly meetings like the one Monday.
"I am glad that you are going to have quarterly meetings because they are absolutely necessary," she said. "I am glad that you are telling me that there is going to be more follow through. But until we see it, I don't think anyone's going to believe it. I think this town is going to continue to be angry until we have results."

title: Oxford's Strand Beach frustrations grow as fencing is erected
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford's Strand Beach frustrations grow as fencing is erected

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Strand Beach project has sparked controversy within Oxford since its inception in 2018. Now, a new town manager, a recently elected commissioner and highly invested residents are taking it upon themselves to assess where the project stands.At Tuesday evening's meeting, Oxford commissioner Dave Donovan used his time during the commissioner comment period to say, "I'd hate for a meeting to go by and not talk about the Strand."
Residents sat up a bit straighter and were excited to hear this.
Recently, protective fencing was erected all over the Strand Beach.
"I mean, my god, what an eyesore," Donovan said.
In order for the town to be in compliance with the Maryland Department of Environment, 85% of the Strand must be covered by marsh and vegetation — as seen from an aerial view — for five years.
The protective fencing, which signifies where the marsh and vegetation will go, covers a large portion of the former beach area.
"I think that's a huge change for people to accept because those used to be beach areas," Commission President Katrina Greer said.
Donovan asked if it would be expensive to take the fencing down, and Greer said it would. "It's $25,000, believe it or not," she said.
The fencing will potentially be up for seasons, but commissioners said they hope that will not be the case. Greer said the fencing helps the plants take hold and without it, they could be installing thousands of plants each year.
"It's the project that keeps giving," Greer said, sarcastically.
The town has been urging the Strand Project's contractor, Underwood and Associates, to complete the living shoreline for several months. On Tuesday, commissioners discussed changing contractors from Underwood and Associates, which the town still has the power to do at this stage of the project.
During the open comments period, resident Jan Greenhawk suggested that the town sue Underwood and Associates.
"I'm going to be short and sweet. I know you're going to closed session and you're going to talk about legal issues," Greenhawk said. "I'm going to give you an opinion, and I think a lot of people in town might agree with this: We need to seek legal action against this contractor. I think he pulled a fast one on the town of Oxford."
Underwood and Associates was unable to comment on the situation before The Star Democrat's deadline.
Currently, there is no ADA accessibility at the Strand Beach and the little walking room there is on the street is consumed by an 80-inch standing puddle.
"(The standing water) has been an outstanding problem for this project for years, and years and years," Donovan said.
There will be an update on the Strand's stormwater issues at the next meeting, which will take place Aug. 12 at 6 p.m. at 101 Market Street.

title: Talbot County passes DAF restrictions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County passes DAF restrictions

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 303
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed new regulations on food processing residuals Tuesday.County leaders said the approved legislation helps Talbot fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, also referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, materials.
The materials often come in the form of animal waste from food processing, which then can be spread as fertilizer. State rules took effect last summer cracking down on DAF residuals, but some counties have since enacted local legislation to quell further resident concerns.
Jurisdictions like Caroline County saw tense debate over the matter. Many Caroline County residents complained of noxious odors from operations storing food processing residuals in open-top storage containers. Last year, Caroline County banned the open-top method.
Similarly, Talbot's legislation requires closed-top storage of food processing residuals. In addition to the open-top storage ban, Talbot's regulations require the storage applicant to:
Receive site plan approval from the county.Obtain an approved nutrient management plan from the state.Remain at least 500 feet from any residential property lines. If all affected property owners consent to a setback reduction, it can be decreased as far as 200 feet.
"We certainly don't want to be the only jurisdiction on the Shore that neglects to regulate this material," County Council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Lesher, Council President Chuck Callahan and council members Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp voted in favor of the legislation. Keasha Haythe, who was absent from Tuesday's meeting, did not vote.
Talbot's Planning Commission and planning officers Brennan Tarleton and Bryce Yelton ironed out the specifics of the regulations since it was drafted last year. Lesher thanked them for their efforts.
"This is one of the more technical issues that we've dealt with," Lesher said, "and I just want to express my appreciation for the staff and for the Planning Commission in working out the details of this."

title: Bay Bridge traffic situation only getting worse
author: MICHAEL SAKATA
content:
Bay Bridge traffic situation only getting worse

 July 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MICHAEL SAKATA | Section: Columns 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Weekends are no longer sustainable on the Eastern Shore. Nor, for that matter, are most weekdays.The 16-mile traffic backups that paralyzed Maryland's Mid-Shore and Upper Shore on July 6, as thousands of weary families spent the waning hours of their holiday weekends languishing on westbound U.S. 50, were unsurprising to those who cross the Bay Bridge and travel this corridor on a regular basis. To their credit, our state and local leaders have used every available Band-Aid to mitigate this crisis — from eliminating the outdated booths at the Bay Bridge's eastbound toll plaza, to closing westbound access roads to weekend through traffic.
Despite their best efforts, though, the situation will only get worse.
As the population of the Eastern Shore continues to climb, regional policymakers work to expand housing inventories in order to meet demand, and the Shore becomes an increasingly popular destination for year-round entertainment and tourism, congestion will only intensify. There will, inevitably, come a time when backups of this magnitude are a daily occurrence and Shore residents are effectively cut off from jobs, emergency services and one another.
Given the inevitability of these trends, and the amount of time it takes for transportation projects to be funded and built in the state of Maryland, we must recognize that the time for action is now. By waiting any longer to commit to a visionary transportation mobility plan, we will only put these Marylanders' lives, livelihoods and quality of life at severe risk.
Given the stakes, Gov. Moore and the Maryland General Assembly are to be commended for committing an additional $500 million to some of our state's most urgent projects this past legislative session. This was a vital first step, but with more than $3 billion in unsatisfied priorities and a statewide network of roads, highways and bridges that continue to crumble with age, it is now time to take a quantum leap forward.
The Maryland Transportation Builders & Materials Association, which represents roughly 240 businesses (and therefore over 100,000 Maryland employees) across the DMV region, has developed a comprehensive regional approach to the U.S. 50 congestion crisis. An approach that recognizes this situation is much bigger than any single project and, therefore, addresses the challenge at multiple chokepoints and safety hazards.
Specifically, our plan calls upon our state leaders to wrap up what has been an interminable Chesapeake Bay Bridge Crossing Study, determine the best strategy for adding significant lane capacity and begin the arduous process of securing the massive funding that will be necessary to move the project forward. We do so, however, knowing that expanded Bay Bridge capacity alone will not solve the problem entirely.
Therefore, we are also calling for action on the following projects — all of which are in the Maryland Department of Transportation's six-year program — and are highlighted in our "25 for 25" campaign. These projects will help our state to meet the demands of the mid-21st century and beyond:
Construction of a grade-separated interchange at U.S. Route 50 and 213 in Wye Mills.Safety improvements at the highly perilous intersection of U.S. 50 and the Easton Bypass.Widening of I-97 to six lanes between U.S. Route 50 and state Route 32.Addition of lane capacity at U.S. Route 50 and Ritchie Highway.Capacity, safety and functionality improvements along the state Route 90 corridor, from U.S. 50 to Coastal Highway.Replacement of the unreliable Sinepuxent Bay drawbridge at the Ocean City Inlet.
To be sure, this is an ambitious plan. In fact, likely the most thorough reimagining of the Eastern Shore's transportation capacity since the "Reach the Beach" program nearly 40 years ago. It is also an expensive ask at a time when our primary sources of transportation revenue are plummeting due to improved gas mileage, reduction in gasoline-powered automobiles and various economic pressures.
However, to suggest that these projects simply cannot be done would imply that they are merely a luxury and not a necessity. As the primary voice of Maryland's transportation industry, we believe that failure to act is no longer an acceptable option. Even in the face of unprecedented fiscal and economic challenges, our elected officials and business leaders must come together — absent the partisan and geographic rivalries that so often act as impediments to progress — and determine how, and not if, we will make this vision a reality.
We simply cannot continue to live like this.
