title: Grassroots lobbying derails Maglev train plans
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Grassroots lobbying derails Maglev train plans

 August 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 772
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Until recently, Maglev trains were being considered for passenger service between Washington, D.C., and Baltimore and eventually between Washington, D.C., and New York City.Unlike traditional passenger trains with locomotives pulling steel wheeled cars on steel tracks, Maglev trains use a powerful combination of electromagnets and levitation.
As a result, Maglev trains can run at top speeds between 250 and 300 miles per hour. That is significantly faster than Amtrak's soon to be launched NextGen Acela, a high-speed passenger train between Washington, D.C., and Boston with top speeds of 160 miles per hour.
After seeing and riding Maglev trains on a trade trip to Japan, Gov. Moore expressed great enthusiasm and strong support for Maglev passenger trains in Maryland.
Despite Moore's enthusiasm and support, Maglev trains are not in Maryland's immediate future, and most likely never will be.
Recently, U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the Federal Railroad Administration is canceling more than $26 million in federal grants to study a Maryland Maglev project.
Duffy noted this project has seen nearly a decade of poor planning, significant public opposition, tremendous costs overruns and nothing to show for it. He noted the project would result in significant unresolvable impacts to federal agencies and federal property, including national security agencies and Fort Meade.
Some will say this decision is comparable to previous Trump administration decisions that negatively impact Maryland such as keeping the FBI headquarters in downtown Washington, D.C., instead of moving it to Maryland and recent news reports about relocating a U. S. Department of Agriculture research center from Maryland.
That is simply not the case with the Maglev decision.
The Maryland Coalition for Responsible Transit (MCRT) has strongly opposed Maglev trains running through Maryland for many years.
The all-volunteer MCRT was formed in January 2020 by a group from Prince George's County and Anne Arundel County to evaluate transportation proposals from a broad array of perspectives, then communicate their findings and recommendations to government decision-makers and also educate the public.
MCRT launched a grassroots lobbying effort with a concise message — stop the proposed Maglev service from being built and operating in Maryland.
Ultimately, their message was heard by and resonated with a wide range of current and previous Maryland Republican and Democratic local, state and national elected officials.
Gov. Hogan, a former and current resident of Anne Arundel County, originally supported the concept. After it generated widespread public opposition, he changed his stance to oppose it.
Members of the Prince George's County Council sent a letter to the Federal Railroad Administration urging rejection of the Maglev proposal.
Angela Alsobrooks, now one of Maryland's U.S. senators, signed that letter when she was a member of that council.
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen has said: "Concerns about the project and its impact on Maryland communities were long running. While its potential was promising, the devil lay in the details, and those details were never fully fleshed out — including how the project would affect residents, our environment and nearby federal agencies."
Despite his enthusiasm for the Maglev project, even Gov. Moore has accepted the Federal Railroad Administration decision. His spokesperson recently said in part, "… this project had challenges that were insurmountable."
Following the decision, Susan McCutchen, a board member at MCRT said the decision brought her a mixture of excitement and surprise.
Her surprise was based in part on the MCRT prevailing despite an enormous amount of lobbying done on behalf of the company that planned to bring a Maglev project to Maryland.
According to media reviews of the company's disclosure reports filed with the Maryland State Ethics Commission, they spent $575,000 on lobbying in 2023 and $603,000 in 2024.
McCutchen has said humbly, "We worked very, very hard — and all volunteer — but it's for our communities, that's the bottom line."
Affirming that the MCRT effort was the result of "very, very, hard work, Maryland state Sen. Alonzo Washington and Maryland state Dels. Anne Healey, Ashanti Martinez and Nicole Williams issued a joint letter saying, "The outcome did not happen by accident. It is the result of relentless and unified opposition from our community and elected leaders — a coalition of residents, advocates, faith leaders, council members and state legislators who stood together to protect our neighborhoods, homes and environmental legacy. We made it clear: Our communities are not for sale, and infrastructure should uplift communities — not divide them."
MCRT's successful efforts are a case study of the awesome power and effectiveness of grassroots citizen lobbying.
Those efforts confirm that in the legislative arena a group of committed, energized, and mobilized citizens can prevail even when they are engaged in a dealing with an opponent who spends in excess of a million dollars to secure a win for their cause.

title: Potential bill on public nuisances workshopped at Caroline County meeting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com

Potential bill on public nuisances workshopped at Caroline County meeting

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners workshopped a potential legislative bill addressing public nuisances at their Tuesday meeting.The commissioners discussed a proposed amendment to the definitions section of chapter 137 of the county's code and a new section addressing public nuisances and their abatement in Caroline County.
As defined in the current legislation, a public nuisance affects an entire area or the public at large, unlike a private nuisance, which affects a single property.
Public nuisance properties can be properties that can cause harm to public health and safety or properties that have been abandoned or unkept. The main priorities for the commissioners with the potential bill are burning trash, temporary use of recreational vehicles and abandoned homes and properties.
The proposed ordinance provides framework for identifying the nuisances, which would include notifying landowners and tenants and providing due process hearings in case of disagreement.
"The county does have the power, as does the health department, the health officer and the secretary of the department of health, all have these powers under the state statutes to abate nuisance," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.
"It doesn't give you a great deal of direction how you're supposed to do it, but you have the power," he said. "So the purpose of ordinances at county level is to give some framework to how public nuisance is identified by the director of planning and codes."
Inspections would be conducted by the county code enforcement office, and coordination with the health department would depend on the nature of the complaint.
Concerns were raised about the feasibility of incorporating appeal hearings into the regular County Commissioners schedule, given the potential for lengthy hearings, but county officials said most of the appeals would not reach the commissioners.
County officials and the county health department agreed to work on the commissioners' concerns within the proposed legislation.

title: Easton approves permit for 54th annual Waterfowl Festival
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton approves permit for 54th annual Waterfowl Festival

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In less than three months, thousands will take to the streets of downtown Easton for the 54th annual Waterfowl Festival.On Monday, the Town Council unanimously approved the festival's permit, along with its transportation plan and food vendors list. This year's festival is slated for Nov. 13-16. Last year, over 25,000 attended, a record-breaking mark.
Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon answered questions about the permit request on Monday.
Kilmon said a key change in this year's transportation plan is the addition of two bus stops, one at the festival building on the corner of South Harrison and South streets, and the other at the Framptom Funeral Home on the corner of North Harrison and Goldsborough streets.
The funeral home is a new venue for a festival art gallery, Kilmon noted.
According to the permit application, festival organizers expect there to be five buses on Friday, Nov. 14; 11 on Saturday, Nov. 15; and six on Sunday, Nov. 16.
Attendees will be encouraged to park at the Easton Elementary, Middle and High schools, along with other locations, including The Country School and Easton VFW Post 5118. Organizers reviewed the transportation plan with a bus charter service, police and economic development leaders.
"We have made every effort to minimize impact on local residents," the plan stated.
The approved food vendors list has 14 locations across town with around 22 total vendors. Kilmon said there are three fewer food trucks than last year.
"As our brick-and-mortar people can take over whatever they need to take over, we are backing down because we do not want to be in the food truck business," Kilmon said. " … We do it for the festival, because it's overwhelming for our local restaurants, especially with all our children."
Town Council President Don Abbatiello asked about an open-container alcohol concern that was noted by the Easton Police Department in its permit review.
"I know it was a concern that people would leave establishments with alcohol and walk around the streets," Abbatiello said. "Even though we don't allow that, it was still occurring. Has there been any reaching out to these different businesses to say, 'you need to do a little bit better tightening of that'?"
Kilmon said organizers, including newly appointed Festival Commission members, have been reaching out to businesses.
"We have expressed our concerns, too," Kilmon said. "We want our people, if you're buying our alcohol, to stay on our own property."
She said the Framptom Funeral Home parking lot will host the festival's tasting pavilion. There will be a fence and festival volunteers in the lot, who she hopes will prevent people from leaving the site with open alcohol containers.
"I think we're going to have better luck keeping our people where they're supposed to be," Kilmon said.

title: Easton council debates how to move forward with food trucks
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council debates how to move forward with food trucks

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After uproar from food truck owners and residents, the Easton Town Council is considering changes to its restrictions on food trucks.On Monday, the council discussed potentially revising a 2011 ordinance that limits food trucks to only operating during special events like festivals.
"I think that should be something we should take on as soon as we can," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
All five council members acknowledged they must keep in mind the town's existing restaurants when making any relaxations to food truck rules.
"2011 was a long time ago, and things change," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said. "But we have to be mindful of our brick-and-mortar restaurants. We don't want to do anything unnecessarily to compete with them."
In the last two weeks, pushback against Easton's food truck rules has been widespread online. A petition garnered over 3,000 signatures.
The outcry came after town code enforcement began to more closely enforce the 2011 rules, prohibiting food trucks from operating in the parking lot of the town's hospital.
The council and attorney Sharon VanEmburgh agreed Monday to look at amending the ordinance by next spring. Then, they focused discussion on a short-term solution.
PILOT PROGRAM
Much of the food truck debate has centered on vendors that had been setting up outside the Shore Medical Center hospital on South Washington Street. Curry said the council received "tremendous" feedback from hospital employees who relied on the food trucks during lunch breaks.
"It's literally impossible to even go pick up a sandwich sometimes with the traffic in our wonderful, little town and get back to the desk within 30 minutes," Curry said.
Curry asked if the town could include the hospital in a short-term fix, such as a pilot program floated Monday. The program would likely be created through a resolution, VanEmburgh said, allowing certain businesses to invite food trucks to their properties.
Easton's program, if approved, would likely include a setback rule from nearby restaurants. VanEmburgh said the best mark may be around 300 feet.
Town Council members debated various provisions that could be included in a resolution to establish the pilot program.
Davis said any pilot program introduced would need to apply to other businesses in town.
"If we're gonna do it for the hospital, we got to be fair across the board to other people," Davis said. "I get the hospital has a need, but you can't just arbitrarily give them favor."
Ward 4's David Montgomery pushed back, saying a pilot program is meant to try out "in a specific time and place." He said the hospital should have "first crack" at a food truck pilot program.
Davis raised the concern that certain food trucks could be excluded from the pilot, providing an example.
"If there's a food truck that specializes in African American food that is not served at the hospital, what do we do in those instances to be fair?" Davis asked.
Montgomery replied, "It just seems to me that you're being obstructionist in these comments.
" ... The hospital has chosen in the past what food truck to invite on their private property," he added. "I think that's their right to do it."
The council also touched on transient license fees that food trucks pay when setting up at permitted festivals or events. Vendors pay $500 for the first two days and $150 for each day after up to 30 days.
"I would not be opposed to waiving that right now while we're in the pilot program," Curry said. "Because you can't expect a food truck to pay $500 to sit outside a hospital or a store or anywhere. Because they'll never recoup."
VanEmburgh said it makes sense to reduce that fee for the pilot program, though she said there probably should still be some fee.
The Town Council is expected to consider a pilot program proposal at a future meeting, potentially on Sept. 2.

 DENTON — Throughout the past two years, solar energy has been a major topic of discussion on the Eastern Shore.The conversation was raised again at the Caroline County Commissioners' bi-weekly meeting Tuesday, where the commissioners dissected a proposed legislative bill on solar.
The solar energy ordnance would bring the county in compliance with state law. The bill focuses on maintaining accessory solar, which is residential solar that is generating power for a property's electrical use.
After discussing several definitions they wanted to revise, the commissioners raised concerns about donating money to the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation. The commissioners have no problem with donating to agricultural land preservation, they said, but they want to make sure the money is going back to farms in Caroline County.
The county contributes $20,000 per year to the land preservation foundation. On top of that, commissioners said, when solar projects come into Caroline County on agricultural land, the solar company has to pay an agricultural transfer fee, which the county also donates to MALPF.
Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter's concern is if the state funding was cut on MALPF would the county still receive financial help to preserve agricultural land.
"If we collect money in Caroline County, I want it to be used to preserve farmland in Caroline County," Porter said.
No official decision was made on donation of the funds, and the county will continue to discuss options at future meetings, the commissioners said.
The county officials will discuss some changes to the proposed bill and move the bill to an official legislative bill with the purpose of having the first reading at the next county commissioners meeting.

title: Oxford's loss of post office, bank impacts residents
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford's loss of post office, bank impacts residents

 August 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Headlines 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Within the past two months, Oxford temporarily lost its post office and permanently closed the Bay Vanguard Bank.Residents are now having to drive to Easton for these services, and many are unhappy with the setup, according to a survey collected by Town Manager Holly Wahl.
Former Town Commissioner Jimmy Jaramillo said there is widespread frustration and disappointment among residents, which he's observed both online and in personal conversations during walks through town.
"As a former commissioner, I'm very concerned. With the post office, there's nothing you can do, that's a freak accident. I'm just glad everyone made it out safely," Jaramillo said. "But the fact that we no longer have a bank in town that local businesses depend on in order to make their business successful. It's very concerning."
A structural fire that occurred June 23 rendered the Oxford Post Office unusable until it's restored. The Commissioners of Oxford are looking for a temporary space in the meantime, but Commissioner Dave Donovan said it has been tricky due to the federal nature of postal mail.
Wahl said the delays in reopening the post office are due to insurance claims and adjuster processes, and the Oxford office may be closed into the new year.
"There is no set timeframe for a return to Oxford. In the interim, customers may continue to utilize neighboring post offices or usps.com for their mailing and shipping needs. We thank our customers for their patience during this time," said Mark Lawrence, strategic communications specialist for the United States Postal Service, in an email to the Star Democrat.
Many Oxford residents are unable to receive mail at home, since mailboxes are not permitted in the town's historic district, Donovan said.
"You know, having to drive all the way to Easton to pick up your mail is a big issue for a lot of people. Some folks get more and more of their stuff via email, but a lot of people don't," Donovan said.
The bank closed after town commissioners decided to take one of their funds out of the local bank and put it into an investment account that accrues more interest.
"But it came to a head in June, when the town had some financial instruments that needed to roll over into new terms as well as a debt facility that the town was negotiating, and the local bank just was not remotely competitive with what we could get from Short United," Donovan said, recounting a time before he was a commissioner. "I mean, it wasn't even competitive."
Wahl said after receiving surveys back from residents, the town is exploring options to restore some banking services.
"We are working with Shore United to see if we can bring a full service ATM into town, and they are looking at the feasibility of doing that and looking at a couple different locations that they could potentially provide that service," Wahl said.

title: Trash dumpsters removed from multiple apartments in Greensboro due to undercharges
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Trash dumpsters removed from multiple apartments in Greensboro due to undercharges

 August 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 395
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — At the Greensboro Town Council meeting, Town Manager Cindy Yost revealed that multiple audits have been conducted on different parts of the town's finances.Within the audits, multiple overcharges and undercharges were discovered.
Yost reported on audits of phone accounts showing the town paying for multiple inactive phone lines. The audit led to about $18,000-$20,000 in savings for the town.
Yost also reported School House, Maple Village, Rolling Meadows and Greensboro Heights apartments were underbilled for trash services for a 23-month period, amounting to more than $18,000 in under paid fees.
The underbilling was due to an error with the flat rate on trash bills. The bill was divided by dumpster size. The town was not charging enough for the dumpsters including when dumpsters were full and over the trash line, resulting in an extra $100 charged by Republic.
The undercharges were deemed by council members to not be the apartment complexes' fault, so they decided to pay up to $24,000 in fees. The town notified the apartment complexes that trash service will end on Sept. 2, and Republic has been notified.
In addition to the issues with the dumpsters, the town discovered that the apartment complexes were being billed a flat rate for water and sewer services, which has been corrected for the next billing cycle.
Yost stated the cost could go up or down depending on residents' usage.
While the town is disappointed this has happened, they are thankful that Yost came in and discovered savings for the town and multiple undercharges.
"This all started looking at a phone bill," Mayor David Spencer said. "We're trying to be as transparent with the citizens as we can be to let you know where we are and where we're going and where we're headed to.
"There's been a lot of mistakes and as the mayor I have to own that. We can't go backward, we have to move forward. I think that we're doing a good job at doing that, and we owe it all to Cindy. She has uncovered a lot of money, a lot of savings for the community. In the end, I think it will turn out well. It's going to hurt for a little while hearing some of the things that have happened. It's going to hurt for some of you that haven't been billed properly, but we need to make it fair to everybody in the community."

title: Open primaries: Idea whose time may never come
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Open primaries: Idea whose time may never come

 August 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 798
 Words 

 Read News Document

 More than 500 years ago, political observer and philosopher Niccolo Machiavelli wrote a timeless and thought-provoking message on resistance to change.He wrote: "It must be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to plan, more doubtful of success, nor more dangerous to manage, than introducing new ways of doing things. For the initiator has the enmity of all who would profit by the preservation of the old ways of doing things and merely lukewarm defenders in those who would gain by the new ones."
This observation is being tested by ongoing efforts in Maryland to change the rules relative to participation in and state funding of partisan primary elections.
This issue is driven in large part by the increasing number of individuals in Maryland who have chosen to register to vote as unaffiliated, often referred to as independents.
In April of this year, more than 22% of registered voters in Maryland are registered as unaffiliated. That number was less than 21% in 2023.
Another 2% of individuals in Maryland have chosen to register with a third party.
The bottom line is almost a quarter of the registered voters in Maryland are not registered as a Republican or Democratic voter and as a consequence, they cannot vote in primary elections.
One can assume this trend will not only continue but also accelerate.
In April of this year, more than 36% of new voter registrations, not changes to existing registrations, were unaffiliated.
In May of this year, five unaffiliated Maryland voters filed a lawsuit in Anne Arundel County District Court. They are working with an advocacy group — Open Primaries Education Fund (not to be confused with the Open Society Foundation funded by George Soros).
The plaintiffs in the suit acknowledge political parties may have the right to exclude citizens from their primary elections, but it is unconstitutional for the state of Maryland to organize and pay for those elections.
They claim the only way the state can be in compliance with the state constitution is if the state Democratic and Republican parties fund their respective primary elections or if both parties allow all qualified citizens, regardless of their party affiliation, to vote in primaries.
The defendant in the lawsuit is the Maryland State Board of Elections, the state agency that manages primary elections.
An assistant state attorney general representing the Board of Elections has requested the Anne Arundel County District Court dismiss the lawsuit based on four claims.
One claim is that a lawsuit filed by only five taxpayers is insufficient to establish standing for such a challenge.
Another claim is that the merits of the unaffiliated voters' challenge have already been considered and rejected in two previous court decisions — one handed down by a state court and one by a federal court.
The Supreme Court of Maryland issued a decision that "voters have no right under the state constitution to vote in the primary elections of a party to which they do not belong."
The U.S. Supreme Court has upheld closed primaries and a political party's First Amendment right "not to associate" and therefore cannot be required to allow unaffiliated voters to participate in their primary elections.
Complicating matters further on a judicial resolution on this matter is the opinion of a former senior voting rights attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union.
He has said the courts are often reluctant to depart from regular procedures on changing election laws and prefer to seek legislative consideration and action.
While pursuing changes in the Maryland General Assembly is always an option, recent history is that pursuing open primary legislation in that arena has failed to get traction.
In the 2023 General Assembly session, one bill was introduced in the Maryland Senate, and one was introduced Maryland House of Delegates, both on open primaries.
Each bill only had one sponsor which is a clear indication that neither bill had even minimal support in the General Assembly.
As a result, neither bill was voted from committee, an essential step on the always challenging process to enact a new law or revise an existing law in Maryland.
Also, no open primary legislation has been introduced in the General Assembly since then.
Going forward, I predict two outcomes on some form of open primaries in Maryland.
I predict, that in every court case, including any appeals to higher courts, eventually the definitive decisions will be that any changes to the election laws must be approved in the General Sssembly and signed by the governor.
I also predict, without widespread public demand for any election law changes in Maryland, they will never be approved in the General Assembly and by the governor.
If my predictions occur, it will affirm that Machiavelli's observation — "There is nothing more difficult to plan, more doubtful of success, nor more dangerous to manage, than introducing new ways of doing things" is as relevant today as it was when he wrote it in 1513.

title: Mobile competition is beneficial
author: Staff Writer
content:
Mobile competition is beneficial

 August 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 177
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I'm not clear why we differentiate between brick-and-mortar businesses and mobile businesses.As a previous owner of a brick-and-mortar business, I had mobile competitors. I took the approach that while I could offer a significantly larger array of products and services, there are customers that will opt for a less comprehensive menu.
I could have started a mobile service too, but the customer base I sought was not those needing or desiring limited mobile options.
So I would advise Easton council to treat mobile businesses like the brick-and-mortar ones. Charge them the same annual fee. Collect the taxes on their income. Collect taxes on the wages they pay their staff. And require the mobile businesses to adhere to the same OSHA, Department of Health, etc. laws and ordinances that all brick-and-mortar businesses are required to follow.
Restaurant owners aren't happy when another restaurant opens. Liquor stores aren't happy when another liquor store opens. But it's called competition.
Maybe … just maybe … mobile competition will get brick-and-mortar businesses to create competitive options rather than asking local governments to stifle them.
TERENCE JOHN
Easton

title: Officials talk local, federal challenges with Cambridge seniors
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Officials talk local, federal challenges with Cambridge seniors

 August 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Local, state and federal officials, including Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), joined senior citizens at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center on Monday afternoon to discuss issues affecting Cambridge's older residents.Cambridge Mayor Lejan Cephas introduced Alsobrooks by describing local policies that help seniors, like the homeownership helper program, and affirming the city's commitment to providing protections for its aging population.
"I can tell you Cambridge is absolutely intentional about our seniors, about our older residents in the city of Cambridge," Cephas said. "We actually put policies in place to provide protections and also the opportunity that you can age and place."
Alsobrooks identified with the audience by describing herself as part of the "sandwich generation," with a 20-year-old child and parents who have been married for 50 years. Her father now cares for her mother, who has dementia. Because of this, Alsobrooks said she is familiar with the struggles senior citizens are facing after recent federal cuts.
The senator went on to slam President Donald Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, saying the brunt of what she called the "Big Ugly Bill" will fall on senior citizens and pointing to significant cuts to Medicaid, Medicare and nutrition programs.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was passed on July 4, extending Trump's 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. The bill made a majority of tax cuts permanent and increased federal spending on border security, defense and energy production while significantly cutting health care and nutrition programs.
Maryland Department of Aging Secretary Carmel Roques said in early iterations of the Big Beautiful Bill, funding for older people in Maryland, primarily through the Older Americans Act, was zeroed out. But the funding was restored in the latest state budget through concerted federal and state efforts, she said.
While officials largely discussed state- and federal-level issues, Cambridge residents like Sandra Snowden sought answers to problems they face at the local level.
"I am politically astute," Snowden said. "And I do understand all that's going on on the national level. I need to kind of bring us down here, to Chesapeake Grove. Right now, we don't have enough money to keep this center going."
Snowden said it currently costs $64 a month for seniors to attend the center two days a week. It costs $5 more for lunch, and there are additional costs for extra activities. The cost of these services vary depending on use and means of transportation, but for Snowden, the cost is too much regardless.
Snowden, who is legally blind, is lives in one of three senior residence facilities in Cambridge. She said her complex has experienced bug infestations, sees high rates of crime and currently has no lighting in the parking lot.
Alsobrooks responded saying she does not have direct oversight of these issues in the city. Cephas and City Manager Glenn Steckman addressed Snowden's concerns directly, saying city officials worked hard with this year's budget to allocate funds towards issues concerning older residents.
The budget currently has $15,000 set aside for senior citizen activities and objectives.
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) encouraged Alsobrooks to maintain open communication so they can have a strong partnership moving forward.
"Whatever comes out at your level, it comes down to this state and just keeping us abreast so we can know what we need to fight for. The seniors, if they want to write a letter or make a phone call and know how it's going to affect the Department of Aging or the Department of Health, that kind of communication level. We need to be able to work with you as a strong partner," Sample-Hughes said.

title: New comprehensive plan discussed in Cambridge
author: Lily Tierney
content:
New comprehensive plan discussed in Cambridge

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester

 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — Last week, the City of Cambridge hosted a charette to devise a new and improved comprehensive plan.The charette was a weeklong intensive and interactive public session where Planning Director Brian Herrmann, alongside a planning committee from consulting firm Able City, began to capture a vision of Cambridge's future.
The new plan outlined five main ideas: make downtown vibrant and multi-generational, encourage great places beyond downtown, reinvent lost Main Street areas, increase waterfront access and recreational amenities, and build a sustainable and equitable future.
The last time the city came up with a comprehensive plan was in 2011. They planned to re-address it in 2021, but due to the pandemic, that never happened.
Under Maryland law, cities must update their comprehensive plans every 10 years to reflect the community's current needs.
Individuals on the planning team specialize in a variety of development topics, ranging from economic development and housing to transportation.
During the weeklong session, there was strong community engagement, said Jason King, a city planner with Able City.
"This week, we started off with that hands-on design session — 135 plus people, 18 tables, two and a half hour event. It was an epic," King said. "For the city of 13,035 people, you know, we ran out of surveys, and we didn't have enough pens."
King said this kind of turn out is expected in a city of 100,000 residents.
Planners and city officials will continue to work on the comprehensive plan in the coming months before submitting a final version to the state.

title: Federalsburg Activities Center hopes to bring joy to the whole community
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg Activities Center hopes to bring joy to the whole community

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — An idea for a space where children could have fun in Federalsburg turned into a place where everyone could have fun.The Federalsburg Activities Center began with a conversation between the Rev. Pam Bockart and the Rev. Stanford Ricks at a meeting in 2019.
Bockart was the Pastor at Christ Church, and she recalled "kids outside just walking the streets having nowhere to go."
She decided to call a meeting about finding something for the children to do. After the meeting, Bockart and Ricks selected a location for a community center project at the old Dollar General building on Morris Avenue in Federalsburg.
Ricks is the vice president of Men for Change, an organization the specializes in "changing our community through service" by mentoring youth in Federalsburg. The group wanted a central location.
A partnership was formed. For the next five years, Bockart, Ricks and a board of stakeholders overcame financial and logistical obstacles to open the Federalsburg Activities Center.
"We started on a journey. We had nothing, no money, just a vision to open up this building," Ricks said, looking around the center, which opened in the former Dollar General building earlier this year.
The group gained ownership of the building with help from its former owner and a loan. But even after the building's ownership was squared away, multiple renovations needed to be done to make the space functional.
After multiple grants, donations from local businesses and an anonymous $400,000 private donation, the Activities Center was renovated and ready for the community.
"Over the five years, we never got frustrated," Ricks said. "That was the great thing to me. The the board that we had, we met every week, we came here, we enjoyed each other, we talked positive and never got frustrated. I think we kind of knew it was going to be a long journey.
"... So now we went from phase one, which was to get the building open. Now were going into phase two of the project, getting the programs up and running in the building."
The current programs at the Activities Center are Men For Change on Friday, bible study on Saturday, senior lunches on Friday, garden club once a month and Make Federalsburg Beautiful meetings once a month. Men For Change sees 30 to 50 kids on Fridays, and the senior lunches see 20 to 40 seniors.
Part of the next phase for the center will be partnering youth with older community members. Board members said older community members tend to feel left out, with a lack of activities catered toward them. The board hopes this partnership will increase seniors' drive and provide mentorship opportunities for local youth.
"We would like to bring the young ones, who are starting their vision, and the old ones, who have their vision, and we want them to kind of get together so that the seniors can tell the younger ones about their story and how to get there themselves that they may have a good life," Ricks said.
Another part of the next phase is adding new programs within the activities center. The board has plans to add a science, technology, engineering and mathematics program; arts and crafts; a coffee club; and a running club. Board members said negotiations for Boys and Girls Club and 4-H partnerships are ongoing.
The board is most excited about the potential of what the activities center can do for the town of Federalsburg.
"There is something in all of us when we give to others," said Wendy Garner, secretary for the board. "We get back as much if not more, and that's what I think all these skills, all these learning curves, whether it's for the kids, the adults, or the seniors — this is a community center."
The board encourages all community members who want volunteer or who have ideas to email fac2024@aol.com.

 FEDERALSBURG — The Federalsburg Town Council hosted a special meeting Wednesday to consult with Ken Decker, a one time was the Caroline County administrator, about becoming Federalsburg's town manager on a contractual basis.The contract would be on a month-to-month basis to help the town address issues while seeking a candidate to permanently fill the position vacated by Sally Slook, who stepped back as town manager due to a family emergency.
"I think the first order of business is to kind of dig in and see what's really going on in terms of the town's finances and sort of their operational challenge," Decker said Thursday.
"The second is to start helping them get ready to hire a permanent town manager because at the moment, what I'm just doing is proposing to provide some contractual managerial administrative services to kind of help them get organized."
Decker has worked as a city manager or county administrator for just over 20 years in Delaware, Pennsylvania and Maryland. He served as the Caroline County administrator from 2011 to 2018.
During the meeting, town officials said current County Administrator Kathleen Freeman had recommended Decker for the role. However, Freeman told the Star Democrat on Thursday that she did not recommend Decker.
Decker and Freeman had a general conversation, in which Federalsburg came up, Freeman said. Decker approached Federalsburg about offering help.
The town councilmembers and Decker spoke about multiple issues at Wednesday meeting.
Federalsburg is in the process of paying off more than $5 million of debt, most of which comes from the town's wastewater treatment facility.
The facility was built to support a housing development in the town that was never constructed, making it outsized to the town's needs.
Mayor Kim Abner said the facility is built to handle 750,000 gallons per day, more than double the current usage.
The town has many issues with taking care of the facility due to improper usage and rates for town residents not being enough to cover the cost of the facility.
"The wastewater and water plant need a thorough look through," Decker said. "I mean, we've talked about the rate study, and even though that there's been a recommendation for that rate study out there, there's been no movement on it. No pun intended, but water and sewer is where you're leaking the most money right now."
While the town didn't make a motion to officially bring Decker on has a contracted town manager, they moved to go into closed session to discuss what a contract would look like for Decker.

title: QA County halts new growth: Moratorium tied to sewer capacity; land preservation, park upgrades approved
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QA County halts new growth: Moratorium tied to sewer capacity; land preservation, park upgrades approved

 August 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Looking at future wastewater capacity, the Queen Anne's County commissioners on Aug. 12 approved a temporary moratorium on residential and mixed-use development.With the area Wastewater Treatment Plant near capacity, the commissioners adopted a moratorium on applications, approvals, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of subdivision, concept plan, site plan or building permit applications for residential or mixed-use projects in Kent Narrows, Stevensville, Grasonville, Prospect Bay, Cloverfields, Bay City and Southern Kent Island.
During the moratorium, the county will not process, consider, review or approve any application, permit or other approval under the County Zoning Ordinance or the Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance for any project in those subdistricts where the total anticipated sewerage allocation exceeds 1,750 gallons per day.
The resolution does not apply to any pending project that already has prerequisite sewer and water allocation for its specific development.
Queen Anne's County has applied for a rerating of the wastewater treatment plant, which if granted would increase capacity by 300,000 gallons per day.
Because of federal Total Maximum Daily Load regulations restricting nutrient and sediment discharge into the Chesapeake Bay, further expansion of treatment capacity at the plant is unlikely.
The county is in the process of updating its 2011 Comprehensive Water and Sewerage Plan. Both that plan and the County Water and Sewerage Allocation Policy may be revised to reflect limited treatment capacity, limited expansion potential and the need to determine how best to allocate sewerage capacity to meet current and future demands.
The county's Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance regulates development based on public infrastructure availability. Commission President Chris Corchiarino said a number of factors have developed since the ordinance was last reviewed, including limited sewer capacity.
With Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the county has also seen an exponential increase in education costs.
"At a time when our enrollment is not going up, our costs have gone up significantly, and that's a cost that is borne by all the citizens," Corchiarino said.
The moratorium will give the county's planning and zoning staff time to take a closer look at zoning, he said.
Land preservation
At no local cost, the commissioners approved the preservation of 117 acres owned by Thompson Farms LLC for review and final approval by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.
Funding will be provided entirely by the Rural Legacy grants program through Program Open Space.
The Thompson Farms LLC property is within the Lands End Rural Legacy Area and will add to the 5,085 acres already preserved. The package includes the Agreement of Sale and Project Agreement signed by the commissioners.
Stevensville park upgrades
Old Love Point Park will see new field lighting. The Department of Parks and Recreation was authorized to contract with Musco Sports Lighting to upgrade the Field Three lights to LEDs for $200,566.
Mowbray Park in Stevensville will also receive new playground equipment. The commissioners approved a $1,139,861 contract with Kompan Inc. to replace the park's current playground.

title: Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth
author: Konner Metz
content:
Here's where Easton leaders stand on growth

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Headlines 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It's a classic debate: build more housing or curb growth?Since joining the The Star Democrat in June 2024, I've seen the housing-growth debate consistently occupy the minds of elected officials, town planners, developers and residents. If you ask a Town Council member or a longtime resident the number one issue that Easton faces, I'd venture to say the answer will be growth-related more times than not.
There's hundreds of housing units in the town's pipeline — 1,127, to be exact. But at the same time, it's well-documented that Easton and Talbot County have an affordability problem, leaving many employees to commute daily from Caroline or Dorchester counties.
So what are the plans to pare down already-heavy traffic and keep the Easton Volunteer Fire Department from transitioning to a paid agency? And at the same time, how can the town still pursue some level of reasonably-priced housing for those that need it most?
It's a complex set of questions I asked the town's top officials, from the mayor, to elected council members, to a surprisingly powerful, six-member volunteer planning board.
The answers aren't clear. Some say slam the brakes. Others believe letting off the gas here and there will do.
There is, however, an approach gaining steam: focus on building from the inside-out, rather than annexing more county land into town or approving sprawling, single-family home developments. Most officials I spoke with endorse that strategy.
No "silver bullet" has emerged or will emerge, many town leaders told me. But a combination of items on the horizon — including a comprehensive plan update, zoning reform and a pause on annexations — will work to manage the town's growth without forgetting about those that seek an affordable place to live.
To hear specifics from town officials, or to find out where Easton's 1,127 units in the pipeline are located, check out my story below.
Thanks for reading.
— Konner Metz

title: The 'missing middle': Why some town leaders see a gap in Easton's housing stock
author: Konner Metz
content:
The 'missing middle': Why some town leaders see a gap in Easton's housing stock

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 712
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Often, the Town Council and Planning Commission are forced to consider projects like a large single-family development or a high-density apartment complex. But the in-between is being lost in the shuffle, some town leaders argue."Missing middle housing" is a phrase used by urban planners, typically referring to townhomes or duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes (buildings containing two, three and four units respectively).
In Easton, this housing has been a frequent topic of conversation as town officials grapple with how to fill affordable housing needs and balance the infrastructure concerns that come with significant growth.
Some town leaders see "missing middle" housing as a key rung in the ladder for residents working toward homeownership.
"It's a big step," Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said. "Owning a home is a tremendous responsibility, and it's a huge milestone in someone's life."
Local real estate agents are noticing the gap, too. Alex Archer, sales manager for The Gerdes Team and a Talbot County resident, said many residents don't have the ability currently to work their way up to buying a single-family home costing hundreds of thousands of dollars. More options in the middle could help that mobility, he said.
"Where's the step to get to that for a lot of blue-collar workers, or for the restaurant workers or for the people who aren't making $150,000 a year?" Archer asked.
Town Council President Don Abbatiello and his wife have experience climbing this ladder. The Abbatiellos first bought a townhome, he said. They later sold it and moved into a single-family home.
But a lot of Easton residents don't have that opportunity since there's not enough affordable housing units available for purchase, Abbatiello said.
"It seems like there's a big drive toward rentals," he said. "But the problem with rentals is you don't build equity."
Tom Klein, an Easton Planning Commission member, said the recently shot-down Fox Chase Estates project had an affordable ownership aspect that he liked. The 365-unit proposal included not just single-family homes, but three-story townhomes, too. It was voted down by Klein and the rest of the commission, though, largely due to connectivity concerns and its placement at the northernmost part of town.
Of affordable rentals, which have carved out notable space in the town's housing pipeline, Klein said: "It still doesn't give people an opportunity to build equity."
A recent draft report from the town's Attainable Housing Task Force takes aim at addressing the missing middle phenomenon in Easton.
Townhomes, duplexes and other missing middle units account for around 20% of the town's stock, according to the draft report, which is undergoing revisions before it is officially presented to the Town Council. The 18-member task force has held discussion on the matter and others as it prepares the report, which is being written by planning and zoning director Miguel Salinas.
The report, referencing census data, states that from 2000 to 2023, around 1,700 new single-family detached homes were built, compared to around 300 single-family attached homes or other middle housing types.
Single-family detached typically refers to a stand-alone house, while attached homes are often townhomes or duplexes.
Michael Ports, vice chair of the Planning Commission, said going straight from an apartment to a detached home can be difficult financially, especially after the pandemic drove up prices.
One potential missing middle housing recommendation the task force may make to the Town Council includes permitting duplexes or townhomes without requiring special approvals or exemptions to the zoning, according to the draft report. Such zoning changes could reduce permitting and time-based costs for developers.
Mayor Megan Cook said such housing types could be crucial for the town's senior population as well.
"We have seniors who have moved here," Cook said. "They maybe now have some health issues, they've lost a spouse or whatnot. They don't need a big home anymore. Maybe they're looking for a smaller footprint."
Gwen Eskridge, an associate broker for Coldwell Banker Chesapeake, lives in Easton. Her daughter and granddaughter both remain at home due to the high cost of homes and rentals in the area.
Development in the missing middle housing range could give them a path toward homeownership, Eskridge said.
"Workforce housing is so critical in this area," Eskridge said. "And I think we really need to start looking into … maybe low-density townhomes or duplexes that would be able to help individuals like my daughter who's living with us."

title: How much growth is too much for Easton? Balance between housing needs, infrastructure unsettled
author: Konner Metz
content:
How much growth is too much for Easton? Balance between housing needs, infrastructure unsettled

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1988
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The predicament on the minds of many Easton residents and leaders continues to be just how much the town can afford to grow.Easton is under a period of significant residential growth with multiple large-scale housing projects under construction. In 2000, the town's population was 11,708, according to census data. Ten years later, it rose to 15,945, and since, it's grown at a slower pace to 17,101 in 2020.
The boom has raised a litany of concerns, from increased traffic to a change in the town's small-town complexion.
Some residents, and a few officials, think Easton should press the brake pedal. But local real estate agents contend that a halt to growth could box out lower- and middle-class buyers and renters.
Martha Witte Suss, an associate broker for Coldwell Banker Realty and Easton resident, said the housing market has been in a crunch since the pandemic. She said there's not enough reasonably priced homes or rentals to satisfy employees who commute from outside Talbot County.
"We have plenty of housing that they can't afford," Suss said. Residential growth, if it focuses on affordability, could cure that dry spell, she added.
Michael Ports, vice chair of the Easton Planning Commission, poses the town's conundrum like this: "What are the housing needs of the people currently, and can we achieve that in a way that doesn't compromise everyone's needs for services?"
It's a question town leaders are taking on, even if there's no easy answer.
This fall, 136 apartments on Elliott Road will begin opening. Two large communities are under construction east of Route 50, combining for over 450 projected single-family homes. Near Easton's downtown, a developer plans to transform two former Perdue AgriBusiness sites into housing projects, totaling 144 units.
In all, roughly 1,127 units are recently finished, under construction or approved by the town's public bodies, according to information from town planners and developers of the 17 listed projects.
The pipeline of projects has yielded varying opinions from town leaders. Some don't want any new large housing projects approved in the next few years. Others prefer a case-by-case approach.
Mayor Megan Cook said the right answer is "probably somewhere in between." The town should focus on the current projects but not be too quick to disregard new ones, she said.
The mayor said growth is a charged topic and especially complicated due to affordable housing needs. No solution is a "silver bullet," Cook and others have repeatedly said.
"It is a balancing act," Town Council President Don Abbatiello said. "There would have to be a project come along that would fit that need, that workforce housing, that affordable housing piece."
In interviews with The Star Democrat, Easton officials weighed in on the town's current list of housing developments. When asked about infrastructure, the most recognized concerns included roads, fire and police services and schools.
They offered thoughts on where the town should focus its residential growth. Most leaned toward building from the inside-out. Planning Commission Chairperson Phil Toussaint is of that opinion. He hopes the sprawling, single-family developments are coming to an end.
"We wouldn't really want to support any development on the outskirts at all," Toussaint said.
And broadly, the 1,127-unit mark can be misleading since some units aren't under construction and may not be for years, Toussaint and others said.
"(People) think they're gonna appear tomorrow," Toussaint said. "They're not."
Single-family home neighborhoods typically take years to build out, such as Easton Village off of St. Michaels Road, a project of around 250 homes first approved in 2003 and just now reaching completion. So far, the 200-home Gannon Range and 252-home Four Seasons projects only have 18 and 11 building permits, respectively, according to Easton planning and zoning director Miguel Salinas.
"It's a daunting number. It's hard to hear," said Cook, who as mayor doesn't have a vote on housing applications. "But at the same time, you look at some of the examples as a community, the neighborhoods that we've had. They're built out over 20 years."
THE PIPELINE
Since town planners prepared a list of Easton housing projects this winter, chatter of "the pipeline" has been frequent at Town Council and Planning Commission meetings. Those two bodies are responsible for approving most of the projects.
The commission is made up of volunteer members and often can only make a recommendation to the council, whose members are elected. But sometimes, the commission holds final say, such as when it approved the 116-apartment Easton Crossing complex on Brookletts Avenue this year.
The five members of the council and six members of the commission offer a range of opinions when it comes to the town's growth.
Town Council Ward 3 representative David Montgomery provided perhaps the most rigid perspective.
"I want to stop for at least five years before we add anything more to this backlog," Montgomery said. "I want to see how fast it actually grows, it's actually built out."
Others were less firm on completely stopping growth, though all council members interviewed for this story said, at the very least, the town needs to be mindful. Some prefer a project-by-project approach, such as Abbatiello, who said future housing proposals need to be the "right fit" for Easton.
"I think right now, there's enough in the pipeline for us to say, 'Let's see how the projects impact the town's resources before we go adding a lot more to that list,'" Abbatiello said.
Planning Commission members have mixed thoughts, too.
Ports, the commission's vice chair, said Easton is "missing a good bit" even with the current project inventory. He said the missing units largely fall between expensive single-family homes and for-rent apartments — a sphere urban planners call "the missing middle."
"The reality is that the median sale price of a home right now is almost twice what a family of four making the absolute average income here in Easton can afford," Ports said. According to Maryland Realtors, the July 2025 median sales price in Talbot County was $545,000, the third highest in the state.
Tom Klein was the commission's lone vote against the Easton Crossing project, citing traffic and parking concerns. He said the need for more affordable housing is clear. But Klein would prefer to have a target number. At times, it feels like Easton is "chasing something" it doesn't know, he said.
"How many more do we need? Do we just keep assuming we keep needing more?" Klein asked. "That, to me, is something I don't really know the answer to. I think it would be helpful to know that so we don't just blindly build."
'MORE AND MORE CROWDED'
Town planners and engineers have processes to gauge the impacts residential projects will have on the town, such as traffic and environmental studies or reviews by the town's nonprofit utility, sewer and water company, Easton Utilities.
Even with project-specific studies, many town leaders believe traffic is a top-of-list concern, along with other infrastructure matters.
Montgomery said town staff should be "much more skeptical about the traffic impact studies" submitted alongside housing proposals. Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis said the traffic issue is obvious to the human eye.
"I don't need a traffic study to tell me that the traffic in Easton, periodically, is a problem at best," Davis said.
Handling traffic backups is a tricky matter, Cook said, since some roads are state-run, others are under county purview and many downtown are maintained by town engineers and public works employees.
Off of Route 328, or Matthewstown Road, 136 apartments are opening soon, while 200 single-family homes will be built just down the road. It's an area residents have flagged during council and state transportation meetings.
"(Route) 328 is going to become busier and busier, and folks, I fear, are going to have more and more challenges getting out to (Route) 50," said Councilmember Robert Rankin, who represents residents in the Route 328 area.
A State Highway Administration planning and environmental study is underway to assess pedestrian and traffic needs on the busy state road that funnels onto Ocean Gateway. Previously proposed concepts by the state include adding left-turn lanes on Matthewstown Road and adding a second through lane on Goldsborough Road as drivers cross Route 50.
Traffic has consistently been brought up as a reason to lean away from annexing land for residential growth outside of Easton's core. Nearly all commission and council members interviewed for this story said they prefer to keep growth within the area encircled by Route 50 and Easton Parkway (322).
The Planning Commission has especially expressed that preference during workshops updating the town's comprehensive plan, which lays out the town's vision for handling growth in the next decade.
In July, the commission rejected the Fox Chase Estates, a 365-unit, mixed-use development proposed near a warehouse and industrial park north of Easton Airport and near the under-construction Shore Regional Health hospital. Town Council members maintain final voting power on the project, though it's unclear when or if it will come before them.
The Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend against the development, citing a lack of connectivity as a main reason. The vote lines up with the commission's recent direction as they draft the new comprehensive plan: build from the inside-out.
"We'd rather see infill," Klein said. "We want to see connected neighborhoods."
That line of thinking, shared by many Town Council members, still leaves Easton with infrastructure challenges, such as downtown streets, utilities and safety. The latter was emphasized by Cook and council members as a chief priority.
Funding for the Easton Police Department and Easton Volunteer Fire Department makes up around 40% of the town's general fund budget. Abbatiello, who volunteers for the fire company, wants to hold off a massive increase in the cost for fire services by maintaining the department's volunteer status for "as (long) as possible."
"The biggest tax increase residents of Easton are ever going to see is if the Town of Easton needs to go to a paid (fire) department," Abbatiello said.
Easton Utilities evaluates water demands annually. According to a statement from Doug Abbott, director of engineering and water/wastewater departments, the utility is using 60% of its water and wastewater capabilities, leaving 40% "to accommodate future growth."
And as for downtown traffic, some town leaders are worried infill will do more harm than good.
"Our streets are becoming more and more crowded, and I am concerned the more that we have infill development, the harder it is to maneuver around this town," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said at a comprehensive plan workshop Aug. 25.
"I just don't accept that assumption," Toussaint, the commission chair, later said. He argued that concentrating growth downtown will take cars off town streets and improve walkability.
Overall, the Aug. 25 meeting yielded a key takeaway: the new comprehensive plan is likely to include a preferred annual population growth rate around 1.75%. Planners initially proposed not to mark an annual growth rate in the plan, a change from the 2010 version, which stamped the rate at 1%.
Town Planner Lynn Thomas said at the meeting that without a growth rate, the plan would use historic projections to determine if the town should consider adopting policies to remedy growth trends either "significantly lower or significantly higher" than expected.
But Town Council members said a rate should be clearly stated to keep the town honest.
"I do think it would be helpful to have at least something to point toward," Rankin said. The Planning Commission will adjust the drafted plan later this fall, likely reinstating an annual growth rate, before hosting a public hearing.
The town's Affordable Housing Board and Attainable Housing Task Force are other bodies taking cracks at addressing the housing-growth debate. The task force is currently producing a list of recommended housing policies for the Town Council to consider.
Cook acknowledged that while town boards and discussions are great, "actionable items" — such as the comprehensive plan and policies — are on the way and will bring true benefits to residents. But nevertheless, she's happy Easton is addressing its growth problem head-on.
"No one else around here is having these conversations, but the Town of Easton is," Cook said. "They're difficult conversations. They're polarizing conversations, they're very emotional conversations. But we're having them."

title: Maryland needs open primaries now
author: Staff Writer
content:
Maryland needs open primaries now

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 320
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Aug. 23, an opinion piece and a letter in the Star Democrat addressed the question of open primaries in Maryland. They both missed the mark by a mile. David Reel declared the reform to be "an idea whose time may never come." No chance, no hope was his message. He is right in one sense. As long as Maryland voters continue to bend under the yolk of the two-party duopoly, nothing of consequence will change.Open primaries. however, are consequential.
Michael Pullen commented on the same subject as well, saying the "open primary issue is not a crisis." He went on to whine about the myriad sins of current national leadership. If criticism of leadership was an effective tool in bringing about a change in that leadership, he might bring more than just another Democratic talking point.
In states with closed primaries, like Maryland, registered members of each party select candidates to run in the general election. This leaves party loyalists (usually from the extreme wings) to choose who everyone else gets to vote for. Two dire consequences result. Voters are repeatedly faced with "the lesser of two evils" choice. This hurts election participation and voter confidence in the system.
Second, and more importantly, a significant portion of registered voters (in Maryland 22%) are excluded from a choice in the primary. Young voters are increasingly registering independent. Over one million voters are affected in our state. This is not democracy. Maryland is one of only 17 states that still have completely closed primaries. A closed primary, paid for by the government, is a violation of the Maryland state constitution and is the basis of an ongoing lawsuit in Maryland. If we believe in democracy and better leadership in government, we need to support the movement for open primaries in Maryland. (To learn more about the lawsuit and how you can support the fight for open primaries in Maryland, check out maryland.letusvote.org/news.
PETER TAILLIE
Greensboro

title: CWDI gives project updates and addresses concerns
author: Lily Tierney
content:
CWDI gives project updates and addresses concerns

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. gave an update on the Cambridge Harbor project at a July 31 community update meeting, outlining a vision built around four zones: Town Center, Walkable Neighborhoods, Maritime Trade, and Community Recreation.CWDI Board President Angie Hengst also addressed community concerns that have caught traction on social media regarding a potential YMCA, a board position and planning committee meetings.
Hengst said CWDI's operations are all "100% above board."
CWDI's Cambridge Harbor project aims to develop Cambridge's waterfront, similar to the Inner Harbor in Baltimore.
The first major step in the waterfront project will be a boutique hotel, which CWDI hopes will open by early 2029, Hengst said. Plans also call for new commercial and residential spaces, townhomes on Byrn Street, and a 1,000-foot fishing pier to replace the condemned Bill Burton pier.
"The biggest thing is that we showed some of the renderings and really zoomed in on those four zones so people could get a better idea of what our actual concept design is, kind of our vision for the site," Hengst said of the July 31 meeting.
These renderings are a guide to understand CWDI's vision, but they are subject to change depending on the developers{span}, she said{/span}.
At the meeting, {span}CWDI members{/span} also addressed community concerns regarding a potential YMCA on the waterfront. CWDI emphasized that no YMCA is planned, though the organization could submit a proposal in 2026.
Hengst said she believes the YMCA rumor got started because an old concept design that had a space for a potential YMCA was shown by mistake at a recent Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods meeting.
During an interview, Hengst addressed other concerns regarding CWDI Treasurer Frank Narr's appointment to the CWDI board. Hengst said Narr's seat on the board was formerly a CWDI-appointed position.
Last year, the policy was changed to have three positions appointed by the Cambridge City Council and three by the Dorchester County Council. CWDI appointed Narr before the policy change, so some people think he should have to be reappointed by the county council.
"I do want to note that when CWDI as an organization made Frank's appointment, it did have to be approved by both the city and the county, so they did approve of that appointment at the time, as with CWDI," Hengst said. "They didn't directly appoint him, but they did approve of the appointment at the time."
Hengst said CWDI has a signed letter from the county council acknowledging Narr as one of their three appointees.
The final concern Hengst addressed were CWDI's Planning Committee meetings, which she said are not open to the public.
Previously, CWDI was in hot water for not allowing the public meetings where they held discussions with elected officials. But Hengst said these specific meetings are for the Planning Committee to work with city officials to compile information that will then be publicly presented at a community update meeting.
"It's our planning committee working directly with the city as they work through the regulating planning and zoning guidelines," Hengst said.
To see the updated renderings of the Cambridge Harbor Project, visit CWDI's website.

title: Doverbrook Apartments will reopen waitlist Thursday
author: Konner Metz
content:
Doverbrook Apartments will reopen waitlist Thursday

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 304
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After a months-long delay, move-in at the Doverbrook Apartments may finally be imminent, according to the project's leader.Don Bibb, executive director of the Housing Commission of Talbot, told The Star Democrat on Aug. 28 that the 64-unit complex will open its waitlist on Thursday morning.
The units, run by the housing commission, were completed in the spring, but they have been empty all summer due to a snag between the commission and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, or HUD. The holdup centered on whether the commission gave proper public review time for its housing choice voucher plan, which outlines waitlist rules and how the complex will assess voucher and income eligibility, among other things.
Bibb said "it took some deliberation" among HUD's Baltimore field office and its headquarters before they determined the Doverbrook project met the public review requirements.
He expects move-in to begin soon.
"We know September is going to be a fairly busy month for getting folks approved and moved in," he said.
In April, 145 people applied for the complex's waitlist. That list will now be scratched, Bibb said. The housing commission will reach out to those that applied for the first waitlist, he added.
The complex was closed in December 2023 for renovations and expansion. Returning residents, who have been temporarily housed by the commission in St. Michaels, will retain priority, Bibb said.
As part of the housing choice voucher plan mandated by HUD, residents will have to undergo income- and voucher-based verification to be approved.
Waitlist applications will open Thursday, Sept. 4 at 8:30 a.m., Bibb said. Applications will be fielded at the Housing Commission of Talbot's office on the site of the Doverbrook Apartments at 705 Dover Rd.
Bibb said anyone looking to apply for the waitlist should bring with them income verification, birth certificates, social security cards and bank statements.

title: As solar looms on horizon, Betterton residents weigh in ahead of public hearing
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
As solar looms on horizon, Betterton residents weigh in ahead of public hearing

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — For the past two Saturday afternoons, residents living near Betterton held informal meetings discussing Halo Betterton Solar LLC.Halo Betterton LLC had submitted an application in April for a 5-megawatt solar project on a 30-acre site at Howell Point Road and Still Pond-Betterton Road which, if built, will be directly across from some of these neighbors.
As brought up in previous council meetings, the town is opposed to the project because the company's plans do not fit with Betterton's comprehensive plan. It takes away any potential to have commercial development in that area.
The informal meetings were conducted by Paul Falcon and Kathryn Klvana at 13959 Still Pond Road and then at the Betterton Volunteer Firehouse, and drew out other neighbors who would be affected by building the installation.
The second meeting that took place at the firehouse was well-attended and included Mayor Donald Sutton, council member Gerry Werner, longtime residents and people passionate about this cause coming from other Maryland regions affected by these facilities.
Sutton said it is good to see so many people come out and express their concerns.
Residents raised multiple objections to the proposed solar installation during the meetings.
Douglas Cregar said his group has researched the project extensively and opposes the installation.
"We've done our research and are against this solar installation here," Cregar said. "Studies show that everyone within a mile will lose 5% in property value. Also, among 35 active solar proposals in Maryland, there is no location like the Betterton area they plan to build on, that is surrounded by residential housing on three sides."
Art Pleasanton raised concerns about emergency services, noting the proposed site would interfere with helicopter medical evacuations.
"If (solar) is built where they want to build it they'd have to do it over a helicopter landing zone," Pleasanton said. "The next nearest one is at Worton at the school. For anyone who thinks this is not an issue, last year a little girl was saved from drowning because we had a way to get her out fast."
Kathryn Klvana expressed frustration with recent state legislation that could override local zoning decisions.
"I'm shocked that with this new law Governor Wes Moore just signed, the state can override local zoning and put this huge solar farm across from our homes," Klvana said. "We moved to this beautiful place to retire. We're zoned community residential. What about our rights?"
Tracy Cameransi, who lives in a small area just outside of town, said she frequently receives calls from solar companies but will not sell to them. She is opening her home for residents to attend the upcoming virtual hearing together.
"We have a small area just outside of town and we get calls all the time from these solar companies," Cameransi said. "We will never sell to them, but what we are doing is opening up our home on Sept. 9 for the Zoom hearing and everyone is invited to attend at 13499 Still Pond Road."
As the town is preparing for a public hearing for the Halo project, a virtual meeting on Sept. 9 at 7 p.m. online, attendees gave their initial impressions concerning the project.
