 CHESTERTOWN — Some 170 people representing a cross-section of Kent County gathered Monday for The Shelter Alliance's inaugural event, an evening focused on the root causes of homelessness, practical pathways to stability and self-sufficiency, and the organization's new leadership under Executive Director Kimrose Goodall.Chestertown resident and Maryland Planning Secretary Rebecca Flora opened the program by introducing Jake Day, Maryland's secretary of Housing and Community Development, noting their shared commitment to approaches that are data-driven and heart-led.
After touring Kent County earlier in the day, Day said the state is grappling with the compounding effects of not building sufficient affordable housing over the last 16 years. He said the Moore administration believes everyone deserves safe shelter and called for collaboration across all levels of government. Day highlighted the Maryland Shelter and Transitional Facilities Grant Program, which funds improvements to emergency shelters and creation of transitional housing, and said the department will partner with The Shelter Alliance to bring resources to Kent County.
Goodall brought the conversation local, noting Kent County ranks third in Maryland for adolescent homelessness. While single men comprise the largest group experiencing homelessness nationally and locally, she said, many single women, mothers with children and a growing number of older adults are also facing uncertain futures.
Goodall outlined The Shelter Alliance's mission to provide a shelter operating 24 hours a day, year-round, paired with individualized, wraparound support. The organization has an eight-member working board, an executive director and a case manager, and coordinates with partner agencies and community organizations to streamline intake and tailor services to each guest's needs. She said the board plans to expand and invited attendees to apply.
During a Q&A, attendees asked about Goodall's vision for a future facility. She said the ideal site would be an existing structure that can be safely adapted to meet diverse guest needs and is near public services, including substance use and mental health support, partner agencies and everyday amenities. Proximity matters, she said, because transportation challenges in Kent County can hinder access to vital programs and resources.
The evening concluded with a presentation honoring board president Carol Niemand for her role in founding The Shelter Alliance and steering the organization to early milestones.
An annual report summarizing The Shelter Alliance's accomplishments was available at the event and will be posted on Facebook and at shelteralliancemd.org, which is scheduled to launch on World Homeless Awareness Day, Oct. 10.

title: New plaques at Harmony Community Park honor Roger Layton, Sarah Mueller
author: Konner Metz

New plaques at Harmony Community Park honor Roger Layton, Sarah Mueller

 HARMONY — Caroline County honored two respected leaders Saturday by unveiling plaques in their names at the Harmony Community Park.Families and friends of Roger Layton and Sarah Mueller gathered for a joint dedication at the park, which is on Route 16 north of Preston and south of Denton.
A fence for the park's ball field got a new addition: a plaque cementing it as Roger Layton Memorial Field, named after the former Caroline County commissioner and longtime youth softball and baseball coach.
In front of the park's pavilion, a large plaque set on brick dedicated the park to Sarah Mueller, a well-known community volunteer and former Character Counts coach at Preston Elementary School. Character Counts coaches teach trustworthiness, respect and fairness to school-age kids.
Current Caroline County commissioners and other officials attended and spoke to the expansive impacts both Layton and Mueller had on the local community.
Stacy Seward, one many local softball players coached by Layton, recalled fond memories of her former mentor.
"He created lasting memories for so many young athletes," said Seward, the county's grants coordinator. "For example, teaching us how to slide in the playground sand at Denton Elementary School, saying 'If I can get my old body down here, you girls can too.'"
Steward said he was key to creating the county's first ever softball travel team.
"He was the true backbone to girls' softball, not only in Caroline County, but to the entire Eastern Shore," Seward said.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said Layton, a commissioner of eight years and former investigator for the State's Attorney's Office, always put Caroline County first.
Daughter Jaclyn Crawford said her father's "real gift was his deep commitment to young people."
"In each role, he was known for his competitive spirit, but above all, his determination to make life safer and better for the community," Crawford said.
In addition to Crawford, other family members of Roger Layton who attended Saturday's dedication included: wife Faye Layton, sister Rena Callahan, stepfather Ronald Sard, granddaughter Madison Weston, cousin Rick Davis and more.
After Layton's sign was unveiled, the curtain was removed off of a large plaque dedicated to Mueller. Husband John Mueller then reflected on his wife's knack for helping people.
"If she heard that you needed something, she'd be the one to offer," her husband said. " ... She was always there first."
He recalled not just her volunteer efforts as a character coach for elementary school kids, but also her assistance in collecting dog and cat food for the local Humane Society.
In addition to John Mueller, his four kids and six grandchildren attended Saturday's dedication, as well as Sarah's mom, Jessie Browne.
Around four years ago, the Mueller family donated $20,000 to the county for upkeep and improvements at Harmony Community Park, including to the pavilion, walking trails and playground.
County commissioners thanked the Mueller family for their donation to the park and spoke about Sarah Mueller's lasting legacy.
"Sarah was more than a neighbor," Porter said. "She was a friend, volunteer, mother and a mentor who gave so much of herself to this community, from her time as a Character Counts coach to her years with the Girl Scouts, where she poured her love into children and back.
"By placing her name here at Harmony Park, we make sure her kindness, spirit and her legacy will always be a part of this place."

title: Concerns over data centers voiced at public meeting
author: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com
content:
Concerns over data centers voiced at public meeting

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 792
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Shouts against data centers were heard from the back of the room during a meeting earlier this month that addressed noise, water and electricity impacts but also stressed potential economic benefits.There is interest in building data centers in Charles County, Jim Chandler, director of economic development for county government, said during the Sept. 20 meeting at Mary B. Neal Elementary School.
There is a 432-acre proposed data center development located on Billingsley Road near the county landfill and recycling center, according to a presentation from NAI Michael.
Charles County is aware of the commercial development interest in the Piney Reach property for a data center, according to a statement from county government sent to Southern Maryland News.
Prince George's County had a protest against data centers because there are concerns about water, electricity and electronic waste, Carlos Childs, a Waldorf resident, said. The Charles County work group for data centers should also include members of the public and surrounding neighborhoods to provide insight, he said.
"They're saying that the Charles County government is supportive of a data center coming here," Childs said. "Which is weird that it wasn't said … or that they even mentioned the Piney Reach [data center] at all."
Childs was told about the proposed Piney Reach center and found the presentation on Google, he said.
So far, the county has not received any development plan submissions. The economic development department views this property "as an opportunity site for a number of industrial-type uses, one of which could be the future use of data centers."
"Data centers need to be carefully located and need regulation," Chandler said.
Phones, computers and GPS systems use data centers, Mark Thompson, chief of commercial development for Charles County, said. Data centers are large, one- to two-story buildings that have computer servers. They have high security to protect information and back up generators.
"For the longest time, you've heard people talking about the cloud … data centers are effectively the cloud," Thompson said.
Water impacts
Data centers require a lot of energy and get extremely hot, making the water use high to cool the systems, Thompson said. They use a closed-loop system, which keeps water in the system.
"We need to look at those things and think about them relative to other commercial uses," Thompson said.
Treated waste water is already being used for cooling at the CPV St. Charles Energy Station, which can be used for the same purpose as data centers, Jason Groth, director of planning and growth management, said.
"Our reclaimed, effluent water is ever-growing," Groth said. "As we grow, as new connections are made to the system, more water is produced. Therefore more reclaimed water is produced."
Economic benefits
Data centers can generate up to 5,000 construction jobs, and data center employees earn around $100,000 a year and generate billions of dollars in state and local taxes, Chandler said.
Data centers offer jobs for engineers, computer technicians, systems maintenance and security, Thompson said, as well as electricians, carpenters and plumbers while the center is being built.
Data centers also have a higher assessed value than homes and generate significant property taxes, Thompson said. The land sold for a data center in Frederick County generated $50 million in recreation taxes.
"That's a significant, significant revenue," Thompson said. "As we are all faced with revenue challenges throughout the state and the counties, we need to be thinking about that as a very important consideration."
The advocacy group Strong Towns Charles County is concerned about being able to support the infrastructure and impacts to wildlife, Maddie Kaba, co-leader of Strong Towns, said.
"We're talking about an initial construction boom now and all the revenue that it's going to bring in, but how are we being responsible with that money and making sure we save some of it," Kaba said.
Traffic, noise addressedData centers don't generate a lot of traffic because there are not a lot of people coming in and out, Thompson said. Cooling centers and generators generate around the same amount of noise as power plants and recycling centers.
Back up generators have to be run every 10 to 15 minutes and create noise, Groth said. To ease the noise, the generators will be built within the data center campus between two buildings.
"The further the building can be set back away from a property line or adjacent use is really key," Groth said.
While data centers should not be compared to the recycling center because it gets rid of harmful plastics and metals, Shelly Posey, a resident who lives outside La Plata, said she liked the idea of using wastewater.
"I won't say that I'm positive, but I'm in the middle," Posey said.
The county is working on a zoning text amendment that will include constraints on data centers if they were to be built, Groth said. It will move through the public process starting in October.

title: Cambridge ordinance proposes updating code on group housing
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge ordinance proposes updating code on group housing

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge's Unified Development Code is "outdated," according to City Planner Brian Herrmann, who has proposed a new ordinance to align the city's code on group housing with state and federal laws.But rumblings on social media express concern over the proposed ordinance, saying it will lead to a proliferation of these types of residences if passed. Herrmann said that will not be the case.
A group home is a residential facility that provides supervised housing and support services for individuals who require assistance.
In the current code, group homes can have no more than eight clients and are allowed in every district. The new ordinance sets out to clarify where and what type of group homes are allowed.
The code only defines two uses: a group home and a set of institutional residential uses like nursing care, intermediate care and child care institutions.
The proposed ordinance would eliminate these two uses and replace them with four new categories: large group homes/large halfway houses, recovery residences, small group homes/small halfway houses, and commercial properties like assisted living facilities, residential care homes and nursing facilities.
The large group homes/large halfway houses, recovery residences and small group homes/small halfway houses will be regulated on the state and federal level.
"So we don't really have much say in it other than we do give a zoning certificate to say that, yeah, you do meet the zoning requirements and we're going to sign off on that," Herrmann said.
Herrmann clarified that the large group homes/large halfway houses would be primarily allowed in institutional, commercial mixed use and maritime resort zones, meaning few are likely to be in typical residential neighborhoods.
On social media, residents have expressed concerns over the ordinance out of fear the group homes will change the makeup of residential neighborhoods.
"I understand all of the concerns. I think everyone would probably have them with their own property. The issue is that we have to follow the rules and we can't just make them up," Herrmann said on aligning the city's code with state and federal regulations.
According to Herrmann, passing the ordinance will enhance the city's ability to register, track and inspect certain facilities, add enforceable conditions, and require a Board of Appeals review for some uses.
"It's a little stricter," he said.
Herrmann said in the past few years, the city has received far less applications to create these types of homes. He said they used to get 12 to 14 applications, but in his time as city planner, they have only received two.
Because downtown Cambridge has a form-based code, which puts more emphasis on what the homes look like rather than their use, Herrmann said the area is less attractive to applicants.
"I guess we just haven't seen as many applicants in the last couple years as we did in the past, which, to me, tells you that we're moving in the right direction. And then if we can get our code up to what it needs to be, and it's a little stricter, I think we'll be even better off," Herrmann said.

title: MACo leaders meet with Talbot officials to discuss 2026 General Assembly
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo leaders meet with Talbot officials to discuss 2026 General Assembly

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Leaders from the Maryland Association of Counties shared predictions for a calmer legislative session in 2026 during a meeting with the Talbot County Council on Tuesday.Michael Sanderson, MACo's executive director, and Jack Wilson, the association's president and current Queen Anne's County commissioner, met for an annual check-in with Talbot officials.
Sanderson reminded the council members of last year's volatile General Assembly session, during which legislators and Gov. Wes Moore (D) had to reckon with closing a $3 billion gap in the state's fiscal year 2026 budget.
Some savings came through cost shifts placing more burden on county governments, the MACo leaders said. But they added that the upcoming 2026 session, and the fiscal year 2027 budget that goes along with it, likely won't be as dire.
"Relatively calm, probably not a big crisis," Sanderson said of his projection for this year's session, which officially kicks off Jan. 14 in Annapolis.
He said the large budgetary concerns are likely to reappear in 2027 as legislators put together a plan for fiscal year 2028.
"The story from last year is gonna repeat itself, but with a year off," Sanderson predicted.
Specifically, the executive director said Maryland's expansive education funding formula, The Blueprint, will influence the 2027 session. And in the short-term, some counties are already coming to grips with increasing cost shares for education.
"Every county is either in the midst or a year or two away from seeing a year where the increase in school spending required under Blueprint requires all the money or even more money than your county's likely to gain in revenue for that year," Sanderson said. "It's an obvious squeeze at the local level."
Talbot County's fiscal year 2026 budget included $55 million in education funding required by The Blueprint's formulas. On top of that, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding to fill new positions.
That mark had been scaled back twice from the original ask the Talbot Board of Education made of the council — first requesting $5.5 million in supplementary funds, then $1.1 million.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, who supported the district's $1.1 million request earlier this year, said it was "short-sighted" for the county to only fund the district's request partially, given that Blueprint requirements are only set to increase in future years. But other council members opted to hold back on dedicating the full request as the county aimed to even out its spending hikes seen in years prior.
Sanderson said on Tuesday that housing legislation will be at the forefront this winter. Recently, Moore signed an executive order that aims to speed up the permitting and building of affordable housing projects.
"I anticipate that being a big fight," Sanderson said. "Whether it's a big fight in the more rural jurisdictions is yet to be seen."
Council Member Lynn Mielke asked how Easton fits into state plans to tackle the housing issue.
Sanderson said there's an opportunity for MACo to advocate for provisions so a potential housing package doesn't "overwhelm" local jurisdictions. He said the association can help push for certain changes to help counties and towns that lack authority in certain areas, such as the variation of impact fees on developers.
"At the same time, we generally want to keep land use decisions local," he added.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners discuss sea level rise projects
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners discuss sea level rise projects

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday, Roy Meyer of the Climate Change Sea Level Rise Commission and multiple engineers presented key sea-level rise mitigation projects to the St. Michaels commissioners.Meyer said the projects were for the wellbeing of the town of St. Michaels residents and tourists.
"If there's one thing that impacts the town and the Maritime Museum in the same way, it's sea level rise and flooding," Meyer said. "So I mean their campus is going to be flooded, our roads are going to be flooded."
The projects, which will be carried out in two phases, will potentially raise road elevations to five feet. An Advanced Systems grant with FEMA and a state grant will help the town cover the cost of the projects.
Phase one involves raising Mill Street, Burn Street, the Harbor walkway and the end of Cherry Street to an elevation of five feet. It also includes demolishing and rebuilding Honeymoon Bridge at a higher elevation and wider size, rebuilding piers at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, installing a larger culvert system where Mill Street meets the tidal area, and adding a north sidewalk along Mill Street.
The cost of Phase one would be more than $5.3 million.
Phase two will address Mulberry Street, Muskrat Park, and Church and Green streets. Phase two features two options, short-term and a long-term solutions.
The short-term would include modifying the parking lot and existing swale in the park to provide immediate relief from flooding by getting water off the streets faster. This solution is expected to be effective for daily high tides until 2050 and cost $708,366.
The long-term approach raises the roads, similar to phase one. It would also move the roads away from the pipe system and allow for overland flow, separating stormwater and tidewater.
Raising to elevation five feet is the ideal solution, but challenges exist with a wall along Church Street near a cemetery and columbarium, engineers said. The long-term approach would cost $896,724.
The commissioners elected to proceed with prioritizing the already advanced Phase one construction plans and will follow up with the Maritime Museum to discuss options.
The commissioners selected the short-term solution for phase two, saying the town will develop a detailed long-term plan for Muskrat Park. The commissioners also said they would defer action on Mulberry Street until more clarity emerges from private development plans.

title: Easton council members to host ward town halls for residents
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council members to host ward town halls for residents

 September 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 459
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Beginning Monday, Easton council members will host ward-specific town halls in hopes of increasing transparency and engaging with constituents.Maureen Curry (Ward 1), Robert Rankin (Ward 2), David Montgomery (Ward 3) and the Rev. Elmer Davis (Ward 4) will each host town halls open to their constituents at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department in the coming weeks.
The town halls were mentioned during Easton's recent election, including by Don Abbatiello, now council president and then Ward 2 representative.
Abbatiello said he aims to attend all four town halls.
"We wanted to make sure that we left no stone unturned when it came to sharing information," Abbatiello said.
Rankin will kick off the meetings with Ward 2 residents on Monday. Montgomery will host Ward 3's discussion on Oct. 9. Davis will lead Ward 4's on Oct. 23, and Curry will wrap it up with Ward 1's meeting on Oct. 27. All four meetings will be held at the Easton fire hall from 7 to 8 p.m.
Abbatiello said the idea to host semi-regular ward town halls birthed from discussions on the campaign trail, with some residents feeling like they didn't have enough access to town information or couldn't attend town meetings, which are typically twice a month at 5:30 p.m.
The council president said the town's done a good job in improving its communication to residents since he joined the council in 2019, especially on its website and social media platforms. The new town halls are a continuation of that effort, he said.
Council members will provide brief presentations to residents at the meetings, updating them on recent projects in town and their respective wards. Then, the sessions will open up for feedback and questions from the public.
"We want residents to be informed and know what's going on," Rankin said. " ... The more we can hear from folks … that really helps us a lot."
Housing, growth and traffic are expected to be major points of discussion, council leaders said.
"The central topic, for me at least, will be growth," Montgomery said. "And I think that's a topic that concerns everybody of Ward 3 because of how residents have to tend to traffic."
Rankin said he expects his discussion to touch on recent development projects and the town's comprehensive plan, which is in the process of being updated for the first time since 2010 and will lay out a vision for the town's growth over the next decade.
Davis said that in addition to growth and development, he expects to field questions on the Easton Police Department and resident concerns about safety.
The Ward 4 representative highlighted the town halls as another avenue to be open with the public.
"Everybody can be included and get some questions answered," Davis said. "Our main goal is to show transparency to the community."

title: Eye of the storm: Communities still rebuilding and recovering after Hurricane Helene
author: Mike Sunnucks Adams MultiMedia
content:
Eye of the storm: Communities still rebuilding and recovering after Hurricane Helene

 September 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks Adams MultiMedia | Section: News 
 
 1182
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A year ago, Hurricane Helene rampaged through Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas and Tennessee with high winds, biblical rains and destructive storm surges and floods that left 252 people dead and caused an estimated $79 billion in damage.A few weeks later, Hurricane Milton slammed Florida and Georgia, killing 46 people and causing another $34 billion in damage.
Helene brought torrential rains and deadly floods to areas of the Carolinas and Appalachia, with warmer ocean water fueling larger and more destructive hurricanes.
Some areas saw historic amounts of rain and major power outages from Helene's monstrous storm clouds.
Parts of Transylvania and Yancey counties in North Carolina were hit with 30 inches of rain. Greenville, South Carolina, saw 21.66 inches.
Heavy rains stretched from Florida to Ohio and Indiana, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
From Western Carolina and Appalachia to Florida's Gulf coast and southern Georgia, communities are still healing and rebuilding from last year's devastating hurricane season.
Those on the frontlines of the recovery efforts say progress has been made, but more work and challenges remain.
'NEARLY EVERY STRUCTURE'On Florida's Gulf coast, Hurricane Helene brought historic storm surges and flooding to the southwestern parts of the state as well as the Big Bend and Tampa Bay areas.
Some of those same areas were hit in October by Hurricane Milton.
"We had widespread flooding during Helene, with nearly every structure in the city taking water, some as much as 5 feet. Milton tore off roofs from condos and knocked down trees and power poles, many residents were without power and water for 7 to 10 days," said Trip Barrs, fire chief in the beach town of Treasure Island in the Tampa-St. Petersburg area.
Other parts of Florida also got hit by both hurricanes.
"Helene impacted some of our coastal areas on Sept. 26 last year, and then Hurricane Milton impacted a much broader area of Lee County mere days later on Oct. 9," said Betsy Clayton, communications director for Lee County, which includes Fort Myers.
That area of southwest Florida experienced a storm surge of more than 5 feet and 6 inches of rain in a short period from Hurricane Helene.
A few weeks later, Milton brought winds of 120 miles per hour, a 6.8-inch storm surge in Lee County and heavy rains. Parts of Florida saw numerous tornadoes.
Lee County collected more than 627,000 cubic yards of debris from the two storms, according to a post-storm analysis.
In Treasure Island, Barrs said roughly a year later that there are "many vacant residential and commercial lots" from the storms.
"We are starting to see some rebuilding and some homes being elevated. Many businesses were not able to reopen, and others are still in temporary facilities," he said.
Other challenges persist.
"Many residents are still not able to rebuild or repair their homes. This is due to a variety of issues: insurance, permitting, old/non-flood compliant structures. Many of our smaller, 1-story hotels will not be able to reopen," Barrs said.
High insurance costs and sometimes delayed, disputed or denied storm claims have been causes for frustrations in Florida, in particular, as well as other states.
Barrs said some hotel rooms have started to come back online, and a beach renourishment project replacing sand lost to the storm surges is slated to start "in the coming months."
Other communities and tourist attractions in Helene's path have also reopened and have been marketing and advertising that to targeted audiences.
That includes Asheville, the popular arts and tourism hub in western North Carolina.
"We're shouting it from our beautiful Blue Ridge mountaintops—the Asheville area is open for business and eagerly welcoming visitors after Hurricane Helene impacted our region in fall of 2024," said Dodie Stephens, vice president of marketing for the Explore Asheville tourism group, earlier this summer.
The group has been advertising in regional drive markets as well as cities with flight connections to Asheville.
"Downtown Asheville was largely unimpacted by the storm last fall and many of the most iconic hikes, overlooks and attractions along the Blue Ridge Parkway are open," she said.
The Biltmore gardens reopened in November 2024 and is hosting an exhibition featuring Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamum through Jan. 4, 2026.
Some areas of the Appalachian Trail damaged by Hurricane Helene have been repaired or reopened. But there continues to be repair work and debris collections in other trail areas in North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia, according to the National Park Service.
There are detour areas along the 2,200-mile trail because of storm damage and remediation.
Some Florida communities saw backlogs and delays with permitting approval after the storms.
That prompted Treasure Island and other localities to take fresh looks at its emergency planning and response, Barrs said.
In Lee County, local officials have been reexamining their communications and social media policies on how to keep the public best informed during major storms and other emergencies.
'HISTORIC DAMAGE'Beyond its coastal impacts, Helene brought major flooding, downed trees and damaged homes, buildings and roadways in Georgia, the Carolinas and Tennessee.
"At one point during the storm, over 1.2 million gallons of water per second flowed over the Nolichucky Dam. In comparison, Niagara Falls' peak daily flow is 700,000 gallons of water per second," said Mark Nagi, regional communications officer for the Tennessee Department of Transportation.
The state also removed more than 720,000 cubic yards of debris from Helene.
"This storm has caused historic damage to bridges and roadways, especially in Upper East Tennessee. TDOT anticipates hundreds of millions of dollars in damage," Nagi said.
Helene's biblical rains and floods damaged and shut down parts of Interstate 40 near the Tennessee, North Carolina border and 49 sections of state and local roadways in the eastern part of Tennessee last year, according to
"Work on full restoration of I-40 in Cocke County continues," Nagi said. "We anticipate the roadway being fully back open in Summer 2026. We have had one lane open in each direction since late October 2024."
Forty-seven of the 49 impacted state and local roadway areas have reopened, with the two remaining areas under contract to be repaired this fall and next spring.
Tennessee surveyors inspected all 490 state-owned bridges that the storm could have damaged.
Nagi said two bridges in Greene and Washington counties were built in a faster "Progressive Design-Build" mode that allowed design and construction phases to overlap.
"Those bridges were each opened in less than 8 months. Without PDB being utilized, it would have probably taken approximately 2 to 3 years to reconnect those communities," he said.
On Sept. 15, North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein called for an additional $13.5 billion in federal funding to help with Hurricane Helene reconstruction.
That includes $8 billion to help rebuild homes and small businesses, $2 billion for local governments financially strained by the storm and its cleanup, and $2 billion to help with reconstruction and full reopening of sections of I-40 hit by the storm.
Stein, a Democrat, also wants Congress to release another $10 billion in previously allocated funds related to hurricane recovery.
"Western North Carolinians are counting on the federal government for help to rebuild homes, support small businesses, and repair roads. I call on Congress to deliver for western North Carolina its fair share and appropriate an additional $13.5 billion in funding for Helene recovery," Stein said in a statement.

title: County weighs ICE Program: Officials seek details on 287(g) jail enforcement model before considering public comment and vote
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
County weighs ICE Program: Officials seek details on 287(g) jail enforcement model before considering public comment and vote

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 654
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County officials say they are seeking more information from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement about the county's eligibility for a 287(g) Jail Enforcement Model program.At an informal community forum Sept. 29 hosted by Eastern Shore Indivisible at the Kent Island branch of the Queen Anne's County Public Library, County Commissioner President Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann updated residents on the status of discussions with ICE.
Corchiarino said the county has not yet been told whether it qualifies for the Jail Enforcement Model, one of three agreements available under ICE's 287(g) program. He emphasized that no plans are in place.
"We're waiting to hear from federal officials," Corchiarino said. "We don't have clear details or expectations yet of what a memorandum of understanding would look like."
Program background
Under the Jail Enforcement Model, correctional officers can be deputized with limited federal authority to serve civil detainers within a county detention facility. Other models under 287(g) include the Warrant Service Officer and Task Force programs, though Corchiarino said Queen Anne's is not pursuing those.
On July 30, the county's Republican Central Committee hosted an informational meeting in Stevensville with James Brooks, community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices. Following that session, Corchiarino said, residents asked county leaders to seek more information about the county's eligibility.
He noted that requirements for correctional facilities vary by jurisdiction in Maryland. In Queen Anne's County, the detention center falls under the authority of the county commissioners rather than law enforcement.
"If we find out we're not eligible, then it's a moot point," Corchiarino said. "If we are eligible, then we'll need to look at requirements and a cost analysis. Any decision would go through public comment and ultimately a commission vote."
There is no set timeline, he said, adding that even if ICE responds soon, the matter would take time before reaching an agenda.
Community questions and concerns
During the forum, some residents voiced concerns about immigration enforcement and civil rights. One man who identified himself as part of the Hispanic community said he had been detained twice "on the west side of the bridge" and carried laminated copies of his birth certificate out of fear.
"What's going to be done to ensure I keep my American rights … without being afraid of the lights in the rearview mirror?" he asked, drawing applause.
Hofmann said the sheriff's office does not have authority to serve civil detainers and in his 30 years could recall only one case involving an ICE civil detainer in the county. He stressed that the role of ICE is separate from the role of county commissioners or the sheriff's office.
"Regardless of origin, whether American or immigrant, there are bad people with warrants for crimes, and we are obligated to enforce the criminal law," Hofmann said.
He added that ICE falls under the umbrella of Homeland Security Investigations and that since 2010 the county sheriff's office has had a designated desk for Homeland Security agents, used in rare but valuable partnerships on cases involving fraud, child pornography and human trafficking.
"What I don't want to do is create fear amongst our community," Hofmann said. "We want people to get the services they need here in Queen Anne's County. We are genuinely here to take care of everyone fairly and equally."
Calls for transparency
Some residents said they want more public collaboration when federal topics arise.
"This affects everyone. It's not just Republicans or Democrats. We should be working together to protect our community," one Grasonville woman said.
A Centreville woman added that she wanted reassurance county law enforcement would remain lawful and not adopt questionable tactics she had heard about elsewhere.
Corchiarino said he considers public input an important factor in any decision.
"A room full of people, that's persuasive for me," he said.
Silvia Gonzalez Roman, co-founder of Eastern Shore Indivisible, said the group invited an ICE representative to the forum but did not receive a response.
"Building community with open dialogue is what it is all about," she said.

title: Workshops held during Oxford Commission Meeting
author: LILY TIERNEY ltierney@chespub.com
content:
Workshops held during Oxford Commission Meeting

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LILY TIERNEY ltierney@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Commissioners of Oxford held several work sessions during the town's Sept. 29 meeting. These included:Town electionsCommissioners discussed the possibility of creating a supplemental municipal voter list in addition to the county's list.
They plan to discuss the matter further at a workshop on Oct. 8 and are actively seeking the public's feedback.
Ethics ordinance recommendations from the Ethics CommissionCommissioners considered revising the ethics ordinance after the Ethics Commission said the current version is confusing from years of edits.
Additional proposals included adding an alternate member, staggering terms for continuity, and clarifying the distinction between the Ethics and Town commissions.
Members of the Ethics Commission suggested narrowing financial disclosure rules, which currently require candidates to report all global property and business interests, to instead focus on conflicts of interest within Maryland.
The Ethics Commission also discussed separate disclosure standards for elected officials, appointed members and staff, and agreed to add a campaign finance section requiring filings at candidacy, election and post-election.
The updates are slated for completion by February ahead of the next election cycle.
Economic development prioritiesThe Oxford Business Association pressed town leaders for clear economic development priorities to guide its work, particularly on tourism and use of accommodation tax revenues, now at historic lows.
Commissioners asked for detailed budgets and proof of return on investment before committing tax dollars, moving away from funding with "no strings attached."
The association's representative said they must consult members before releasing past financials. They agreed performance metrics, like website analytics, which are currently hindered by technical issues, will be needed once town priorities are defined.
Short-term rental permitting processCommissioners considered adopting a software called Granicus to crack down on unlicensed short-term rentals, estimating 35 to 44 units operate in town but only five hold permits.
The program, already in use by Talbot County, would cost Oxford $2,000 a year.
The software would also help enforce a proposed rule requiring license numbers in rental ads, which officials say are easier to track than actual bookings.
Breezeline franchise agreementCommissioners are reviewing their franchise agreement with Breezeline, weighing whether to stay with the old terms or adopt a new template that covers only cable.
The draft also drops the 2% public, educational and government funding, meaning the town would need to add a franchise fee of up to 5% to recoup costs.
Commissioners said they'll hold a public hearing, likely after the holidays, to gather resident feedback on service quality before entering negotiations.
Utility payment processingCommissioners are exploring new approaches to utilities and services, including an online portal for utility bill payments that would allow credit card use but carry a 1.5% to 3.5% transaction fee which will likely be passed on to residents rather than absorbed by the town.
An Automated Clearing House payment option through Shore United Bank is also being considered, with specific cost proposals to be discussed at a future meeting.
Electric fees paid by the townThe Electric Vehicle Institute has offered to replace the current chargers with faster, pay-as-you-go chargers that would eliminate the current expense of $600.
Commissioners will also separately review electricity costs tied to the watermen's boat slips, citing the town's commitment to its working waterfront.

title: Data center pause underscores local concerns about widespread impacts
author: Peter Riccio and Holliday Woodard Capital News Service
content:
Data center pause underscores local concerns about widespread impacts

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Peter Riccio and Holliday Woodard Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 958
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — A proposed data center project in Prince George's County, Maryland, was paused on Sept. 16 to give a task force time to evaluate potential impacts on public health, the environment and energy demand.The Prince George's project is controversial, underscoring growing public concerns over the proliferation of data centers nationwide.
Data centers can range from massive warehouse-sized facilities to office buildings and are the physical backbone of everything digital.
The growth of these centers has surged, with 44 operational or planned data centers in Maryland, according to Data Center Map. Prince George's County is one of the latest battlegrounds where local opposition has slowed what data center supporters insist would be a major boom to the economy.
"The only reason the county is considering data centers is for money," Prince George's County Council Member Wala Blegay said in an interview with Capital News Service. "The reality is that our commercial tax base is very low. We're mostly relying on residential (taxes) because our residents are not able to get relief on the high property taxes that we have here. That is why we are looking at data centers."
Blegay's District 6 borders the District of Columbia and is mostly inside the Capital Beltway, encompassing communities including Suitland, District Heights, Marlow Heights, Camp Springs and Forestville.
The county council created the Qualified Data Center Task Force in April 2025. The council faced local protests at their three meetings in July from residents concerned about energy consumption, electric bills and environmental factors.
On Sept. 16, the council approved a resolution pausing the development of current and future data center projects until the task force has completed its work. The task force is expected to release its findings in November.
"There is no point in having a task force if all of these projects can move forward," Blegay said. "We're studying all of these infrastructure issues. So we're talking about the next three months, we're going to be passing legislation to address that… and we don't want people to rush out and expedite their process, so they'll get ahead of us."
Prince George's County Executive Aisha Braveboy told Washington's WTOP radio that the county council's 2021 decision to speed up the data center approval process "was a huge mistake because the residents have a stake in where these data centers are located."
"I'm in support generally of data centers," Braveboy said. "I do believe it's a really good economic tool in the right locations."
"I think we gotta look at what the land use implications are and be really thorough in these decisions," Del. Ashanti F. Martinez, D-Prince George's, said in a Sept. 18 Instagram post. "You know, at the state level we try to provide as much oversight as possible, and I'm really concerned that we are moving a little fast on the data center conversation."
Access to electricity and the price residents pay are critics' primary concerns, as the average monthly electric bill for Maryland, according to poweroutage.us, stands at $167.55. Electric bills are expected to slightly rise with the anticipated new data centers, according to a letter from the Office of People's Council for the State of Maryland.
"What we know is that no data center is going to be turned on, especially with high gigawatts, not within the next four to five years, because of all the issues with electricity and energy sourcing," Blegay said.
Maryland currently does not produce enough electricity on its own, so it relies on importing the shortfall from outside the state.
"Historically, Maryland has imported about 40% of its annual electric needs from other states," according to a 2024 fact sheet from PJM, a transmission organization that coordinates the use of wholesale electricity among 13 states and the District of Columbia.
As of last year, data centers accounted for about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption, according to a report from the Department of Energy (DOE).
"(AI is) a much more significant data hog than any type of search you have today, and it's something that is exponentially growing with the types of searches Americans are doing," Michael Kratsios, director of the White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy, told a Sept. 10 hearing of the Senate Commerce, Science & Transportation Committee's science, manufacturing, and competitiveness.
The increased use of AI has provided an opening for Republicans who advocate a renewed reliance on traditional fuels to meet the energy demand. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, for example, wants "good, old-fashioned" coal and gas to provide U.S. power needs.
"When you had 94% of new power generation in America over the last four years, be it wind and solar, that probably isn't nearly enough to produce the kind of energy that we need to power the AI revolution," Moreno said at the subcommittee hearing.
But Sen. Edward Markey, D-Massachusetts, warned that "Americans' electricity bills are going to rise by as much as 25% over the next four years — 25% because of data center demand. It's not just a future fear, it's a present problem."
"So, Mr. Kratsios, do you think it's appropriate that the administration is forcing Americans to pay more on their electricity bills while using their taxpayer dollars to make the problem even worse by funding the unfettered growth of the AI industry?" Markey asked.
"I do not believe there's been an administration in American history more committed to growing power generation for the American people and lowering energy costs for everyday Americans," Kratsios responded. "And I'm proud to work for a president and administration that has that level of commitment."
In October, PG County will host another public council meeting to continue discussions about the data center. By the end of November, the Prince George's County Qualified Data Center Task Force will report its findings, giving the council six months to decide on next steps, according to the resolution.

Christina Robinson not seeking reelection in Greensboro

 GREENSBORO — At the last Greensboro Town Council meeting, Mayor David Spencer took time to highlight a council member who is not running for reelection, Christina Robinson."I just want to say that I really didn't know you prior to sitting on the board with you, and it has been an absolute pleasure," Spencer said. "You are very thoughtful, thought provoking, and you're always looking out for others that sometimes the things that I know I don't think of, and it's sometimes the things that us men don't think of, and you look at a different viewpoint, and that's always good. It's beneficial to the community and everybody here, and it's been a pleasure."
Robinson said she was not seeking reelection because she does not see herself in government long-term.
"I never really wanted to be a politician," Robinson said. "I just have never had an interest in it. I've always been involved in the community, I enjoy just getting in and getting to work, so that's what I've always done."
While Robinson said she never wanted to run in 2023, a seat opened up on the council and some community members encouraged Robinson to run. Robinson won the special election with 47 votes, more than twice the votes of her two oponents.
"I got involved because I didn't necessarily agree with or like the way the town was heading," Robinson said. "So a couple of community members asked me if I would run. I never thought that I would get elected because I was never one of the most liked citizens because I was very outspoken in the past with prior council administrations that we've had."
Robinson's seat is one of two that will be up for election in November. The other seat is occupied by Councilmember Pete Brelia, who is seeking reelection.
Candidates for the Town Council seats must file a certificate of nomination in the Town Office by Oct. 7. Candidates must be a qualified voter of the town, be at least 18 years old and have lived in Greensboro for at least a year prior to the election.
The two winners selected by voters on Nov. 4 will serve four-year terms.

title: Oxford tackles short-term rental compliance issues
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford tackles short-term rental compliance issues

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Oxford currently has somewhere between 35 and 44 short-term rentals, but according to Town Commissioner Dave Donovan, only five are licensed.Donovan proposed an ordinance at Monday's Town Commission meeting amending town code to hold operators liable for non-compliance and gather accurate data on the number, location and rental frequency of short-term rentals in town.
The information will help commissioner make better-informed policy decisions, Donovan said.
He believes the primary issue with short-term rental compliance is operators forgetting or neglecting to register.
"I suspect that the real problem with compliance, at least in the last couple years, is that people in town just forgot," Donovan said. "And, obviously that's not okay, but also, you got to do something to make sure they remember."
The town's current short-term rental rules fine operators that are not licensed $100 to $200 every day they remain unlicensed. Donovan said this is difficult to enforce, especially considering unlicensed rentals are hard to track because they advertise online without physical signs.
The proposed ordinance would fine short-term rental operators who do not comply a flat fine of $1,000 a month, which Donovan said will likely be more effective. It would also make the act of advertising a short-term rental property without a license a violation, requiring owners to remove listings if not properly registered.
"The agents are the ones that really should, and most likely do, understand the requirements of the local ordinances, whether it's here, or Easton, or Trappe, or St. Michaels or the county. And so, there's really no excuse," Donovan said.
The current ordinance restricts licenses to "natural persons," which prevents corporations and investment groups from buying multiple properties for short-term rentals.
"I think it's very clever. It really provides a tremendous disincentive to the true out-of-towners, the true real estate investment companies that just want to come into a town like ours and buy up chunks of it and run a short-term rental business, because they can't," Donovan said.
There will be a public hearing on this proposed ordinance at the Oxford Town Commissioners meeting on Oct. 28.

title: Greensboro discusses a change from quarterly to monthly water bills
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chesub.com
content:
Greensboro discusses a change from quarterly to monthly water bills

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chesub.com | Section: News 
 
 236
 Words

 GREENSBORO — During the monthly Greensboro Town Council meeting, the council discussed potentially changing water bills from quarterly to monthly.Town Manager Cindy Yost met with the town's billing company Edmunds Gov Tech. Yost said during the meeting, the billing company stated that a lot of towns are returning to monthly billing for the benefits to their residents.
"The benefit for residents, of course, is better budgeting, improved usage awareness, too, and fewer surprises," Yost said. "So, if they fill a pool up or if they have a leak on their commode or something like that, this is going to pick it up a lot faster."
Yost said multiple residents have come into the town struggling to pay their quarterly water bills.
Yost also mentioned the benefits changing the water bills would have for the town.
"Enhanced cash flow, I mean, that's a given." Yost said. "You're going to get paid on a monthly basis. Faster leak detection, which is going to be huge for us, and a stronger customer engagement because we're going to be out there on a monthly basis interacting instead of the quarterly."
Greensboro is not the only town thinking of making a change to its fee schedule. Federalsburg is in discussions to change water and sewer billing from monthly to quarterly.
The Greensboro Town Council made a motion to move the discussion to an ordinance introduction with a public hearing at their Oct. 16 town hall meeting.

title: Gov. Moore fights for the Shore
author: Staff Writer
content:
Gov. Moore fights for the Shore

 October 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 336
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I've been a Republican all my life — as the mayor of my town, as a delegate who defeated a Democratic incumbent to serve in Annapolis, and when I voted for Donald Trump in the last presidential election.There's no doubt I'm a Republican, but I'll proudly cross that party line to back Gov. Wes Moore and his mission to build a Maryland that leaves no one behind.
I was born in Salisbury, raised near Crisfield and served the people of Delmar for two decades — I know what it's like to live in a community that feels forgotten by Annapolis. I've worked with a lot of local leaders and several governors, trust me when I tell you, Wes Moore is different.
In two and half years, he's made 51 visits to the Eastern Shore and just last week was the first governor to visit Smith Island since 1999. But he doesn't just come to the Shore; he brings investment with him.
Since taking office he's put $1.9 billion in education funding here; he's made historic investments in rural health care and hospitals opening TidalHealth in Salisbury and breaking ground on the University of Maryland Shore Regional Medical Center; he's put a $10 million investment to improve our waterways up and down the Shore; and he's cut through the red tape to open and expand businesses in places like Caroline County and Dorchester County.
But perhaps most importantly, he's focused two of the state's strongest poverty fighting initiatives in our rural communities. His ENOUGH Act includes funding to Dorchester and Caroline counties to end generational childhood poverty, and Cambridge was named as one of the first Just Communities giving them priority access to funding that will help increase assets, home ownership and home values.
We are seeing momentum across the state and in our own communities that we just can't afford to lose. I've endorsed him, I believe in him, and I'm proud to work alongside him, because I know Gov. Moore fights for the Shore.
CARL L. ANDERTON JR.

title: Federalsburg council member confronts colleagues over emails calling her 'rogue'
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Federalsburg council member confronts colleagues over emails calling her 'rogue'

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 816
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — A Federalsburg council member expressed frustration with her colleagues Monday night, claiming they failed to defend her when she was accused of taking action without council approval.Council member Brandy James alleged former contractual town manager Ken Decker called James a "rogue council member" in emails exchanged with town council members.
James said that in the emails, Decker accused her of taking actions without the full council's approval.
"I've never been a rogue, as I was termed in the emails, council member," James said during Monday's Town Council meeting.
"Anything that I have done I have done with everyone's up here OK. I have a whole stack of emails where I was called these names, and you all just stood by and not said a thing, but I'm a big girl, but I have all of this that shows anything that I have ever done, it has shown that you all have said, 'OK,'" James said.
According to James, the email exchange claims James acted alone in hiring a cleaning crew to clean town hall after the building was closed for mold remediation. James said the decision to bring in a cleaning crew was approved by the Town Council.
"You all OK'd all this," she said. "Now all of this that's being alleged in here is making me a rogue council member, but none of you spoke up. So, to me it sounds like you're going along with it."
While Decker said he could not remember the emails James referenced, he said any issues he had with the town were normal professional issues, not personal ones.
Decker elected not to renew his contract with the town after he served 30 days in the contractual town manager role in September.
"I don't think there's a lot to be accomplished by trying to go in and get into the details about interactions I had with individual members of the council," Decker told the Star Democrat on Tuesday morning.
Decker said he thought he worked well with the town but didn't think he could help the town do what needed to be done.
"If councilwoman James is unhappy about something I wrote, I'm not hard to find," Decker said.
Council member Ian Ferguson told the Star Democrat on Tuesday morning that Decker sent the emails James referenced. Ferguson said he did not say anything in James' defense because Decker is allowed his opinion.
"Now, I can see the point that she's making of 'Hey, you know, you don't got my back, and I feel this is wrong,' and that's fair. She has a valid point to that," he said. "But at the end of the day, I looked at it more like we have larger things to worry about than somebody throwing names and shade or whatever you want to call it at people. … My focus was getting the MOU passed, and the wastewater treatment plant up to snuff and getting rates set for that."
James' comments were raised after a discussion about the town's water billing schedule. The town discussed raising water and sewer rates in meetings throughout September, a recommendation made by Decker to increase revenues and tackle the town's $5 million debt.
During public comment at the meeting Monday, a resident raised a question about whether the town was considering switching from quarterly to monthly billing for water and sewer. Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said there was discussion by the town but there was not a motion made to change its billing schedule.
James said that she had made this motion at a prior meeting and that it was passed by the council. According to the town minutes for the council's July meeting, a motion was made by James to change water bills from quarterly to monthly and was seconded by Mayor Kimberly Abner and passed 5-0.
Ryan clarified to the Star Democrat that the motion could have been to further a conversation, but the motion to switch to monthly could not be passed without an ordnance with approved legislation.
James said that in previous meetings and closed sessions, there were conversations about potentially moving the town water billing to a monthly schedule to ensure more consistent revenue to the town.
James said when a county official visited the town of Federalsburg, the official said, "Town of Federalsburg, you have three to four months out of the year where you had zero income coming in, and that's where one of your shortfalls are."
"Three to four months, and that's one of the reasons why we couldn't make payroll," James said.
"...Y'all forgot that, and that was where the discussion with staff came in of how can we make sure income is still coming in during those three or four months that we have no income. That was where the inception of monthly billing payment, but how conveniently everybody forgot."
The council introduced an ordinance Monday to raise water and sewer bills by 20% and will hold a public hearing at its Nov. 3 meeting.

title: Tensions flare over rezoning, shoreline project at Cambridge council meeting
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Tensions flare over rezoning, shoreline project at Cambridge council meeting

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — There were a few tense moments at the Oct. Cambridge City Council meeting.During the open comment period, a resident called commissioners' discussions "spirited." At points during the meeting, commissioners spoke over each other and exchanged sharp words.
Tensions arose after Commission President Sputty Cephas made a motion to hear two rezoning ordinances together, meaning the vote for one ordinance would be postponed to another meeting. The applicant behind the delayed ordinance walked out of the meeting as a result, threatening to withdraw their application.
Jim Cheney with Quality Housing of Cambridge received approval from the Planning Commission to rezone three parcels into mixed-use Downtown Waterfront Development District zoning, opening those parcels up for potential commercial development.
Currently, two of the parcels are zoned as general commercial while the third is residential.
Cheney was represented by his attorney, Jesse Hammock, who came to speak during Ordinance 1255's public hearing Oct. 6 and did not seem pleased when the vote was taken off the agenda.
Cheney's neighbor, Benito Lake, is the applicant behind the other rezoning ordinance. Lake put in an application to rezone two of his parcels for the same use as Cheney.
Lake is a month behind Cheney in the rezoning process.
When the council decided to defer the second reading of Ordinance No. 1255 to be heard alongside Ordinance No. 1258, Cheney's attorney withdrew his client's application and walked out of the meeting.
City Attorney Patrick Thomas said with the applicant withdrawing, there may be no party to present the case, raising legal issues with approving the rezoning.
City staff and commissioners discussed whether they or the Planning Commission could initiate rezoning, and Thomas said they would need to research it but cautioned against rezoning a property without the owner's consent.
Commissioners and staff expressed intent to make contact with parties soon to align and potentially proceed collectively, acknowledging that delays could further complicate the multi-parcel rezoning.
Commissioners still held a public hearing on Ordinance No. 1255, though they did not hold a vote. Resident Sharon Smith expressed concerns over access to one of the parcels. City Planner Brian Herrmann responded, saying there is a paper street, a roadway that exists on city maps but has not been constructed.
Shoreline project debate
Tensions flared again when discussing renewing the consulting contract for Cambridge's shoreline project, which aims to thoroughly assess the factors and conditions that contribute to current and potential future flooding issues.
When speaking about the current consultant's contract, which has expired, some commissioners said they lacked a clear understanding of the project's deliverables and progress, hindering their ability to support the contract renewal.
But City Manager Glenn Steckman said delaying the shoreline project exposes the city to ongoing flood damage and potential catastrophe if there is a major storm.
Mayor Lajan Cephas, who is not able to vote on the matter, expressed agitation at the ongoing discussion and suggested Larry White, the current consultant for the project, come speak to the commissioners directly.
Sputty Cephas made a motion to defer the item so commissioners can have further conversations. He began speaking about why he made the motion, and Lajan Cephas cut him off, saying, "Well, I've attended the meetings."
Sputty Cephas asked, "May I finish?" Lajan Cephas responded, "No, I'm going to finish."
A few commissioners chuckled.
"I'm just to the point where I'm over talking about this, and Mr. White needs to come here and get the full opportunity to give a presentation, not shortened, not edited, so every single question can be asked, and then you can make that determination as commissioners whether you are going to save our shoreline or not, and let that be on the record," Lajan Cephas said, closing the discussion.
The specific terms of the flood mitigation consultants contract remain unresolved and will be the subject of a future meeting.

author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com

Denton approves Sharp Road Park playground's first phase

 DENTON — The Town of Denton approved the first phase of Sharp Road Park's playground construction at the Denton Town Council meeting on Monday.Phase one of the playground features equipment that's designed to look like first responder vehicles. The hope for the park as a whole is to honor first responders and veterans of Caroline County.
"We've got a lot of first responders that live in our community, and we want to make sure that we've got a place to acknowledge them. So that's something we're really excited about," Mayor Abby McNinch said.
The council approved a proposal in the amount of $294,699 from Kompan Inc. to furnish and install playground equipment at Sharp Road Park.
The town received $300,000 in grant funding from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources Community Parks and Playgrounds program for phase one of the project.
The DNR grant funding will be used to fund $274,426.86 of the playground costs, and the remaining grant funding will be used to fund engineering costs related to the project. The Town will fund the remaining $20,272 for playground surfacing.
Denton has additional play equipment planned for a second phase of construction, but the town will need to secure additional funding from the state to complete phase two.
The park is expected to receive multiple upgrades in the near future, which started with a mural honoring first responders on the basketball court created by Terae Warner, a local business owner and basketball coach, and artist Shelton Hawkins.
More additions expected at Sharp Road Park include an outdoor exercise circuit, flag court and highly anticipated dog park.
"It seems like everybody's most excited about the dog park," McNinch said. "We've heard the community about that, and that's something we're looking forward to putting in as well."
The flag court will include flags representing different branches of the military.
Caroline County has started construction on the baseball field, softball field and multipurpose field at the park with hopes of the fields being finished by December.
McNinch said that the upgrade of Sharp Road Park has been a goal of hers since she entered office.
"You'll have the dog walkers, the people that are walking the trail, then the little kids that are playing, the kids that are playing soccer, basketball, all of it. It really becomes a community asset and kind of what we've envisioned for a long time, so we're excited," McNinch said.

title: Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Candidates in future campaigns will face new fundraising restrictions and reporting requirements thanks to a new law passed by the Easton Town Council.After nearly six months of fine-tuning, Easton passed its first campaign finance ordinance on Monday.
It will limit campaign contributions to $1,000, ban contributions from political committees and organizations, and require campaign treasurers to submit detailed financial reports before and after the election.
Council members said the ordinance is a win for transparency in Easton's elections. All five voted in favor of the new regulations.
"I think that (we) have done an excellent job of putting together an ordinance which achieves our goals of providing transparency in elections," said Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook.
The ordinance was introduced in April, amid a heated and politically charged race between current Town Council President Don Abbatiello and former President Frank Gunsallus.
There were largely no requirements for candidates to report specific contributions made to their campaigns during this year's election. Financial disclosures submitted by candidates when they filed for candidacy didn't include campaign donations. Montgomery, Cook and others argued that there should be more transparency on which organizations and people make donations to candidates.
Now, future candidates must name a campaign treasurer, who is responsible for sending the town office documentation of each donation, whether from an individual, business or organization.
The council has made several edits to the campaign ordinance ordinance since April, including raising the maximum donation mark from $250 to $1,000 and exempting spouses or domestic partners of candidates from the $1,000 limit.
Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said Monday that concerns he had about a political committee donation ban in the ordinance breaching First Amendment standards were quelled after discussion with Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh.
Rankin said individuals involved in political organization can still donate on behalf of themselves. And the ordinance doesn't stop political committees from making "independent expenditures" supporting a candidate, as long as the money doesn't go to the candidate directly.
Political groups will be required to file reports to the town if their expenses for an election cycle are $100 or more.
Town elections are nonpartisan.
Resident Lance Simon, a vocal advocate for the ordinance, thanked council members for supporting the new restrictions and said he hopes it can be "up and running" soon to allow enough time for it to be properly implemented. The town's next election is scheduled for May 2027.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who expressed concerns with the first draft of the ordinance potentially blocking some residents from running for office due to fiscal limits, said Monday that the final version is in a better place.
Davis thanked Cook and Montgomery for sponsoring the ordinance and bringing transparency to future town elections.
"I think the work has been done," Davis said. "I think we have really mulled it over a lot."

title: Betterton pushes back: Town says Halo Solar plan would threaten safety, growth and historic character
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Betterton pushes back: Town says Halo Solar plan would threaten safety, growth and historic character

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1060
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — Residents of this small Kent County town say they support renewable energy — just not in the middle of their gateway.On Sept. 9, nearly two dozen people joined an online public hearing before the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) to oppose a proposal from Halo Solar LLC. The company is seeking a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) to construct a 5-megawatt solar generating facility at the corner of Howell Point and Still Pond-Betterton roads — an area town officials say is the last viable space for residential and commercial growth.
Presiding over the hearing was Public Utility Law Judge Christine Burke, who first heard from Halo representatives before opening the floor to community comments.
Town officials: "Not at this location"
Betterton leaders emphasized they are not opposed to solar power but strongly object to this site, which they called the "gateway to Betterton." The town, population 298, has been working for years to balance conservation with limited development.
"This town has been incorporated for almost 120 years, going from a popular tourist attraction to residential," said Councilman Wayne Gilchrest. "This project would be sealing the town's fate for at least ten years."
Mayor Donald Sutton said the proposed structure would block the town's designated helicopter landing zone, posing a public safety risk. "It's zoned residential and commercial — the only area we have for expansion," Sutton said. He proposed a compromise: scale the solar farm down to 10 acres, leaving 20 available for future development.
Town Manager Tom Mogle added that Betterton's award-winning wastewater treatment plant, built in 2017, depends on new dwellings to offset its high operating costs. "We've invested heavily — rebuilding the boardwalk, restoring the bathhouse, improving Ericsson Avenue — all with a vision of balancing conservation with growth," he said.
Developer presents plan
Michael Lossia, a founder of Halo Solar, gave a brief presentation describing "Betterton Solar" as a 15-foot-high array of bifacial panels on a single-axis tracking system surrounded by fencing, evergreens, and other vegetation. The project, engineered by Kimley-Horn, is one of 15 Halo developments on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
"With that, I'll turn it back to you, Judge," Lossia said after a short summary — leaving residents eager to respond.
Residents: "A bad idea for a small town"
Helen Martin, who lives about 125 feet from the proposed site, said the project would destroy local ecosystems, cause soil erosion, and disrupt migratory bird patterns. "It's only six blocks from the beach — our biggest tourist attraction," she said. "Betterton is on the National Register of Historic Places. We need to keep that charm."
John Erikson questioned why a commercial solar farm would be allowed in a residential community. "There's a reason these projects aren't built in towns," he said. "This would be the only one like it in Kent County."
Paul Falcon, who lives directly across from the parcel, presented photos showing what he described as an "unsightly" buffer of fencing and metal panels. "The facility would be the size of five Walmart Supercenters," he said. "It would dominate the landscape, taking up one-third of the town's footprint. Are we expected to live with something that looks like a strip mine?"
Concerns over planning, housing, and costs
Professional planner Creigh Rahekamp argued the project would undermine the county's need for workforce housing. "Employers already struggle to find skilled workers because housing is too expensive," he said. "Halo picked the one site in town that eliminates its only growth opportunity. That's completely wrong."
Retired teacher David Paltrineri compared the situation to Middletown, Delaware, where an Amazon warehouse spurred traffic and overcrowding. "I saw firsthand what happens when growth is driven by outside interests without careful planning," he said.
Resident Kathryn Klvana said she was shocked to learn the state could override local zoning. She also questioned the validity of Halo's impact studies, saying glare analyses failed to consider larger vehicles such as trucks, farm equipment, or crop-dusting planes. She warned that stormwater runoff could carry contaminants into a Department of Natural Resources critical area and questioned what would happen in the event of a fire.
Klvana and others also feared higher energy costs and lower property values.
Loss of landing zone sparks safety fears
Art Pleasanton, representing the Betterton Volunteer Fire Company, said the proposed solar site would eliminate the town's emergency helicopter landing zone — a crucial asset during summer rescues.
"The biggest day this summer, we had 1,000 people on the beach," he said. "When a young girl nearly drowned, lifeguards pulled her out, gave CPR, and we airlifted her from that field. Her life was saved. If we lose that zone, the next one is 7.3 miles away — a 14-minute trip. Save our landing zone so we can save lives."
Property values and land use
Several speakers cited studies showing homes near large solar fields lose an average of 8% of their property value. Retired engineer Douglas Cregar said Halo had purchased enough land to host a 7-megawatt system, far larger than proposed.
Janet Christensen-Lewis, chair of the Kent Conservation and Preservation Alliance, said the project would "hamstring a well-governed town's growth agenda in favor of an extractive corporate use."
She noted that Maryland's Chapter 623 directs regulators to weigh renewable energy benefits against the loss of scarce housing land. "Halo will get guaranteed income from subscribers," she said. "Betterton residents get first dibs on subscriptions — crumbs."
A call for the PSC to visit
Pat Whitmore urged the commission to look beyond Betterton. "This isn't happening in isolation," she said. "Halo has projects in Kennedyville, Rock Hall, and Warwick. They're taking farmland and siting projects on town growth areas. Why not build on developed land like landfills?"
Tom Deliberto, a Betterton Planning Commission member and attorney, called the project's energy contribution negligible. "The gain to Maryland's renewable portfolio is 11-thousandths of 1 percent," he said. "Proportionally, it's like taking 34 square miles of Baltimore County for a fraction of a percent of power."
Mark Mendez of Glen Street made the final appeal: "This is your chance to say no. Come see the town — see how out of place this would be."
Next steps
Judge Burke closed the session by reminding participants that all comments — oral, mailed, or electronic — will be considered when she drafts her proposal order. Additional comments can be submitted through Dec. 8, following an in-person hearing scheduled for Dec. 1 (location to be determined).
Case documents and comment forms are available on the PSC website at psc.state.md.us, under Case No. 9786.
