title: Denton election cancelled: Lister runs unopposed
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton election cancelled: Lister runs unopposed

 October 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 447
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Dallas Lister will regain his seat on the Denton Town Council after no candidates filed to run against him in the town election scheduled for Nov. 4.Lister was first elected to the council in 2015 and will be entering in his third term.
"It's a good thing. I think that we have a couple projects that are going that we're trying to get done," Lister said in an interview Thursday.
Lister has been a proponent of multiple projects within the town government. Some he highlighted were raising the compensation for town employees and lowering taxes.
"So over the last 10 years, we, as the council, have worked together pretty intimately to improve a couple of major areas," Lister said. "One has been employee compensation as well as employee benefits. We had a lot of turnover during my initial election, in that period of time, and a lot of problems with balancing budgets. So we changed a couple of things where we quit prioritizing balancing the budget on employees payroll and staff."
"...Then we started working aggressively to lower the tax rates to make that it's a more competitive community to live in as well as want to build your business in on the Eastern Shore. So we've been successful with both of those areas," Lister said.
Lister highlighted Scott Getchell as one of the employees the town brought in after the retirement of former town administrator.
"We have a very excellent town administrator in a Scott Getchell at this time, which we were able to work towards finding that replacement when our previous town administrator retired. So this was a integral part of changing the town administration and make up for the community," Lister said.
Looking forward with the council, Lister hopes to bring more people and jobs to the town of Denton.
"Kind of the things that we've prioritized as a council now are to to continue with economic growth and to bring jobs to the community so that we're not as much of a bedroom community as much as a established community where people work as well as live here," Lister said. title: Subcontractor strike causes major sewer line break in Greensboro, town says
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Subcontractor strike causes major sewer line break in Greensboro, town says

 357

 GREENSBORO — At around 3:30 p.m. Friday, the Town of Greensboro received a call about sewage water in the road on Route 313 and Bridgetown Road, town officials said.Upon arrival, Greensboro Public Works found a sewer main pipe break on Bridgetown Road. Greensboro Town Manager Cindy Yost said the sewer line is connected from Greensboro to Goldsboro. Friday evening, she said the town had asked Goldsboro residents to use less water while repairs were underway.
"We've had to go in and shut down the pump station to Goldsboro, and hopefully that'll keep it from coming forward," Yost said. "Then we've got some trucks coming in, too, to help with that load. So, hopefully we can manage that with Goldsboro and not create any issues for them at the current time."
She said the town hoped to have the issue resolved by the morning.
After investigation, the town discovered that a subcontractor from Sure Shot Drilling was boring on the property. Yost said the subcontractor hit the main sewer pipe, then covered the pipe with plywood, put an orange flag around the pipe and left the scene without contacting the town.
According to Yost, the town contacted Sure Shot Drilling after discovering the break, and the company said workers had contacted Miss Utility, the company responsible for marking the location of power lines, sewer lines and water lines ahead of construction work.
The town manager said Sure Shot Drilling officials told her the area was not marked, so the contractor boring in that area was unaware the pipe was there.
Sure Shot Drilling could not be reached for comment due to the office being closed at the time the Star Democrat called.
Yost said the town was not contacted by Miss Utility ahead of Friday's construction work and was unaware of boring being done in the area that day.
"This is a huge sewer main. We should have been contacted. We were not," Yost said. "So, right now we've got emergency crews out here. We've got our local police out here on the road. We've called MDE because of the sewage going into the creek. So, we're hoping that we can get this fixed tonight."

 DENTON — Cheryl Beulah, executive director of Aaron's Place, discussed the food pantry's potential new location with the Caroline County Commissioners on Tuesday.The proposed location on Meeting House Road will allow Aaron's Place to work in partnership with His Hope Ministries and the Chesapeake Culinary Center to provide a year-round homeless shelter and multiple different classes, additions and food storage locations, Beulah said.
Plans for the location have been in the works for the past two years while volunteers from Aaron's Place and His Hope Ministries have resolved issues with the Environmental Protection Agency resulting from a covenant on the property.
The EPA covenant came after the property was contaminated with volatile organic compounds in the 1980s, Beulah said at the meeting Tuesday. Extensive testing has been conducted over the years, with the contamination shrinking due to a large pumping and air system installed by the previous owner, Russel Metals.
The EPA covenant is restrictive, primarily concerning water usage, but the EPA has indicated that as long as the project does not break the wellhead and uses water according to county instructions, it can proceed. The EPA also said that if three negative VOC tests are obtained after the project is on the property, it would consider removing the covenant.
Beulah told the commissioners how great the location will be for the community after all renovations were completed.
"To take that big piece of building, that building and that property, clean it all up, fix it all up and have it as a resource center to serve the people in the community. All the agencies that can come together will come together under one roof, joining forces together, joining resources together, and providing us a significant services in our community," she said.
The commissioners asked Beulah and the group questions about what services will be included at the new location. The group responded with a full analysis of the building.
"So, it's three main components, three main partners. Aaron's Place, His Hope Ministry and the Food Aggregation, those are the three main ones," Beulah said.
The group said the project requires significant funding. They are forming a capital campaign committee and exploring various funding opportunities around the state, Beulah said, and wanted to make sure they had the commissioners' support for the project before proceeding.
While the commissioners did not suggest a certain amount of money to support the project, the commissioners all said they will support the project and provide any help they can offer.

title: Hornberger to introduce citizenship check for voters
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Hornberger to introduce citizenship check for voters

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: State News

 ANNAPOLIS — Cecil County Del. Kevin Hornberger (R) says he likely has bipartisan support for a resolution he plans to bring before the Maryland General Assembly in January that would require the Maryland State Board of Elections to verify the citizenship of every registered voter in Maryland."Virginia and Colorado — both fairly 'blue' states — are already doing this," Hornberger said. "So I say, 'Hey, State of Maryland, you need to participate in this program.'"
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlement program is an online service that verifies a benefit or license applicant's immigration status for US citizenship. It does likewise for those who are naturalized, acquired or US born, giving this information to agencies to assure only those allowed get these entitlements. That includes the right to vote, Hornberger said.
"This tells the Board of Elections to participate," Hornberger said. "I think we'll have bipartisan support."
Party affiliation is not the issue, Hornberger said, even though Democrats told Republican members of the General Assembly that this was unnecessary. "They said you guys are offering solutions to a problem that doesn't exist. Well, guess what?"
The recent arrest of an Iowa public schools superintendent — who previously resided in Maryland — is what made Hornberger pursue the SAVE Act legislation.
"He was in this country illegally and he was registered as a Democrat in Maryland," he said.
Calling Maryland "one of the largest immigration states in the country," Hornberger said the SAVE Act wouldn't carry any penalties.
"It's just saying they can't vote," he said. If the resolution gets approved, Hornberger said it would make elections fair. "Every board in Maryland would have to use the federal voter registry database to assure that everyone registered to vote in the state of Maryland are legally residents."
The bill would first go before the House Ways and Means Committee, of which Hornberger is a member.

title: St. Vincent de Paul expands operations during a time of increasing need
author: Konner Metz

 EASTON — The completion of an expanded St. Vincent de Paul food pantry couldn't have come at a better time for Talbot County residents in need.John Plaskon, president of the Easton chapter of St. Vincent de Paul, said at a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Wednesday morning that Tuesdays and Saturdays — the pantry's distribution days — are becoming busier.
"There's more cars coming through lately than ever before," Plaskon said.
Volunteers for the nonprofit organization on Canvasback Drive will be better able to accommodate increased need thanks to a 2,560-square-foot expansion. Town, county and state officials joined St. Vincent de Paul to cut the ribbon Wednesday on a larger pantry, thrift store and advisory offices.
"We are a community of tremendous opportunity, and we're very thankful for what we have," Easton Mayor Megan Cook said. "But we're also a community of tremendous need. And the mission of St. Vincent de Paul really does help with that."
Plaskon said after the event that the expansion project, led by Willow Construction, cost nearly $1.4 million. Between funds from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development and Talbot County Council, and gifts from local donors, that mark was fully funded.
County Council President Chuck Callahan said acts of philanthropy in the county impress him, including St. Vincent de Paul's work. Callahan chairs the board of the Neighborhood Service Center, a nonprofit on the other side of town.
"It's a big effort on all of us, and that's really what this community is all about," Callahan said.
The relocated food pantry allows volunteers more space to operate on busy pickup days. A refrigerator and freezer were added to the end of the food pantry, along with other new equipment.
St. Vincent de Paul broke ground on the expansion in August 2024. It was a three-phase endeavor that Plaskon said "flowed pretty smoothly" over the last year and change.
The nonprofit's new thrift store has raked in more money, which goes toward the food pantry and advisory offices. Plaskon said weekly returns have risen 35% to around $9,000 a week.
Plaskon recently took over as president of the organization, which is made up of over 300 volunteers and has no paid employees. On Wednesday, he presented a proclamation honoring former president Alex Handy, who served in the role for 16 years.
Handy had similar praise for his successor.
"I am so grateful for having John step forward in that meeting and ever since, taking over this project," Handy said. "He has done a miracle amount of work here, and I can't thank him enough for steering us and steering this project to a wonderful culmination today."
Just before the ribbon was cut, the Rev. James Nash, pastor of Sts. Peter & Paul Church in Easton, told St. Vincent de Paul volunteers just how important they are to the community.
"A lot of the people on the day of food pickup, they will come here an hour and a half early or two hours early, just to sit," Nash said. "So you not only provide food. ... You give people the chance to just shut down for an hour or an hour or 20 minutes. ... And you offer them a place to come that's safe, where they feel heard, where they feel cared about."
Nash said he's seen other St. Vincent de Paul chapters during his career. The Easton one stands out.
"Nothing like this, nothing like this," Nash said of other chapters. "You all have a lot to be proud of."

title: Talbot council, Eastern Shore legislators share heartburn over state mandates
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot council, Eastern Shore legislators share heartburn over state mandates

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There's still more than two months until the 2026 Maryland General Assembly kicks off, but on Tuesday, local officials struck a chord of financial concern over the state's propensity to push down costs on county governments.The heartburn was shared during a joint meeting between the Talbot County Council and three elected officials in the General Assembly — Dels. Chris Adams and Tom Hutchinson and Sen. Johnny Mautz, all Republicans who represent multiple Mid-Shore counties.
At one point, council member Dave Stepp asked the legislators which additional cost burdens the state may place on counties heading into fiscal year 2027.
"Name it," Adams responded.
"I think that the assumption that there'll be additional burdens and additional costs is probably a safe assumption," Mautz said.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher pointed out the state legislature's choice last fiscal year to require counties pick up a portion of teachers' pensions payments, which are run through a state program. Talbot's share was $440,000, which prompted an increase, albeit slight, in the property tax rate for residents.
Lesher said if the state wants counties to increase financial responsibilities for the pensions, counties should be granted authority over the program, too.
"We're just being handed the bill," Lesher said. "And if they want to share this responsibility, share the authority. But obviously there's no interest in doing that."
It's unclear exactly which cost shifts could be at play with session still weeks away, but the Republican legislators and county officials spent much time during Tuesday's meeting discussing The Blueprint, Maryland's expansive funding and improvement plan for education.
In fiscal year 2026, the county was required by the Blueprint to include $55 million in education funding in its budget. That share will sharply increase in future years, according to reports from the state Department of Legislative Services as of the spring.
In Talbot County, the required funding mark could hit $90 million by fiscal year 2034, a hike school officials described as "sobering."
On Tuesday, Talbot County Finance Director Martha Sparks shared concerns with discrepancies state agencies have had when calculating the minimum funding marks counties must dole out to areas such as education and health departments.
Sparks said in the past, "core funding" required by the Maryland Department of Health to go to local health departments was off by around $250,000. The discrepancies have put other counties in more of a bind, she acknowledged, but still impact Talbot since the notice of changes from the state agencies come after the county has already significantly completed or passed its budget.
"These differences in funding have been small, relatively so," Sparks said. "They're still large for us. We want our budget to be right."
HOTEL TAX COLLECTION
Sparks and the Eastern Shore legislators opened Tuesday's meeting with a short discussion on Senate Bill 979, a law which will soon require the Comptroller's Office to collect certain accommodations tax information from companies such as Airbnb and Vrbo. Currently, counties are the collectors.
Hutchinson said while the bill gained support from some jurisdictions, it could actually hurt Talbot County since the finance office has a "terrific" collection system.
"In Talbot County, the bill was a negative to them," he said. "To other counties … where they don't really have a process in place, they were somewhat supportive of it."
Lesher said if the state assumes the collection duties, Talbot County could lose timely access to important tourism and rental data. Legislators were optimistic that Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) is open to allowing an opt-out to the bill mandating the state take over collection.
"I think it'd be helpful if the council would say, 'We don't want the state to collect this,'" Mautz said.

title: 'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — On Sundays, when the pews should have been packed, the Rev. Dennis Morgan would walk into St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Vienna and, at most, see two parishioners prepared for sermon.That is until Sept. 21, when the parish had its final service and St. Paul's closed its doors for good. The church's closure was not the town's first this year.
St. Paul's was deconsecrated just months after Vienna United Methodist Church, located directly across the street, stopped its services, Morgan said.
"It's a very, very bittersweet time," he said. "You know, realizing that it must be done, but, at the same time, you know, it's heartbreaking."
The church closures are the consequence of attendance trends seen in Vienna and across the country.
About 33% of adults in the United States attend religious services in person as of February 2025. This is a dramatic decline from 2007, when 50% of adults attended religious services in person, according to a recent Pew Research Center study.
"There have been really low numbers at St. Paul's for several years, and it just wasn't sustainable," said Administrative Assistant to the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton Lynn Anstatt.
In 2020, there were 18 parishioners on the books at St. Paul's, with roughly eight members attending services weekly. This dropped to 11 members on the books with around two attending weekly services by 2025, Morgan said.
He said the pandemic and static population of Vienna largely contributed to decreased attendance of all the churches in the area. Only a handful still hold weekly services.
Keeping St. Paul's open and active had become an existential question for Morgan.
"We could have kept the property going probably for quite a while, but we had no mission, no outreach and we questioned the 'why' of it more than the 'how' of it," the pastor said.
Morgan was in conversation with the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton for around three years in an attempt to keep the church open. But after seeing minimal improvement, he could no longer justify keeping the parish going.
"The church is still available to use although it has been deconsecrated, so we do have access to the church. But in terms of services and everything, that does come to an end," Morgan said.
The decommissioning of St. Paul's comes after more than 300 years of active service in Vienna.
There are now no Episcopal Churches in Vienna, but because attendance was so low and the church was not involved in the community, Morgan doesn't think the deconsecration will have much negative impact on the larger Vienna community.
Many community members have family buried in the cemetery on the property and have inquired with Morgan about the cemetery's future.
"The difficult decision to close the church, despite such a vast legacy, was driven by factors such as declining membership and the increasing costs of maintaining historic structures," former parishioner of St. Paul's and Vienna resident Susan Donaghue wrote in an email to the Star Democrat. "The conclusion of ministry at St. Paul's marks the end of an era for the town of Vienna and the community it so faithfully served."

 GREENSBORO — The aftermath of a sewer main pipe break will cost the town of Greensboro around $300,000 to fix, but the town plans to be reimbursed for the cost.At around 3:30 p.m. last week, the Town of Greensboro received a call about sewage water in the road on Route 313 and Bridgetown Road, town officials said.
Upon arrival, Greensboro Public Works found a sewer main pipe break on Bridgetown Road. Greensboro Town Manager Cindy Yost said the sewer line runs from Greensboro to Goldsboro. Friday evening, she said the town asked Goldsboro residents to use less water while repairs were underway.
After investigation, the town discovered that a subcontractor from Sure Shot Drilling was boring on the property. Yost said the subcontractor for Cherrywood Solar hit the main sewer pipe, then covered the pipe with plywood, put orange netting around the pipe and left the scene without contacting the town.
Now almost one week after the main pipe break, the town still continues work at the site to resolve the broken pipe 19 feet underground.
According to Yost the town called Spring and Associates, a horizontal directional drilling, to begin the process of fixing the pipe on Friday. The plans state that this particular pipe is 19 feet underground and while drilling down and getting to 17 feet, the road began to slide.
The town signed a contract with Spring and Associates on Saturday night. After the contract was signed Spring and Associates began to bring more equipment into Greensboro, but equipment delivery was delayed until Monday because of the wind storm this past weekend.
After more difficulties on Monday, Spring and Associates are still bringing in equipment from Virginia.
Yost said the town has two pump trucks operating around the clock at the Goldsboro pump station to prevent any issues for the town of Goldsboro.
Yost said that with the costs for contracting with Spring and Associates, Premier, the State Highway for guard rail removal, power companies for telephone pole removal, flaggers and their town staff, the repair will run up to $300,000.
The town is fronting the bill and has reached out to CherryWood solar contractors, NextEra to request they cover the cost, but has not yet received a response and plans to reach out to confirm.

title: Greensboro moves toward monthly utility billing

 The Town of Greensboro presented two ordinances that would change some of the towns billing from quarterly to monthly at the Greensboro Town Council Meeting on Thursday.The council introduced a resolution to change trash billing from quarterly to monthly at $16.50 per month per single-family residence, including multi-family units.
A second resolution was introduced to establish water and sewage rates effective Dec. 1, changing from quarterly to monthly billing.
"The benefit for residents, of course, is better budgeting, improved usage awareness, too, and fewer surprises," Town Manager Cindy Yost said to the Star Democrat on Oct. 3 when the proposed water bill changes were first discussed at a town meeting. "So if they fill a pool up or if they have a leak on their commode or something like that, this is going to pick it up a lot faster."
The proposed change from either monthly to quarterly or quarterly to monthly has been discussed around Caroline County throughout this year.
The town of Federalsburg is in discussions to change water and sewer billing from monthly to quarterly.
According to Yost, the benefits for the town would be enhanced cash flow and improved public works procedures.
"Enhanced cash flow, I mean, that's a given." Yost said. "You're going to get paid on a monthly basis. Faster leak detection, which is going to be huge for us, and a stronger customer engagement because we're going to be out there on a monthly basis interacting instead of the quarterly."
A public hearing was scheduled to discuss both proposed ordinances at the Nov. 6 meeting.

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council last week approved a bill allowing it to accept money from a statewide cannabis reinvestment fund, which currently has around $730,000 allocated for the county.Maryland's Cannabis Reform Act in 2023 created a Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund, designed to allocate 35% of the collected taxes from cannabis sales back into communities most affected by the disproportionate enforcement of previous cannabis laws.
County Attorney Patrick Thomas said at the council's meeting on Oct. 14 that the county can't use the money until it passed the bill, which effectively establishes Talbot's own reinvestment fund and a commission to administer the funds. Talbot Family Network, the board responsible for the county's youth and family services, will serve as the commission.
After the public hearing yielded no comments, the council moved the bill to third reading and approved it 4-0. Council member Lynn Mielke abstained.

title: Sewage seeping onto streets sparks Cambridge flood debate
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Sewage seeping onto streets sparks Cambridge flood debate

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 506
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge city commissioners met for a work session Monday to review a presentation from the "Make Cambridge Resilient" team and to ask questions about the project — and there were many.The initiative is a shoreline and stormwater flood risk-reduction project, but some commissioners and elected officials have expressed concerns about its scope and goals. The design phase is now 30% complete, but without secured funding and support from the city, county and elected officials, the effort may stall.
Current goals include:
Designing and constructing a living shoreline.Creating a stormwater system with nature-based water storage and control features.Gathering public comments.Institutionalizing floodplain management and flood risk reduction.Developing a green infrastructure plan.Implementing additional nature-based solutions.Reactivating and maintaining the stakeholder group.Providing support to property owners to identify risk-reduction strategies.
During recent City Council meetings, Commissioner Brett Summers raised concerns about toilet paper in the street, an issue caused by floodwater entering the sewer system through manhole defects. Director of Public Works Wayne Suggs said during the meeting that three spots remain where sewage and floodwater are still connected.
Suggs said three elements must be addressed to control these issues: top-down flooding, pump station capacity limits and creek water entering the system.
The Trenton Street Pump Station, which takes in most of the city's stormwater, is 97 years old and failing. When floodwater enters wastewater lines, it is pumped to the nearly century-old station, which doesn't have the capacity to handle it. As a result, toilet paper and sewage rise onto the streets.
"So can this project help us with that problem — and when?" Summers said.
Project Manager Larry White responded that adding pumps at the end of streets, repairing older infrastructure and constructing a living shoreline will help with sewage issues, but the project itself does not cover wastewater.
The city has published a bid to rehabilitate the Trenton Street Pump Station, but it's a $7 million project.
"Even if we moved and we awarded the bid tomorrow for Trenton Street, it will be 18 months before that system can be brought online," City Manager Glenn Steckman said.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said a mutual understanding of the project's goals is lacking and needs to be developed.
Del. Tom Hutchinson (R- Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) expressed concerns about the project, saying there has been mixed feedback from constituents and comparing the initiative to the "failing" Strand Beach project in Oxford.
Other concerns included insufficient outreach — particularly to Black and Hispanic communities and city park users — a lack of coordination with state agencies such as the Department of Natural Resources and the Maryland Department of the Environment, and long-term maintenance responsibilities.
Hutchinson said he contacted stakeholders listed on the project's website and many raised similar concerns.
"I had the opportunity to talk to DNR Secretary Kurtz, and he wasn't aware of the project," he said.
Some stakeholders, including Debbie Cornwell with the Maryland Department of Planning, expressed concerns about transparency.
Commissioners agreed to make the council chambers available for future public "Make Cambridge Resilient" meetings to improve transparency, but no further action was taken during the work session.

 DENTON — On Tuesday, The Caroline County Commissioners enacted a legislative bill on establishing a fund to receive payments of compensatory preservation contributions to Caroline County when solar energy systems are developed on a parcel of land identified as Class 1 or 2 soils.The county has discussed this bill in workshops since September. After many adjustments to logistical wording of the bill, the county passed the legislation.
"It is earmarked for an additional contribution to the Maryland Ag Land Preservation Fund, which is used to purchase Ag Land Preservation easements on existing farmland," Breeding said. "So basically, the MAUPH program enters into easement agreements with farmers that basically states that they will never develop put solar or build housing or any other form of development on the farmland, so it basically preserves it as agricultural land forever."
Caroline County has seen multiple solar arrays go up on farmland in the county,
The fee for this contribution will be determined at final site plan approval and must be paid before a building permit is issued. The county has been informing solar projects about this forthcoming change through its website and email communications since the initial discussion of the change.
The bill applies to any project with Class 1 or Class 2 soils, regardless of zoning district. However, it does not apply if the land is within town limits.
The county is happy to have the bill done, during the commissioners meeting Breeding thanked all working parties of Caroline County for their contributions to the bill.
"It's been a long process. It's been a lot of nuance details that we had to work through, and it feels good that we've been able to to get this accomplished, and we look forward to preserving the agricultural heritage of Caroline County," Breeding said.

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners have discussed the sale of Daysprings Townhomes throughout 2025, now the sale looks like it may happen.At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman said that paperwork with legal teams are being prepared and negotiations are ongoing on the potential sale of Daysprings Townhomes.
"We're down to just what I would say wording, not much left to get that contract finished and I don't need to speak for Stewart, but he's drafted up the letters to notify the tenants and all of those things. So we're making really good progress on Daysprings," Freeman said.
The Dayspring Townhomes complex is located just outside Ridgely on School Street. The initial property was built in 1994 by Interfaith Housing Development, a former local nonprofit that worked with the county.
That nonprofit ceased operations a handful of years ago, leaving the low-income housing complex in the hands of its owners, Caroline County, and the contracted property management company, East Coast.
According to Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding, the decision to sell is due to a lack of funding to properly repair the complex.
"There's limited state money available to renovate the apartments that are there, and it's very difficult to get a hold of the money. So really the the best path moving forward is to sell it to a private company and just have them renovate as needed to make it fair market value housing," Breeding said.
According to Freeman, once the contract is signed, the county will notify tenants of the sale and advise them with an option to extend their lease for one year. The apartments will be sold to a private entity who will rent the units at market rate.
According to Freeman, the purchaser intends to renovate the apartments, but the timeline is unknown. The county will offer relocation assistance to all tenants.
The county will follow state requirements with the sale of Daysprings Townhomes and the movement of the tenants.
